Uniform Title: Mahānirvāṇatantra Main Title: Mahānirvāṇatantra with the Commentary of Hariharānanda Bharati Commentator: Hariharānanda Bharati
Editor: Arthur Avalon;
Alternate Name: John Woodroffe.
Description: Data entered from the Tantrik Series, Volume 13, edited by Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe).
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.
Publisher: Luzac and Company. Publication year: 1926.
Place of publication: Calcutta;
Country of publication: India; Title: Mahānirvāṇatantra.
The First Chapter:
On a beautiful peak of the lord of mountains, adorned with various jewels, strewn with diverse trees and creepers, and filled with the songs of various birds. || 1 ||
Oṃ, salutations to Brahman!
Oṃ, I am Brahman; I am indeed Brahman.
Having established the sixfold tradition (ṣaḍāmnāya), Sadāśiva, whose power is immeasurable, has sent forth [this teaching].
By his primordial power (*ādi-śakti*),
he proclaimed the entire great *Nirvāṇa-tantra*, the bridge across the ocean of the Kula lineage,
while repeatedly recollecting the Supreme Brahman and repeatedly chanting the name of the Guru’s feet.
I shall explain the independent word of Śambhu according to my understanding.

When the Kali Yuga arrives— characterized by the destruction of all meritorious deeds taught in the Vedas and other scriptures, and the promotion of infinitely censurable sinful actions— how can there be deliverance for those men who are indifferent to the contemplation of the Supreme Self and are addicted to various kinds of sinful karma?

Thinking, "Will this come to pass? Pārvatī questioned Sadāśiva—who was standing on the peak of Kailāsa and possessed of compassion—regarding the means for their deliverance; that very [question] she expressed as follows: "O Lord of Mountains..."
(2) Delighted by the fragrance of flowers from all seasons, it was most enchanting;
it was fanned by breezes rich in coolness, sweetness, and gentleness.
Resounding with the sweet sounds of the musical performances of hosts of apsarases,
shaded by the cool shadows of trees with steady shade, and lovely with its lush splendor.
In the interior of the forest resounded by flocks of intoxicated cuckoos, which is always frequented by the King of Seasons together with his own retinue; || 4 ||

With the words beginning with "śikhara," [it is said]: there, upon that peak of the lord of mountains— the summit of Kailāsa, the sovereign of mountains— having seen Śiva, who maintains silence and is a silent sage, [he acted] out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Desiring the welfare of people, the goddess Pārvatī, being modest and bowed with humility, spoke to Śiva"—this is established by the words found in the eleventh verse.
By the phrase "observing a vow of silence" (*maunadharam*), the lack of opportunity for conversation is indicated. [The remaining words] begin with "in the beautiful" (*ramye*).

The thirteen words ending in the locative case are qualifiers of the term *girīndraśikhare* (on the peak of the king of mountains). It should be understood that the words ending in the accusative case, such as *carācarajagadgurum* (the teacher of the world of moving and unmoving beings), qualify the term *śivam*. One delights—that is, one plays—there.
In that delightful place, frequented by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and others— the suffix *yat* being applied in the sense of location according to the rule *poradupadhāt*— it was adorned with various jewels,
shining with many gems such as rubies and emeralds, and filled with diverse trees and creepers.
It was pervaded by many trees and many creepers,
and it was filled with the sounds of various kinds of birds, accompanied by the cries of diverse winged creatures. || 1 ||
It was made fragrant by the exceedingly captivating scents associated with all the flowers belonging to the seasons, beginning with spring; thus,
it was rendered most enchanting and delightful by its coolness.
It was fanned by breezes endowed with fragrance and gentleness.

"By the hosts of Apsarases," and so forth: [it refers to] that which is made resonant—i.e., filled with sound—by the deep-toned music (*kaladhvani*) performed by the groups (*gaṇa*), the assemblies (*samūha*) of Apsarases; [and it refers to] those trees whose shadows (*chāyā*) are steady (*sthirā*), meaning unshakable (*acañcalā*).
In a place covered by shadows, which is shaded; that which is both smooth and glossy is "snigdhamañjula," meaning smooth and beautiful—in such a place.

"Mattetyādi": In that [place] where the interior of the forest (*vipināntara*)—the midst of the woods—is resounded (*saṅghuṣṭa*), filled with the noise, by a multitude (*sandoha*), a swarm, of intoxicated cuckoos;
and which is at all times (*sarvadā*), at every moment, [frequented] by its own groups (*svagaṇaiḥ*), such as bees and the like.
It was attended by the spring, the king of seasons.
There, surrounded by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and the Gaṇas of Gaṇapati, [he beheld] the Lord, the teacher of the world of mobile and immobile beings, who observed a vow of silence. (5)
To Sadāśiva, who is eternal bliss, an ocean of the nectar of compassion,
white as camphor and the kunda flower, the all-pervading Lord composed of pure sattva.
Clad in the directions as his garment, the protector of the distressed, the lord of yogis, beloved by yogis, adorned with a circle of matted locks sprinkled with droplets from the Ganges; (7)
Adorned with supernatural powers, peaceful, garlanded with serpents, and bearing a skull-cup;
three-eyed, the lord of the three worlds, and the bearer of the excellent trident. || 8 ||

"By the Siddhas," and so forth: by the Siddhas who are of divine origin, by the Cāraṇas, by the Gandharvas, and by the hosts of Gaṇapati—those groups whose lord is Gaṇapati. "Enveloped" means surrounded. "The God" means the radiant one. "The teacher of the moving and unmoving world" refers to the teacher of all that is mobile... [the rest of the sentence continues with the description of the immobile].
The father of all beings—those that move, those that do not move, and those that are stationary. || 5 ||
"Sadā," and so forth: [he is] that from whom, or for whom, there is always (*sadā*)—that is, at all times (*sarvadā*)—auspiciousness (*śiva*), or well-being (*kalyāṇa*).

Or, he is that for whom there is always bliss (*ānanda*); that is, he whose bliss is real (*sat*) or who abides in it at all times. Or, he is that which gladdens (*ānandayati*) the virtuous (*sataḥ*, i.e., the *sādhus*). He is an ocean of the nectar of compassion (*karuṇāmṛtasāgara*), [the embodiment] of mercy.

The ocean of nectar; white as camphor and the *kunda* flower, meaning as bright as camphor and the *kunda*; consisting of pure *sattva*, meaning preeminent in the quality of stainless purity; the all-pervading Lord, the omnipresent one. || 6 ||
"Digityādi" and so forth. "Digaṃbara" means one whose garment (ambara) is the directions (diś);
the meaning is that he is devoid of clothing. "Dīnanātha" means the protector of poor people. "Yogīndra" refers to one who possesses yoga, which is meditation upon the Supreme Self.

The most excellent; beloved by yogis—that is, cherished by practitioners of yoga—or that whose beloveds are the yogis. Adorned with a mass of matted locks (*jaṭāmaṇḍala*), a collection of matted hair, which has been sprinkled by the droplets of the Gaṅgā scattered here and there. || 7 ||
"Vibhūti," and so forth: *vibhūtibhūṣitam* means adorned with ashes;
*śāntam* means one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is restrained; *vyālāḥ* refers to serpents, which constitute his garland (*mālā*);
*kapālinam* means one who possesses a human skull (*nṛkapāla*); and *locanāni* are those by which [he] is looked upon or seen.

Him who has those three eyes; the Lord of the Three Worlds, the presiding ruler over the three worlds; the bearer of the excellent trident—one whose nature it is to bear either the trident that is supreme among tridents, or both the trident and the boon—thus he is the "bearer of the excellent trident" (triśūlavaradhārī).
To him. || 8 ||

(4) [I bow to Him] who is easily pleased, consisting of pure knowledge, the bestower of the fruit of absolute liberation, free from conceptual construction, free from fear, devoid of distinctions, and stainless. 9.

Beholding the God of gods, the benefactor of all, who is free from affliction and possesses a gracious countenance, the goddess Pārvatī, desiring the welfare of the worlds, spoke to Śiva while bowing low with humility.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, my protector, ocean of compassion!
I am dependent upon you, O Lord of gods, and I am always an executor of your commands.
Without your command, it is not at all possible for me to say anything.
If you have even a slight trace of compassion toward me, or if there is affection for me, then let that which has been reflected upon by my mind be reported.
"Quickly," and so forth. "Quickly" means one whose satisfaction or contentment is immediate.
"Consisting of knowledge" means having the nature of that knowledge which is the true comprehension of all categories of existence. It is the bestower of the fruit of liberation (*kaivalya*).

The giver of the fruit whose nature is *nirvāṇa*; "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*) means that from which various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have departed; "free from affliction" (*nirātaṅka*) means that from which distress, fever, and fear have departed; and "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*) means devoid of manifold differences.
It is stainless and imperceptible to the ignorant. || 9 ||
"Of all," and so forth. Regarding the question of what Pārvatī said to Śiva—who is "nirāmaya," meaning one from whom *āmaya* (disease) has departed—she says:
"The illustrious Pārvatī said: 'O God of gods,' and so forth. O Lord of Gods!
I am the controller even of the gods, beginning with Indra; since I am dependent on you and have come under your sway, I am always, at all times, an executor of your commands.
Therefore, without your permission, I am not able to speak or say anything at all.
It is possible. || 11 || 12 ||
"O Great Lord, other than you, who else in the three worlds could possibly be capable of severing this doubt—someone who is omniscient and a knower of all scriptures? (13)
Śrī Sadāśiva said: O highly wise one, my beloved as life itself, tell me what is being said,
which is something that should not even be told to Gaṇeśa or to Skanda, the commander-in-chief.
I shall speak before you that which may be most secret;
for what is there in the three worlds that ought to be hidden from you? (15)
"O Goddess, you are my very form; there is no difference between you and me.
O omniscient one, do you not know? Why do you ask as if you were ignorant? (16)
Having heard these words of the god, the virtuous Pārvatī, her mind filled with joy and bowed in humility, questioned Śaṅkara.

Regarding the phrase "tvadanya" (other than you): it is a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "one other than you" (*tvattaḥ anyaḥ tvadanyaḥ*). Alternatively, "tvat" is a separate word ending in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*) [governing the following "anya"]. || 13 ||
Desiring to know the matter that Pārvatī wished to ask, the illustrious Sadāśiva said:
"What is it being said? and so forth. By mentioning Gaṇeśa as well as Skanda Kārtikeya, the commander-in-chief, the Blessed Lord Mahādeva [intended to] indicate their status as great heroes.
It is indicated that because of his extreme affection, there is a fitness for him to express even the most secret matter by force. || 14 ||
"Before you" (*tavāgre*) means: what object is there to be hidden even from you, that is, before you (*tvadagre*), in all the three worlds?

The meaning is that there is nothing at all. Regarding the form *agre*: from the word *agra* ending in the locative case, the suffix *tasi* is applied in its own sense (without changing the meaning) according to the rule *ādyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*. || 15 ||

Regarding "my form" (*mama rūpa*) and so forth: it is called *rūpā* because it is that which is formed (*rūpyate*), meaning a specific act of forming is prescribed; the suffix *-ac* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, "my form" means she who possesses my form. However, if the reading is *matsvarūpā*, it means she whose single, identical form is the same as mine.
As if ignorant, as if lacking knowledge. || 16 || 17 ||
The venerable Ādyā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, best among those who know all dharmas!
Formerly, by the compassionate Blessed One, the inner controller of Brahmā—" (18)
The four Vedas were revealed there, augmented by all the dharmas,
and therein the regulations for the castes, stages of life, and so forth were firmly established.
In the Kṛta Yuga, virtuous men on earth, pleasing the gods and the ancestors through the aforementioned sacrifices of yoga and other ritual acts, were of meritorious character.
Through the study of sacred texts, meditation, austerity, compassion, and charity, they have conquered their senses;
they possess great strength, great heroism, and great courage and prowess.
In response to the inquiry as to what Pārvatī asked Śaṅkara, [the text] says: "The Blessed One said," and so forth. O Blessed One (*bhagavan*), endowed with sovereignty and other such qualities;
O Lord of all beings (*sarvabhūteśa*), the controller of all creatures. Just as...

With the intention that "just as you have indeed delivered the worlds through the instruction of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Saṃhitās during the Satya and Tretā ages, so too in the Kali age— a time of sin where wicked deeds prevail— you alone, being compassionate, must uplift human beings by some means," he says:
"By the compassionate one," and so forth. || 18 ||

"Manifested," and so forth. Those in whom all dharmas are augmented—that is, increased—are "those in whom they are spoken," and so on. In the Kṛta Yuga, the Age of Truth; on earth, that is, upon the ground;
human beings of virtuous character.

The connection with the words situated in the fifth verse is as follows: "they remained pleasing and satisfying the gods and the ancestors through those ritual acts such as sacrifices—which were spoken of in the Vedas, which consisted of the aforementioned sacrifices and yogic offerings, and which served as means for crossing over [to liberation]. || 20 ||

"Self-study," and so forth: self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the study of the Vedas; meditation (*dhyāna*) is reflection upon the Supreme Self; austerity (*tapas*) consists of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances; compassion (*dayā*) is the desire to destroy the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest; and charity (*dāna*) is the giving away of wealth and other goods acquired through righteous means.

The offering was made into the vessel by all of them; these were distinguished men. The word "were" (*āsan*) must be construed with all the participial words beginning with "having conquered the senses" (*jitendriyāḥ*). "Having conquered the senses" means those who have brought their eyes and other faculties under control.
(7) Mortals who frequent the temples of the gods are like gods themselves, firm in their vows;
all are devoted to truth and righteousness, virtuous, and speakers of truth. || 22 ||
The kings, whose resolutions were true and who were devoted to the protection of their subjects,
regarded the wives of others as their own mothers and the sons of others as their own children.
At that time, regarding the wealth of others, men viewed it as if it were a clod of earth;
they were always devoted to their own duty and remained on the path of the righteous.
None were speakers of falsehood, nor were any ever devoted to negligence; there were no thieves, no doers of harm to others, and none of evil intent. (25)
They were neither envious, nor excessively angry, nor overly greedy, nor lustful;
all possessed pure inner hearts and were always joyful in mind. (26)

They possess great strength (*mahābala*) and great capability (*mahāsāmarthya*). According to Amara, the term *bala* refers to bulk, capability, and an army. They are of great heroism (*mahāvīrya*), great majesty (*mahāprabhāva*), or great splendor (*mahātejas*).
According to the Medinīkośa, *vīrya* denotes majesty and semen, while *tejas* denotes both splendor and capability.
Those whose courage, prowess, resolve, and heroism are great are called "possessors of great courage and prowess. || 21 ||
"Devāyatana," and so forth. "Devāyatanagāḥ" means those who go to the temples of the gods.

Although they are "martyāḥ," meaning subject to death, they are "devakalpāḥ," meaning slightly less than gods; that is to say, equal to gods. They are "sādhavaḥ," meaning those whose vows and observances are firm.
Those who abide by their respective duties; speakers of truth—truth being the expression of things as they actually are—and those who speak it. || 22 ||
"Kings," and so forth. Those whose mental activity consists of truthful resolve.
Toward the wives of others—that is, other men's wives—and toward the sons of others—that is, the children of another. || 23 || 24 ||
"Not," and so forth. "Not delighting in negligence" means they are attentive. "Not evil-minded" means they do not have corrupt intentions. || 25 ||
"Not so," and so forth. They are not envious, nor do they hate the virtue of others; they are not excessively angry, nor are they full of wrath.
Those whose minds and hearts are such that there is joy in them at all times—[they are the ones who attain this]. 26.
The lands were rich with every kind of crop, the rain-clouds poured forth at the proper season, the cows abounded in milk, and the trees were laden with fruit. (27)
There was no untimely death there, nor famine, nor disease;
[the people] were always joyful, well-nourished, healthy, and endowed with splendor, beauty, and virtue.
The women were not unfaithful, being solely devoted to their husbands. (28)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who abide by their own proper conduct and worship according to their respective duties have reached the path of liberation.
When the Kṛta age had passed and the Tretā age had begun, seeing the transgression of dharma,
mortals were no longer capable of accomplishing their desired goals through the rituals prescribed in the Vedas.
Human beings, whose minds are agitated by anxiety, are not capable of performing Vedic rites which cause much affliction and require numerous means. (31)
Those whose minds are always timid are neither able to abandon nor to perform the scriptures consistent with the meaning of the Vedas that exist on earth in the form of Smṛtis. (32)
Then, having manifested yourself, you delivered the worlds— rendered weak by austerity and Vedic study— from the sin that bestows suffering, grief, and disease.
Regarding the "grounds" (bhūmayaḥ): they are the rain-clouds (parjanyā meghāḥ). || 27 ||
"Not so," and so forth. In that regard, during the Kṛta Yuga: *rujaḥ* means diseases; *sadārogyāḥ* refers to those who possess constant health;
*tejorūpaguṇānvitāḥ* means endowed with brilliance, beauty, and other such qualities. || 28 ||
"Brāhmaṇas," and so forth; "sacrificing" means worshipping the Supreme Lord. || 29 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "kṛte" and so forth: when the Kṛta age (Satyayuga) has passed and gone by, and the Tretā age has arrived, mortals— meaning human beings— are no longer capable or competent in accomplishing their own desired goals through the rituals prescribed in the Vedas.
[They] came to be. And when there are many means—that which possesses many means is "bhūrisādhana"—who else besides you exists for living beings in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra? (p. 9)
He is the sustainer, the protector, the deliverer, the lord who acts for one's welfare like a father. || 34 ||

Furthermore, when the Dvāpara age arrived— devoid of the merits prescribed by the Smṛtis, with half of the Dharma lost, and men overwhelmed by mental anguish and physical disease— it was you alone who rescued those people through the instruction of the Saṃhitās and other works.
When the sinful Kali age has arrived, which destroys all dharma, characterized by evil conduct, wicked proliferation, and the promotion of corrupt actions; || 36 ||

For this very reason, it causes much affliction (*bahukleśakaram*), meaning it is the producer of many afflictions (*kleśa*). Alternatively, that which is performed—that is, brought to completion—by means of many afflictions is "that which causes much affliction.

The suffix *kṛt* is applied here in the sense of the object (*karman*) by virtue of the rule of general usage (*bāhulaka*). For this very reason, [it is difficult] to perform such a Vedic ritual action.
With their minds agitated by anxiety, men became unfit;
and when men were always of timid heart and perpetually restless in mind,
they were unable to abandon that Vedic rite because of hearing of various faults associated with its abandonment.
Because they were difficult to accomplish due to the abundance of afflictions, they were not able to perform it at that time;
therefore, having seen the transgression of Dharma, the overstepping of Dharma, or the perversion of Dharma,
they manifested upon the earth the Smṛtis and the Śāstras endowed with the meaning of the Vedas.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "You have rescued (*atārayaḥ*)," that is, you have caused to cross over, the people of the worlds who were weak in austerity and Vedic study, from sin. (30–33)

Regarding the phrase "you": since you are of such a nature, the construction should be understood as "without you. In the "terrible ocean of saṃsāra," that is, in the fearsome sea of worldly existence; the "Lord" is the Master of the universe.

"Then," and so forth. "Abandoned by the merits prescribed in the Smṛtis" means abandoned or forsaken by those merits and virtues that have been declared in the Smṛti texts. "In the case of the destruction of half the dharma" refers to one who destroys (lumpati) half of the dharma;
thus, he is "the destroyer of half the dharma. This refers to [the state] "abandoned by the merits prescribed in the Smṛtis."
It should be understood that the phrase "upon the loss of half the Dharma" is an adjective either of "in the Dvāpara [age]" or of "among men. *Ādhi* refers to mental anguish. || 35 ||
"Upon his arrival," and so forth. "In one of evil conduct" means in that place where there is wicked behavior. || 36 ||
The Vedas are not the source for those [Smṛtis]; how then could there be remembrance [of them]—for they are endowed with various Itihāsas and reveal manifold paths? (37)
O Lord, there will be the destruction of many ancient [traditions];
at that time, people will become averse to dharma and righteous deeds. (38)
They were unrestrained, intoxicated with pride, and always devoted to evil deeds;
they were lustful, greedy, cruel, harsh, foul-mouthed, and deceitful. (39)
They will have short lifespans and dull intellects, overwhelmed by disease and grief;
they will be devoid of fortune, weak, base, and devoted to low conduct. (40)
Devoted to associating with the base, they are stealers of others' wealth;
these wicked men are intent on censuring others, harming others, and slandering others. (41)
Free from the fear or suspicion of sin regarding the abduction of others' wives, they are penniless, filthy, wretched, impoverished, and long-suffering from disease. (42)
Brahmins who behave like Śūdras, who neglect the twilight prayers, who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and who are greedy, ill-behaved, and evildoers; 43.
"Not so," and so forth. "Prabhavaḥ" means capable. || 37 || 38 ||

"Unrestrained," and so forth. Those for whom the "shackle"—the fetter consisting of the Vedas and other such things—has been cast off are "ucchṛṅkhalāḥ," meaning they are free from bondage. "Lolupāḥ" means excessively greedy. "Krūrāḥ" means merciless. "Niṣṭhurāḥ" means speakers of harsh words.
Durmukhas means those with foul mouths; śaṭhas means those who are deceitful and crooked. || 39 ||
Regarding the phrase beginning with *svalpa*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "those who have short lives and are dull-witted. (40)
"Base" means wicked people, the evil-minded. || 41 ||

"Regarding 'another's wife' and so forth: those devoid of fear or apprehension regarding the sin of abducting another's wife are those who lack agitation or dread concerning the evil resulting from such abduction. 'Defiled' means corrupted by impurity. 'Miserable' means possessed of distress. 'Poor' means fallen into misfortune. || 42 || 43 ||
(11) They are speakers of untruth, fools, hypocrites, and practitioners of wicked sophistry;
they are sellers of their daughters, outcasts (vrātyas), and those who have turned their backs on austerity and religious vows. 44.
Devoted to recitation and worship for the sake of deceiving the world, these heretics consider themselves learned, yet they are devoid of faith and devotion. (45)
Having whatever food and conduct they please, these hired servants and attendants of Śūdras eat the food of Śūdras; they are cruel and lustful for sexual pleasure with Vṛṣalīs. || 46 ||
Out of greed for wealth, they will give their own wives to those of low birth;
the only remaining mark of Brahminhood will be the wearing of the sacred thread. (47)
There is no restriction on drinking and so forth, nor any discrimination between what is fit and unfit to eat;
he is constantly reviling the scriptures of Dharma and is perpetually hostile toward the virtuous. (48)
Not even a mere conversation about virtuous stories ever entered their minds;
yet you have composed the Tantras for the sake of uplifting all living beings. (49)
Regarding the passage beginning with *asatya*: "hypocrites" (*dāmbhikāḥ*) refers to those possessing hypocrisy (*dambhaḥ*), which is the flaunting of religious merit (*dharmadhvajitvam*).
"Outcastes" (*vrātyāḥ*) refers to Brahmins who have not been consecrated even until the age of sixteen and whose *gāyatrī* has fallen away; this is to be connected with the preceding verse. || 44 ||
"Worldly," and so forth. Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*) are those who possess the practice of vows such as the red robes and the girdle of muñja grass that are outside the Veda.
"Devoid of faith and devotion": faith (*śraddhā*) is firm conviction in the Veda and its like; devotion (*bhakti*) is—
They are devoid of those two activities that produce joy. || 45 ||

"Of what food," and so forth. *Bhṛtakas* are those whose livelihood depends on being maintained; for this very reason, they are servants even to Śūdras. *Krūra* means hard-hearted. *Vṛṣalīratikāmukas* are those who desire sexual pleasure with a Śūdra woman (*vṛṣalī*). (46–48)
Regarding the passage beginning with "sat" and so forth: in the phrase "merely engaging in virtuous conversation," the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "tu" (but/rather).
(12) Therein are the various collections of the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*, which grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation;

the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the mantras and yantras of the goddesses and gods; and many *nyāsas* (ritual placements) characterized by the processes of emanation, maintenance, and so forth. || 50 ||
The bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and others have been described extensively;
the deities, possessing the states of the Paśu, Vīra, and Divya, bestow the accomplishment of mantras.
The corpse posture, ascending the funeral pyre, the practice with a shaven head,
and the rites of the creeper practice— you have described these thousands of times.
The animal state and the divine state have been set aside by [the Lord] himself;
in the Kali age, the animal state does not exist, so how could the divine state come to be? (53)
The animal himself should fetch the leaf, flower, fruit, and water;
he should not look upon a Śūdra, nor should he think of a woman even in his mind. (54)
Divine, consisting mostly of deities, with a perpetually pure inner organ, he transcends dualities, is free from passion, equal toward all beings, and patient. (55)
"Regarding 'nigama' and so forth: in those [scriptures] such as the Tantras, [the powers] are characterized by creation, maintenance, and so on;
that is, they have the nature of creation, maintenance, and so forth. (50)
"Having bound the lotus posture," and so forth; the word "where" is to be supplied, and by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the released lotus posture and others is intended. || 51 ||
Regarding "the corpse-seat" (śavāsana): here too, the word "where" (yatra) is to be supplied. The corpse-seat is the seat of a dead body. || 52 || 53 ||

In order to demonstrate the reason for the absence of both the state of a bound soul (paśubhāva) and the divine state (divyabhāva) in the Kali age, [the author] first shows, in two verses beginning with "patram," those actions that are to be performed by the bound soul and the divine being respectively. He should "bring" (āharet), meaning he should fetch it. 54.

"And divine" (divyaḥ): the word "should be" (bhavet) is to be supplied. "Abounding in deities" (devatāprāyaḥ) means equal to a deity. "Beyond the pairs" (dvandvātītaḥ): "pairs" (dvandvāni) refers to dualities such as pleasure and pain, cold and heat;
he is beyond them, having transcended them, being one whose nature is to endure them.
For those joined with the impurities of the Kali age, whose minds are always unstable, and who are addicted to sleep and laziness—how can there be purity of being? (56)
The rites of heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) are proclaimed as consisting of the five principles (pañcatattva):
liquor, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union.
These five principles have been taught by you, O Śaṅkara. (57)
Men born in the Kali age will be greedy, devoted solely to their genitals and bellies;
out of greed they will fall there, and they will not perform spiritual practice.
Having drunk much honey for the sake of sensual pleasure, they will become intoxicated with pride and devoid of discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful. (59)

This is the meaning. "Vītarāga" means one from whom passion (*rāga*)—whether defined as attachment, affection, or envy—has departed (*vīta*) or gone away (*gata*) specifically (*viśeṣeṇa*). According to the lexicon, "passion" (*rāga*) refers to both attachment and envy. "Sarvabhūtasama" means equal toward all beings, being devoid of passion, hatred, and so forth.
One who is patient (*kṣamī*) is one who possesses forbearance (*kṣamā*), which consists in not practicing retaliation when harm has been inflicted by another. 55.
Having thus demonstrated the rites to be performed for those who are bound as animals and those who are divine,
[the author] now addresses those whose minds are perpetually fickle, who are addicted to sleep and laziness,
and who are characterized by various kinds of evil deeds.

In order to demonstrate that for those humans born in the Kali age— who are unfit for the means of accomplishing the ritual acts pertaining to the animal (paśu) and divine (divya) [states]— the states of being an animal and being divine are not achieved, he says "Kali," and so forth. (Verse 56)
"O Vīra," and so forth. O Śaṅkara, O benefactor of the world, the five principles beginning with wine (*madya*) have been declared—those in which [the rites] are performed.
The grammatical connection is that such ritual acts of *vīrasādhana*, including the five principles of wine, meat, and so on, have been proclaimed by you. (57)
Regarding the phrase "born of the Kali age": therein, within the five principles beginning with wine (madya). || 58 ||
"Of the senses" means: *madhu* is wine. || 59 ||
(14) Many robbers on earth will be violators of other men's wives; intoxicated by their power, those wicked ones will not exercise any discrimination regarding the source of their sins. (60)
Due to the fault of excessive drinking and other such vices, many on this earth become diseased, deprived of strength, deprived of intellect, and possessed of impaired senses. (61)
In lakes, pits, and deserts, as well as from palaces and even from mountains,
men overwhelmed by intoxication will fall and die.
Some will quarrel even with their elders and kinsmen;
some will remain silent as if dead, while others will be excessively talkative.
O Lord, those cruel ones who perform what should not be done and who destroy the path of dharma—[regarding] those actions which were described by you for the sake of their welfare; || 64 ||
I think, O Mahādeva, that these [teachings] have become perverted among humans; for who indeed will practice yoga, or who at all will undertake the various types of renunciation? (65)

O Lord of the World, due to the influence of the dharma of the age and their own inherent nature, men in the Kali age will become exceedingly wicked and will in every way be doers of evil; [thus, they will fail to perform] the recitation of hymns, the writing of mantras on yantras, and the preliminary rites (puraścaryā).
"Ravishers of others' wives," and so forth: those who violate the wives of others, that is, those who commit acts of aggression against them;
"robbers" means thieves; "in a lake" refers to a reservoir of deep water; "in a wilderness" means on a path far from a village, devoid of trees, creepers, and the like. (Verses 60–62)

"Some" refers to the elders, such as parents and others. "Silent" means not speaking anything at all. "Yoga" refers to the means of elevation consisting of various meritorious acts prescribed in the Tantras and other scriptures.
Puraścaryā means puraścaraṇa (the preliminary preparatory rite). || 63–66 ||
O Lord of the Wretched, O Master, please tell us out of compassion the means for that [attainment], which increases longevity, health, and luster, and augments strength and vigor. (67)
It bestows knowledge and wisdom upon men and brings about auspiciousness without effort;
by it, people shall become possessed of great strength and prowess. (68)
Men with pure minds, intent on the welfare of others, acting kindly toward their parents, devoted to their own wives, and turning away from the wives of others. (69)
They are devoted to the deities and their gurus, and they support their children and kinsmen. || 70 ||
O knowers of Brahman, possessors of the knowledge of Brahman, whose minds are intent on the contemplation of Brahman—
tell us what is beneficial for our welfare so that we may achieve success in the course of worldly life.
Who in the three worlds, apart from you, is the protector of all people regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life? (72)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Inquiry into the Means for the Liberation of the Living Soul," in the *Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra*, the most excellent of all tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas, within the dialogue between the venerable Primordial Goddess and Sadāśiva. 1.
"Of them," and so forth. "Of those men. *Āyurārogyavarcasyam* means beneficial for longevity (*āyuḥ*), health (*ārogya*), and luster (*varcas*), that is, for vitality (*tejas*). || 67 ||
"Knowledge," and so forth; by which means. || 68–70 ||

"Knowers of Brahman" means those possessed of wisdom who understand that all is indeed Brahman through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). "Of the worldly course" means of the maintenance of the world. 71–72.
Thus ends the first chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. Regarding the second chapter:
having heard these words of the Goddess, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, [spoke].
The ocean of great compassion spoke the truth in its true essence.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
"Well asked, O highly fortunate one, you who act for the welfare of the worlds!
No such auspicious question has ever been posed by anyone before."
"You are blessed, you are grateful, and you are beneficial for those born in this degenerate age;
O auspicious lady, whatever has been spoken by you is true, truly according to the facts. (3)
O Supreme Goddess, you are omniscient, the knower of the three periods of time, and the knower of Dharma; O Beloved, the past, the present, and the future are all endowed with Dharma through you.
Oṃ, salutations to Brahman.

Śaṅkara, now praising Pārvatī— who has asked the question regarding the means for the deliverance of her life— and that very question, begins to give her a reply, starting with the words "iti" and so forth.
The benefactor of the world, the producer of welfare for all people;
an ocean of great compassion, a sea of great mercy. || 1 ||
"Omniscient," and so forth; "bhavat" means the present. || 4 ||

O Goddess of the gods, for the twice-born and others who are distressed by the impurities of the Kali age, there is no doubt that [this occurs] according to reality, according to principle, and according to what is appropriate. (p. 17) 5.
For those who do not investigate the pure and the impure, there is no purification through Vedic rites;
nor can men achieve their desired goal through the Smṛtis, such as the Saṃhitās and others.
Truth, truth, and again truth—truth, truth is what I speak.
For in the Kali age, O beloved, there is no way [to liberation] without the path of scripture.
O Śivā, in the past I myself declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other texts that in the Kali age, the wise man should worship the gods according to the procedures prescribed in the Āgamas.
He who, transgressing the scripture of the Kali age, proceeds by another path—there is no goal for him;
this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 9 ||
I am the one to be propounded by all the Vedas, Purāṇas, Smṛtis, Saṃhitās, and so forth; there is no other Lord in the world besides me.

Regarding the word *kali*: [it refers to] those who are wretched due to the impurities of the *kali* age—those characterized by miserable states caused by the misdeeds associated with the *kaliyuga*, and who are devoid of discrimination between the pure and the impure (*medhya-amedhya*), that is, lacking discernment between what is sacred and what is profane. Therefore...
In this way, purification for the twice-born and others—beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—cannot be achieved through *śrauta* rites, that is, rites prescribed in the Vedas. || 5–6 ||
"It is true. The particle "hi" is used for emphasis. || 7 ||

"Śruti," and so forth. O Śivā, the wise and discerning one should worship—that is, honor—the gods according to the procedures prescribed in the Āgamas; this is the connection [of the meaning], that it was previously stated by me myself in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other such texts. (8-9)

In order to establish the authority of his own doctrine, he first declares the absolute supremacy of the Self itself, saying "by all," and so forth. The word "yataḥ" (since) is to be supplied. "Pratipādyaḥ" means that which is to be made to understand. || 10 ||
And they all proclaim my station, which purifies the world;
yet people who have turned away from my path are heretics and slayers of the Veda. (11)
Therefore, O Goddess, whatever action one performs while abandoning my teaching shall be fruitless, and the performer shall also become a denizen of hell. (12)
The fool who, having abandoned my teaching, resorts to another doctrine, is a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of his father, and a slayer of women; of this there is no doubt. (13)
In the Kali age, the mantras proclaimed in the Tantras are effective and bestow results swiftly;
they are recommended for all rites, such as recitation, sacrificial offerings, and ritual actions. (14)
Those belonging to the Vedic tradition were devoid of vigor, like snakes whose poison has been removed;
they were fruitful in the Kṛta age and others, but in the Kali age they are like the dead.
"They declare"—all those [scriptures] beginning with the Vedas declare, that is, they teach, my station, my own abode, which purifies the worlds, meaning it produces purity for the worlds;
the ellipsis is "they would become killers of Brahman. || 11 ||
"From this," and so forth. Having "abandoned," that is, having completely relinquished, that action. || 12-13 ||

Now, demonstrating that the mantras declared in the Vedas lack efficacy and fail to produce their respective fruits in the Kali age, [the author] states that because only the mantras proclaimed in the Tantras are effective, they grant results immediately.
He speaks of its extreme excellence because it bestows various fruits, starting with the words "In the Kali age," and so forth. || 14 ||

"Devoid of potency," and so forth: those mantras of the *śrauta* class, proclaimed in the Vedas, which were effective and productive of their respective fruits in the *satya* and other ages— all those mantras in the *kali* age are devoid of potency (*nirvīrya*), like serpents deprived of venom, lacking luster, as if dead.
The syntactical connection (anvaya) is that they should be understood as the producers of their respective fruits. || 15 ||
Just as dolls made of cloth on a wall, though endowed with all the sense organs, are incapable of performing actions, so too are other collections of mantras. (16)
An action performed with other mantras is like sexual union with a barren woman;
there shall be no attainment of fruit therein, for it is merely labor alone. (17)
The man who, in this Kali age, desires success through paths proclaimed by others is like a foolish person who, while thirsty on the banks of the Ganges, digs a well.
Having abandoned the Dharma arising from my own mouth, he seeks another Dharma;
like one who, having left the nectar in his own home, desires milk from a goat. (19)
There is no other path for the sake of liberation, nor for the attainment of happiness in this world or the next,
such as the path proclaimed in the Tantra for the sake of both liberation and happiness.
The tantras have been taught in many ways and are endowed with various narratives, as well as numerous injunctions for both the perfected ones (siddhas) and the practitioners (sādhakas). (21)
"Like dolls," and so forth. Just as these dolls (*pāñcālikā*)— constructed from cloth, ivory, and other materials— which stand against a wall and are endowed with all the senses,
are incapable and powerless in performing actions, even so are others who are distinct from those mentioned in the Tantras.

The "masses of mantras" (mantrarāśayaḥ) are collections of mantras; they should be understood as those which accomplish their respective tasks in the Kali age. According to Amara, a "pāñcālikā" is a doll made of cloth, ivory, or other materials.

"Anye" and so forth: just as union with a barren woman does not bring about the fruit in the form of offspring, so too is the ritual action performed with other mantras; when that ritual action has been performed, [it is ineffective].
The accomplishment of the fruit—the realization of the result—would not occur; there would be nothing but mere exertion. The word "hi" indicates that this is certain. || 17 || 18 ||
"From my mouth" means spoken from my own face. "Seeks" means desires. "Up to the Arka tree" means originating from the *arka* plant. || 19 ||
"Not another" means [he does not go] to that other world. || 20 || 21 ||

(20) O Dear One, due to the diversity of qualified practitioners and the abundance of bound souls (paśus), the dharma proclaimed in the Kula tradition has been taught in some places for the sake of secrecy. || 22 ||
Some [mantras] that cause the activity of the individual soul (jīva) have also been mentioned;
O beloved, various kinds of gods and many types of goddesses have likewise been described. (23)
The Bhairavas, Vetālas, Vaṭukas, Nāyikās, and Gaṇas;
the Śāktas, Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Sauras, Gāṇapatyas, and others. || 24 ||
There are various mantras and yantras, numerous means for attaining success, which are accomplished through great effort and grant the results as described. (25)
O beloved, in whatever manner, by whomever, and at whatever time questions were asked, I spoke in that very same way for the benefit of each person.
For the benefit of the entire world and for the welfare of all living beings,
O Pārvatī, in accordance with the dharma of the age and according to reality.
The questions you have asked are such as have never been asked by anyone before;
out of affection for you, I shall declare that which is the essence of essences, higher than the highest. (28)

"Regarding the passage beginning with 'adhikārī' (the qualified practitioner): O beloved, for the sake of the distinction among qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), specifically due to the particularity of those [practitioners] and because of the abundance of bound souls (*paśu*), the Dharma taught in the Kula tradition—spoken according to the Kula conduct—is declared in some places for the purpose of concealment. (22)

"Jīva," and so forth. The phrase "according to the distinction of the qualified practitioners" (adhikārivibhedena) is to be supplied [to the previous verse]. Regarding the word "api" (also/even), its connection should be made with the phrase "those which cause the activity of the individual soul" (jīvapravṛttikārīṇi). || 23 || 24 ||

"Various," and so forth. "Those with accomplished means" (*siddhopāyāni*) refers to those in which the means (*upāyāḥ*) are accomplished (*siddhāḥ*), that is, possessed of perfection (*siddhimantaḥ*). || 25 ||

"Yathā" and so forth: in whatever manner and of whatever kind the questions are, in that very same manner and of that very same kind is the answer. The phrase "for the benefit of all the world" should be construed with the words "the question which has been posed by you. (26–28)
"O Goddess of the Gods, having extracted the essence of the Vedas, the Āgamas, and especially the Tantras, it is being told by me before you. (29)
Just as among men those who know the tantras are preeminent, just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers,
and just as I am among the lords of the three heavens, so is this [work] among the scriptures.
O Śivā, what is the use of the Vedas, what use the Purāṇas, and what use the many scriptures?
When this Great Tantra is understood, one becomes the master of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 31 ||
Since I have been appointed by you for the welfare of the world,
I shall therefore tell you that which will bring benefit to the universe.

O Goddess, when the welfare of the universe is accomplished, O Supreme Sovereign, the Lord of the Universe, the Soul of the Universe, becomes pleased; for the entire universe is dependent upon Him. (33)
"Of the Vedas," and so forth. "Essence" (sāra) means the stable portion. || 29 ||

Now, he states the superiority of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra* over all other tantras by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). The ellipsis to be supplied is "those who know the tantras are the best. This refers to the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*. (30, 31)
"From which," and so forth. "Viniyojitaḥ" means set in motion or impelled. || 32 ||
Now, one might ask: "What benefit do you gain from explaining the means for producing the welfare of the world?
To this, he says, "When [it] is done," and so forth. O Goddess, when the welfare of the world is accomplished, Viśveśa—the Supreme Lord and ruler of all of us, including ourselves—is pleased.
It occurs. One might ask: how can affection arise toward the Supreme Lord from the production of the welfare of the universe?

To this he says, "the soul of the universe" (*viśvātmā*). Since the Supreme Lord is one for whom the universe is within himself, therefore, through the production of the welfare of the universe, affection arises toward him.
[This is] the state of being. [Objection: But how could he possess the nature of the universe?
To this he says, "Since the universe," and so forth. Since the universe rests upon him—that is, it exists resting upon that Supreme Lord—therefore he is the self of the universe. || 33 ||
He alone is of the nature of existence, the Truth, non-dual, higher than the highest;
self-luminous, eternally full, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. (34)
Changeless, without support, without distinction, undisturbed;
beyond the qualities, the witness of all, the self of all, the all-seeing, the omnipresent. || 35 ||
He is hidden within all beings, all-pervading, and eternal;
he appears as the qualities of all the senses, yet is devoid of all senses. || 36 ||

Now, in order to declare that because it is real, because it generates joy for all, and because it is the cause of nirvāṇa, the Supreme Self alone is the one to be meditated upon, worshipped, and easily propitiated— firstly, [the text speaks] of the Supreme Self alone.

With the verses beginning with "He alone is one," etc., [the author] establishes that while He is reality, all other objects are false. That Supreme Lord alone—who is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) and whose very essence is being (*sat-svabhāva*)—is the sole reality;
everything else, every other object, should be known as unreal. [The following] provides the reasons for His reality:

Demonstrating this, he says "non-dual" (*advaita*) and so forth: because it is non-dual—devoid of a second of either a similar or dissimilar kind—it is therefore *para*, meaning superior even to Brahmā and others. It shines by itself alone, through its own self; thus, it is *svaprakāśa* (self-luminous).

The meaning is that it is independent of the light of the moon, the sun, and so forth. "Always full" means eternally undivided. "Characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss" means its essential nature consists of that consciousness and bliss—knowledge and joy—which are both ever-present and eternal. || 34 ||
Changeless: devoid of modification, for modification is the alteration of nature (prakṛti).
Supportless: devoid of a substratum. Undifferentiated: devoid of internal distinctions. Unperturbed: devoid of agitation. Beyond the qualities: beyond qualities such as cold and heat.

He has transcended and gone beyond pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as goodness (*sattva*) and the other qualities. He is the witness of all, the direct observer of the auspicious and inauspicious actions of everyone. He is the self of all, the very nature of everything. He is the seer of all, the beholder of every object. He is the all-pervading Lord (*vibhu*).
He who has attained all sovereign powers. || 35 ||
He is hidden and concealed within all beings, both moving and unmoving; he is all-pervasive, having the nature of permeating every object; he is eternal, devoid of beginning or end;
and he is the manifestation of the qualities of all the senses and of all the *guṇas*.
That which, being of such a nature, does not manifest those objects; it is devoid of all sense organs, being empty of the entire collection of senses such as the eye and so forth. || 36 ||
Transcending the world, yet the cause of the world, beyond the reach of speech and mind; he, the omniscient one, knows the universe, but no one knows him. (37)
The entire world, the three realms with all that is moving and unmoving, is dependent upon him; supported by him, this inconceivable universe persists. (38)
Relying upon its reality, it appears as distinct entities, like real things;
by that very cause, O Maheśvarī, we have been born. (39)
He alone is the Supreme Lord, the cause of all beings;
because he effects the creation within the worlds, he is celebrated as the Creator, Brahman. (40)
O Goddess, Viṣṇu is the protector and I am the destroyer by His will;
Indra and all the other guardians of the worlds are subject to His authority.
Devoted each to their own respective duties, they rule by his command;
you are his supreme Prakṛti, worthy of worship in the three worlds.
He has transcended the world and passed beyond it; he is the cause of the world and the seed of the universe.

He is beyond the reach of speech and mind, being an object neither of words nor of thought. That omniscient Supreme Self knows and perceives the entire universe, the whole world; [meditate upon] that Supreme Self.
No one knows this; therefore, the meaning is that the Supreme Self alone is real, whereas every object distinct from Him is unreal because it does not possess such a nature. || 37 ||

"Dependent on that," and so forth. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied. Since the entire world is dependent on that—that is, subject to the control of the Supreme Self—the three worlds, together with all moving and stationary beings, exist by taking Him as their support.
One should remain established by taking refuge in the Supreme Self. This world, which is beyond deliberation and beyond removal,
appears as if it were real and existing as distinct entities— such as "this is earth," "these are waters," and "this is air"— by relying upon the reality of the Supreme Self as its own reality.
The grammatical connection is "it shines forth. We are Śaṅkara and the others. || 38 || 39 ||
"Because of the cause," and so forth. "One" means alone. "By His will" means by the will of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
Because he performs the act of creation within the worlds, Brahmā is celebrated—that is, designated—by the title "the Creator. It is precisely by His will that he protects the created world.
(24) Directed toward their respective objects by Him in His form as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), they perform their own respective actions; they are never independent. 43.
Out of fear of him the wind blows, out of fear of him the sun shines;
at his command the clouds rain in due season, and the trees in the forest put forth their flowers.
He measures time within time; he is the death of death and the fear of fear.
He is the Blessed One, knowable through the Vedanta, who is indicated by the word "That" (Tat).
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, all the gods and goddesses are composed of that;
indeed, the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is composed of that. (46)
When he is satisfied, the world is satisfied; when he is gratified, the world is gratified.
O Goddess, by propitiating him, the gratification of all beings is achieved. (47)
Viṣṇu is celebrated as the protector; and because of his act of withdrawal, I am celebrated as the destroyer.

Regarding the words "Indra and the others": those world-protectors such as Indra and the rest, who are subject to him—that is, dependent upon the Supreme Lord—are all, while intent upon their respective offices, [governing] the worlds by his command.
The grammatical connection is "he teaches. (40–42)

"By him," and so forth. By that Supreme Self, they are "joined to their respective objects," meaning they are set in motion toward this or that object; they are not independent, nor are they self-reliant. 43–44.
"Kālam" and so forth. At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), he even brings time itself to its end, causing it to go to destruction.
"Of fear" (*bhiyaḥ*) means of fear (*bhayasya*). He is indicated by the words "yat" and "tat," being made known by those two pronouns. || 45 ||
"Everything," and so forth. "Consisting of that" means having the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass—that is, from the creator Brahmā up to a cluster of grass—the entire, complete world is composed of that.
It becomes the very nature of the supreme Brahman. || 46 ||
"In that," and so forth. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "In that" means in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). || 47 ||
Just as the sprout-like branches of a tree are satisfied by the sprinkling of water at its root, so too are all the immortals and others satisfied by the performance of that [rite]. (48)
O beloved, O lady of excellent vows, know this: just as they become pleased through your worship, meditation, adoration, and recitation, so too do the beautiful ones. 49.
Just as rivers flow toward the lord of rivers even against their will, so too,
O Pārvatī, ritual acts such as worship and the like are directed toward Him.
O Śivā, whatever deity one may worship with faith for the attainment of whatever goal,
the Supreme Overseer bestows all those very things through those respective hosts of deities.
O beloved, what is the use of speaking much more here before you?
He alone is to be meditated upon, worshipped, and easily propitiated; without him, there is no path to liberation.
There is no exertion, nor fasting, nor does bodily affliction exist;
there is no restriction regarding conduct and the like, nor are there numerous ritual services.

He provides an illustration for the gratification of all through the propitiation of the Supreme Brahman with the verse beginning "of the tree" (taroh) and so forth. "Its branch-fingers" refers to the branches and sprouts of the tree.
"From its performance" means from the propitiation of the Supreme Lord. || 48 ||
"Yathā" and so forth; "from worship" means from mental veneration. || 49 ||
"Yathā" and so forth: "taduddeśyāni" means those rites, such as worship (arcā) and others, for which that Supreme Self is the intended object (uddeśya). || 50 ||

"Whosoever," and so forth. "For the attainment of whatever"—that is, for the acquisition of whichever fruit—[He is] the "supervisor," the instigator of all living beings toward their respective actions. (51)
"Not with much," and so forth. "Easily propitiated" (sukhārādhya) means one who is to be worshipped or served with ease. || 52 ||
Demonstrating precisely its ease of attainment, he says: "No exertion," and so forth. "Exertion" (āyāsa) means fatigue. || 53 ||

(26) O Mistress of the Kula, there is no consideration of direction or time, nor any requirement for the application of mudrās; since this is the means for its realization, who else would one resort to besides it? 54.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Inquiry into the Means for the Liberation of the Living Soul," in the *Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra*, the most excellent of all Tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas, within the dialogue between the venerable Primordial Goddess and Sadāśiva. || 2 ||
That Supreme Self. || 54 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. The third chapter:
The Śrī Devī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, teacher of teachers of the deities;
you are the speaker of all the scriptures, as well as of the mantras and their means of accomplishment.
That which has been described as the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest—by worshipping whom a mortal attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 2 ||
"O Blessed One, by what means does the Supreme Self become propitious? O Lord, what is His practice, and what mantra is proclaimed for Him? (3)
What is the meditation and what is the ritual procedure for the Supreme Lord, the Highest Self?
O Lord, please tell me out of compassion so that I may hear it according to its true nature. (4)
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O beloved of my life, to the supreme reality that is most secret.
Om, salutations to Brahman.

Having heard that for the sake of liberation the Supreme Self alone is to be meditated upon, worshipped, and easily propitiated, the Goddess— desiring to know the method of such meditation and praising Sadāśiva— spoke, beginning with "O God of gods," and so forth. [She addressed] the deities...
From the Guru, who is even greater than Bṛhaspati, one finds—that is, obtains—the reality of that Supreme Self according to its true nature, that is, in its actual state. || 1–4 ||
(28) "O auspicious one, this secret has not been revealed anywhere.
Out of affection for you, I shall speak of that which is supreme and dearer to me than my own life. (5)
That which is to be known is that Supreme Brahman, consisting of existence, consciousness, and the universe;
likewise, O Maheśvarī, it is characterized by its essential nature or by its defining attributes.
The essential nature of Brahman is remembered as pure existence alone, devoid of distinctions, beyond the reach of speech and mind, and the true being of the three worlds.
That is to be known everywhere through the practices of samādhi by those who possess equal vision toward all things,
who have transcended dualities, who are free from conceptual construction, and who are devoid of the superimposition of the body upon the Self.
Then, at that time, Sadāśiva said: "The supreme secret," and so forth.

"The supreme secret" means the most profound mystery; "the supreme reality" (paraṃ tattvaṃ) is the Supreme Brahman. According to the lexicon, *tattva* refers to the true nature of Brahman (*yāthārthya*). "Secret" (*rahasya*) means hidden (*guhya*). || 5 ||

"Jñeyam," and so forth. O Maheśvarī, that which consists of existence, consciousness, and the universe—existence (*sat*) being eternally abiding, consciousness (*cit*) being sentience, and the universe (*viśva*) being the entire world—that which is this very nature, most secret, is the Supreme Brahman. It is by way of its essential nature (*tattvasvarūpeṇa*), that is, by way of the nature and defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman.

Or rather, it is to be known correctly through extrinsic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Those by which an object (*padārtha*) is characterized—that is, known—are "characteristics. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). (6)

Now, in response to the inquiry, "What indeed is the nature of that reality by which the Supreme Brahman may be known?", he defines the nature of Brahman with the words beginning "sattāmātram" (mere existence). That which is mere existence...
It is the nature of pure ultimate reality; it is without distinction, devoid of internal differentiation;
it is beyond the reach of speech and mind, ungraspable by words or thought;
it is the true manifestation of the three worlds, which are otherwise unreal and illusory.
For that knowledge of the true Veda is remembered as the very nature of Brahman.

And he states, beginning with the word "samādhi," that this nature of Brahman is to be known only by the paramahaṃsas: "by those who possess equal vision everywhere" means by those whose vision is equal—that is, the same—toward all things, such as enemies, friends, and so forth; and "by those who have transcended the pairs [of opposites]."

By yogis who have transcended pleasure, pain, cold, heat, and the like; who are free from conceptualization and devoid of various kinds of mental constructions; who are divested of the superimposition of the body upon the self and are devoid of the notion that the self resides in the body; and by means of the yoga of meditative absorption (samādhi).
Concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind.
That from which the universe has arisen, by which that which is born subsists, and in which all things dissolve—that is to be known as Brahman by its characteristics. (9)
O Śivā, that which is to be known through the intellect as one's own essential nature (svarūpa) is indeed [the goal] characterized by defining marks;
for those who desire to attain it through such marks, the means (sādhana) has been prescribed therein.
I shall proclaim the means for its accomplishment; listen attentively, O beloved.
First, I shall describe the extraction of the mantra of the Great Lord.

Yogas are such means as single-minded devotion to the Supreme Lord, right vision, and so forth; by these instruments, that Brahman becomes known. Alternatively, *samādhi* refers to the Supreme Lord, in whom the mind is concentrated (*samādhīyate cittam asmin*); here the suffix *ki* is used in the sense of a locus according to the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*. In that [state],...
By those people who possess the yoga of right vision and so forth, through their yogas of meditative concentration.
Showing the incidental characteristics (taṭasthalakṣaṇas), he says "from which the universe," and so forth:

from which, as the cause, the entire universe—the whole world—has emerged and been born; and once born, the existing universe remains supported by that [Brahman] as its substratum; and at the time of dissolution, all...

That Brahman, in which moving and non-moving beings dissolve and become absorbed, is to be known and understood through these defining characteristics as presented from an external standpoint. || 9 ||

To demonstrate that there is no difference in Brahman— the object to be known— between its essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) and its incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*), he says "by the cognition of its own nature," and so forth: O Śivā, that very Brahman which is to be known— that is, cognized— as the cognition of its own nature is indeed Brahman.

It may also be known through extrinsic characteristics (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*). For those people who wish to realize Brahman through its essential characteristic (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), there is no dependence on means; however, for those who wish to realize it through extrinsic characteristics alone— [the following applies].
In order to state the means of realization (*sādhana*), he says "by characteristics" (*lakṣaṇaiḥ*) and so forth. Among those [characteristics],
namely the essential characteristic (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) and the incidental characteristic (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*),
for those people who desire to attain— that is, to realize— Brahman by means of the incidental characteristics...
The means of accomplishment has been prescribed. || 10 ||

"Regarding the passage beginning with *tat* and so forth: O beloved, I shall explain that means (*sādhana*)—the means for realizing Brahman, which is known through its extrinsic characteristics (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*). Listen attentively, being fully focused. In that regard, while the means is to be explained, first, at the outset..."
I shall now describe the extraction of the mantra of Maheśvara, the Great Lord.
Having first extracted the *praṇava*, one should utter the words "sat" and "cit";
at the end of the [third] word, "brahma"—this is proclaimed as the extraction of the mantra. (12)

When joined according to the sequence of conjunctions, this mantra is considered to consist of seven syllables; O Goddess of the Gods, when devoid of the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), this mantra becomes six-syllabled.
This is the supreme of all mantras, directly bestowing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
herein there is no dependence on [the attainment of] supernatural powers (siddhi) and the like, nor is there any defect regarding enemies, friends, and so forth.

There is no requirement for a lunar day, nor a constellation, nor likewise the calculation of zodiac signs; there is no restriction regarding noble or ignoble lineages, nor is any purificatory rite required here.
This mantra is effective in every way; no deliberation need be made in this matter.
If, through merits accumulated over many births, a true guru is obtained, then by learning [the truth] from his mouth, one attains the fruition of birth. (16)

He explains the extraction of the mantra itself with the words beginning "the *praṇava*," and so forth. First, having extracted the *praṇava*, which is the syllable *oṃ*, one should thereafter utter and speak the word *saccit*. At the end of the word *saccit*, one should utter "one Brahman."
And from that, the mantra consisting of the form "Saccidekaṃ Brahma" is produced.
This very extraction of the mantra has been proclaimed and explained. || 12 ||

Regarding the term *sandhi*: O Goddess of the gods, this mantra, when joined and united according to the sequence of *sandhi*, is considered to consist of seven syllables (*saptārṇa*). By omitting the *tāra*—that is, by excluding the *praṇava* (Oṃ)—this very same previously mentioned mantra becomes six-syllabled (*ṣaḍvarṇa*). || 13 ||

Now he praises this mantra with the words beginning "sarva" and so forth. This mantra is the most excellent and supreme among all mantras. He explains its status as the most excellent of all mantras with the words beginning "sākṣāt" and so forth. || 14 ||
"Not the lunar day" (na tithiḥ): the ellipsis is that "the lunar day is not to be taken into account. || 15 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate the supreme excellence of the person who receives this mantra, he says "vahni" and so forth: "Having learned this mantra from his mouth," that is, from the mouth of a true guru. || 16 ||
Having placed the fourfold aims within his grasp, he rejoices both in this world and in the next. || 17 ||
He is blessed, he has accomplished his purpose, he is successful, and he is righteous;
he has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.
He was proficient in all scriptures and established in all the worlds,
for him the great jewel of the mantra had reached the vicinity of the path of his ears.
Blessed is his mother and father; O Śivā, his lineage is pure.
His ancestors, being satisfied, rejoice together with the gods, their bodies bristling with joy as they sing this song of praise.
"In our family, a most excellent man has been born who teaches the Brahman; what need have we for funeral cakes at Gayā, or for sacred pilgrimage sites, or for ancestral offerings and libations? (21)
What need is there for gifts, what for recitations or burnt offerings, and what for other manifold means?
We have attained imperishable satisfaction through the spiritual practice of this virtuous son.

"Caturvargam" (the fourfold group): the group or collection characterized by dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is the "caturvarga. As Amarasimha states: "Trivarga consists of dharma, kāma, and artha; caturvarga includes mokṣa as well. "Paratra" means in the other world. "Niṣṇātaḥ" means skillful or proficient.

"Reached the vicinity of the path of the ears" means having reached the proximity of the range of hearing. "The mantra itself is the great jewel. (Verses 18–19). Regarding the word "pitaraḥ": it is that which is sung, thus "gāyanī"; here the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) by virtue of the rule "lyuṭ vā" being applied extensively (*bāhulakāt*). "Adorned with horripilation" means attained through the bristling of the hair.
Those whose bodies (*vigraha*) were thus; [even in the reading *pulakāṅkitavigrahāḥ*, the meaning of *aṅkita* is "marked" or "stamped"]. || 20 ||
He spoke that very verse with the two beginning with "In our family" (asmatkule), etc.
"One who instructs in Brahman" means one who possesses instruction in Brahman. "Satisfied with the imperishable" means possessing mantras that grant indestructible satisfaction. || 21 || 22 ||
Listen, O Goddess, who are adored by the world; I speak what is true, truly true.
For those who worship the Supreme Brahman, what need is there for any other means? (23)
Merely by receiving the mantra, an embodied being becomes identical with Brahman;
O Goddess of gods, for one who has become Brahman, what is there left to be attained within the three worlds? (24)
What can the enraged planets, vetālas, ceṭakas and the like, piśācas, guhyakas, bhūtas, ḍākinīs, mātṛkās and so forth do? At the mere sight of him, they flee with their faces turned away. (25)
Protected by the Brahma-mantra and enveloped in Brahmanic splendor, why should he fear the planets and other such influences? He is like another sun.
Seeing him, they were overcome with fear like elephants seeing a lion;
they fled and perished like moths in a fire.
There is no evil whatsoever for that embodied being who is established in Brahman, who is purified by truth, pure, and intent on the welfare of all living creatures;
for who would seek to cause him harm, except one who seeks his own destruction? (28)
"Listen," and so forth. By "other means" (*sādhanāntaraiḥ*) is meant by specific means (*sādhanaviśeṣaiḥ*). || 23 ||

"By the mantra," and so forth. What is there to be attained? What is there to be gained? Rather, the meaning is that every single thing has already been attained. (24) By the mere sight of him who has become Brahman, the planets and other malevolent forces turn their faces away and flee. (25) "Protected," and so forth.

A person who has become one with Brahman—does he fear the planets and other such beings? Having become fearless, why would he fear? Rather, the meaning is that he does not fear. Like Mārtaṇḍa, that is, like the sun. Regarding the passage beginning with "him":
those planets and others flee from him, the worshiper of the Supreme Brahman; they run away like moths.
Like moths; || 27 || of the pure one, whose internal organ (antahkarana) is stainless. || 28 ||
Those wicked and sinful people who harbor malice toward one who teaches the Supreme Brahman commit an act of treachery against themselves, for they are not distinct from the True Being. (29)
He is the benefactor of all, virtuous, and the doer of what is pleasing to everyone;
O Goddess, when harm is done to him, who could possibly remain free from affliction? (30)
If a practitioner does not know the meaning of the mantra and the consciousness of the mantra, his mantra will not be perfected even if recited ten million times. || 31 ||
Therefore, O beloved, I shall explain its meaning and consciousness; listen.
By the letter *a*, he is the protector of the world; by the letter *u*, he is the destroyer.
By the letter *ma*, the creator of the world is expressed; this is declared to be the meaning of the *praṇava*.
By the word *sat*, that which always abides—the consciousness of pure awareness—is proclaimed. (33)
O Īśānī, that which is one and non-dual is called Brahman because of its vastness;
O Goddess, this meaning of the mantra has been told, which bestows the desired accomplishments upon the practitioner. (34)

"Those who," and so forth. Those who are sinful, characterized by evil, wicked, and base individuals, who harbor malice toward a person who teaches the Supreme Brahman—that is, who inflict harm upon him—those sinners commit nothing but treachery against themselves. [The phrase] "toward one who teaches the Supreme Brahman" means...

Because the rule "the object of those [verbs] meaning anger, malice, envy, jealousy, and censure is the recipient of the anger" (*krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ*) prescribes the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*), the fourth case (*caturthī*) is applied by the rule "the fourth case is used for the recipient" (*sampradāne caturthī*). Showing the cause for the production of harm to himself through the act of committing treachery against those who instruct him in the Supreme Brahman, he says: "They are not distinct," and so forth.

Because they are not distinct or separate from that person who is virtuous, established in Brahman, and a teacher of Brahman, the implication is that they are merely committing treachery against themselves. (29) But he, on the other hand, is one who is firmly grounded in Brahman. (30)

"Regarding the meaning of the mantra": for that practitioner (*sādhaka*), since [the mantra] does not become effective, he therefore first explains the meaning of the *praṇava* (OM) with the words "by the letter A," and so forth. || 31 || 32 ||
Now, he explains the meaning of the terms *sat*, *cit*, and so forth, beginning with the words "by the word *sat*" and so on. || 33 || 34 ||
This consciousness of the mantra is indeed its presiding deity;
O Supreme Goddess, knowledge of that bestows accomplishment upon devotees. (35)
O Goddess of gods, its presiding lord is all-pervading and eternal;
it is inconceivable, free from affliction, beyond speech, and stainless.
O Pārvatī, by means of Vāk, Māyā, Kamalā, and so forth—devoid of the Tāra—the various Vidyās, Māyā, and Śrī are bestowed in every direction. (37)
With the *tāra* (oṃ) or without the *tāra*, each individual word, or even by means of pairing them two by two—this mantra may thus become manifold. (38)

Now, [the author] explains the consciousness of the mantra with the words beginning "in the mantra" (*mantra* etc.). O Supreme Goddess, the connection of the sentence is as follows: you should know that the very knowledge which belongs to the deity who presides over that mantra is indeed the consciousness of the mantra. And that is the knowledge of the presiding deity.
It shall become the bestower of perfection upon devotees. || 35 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to who the presiding deity of this mantra is, he says "of this" and so forth: O Goddess of Gods, [the mantra is] all-pervasive (sarvavyāpin), having the nature of pervading all objects;
eternal (sanātana), being devoid of prior non-existence and destruction; and inconceivable (avitarkya), being beyond logical deduction.

Formless, meaning devoid of shape; beyond speech, meaning transcending words; stainless, meaning not being an object of the mind, eyes, and other senses—that Brahman shall be the presiding deity of this mantra. || 36 ||

"Speech," and so forth. O Pārvatī, by means of that mantra previously mentioned— which has "Aiṃ," "Hrīṃ," and "Śrīṃ" as its initial seed-syllables (*bīja*), and which is devoid of the *tāra* (the *praṇava*)— various kinds of knowledge (*vidyā*) of many types are bestowed in due order.

Various *māyās* are bestowed upon every face; such is the *śrī*, the Goddess Lakṣmī, that is bestowed. Just as knowledge (*vidyā*) is bestowed by means of this mantra: *aiṃ saccidekaṃ brahma*; so too is *māyā* bestowed by means of this: *hrīṃ saccidekaṃ brahma*. *Śrīṃ*.
But by the statement "Brahman is one, consisting of Truth," [it is indicated that] Śrī [is also Brahman]. || 37 ||

Now, with the words beginning "by means of the *tāra*," he establishes the various forms of this very mantra: each individual word of the previously mentioned mantra, or the entire word, should be joined with the *tāra*, that is, the *praṇava*.
The seer of this [mantra] is indeed Sadāśiva; its meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is the Supreme Brahman, the inner controller of all, devoid of attributes (nirguṇa). || 39 ||
The application for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life has been proclaimed;
now listen, O beloved, as I describe the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa). 40.
O Maheśvarī, [one should recite] "Tāram," "Saccidekam," and "Brahma" for the entire [mantra], [placing them] on the thumb, forefinger, middle finger, and ring finger respectively. (41)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, on the palms and backs of the two little fingers,
[one should place] *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* at their ends, respectively.

Alternatively, it should be understood as being characterized by the omission of the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), that is, by the abandonment of the *praṇava*. Consequently, this mantra becomes manifold. Furthermore, according to the sequence of pairs, this aforementioned mantra—whether accompanied by the *praṇava* or devoid of it—becomes manifold, meaning it takes many forms. [The mantra] accompanied by the *tāra*...

Each word devoid of that [the *praṇava*] is as follows: *oṃ sat*, *oṃ cit*, *oṃ ekam*, *oṃ brahma*; and *sat*, *cit*, *ekam*, *brahma*. A complete word, whether connected with the *praṇava* or unconnected with it, is as follows: *oṃ saccidekaṃ brahma*.
"Sat-cit-ekaṃ Brahma. According to the sequence of pairs: *oṃ* Sat-Brahma; *oṃ* Cit-Brahma;
*oṃ* Ekaṃ Brahma; *oṃ* Sat-Cit; *oṃ* Cit-Ekaṃ; Sat-Brahma; Cit-Brahma;
Ekaṃ Brahma; Sat-Cit; Cit-Ekaṃ. Thus [ends verse 38].

Now, he states the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details of this mantra with the verse beginning "The Seer" and so forth, consisting of one and a half [verses]. Of this mantra: "the inner controller of all" means the internal regulator of all.
