Sadāśiva is the seer of this mantra; the meter (*chandas*) is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is the supreme, attributeless inner controller of all.
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), desire (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*), with Brahmā as the deity.
Salutation to Sadāśiva, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *anuṣṭubh* meter (*chandas*), on the mouth;
salutation to the deity, the inner controller of all, the supreme Brahman devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa-paramabrahman*), on the heart.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa. Having thus performed the *ṛṣinyāsa*, the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* are to be performed; therefore, he speaks [the following] beginning with "aṅganyāsa" etc., in order to describe those two. (39–40)

Between those two, he first describes the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the two and a half verses beginning with "Tāram" and so forth: "O Maheśvarī, O Goddess worshipped by the gods,
[perform the nyāsa] with the mantras ending in *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*."
The practitioner, being well-composed, should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) according to the prescribed rule of placement, including the internal elements *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*.
In this very manner, the procedure is ordained from the heart up to the hands. (43)
Then one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with either the root mantra or the syllable Om,
O Pārvatī, using the middle and ring fingers of the right hand.
Holding the left nostril with the right hand,
the practitioner of mantra should fill the breath through the right nostril while reciting the root mantra eight times.

Holding the right nostril with the thumb through the practice of breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should recite [the mantra] thirty-two times; thereafter, [one should exhale] through the right nostril.
Chanting the mantra sixteen times, one should very gradually exhale the breath;
likewise, through the left nostril, one should perform inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
Again, one should perform [the rite] to the south as before, O Goddess worshipped by the gods;
thus has the procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma) been declared for the practice of the Brahma-mantra.

The syllable *praṇava*, which is distinguished by the words *hūṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, *phaṭ*, *rūpa*, *tāra*, *sat*, *cit*, *ekam*, and *brahma*; immediately following that, the entire phrase *oṃ saccidekaṃ brahma* [is assigned] to the thumb, forefinger, middle finger, ring finger, and the two little fingers.

The practitioner, being well-composed and extremely attentive, should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the palms and backs of the hands according to the prescribed method and in due order. The sequence is as follows: *Oṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *Sat* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *Cit* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*.
*Hūṃ* with the two ring fingers; *Vauṣaṭ* with the two little fingers for Brahman; *Oṃ Saccidekaṃ Brahma Phaṭ* with the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the *karanyāsa*.
Now, the *aṅganyāsa* is performed with half [of the verse], beginning with "at the heart" (*hṛdi*) and so forth, extending from the heart to the hands.
In this very manner, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is prescribed: *oṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *sat* to the head, *svāhā*;
*cit* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *ekam* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hūṃ*; *brahma* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. *Oṃ sat-cit-ekam brahma*.
With the palms and backs of the hands, [utter] "phaṭ. || 41–43 ||
Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should perform *prāṇāyāma*;

this he states with the words beginning "prāṇāyāmam. Immediately thereafter, by means of the root mantra beginning "Oṃ, Brahman is existence-consciousness-unity," and by the *praṇava*, the syllable "Oṃ," [one should perform it] in the cause.
Then, one should perform meditation, which accomplishes the desired goal of the practitioner. (49)
In the center of the lotus of the heart, there is that which is without distinction or desire,
to be known by Hari, Hara, and Brahmā, attainable through meditation by yogis,
the very nature of existence and consciousness, which destroys the fear of birth and death.
I praise Brahman, the consciousness that is the seed of the entire universe.

Or one should perform *prāṇāyāma*. Now, in response to the question of how *prāṇāyāma* is to be performed, the author states its procedure in four and a half verses beginning with "madhyama. O Pārvatī, [of] the right hand...
Holding the left nostril with the middle and ring fingers,
the practitioner-mantrin, while reciting the root mantra eight times, should fill the air through the right nostril. Then...
Holding the right nostril with the thumb of the right hand,
one should recite the root mantra thirty-two times through the practice of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*). Then,
while reciting the root mantra sixteen times, [one should exhale] through the right nostril alone.

One should exhale the breath very slowly. Then, one should likewise perform inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) through the left nostril; the meaning is that one should produce the breath by drawing it in, holding it motionless, and releasing it in that same sequence as before. As previously described.

Again, one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) from the right side as well. This is declared to be the procedure for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) in the practice of the Brahma-mantra. Regarding the nature of inhalation and the others, Yogi-Yājñavalkya says:
"Drawing the breath upward through the nose is called *pūraka* (inhalation);
holding the breath motionless is *kumbhaka* (retention); and being released [from the breath] is *recaka* (exhalation). Thus [ends the section]. 44–48.
Having thus performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform meditation on the Supreme Brahman;
this is stated by the words beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*). || 49 ||

Now, he describes that meditation with the words beginning "hṛdaya" (heart). The grammatical construction is: "I praise—that is, I meditate upon—the Consciousness, the sentient Brahman, situated in the center of the heart-lotus.
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *īḍ* is employed here in the sense of meditation (*dhyāna*).

"Without distinction," and so forth, are the qualifiers of Brahman. "Without distinction" means devoid of various kinds of differentiation. "Without activity" means free from desire, which implies having attained all sovereignty. It is to be reached through meditation.

It must be understood through meditation: that which destroys the fear of birth and death and removes the terror caused by the signs of birth and death. Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Brahman with mental offerings, (p. 38) [one attains liberation].
One should worship with supreme devotion for the sake of attaining union with Brahman.
One should offer fragrance as the earth-element (mahītattva) and flowers as the ether-element (ākāśa).
One should offer incense as the air-element (vāyutattva) and present the lamp as the fire-element (tejas).
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) to the Supreme Self (paramātman) by means of the water-element (toyatattva).
Then, having mentally recited the great mantra, the supreme practitioner should offer it to Brahman and subsequently commence the external worship.
The materials have been set forth: perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
garments, ornaments, and the like; as well as various kinds of food and drink. (54)
Having purified [the offering] with this mantra and meditated upon the eternal Brahman,
the wise man, closing his eyes, should offer it to the Supreme Self.
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is absorbed in the yoga of Brahman-action, Brahman alone is to be attained. 56.
The meaning is that its nature is pure consciousness, its nature is eternally abiding, and its nature is knowledge;
it is the seed of all worlds, the cause of the entire universe. || 50 ||

Having thus meditated upon Brahman, one should perform its worship; this is stated by the words beginning with "having meditated" (*dhyātvā*). "Mental" (*mānasaiḥ*) means those formed by the resolve of the mind. "For the sake of union with Brahman" (*brahmasāyujyahetave*) means for the purpose of attaining the state of Brahman. "Brahmabhūyam" means the state of being Brahman (*brahmatvam*).

"Amarasiṃha also states that [this] is 'union with Brahman' (brahmasāyujya). He describes these very metaphorical mental offerings with the words beginning with 'fragrance' (gandha) and so forth. || 51 || 52 ||
"Then" means: having offered the great mantra consisting of "Oṃ, Brahman is one, being-consciousness," and so forth;
that is, having given the fruit caused by the recitation of the great mantra.
He describes the external worship itself with the words beginning "upasthitāni" (those present). "Upasthitāni" means those standing nearby.
"Anena" refers to the mantra that will be spoken immediately following this [at verses 53–55].

Now he states the mantra for the offering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, beginning with "brahmārpaṇam. That by which something is offered or given is the *arpaṇa*, such as the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) and other vessels; that too is Brahman alone.
Even the oblation being offered, such as clarified butter and the like, is Brahman alone.
Then, having opened his eyes and recited the root mantra according to his capacity,
he should offer that recitation to Brahman and recite the hymn of praise and the armor-verse (kavaca).
Listen, O Maheśānī, to the hymn of praise to Brahmā, the Supreme Self;
having heard it, O Goddess, the practitioner attains union with Brahman. (58)
Salutations to You, the Existent One, the refuge of all worlds; salutations to You, Consciousness, whose nature is the form of the universe;
salutations to the non-dual Reality, the bestower of liberation.
Salutation to Brahman, the all-pervading, who is devoid of qualities. || 59 ||
You alone are the refuge; you alone are the most excellent;
you alone are the cause of the universe, possessing universal form. Fire is indeed Brahman; the oblation offered by the agent, who is Brahman, is also Brahman.
The meaning is that the fire, the agent, and even the act of offering are Brahman alone.

Thus, by that person who possesses *samādhi*—which is one-pointedness of mind—directed toward Brahman itself in its aspect as action, Brahman alone is to be reached and attained, and not any other fruit; this is the meaning. || 56 ||
"Then," and so forth. "Having opened" means having uncovered. "The root" refers to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
"Made over to Brahman" (*brahmasāt*) means dependent upon Brahman. || 57 ||
Regarding the word "stotra": he attains union with Brahman; that is, he reaches the state of Brahman. || 58 ||

Now he states that hymn of praise, beginning with "Salutations to You" (*namaste*): *sate* means to the eternal, the ever-abiding; *sarvalokāśrayāya* means to the one who has become the support for all the worlds; *cite* means to consciousness;
*viśvarūpātmane* means to Him whose self possesses the form of the universe; and *advaitatattvāya* means to the non-dual reality.

To Brahman, the most vast, and therefore all-pervasive—that is, having the nature of pervading all things; to the one devoid of qualities, meaning free from the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest; to the reality that is free from internal distinctions based on similarity or dissimilarity. || 59 ||
(40) You alone are the creator, protector, and destroyer of the world; you alone are the supreme, immovable, and free from conceptual construction.
You are the fear of fears, the terrifying of the terrifying, the refuge of living beings, the purifier of the purifiers,
and the sole sovereign over those who occupy the highest stations.
The supreme protector of others among all protectors. || 61 ||
O Supreme Lord, illuminator of all forms, indefinable, inaccessible to all the senses,
Truth, inconceivable, imperishable, all-pervading, unmanifest Reality.
May the Sovereign Lord, the illuminator of the world, protect us from misfortune. || 62 ||

"Thou," and so forth. "One" means primary or absolute. "Refuge-worthy" (*śaraṇya*) means fit for refuge or protection; here the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of "fit for that. "Excellent" (*vareṇya*) means worthy of being chosen;
the meaning is that it is to be worshipped by those who fear the sufferings of birth, death, and so on. "Supreme" (*param*):
Supreme; non-conceptual, meaning devoid of various kinds of mental constructions. || 60 ||

"Of fears," and so forth: [he is] the terrifying among the terrifying, the awe-inspiring among the awe-inspiring; the purifier among the purifiers, the generator of purity among those things that produce purification; among all places (padānām), that is, locations.
Or rather, it is the controller and regulator even of those such as Brahmā and others who possess a station that is "mahoccais" — exceedingly elevated;
that is, even among the most excellent beings. || 61 ||

"O Supreme Lord," and so forth. "Supreme Lord" (pareśa) means the sovereign even over others such as Brahmā and the rest. "O Master" (prabho) means O Controller. "Inexpressible" (anirdeśya) means incapable of being described by words.
"Beyond the reach of all senses" (sarvendriyāgamya) means unattainable by all the senses, such as the eyes and the rest. "Truth" (satya).

O You who possess the ultimate truth; O Inconceivable One, who is not even an object of the mind; O Imperishable One (Akṣara), so called because You do not perish or move; O Unmanifest One (Avyakta), devoid of form and other such qualities; O Illuminator of the worlds...
May He, the Lord even of the moon, the sun, and so forth— or alternatively, where *jagadbhasaka* (the destroyer of the world) and *adhīśa* (the supreme lord) are distinct words—
protect [us] (*pāyāt*), that is, save us from *apāya*,
which is the separation from devotion, wisdom, and the like. 62.
We remember that one alone;
we mutter that one alone; we bow to that one who is the witness of the universe—the one eternal treasure, the Lord who is without support.
We go for refuge to the ship that carries one across the ocean of existence. || 63 ||
Whoever, having become pure and restrained, recites this hymn of the five jewels dedicated to Brahmā, the Supreme Self, shall attain union with Brahman.
One should recite this daily at dusk, especially on Mondays;
the wise person should cause their kinsmen who are devoted to Brahman to hear and understand it.
Thus, O Goddess, the five jewels of the Great Lord have been told to you.
Now hear, O lady of beautiful limbs, the armor named *Jaganmaṅgala*, by the recitation and wearing of which one certainly becomes a knower of Brahman. (66)
May the Supreme Self protect my head; may the Supreme Lord protect my heart;
may the Protector of the World protect my throat; and may the all-pervading All-Seeing One protect my face.
May the Soul of the Universe protect my hands; may He who consists of consciousness protect my feet;
may the eternal Supreme Brahman protect every limb at all times.

"tat" and so forth. "That" refers to Brahman. That in which the universe is deposited is the "nidhāna," meaning it is the substratum of the universe. It is "nirālamba," meaning devoid of any external support. || 63 ||

Now, he describes the fruit resulting from the recitation of this hymn called the *Pañcaratna* (The Five Jewels), beginning with the words "The Five Jewels," etc. "Prayataḥ" means pure. "Adaḥ" refers to this hymn. (64–65)
Having recited the hymn of praise (stotra), the armor (kavaca) must be recited; therefore, he begins to describe that with the words "iti" (thus). || 66 ||
He speaks of that very Brahma-armor, beginning with "the Supreme Self" and so forth. "Consisting of consciousness" means having the nature of pure awareness. || 67 || 68 ||

(42) Sadāśiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this armor (*kavaca*) which is the auspiciousness of the world; the meter (*chandas*) is *anuṣṭubh*, and the deity (*devatā*) is the Supreme Brahman. Its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life. || 69 ||
Whoever recites the Brahma-kavaca preceded by the ritual placement upon the seers (ṛṣinyāsa),
having attained the knowledge of Brahman, shall become truly one with Brahman.
If one writes [this] on birch bark, places it in a pill, and wears it on the neck or on the right arm, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 71 ||
Thus has this supreme armor of Brahman been revealed to you;
one should bestow it upon a beloved disciple who is wise and devoted to the guru.
Having recited the hymn of praise and the armor-rite, the foremost of practitioners should prostrate.
Salutations to you, the Supreme Brahman; salutations to you, the Supreme Self.
Salutations to you who are devoid of qualities; repeated salutations to you whose nature is pure existence.

Now, he states the seer (ṛṣi) and other details of this armor (kavaca) with the words beginning "Śrī Jagat," and so forth. Then, he states the fruit arising from the recitation of the Brahma-kavaca with the words beginning "He who," and so forth. That [recitation] in which the ritual placement of the seer (ṛṣinyāsa) precedes; and the ṛṣinyāsa belongs to this [text] named Śrī Jaganmaṅgala.
Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of the armor (kavaca); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); the Supreme Brahman is the deity (devatā).

Its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, in the recitation of the armor known as the Śrījaganmaṅgala. Salutation to Sadāśiva, the seer, upon the head; salutation to Anuṣṭubh, the meter, upon the mouth.
Salutation! Salutation to the deity, the Supreme Brahman, in the heart.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, in the recitation of the armor (*kavaca*) known as the *Śrījaganmaṅgala*. Having approached and attained [it], one becomes composed of Brahman, having the nature of Brahman. (Verses 69–71)

Thus [it is said]. "To you" (*te*) means before you or for your sake. "One should bow to the Supreme Self"—this is the ellipsis. "The foremost of practitioners" (*sādhakāgraṇīḥ*) means the best of practitioners. He expresses that very act of bowing with the words beginning with "namaḥ" (salutation), etc. (verses 72–74).
Whether verbal, physical, or even mental, according to one's capacity, purification of intention is prescribed for the propitiation of the Supreme Lord. (75)
Having thus worshipped together with his own people and kinsmen,
the wise man should partake of the great grace (mahāprasāda) of Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
In the worship of the Supreme Lord, there is neither invocation nor dismissal;
at all times and in all places, one should accomplish the means to Brahman.
Whether un-bathed or having bathed, whether having eaten or being hungry, one whose mind is ever pure should worship the Supreme Self. (78)
Whatever food, drink, or other offerings are given to the Supreme Lord with this Brahma-mantra, that alone is truly great and purifying. (79)
In the waters of the Gaṅgā or on stone and such, there exists the defect of being touched;
however, in an object offered to the Supreme Brahman, there is neither the state of being touched nor the state of being untouched.

Now, one might object that all three types of salutation—physical, verbal, and mental—should be performed toward the Supreme Self, or at least one of them; to this he replies with the words "verbal," etc.
According to his understanding, [he offers] physical and verbal [salutation] to the Supreme Brahman.

Or one should perform a mental prostration. Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that for the Supreme Brahman, only a physical prostration is appropriate, and not vocal or mental ones? To this, he says: "In worship," and so forth. *Bhāva-śuddhi* is the purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). || 75 ||
"Thus," and so forth. "Having worshipped the Supreme Self"—this is the ellipsis. "One should accomplish" means one should bring [the goal] to completion. (76–78)

Now he begins to describe the majesty of the great grace (*mahāprasāda*) of Brahman with the words "by this," and so forth. [This refers to] by means of the Brahma-mantra consisting of "Oṃ Saccidānanda" and so on, or that consisting of "Brahmārpaṇam" and so on, [upon] stone and other materials.
On the Śālagrāma stone and so forth. || 79 || 80 ||
Whether it be cooked or even uncooked, having consecrated it with this mantra and dedicated it to Brahman, the practitioner should eat it together with his own kin. (81)
In this matter, there is no consideration of caste, nor any discrimination regarding food leavings and the like;
there is no restriction of time here, nor likewise any concern for purity or impurity.
At the proper time, in the proper place, and according to the appropriate manner, one should partake of the food offering (naivedya) dedicated to Brahman without hesitation. 83.
O Goddess, even that food brought by a dog-cooker, or even that which has issued from a dog's mouth, is purifying and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (84)
O you who are worshipped by the gods, what more need be said regarding human beings and others? What fruit would arise from partaking of the food offering (naivedya) of the Supreme Lord? (85)
Whether one is burdened by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or joined with other sins, one is liberated by receiving his grace even once; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts at thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas),
a mortal obtains that same fruit by resorting to Brahmārpita.
Whatever fruit one enjoys by performing sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, one shall obtain ten million times that much by consuming the consecrated food (naivedya) of Brahman. 88.
Even with thousands of tongues and hundreds of millions of mouths,
it is not possible to describe the greatness of the Mahāprasāda.

"Ripened" means by means of the mantra consisting of "Oṃ Tat Sat," and so forth. "Not here" means not in this regard, namely, when there is the great grace of Brahman. "Brought" means that even food brought by a *śvapaca*—a *caṇḍāla*—becomes purifying once it has been dedicated to Brahman.
It would be; it attains, it obtains. || 81–89 ||
Whether situated anywhere at all, having obtained the nectar offered to Brahman and having taken hold of it—be they even mere skeletons—they shall attain union with Brahman. (90)
If food belonging to a low caste should be prepared for a Brahmin,
that food must be accepted even by Brahmins who have reached the further shore of the Vedānta.
No distinction based on caste should be made regarding the grace of the Supreme Self;
he who harbors impure thoughts toward it becomes a perpetrator of a great sin.
O beloved, one might better commit a hundred sins or even kill a Brahmin than show contempt for food offered to the Supreme Brahman.
O auspicious lady, those foolish men who discard food, water, and other offerings consecrated by the great mantra cause their ancestors to fall into the depths.

Those who harbor hatred toward the food offerings dedicated to Brahmā fall themselves into the Andhatāmisra hell, where they remain until the dissolution of all things; for them, there is no atonement.
In this practice of the Great Mantra, all actions become meritorious, deep sleep becomes equivalent to virtuous deeds, and acting according to one's own will is prescribed here. 96.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yatra" and so forth: *amṛta* means wine (*śīdhu*). *Kīkaśa* refers even to a *cāṇḍāla*. || 90 ||
"Yadi" means: belonging to a low caste, such as a *caṇḍāla* and so forth; "meditated upon in Brahman" means it has been offered to Brahman. || 91 || 92 ||

"Varam," and so forth. *Varam* means slightly dear. According to Amara: "The word *vara* [is used] after *deva* [in the sense of a boon]; it is best (*śreṣṭha*) in three genders, and neuter in the sense of 'slightly dear'. *Avahelanam* means contempt or disregard. || 93 || 94 ||

"By himself," and so forth. In the hell called Andhatāmisra, there is a "submersion" (saṃplava) of the summoned universe into the water—that is, a complete immersion lasting until that time, meaning until the time of universal dissolution (pralaya). "Redemption" (niṣkṛti) means deliverance. || 95 ||
"Meritorious," and so forth. Even all non-meritorious actions become meritorious; the meaning is that they behave as if they were meritorious. || 96 ||
(46) What has he to do with Vedic practices, or even with Tantric ones?
For the wise man established in Brahman, conduct according to his own will is declared to be the rule. || 97 ||
There is no fruit from performing this, nor is there any fault from not performing it; there is neither obstacle nor transgression resulting from the practice of this Brahma-mantra. (98)

In this Dharma, O Great Goddess, there should be one who speaks the truth, has conquered his senses, is devoted to helping others, is free from changeability, and possesses a virtuous disposition. (99)
Free from envy, devoid of hypocrisy, compassionate, and pure in mind, he brings joy to his mother and father and is devoted to their service. (100)

One who hears Brahman, who contemplates Brahman, whose mind is intent on the search for Brahman, who has a restrained self and firm intellect, should meditate upon himself as being directly Brahman. (101)
A practitioner of the Brahma-mantra should avoid speaking falsehoods, harboring thoughts of ill-will toward others, and sexual intercourse with the wives of others. 102.
"O Goddess, one should say 'Tat Sat' at the commencement of all rites;
the phrase 'May there be offering to Brahman' is for the acts of eating and drinking. (103)
Whatever means ensures the successful course of worldly life for mortals—that alone is the duty to be performed by those who know Brahman; this is the eternal dharma. (104)

"Kimiti," etc. For the wise one (*viduṣaḥ*), who knows that "everything is indeed Brahman," conduct according to one's own will (*svecchācāra*) is itself the injunction (*vidhi*). This refers to this one who is established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhasya*). 97–98.

"In this [verse], beginning with 'asmin'... "Sadāśayaḥ" means having a virtuous intention. "Mātsaryahīnaḥ" means free from envy, that is, devoid of hatred for the welfare of others. "Adambhī" means free from deceit. "Tayoḥ" refers to those two, the mother and father. (99) (100)

"Brahman," and so forth. "Self-controlled" means one whose mind is restrained. "Meditating" means contemplating that Brahman truly exists. "The offering is Brahman" refers to the statement [of the mantra]. "The course of worldly life" means the maintenance of the world. (101–104)

(p. 47) Now I shall describe the ritual of the twilight worship (sandhyā-vidhi) of the Brahma-mantra belonging to Śambhu, by performing which human beings on earth attain the perfection of Brahman. || 105 ||
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, in the appropriate place and upon the appropriate seat,
the best of practitioners, having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman as before, [should perform the rites].
O Goddess, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
having offered the recitation according to the rules, the wise person should prostrate as before.
This twilight ritual has been described by me as being in every way essential for the accomplishment of Brahman;
through its performance, the practitioner of mantra becomes pure in heart. (108)
O lady of beautiful limbs, listen to the Gāyatrī, which destroys all sins:
having uttered "Parameśvarāya" (to the Supreme Lord) in the dative case, one should say "vidmahe" immediately thereafter. (109)
"O Dear One, one should say 'we meditate' (*dhīmahi*) with reference to the supreme reality (*paratattva*) as the goal.

Now, regarding the phrase 'which twilight' (*yāṃ sandhyām*): it refers to the attainment of Brahman (*brahmasampatti*), which is the perfection whose nature is Brahman. He explains that very procedure for the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vidhi*) starting with the words 'in the morning' (*prātaḥ*) and so forth."
"By means of its performance," that is, by means of its practice. || 105–108 ||
He speaks of that very Brahmagāyatrī with the half-verse beginning "Parameśvaram" and so forth:
"O Dear One, O Īśānī, having uttered the word 'Parameśvara' ending in the fourth case (the *ṅe* vibhakti), one should say the word 'vidmahe'. Immediately after that, [one says] 'vidmahe'."

Immediately after the word [parasmai], one should utter the word *paratattvāya*. After the word *paratattvāya*, one should utter the word *dhīmahi*. Immediately after that word *dhīmahi*, one should utter *tanno brahma pracodayāt*. And then, [one says] *parameśvarāya vidmahe*.

The *Brahma-gāyatrī* was thus established as: "We meditate upon the Supreme Reality; may that Brahman inspire us. As for the meaning of the *Brahma-gāyatrī*: "Upon the Supreme Reality," that is, upon the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*); "in order to attain the Supreme Reality," that is, the Supreme Lord; "that which is Brahman," we—
We know, we reflect upon, and we meditate upon that Brahman; O Īśānī, may that Brahman impel us. This is the Śrī-Brahma-Gāyatrī, which bestows the four aims of human life. (110)
Whether it be worship, sacrifice, bathing, drinking, or eating—
whatever action one performs, one should accomplish it with the Brahma-mantra.

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and bowed to the Guru who bestows the Veda, and having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity; then, as before, one should bow to the Veda—this is remembered as the morning ritual (*prātaḥ-kṛtya*). || 112 ||
The preliminary rite for this [mantra] consists of thirty-two thousand recitations;
the fire-oblation is one-tenth of that, and the libation is one-tenth of that.
O beautiful one, the sprinkling [of water] should be done with a tenth part of that, and again with a tenth part of that;
the practitioner of mantras should feed Brahmins during the rite of *puraścaraṇa*. (114)
In this [practice], there is no consideration of what is fit or unfit to be eaten; there is nothing to be rejected and nothing to be accepted.
There is no rule regarding the purity of time, nor any determination of place. (115)
"May it impel us"—that is, it may urge us forward, meaning it may enjoin us toward virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). || 109 || 110 ||

"Regarding 'worship' (pūjanam): the ellipsis is that one should accomplish the respective rites. Now, he describes the morning duties with the words beginning 'in the Brāhma [period]' and so forth. 'The mantra' refers to the mantra beginning with 'Oṃ, Brahman is the one reality of consciousness-existence' (oṃ saccidekaṃ brahma) and so on. || 111 || 112 ||

Now, he describes the procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* of the Brahma-mantra with the verse beginning "thirty-two," and so forth. The *puraskriyā* of this Brahma-mantra is the *puraścaraṇa*. The fire-oblation (*havana*), which is the *homa*, is to be performed with a tenth part of that—that is, with a tenth part of the recitation (*japa*).

"From a tenth part of that" means from a tenth part of the *homa*. "By a tenth part of that" means by a tenth part of the *tarpaṇa*. "Sprinkling" (*secanam*) refers to cleansing (*mārjanam*). "By a tenth part of that" means by a tenth part of the cleansing. Regarding "edible offerings" (*bhakṣya*) and so forth: here, [this applies] to the *brahma-mantra*.
In the rite of *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary practice), verses 113–115.
Whether having eaten or not having eaten, whether having bathed or indeed not having bathed, the practitioner should accomplish the supreme mantra according to his own will. (116)
O fair-faced one, [this is achieved] without exertion, without affliction, without hymns and armor,
without ritual placement (nyāsa), without gestures (mudrā), and without the bridge (setu).
Even without the recitation of the *cauragaṇeśa* and other mantras, and without the *kullukā*, the direct realization of the Supreme Brahman will certainly occur spontaneously. (118)
In this great destroyer [of ignorance], mental resolve is proclaimed; for the practice of the Brahma-mantra, purity of intention is prescribed. (119)
O Goddess, the practitioner of Brahman should contemplate everything as consisting of Brahman;

for him, there is no transgression nor any deficiency in the constituent parts [of the rite]. Indeed, in the practice of Mahāmanu, even that which is deficient in its parts certainly becomes complete in all its limbs.
In this terrible and most difficult age of Kali, devoid of austerity,
the practice of the Brahma-mantra is the only seed for crossing over.
Many means of accomplishment have been taught in various tantras, scriptures, and so forth;
yet, O Maheśvarī, they are impossible to achieve for those with weak vitalities in the Kali age.

"Unconsumed," and so forth. "Unconsumed" (*abhukta*) means that which has not been consumed; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *arśa-ādibhyo'c*. "The bridge" (*setu*) refers to a specific type of recitation (*japa*). "The *kullukā*" is also a specific type of recitation; [the practice] is performed without that. One should "cultivate" (*bhāvayet*), meaning one should contemplate. (116–119)

"And not," etc. For this great mantra, there shall be no transgression resulting from the deficiency of its limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth. Even if it is "deficient in limbs" (*vyaṅga*), that is, lacking some of its constituent parts. || 120 || 121 ||

[Objection: But surely, in many tantras and other scriptures, you yourself have stated that there are numerous practices (*sādhana*) which are seeds for liberation (*nistārabīja*); so how can it be said that in the Kali age, the practice of the Brahma-mantra alone is the seed for liberation? To this, he says "the practices," and so forth. Here...
Although this is so, nevertheless—the word "nevertheless" (tathāpi) is to be supplied. || 122 ||
O beloved, those of short lifespan have meager livelihoods and lives dependent on food;
they are greedy, preoccupied with the acquisition of wealth, and always fickle-minded. (123)
For those whose intellects are unsteady in concentration and who cannot endure the hardships of yoga, this path of Brahman has been proclaimed for their welfare and liberation. 124.
In the Kali age, truth indeed does not exist, it truly does not exist; this is the truth I declare, O Goddess: that without the initiation of Brahman, there is no liberation or happiness.
One should perform the morning rites early in the morning and observe the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at the three junctions of the day;
one should perform worship at midday—this is the rule in all tantras.
However, O Śivā, in the worship of the Supreme Brahman, the rule depends on the desire of the practitioner.

Where injunctions are mere servants and prohibitions have no power even as masters, where desired success is attained through acting according to one's own will—who else would one resort to but that? (127)
Having approached a guru who possesses knowledge of Brahman, who is peaceful and of steady mind, and having taken hold of his lotus feet, one should pray with a spirit of devotion. || 128 ||

Showing the reason for their incurability, he says "of short life," and so forth. The word "since" (yataḥ) is to be supplied. "Those whose vital breaths are dependent on food" means those whose life-forces have come under the control of food. || 123 ||

"In samādhi," and so forth. Samādhi is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; it is therein [that they dwell]. "Unable to endure the afflictions of yoga" means those whose nature is not to endure the afflictions caused by the performance of various ritual acts which serve as the means for crossing over [to liberation].

124–125. Making the formal proposition that in the Kali age there is no initiation other than the Brahma-initiation (brahmadīkṣā) that leads to liberation and happiness, he says "In the Kali [age]," and so forth.
"Morning," etc.: the rule is simply the desire of the practitioner, in the case of the worship of the Supreme Brahman. || 126 ||

Now, he begins to describe the procedure for the instruction in the Brahma-mantra with the words "the knower of Brahman," and so forth. "Peaceful" (śāntam) means devoid of passion, hatred, and the like. "By way of devotion" (bhaktibhāvataḥ) means through the yoga of devotion. In response to the expectation of what one should pray for, he says "consisting of compassion" (karuṇāmayetyādi), and so forth.
O Lord of compassion, Lord of the wretched, I have come to you for refuge;
O you whose wealth is glory, place the shade of your lotus feet upon my head. (129)
Having thus prayed to the guru and subsequently worshipped him according to one's capacity,
one should stand silently before the guru with palms joined in reverence.
The Guru, having duly considered the characteristics of the disciple as they have been described,
should compassionately bestow the great mantra upon that worthy disciple after summoning him.
Seated upon his throne, facing either east or north, the wise teacher should bring the disciple to his left and gaze upon him with compassion.

Then, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages upon the head of the disciple, the practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of the disciple's desired accomplishment.
The true guru, a treasury of compassion, should cause the mantra to be heard seven times in the right ear of Brāhmaṇas and in the left ear of others. || 134 ||
O Kālikā, the method of instruction for the Brahma-mantra has been declared;
here there is no requirement for worship and the like—one should perform the mental resolve (saṃkalpa). 135.
"Regarding 'the guru' and so forth: as it has been stated concerning the characteristics of a disciple, such as 'one who is peaceful, self-controlled, and humble,' and so on. (131)
"Having sat down," and so forth. The "knower" (jñānī) is the teacher who possesses the knowledge of Brahman. "With compassion" means with a gaze endowed with mercy. || 132 ||
"Tataḥ" and so forth refers to the mantra beginning with "Oṃ, Brahman is one, being-consciousness," and so on.
"Dakṣa," and so forth. "Vāmataḥ" means in the left ear. The mantra is the very one previously mentioned. || 133 ||
Regarding the word "upadeśe": here, in the injunction for the instruction of the Brahma-mantra, one should "caret," that is, perform it. || 135 ||
Then, the Guru should raise up the disciple who has prostrated like a staff at the lotus feet of the venerable Guru, while affectionately reciting this mantra: (136)
Arise, my child; you are liberated. Be devoted to the knowledge of Brahman.
With your senses conquered and speaking the truth, may strength and health ever be yours. (137)
Then, having risen, the best of practitioners should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to his ability, or even his own fruit; and,
remaining under the command of the guru, he should roam upon the earth like a god.
Merely by grasping the mantra, one becomes its very self and absorbed in it;
O Goddess of gods, for one who has become Brahman, what is the use of other numerous means? (139)
Thus, O beloved, the initiation of Brahman has been briefly described to you.
One should take recourse to the initiation of Brahman solely through the compassion of the Guru. (140)
Śāktas, Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Sauras, and likewise Gāṇapatyas—both Brahmins and those other than Brahmins—are all eligible for this. (141)
"Then," and so forth. "Then" means after hearing the mantra. "The child" refers to the disciple.
He states that very mantra beginning with "Arise, child," and so forth. || 136 || 137 ||
"Then" (tataḥ) means his own wealth or himself. || 138 ||
"Mantra," and so forth. "Tadātmā" means one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is established in Brahman.
"Tanmayaḥ" means having the nature of Brahman. || 139 ||
Demonstrating that there is no restriction regarding time and so forth for the reception of the Brahma-mantras, he says "guru" and so forth. || 140 ||

He states with the words "Śāktāḥ" and so forth that all Brāhmaṇas and others—both those who have received instruction and those who have not—possess the right to this Brahma-mantra; here, [the reference is] to the Brahma-mantra. || 141 ||
"O Goddess, by the grace of this mantra, I am the conqueror of death, the God of gods, the teacher of the world, acting according to my own will and free from conceptual constructs. (142)
Brahmā, the Brahman-sages, the gods, and likewise the divine sages have previously worshipped this very Brahma-mantra from me.
O beloved, from the mouths of the celestial sages, the sage-kings received it;
having worshipped it, they became one with Brahman through the grace of the Supreme Self.
O Great Goddess, in the Brahma-manvantara there is no deliberation whatsoever;
the Guru should indeed bestow his own mantra upon the disciples without hesitation. 145.
A father may initiate his sons; a brother, his brothers; a husband, his wife; a maternal uncle, his sister's sons; and likewise, a maternal grandfather, his grandsons. (146)

He says, beginning with "I," that it was solely through the grace of this mantra that he attained such states as being the Conqueror of Death (*mṛtyuñjaya*); the ellipsis is "I became the Conqueror of Death. || 142 ||

He states, beginning with "him" (*amum*), that the state of being Brahman arose in Viriñci and others solely through the worship of this mantra; the phrase "having received from me" (*matto gṛhītvā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. They were "worshippers" (*upāsitāḥ*), meaning they performed [the practice] with faith. This is according to the rule beginning with *gatyarthākarmakaśliṣaśīḍ*.
The suffix *kta* is used in the active sense (*kartari*). The Brahman-sages are Bhṛgu and others; the gods are Indra and others; the divine sages are Nārada and others. || 143 ||
"Devarṣi" means from the mouth of the celestial sage, that is, from the mouth of Nārada. "Sages" refers to Vyāsa and others;
"royal sages" refers to Janaka and others. || 144 ||

He states in two verses beginning with "brāhme" that even though this Brahma-mantra has been received by oneself, it should be given to disciples by the guru, and it should also be given to sons and others by their fathers and others; [he says this] while not deliberating— that is, disregarding— the fault incurred by the act of giving one's own mantra.
The fault that exists in bestowing one's own mantra, as well as in the initiation of a father or others, does not exist at all once the Great Mantra of Brahman has been mastered. (147)
Having heard this from the mouth of a knower of Brahman by whatever means possible, a man who has become one with Brahman is purified and is no longer stained by merit or sin. || 148 ||
Those householders, such as Brahmins and others, who are devotees of the Brahma-mantra and take delight in the excellence of their respective castes, are especially worthy of worship and honor. (149)
Ascetics are directly Brahmins, while others are equal to Brahmins;
therefore, everyone should honor those who know Brahman and are consecrated by Brahman.
And those men who hold them in contempt are slayers of Brahmins;
they fall into a terrible hell for as long as the sun and stars exist. 151.
Whatever sin is declared for the killing of a woman, and whatever sin for the destruction of an embryo—ten million times that sin results from reviling a devotee of Brahman. (152)

Surely, for those sons and others who, transgressing prohibitive statements such as "one should not receive the mantra from one's father" and "likewise from one's maternal grandfather," receive the Vedic mantra from their father and so forth, [what would happen] regarding the giving of their own mantra?

Regarding the fact that a guru who, disregarding those various prohibitory statements, bestows his own *brahman-mantra* upon disciples would incur sin, he says "In the giving of one's own mantra," etc.; the word "the fault" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 147 || 148 ||

"Brahmamantretyādi" (beginning with "brahmamantra"). The word "yataḥ" (since) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Brahmamantropāsitāḥ" means those who have worshipped the Brahma-mantra. This is a *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* compound, according to the rule "gamyādīnām upasaṃkhyānam" (the addition of words such as *gamya* [to the list of those ending in the accusative]). || 149 ||
Regarding the term "brāhmaṇas": the brāhmaṇas would be the ascetics who have renounced the world;
the others are the kṣatriyas and so forth. || 150 ||

Now, with the two verses beginning with "And those who," he states that those people who revile the worshippers of Brahman are the locus of all sins: "those" refers to the ones initiated for the sake of Brahman; "they despise" means they disregard them.

As long as the sun and stars remain, so long shall this endure. Just as one who has committed the murder of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*) or the destruction of a fetus (*garbhaghātana*) is liberated from all sins through the instruction of Brahmā, even so do they attain union with Brahmā (*brahmasāyujya*) through your practice. (153)
Thus, in the glorious Mahānirvāṇa Tantra— the supreme among all supreme tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas, in the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva—
this is the section titled "The Exposition of the Instruction on the Supreme Brahman" in response to the inquiry concerning the means for the liberation of the living soul.
The Third Chapter (Ullāsa) || 3 ||
Union with Brahman (brahmasāyujya) is the state of being Brahman (brahmatva). || 153 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
The fourth chapter:
Having heard the complete method of worshiping the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Goddess—
Endowed with supreme bliss, she questioned Śaṅkara. || 1 ||
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord, that supreme worship of Brahman which you have described is beloved by all the worlds and directly bestows the state of Brahman.
O Lord of the Universe, I am satisfied, drenched by the nectar of your words, which bestow splendor, intelligence, strength, and sovereignty, and are the means to attain happiness.
As it has been said, O Ocean of Compassion: "Just as [beings] attain union with Brahman through the service of Brahman, so too do they [attain it] through my practice. (4)
Oṃ, salutations to Brahman.
In response to the inquiry, "What does the Supreme Goddess ask Śaṅkara?", he says:
"That which has been told," and so forth. (1–2)

"Teja" and so forth. The ellipsis is: "I am satiated having heard that meditation upon Brahman. [She is] "plunged in the nectar of your speech," meaning submerged in the ambrosia consisting of your words. || 3 ||
Regarding what was said, and so forth: O ocean of compassion, O sea of mercy,
just as people attain *brahmasāyujya*— that is, the state of being Brahman— through the service and worship of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*), even so [may it be] for me.
(57) O Lord, I desire to know this supreme means of mine which you have described as that which produces union with Brahman.
What is its ritual procedure, by what path is it accomplished, and what mantra is prescribed here? What also are the meditations, worship, and other rites?
O Lord, you ought to explain this in full detail, with all its remaining points, right down to its very root—
something that brings me joy and confers benefit upon the worlds.
For who else but you, O Śambhu, is the preceptor and physician for the diseases of worldly existence?
Having heard these words of the goddess, Maheśvara,
the god of gods and lord of Pārvatī, spoke to Pārvatī with supreme affection.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to the reason for your worship,
by which one attains union with Brahman through your practice.

The syntactical connection with the words found in the second verse is as follows: "I desire to know—to understand—what the reason is for that which you have stated, namely, that they attain the state of Brahman even through spiritual practice (sādhana). || 4 ||

"Etad ityādi" and so forth. O Lord, what is the nature of that supreme and most excellent means of mine which you have described as producing union with Brahman—that is, generating the state of Brahmanhood? This too I desire to know. || 5 ||
Of that, my proof; here, in my proof. || 6 ||
"Along with the remainder," and so forth. "With the remainder" means up to the very end of what remains.
"From the root" means beginning from the root. "Except for you" means without you. "The great physician for the disease of existence" means the king of healers for the disease that is birth. || 7 ||
"Thus," and so forth; the words "he spoke the reply" are to be understood as the ellipsis. || 8 ||
In response to the expectation of what answer the Lord of Pārvatī gave to Pārvatī, he says:

"Listen, O Goddess," and so forth. O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O you who possess great merit, for this reason—that is, by means of your practice (*sādhana*)—people attain union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*), that is, the state of being Brahman.
The syntactical connection is: "Listen as I describe to you that which is the cause for your propitiation. || 9 ||
(58) You are the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), the manifest [form] of Brahman, the Supreme Self.
From you the entire universe is born; O Śivā, you are the mother of the world. 10.

O auspicious lady, this entire world, from the Great Principle (Mahat) down to the subtle atom, including all that is moving and unmoving, was created by you alone; this universe is dependent upon you.
You are the primordial source of all sciences and our own place of birth;
you know the entire universe, yet no one knows you.
You are Kālī, Tāriṇī, Durgā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Bhuvaneśvarī; you are Dhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Bhairavī, and Chinnamastakā.
You are Annapūrṇā, the Goddess of Speech; you are the Goddess whose abode is the lotus. You are the embodiment of all powers, and your body consists of all the gods.

Now, in order to state that the fact of the *sādhana* of Parameśvarī being the generator of union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*) is due to its possessing the very same conformity to Brahman (*brahmasārūpya*), he begins [the explanation] with the words "You are the supreme Prakṛti," and so forth. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied. He who possesses the supreme *māyā* or *śakti* is [the Supreme Lord].
The word *parama* means that which moves through and pervades everything; thus it is the *ātman*. Since he is both supreme (*parama*) and the *ātman*, he is the *paramātman*.

The grammatical construction should be understood as follows: "Because you are the direct, supreme (*parā*), and most excellent (*atyutkṛṣṭā*) nature (*prakṛti*) of that *paramātman*, Brahman. || 10 ||
That which has the principle of Mahat as its beginning is "mahadādi" (beginning with Mahat).
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "O Primordial One" (*kiñca tvamādyā*): "Primordial" means being the first.

You are not only the mother of other worlds, but you are also the birthplace—the source of origin—for us as well, such as Śaṅkara and others. Because you are the mother of the world, you are the entire world.

You know [all]; yet because you are born from him, no one knows you. (12) Furthermore, "You are Kālī," and so forth. (13) Vāgdevī is Sarasvatī; Kamalālayā is Lakṣmī; "your body" is the ellipsis for "tanuḥ. (14)
You alone are subtle and you are gross; you possess the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest. Though formless, you also have form—who is worthy of knowing you? (15)
For the sake of the affairs of your lay devotees, for the welfare of the worlds, and for the destruction of the Dānavas, you assume various kinds of bodies. (16)
You are four-armed, two-armed, six-armed, and likewise eight-armed;
for the sake of protecting the universe, you alone bear various weapons and missiles.
The practice of mantras, yantras, and so forth, according to their various specific forms, has been taught in all the tantras; likewise, the three states of being have been taught. (18)
In the Kali age, the state of being a mere animal does not exist, yet even the divine state is difficult to attain;
however, the practices of heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) are directly manifest in the Kali Yuga.
O Goddess, in the Kali age, spiritual accomplishment does not arise without the conduct of the Kula;
therefore, one should practice the Kula-sādhana with every effort. (20)
O Goddess of gods, through the conduct of one's family, the knowledge of Brahman arises;
a mortal endowed with the knowledge of Brahman is liberated while living, without a doubt. || 21 ||

"Thou art," and so forth. Subtle means having the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Because it possesses a gross form, it is manifest; yet because it possesses the nature of atoms, its own form is unmanifest—such is its state. In reality, although thou art formless and devoid of shape, thou art possessed of form.
You are distinguished by your specific forms; therefore, who is capable—meaning, who is worthy—to know or understand you? No one at all. || 15 ||

Now, if in reality I am indeed formless, for what purpose do I assume various forms? To this he replies with the words "of the worshippers," and so forth (verse 16). Showing those very various bodies, he says "four-armed," and so forth (verses 17 and 18).

Now, because of the prevalence of the animal state (*paśubhāva*) and so forth, and since in the Kali age only the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*) exists, one should practice only those rites of heroic accomplishment (*vīrasādhana*) that grant immediate results; this is precisely what he states with the verses beginning "the animal state" (*paśubhāva*). (19–21)
(60) By means of knowledge, everything impure becomes pure through knowledge.
When the knowledge of Brahman has arisen, neither purity nor impurity exists. || 22 ||
For one who knows the Supreme Brahman, which is all-pervading and eternal—for him who knows that everything is Brahman, what impurity could there be before it? (23)
You are the goddess who embodies all forms, the supreme mother of all;
O Goddess of gods, when you are pleased, there shall be satisfaction for everyone.
At the beginning of creation, you alone existed, consisting of darkness and beyond the reach of the senses;
from you, the entire universe was born through the desire to create of the Supreme Brahman.
This universe, beginning with the principle of Mahat and ending with the gross elements, has been created by You;
yet that Brahman, the cause of all causes, is merely the instrumental cause.
It is of the nature of existence, all-pervasive, and stands encompassing everything;
it is eternally of a single form, pure consciousness alone, untainted within all things. (27)
It does not act, nor does it eat; it neither goes nor stands.
It is truth, knowledge, without beginning or end, beyond the reach of speech and mind.
The pure, the purifier. || 22 ||

"Yaḥ" (He who): eternal, being of one and the same nature at all times. || 23 || 24 || "Beyond the range" (agocaram), because it is devoid of form, it is also not an object of speech or mind. || 25 ||
"Mahat," and so forth. "Up to the elements" means up to the earth.
"The cause of all causes" means the instrumental cause even of all the causes beginning with Mahat. || 26 ||
"Of the nature of existence," and so forth. "Of the nature of existence" means having a permanently abiding essential form.
"Pervading all," meaning having completely enveloped every object, it remains within all things yet is untainted and unattached. || 27 ||
"Not so," and so forth. She neither eats nor consumes. Truly, according to the nature of reality, knowledge—relying on that mere will—is you, the supreme Mahāyoginī.
You create, protect, and destroy this entire world of moving and non-moving beings. || 29 ||
Your form is Mahākāla, the agent of the world’s destruction;
at the time of the great dissolution, Kāla shall swallow everything.
Because she impels all beings, she is celebrated as Mahākāla;
and because she impels Mahākāla, you are the primordial, supreme Kālikā.
Because she devours time (kāla), Kālī is the primordial form of all;
because she is both time and the first-born, the primordial Kālī is thus celebrated.
Furthermore, having attained your own true nature, which is formless and of the nature of darkness,
you alone remain— beyond speech and yet accessible to the mind.
Though possessing form, you are also formless; through your illusory power (māyā), you assume many forms.
You are the beginning of all things, yet you are without beginning; you are the creator, the destroyer, and the protector.
Its essential nature is the comprehension of all categories of existence; it is without beginning or end, meaning that which has no beginning—no cause—and no end—no destruction. || 28 ||
"tad ityādi" and so forth. "Tadicchāmātram" means the mere will of the Supreme Brahman. "Ante" means at the time of dissolution (pralaya). || 29 || 30 ||
"From reckoning," and so forth; "from reckoning" means from devouring. (31) She whose form is the beginning is the one whose nature is the cause. (32)
"Again," and so forth. "Formless" means devoid of shape. "Beyond speech" means transcending words. "Inaccessible to the mind" means unattainable even by the intellect. || 33 ||
"Having forms," and so forth: You are the beginning of all, being the cause of everything;
because you are the cause of all, there exists no beginning—that is, no cause—of you who are thus constituted. || 34 ||
Therefore, O auspicious lady, it has been told to you: the fruit that one who is initiated by means of the Brahma-mantra attains, that same fruit shall be yours through this practice. (35)
O Goddess, due to the differences in conduct, disposition, place, time, and authority, this secret practice has been taught in some instances as being hidden.
Those mortals who are authorized therein shall partake of the fruit thereof;
such men, their sins having been removed, shall cross over [to liberation]. || 37 ||
Through merits accumulated over many births, one may obtain an inclination toward the family tradition;
with a self purified by the family tradition, one becomes truly identical with Śiva. (38)
Where there is an abundance of enjoyment, what talk can there be of yoga?
Even in yoga, there is an absence of enjoyment; but the Kaula partakes of both. 39.
He states with the words "Therefore," and so forth, that this alone is the reason for attaining the state of Brahman through your practice. || 35 ||

Now, regarding what was asked by the Supreme Goddess—namely, "By what path is accomplishment achieved? and "What is my supreme accomplishment like?"—all rites are to be accomplished by the very path described by me; it is by the path spoken by me that [accomplishment is attained].
He begins to give the reply—“That which is the means for the obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*) is itself your means”—with the words “By various practices,” and so forth.
“By various states” (*nānā-bhāvena*); “due to distinction” (*vibhedāt*), meaning due to specific differences; “in some places,” such as in the Tantras and other texts. (36)
"Ya" refers to wherever there is either a secret practice or a manifest practice. || 37 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate that in this most degenerate Kali Yuga all rites must be accomplished solely through the path of the Kula, Mahādeva, desiring to praise that very path, first extols those people who abide by that path with the verses beginning "bahujanma" and so forth.
He is manifestly composed of Śiva; he is manifestly the very nature of Śiva. || 38 ||
Regarding the phrase "wherein": in which means there is an absence of enjoyment, that is, a lack of worldly experience.
One attains both; one obtains both yoga and enjoyment. || 39 ||
O lady of excellent vows, if even one who knows the reality of the Kula is honored by someone, all the gods and goddesses are thereby honored; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Whatever fruit one might obtain by giving away the earth filled with gold,
one obtains ten million times that merit from the worship of the Kaulika.
Even a dog-cooker (outcaste) who possesses knowledge of his lineage excels a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Brāhmaṇa devoid of the conduct of his lineage is the lowest of dog-cookers.
There is no dharma higher than the Kaula dharma within my own knowledge;
by the mere performance of which a man becomes a knower of Brahman. (43)
I tell you the truth, O Goddess; take this to heart and understand it:
there exists no dharma higher than Kaula, the supreme among all dharmas. (44)
This supreme path, though hidden amidst the confusion of worldly beings, will soon become manifest when the powerful Kali age has fully set in. (45)
When the Kali age has fully flourished, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth:
on this earth, human beings will remain as mere beasts, unless they belong to the Kaulas. 46.
But when the Vedic initiation as well as the Puranic initiation no longer remains, O lady of beautiful hips, at that very time the powerful Kali age shall prevail.
"Single," and so forth; the ellipsis is "worshipped by him. || 40 || 41 ||
"Śvapaca," and so forth. "Surpasses" means that he excels because of his possession of the highest state. || 42 ||
Showing the reason for the Kaula dharma being the supreme among all dharmas, he says:
"By the mere performance of which," and so forth. || 43 || 44 ||
"This," and so forth. "In the throng of beasts" means in a multitude of animals. "Having gathered" means having come together properly. || 45 || 46 ||

Now, in connection with the conduct prescribed for each respective age (*yuga*), he briefly describes the characteristics of the predominance of the Kali age with the words beginning "When indeed... and so forth. O Varārohe, O most excellent one! (47)

But when the examination of merits and demerits, which originates from the Veda, no longer remains fixed upon the auspicious and peaceful [Śiva], at that very moment the powerful Kali age shall prevail. (48)
O Mistress of the Kula, when the river of love is in some places cut off and in others broken, then indeed the Kali age shall prevail. (49)
But when kings of Mleccha descent, greedy for wealth, come to be,
O highly wise one, then indeed Kali shall prevail.
When women become exceedingly difficult to restrain, harsh, and addicted to quarreling,
and when they revile their husbands, at that very time the powerful Kali age prevails.
But when men on earth, conquered by women and slaves to their desires, act with malice toward their gurus, friends, and others, at that very time Kali becomes powerful.
When the earth yields little fruit, when the clouds rain but sparingly,
and when trees do not bear fruit properly— then indeed is the Kali age powerful.
When brothers, kinsmen, and ministers strike one another out of greed for even a single grain of wealth, at that very moment the powerful Kali age prevails.
When liquor, meat, and the like are openly available, free from censure and punishment,
and people practice drinking in secret, then indeed the powerful Kali age has set in.
O peaceful one, O you whose mind is restrained! || 48 || The Gaṅgā is a river of supreme delight. || 49 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with *yadā tu*: "extremely difficult to subdue" (*atidurdāntāḥ*) means those who are subdued only with great difficulty; that is to say, they are to be disciplined with extreme hardship. "Harsh" (*karkaśāḥ*) means cruel.
"They will revile" (*garhiṣyanti*) means they will censure. (Verses 50–52) "Scant-rainers" (*stokavarṣiṇaḥ*) means those whose nature is to rain only slightly.
Driven by a craving for wealth and a longing for even a small portion of riches.

"Prakaṭe" and so forth: When liquor, meat, and the like become manifest and openly displayed—even though they are free from censure and punishment—and when people practice drinking in secret, at that very time the powerful Kali age is to be known [to have arrived]. || 55 ||
Just as there was the practice of consuming wine and other substances during the ages of Satya, Tretā, and Dvāpara, so too in the Kali age one should act in accordance with the path of the Kula. (56)
Kali does not afflict those who follow the traditions of their lineage, who are purified by truth, who have conquered their senses, whose conduct is manifest, and whose nature is compassionate. (57)
Those who are devoted to serving their gurus, who are devoted to the lotus feet of their mothers, and who are devoted to their own wives—indeed, the Kali age does not afflict them. 58.
Those who are devoted to the vow of truth, established in truth, dedicated to the dharma of truth, and whose family traditions are rooted in truth—Kali does not indeed afflict them. (59)
The Kali age does not indeed afflict those who, having purified the principles through the family lineage, bestow them upon a yogi of truthful speech. (60)
Those who are free from violence and envy, devoid of hypocrisy and hatred,
and firmly established in the duties of their own lineage— Kali does not afflict them.
Those who associate with the Kaulikas, dwell among the virtuous of the Kula, and perform the service of the Kula—indeed, the Kali age does not afflict them. (62)
Wearing various disguises, the Kaulas remain steadfast in the Kula practices;
they serve you through these Kula observances, and indeed, the Kali age does not afflict them.

"Satyatretā," and so forth; the ellipsis is "as if he had openly practiced the consumption of liquor and other such things. (56) "He does not obstruct them" means he does not cause them distress. (57)
"Respectful," and so forth. "Yuktāḥ" means joined together; "anuraktāḥ" means possessing affection. || 58 ||
Those who possess the truth of the family practice (kulasādhana) are those who apply themselves correctly to the family practice; the "principles" (tattva) refer to wine, meat, and so forth.

"Free from violence" (hiṃsā): they are devoid of violence and envy; for violence is an action conducive to the separation of life, while envy is hatred toward the welfare of others—they are free from these two. "Dwelling" (vasatiṃ) means a residence. 61–65.
Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, visiting sacred fords, religious vows, and libations—those who perform these according to their family traditions are not afflicted by the Kali age. (64)

The rites of sprinkling water for the living and other consecrations, as well as the ceremonies such as the ancestral *śrāddha*, which people perform according to family traditions—Kali does not indeed obstruct those who do so. (65)
Those who bow with devotion to the reality of the Kula, the substance of the Kula, and the Kula-yogi themselves—Kali does not indeed afflict them. (66)
Kali is a servant to the virtuous—those who are free from crookedness, falsehood, and malice; those who are pure, who follow the path of their lineage, and who are devoted to helping others. (67)
O beloved, there is one great virtue in the multitude of faults of the Kali age:
for the Kaulas who are true to their vows, prosperity comes by mere intention.
But in another age, O Goddess, mental merit and demerit belonged to men;
however, in the Kali age, there is merit alone and no evil deed.
Those men who are devoid of family traditions, who constantly speak untruths, and who are intent on harming others, are the servants of the Kali age.

Those who are not devoted to the path of their own family, who lust after the wives of others, and who hate those established in the family tradition—these should be known as the servants of the Kali age. (71)
In connection with the conduct of the ages, O auspicious Pārvatī, the characteristics of the predominance of the Kali age have been briefly described for your pleasure.
The reality of the *kula* consists of the woman’s flowers and so forth; the substance of the *kula* consists of wine, meat, and so forth. 66.
"Kauṭilya," and so forth. "Those whose vow is the service of others" (*paropakāravratinaḥ*) refers to those who possess a vow consisting of the service of others. || 67 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the Kali": [it refers to] the collection of defects and that which possesses the collection of defects. "O Goddess, while other [ages] such as Satya and Tretā were manifest, all dharmas here in this Kali age are weak;
only a single Truth (satya) alone shall remain. Therefore, one should become composed of Truth. (73)
O lady of excellent vows, know this to be true: whatever action a man performs by relying upon truth and dharma, that very action is fruitful. 74.
For there is no dharma higher than truth, and no evil greater than untruth;
therefore, a mortal person should, with their whole being, take refuge in truth alone. 75.
Worship devoid of truth is in vain; recitation devoid of truth is in vain;
austerity devoid of truth is useless, like sowing seeds in barren soil. (76)
The Supreme Brahman is the embodiment of truth; truth indeed is the highest austerity.
All ritual actions have truth as their root, for there is nothing higher than truth.
Therefore, I have declared that in the Kali age, when evil is rampant,
even the family tradition must be performed with truthfulness and manifest sincerity.
For truth is lost through concealment; there is no secrecy without falsehood.
Therefore, the Kaulika should perform the Kula practice openly. (79)

Desiring to declare that when the Kali age prevails, the family tradition must be made manifest through truth alone, Mahādeva, wishing to praise truth, said: "In this manifest [age]," and so forth. (73–74)
"Not," and so forth. From the untrue, that is, from the false. "In every way" means with all effort. Regarding the word *ātman*:
"Ātman [means] effort, fortitude, intellect, nature, Brahman, and body"—so says Amara. "One should take refuge" means one should properly practice it. || 75 ||
In "ūṣare," meaning a place containing alkaline soil; for this very reason, because all actions have truth as their foundation—this is the sense. In "duṣkṛte," meaning toward a sinner. (Verses 76–78)
"It is diminished" means it becomes inferior; it becomes abandoned—this is the meaning. || 79 ||
(68) For the sake of protecting the family dharma, falsehood is not to be considered contemptible;
as it is said in the Kula-tantras, [falsehood] is not censured even in the powerful Kali age. 80.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma has four feet; in the Tretā, it is diminished by one foot;
in the Dvāpara, O Goddess, it has two feet; and in the Kali age, it consists of only a single foot.
Even there, truth is powerful, while austerity is lame and compassion is likewise;
if the foot of truth is severed, the destruction of dharma arises.
Therefore, relying upon truth, one should accomplish all actions. (82)
O Mistress of the Family, where there is no means [of attainment] other than family conduct, if one enters into falsehood therein, how could there be supreme bliss? (83)
In every way, a person whose soul is purified by truth should perform all actions prescribed for their respective caste and stage of life according to the path uttered from my mouth. 84.
Initiation, worship, recitation, fire-oblation, the preparatory rite, and the libation; the investiture for vows, the rite for a male child, and likewise the parting of the hair. || 85 ||

[Objection: "But surely, it was stated by you yourself in the *Kulatantres* that 'in order to protect the family dharma (*kuladharma*), falsehood is not to be practiced, for it is contemptible'; so how is it now said, 'Therefore, the Kaulika should perform the Kula-sādhana openly'? To this, he says:
"Of the family dharma," and so forth. || 80 ||
"Kṛte" and so forth. In the Kṛta age, i.e., the Satya-yuga, Dharma existed with four quarters; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Because the rule regarding the addition of suffixes at the end of a compound is not universal, there is no elision of the final syllable of the word "pāda.
The ellipsis is that "only a quarter (pādamātra) of Dharma remains. || 81 ||

Regarding the phrase "tatrāpi" and so forth: even there, that is, even in the case of a single quarter-verse (*pāda*), compassion (*dayā*) is also lame. "Lopa" means it is elided; the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of that action (*karman*). || 82 ||

Regarding "family custom" (*kulācāra*): in this powerful Kali age, *niḥśreyasa* is liberation (*mukti*). And what is that? It is all ritual action therein, beginning with initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth. "Puraścaraṇa and libation" (*tarpaṇa*) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). (83–85)
One should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), as well as the naming and tonsure ceremonies, the funeral rites, and the ancestral *śrāddha*, in accordance with the scriptures. (86)

The Śrāddha at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), the autumnal festival, a pilgrimage, the entry into a new house, and the wearing of new garments and the like—(these should be performed). || 87 ||
The consecration of step-wells, wells, and tanks, as well as rites for auspicious lunar days, the commencement and dedication of houses, and likewise the installation of deities; || 88 ||

The duties pertaining to the day, the duties pertaining to the night, and likewise the duties pertaining to the lunar phases (parvan), as well as those pertaining to the seasons, months, and years—both the obligatory (nitya) and the occasional (naimittika). || 89 ||
Whatever is to be done and whatever is not to be done, whatever is to be abandoned and whatever is to be accepted—all that a person should accomplish according to the procedure taught by me. (90)
If, through delusion, evil intent, or even lack of faith, one should not perform [this],
he shall be ruined from all his ritual acts and become a worm in excrement.
O Great Goddess, if in this powerful Kali age one abandons my teaching,
whatever action is performed at any time will lead to the opposite result.

The phrase "name and tonsure" means both the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) and the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*). By the expression "new clothes, etc.," new ornaments and so forth are included. [It also includes] the commencement and consecration of a house.
The meaning is: the commencement of building a house and the consecration of the house. || 86–90 ||

He states through the verses beginning with "one should not [act]" that in the powerful Kali age, for a person who performs actions while transgressing the doctrine of Sadāśiva, there is the state of great sin (mahāpātaka) and the fruitlessness of the actions being performed; this is due to delusion (moha), which is a lack of discrimination (aviveka).
By lack of faith, that is, by the absence of trust. || 91 || 92 ||
(70) An initiation not approved by my own view destroys the life-force of the practitioner;
even his worship is fruitless, O Goddess, like an oblation poured onto ashes.
The deity becomes angry with him, and he encounters obstacles at every step. (93)
O Mother, when the Kali age has fully set in, he who, knowing my scripture,
performs ritual acts through other paths shall become a perpetrator of great sin.
The man who performs his vows and marriage by any other path goes to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (95)
If one commits the murder of a Brahmin while under a vow, he becomes a Vrātya Mānavaka;
he is merely a carrier of the sacred thread, and he is even lower than a Caṇḍāla. (96)
Even if she has been married, a woman who [knows this] is to be censured;
O Mistress of the Family, the husband too becomes a sinner through such association.
Day by day, that man incurs the sin born of approaching a prostitute.
The deities do not accept water or other offerings from his hand, nor do the ancestors eat them, because that [food] is like filth and pus. (98)
The offspring of those two is a *kānīna*, excluded from all religious duties;
he has no entitlement to rites for the gods, the ancestors, or family traditions. (99)
That which is offered as an offering of ashes is "arpaṇa"; [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The compound *bhasmanyarpaṇam* is a locative *tatpuruṣa*, meaning "offering in the ashes. The intended sense is "that which has been offered into the ashes" (*bhasmārpitam*).
Alternatively, the reading may simply be *bhasmārpitam*. (93–95)

Regarding the passage beginning with "vrate" and so forth: even a boy who has undergone the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) by another path would become a *vrātya*, meaning he would be devoid of the [proper] purificatory rites. || 96 ||
"Married," and so forth: one should know that a woman who has been married by another method is censured—that is, she is blameworthy. Alternatively, there is the reading "tāṃ tu garhitām.
Due to association with the non-Śāmbhava path, one should perform the installation of the deity.
In that case, the presence of the deity will not occur in any way;
there is no fruit here or in the hereafter, only physical suffering and the depletion of wealth. (100)
If a man performs a śrāddha rite while disregarding the injunctions declared in the scriptures, that śrāddha becomes fruitless, and he too shall go to hell along with his ancestors. (101)
Then that mass, consisting of blood and impurities, becomes like water;
therefore, a mortal should with great effort take refuge in the doctrine of Śaṅkara.
What is the use of saying much more here? I speak the truth, the absolute truth:
O Goddess, every action performed that is not dedicated to Śambhu is entirely fruitless.
Let alone the supreme dharma; even the former dharma perishes for one who is devoid of the Śāmbhava conduct. For such a person, there is no escape from hell.
O Great Goddess, that very practice which constitutes the means for the daily and occasional rites according to the path proclaimed by me is indeed your own practice. 105.
From the union with a woman married by another rite—
that is, for him who has engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman wedded according to a different ritual procedure.

He states the reason for not accepting food, water, and so forth given by their hands in the passage beginning with "yataḥ" (since). "Tat" refers to that food, water, and so on. "Tayoḥ" refers to those two: the woman who was wedded by another path and the man who wed her.
"Asya" refers to this son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*). (Verses 97–99)
In that regard, [it refers to] the image of the deity established on the path of Aśāmbhava. || 100–103 ||
Expiation is deliverance. || 104 || 105 ||

(72) Listen now as I describe from my own mouth the special propitiation performed there, which, combined with mantras, yantras, and other means, serves as the medicine for the diseases of the Kali age. 106.
