Thus, in the glorious Mahānirvāṇatantra— the supreme among all supreme tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas, and the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva— this is the section titled "The Commencement of the Means for Accomplishing the Supreme Prakṛti," following the inquiry into the means for the liberation of the individual soul.
The Fourth Chapter (Ullāsa) || 2 ||

"Bheṣaja" means medicine. "Gadataḥ" means from me, as I am speaking. Since the word "mama" (of me) is intended to express the sense of the ablative case as a residual relation (*śeṣa*), the genitive case is used according to the rule "the sixth [case] is used for the remainder" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*).
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. In the fifth chapter,
the venerable Sadāśiva said:
You are the primordial, supreme Śakti, whose very nature is all powers;
by your power we are empowered for creation, maintenance, dissolution, and the rest.
Your forms are infinite, possessing various colors and shapes; who is able to describe them, which are accomplished through manifold efforts? (2)

By a mere fraction of your compassion, the rites for their worship and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) have been described, according to my understanding, within the family tantras (*kulatantra*), the scriptures (*āgama*), and so forth. (3)
This secret practice has never been revealed anywhere;
O auspicious one, it is only through its grace that such compassion for me exists in you. (4)
Oṃ, salutations to Brahman.
Having set out to describe specifically the special mode of worship joined with mantras, yantras, and so forth, the venerable Sadāśiva said: "You are the primordial, the supreme," and so on. (1)
"Thine" (*tava*): those forms which possess various colors and shapes; "various" (*nānā*) means many, and "colors" (*varṇa*) and "shapes" (*ākṛti*) refer to their respective appearances. || 2 ||
By a mere fragment of compassion, by a tiny drop of mercy—toward those [beings] of your various forms. || 3 ||
But that which is being stated hereafter pertains to this secret means of accomplishment (guptasādhana). || 4 ||
(74) Since you have now asked, I am not able to conceal it.
I shall tell it for your pleasure, O beloved who is dearer to me than my own life. (5)
It is the pacifier of all suffering, the warder-off of all calamities, the root of attaining you, and the cause of your own satisfaction before long. (6)
O beloved, for men who are distressed by the impurities of the Kali age, whose lifespans are short,
and who are attached to great exertions, this alone is the supreme wealth.
In this [rite], there is no abundance of ritual deposits (nyāsa), nor is there restraint such as fasting;
it is easily accomplished, not burdensome, and bestows great fruit upon devotees.
In that regard, first listen, O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, to the sequence for the extraction of the mantra, by the mere hearing of which one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). (9)
The Lord of Breath (H) mounted upon Taijasa (R), possessing Bheruṇḍā (U) and the Sky-drop (M)—
having extracted this seed-syllable, O Dear One, one should extract the second.
The twilight is mounted upon the red [color], joined with the moon in the left eye;
hear the third, O auspicious one: Prajāpati is situated within the lamp. (11)
That is the secret practice. || 5 || 6 ||
From this point onward, that which is being described is precisely the secret means (guptasādhana). || 7 ||
In this regard, concerning the proof that is being stated hereafter: "abāhulya" means being devoid of multiplicity; that [is the nature] of that proof.

He explains that very sequence for extracting the mantra with the words beginning with "prāṇeśa" (the Lord of Breath). "Mounted upon Taijasa": *taijasa* is the letter *ra*; mounted upon that. "The Lord of Breath" (*prāṇeśa*) is the letter *ha*. "Bheruṇḍā endowed with the Sky-dot": *bheruṇḍā* is the vowel *ī*; the "Sky-dot" (*vyomabindu*) is the *anusvāra*.
One should formulate [the mantra] as distinguished by those two. Thus, having extracted this seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, one should extract the second seed-syllable.
And what is that seed-syllable? To this he says "Sandhyā," and so forth. Sandhyā is mounted upon the letter *ra* (repha).
It is joined with the palatal *śa*, the left eye (*vāmanetra*), and the moon (*indu*). The left eye is the vowel *ī*; the moon is the *anusvāra*.
Joined with those two [the vowels *u* and *ū*], along with the *bindu* of Govinda, it brings happiness to practitioners.
O Supreme Goddess, at the end of the three seed-syllables is the word of address. (12)
O Śivā, this ten-syllable mantra is said to extend up to Vahnikāntā;
this goddess is the supreme sovereign, consisting of all vidyās.
The lord of practitioners should recite each of the three seed-syllables three times for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha. (14)
Excluding the first three seed-syllables (bījas), there is also a ten-syllable mantra consisting of seven syllables;
furthermore, the seven- and eight-syllable mantras beginning with Kāma, Vāgbhava, and Tārā are each of three types.
It should be joined together. Thus, the second seed-syllable, *śrīṃ*, has been extracted.

"O auspicious lady, hear the third seed-syllable. To explain what that seed-syllable is, he says: "situated in the lamp," and so forth. "Situated in the lamp" means situated in the letter *ra* (the lamp), [and] Prajāpati is the letter *ka*.

"Joined with Govinda-bindu": Govinda is the letter *ī*, and the bindu is the anusvāra; it should be joined with these two. Such a *ka* brings happiness to practitioners, meaning it bestows bliss. And thus, "krīṃ" is the third [syllable].

The seed-syllable has been extracted. At the end of the three seed-syllables, one should utter the address "O Supreme Goddess" (parameśvari), which has "svāhā"—the beloved of fire—as its concluding limit. By joining all these words together, it becomes: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā*.

The mantra has arisen. O Śitā, this mantra is said to consist of ten syllables (*daśārṇa*). However, if the reading is "ending with Vahnikāntā," then the mantra is the subject and this [phrase] should be understood as its qualification. She consists of all vidyās; she is the very nature of all vidyās.
The Goddess who is the essence of mantra is the Supreme Sovereign, known as Vidyā. 11–13.

"Ādyaiḥ," and so forth. Among the three seed-syllables beginning with *hrīṃ* that constitute the beginning of this very mantra, one should take each individual seed-syllable—namely *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, or *krīṃ*—or else all three seed-syllables together: *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, and *krīṃ*.
For the sake of accomplishing the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, the supreme practitioner, the lord of practitioners, should recite [these mantras].
Thus, there were five mantras. 14.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bījam" (the seed-syllable): having set aside or omitted the first three seed-syllables, *hrīṃ* and so forth, the Parameśvarī Vidyā consists of ten syllables; furthermore, O Parameśvarī, she who consists of seven syllables is also that which takes the form of *svāhā*, being thus seven-syllabled as well.
From the word of address "Daśārṇa," one should utter the word "Kālike.
Again, one should speak the first three seed-syllables (bījas), and then the wife of Fire (svāhā). (16)
This is declared as the sixteenth [vowel], hidden in all tantras;
when preceded by the bride (V) or by the Praṇava (Oṃ), it becomes this seventeenth [vowel] in two ways. (17)
Indeed, your mantras are innumerable, numbering in the tens of millions and even more;
yet, O beloved, twelve mantras have been described here in brief.
Whatever mantras have been proclaimed in whichever tantras,
all of those are your mantras, because you are the primordial nature.

[This] may be so. Together with this, there have been six mantras. If the Supreme Goddess, whose first seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *klīm*, *aim*, or *oṃ*—such as Kāma, Vāgbhava, Tārā, and the rest—and who consists of seven syllables in the form of a mantra, were [to be recited], then: *klīṃ parameśvari*.

The form "svāhā" is *ai*, the form "parameśvari svāhā" is *oṃ*, and the form "parameśvari svāhā" is also the eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣarī*). Thus, this eight-syllabled mantra has become threefold. Together with these three, there came to be nine mantras. || 15 ||

"Daśārṇa," and so forth: after the address "O Daśārṇa," one should utter the word "Kālike. After that, one should again utter the triad of seeds beginning with *hrīṃ*. Immediately following that, one should utter the word "svāhā," which is the consort of fire (*vahnijāyā*).

By joining all the words together, the mantra *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari kālike hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ svāhā* is produced. This sixteenth [mantra], consisting of sixteen syllables and being the very essence of the mantra, is the Supreme Goddess Vidyā; though hidden in all the Tantras, it has been revealed by me for your pleasure.
"Samākhyātā" means correctly explained. Together with this, there are ten mantras.
If this sixteenth mantra begins with "strīṃ," or with a seed-syllable (*bīja*), or with the *praṇava*, or with the syllable *oṃ*, then it is as follows: *strīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ krīṃ parameśvari*.

The form beginning with *kālike hrīṃ śrīṃ krīṃ svāhā* and the form beginning with *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ krīṃ parameśvari kālike hrīṃ śrīṃ krīṃ svāhā* constitute the seventeenth [mantra], which consists of seventeen syllables. Thus, this seventeenth mantra has become twofold.
Together with these two, there were twelve mantras. || 16–18 ||
He states the reason why all the mantras taught in the entire Tantra are related to Pārvatī: "Because you are the primordial Prakṛti. (19–20)
(77) Indeed, there is but one single means for accomplishing all these mantras;
I shall declare it for your pleasure and likewise for the welfare of the world. (20)
O Goddess, without the practice of the Kula way, the mantra of Śakti does not bestow success;
therefore, one devoted to the Kula practice should accomplish the sādhana of Śakti.
Liquor, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union—these five principles (pañcatattva) are proclaimed for the initial rite of worshiping Śakti. (22)
Without the five principles (pañcatattva), worship leads to malevolent magic; for such a person there will be no attainment of the desired goal, and obstacles will arise at every step. (23)
Just as no sprout can arise from sowing seeds upon a stone, there is no production of fruit in a worship that is devoid of the five principles (pañcatattva). || 24 ||
O Goddess, without the morning rites one has no authority for ritual acts;
therefore, I shall first explain the appropriate morning rites as they should be performed. (25)
In the final half of the last watch of the night is the dawn;
at that time, the practitioner, having risen and abandoned sleep,
should take his seat and meditate upon the Guru— two-eyed and two-armed— upon a white lotus on the crown of his head.
He states that very means of accomplishment with the words beginning "the family practice" (kulācāra) and so forth. || 21 ||

Since the worship of Śakti is fruitless without the five principles (pañcatattva), it must necessarily be performed with the five principles; thus he says, beginning with "madyam" [wine] and so forth.
[The term] *abhicāra* refers to the act of violence (*hiṃsākarma*); according to Amarasimha, "the act of violence is *abhicāra*."

He describes the morning duties with the words beginning "of the remaining watch of the night" (*rajanīśeṣayāmasya*). The "remaining half" of the last watch of the night—the final four *daṇḍas*—is the time of dawn (*aruṇodaya*). At that very time, during that dawn, [one should perform the rites].
Having abandoned sleep and cast off lethargy, the practitioner rises; having thus prepared his seat,
he puts on white garments and applies white garlands and unguents.
He displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, is peaceful, and possesses a form composed of compassion. || 27 ||
His body is embraced by Śakti, who holds a blue lotus in her left hand;
his face is smiling and serene, bestowing the desired objects upon the practitioner. || 28 ||
Having meditated thus, O Mistress of the Family, and having worshipped with mental offerings, the mantra-practitioner should recite the supreme seed-syllable of Speech.
Having performed the recitation according to one's ability and offered it into the right hand, the wise person should then prostrate to the true guru with this mantra: (30)

The grammatical connection is as follows: being seated upon a seat, one should meditate on the Guru situated upon a white lotus, a white *padma*, on the crown of one's head. The words beginning with "two-eyed" (*dvinetra*) ending in the accusative case are adjectives qualifying the Guru, as are those beginning with "white. "Clad in white garments" (*śvetāmbaraparīdhāna*) refers to that which is worn.

*Parīdhānam*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The lengthening of the vowel in *parī-* is an archaic Vedic feature (*ārṣa*). Thus, it means "one whose lower garment (*parīdhāna*) consists of white cloth (*śveta ambara*). *Anulepanam*: that which is smeared upon is "ointment" (*anulepana*), such as sandalwood paste. It refers to one whose garlands (*mālya*) and ointments (*anulepana*) are white.

Regarding the passage beginning with "vara" (the boon): "one whose hands possess the boon and fearlessness" means one whose two hands hold the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and dispelling fear (*abhaya*).

"Peaceful" (*śānta*) means devoid of passion, hatred, and the like. "We meditate upon Him whose body consists of compassion" (*karuṇāmayavigraham*) means one whose physical form (*vigraha*) is characterized by an abundance of mercy (*karuṇā*).
His body is embraced by a woman who holds a blue lotus in her left hand and possesses a spear (*śakti*); she embraces his form with her left hand while holding a lotus. || 27 || 28 ||

"Thus," and so forth. O Kuleśānī, the practitioner (mantrī), that is, the seeker (sādhaka), having thus meditated upon the Guru and having worshipped him with mental offerings— those conceived by the mind such as water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and so forth— [attains] the supreme...
One should mutter the supreme seed-syllable *aim*, which originates from speech. The phrase "the muttering of the seed-syllable *aim*" is the understood remainder [of the sentence].
Salutations to you, the true Guru, who destroys the fetters of existence, who reveals the vision of wisdom, and who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (31)
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who is the Supreme Brahman in human form, who removes ignorance, and who illuminates the Kula-dharma. || 32 ||
Having thus prostrated before the Guru there, one should meditate upon one's own deity;
having worshipped that deity as before, one should perform the recitation of the root mantra.
Having recited [the mantra] as much as possible, the wise one should offer it into the left hand of the Goddess and prostrate before the chosen deity with this mantra.
Salutations to her who possesses all forms, the mother of the universe;
salutations again and again to you, the primordial Kālikā, the creator and the destroyer. (35)
Having paid obeisance, one should go outside, leading with the left foot;
having discharged urine and feces, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
In response to the expectation of "by which mantra?", he states that very mantra:

"For the destruction of the bonds of existence" (*bhavapāśavināśāya*). This means: for the destroyer of the bond consisting of *saṃsāra*. [And] "to the one who reveals the vision of knowledge" (*jñānadṛṣṭipradarśine*), meaning to the one whose nature is knowledge...
To him whose nature it is to demonstrate his view. || 31 || 32 ||

"Having prostrated," and so forth. Having thus prostrated—that is, having bowed down with excellence through an excess of devotion and faith—the practitioner (sādhaka) should contemplate, that is, meditate upon, his own deity seated there upon the white lotus on [the crown of] the head. Then, as before...

Having worshipped that one's own deity with mental services as if toward a guru, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the root mantra beginning with *hrīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *krīṃ*, and so forth. (33–34) He states that very mantra: "Salutation to all... (35–36).
Then, having gone to the vicinity of water and performed his bath according to the prescribed rule, he should first sip water and thereafter enter the water. (37)
Standing in water reaching up to the navel for the removal of impurities,
having bathed once and likewise emerged [from the water], one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the mantra.

The foremost of practitioners, the Kula-sādhaka, having sipped water three times with the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva ending in *svāhā*, and having wiped [his mouth] twice, should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
O Dear One, having drawn the family-diagram containing the essence of the mantra upon water, the wise one should recite the root-mantra twelve times over it.
Having meditated upon water as being of the nature of light (tejas), the preceptor, addressing the Sun,
offers three handfuls of that water; having sprinkled his own head with that very water in three ways, he should block the seven apertures.

"Then," and so forth. "In the vicinity of water" means near a body of water. He explains the very procedure for bathing with the verses beginning with "First, the waters," and so on. "Apo" means waters. "In salile" means in the water. (37) "With mantras, the rite is *māntra*. (38)

Showing the very mantras for the ritual sipping (ācamana), he says "ātma" and so forth. The meaning is: by means of the mantras consisting of the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, which end with "svāhā"—namely, "Svāhā to the principle of Ātman," "Svāhā to the principle of Vidyā," and "Svāhā to the principle of Śiva."
The foremost of practitioners, the best of adepts— the Kula practitioner—
having sipped the waters three times (three rounds), drunk them twice (two rounds), and wiped [his mouth] twice (two rounds), having thus performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana),
[should recite] any one among the mantras beginning with Hrīḥ.

The wise and steadfast practitioner, having drawn such a *kulayantra* consisting of a triangle within the womb of the mantra— that is, within water— should recite the root mantra, consisting of *hrīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *krīṃ*, and so forth, twelve times over that *kulayantra*.
"One should recite twelve times"—this is the connection with the second [verse]. || 39 || 40 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the nature of light": the teacher or practitioner, having meditated upon the water associated with the *kula*-yantra as being of the nature of light, and having offered three handfuls (*tryañjali*) of that water— namely, the water associated with the *kula*-yantra—
directed toward the sun, by means of that very [water]...
Then, for the sake of pleasing the deities, having immersed himself three times within the water, he should rise, wipe his limbs, and put on two clean garments. (42)
With either clay or ashes, one should apply a *tripuṇḍra* together with a *bindu* on the forehead as a *tilaka*, while binding the hair with the *Gāyatrī* mantra. (43)
The practitioner of mantras should perform both the Vedic and the Tantric twilight devotions (sandhyā) according to their proper sequence; now listen as the Tantric rite is described. (44)
Having sipped water as before, O Śivā, one should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) with waters.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, please be present in these waters! (46)

Having sprinkled one's own head three times with water from the vessel connected to the *kulayantra*, one should block the seven apertures— the openings of the ears, eyes, nostrils, and mouth— with the fingers of both hands. || 41 ||

Then, thus: after the closing of the seven apertures, having made a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the propitiation of the deities, one should immerse oneself three times in the water; then, having emerged and wiped the body, and having sprinkled it with water using a cloth, one should put on two clean garments—that is, washed clothes.
"Ācchādayet" means he should clothe [him]; that is the meaning. || 42 ||

Regarding the phrase "with clay": then, having bound his hair-knots with the Gāyatrī mantra—that is, having tied up his locks—he should apply a *tripuṇḍra* mark or a *tilaka* on his forehead using either excellent clay or similar sacred ash, accompanied by the *bindu*. || 43 ||

Regarding the phrase "the Vedic": then the practitioner, the seeker, should perform and carry out both the Vedic and the Tantric twilight devotions (*sandhyā*) precisely according to their respective sequences. Between those two, listen now to the Tantric twilight devotion.
It is being told by me. || 44 ||

He describes the Tantric twilight ritual (sandhyā) with the words beginning "having sipped water" (ācamya) and so forth: "O Śivā, having sipped water as before, one should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) into the water. (45)
Now, in response to the expectation of which mantra or which sacred sites (tīrthas) one should invoke, he says "Gaṅge ca" and so forth. "Sannidhim" means proximity. || 46 ||
With this mantra and the gesture known as the hook (aṅkuśamudrā), the wise one, having invoked the sacred ford into the water, should recite the root-mantra twelve times. (47)
Then, one should cast three drops of that water upon the ground using the combination of the middle and ring fingers, preceded by the recitation of the root mantra.
Having sprinkled his own head seven times with that water,
he should then take it in his left hand and cover it with his right hand.
Having recited the five seed-syllables of Īśāna, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Vahni, and Indra,
one who knows the Vedas should take water in his right hand.

"By means of the mantra": the wise practitioner, by means of this mantra just mentioned and with the gesture known as the *aṅkuśa* (the hook), having invoked the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) into the water, should recite the root mantra twelve times over that very water. As for the *aṅkuśa* gesture: [it is as follows].
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Then, having formed the right fist with the index finger in the shape of a goad, this great mudrā called the 'Goad' is capable of attracting the three worlds. (47)
"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, that ritual action in which the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) precedes is called "preceded by the recitation of the root mantra.
By means of the joining of the middle and ring fingers, one should [offer] drops from that water three times, i.e., in three ways, onto the ground.
One should cast it away. || 48 ||

"Seven times" means: having first uttered the root mantra, one should sprinkle one's own head—that is, one's own crown—with that very water seven times by joining the middle and ring fingers; thereafter, [one should place it] in the left hand.
Having taken up water and grasped it with the right hand, one should cover [the vessel] with it. || 49 ||

"Īśāna," and so forth. Having covered [the vessel] with the right hand, one should recite four times—that is, fourfold—the five seed-syllables *ha*, *ya*, *va*, *ra*, and *la*, which have Īśāna, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Agni, and Indra as their presiding deities; then, that water...
One should bring it together with the right hand. || 50 ||

Having beheld [it] and meditated upon it as consisting of light, the practitioner, having drawn [the breath] in with the iḍā, should expel the impurity within the body through that which is called piṅgalā. (51)
Having drawn [the water] out and reciting the weapon-mantra over a vajra-stone in front of him,
the mantra-practitioner should strike it three times and then wash his hands.
Having sipped water (ācamana) with the prescribed mantra, one should offer the arghya oblation to Sūrya.
Having uttered "Tāra-māyā-haṃsa" (Oṃ Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ), followed by "Ghṛṇi Sūrya," and saying "This arghya is for you," one should offer it while pronouncing "Svāhā."
Then, one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Gāyatrī, the Supreme Deity,
in her three forms according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas), at dawn, midday, and evening.
In the morning, one should meditate on Brāhmī, red in color, two-armed, and youthful;
she holds a water-pot filled with sacred water and a rosary of clear beads, wears a garment of black antelope skin, is mounted upon a swan, and possesses a pure smile. (56)

Regarding the word "vīkṣya" (having beheld): the practitioner, having beheld— that is, looked upon— that water brought in his right hand, and having meditated upon it as consisting of light, that is, as the very form of light, draws it in through the *iḍā* channel and,
by means of the channel called *piṅgalā*, [purifies] the impurity within the body with that water.
One should expel and cast out the evil within the body. || 51 ||

"Having extracted": the practitioner, the *sādhaka*, having thus extracted the impurity within the body, should strike—that is, hit it—three times with the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*, while uttering and reciting it, upon a diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*) imagined by the mind in front of him. Immediately after that:
He should wash his hands and rinse his mouth.
"Perform the ritual sipping (ācamya). Then, having performed the ritual sipping with the aforementioned mantra, one should present—that is, give—an arghya offering to Sūrya. || 53 ||

Now, by which mantra should the *arghya* be offered to the Sun? To this he says: "Tāra," and so forth. Having first uttered *tāra*, *māyā*, and *haṃsa*, then after that having uttered *ghṛṇi-sūrya*, and then after that having uttered "this *arghya* to you" (*idam arghyaṃ tubhyam*).

Immediately thereafter, pronouncing and reciting "svāhā," the practitioner should offer arghya to the Sun. The meaning is that he should present the arghya with the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsa ghṛṇisūrya, this arghya is for you, svāhā. || 54 || 55 ||

Demonstrating the threefold nature [of Gāyatrī] through the distinctions of her qualities—such as being a queen—at dawn, midday, and sunset, he describes the meditation on Gāyatrī itself with the verses beginning "In the morning, the Brāhmī... and so forth.
Regarding the word "in the morning" (*prātaḥ*): she is of red complexion; "red" means crimson.
At midday, one should meditate upon her as Śyāmavarṇā Vaiṣṇavī, four-armed, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, and seated upon Garuḍa. (57)
One should constantly meditate upon the youthful goddess, whose pair of breasts are full and high, who is adorned with a forest garland, situated in the center of the orb of the sun. 58.
In the evening, the ascetic should meditate upon the boon-granting goddess Gāyatrī—
white in complexion, clad in white garments, and seated upon the bull-throne.
She has three eyes, bestows boons, and holds a noose, a trident, and a human skull with her lotus-like hands; she is aged, her youth having faded away.
She who possesses that color; she who is two-armed, having two arms; [holding] in her hands a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) filled with holy waters such as those of the Gaṅgā, and a clear rosary of beads.

Wearing [it], that is, bearing it; wearing a garment of black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), meaning she is clothed in a garment in the form of dark hide; mounted upon a swan (*haṃsa*), where a swan is a particular kind of bird, she has ascended it; possessing a pure smile, where "pure" (*śuci*) means holy, bright, and radiant.

One should meditate at dawn upon Goddess Gāyatrī, who is thus characterized: she whose face bears a slight smile, who is a maiden (kumārī), who is a girl (kanyā), and who is Brāhmī, the power (śakti) of Brahmā. The grammatical construction should be understood in this same manner for what follows as well. || 56 ||
"At midday" means that Gāyatrī. || 57 ||
"Pīnā" means one whose pair of breasts is full, large, high, and elevated; she who is thus characterized. || 58 ||
"At eventide," and so forth. A *yati* is one who has conquered the assembly of the senses;
as Amarasimha states: "Those who have conquered the collection of their senses are *yatins*, and they are also called *yatayas*.
[She is] one who has taken refuge upon the bull-throne (*vṛṣāsana*); he whose seat is in the form of a bull is the Bull-seated One (*vṛṣāsana*).
She who has made Śiva himself her refuge—that is, she whose own support is he—or rather, she who has made that which consists of his bull-seat (vṛṣāsana) her refuge;
such is she. || 59 ||
"Three-eyed" means possessing three eyes. "Human skull" means a human cranium. "With fading youth" means with destroyed or vanished youthfulness. || 60 ||
Having meditated thus, one should offer three handfuls of water to Mahādevī and then recite the Gāyatrī ten or even a hundred times. (61)
Listen to the Gāyatrī, O Goddess of gods; I shall recite it to you with devotion.
Having uttered the word "Ādyāyai," one should then say "vidmahe. (62)
"Let us meditate upon the Supreme Sovereign; may that Kālī inspire us.
This is your Gāyatrī, which destroys even the greatest sins. (63)

Reciting this at the three junctions of the day, one shall obtain the fruit of the twilight rites (saṃdhyā). Thereafter, O auspicious lady, one should offer libations to the gods, sages, ancestors, and deities.

I offer libations with the Praṇava, followed by the name [of the deity] and the word "namaḥ. However, in the case of Śakti, one should utter Māyā in place of the Praṇava and the word "dviṭha" (svāhā) in place of "namaḥ."
"Thus," and so forth. To Mahādevī Gāyatrī, "tenfold or even hundredfold" means ten times or a hundred times. || 61 ||
With the words beginning "the Gāyatrī," he begins to speak of the Gāyatrī; "bhāvataḥ" means with affection. || 62 ||

He [the author] states that very *gāyatrī* with the words "to the Primordial One" (*ādyāyai*) and so forth. First, having uttered the word "to the Primordial One," one should thereafter utter the word "we know" (*vidmahe*). Thereafter, one should utter: "we meditate upon the Supreme Sovereign" (*parameśvaryai dhīmahi*), and "may Kālī impel us thereto" (*tannaḥ kālī pracodayāt*). This is the method of application.
"Let us know the Primordial One; let us meditate upon the Supreme Sovereign; may that Kālī inspire us"—such was the Gāyatrī. As for the meaning of this Gāyatrī:
"To the Primordial One, the Supreme Sovereign"—in order to attain the Primordial Supreme Sovereign, whom we...
We know, we reflect upon, and we meditate upon that Kālī, who is most renowned as the cause of the universe;
may she impel us—that is to say, may she direct us toward virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. Thus ends verse 63.
"At the three junctions of the day" means this Gāyatrī of yours alone. "Then," however, means immediately after the recitation of the Gāyatrī. || 64 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which specific mantras should be used to satiate the gods, sages, ancestors, and deities, he states the mantra for the libation (tarpaṇa) beginning with "the Praṇava": first one should utter the Praṇava, the syllable Oṃ; then [one should utter] the name followed by the word "saha" (together).
At the end of the *mūla-mantra* and at the end of *sarvabhūta*, one should utter the word *nivāsinyai*.
One should likewise recite *sarvasvarūpām* joined with the feminine suffix *ṅī*, as well as *sāyudhā*. (66)
In the same manner, [one offers] the one with the veil (sāvaraṇā) and the fourth [deity], as well as the one higher than the highest (parātparā);
then, "To the primordial Kālikā, this arghya," and then the word for the twice-born (dviṭhaḥ).
Having offered this *arghya* to Mahādevī, the wise practitioner should recite the root mantra.
Having performed the recitation according to his capacity, he should offer it into the left hand of the Goddess.

One should utter the name or designation accompanied by the second case ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*). Following that, one should utter the words "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*) and "salutation" (*namaḥ*). However, if there is capacity—that is, when it is possible—in place of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), one should utter the *māyā*-seed-syllable *hrīṃ*; and in place of "salutation" (*namaḥ*), [one should utter the appropriate seed-syllable].
One should utter the word "svāhā" twice. With this mantra, "oṃ devāṃs tarpayāmi namaḥ," one should satisfy the gods; with "oṃ ṛṣīṃs tarpayāmi namaḥ," the sages;
and with the mantra "oṃ pitṝṃs tarpayāmi namaḥ," the ancestors; and [with] "hrīḥ," the primordial Kālī.
By the mantra "tarpayāmi svāhā," it is indicated that one should satisfy the primordial Kālī. || 65 ||

"Ending with the root," and so forth: at the end of the root mantra *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā*, one should utter the word *sarvabhūta* (belonging to all beings), and at the end of that, the word *nivāsinyai* (to her who dwells). Then, one should utter *sarvasvarūpām* (the one whose nature is everything) joined with the feminine suffix *ṅī*. After that, likewise [the word] joined with *ṅī*.

One should also utter the word "sāyudhā" (armed). Then, in the same manner, one should utter "parātparām" (the one higher than the highest) with the dative case-ending. Then one should say: "ādyāyai kālikāyai te idam arghyam" (to the primordial Kālikā, this is the water-offering for you).
Then one should utter the word "svāhā," which consists of two "ṭha"s. By joining all these words together: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ*.

"O Supreme Goddess, Svāhā! To her who dwells in all beings, who is the embodiment of all, who is equipped with weapons and attendants, who is higher than the highest, the primordial Kālikā—to you, this is the arghya; Svāhā!"—such was the mantra. || 66 || 67 ||

"By this": having offered *arghya* to Mahādevī with this very mantra just mentioned, the wise and steadfast practitioner should mutter the root mantra. Having performed the recitation according to his capacity, he should offer the fruit born of that recitation into the left hand of the Goddess.

Having prostrated before the Goddess and taken water for the purpose of worship, the practitioner, having bowed to the sacred ford (tīrtha), should recite the hymn while remaining intent on meditation upon the deity. (69)
Having entered the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), one should cleanse one's hands and feet;
then, one should prepare the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya) in front of the door.
The wise one should fashion a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and the form of the earth;
having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), he should place the support (ādhāra) therein.
Having washed the vessel with the Astra mantra and filled it with the Hrdaya mantra,
one should place in it fragrance and flowers, and then invoke the sacred waters (tīrthas).
Having worshipped the orbs of fire, sun, and moon within the water of the supporting vessel, one should consecrate it ten times with the seed-syllable *māyā*.
"Having prostrated," etc.: Then the practitioner, having prostrated before the Goddess,

taken water for the purpose of worship, and having bowed to the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), while reciting a hymn and being intent on meditation upon the deity, arrives at the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), the house of sacrifice.
One should cleanse and wash one's hands and feet; then, in front of the door, one should prepare—that is, arrange—the general *arghya* offering. || 69 || 70 ||
Now, as to what the general *arghya* (offering water) is called, he says "the triangle," and so forth.

A wise person—that is, one who is discerning—should construct a mandala that is a combination of these: a triangle, a circle, and the form of the earth; namely, a triangle, circle, and the form of the earth. First...

The meaning is that one should construct a mandala consisting of a triangle, then outside of that a circular circle, and then outside of that a square representing the earth-disk (*bhūbimba*). In that constructed mandala, one should worship the *Ādhāraśakti* (Supporting Power) with scents, flowers, and other offerings, using the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti."
Having performed the worship, one should employ—that is, place—some kind of support for the setting out of the vessel for the general *arghya* offering upon that very same prepared maṇḍala. || 71 ||

Regarding the phrase "with the Astra-mantra": having washed the vessel with the Astra-mantra *phaṭ* and placed it upon its support (*adhāra*), one should fill it with water using the Hṛdaya-mantra and the *namaḥ*-mantra;
then, having cast into it sandalwood paste and other fragrances as well as flowers, thereafter, in that [vessel]—
One should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas). || 72 ||
Regarding "the support" (ādhāra): then, having worshipped the orbs of Fire, Sun, and Moon within those— the support, the vessel, and the water— namely,
the orb of Fire in the support, the orb of the Sun in the vessel, and [the orb of the Moon] in the water.
One should display the *dhenu-yoni* [mudrā]; this is remembered as the general *arghya*.
Then, one should worship the deities of the gateway with that water and flowers. (74)
One should then worship Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and likewise Yoginī; then Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as Lakṣmī and Vāṇī. (75)
Touching the left branch slightly while leading with the left foot,
the wise practitioner should enter the pavilion while recollecting the lotus feet of the Goddess.

The meaning is that one should worship the moon-mandala with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the mantra to be described hereafter. One should consecrate that water ten times—that is, ten repetitions—with the seed-syllable of Māyā, namely the syllable *hrīṃ*. || 73 ||

"One should display" means that thereafter, one should display the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās over it. This very [offering] is known as the general *arghya*. Following that, one should worship the deities of the gateway with water and flowers—that is, with the water and flowers belonging to the general *arghya*.
As for the Dhenu-mudrā:
"The little fingers and ring fingers are again joined with their tips facing one another;
likewise the index and middle fingers [are joined]—this is the Dhenu-mudrā, which bestows nectar. (74)
Showing those very door-deities whom one should worship, he says "Gaṇeśam" and so forth. With the mantra "Gāṃ Gaṇeśāya namaḥ," [one worships] Gaṇeśa;
with the mantra "Kṣāṃ Kṣetrapālāya namaḥ," [one worships] Kṣetrapāla; and with "Vāṃ Vaṭukāya namaḥ," [one worships] Vaṭuka.
With this [mantra], one worships Vaṭuka; with "Oṃ Yoginyai Namaḥ," one worships the Yoginī; with "Gāṃ Gaṅgāyai Namaḥ," one worships Gaṅgā; with the mantra "Yāṃ Yamunāyai Namaḥ," one worships Yamunā;
with "Śrīṃ Lakṣmyai Namaḥ," one worships Lakṣmī; and with "Aiṃ Sarasvatyai Namaḥ," [one worships Sarasvatī].
One should worship and honor Speech with mantras, perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 75 ||

"Something" means as follows: then, touching slightly the left branch— that is, the left of the four wooden posts standing at the door— the wise practitioner, while recollecting the lotus-feet of the Goddess, should proceed with his left foot foremost.
One should enter the pavilion—the sacrificial pavilion for the Goddess, the sacrificial hall for the Goddess. || 76 ||
(Wearing the sacred thread) over the right shoulder, he should worship Vāstvīśa and Brahmā in the south-western direction;
then, he should sprinkle the sacrificial hall with water from the general *arghya* vessel. (77)
Immediately thereafter, the supreme practitioner, by means of divine visions and with weapons [of mantras],
should dispel the divine obstacles and those moving through the intermediate space.
One should ward off terrestrial obstacles with three strikes of the heel;
likewise, one should [fumigate] the sacrificial pavilion with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and camphor.
One should fumigate [the area] for one's own seating; having drawn a square and a triangle there, one should worship with the heart-mantra "to Kāmarūpa. (80)
There, having spread out a seat at will from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should worship the seat with the mantra: "Salutation to the Lotus-seated One."

"In the southwest," and so forth. Having entered the pavilion, one should worship and honor Vāstveśa and Brahmā in that very southwest direction with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, using the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, while employing the water of the general *arghya*.
One should sprinkle and drench the sacrificial hall. || 77 ||

Regarding the word "immediately" (*anantaram*): immediately after that, the supreme practitioner (*sādhakendra*), by means of divine glances—divine vision being a gaze devoid of blinking—and by means of those observations, beholds them; they are "divine" (*divya*) because they exist in heaven (*divi*).

One should dispel and ward off obstacles. One should dispel the obstacles moving in the intermediate space and those situated in the sky with water and the *astra* mantra, "phaṭ. However, one should dispel the terrestrial obstacles—that is, those arising from the earth—with three strikes of the heel.

One should ward [the obstacles] off with blows from the soles of the feet. Then, one should fumigate and perfume the sacrificial pavilion with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and camphor. Thereafter, for the purpose of one's own seating, one should draw a triangle, and outside of that, a square and a four-cornered [figure].

Having drawn the maṇḍala, one should worship the presiding deity of that drawn maṇḍala—who can assume any form at will—with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, using the mantra: "To Kāmarūpa, the heart; obeisance to Kāmarūpa. (78–80)

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): having first spread and covered a seat in that mandala according to one's desire, one should utter the seed-syllable *klīm*, and thereafter say "to the Support-Energy" (*ādhāraśakti*).
And after the Support-Energy, [one says] "to the Lotus-Throne" (*kamalāsanāya*).
Having sat upon his seat, facing either east or north, the wise practitioner, bound in the *vīrāsana* posture, should purify the *vijayā*. (82)
Having uttered Tāra and Māyā, [one should say]: "O Amṛte, O Amṛtodbhave, O Amṛtavarṣiṇi; then, attract the nectar twice. (83)
"Grant me success," he should say; then "Kālikā me" (Kālikā for me);
thereafter "vaśamānaya ṭhaṭha" (bring under control, ṭhaṭha). This is the mantra for the purification of consciousness. || 84 ||
Having recited the root mantra seven times over the Vijaya vessel,
one should display the Āvāhanī and other mudrās, as well as the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās.
One should say "namaḥ. Through this application, the mantra "klīm ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ" is formed. With this very mantra, one should worship the seat and its presiding deity.
Vijayā and Bhaṅgā. || 82 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to which mantra one should use to purify Vijayā,

he states the very mantra for that purification in two verses beginning with "Tāram": first, having uttered the *tāra*, the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and the *māyā* seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, and thereafter [the word] *amṛte*.
One should say, "O source of nectar, O showerer of nectar. Then one should say, "Nectar.
Then one should say twice, "Draw [it] forth. And then one should say, "Grant success.
After that, one should say, "To me, O Kālikā. And then, "Bring [them] under control."

One should say "Ṭha-dvandva svāhā. By joining all the words together, the mantra is formed as follows: *Oṃ hrīṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtam ākarṣaya ākarṣaya siddhiṃ dehi kālikāṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā*. This is for the purification of consciousness (*saṃvit*).
This very same rule prescribed by Manu is declared for the purification of hemp (bhaṅgā). || 83 || 84 ||

Regarding the phrase "the root mantra": having recited the root mantra seven times over the *vijaya* [flower], that by which [the deity] is invoked is the invocation mudrā (*āvāhanī-mudrā*). That which has this as its first is "beginning with the invocation" (*āvāhany-ādi*).
That which is both this and a mudrā is the "mudrā beginning with the invocation" (*āvāhany-ādi-mudrā*); it refers to that.
One should display the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās above the *vijaya* [mudrā]. Regarding the *āvāhanī* and other mudrās, as stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* (p. 91):
"The Guru [is worshipped] in the thousand-petaled lotus according to the *saṅketa* mudrā."
One should satisfy the Goddess in three ways, reciting the root mantra while [visualizing her] in the heart.

One should offer oblations into the mouth of Kuṇḍalī with this mantra ending in *svāhā*: "Vāgbhava, the pair of *vada*s, then the word *vāgvādini*, followed by: 'O you who bring all beings under control, remain firm on the tip of my tongue! (87)
Having accepted [the teachings], one should bow to the Śrī Guru above the left ear;
to Gaṇeśāna on the right, and to the Primordial Eternal One (Sanātanī) in the middle.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should become intent on meditating upon the Goddess.
One should place the hollowed palms facing downward; this is the mudrā for invocation (āvāhanī). However, when it is performed in the reverse manner, it becomes the mudrā for installation (sthāpanī).

This same [mudrā], when formed with the fists having the thumbs pointing upward, is the Sannidhāpanī; this same [mudrā], when formed with the fists having the thumbs tucked inside, is the Sannirodhinī. || 85 ||

Regarding "the Guru": with the mantra "Ai! I satisfy the venerable Guru Amukānandanātha; obeisance," one should duly satisfy the Guru three times with the *vijayā* [wine] in the thousand-petaled lotus of the *sahasrāra*, using the *saṅketamudrā* as instructed by the Guru, which is the *tattvamudrā*. The root [mantra is]: Ai! I satisfy the venerable Guru Amukānandanātha; obeisance.
While reciting the mantra, one should satisfy the Goddess Vijayā within the heart three times with the mantra "I satisfy the primordial Kālī, svāhā," using the *tattvamudrā* itself.
Regarding "Vāgbhava": first, one should utter the Vāgbhava seed-syllable *aiṃ*.
Then, one should utter the pair of *vada* syllables. Then, one should utter the word *vāgvādini*. Then, one should utter:
*mama jihvāgre sthirībhava sarvasattvavaśaṅkari*. By means of this conjunction: *aiṃ vada*.

"Speak, O eloquent one! Be firm upon the tip of my tongue, O subduer of all beings!"—this mantra has been produced. With this very mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer oblations of *vijayā* into the mouth of the *kuṇḍalī*. || 87 ||

"Having accepted" means: having thus accepted or grasped the dissolution of the consciousnesses, one should bow to the Śrī Guru with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Śrī Gurus" at the upper region of the left ear;
[and likewise] on the right, at the upper region of the right ear.
The wise practitioner should place all the materials for worship on the right;
on the left, he should place well-perfumed water and whatever substances belong to the *kula*. (89)
Having sprinkled all the materials with water from the general *arghya* vessel while reciting the root mantra ending with the weapon (*astra*) mantra, one should encircle them with a stream of water;
O Goddess of Gods, one should perform the enclosure of fire using the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*).
Taking a flower combined with sandalwood paste in both hands,
one should rub it with the Astra-mantra and cast it away for the purification of the hands.

O Śivā, having performed three successive upward claps with the index and middle fingers on the palm of the left hand, one should then perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana) with the Astra-mantra and snapping sounds, and thereafter perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

One should bow to Gaṇeśāna with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa. With the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to Sanātanī, Ādyā, Kālī," one should bow to Sanātanī, Ādyā, and Kālikā in the middle, at the region of the forehead. || 88 ||
He worships. The materials for worship are flowers and so forth; the family substances are liquor and so forth.

"Ending with the weapon-mantra": then, having sprinkled and consecrated all objects with the root-mantra ending in *phaṭ*, with the root-mantra itself, and with the water of the general *arghya* offering, one should encircle them with a stream of water. O Goddess, then—
One should perform the enclosure of fire as a protective barrier using the seed-syllable of fire, "raṃ."

Regarding "the flower": then, for the purification of the hands, having taken and grasped a flower combined with sandalwood in both hands, one should rub that flower with the mantra *phaṭ* (the Astra-mantra) and cast it away. || 91 ||

Regarding *tarjanī*: O Śivā, then, having struck three successive claps (*tāla*) on the palm of the left hand with the index and middle fingers, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) by means of the *astra* mantra "phaṭ," using finger-snaps and the sounds of the fingers.
Then, immediately after the binding of the directions, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having placed his hands, palms upward, upon his own lap, the best of practitioners should fix his mind on the *mūla* and [awaken] the *kuṇḍalī* by means of the syllable *huṃ*. (93)
Having raised her up together with the Earth by means of the Haṃsa-mantra,
one should bring her to the Svādhiṣṭhāna and unite that principle with the [higher] principle.
One should dissolve the earth, which is conjoined with smell and the other [objects] and associated with the nose, into water;
one should dissolve water, together with taste and the rest and the tongue, into fire.
Having dissolved fire together with form and the other [objects] along with the eye into air, one should dissolve air—conjoined with touch and the other [objects] and the skin—into space. || 96 ||
One should dissolve the sky along with sound into the ego;
that [ego] into the Great Principle (mahat); the Great Principle into primordial nature (prakṛti); and that [nature] one should dissolve into Brahman. (97)
He describes the very method for performing the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) with the words beginning "on his own lap" (*svāṅke*).
The best of practitioners, having placed his two hands palms-upward on his own lap and having fixed his mind on the *mūla*, the *mūlādhāra* cakra, [utters] by means of the syllable *hūṃ* alone.

Having raised Kuṇḍalī by means of the *haṃsa* mantra— that is, the mantra consisting of the word "haṃsa"— one should bring that power (*śakti*), together with the element earth, to the *svādhiṣṭhāna*,
which is the *svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra*; there, one should dissolve the principle (*tattva*) of earth and so forth into the principle of water and so forth.
One should employ [it] and dissolve [it]. || 93 || 94 ||

Demonstrating precisely the manner of dissolving the elements beginning with earth into the elements beginning with water, he says "gandhādi" and so forth. That which has smell as its first [quality] is "gandhādi";
such is that which is both smell and the sense of smell (the nose), hence "gandhādighrāṇa," by means of that.

One should withdraw and dissolve the earth, joined with the waters, into the water. Regarding the reading "ghrāṇādi," that which is smelled—that is, perceived by the nose—is "ghrāṇa," namely odor itself.
In this same manner, one should likewise dissolve the water and the other elements into fire and so forth. (95–96)

Regarding the term *ahaṅkāra*: one should dissolve the ether (*vyoma*), together with sound—that is, accompanied by sound—into the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*). One should dissolve that principle of ego into the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*), and dissolve the Great Principle into primordial nature (*prakṛti*). One should dissolve that primordial nature into Brahman.
One should cause it to dissolve. || 97 ||
Having thus dissolved [the body], the wise one should contemplate within the left side of the belly a man who is black in color, with red beard and eyes. (98)
Wearing red skin, wrathful, and the size of a thumb;
he is the embodiment of all sins and remains perpetually with his face turned downward. || 99 ||

Then, having meditated upon the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, which is smoke-colored, at the tip of the nose, the foremost of practitioners should fill the breath with sixteen measures (*mātrā*) using that [syllable]; by means of this, he should dry up the body consisting of sin. 100.
Having meditated on the syllable *raṃ* of red color at the navel,
one should burn the body of one devoted to sin with the fire born from it by means of sixty-four breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*).
"In this manner" means: the wise practitioner,

having thus dissolved the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth in this way, should contemplate within his left side— that is, in the left abdomen— a black-colored person who is the very embodiment of all sins.
The words ending in the accusative case, such as *raktaśmaśruvilocanam* and so forth,

are qualifiers of the person who is the very embodiment of all sins. *Raktaśmaśruvilocanam* means one whose beard and eyes (*śmaśruvilocane*) are red (*rakte*), that is, of a crimson color (*lohitavarṇe*).
Thus it was. || 98 || 99 ||

"Then, thus": immediately after that, having meditated upon the smoke-colored seed-syllable *yaṃ* at the left nostril, the practitioner, while reciting that very seed-syllable, should fill or draw in the air through that left nostril with sixteen *mātrās*.
The foremost of practitioners, the best of adepts, by means of that filled wind, should dry up the sinful body—the body of one whose nature is evil—within himself, within his own self. || 100 ||
"Not non-existent. Then, having meditated on the red-colored seed-syllable *raṃ* at the navel,
while reciting that very seed-syllable, one [should burn] one's own addiction to sin with the fire produced from that seed-syllable *raṃ* by means of sixty-four *kumbhaka* breath-retentions.
One should burn the body. || 101 ||
Having visualized the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, white in color, upon the forehead,
one should flood it with the water of nectar by means of thirty-two exhalations.
Having immersed [the body] from the feet up to the head,
one should thereafter contemplate the newly arisen body as consisting of the deity.
Visualizing the yellow-colored seed-syllable of the earth at the *mūlādhāra*,
one should strengthen one's own body with that divine vision.
Placing the hand upon the heart while uttering "Ā Hrīḥ Kroḥ Haṃsaḥ," one should establish the life-breaths of the Goddess in her body by means of the mantra "So 'ham. || 105 ||

Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), O Ambikā, one who is intent on the state of the Goddess and whose mind is composed should perform the ritual placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa).

Regarding the phrase "on the forehead": then, having visualized the white-colored Vāruṇa seed-syllable *vaṃ* on the forehead, while muttering that very seed-syllable, [one should sprinkle] with thirty-two exhalations the water in the form of nectar that has fallen from the Vāruṇa seed-syllable as ambrosial fluid.
One should cause the burnt body to be immersed [in water]. || 102 ||

He causes it to arise. Thus, having flooded the body from the feet up to the head, he should thereafter contemplate—visualize—the newly arisen body as consisting of the deity, having the very nature of the deity's body. || 103 ||

Regarding the word "pṛthvī" (earth): Then, while meditating upon the seed-syllable of earth (*pṛthvībīja*) in the form of the yellow-colored syllable *laṃ* at the *mūlādhāra*, one should solidify one's own body by means of that *laṃ* seed-syllable and divine vision. || 104 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the heart": then, having taken and placed his hand upon the heart while uttering *ā* *hrī* *kro* *haṃsaḥ*, the practitioner, with the mantra *so'ham* ("I am that"), should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the Goddess within that fresh body by means of the mantra *ā* *hrī* *kro* *haṃsaḥ* *so'ham*.
The meaning is that one should effect the establishment of the Goddess's vital breaths within that body. || 105 ||
Devoted to the state of being the Goddess, intent on the contemplation that "I am of the very nature of the Goddess.
(106) Brahmā is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*) of Mātṛkā, Gāyatrī the meter (*chandas*), the Goddess Mātṛkā the deity (*devatā*), and the consonants the seed-syllable (*bīja*). (107)
The vowels are the powers (śaktis), and the creation (sarga) is proclaimed as the pin (kīlaka). O Great Goddess, this is the application and practice in the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa).
Having thus performed the placement of the seers (ṛṣinyāsa), one should perform the placement of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa). 108.
Aṃ and āṃ are in the center of the ka-group; iṃ and īṃ are in the center of the ca-group;
uṃ and ūṃ are in the center of the ṭa-group; and eṃ and aiṃ are in the center of the ta-group. || 109 ||

O fair-faced one, the mantra for the six limbs is declared as follows: the letter *auṃ* in the center, followed by the consonants from *pa* to *kṣa*, with the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga (*sarga*) placed between them. 110.
Having performed the ritual placement according to the rules of nyāsa, one should meditate upon Mātṛsarasvatī.

Now, desiring to demonstrate the very sequence for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā*, he states the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details of the *mātṛkā* with the words beginning "of the *mātṛkā*" and so forth. "Emission" (*sarga*) means the creative outpouring (*visarga*). "The state of being employed in application" (*viniyogaprayogitā*) means the quality of being applied in a ritual application; that is, the application is to be put into practice.

This is the meaning. For this Mātṛkā, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), the goddess Sarasvatī in the form of Mātṛkā is the deity (devatā), the consonants are the seed-syllables (bīja), the vowels are the powers (śakti), and the visarga is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa during the ritual placement of the script (lipinyāsa). [The placement is] on the head...

Salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi). Salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (chandas), in the mouth. Salutation to the goddess Sarasvatī, the mother (mātṛkā) and deity, in the heart. Salutation to the consonants, the seed-syllables (bīja), in the secret place. Salutation to the vowels, the powers (śakti), in the two feet. [Salutation] to all the limbs.

"Obeisance to Visarga, the Kīlaka. The application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa through the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa). Having thus performed the placement of the sages (ṛṣinyāsa), one should perform the placement of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa). || 107 || 108 ||

He explains the sequence for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs with the words "aṃ āṃ in the middle," and so forth: the *ka*-group situated between *aṃ* and *āṃ*; the *ca*-group situated between *iṃ* and *īṃ*; the *ṭa*-group situated between *uṃ* and *ūṃ*; the *ta*-group situated between *eṃ* and *aiṃ*; [and] *oṃ*.

Oṃ! [I bow to her] whose face, arms, waist, and chest are divided by the fifty letters, with the *pavarga* situated in the center, between the *bindu* and *visarga*, and between the *anusvāra* and *visarga*. (p. 97)

I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses three eyes and a radiant luster; she bears upon her lotus-like hands a crescent moon bound to her shining crown, full and lofty breasts, a ritual seal (mudrā), a rosary of beads, a jar brimming with nectar, and the [scriptural] knowledge. 112.

The syntactical connection is as follows: having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in due order according to the rules of placement upon the six limbs—the heart and so forth—by assigning the phonemes beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa* to the thumbs and so forth, one should meditate upon Mātṛsarasvatī. For example: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ*.

Ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā). Uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ Ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ). Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ...
Dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ to the two ring fingers, huṃ. Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ. Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ.
*Phaṭ* with both palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the *karanyāsa* (hand assignment).
The *nyāsa* for the heart and other limbs is as follows: *Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* (To the heart, salutation); *Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ śirase* (To the head...).
Svāhā! Um Ṭaṃ Ṭhaṃ Ḍaṃ Ḍhaṃ Ṇaṃ Ūṃ, Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā)!
Eṃ Taṃ Thaṃ Daṃ Dhaṃ Naṃ Aiṃ, Huṃ to the armor (kavaca)! Oṃ Paṃ Phaṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ Maṃ Auṃ, Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya)! Aṃ Yaṃ Raṃ...
Laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ astrāya phaṭ.
This very mantra is declared and taught for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 109-111 ||
He describes the meditation on Mātṛsarasvatī itself with the words "by means of the fifty letters. The grammatical construction is: "I take refuge in, I worship, the goddess of speech, Sarasvatī.
In what manner does he describe the goddess of speech?
She whose face, arms, palms, waist, and chest were divided by the fifty letters—
that is, she whose face, arms, palms, waist, and chest were each distinctly marked by the fifty phonemes— such was she. In that regard:
Two-armed and two-footed; furthermore, of what nature [is she]?
One who has a crescent moon bound upon her radiant crown—wherein "radiant crown" refers to a shining diadem, and "crescent moon" refers to a fragment of the moon.

By whom [she was seen]. According to Amara: "Cūḍā, kirīṭa, and bound hair—these three are called mauli. Furthermore, of what nature was she? "Possessing full and lofty breasts"—that is, one whose breasts (stanau) were *āpīna* (exceedingly large) and *tuṅga* (elevated). Furthermore...
In what manner? With her lotus-like hands— her lotus-palms— she holds the *jñānamudrā*,
the rosary of beads (*akṣamālya*), the jar rich with nectar— a vessel filled with ambrosia— and the *vidyā*.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess Mātṛkā, one should assign her to the six cakras:
the letters *ha* and *kṣa* in the lotus at the center of the eyebrows, and the sixteen vowels in the throat. (113)

Having performed the placement of the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* in the heart-lotus, the practitioner of the Kula should place those from *ḍa* to *pha* at the region of the navel, and those from *ba* to *la* upon the linga.
One should arrange the letters from *va* to *sa* on the four-petalled [lotus] at the *mūlādhāra*;
having thus mentally assigned them internally, one should then assign the letters of the Mātṛkā externally.

Bearing [it], that is, holding it; again, of what sort? Possessing a pure radiance—that is, she whose radiance is pure and bright; again, of what sort? One who possesses three eyes—such was she. || 112 ||
"Having meditated thus": having meditated in this manner upon the Goddess Mātṛkā, one should perform her placement (*nyāsa*) within the six wheels (*cakras*).

He explains the sequence for the placement of Mātṛkā within the six wheels with the words beginning "hakṣau" and so forth: in the two-petaled lotus called Viśuddha, located between the eyebrows, are the letters *ha* and *kṣa*.

One should place the phonemes. In the throat, upon the sixteen-petaled lotus located at the throat known as Ājñā, one should place the sixteen vowels. In the heart-lotus called Anāhata, which has twelve petals, the practitioner of the Kula (kulasādhaka), having placed the twelve phonemes from *ka* to *ṭha*, [should proceed].

One should place the ten syllables from *ḍa* to *pha* upon the ten-petaled lotus called Maṇipūraka situated at the region of the navel. One should place the six syllables from *va* to *la* upon the six-petaled lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna situated at the region of the genitals. Upon the four-petaled [lotus]...

One should place the four letters from *va* to *sa* in the *mūlādhāra*. Just as in the lotus located between the eyebrows, there are *haṃ namaḥ* and *kṣaṃ namaḥ*; in the lotus at the throat, there are *aṃ namaḥ*, *āṃ namaḥ*, *iṃ namaḥ*, *īṃ namaḥ*, *uṃ namaḥ*, *ūṃ namaḥ*, and *ṛṃ namaḥ*.

Salutation to Ṛṃ; salutation to Ḷṃ; salutation to Ḹṃ; salutation to Eṃ; salutation to Aiṃ; salutation to Oṃ; salutation to Auṃ; salutation to Aṃ; salutation to Aḥ. Within the lotus situated at the heart: salutation to Kaṃ; salutation to Khaṃ; salutation to Gaṃ; salutation to Ghaṃ; salutation to Ṅaṃ; salutation to Caṃ.
Namaḥ chaṃ, namaḥ jaṃ, namaḥ jhaṃ, namaḥ ñaṃ, namaḥ ṭaṃ, namaḥ ṭhaṃ;
to the lotus situated at the navel: namaḥ ḍaṃ, namaḥ ḍhaṃ, namaḥ ṇaṃ, namaḥ taṃ, namaḥ thaṃ, namaḥ daṃ, namaḥ dhaṃ, namaḥ naṃ.
Namaḥ paṃ, namaḥ phaṃ, namaḥ. In the lotus located at the *liṅga*: baṃ namaḥ, bhaṃ namaḥ, maṃ namaḥ, yaṃ namaḥ, raṃ namaḥ, laṃ namaḥ. In the *mūlādhāra*:
vaṃ namaḥ, śaṃ namaḥ, ṣaṃ namaḥ, saṃ namaḥ. Thus, in the six *cakras*.
The sequence for the deposition of the *mātṛkā* (p.

99): [One should deposit them] on the forehead, the face, the circles of the eyes, the ears, the nose, the two cheeks, the lips, the teeth, the head, the mouth, the shoulders, the joints, and the tips of the fingers. 116.
On the two sides, at the back, at the navel, in the abdomen, at the heart and the shoulders, at the part of the hump, and then starting from the heart in the pair of hands and feet. (117)
One should assign the letters of the Mātṛkā in their proper order to the belly and the mouth;
having thus performed the assignment of the script (lipi), one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having recited the seed-syllable of Māyā sixteen times, one should fill one's own body with the left breath and retain it for sixty-four [counts].
In this manner, having mentally deposited the letters of the Mātṛkā within the interior of the Mātṛkā-letters, one should also deposit them externally. (113–115)

He describes the sequence for the external placement (*bahirnyāsa*) of the letters of the *mātṛkā* with the words beginning "on the forehead" (*lalāṭa*). The connection with the third [verse] is that one should place the letters of the *mātṛkā* in due order on the forehead, the circle of the mouth, and so forth; for example, *aṃ namaḥ* on the forehead and *āṃ namaḥ* on the circle of the mouth.
Salutation to *Iṃ* on the right eye; salutation to *Īṃ* on the left eye; salutation to *Uṃ* on the right ear; salutation to *Ūṃ* on the left ear; salutation to *Ṛṃ* on the right nostril;
salutation to *Ṝṃ* on the left nostril; salutation to *Ḷṃ* on the right cheek; salutation to *Ḹṃ* on the left cheek.
*Namaḥ* to the upper lip, *eṃ*; *namaḥ* to the lower lip, *aiṃ*; *namaḥ* to the row of upper teeth, *oṃ*;
*namaḥ* to the row of lower teeth, *auṃ*; *namaḥ* to the head, *aṃ*;
*namaḥ* to the cavity of the mouth, *aḥ*; *namaḥ* to the tips of the ten joints of the arms.

In sequence: *kaṃ namaḥ*, *khaṃ namaḥ*, *gaṃ namaḥ*, *ghaṃ namaḥ*, *ṅaṃ namaḥ*, *caṃ namaḥ*, *chaṃ namaḥ*, *jaṃ namaḥ*, *jhaṃ namaḥ*, *ñaṃ namaḥ*. At the tips of the ten joints of the two feet, in sequence: *ṭaṃ namaḥ*, *ṭhaṃ*... [and so on].
*Namaḥ* to *ḍaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *ḍhaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *ṇaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *taṃ*, *namaḥ* to *thaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *daṃ*, *namaḥ* to *dhaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *naṃ*. On the right side:
*paṃ namaḥ*; on the left side: *phaṃ namaḥ*; on the back: *baṃ namaḥ*; at the navel: *bhaṃ*.
Salutation to *maṃ* in the belly; salutation to *yaṃ* in the heart; salutation to *raṃ* on the right shoulder;
salutation to *laṃ* on the left shoulder; salutation to *vaṃ* in the region of the hump;
salutation to *śaṃ* in the pair of hands to the east of the heart; salutation to *ṣaṃ* in the pair of feet to the east of the heart.
"Saṃ namaḥ," "haṃ namaḥ," "laṃ namaḥ," and "kṣaṃ namaḥ"—this is the sequence for the external placement (vahirnyāsa) of the letters of the Mātṛkā, performed upon the belly and the face. || 116–118 ||
Now, one might ask: how should one perform *prāṇāyāma* during the practice (*sādhana*) of a goddess-mantra?
To this he says, beginning with "the *māyā*-seed," and so forth. A wise and steadfast person, having recited the *māyā*-seed—the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*—sixteen times, that is, sixteen repetitions;
Holding the two nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, the wise one, reciting the seed-syllable thirty-two times, should exhale the air through the right [nostril]. (120)
Repeating this three times over and over again is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Having thus performed the *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform the *ṛṣinyāsa*.
The seers of this mantra are Brahmā and likewise the Brahman-seers;
the meters are the Gāyatrī and others; and the primordial deity is Kālī. 122.
The first seed-syllable is the "seed," which is proclaimed as the power (śakti) Māyā; Kamalā is declared the "pin" (kīlaka). One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in these locations:
on the head, face, heart, private parts, feet, and all the limbs. (123)

One should fill one's own body with air through the left nostril. Then, holding both nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, one should retain the breath (kumbhaka) by making it steady while reciting the *hrīṃ* seed-syllable sixty-four times. Then...
While muttering the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* thirty-two times, one should exhale and release the breath through that same right nostril. One should perform this by repeating it three times.
This is known as *prāṇāyāma* in the practice of the Goddess’s mantra.
The meaning is that the procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma) has been declared. || 119–121 ||

Showing the sequence of the Ṛṣi-nyāsa, he states the Ṛṣi and other details of that mantra with the words "of this mantra" and so forth: "Of this mantra, *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā*, the first seed-syllable is *krīḥ*; the seed-syllable of Māyā is *hrīḥ*; [the seed-syllable of] Kamalā is *śrīḥ*."

The seed-syllable (*bīja*). One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth upon these locations. To specify which locations these are, he says "the head" and so forth. For instance, for this mantra, Brahmā and the Brahman-seers are the seers, the *gāyatrī* and other meters are the meters (*chandas*), and the primordial Kālī is the deity.
*Krī* is the seed-syllable, *hrīḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *śrīḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*).

For the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, this is the application (*viniyoga*) in the rishi-assignment (*ṛṣinyāsa*). *Namaḥ* to Brahmā and to the Brahman-rishis upon the head; *namaḥ* to the rishis upon the mouth.

Salutation to the meters, beginning with Gāyatrī. Salutation to the primordial deity Kālī in the heart. Salutation to the seed-syllable *krīṃ* in the secret place. Salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hrīṃ* in the two feet.
Salutation to the wedge (*kīlaka*) *śrīṃ* in all the limbs.

With the root mantra, one should perform the placement [of mantras] with both hands from the feet up to the head, and from the head down to the feet, either seven times or three times. This is the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), which bestows the attainment of the results as described. (124)
The assignment of limbs (aṅgakalpanā) should be performed with the seed-syllable of whichever vidyā one possesses;
or else, O Dear One, it may be done with the root-mantra, even without the six long vowels. 125.

The wise one should [assign] *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* respectively to the two thumbs, the two index fingers, the two middle fingers, the two ring fingers, the two little fingers, and to the palms and backs of the two hands. (126)
Salutation. For the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, there is the application (viniyoga) in the rishi-nyāsa. Thus ends the procedure for the rishi-nyāsa. 122–123.
Now, he describes the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the words beginning "with the root," etc.
From the feet to the head— that is, starting from the feet up to the head,
and starting from the head down to the feet— one should perform it with both hands using the root mantra.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), placing it sevenfold, that is, seven times, or threefold; [the phrase] "from the head" (*mastakāt*) uses the ablative case in the sense of the accusative or the locative when a verbal suffix ending in *lyap* is elided. 124.

Now, he explains the procedure for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs with the verse beginning "yadbījādyā" and so forth. That which has a seed-syllable as its first part is "yadbījādyā"—that is, the *vidyā* consisting of the mantra.
Because of the prohibition "without the six long vowels in the latter half," it begins with the vowel *ā*.
The meaning is that the assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) should be performed by means of that seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels;
that is, the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), beginning with the thumb and the heart, must be performed. Alternatively, O Dear One, [it may be done] without the six long [vowels].

The assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) should be performed using the root mantra itself, which is devoid of the six long vowels such as ā and the others that are [ordinarily] to be supplied. || 125 ||

He describes the sequence for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) beginning with the thumbs and so forth, by means of the verse beginning with "to the two thumbs" (*aṅguṣṭhābhyām*), which consists of one and a half verses. The meaning is that "namas to the two thumbs" is said with reference to the two thumbs. The same syntactical connection applies to what follows as well.
The wise practitioner, being disciplined, should [perform the ritual] gradually, step by step:
*hrāḥ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *hrīḥ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *hrūḥ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *hraiḥ* to the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*; *hrauḥ* to the two little fingers.
With the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ* and *hraḥ*.
First, *namaḥ* for the heart; *vahnivallabhā* (svāhā) for the head;
*vaṣaṭ* is said for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *hum* is uttered for the armor (*kavaca*). || 127 ||
Having thus performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence with "vauṣaṭ to the three eyes" and "phaṭ to the weapon," one should perform the placement of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa).
The foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (Kūrma), Śeṣa, and likewise the Earth;
then the ocean of nectar, the Island of Jewels (Maṇidvīpa), and the Pārijāta tree. || 129 ||
And having fashioned a house of wish-fulfilling gems and an altar of jewels and rubies,
the Hero should place the lotus seat there within the lotus of his heart.

*Phaṭ* with both palms and backs of the hands; *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā* with the two thumbs—thus one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the six limbs beginning with the thumbs; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. || 126 ||
Now he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs, beginning with the heart and so forth, using the formula "Salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*) and so on.

The meaning is that first, with respect to the heart, "salutation" (*namaḥ*) is uttered. The same construction applies to what follows. *Vahnivallabhā* (the beloved of fire) is *svāhā*. [The mantra is: *hrāḥ*, salutation to the heart.

*Hrīḥ*, *śirase svāhā*; *hrūḥ*, *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *hraih*, *kavacāya huṃ*; *hrauḥ*, *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*; *hraḥḥ*, *astrāya phaṭ*. Or likewise, in sequence: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā*, *namo hṛdayāya*. Thus [the limbs].

The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the six limbs, beginning with the heart. Having thus performed the placement for each of the six limbs according to this procedure, he should carry out the placement of the seat (*pīṭhanyāsa*). || 127 ||

Demonstrating the very sequence for performing the ritual placement (*pīṭhanyāsa*), he says "the foundational power" (*ādhāraśakti*) and so forth: the Hero (*vīra*) should place the foundational power in the lotus of the heart—the heart-lotus;
in that very place, one should also place Kūrma and the others. Therein...
Upon a pedestal of jewels and rubies: "Obeisance to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) within the lotus of the heart;
obeisance to the Tortoise; obeisance to Śeṣa; obeisance to the Earth;
obeisance to the Ocean of Nectar; obeisance to the Jewel Island; obeisance to the Pārijāta tree."
Homage to the House of the Wish-fulfilling Gem; homage to the Lotus Seat upon the pedestal of jewels and rubies. || 129 || 130 ||
On the right and left shoulders, on the left hip and likewise on the right hip, one should place Dharma, Jñāna, Aiśvarya, and Vairāgya in successive order. (131)
On the side of the face and on the right side of the navel, the best of practitioners [should place] those very same [seeds], Dharma and the others, preceded by Naṃ, in their proper order. (132)
One should [meditate upon] Ānandakanda, Sūrya, Soma, and Hutāśana in the heart;
likewise, Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, joined with the Bindu and the initial syllables, as well as the filaments, the pericarp, and the presiding goddesses of the seat (pīṭha) within the petals. 133.
Maṅgalā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Jayantī, Aparājitā,
Nandinī, Nārasiṃhī, and Vaiṣṇavī are the eight presiding goddesses.
"Dakṣa," and so forth: one should sequentially place Dharma and the others upon the right shoulder and the other limbs.
For example: "Homage to Dharma" on the right shoulder; "Homage to Jñāna" on the left shoulder; "Homage to Aiśvarya" on the left hip; and "Homage to Vairāgya" on the right hip.

Regarding the passage beginning with "mukha" and so forth: the best of practitioners should place those very same qualities, such as *adharma* and the rest, preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*) in the mouth and other locations, respectively and in due order. For example: "Oṃ, homage to Adharma in the mouth"; "Oṃ, homage to Ignorance on the left side"; [and] in the navel...
"Salutation to Anaiśvarya (lack of sovereignty) on the right side; salutation to Avairāgya (lack of dispassion)," thus [he says]. || 132 ||
"Ānanda," and so forth: one should place the Ānandakanda and the others in the heart.

Together with the initial syllables joined with the *bindu* (the nasal *m*) and accompanied by their respective vowels, one should place *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* in that very same location. For example: "Obeisance to Ānandakanda" (*ānandakandāya namaḥ*) in the heart.
"Salutation to Sūrya, salutation to Soma, salutation to Agni, salutation to Sat-tva,
salutation to Raj-as, salutation to Tam-as, salutation to the filaments, salutation to the pericarp"—
thus one should place the presiding deities of the pedestal upon the petals of the heart-lotus. (133)
Regarding those who are the presiding goddesses of the seats (*pīṭhanāyikā*) that one should place upon the petals, he says: "With one [verse], Maṅgalā," and so forth.
