Just as on the petals of the heart-lotus, one should place them in sequence: *namaḥ* to Maṅgalā, *namaḥ* to Vijayā, *namaḥ* to Bhadrā, *namaḥ* to Jayantī, *namaḥ* to Aparājitā, and *namaḥ* to Nandinī.
Salutation to Nārasiṃhī; salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; salutation! || 134 ||
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhonmatta, Bhayaṅkara, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhārī—these are the eight Bhairavas.
One should place these upon the tips of the petals and then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 135 ||
Taking fragrant flowers with the *karakacchapa* mudrā and placing both hands at the heart, one should meditate upon the eternal Goddess.
Meditation is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as being with form and without form;
that meditation of yours which is without form transcends the sphere of speech and mind. (137)

Unmanifest, all-pervading, and devoid of such distinctions as "this" or "thus," it is inaccessible to ordinary yogis, yet reachable by them through great hardships and manifold forms of self-restraint.

Regarding "Asitāṅga": one should place these eight Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, upon the tips of the petals; that is, in sequence upon the tips of the petals of the heart-lotus: "Obeisance to Asitāṅga Bhairava," "Obeisance to Ruru Bhairava," and "Obeisance to Caṇḍa Bhairava."
"Salutation to Bhairava, intoxicated by anger; salutation to Bhairava, the terrifying;
salutation to Bhairava, the bearer of the skull; salutation to Bhairava, the formidable;
salutation to Bhairava, the destroyer. Having thus performed the ritual placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*), then—
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 135 ||

He says "Gandha. Then, having taken up and grasped the perfumes and flowers with the *karakacchapa* mudrā as instructed by the Guru, and having placed his hands together at his heart, he should meditate upon the eternal Goddess, who is devoid of beginning and end. || 136 ||

Regarding "meditation" (*dhyāna*): O Goddess, your meditation is said to be twofold, according to the distinction between with-form (*sarūpa*) and formless (*arūpa*). Between those two, that meditation of yours which is the object of meditation (*dhyeya*)—the formless, being devoid of form—is beyond the reach of speech and mind (*avāṅmanasagocara*). Of speech...

And that which has become an object for the mind—that which is meditated upon—is *dhyāna*. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*) by virtue of the rule of frequent usage (*bāhulaka*). || 137 ||

"Unmanifest," and so forth. This means it is devoid of such-and-such [specific qualities], being free from any established tenet that asserts "this is exactly like this. "Inaccessible" means unknowable. "With hardships" refers to vows such as the *prājāpatya* and others. "Tranquility" (*śama*) is the restraint of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). That...
Those for which "peace" (śama) is the first are "those beginning with peace" (śamādayaḥ). And since those [qualities] beginning with peace are many, it is by means of them. 138.
For the purpose of steadying the mind, for the swift attainment of one's desired goal, and for the awakening of subtle meditation, I shall describe gross meditation to you. (139)
For the formless Kālikā, the Mother of Time of great splendor,
a conceptualization of form is fashioned according to her qualities and activities.
I meditate upon her whose limbs are like a cloud, who has the moon as her crest-jewel, three eyes, and wears red garments;
she holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting with her two hands, rests upon a radiant red lotus,
and stands before the dancing [Lord Śiva] while drinking sweet honey-wine.
Beholding the time, I worship Kālikā, whose beautiful face has blossomed like a lotus.
Having meditated thus and placed a flower upon his own head,
the practitioner should worship with supreme devotion through mental offerings.
Regarding "by the mind": "swiftly" connects with what precedes it. || 139 ||

[An objection: "Surely, gross meditation is possible only for an object that possesses form; but since I am devoid of form and empty of beginning and end, how can you speak of gross meditation for me? To this, he says: "For the formless," and so forth. (140)

He describes the coarse meditation (*sthūladhyāna*) itself with the words "Meghāṅgīm. The grammatical construction is: "I worship the primordial Kālikā. Of what nature is Kālikā? She is "Meghāṅgīm," meaning she whose body (*aṅga*) is like a cloud (*megha*). Furthermore, of what nature is she?
She who has the moon as her crest—she upon whose head the moon is situated; furthermore, of what nature is she?
She who has three eyes—she whose eyes are three; again, of what kind is she? [Bestowing] fearlessness and the boon with her two hands.
Bearing [it], bestowing [it]; again, of what kind? Seated upon a blooming red lotus—blooming means fully opened; a red lotus is a crimson water-lily;
seated there, resting upon it. Furthermore, of what nature? Sweetly...
Having drunk the *mādhvīka* liquor produced from *madhūka* flowers, she beheld Mahākāla dancing before her; she was one whose excellent face (*mukhaśreṣṭha*) was thus blossoming with joy. || 141 ||

"Thus": having meditated upon Ādyā Kālī in this manner, the practitioner, having placed upon his own head the flower held with the *karakacchapa* mudrā, should worship the Goddess with supreme devotion through mental offerings. || 142 ||
One should offer the heart-lotus as a seat with the nectar flowing from the thousand-petaled lotus;
one should offer water for the feet at the feet, and present the mind as the guest-offering (arghya). (143)
With that nectar, one should prepare the ceremonial rinsing (ācamana) as well as the water for bathing;
the garment is the element of space (ākāśatattva), and the fragrance is the element of smell (gandhatattva).
One should conceive of the mind as the flower; one should conceive of the vital breaths as the incense.
One should take the element of fire for the purpose of the lamp, and the ocean of nectar as the food offering.

The unstruck sound (anāhatadhvani) is the bell, the wind-element (vāyutattva) is the fly-whisk (cāmara), the activities of the senses are the dance, and likewise, the flickering of the mind is the [fluttering of the whisk]. || 146 ||
One should offer various kinds of flowers for the sake of accomplishing one's own spiritual disposition (bhāva), while remaining free from deceit, egoism, passion, and pride. (147)
Absence of delusion and absence of hypocrisy, as well as absence of hatred and absence of agitation, along with absence of envy and absence of greed—these are proclaimed as the ten flowers. (148)
He demonstrates the worship of the Goddess through mental services by means of the verses beginning with "the heart-lotus" (hṛtpadma). One should offer the heart-lotus as a seat to the Goddess,
[anointing it] with nectar flowing from the thousand-spoked [cakra].
One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the two feet of the Goddess with nectars falling from the thousand-petaled lotus; the same construction applies hereafter as well. || 143 ||
"By that" means by that nectar fallen from the thousand-spoked [cakra]. || 144 ||
The ocean of nectar, the sea of immortality. || 145 || 146 ||

Regarding the word "flower": for the sake of establishing one's own state (*ātmano bhāvasiddhaye*), that is, for the accomplishment of the object intended by oneself, [the author] describes various kinds of flowers to be offered to Kālī in two and a half verses beginning with "free from deceit" (*amāyam*). Of deceit (*māyāyā*)...

Absence of deceit is the first flower. Absence of egoism—egoism being the conceit of excessive self-worship—is the second flower. Passion and anger—their absence is non-passion—is the third flower. Intoxication...
The absence of that mental restlessness caused by wealth, knowledge, and so forth—that is "non-intoxication" (amada), the fourth flower. || 147 ||
Delusion (*moha*) is lack of discrimination; its absence is non-delusion (*amoha*), the fifth flower.
Deceit (*dambha*) is hypocrisy; its absence is non-deceit (*adambha*), the sixth flower.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is aversion; its absence is non-hatred (*adveṣa*), the seventh flower. Agitation (*kṣobha*)...
(107) Non-violence is the supreme flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower;
compassion, forgiveness, and the flower of knowledge—these five flowers are beyond compare.
Thus, one should worship with these fifteen flowers that consist of pure dispositions. (149)
An ocean of nectar, a mountain of meat, a parched mountain of fish, heaps of mudrās, excellent devotees, and likewise milk-rice (pāyasa) smeared with ghee. || 150 ||

Having offered the nectar of the lineage, its flower, the water for washing the seats, and the oblation (bali) for lust and anger—the two creators of obstacles—one should perform the recitation (japa). 151.
The garland is said to consist of the letters, held together by the thread of Kuṇḍalinī.

Futile movement here and there is its absence; freedom from agitation is the eighth flower. Envy is hatred of another's prosperity; its absence, non-envy, is the ninth flower. Greed is [the desire] even when the acquisition of wealth and such occurs in many ways.
Furthermore, the further increase of desire is its absence, which is non-attachment (*alobha*), the tenth flower.
Thus, the ten flowers have been proclaimed. || 148 ||

Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the cessation of causing pain to others. Restraint of the senses (*indriyanigraha*) is the control of the eyes and other faculties regarding their objects. Compassion (*dayā*) is the desire to destroy the suffering of others without motive. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the non-practice of retaliation when harm has been inflicted by another. Knowledge (*jñāna*).

Skill in discerning the essential from the non-essential. "States" (*bhāva*) refers to those things which are cultivated or contemplated; thus, it means "by means of those states that are being cultivated. (149)
Regarding "sudhāmbudhim": *sudhāmbudhim* means an ocean of liquor; *ghṛtāktam* means mixed with clarified butter. || 150 ||
Regarding "the nectar of the Kula" (*kulāmṛtam*): the nectar of the Kula is a specific kind of nectar produced by Śakti.

Its "flower" (*tatpuṣpam*) is the flower of the Kula, meaning the flower of a woman (*strīpuṣpam*). "The water for washing the seats" (*pīṭhakṣālanavāri*) is the water used for washing the specific limbs of a woman. || 151 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of rosary is used for the practice of internal recitation (*japa*) and what the procedure for that recitation is,
he says "the rosary" and so forth.
It is composed of syllables (*varṇamayī*), meaning it takes the form of syllables, and is strung together, held in place by the thread in the form of Kuṇḍalinī.
It is prescribed for recitation performed with a rosary. || 152 ||
Having uttered the mantra together with the *bindu*, one should recite the root mantra;
this, beginning from the letter *a* and ending with the letter *la*, is known as the *anuloma* (direct order). || 153 ||
One should again recite the mantra beginning with the letter *la* and ending with *śrīkaṇṭha*;
this is renowned as "in reverse order," and the letter *kṣa* is called the "meru. (154)
Then, having recited one hundred and eight times the eight groups [of syllables] ending with the final letters of each group, together with the root-mantra, one should offer it with this.
O Mother Kālī, primordial one, who dwells within the innermost self of all and whose nature is the light within one’s own heart, accept this internal recitation; salutations be unto you! (156)
Having offered this recitation, one should prostrate with eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga) with devotion;
having thus performed the internal worship, one should commence the external worship.

"Accompanied by the bindu" means that one should utter the phonemes from 'a' to 'la' together with the anusvāra (bindu), and then recite the root mantra; one should chant it as follows: *aḥ / hrīḥ / śrīḥ / krīḥ / parameśvari svāhā*. This very method of chanting is known as *anuloma* (in the direct order). || 153 ||

"Again," and so forth. Again, beginning with the letter *la* situated at the end of the syllable *ha*, one should recite the mantra while pronouncing the letters ending in *a*—up to *śrīkaṇṭha*—along with the *bindu*. For example: *laṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari*.
*Svāhā* | *Haṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā*—thus it is. And this is renowned as the *viloma* (reverse) [mantra]. The letter *kṣa* is said to be the *meru* (axis) of the garland. || 154 ||

"Eight," and so forth. Immediately thereafter, one should recite the root mantra, which consists of eight syllables, together with the final letters of the eight groups—namely *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *ṣa*—along with their bindus (*visargas*), in the forms of *aḥ*, *ṅ*, *ña*, *ṇ*, *na*, *ma*, *va*, and *la*. By means of this...
Immediately after this, by means of the mantra that will be spoken. || 155 ||

He states the mantra for the dedication of the recitation (*japa*) itself as "O you whose abode is the inner self of all" (*sarvāntarātmanilaye*). This means: O you whose abode—meaning the heart, the inner self, the dwelling place—is within all beings. || 156 || 157 ||
(109) Listen now as the consecration of the special *arghya* is first described;
by its mere installation, the deity becomes well-pleased. (158)
Upon seeing the arghya vessel, the yoginīs, the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā, and even the Bhairavas dance with joy and bestow spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). || 159 ||
On the ground in front of one’s left, with the water of the general *arghya*, [one should draw] a triangle containing the syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), a circle, and a square. (160)
Having drawn [the diagram], one should worship there, preceded by the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ),
ending with the word "namaḥ" and the syllable "ṅe" for Ādhāraśakti.
Then, having placed the washed support upon the mandala,
[one should worship] the fire-mandala ending with the syllable *maṃ*, consisting of ten kalās.
Having worshipped with [mantras] ending in "namaḥ," the practitioner should wash the arghya vessel and place it upon the support (ādhāra) there with the Astra mantra. || 163 ||
Regarding "of the special arghya": therein, at the commencement of the external worship. 158 || 159 ||

He explains the consecration of the special *arghya* with the words beginning "on one's left" (*svavāme*). On one's left means on the left side of oneself. On the ground in front means on the earth directly before one.
By means of the water of the general *arghya*, the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) is placed within the womb [of the vessel].
Having first drawn such a triangular mandala, and having drawn a circular [mandala] all around its exterior, and outside of that a square four-cornered mandala—
therein, in that mandala, she whose [mantra] is preceded by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, the seed of *māyā*.

One should worship the Support Power (Ādhāraśakti), which is of such a nature—ending in the feminine nominative case—and which has the word "namaḥ" at its conclusion or end. The meaning is that one should honor the Support Power with the mantra: *hrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*. || 160 || 161 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): after the worship of the *ādhāra-śakti* (the foundational power), one should place and establish the washed vessel upon its mandala; having first uttered "mam," and then having uttered the fire-mandala ending in the suffix *-ṅ*, and then...

Having addressed the vessel as "to the one whose orb is like the sun" and "to the essence of the digit at the end of the twelve," he should worship it with the word "namas" at the end; he should then fill the vessel with the root mantra itself. (164)
Having filled three parts with impure substances and the remaining part with water,
the practitioner, O Ambikā, should offer perfumes and flowers there and worship with this [mantra].
The sixth vowel joined with the bindu, ending in the letter ṅa, is indeed the lunar mandala;
at the end of the sixteenth [digit], from the word "kalā," one should also say "ātmane namaḥ. (166)

One should say, "to the one whose self consists of ten digits. By this conjunction, the mantra becomes: *maṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane*. Having worshipped the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*) in the foundation (*ādhāra*) with this mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should [purify] the arghya-vessel with the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*.
One should wash it. The practitioner should place the washed arghya vessel upon that support. || 162 || 163 ||

"Amityādi" and so forth. First, having uttered "am arkamaṇḍalāya," one should then say "dvādaśānte kalātmane. Through this conjunction, the mantra "am arkamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane" is produced. By means of this very mantra ending in "namaḥ," [one should perform the worship].
One should worship—that is, honor—the solar orb, which is the presiding deity of the vessel and the arghya-vessel;
one should fill the arghya-vessel with the root mantra alone. || 164 ||
Now, with what substance should one fill the vessel? To this he says: "one-third.

Having filled one-third of the vessel with *ali*, that is, with wine, the practitioner should fill the remainder with water. There, having placed fragrance and flowers in that water, immediately after this—
One should worship the moon-maṇḍala right there with the mantra that is about to be recited. || 165 ||

He states the mantra for the worship of the moon-maṇḍala with the words beginning "the sixth," etc. Having first stated the sixth vowel accompanied by a bindu—that is, endowed with the anusvāra—one should then say "to the Self (ātmane namaḥ)" after the word *kalā*. By way of combination, [the mantra is]: *ūṃ candramaṇḍalāya*.
"Obeisance to the one whose self consists of sixteen digits"—this is the mantra used for the worship of the lunar disc. || 166 ||
Then, having prepared a leaf from the *śrīphala* tree smeared with red sandalwood paste, along with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), one should place them therein. (167)
Having invoked the sacred site (tīrtha) with the root mantra and visualized the Goddess there,
one should worship her with scents and flowers and recite the root mantra twelve times.
Having shown the *dhenu-mudrā*, he should display the incense and the lamp;
then the practitioner, having poured a little of that water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, [should proceed]. || 169 ||
The knower of mantras should sprinkle himself and the objects to be offered with that [water];
until the completion of the worship, he must not move the arghya vessel. (170)
O lady of pure smiles, this consecration of the special arghya has been explained;
now I shall describe the King of Yantras, which bestows all human goals.
The womb of illusion (māyāgarbha) is a triangle, and outside of that is a pair of circles;
between those two, sixteen filaments are arranged in pairs of pairs.
Then, thus: thereafter, having prepared a leaf belonging to the *bilva* tree associated with the fruit of Śrī, smeared with red sandalwood (*raktacandana*),
accompanied by unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and provided with *dūrvā* grass and flowers, one should place [the offering] therein.
One should cause it to be placed, that is, one should establish it, at the foremost part of the special *arghya* offering. || 167 ||
"By the root [mantra]" means: having visualized—that is, having contemplated—therein, in the water for the special *arghya* offering. || 168 ||

Saying "O Cow," having displayed the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās upon the special *arghya* water, one should likewise display the incense and lamp right there. That water is the special *arghya* water. || 169 ||
"Ātmānam" means one should sprinkle or moisten;
that is, with the water poured into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel. || 170 ||
Regarding the word "viśeṣa": it means that which bestows all human goals—that is, the giver of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 171 ||

He describes the procedure for drawing the King of Yantras with the words beginning "māyāgarbham" and so forth. One should first draw a triangular mandala that has the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* (māyā) in its interior; then, outside of that, one should draw a pair of circles surrounding it on all sides.

One should draw two circular maṇḍalas. In the center of those two circular maṇḍalas, one should draw [deities] in pairs according to their sequence; outside of that, an eight-petaled lotus; and outside of that, a square enclosure (bhūpura).
It was provided with four gates, beautifully lined, and most enchanting.
In a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, smeared with the secretions of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, and joined with self-arisen flowers, sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron; || 174 ||

Or else, being free from indolence, while reciting the root mantra, one should draw the king of diagrams with a golden stylus or even with a thorn from a *mālūra* fruit, for the sake of attaining the state of the deity. (175)
Alternatively, one should have the yantra fashioned by a skilled artisan upon crystal, coral, or lapis lazuli, using lines for the *utkīla* [piercing] marks.

One should draw sixteen filaments. Outside of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus outside the two circular mandalas. Outside of that lotus, one should draw [the enclosure] provided with four gates on all sides and well-lined with lines.
One should draw a square enclosure (bhūpura) endowed with beautiful lines, most charming and exceedingly delightful.

Now, as to the question of on what substrate this yantra should be drawn and by what instrument, he says "svārṇe" and so forth. It should be smeared with *kuṇḍa* and *gola*, that is, smeared with specific flowers fashioned from particular powers (*śakti*), or with self-arisen flowers (*svayambhūkusuma*).
In a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper— either smeared with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron combined with specific flowers fashioned from *śakti*,
or smeared with pure *kuśīda* or red sandalwood—
one [should offer] with a golden [spoon].

Reciting the root mantra, one should draw the king of diagrams (*yantrarāja*) with a stylus made of gold, or with a thorn from a *mālūra* or a *bilva* tree, for the sake of accomplishing the state of the deity and for the fulfillment of the deity’s pleasure. (174–175)

Alternatively: Or else, one should have a mechanical device made from crystal, coral, or lapis lazuli by a skilled artisan—a craftsman endowed with great proficiency in his own craft—using incised lines, that is, lines carved out by engraving. || 176 ||
Having established it in a pure location, one should place it within the temple;
thus, malevolent spirits, as well as the fears of planetary influences and diseases, will perish. (177)
His mansion rejoices in the happiness, prosperity, sons, and grandsons of the giver;
by the grace of the yantra, he shall become a donor, a protector, and illustrious. (178)
Having thus drawn the yantra and placed it before him on a jeweled lion-throne,
and having worshipped the deities of the pedestal according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the pedestal,
he should worship the root deity in the center of the pericarp.

I shall describe the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) as well as the ritual procedure for the wheel (cakra), by the mere performance of which the deity becomes well-pleased; the perfection of mantra will surely occur and the fulfillment of one's desires arises. (180)
Since this was fashioned by Viśvakarman by taking a portion from each of the gods, it is therefore called a *kalaśa*.

"Śubha," and so forth. Having fashioned the King of Yantras, which is "established in auspiciousness"—meaning that such a state of auspicious establishment has arisen for it—whosoever installs it within a residence, for him the malevolent spirits perish; such is the grammatical connection. || 177 || 178 ||

"Thus," and so forth. Having thus drawn the yantra according to the prescribed method and having placed it before one on a jeweled lion-throne (ratnasiṃhāsana), and having worshipped the deities of the pedestal (pīṭhadevatā) according to the procedure stated for the deposition upon the pedestal (pīṭhanyāsa), [one should worship] the root deity in the center of the pericarp, within the interior of the seed-vessel of the lotus.
One should worship. || 179 ||
Now, he begins to explain the procedure for the worship of the Great Goddess by means of the five principles (pañcatattva), beginning with the word "kalaśa" and so forth. || 180 ||
He explains the term *kalaśa* with the verse beginning "A portion" (*kalām*), etc. (verse 181).

Thirty-six finger-breadths in length, sixteen finger-breadths in height, with a neck of four finger-breadths and a mouth of six finger-breadths; the base is measured at five finger-breadths—this is the rule for the construction of the jar. (182)

For the pleasure of the deity, one should have a jar made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, clay, stone, or even glass; it should be unbroken and without flaws. One should avoid stinginess regarding the expense. (183)
A golden vessel is said to bestow enjoyment, a silver one grants liberation;
a copper one should be known as producing affection, and one made of bell-metal increases nourishment.
Glass is said to be effective for subjugation rites, stone for the rite of immobilization,
and earthenware— when well-observed and well-polished— for all ritual purposes.
On one's own left side, there is a hexagon; in its center is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having drawn a circle outside of that, one should then draw a square outside of that.
Now, he describes the method for constructing the jar with the words beginning with "thirty-six" (*ṣaṭtriṃśat*).
That which has a measurement of thirty-six finger-breadths is "thirty-six finger-breadths"; such is its length, and it is likewise its width.

"Of such a nature": one should have a jar made that is sixteen finger-breadths high—that is, whose height has a measurement of sixteen *aṅgulas*. The remainder [of the description] is that the neck (*kaṇṭha*) of that jar should be four finger-breadths, meaning its mouth is measured at four *aṅgulis*.

One should fashion the base at the lower part to be six finger-breadths (ṣaḍaṅgula) in measure, while the [upper] part should be made five finger-breadths in measure; this very rule is prescribed for the construction of the jar.

Indeed, in response to the inquiry as to which specific objects the jar should be fashioned for, he says "made of gold," and so forth. *Akṣata* means unbroken; *avraṇa* means free from holes. || 183 ||
"Golden" means made of gold; "a jar" is the word understood to complete the sense. || 184 || 185 ||
"On one's own left," and so forth. Having drawn a hexagonal mandala on one's own left side,
and having drawn a single void (śūnya) representing the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) in the center of that hexagonal mandala,
[one draws] a circle outside that hexagonal mandala.
Having drawn a mandala, one should then draw a four-cornered mandala outside of that as well.
Having fashioned the mandala with either vermilion powder or red sandalwood paste, one should worship the deities of the support (ādhāradevatā) therein.
One should extract the Māyā and the Ādhāra-śakti, ending with "namo. || 187 ||
Having washed the base with *namaḥ*, one should place it upon the mandala;
having washed the jar with the *astra* mantra, one should set it down upon that base.

Reciting the root mantra while pronouncing the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, joined with the nasal bindu, the practitioner of mantra should fill [the vessel] by means of the causal syllable.
At the Ādhāra, Kumbha, and Tīrtha [cakras], the wise one, devoted to the state of the Goddess, should worship the spheres of Fire, Sun, and Moon as before. (190)
Having adorned the water-pot with red sandalwood, vermilion, red garlands, and ointments, one should perform the fivefold refinement (pañcīkaraṇa).

Now, with what substance should this mandala be drawn? To that he says: "Sindūra," and so forth. Regarding that mandala: Now, by which mantra should one worship the supporting deity? To that he says: "Māyām," etc. First, one should extract the seed-syllable *māyā*, *hrīḥ*; then [the vocative] *ṅe*.

One should extract the *ādhāraśakti* ending with *namaḥ*. By means of the conjunction, the mantra "hrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ" is produced for the worship of the presiding deity of the base (*ādhāra*). || 187 ||
"Namaseti" means with the mantra "namaḥ" (namas), as stated by Manu; "astreṇa" means with the mantra "phaṭ".

Regarding the passage beginning with "kṣakāra": while reciting the root mantra together with those letters whose first is the letter *kṣa* and whose last is the letter *a*, joined with the bindu—that is, accompanied by the anusvāra—namely: *kṣaṃ laṃ haṃ saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ maṃ*.
Bhaṃ baṃ phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aṃḥ aṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ.
Reciting the mantra "Aṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Krīḥ Parameśvari Svāhā," the practitioner-mantrin should fill the jar with the causal substance, which is wine. || 189 ||
He supports it; "tīrtha" means liquor. As before, it is as in the consecration of the special *arghya* offering. || 190 || 191 ||

Having struck it with a blade of *darbha* grass while uttering "phaṭ," one should envelop it with the seed-syllable "hūṃ. Having gazed upon it with divine vision while uttering "hrīṃ," one should perform the sprinkling with "namaḥ. (192)
One should offer perfume three times with the root mantra; this is declared to be the "fivefold process" (pañcīkaraṇa).
Having bowed to the jar and offered a red flower, one should purify it.
Oṃ! There is but one Supreme Brahman, eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle;
by means of that, I destroy for you the sin of killing a Brahmin born of your thought. 194.
O Goddess, who dwells in the center of the solar disc, who arises from the abode of Varuṇa, and who consists of the seed-syllable Amā—may [this person] be liberated from the curse of Śukra. 195.
Now, what indeed is this "fivefold compounding" (*pañcīkaraṇa*)? To that he says "phaṭ," and so forth.

Having struck the jar with the *phaṭ* mantra and with *darbha* grass—that is, *kuśa* grass—one should envelop it, meaning one should surround it, with the *hrūṃ* seed-syllable using the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*. [One should do this] with the *hrīṃ* seed-syllable.

Having gazed at the flask with divine vision and having beheld it with a reverential mantra, one should perform the sprinkling and consecration of the flask. One should offer perfume into the flask three times with the root mantra. This very [is the procedure].
The "fivefold process" (pañcīkaraṇa) has been described; the ellipsis is that one should purify the wine. || 192 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which specific mantras one should use to purify the liquor, he states the purification mantras themselves in their proper order, beginning with "ekameva": "O Goddess Sudhā, [you who are] certainly (dhruvam) eternal (nityam),
consisting of the gross and the subtle (sthūla-sūkṣma-mayam), that is, whose nature is both gross and subtle."

The grammatical connection is as follows: "I shall destroy that sin of Brahman-slaughter arising from your hair by means of that Supreme Brahman which exists as one alone and without a second. || 194 ||
"Sūrya," and so forth. O you who are born from the abode of Varuṇa—the abode of Varuṇa being his home, the ocean; O you whose origin and birth are from that!
For this very reason, O you who consist of the seed of Amā—Amā being the immortal, eternal, lunar sixteenth digit (kalā).

That which is the seed-syllable (bīja) of the moon is its very nature; therefore, O Goddess Sudhā, who dwells in the center of the solar disc—that is, who resides within the solar disc—be released from the curse of Śukra, let yourself become liberated. || 195 ||
If the *praṇava* is the seed of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman, by that truth, O Goddess, may your sin of killing a Brahmin be removed. (196)

Hrīṃ! Haṃsaḥ! The pure one dwelling in the light, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling on the altar, the guest dwelling in the house, the dweller among men, the dweller in the best, the dweller in Truth, the dweller in the sky, born from the waters.
Born of the cow, born of the cosmic order, born of the mountain—He is the Great Cosmic Order. || 197 ||
With the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, conjoined with the six long vowels, one should utter the word "liberated" at the end of the phrase "released from the curse of Brahmā.
Then, after saying "Salutation to Sudhādevī," one should recite this seven times to dispel the curse of Brahmā. (198)
The goad (aṅkuśa) joined with six long vowels, followed by the illustrious Māyā;
then the nectar (sudhā), and thereafter the phrase "release from the Brahman’s curse";
then the pair [of words] "causing the flow of nectar," ending with the *dviṭha* (svāhā)—this is declared to be the mantra. (199)

Regarding the phrase "of the Vedas": O Goddess Sudhā, by that truth which is the seed of the Vedas in the form of the *praṇava*—that *praṇava* which is the very nature of Brahman, the blissful one whose essence is bliss—may your slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*) be removed; may it perish.

Regarding the term "by Vāruṇa": at the end of the word *brahmaśāpaviśabdasya*, one should utter the word *mocitāyai*. After that, one should say *sudhādevyai namaḥ*. By this combination, the mantra *brahmaśāpavimocitāyai sudhādevyai namaḥ* is formed. This...

This mantra—consisting of the seed-syllable of Varuṇa (*va*) conjoined with each of the six long vowels (*vī*, *vū*, *vai*, *vau*, *vaḥ*), or as appropriate—is recited seven times as follows: "Obeisance to the Goddess Sudhā, who is liberated from the curse of Brahmā. When recited thus sevenfold, this mantra removes the curse of Brahmā.
One becomes a liberator from the curse of Brahmā. || 198 ||

Regarding "the goad": first, one should utter the word *kro*, joined with the six long vowels (*aṅkuśam*). After that, one should utter the word *sudhā* (nectar), joined with the illustrious *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) and the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*. Then, one should utter the words "release from the curse of Kṛṣṇa. Thereafter, [one utters] *amṛtaṃ*.

One should speak thus; then one should speak the pair while causing [the substance] to flow. Having thus liberated [the disciple] from the curse through this very application (*yojanā*), one should worship there with a concentrated mind the deity Ānandabhairava as well as Ānandabhairavī. (200)
At the end of the word *hasakṣamala*, one should utter *varayū*.
The mantra is considered to be *Ānandabhairava* ending in *ṅe* and concluding with *vaṣaṭ*. || 201 ||
Her face is turned away and her beautiful-eyed ear is turned toward the left;
the mantra for her worship ends with "vauṣaṭ" and is addressed to the Goddess Sudhā. (202)
Having meditated there on the state of their essential identity (sāmarasya) and having visualized the substance as drenched in that nectar,
one should recite the root mantra twelve times over it.

The mantra is formed as: *krā krī krū krai krau kraḥ śrī hrī sudhākṛṣṇaśāpaṃ mocaya amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya*. This mantra is said to end with the two *ṭha*-syllables (*svāhā*) and is thus declared to conclude with *svāhā*. || 199 ||

"Thus" means: having liberated [the substance] from the curse of Brahmā by means of the six mantras previously mentioned according to the sequence thus stated, one who is composed should [visualize] therein, in that liquor,
the god Ānandabhairava and likewise the goddess Ānandabhairavī.
One should sacrifice while remaining attentive. || 200 ||

He states the mantra for the sacrifice of both [deities] with two verses, beginning with "hasa": at the end of the word *hasakṣamala*, one should utter the joined term *varayū*; then, one should utter *ānandabhairava* in the dative case (*ṅe*). By way of conjunction: *hasakṣamalavarayū*.
The mantra "Ānandabhairavāya" has been produced;
this mantra is considered to end with *vaṣaṭ*, that is, it concludes with the word *vaṣaṭ*. (201)

"Of this," and so forth. Of this [mantra] *hasakṣamalavarayūm*, its "face"—meaning the beginning—is to be recited in reverse. In the ear, in place of the letter *ū*, the left eye, the letter *ī*, is to be recited.
Then, one should recite *sudhādevyai*. By way of this arrangement:
The mantra is born as: *sahakṣamalavarayī ānandabhairavyai sūdhādevyai*.

For the worship of this Ānandabhairavī, this very mantra is intended to end with *vauṣaṭ*, that is, with the word *vauṣaṭ*. As for the meditation (*dhyāna*), it will follow for both [mantras] hereafter.
He will say [this]. || 202 ||

Regarding the term *sāmarasya*: having meditated upon the *sāmarasya*— the state of oneness— of those two, Ānandabhairavī and Ānandabhairava, within that wine, one [partakes of] that substance which is flooded with their nectar, that is, flooded with the nectar whose nature is that *sāmarasya*.
Having clearly visualized and contemplated the liquor, one should recite the root mantra twelve times over that liquor. || 203 ||
Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra while perceiving [the deity] as the divine being, one should then display the incense and the lamp, preceded by the ringing of the bell. (204)
Thus, the consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha) is always required for the worship of the gods,
as well as for vows, fire-offerings (homa), marriages, and likewise for festive rites.
Having brought meat and placed it upon a triangular maṇḍala in front,
one should sprinkle it with *phaṭ* and consecrate it three times with the seed-syllables of wind (*ya*) and fire (*ra*).
Then, having enveloped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should protect it with the Astra mantra; having rendered it nectarine with the Dhenu mudrā, one should utter this mantra: || 207 ||
O Goddess who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu, and O Goddess who dwells upon Śaṅkara, purify my flesh; establish that supreme state of Viṣṇu. (208)

"By the root [mantra]" means: then, with the perception that it is the deity, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) into the liquor (*madya*) with the root mantra; preceded by the ringing of a bell, one should also display incense and lamps over it. [This refers to] the *tīrtha*, which is the liquor. 204–205.
Now, he describes the procedure for preparing the meat in three [verses], beginning with "the meat":

Having brought the meat and placed it before one on a triangular mandala, one should sprinkle or consecrate it with the *phaṭ* mantra, [purifying it] by means of the two seed-syllables of air and fire, *ya* and *ra*.
One should consecrate it three times with the two seed-syllables. || 206 ||

Regarding "with the armor" (*kavacena*): then, having enveloped the flesh with the armor-seed syllable *huṃ*, one should encircle it with the *avaguṇṭhana*-mudrā and protect it with the *astra*-mantra, the *phaṭ*-mantra;
[and] with the *dhenu*-mudrā and the *vaṃ*-seed syllable.
Having rendered the meat immortal, one should utter—meaning recite—this mantra which will be described immediately hereafter. || 207 ||

He states that very mantra: "Of Viṣṇu," and so forth. That Goddess who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu, and that Goddess who dwells upon the chest of Śaṅkara—may she purify the flesh for me. By offering flesh thus purified, my [offering] shall have her as its primary essence.
Make it the station of Viṣṇu.
Having thus brought a fish and consecrated it with the aforementioned mantra, the wise practitioner should empower that fish with this mantra: (209)
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant one who increases prosperity.
May he deliver me from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality. 210.
In the same way, O Dear One, having taken up the mudrā, one should purify with this [mantra]: "Oṃ!
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched out in the sky. (211)
The wise, praising with inspired hymns and ever-watchful, kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 212.
Alternatively, one should purify all principles by means of the root alone;
for what need has one who has faith in the root for the leaves and branches? (213)
Whatever substance has been purified by the root mantra alone is declared by me to be most excellent for pleasing the deity. || 214 ||
Just as time is short and there is no opportunity for the practitioner, one should purify everything with the root mantra and offer it to Mahādevī. || 215 ||

Now, he states the procedure for the consecration of fish with the verse beginning "In this way" (ittham) and so forth. "With the aforementioned mantra" means with the mantra described for the purification of meat; by this, that which was stated previously is intended. || 209 ||
He states that very mantra: "We worship Tryambaka... (RV 7.59.12). || 210 ||

He states the mantra for the purification of the *mudrā*: "That of Viṣṇu... (*tad viṣṇoḥ*). The wise (*sūrayaḥ*), meaning the learned, always behold that most excellent station of Viṣṇu, which is imperceptible to the ignorant.
Here he provides an illustration with the words "in heaven" (*divi*) and so forth: the eye spread out (*ātataṃ*) in heaven.
It remains beyond the range of the blind, like the sun. || 211 || 212 ||
Alternatively: "all principles" refers to wine and the other [substances]. (213–215)
(121) And herein there is no transgression, nor is there any defect caused by the deficiency of auxiliary factors;
"Truth, truth, and again truth"—such is the teaching of Śaṅkara. (216)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The True Consecration of the Extraction of Mantras and the Installation of the Vessel," in the Śrī Mahānirvāṇatantra— the supreme among all supreme tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas— within the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva.
"No," [it is said]. Here, it refers to the offering of all the *tattvas*, which have been purified by the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) itself, to Mahādevī. || 216 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
The sixth chapter:
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord, if you have compassion for me, please explain in detail that fivefold reality (pañcatattva) which was mentioned by you regarding the rites of worship and so forth.
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī are the three excellent types of liquor;
that same liquor is said to be of various kinds, such as that produced from palm and dates.
Likewise, according to the distinction of regions and the variety of different substances, this [offering] is proclaimed in many ways as being praiseworthy for the worship of the deity. (3)
By whomsoever it may have been produced, or by whomsoever it may have been brought, there is no distinction of caste here; once purified, it bestows all accomplishments.
Oṃ, salutations to Brahman.
Desiring to hear specifically about the five principles (*pañcatattva*), beginning with wine, the illustrious Goddess spoke, starting with the words "That which by you... and so forth. (1)
Thus requested by the Goddess, Śrī Sadāśiva said: "Gauḍī," and so forth.

Gauḍī is that which is produced from molasses; paiṣṭī is that which is produced from flour; mādhvī is that which is produced from the flowers of the *madhūka* tree. These are the three kinds, the three varieties, of the excellent *surā*.
The best [liquor] has been described; that very liquor is indeed *surā*. Demonstrating the various types of *surā*, he says "tāla-kharjūra" and so forth. This is *surā*. (2) (3)
"By which" means brought or led; here, it refers to the realm of the gods. || 4 ||
Meat is said to be of three kinds: that which moves in water, on land, and in the sky.
Therefore, whatever has been brought forth by whomever, having been slain for the sake of pleasing the deities, all of that shall indeed be [efficacious]; of this there is no doubt. (5)
The will of the practitioner is powerful regarding an object to be given to the deity;
whatever substance is dear to oneself, that very thing one should offer to the beloved [deity]. (6)
O Goddess, in the ritual of offering the sacrifice, the male is prescribed as the sacrificial animal;
however, the female animal must not be killed there, according to the teaching of Śambhu.
The three types of fish considered superior are the śāla, the pāṭhīna, and the rohita;
those that are devoid of bones are middling, while those with many bones are inferior.
Nevertheless, even these should be offered to the Goddess, provided they have been thoroughly roasted.
The *mudrā* is also said to be of three kinds, according to the distinction of superior and so forth.
It should be auspicious, resembling the orb of the moon, produced from rice grains,
or else made from barley or wheat, cooked in ghee and pleasing to the mind.
This supreme mudrā consists of medium grains such as rice and so forth;
it is proclaimed as inferior when made from other seeds that have been parched.

He demonstrates the threefold nature of meat with the verse beginning "jalacara" and so forth: *jalacara* is the meat of turtles and the like; *bhūcara* is the meat of goats and the like; *khecara* is the meat of partridges, hārītas, and the like.
All that is meat. (5) One should prepare—that is, offer—it.
Regarding the term "balidāna" (sacrificial offering): "puruṣaḥ" refers to one delimited by masculinity; [this applies] there, in the injunction for the sacrificial offering.
Regarding "mudrā": that which resembles the lunar orb—that is, similar to the moon's disc—is white and made from rice grains, such as *śaṣkulī* and the like;
that which arises from parched grain and the like is *lāja* and so forth. (9–10)
Meat, fish, ritual gestures (mudrā), and whatever fruits and roots there may be—this is declared to be the purity of these items when offered as nectar to the deity. (11)
O Goddess, without purification, the offering of the cause, the worship, and likewise the libation become fruitless; the deity does not become pleased.
Drinking liquor without purification is merely consuming poison;
the practitioner becomes chronically ill and dies before long from a short lifespan. (13)
O Maheśānī, in this powerful Kali age devoid of vitality, the remaining reality is to be known as one's own exclusive [nature], free from all defects. (14)
Alternatively, O beloved of Prāṇa, the self-originated (svayambhū) and other flowers mentioned here are prescribed as substitutes for them; such a substitute is proclaimed to be kusīda.
One should never offer unpurified substances—whether roots, leaves, flowers, or fruits—to Mahādevī; for by offering them, one will surely become a denizen of hell.
"Meat," and so forth. When nectar is offered to the deity—that is, when wine is presented—these [substances] beginning with meat are declared, or stated, to have the designation "purity. || 11 ||

Showing the purpose for establishing the perception of purity regarding meat and other such things, he says "without purity" and so forth: "Without purity, [there would be] meat and the like; without a cause, the offering of wine. (12)
"Pureness" refers to meat and so forth. "Before long" means after only a very short time has passed. || 13 ||

Regarding the phrase "the remaining reality": the remaining reality is sexual union (*maithuna*). "Powerless" means devoid of energy (*nirvīrya*) and luster (*nistejasi*). "One's own" means one's personal power (*śakti*). || 14 ||

"Or else," and so forth. Here, regarding the prescription of the remaining principles (*śeṣatattva*): "in its substitute" refers to the substitute for flowers, such as *svayambhū* (mushroom) and the like; "usury" (*kusīda*) refers to red sandalwood. || 15 ||
Regarding the practitioner who offers unrefined liquor, meat, and so forth to Mahādevī, the text states that he goes to hell, beginning with the words "aśodhitāni" (unrefined). || 16 ||

One should perform the installation of the Śrīpātra with one's own [consort] endowed with virtue and character, or one should consecrate [the disciple] with the Kāraṇa [vessel] or with the water from the general arghya vessel. (17)
First, having uttered the *bālā* [mantra], one should then say "to Tripurā";
at the conclusion of the word "namaḥ," one should pronounce this *śakti*.
At the end of the word "pavitrīkuru," say "mama śaktiṃ kuru" twice. || 19 ||
When a woman who has not been initiated utters the Māyā-mantra into the ear, other Śaktis should be worshipped; they are not worthy of being subjected to the act of beating.
Then, between the self and the yantra, having drawn a triangle containing the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*),
a circle, and a hexagon, one should draw a square on the outside.
"Śrīpātra," and so forth. "Together with his own Śakti"—the ellipsis being "he should consecrate his own Śakti. "With the cause," that is, with wine. || 17 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to by which mantra one's own power (śakti) should be consecrated, he states the mantra for that consecration in the verse beginning with "At the outset" and continuing for one and a half verses: "At the outset, having uttered 'Bālā'—that is, *aiṃ*, *klīṃ*, *sauḥ*—one should then say 'to Tripurā'. Then, at the end of that... [he speaks of] what has been recited.

At the end, following the word *namaḥ*, one should utter or recite this *śakti* [mantra]. And at the end of the word *pavitrīkuru* which is recited thereafter, one should say "make my power [effective] (*mama śaktiṃ kuru*). Then one should say "dviṭhaḥ svāhā. By way of construction: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripurāyai namaḥ imām*.
"Sanctify my power; make my power [effective], svāhā!"—this is the mantra that arose for one's own consecration. || 18 || 19 ||
"Uninitiated" refers to Māyā, whose seed-syllable is Hrīḥ. The others seated there are non-different from one's own self in the acts of striking and sexual union. || 20 ||

"Then," and so forth. Immediately thereafter, between the self and the Yantra-king— that is, between oneself and the King of Yantras— one should draw a mandala consisting of a triangle whose interior contains *māyā* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*), a circle outside of that, and a hexagon outside of that.
Beyond that as well, one should draw a square mandala with four corners.

In the corners of the [triangular] diagram, the best of practitioners should worship Pūrṇaśaila, Uḍḍīyāna, Jālandhara, and Kāmarūpa— each accompanied by the word "namaḥ" at the end and enriched with its own initial seed-syllable (bīja). (22)
One should worship the six limbs in the six corners with the root mantra itself; then one should worship the Triangle, Māyā, and the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) with the mantra ending in "namaḥ."
Having established the vessel whose base has been washed with *namaḥ*, one should worship there, as before,
the digits (*kalā*) of Fire upon the circle, using their respective initial syllables.
"In the corner" means: then,
it should be joined with the seed-syllable consisting of the first letter of one's own name related to the name of oneself, enriched by the seed-syllables of one's own name and so forth,
ending with the dative case and the word "namaḥ," and accompanied by the dative case.

The best of practitioners should worship Pūrṇaśaila, Uḍḍīyāna, Jālandhara, and Kāmarūpa— which have "namo" at the end [of their names]— in the four corners of the square maṇḍala, specifically in its four corners. Pūṃ.
With the mantra "Oṃ, salutation to Pūrṇaśaila-pīṭha," one worships Pūrṇaśaila in the first corner; with "Uṃ, salutation to Uḍḍīyāna-pīṭha," one worships Uḍḍīyāna in the second corner;
and with "Jāṃ, salutation to Jālandhara-pīṭha," one worships Jālandhara in the third corner.
The meaning is that one should worship Kāmarūpa in the fourth corner with the mantra: "Obeisance to Kāmarūpa-pīṭha. || 22 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the six corners": then, one should worship the six limbs—the presiding deities of the hexagon—within the six corners of the hexagonal mandala using the mantras: *hrāḥ namaḥ*, *hrīḥ namaḥ*, *hrūḥ namaḥ*, *hraiḥ namaḥ*, *hrauḥ namaḥ*, and *hraḥ namaḥ*.

One should worship the triangle and the presiding deity of the triangle with the root mantra itself. Regarding "māyām" and so forth: first, one should utter the *māyā* seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, and then the *ādhāraśakti* (supporting power) together with the word *namaḥ* at the end. By way of combination, [the mantra is] *hrīṃ*.
The mantra "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti" is thus produced. With this mantra, one should worship the deity of the foundation (ādhāradevatā) within the maṇḍala. || 23 ||
"Namasa" means: then, having washed the *ādhāra* with the *namas* mantra,

one should place it upon that mandala as before— just as when setting up the water jar (*kalaśa*)— and then [place] the digits of fire (*vahneḥ kalāḥ*) upon the *vṛtta*, that is, upon the circular mandala placed on the *ādhāra*.
Dhūmrārcis, Jvalinī, Sūkṣmā, Jvālinī, Viṣphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā. (25)
The ten digits (kalās) of Fire are to be worshipped with [mantras] ending in "namaḥ" along with the fourth case-ending (dative). || 26 ||
Having offered "Salutation to the fire-maṇḍala," and at the end of the ten [syllables], "to the one whose self is the kalā," and finally giving "namas," one should worship the fire-maṇḍala.
Then, having brought the arghya vessel and purified it with the syllable *phaṭ*,
one should place it upon its base and worship the twelve digits (*kalā*) of the Sun with the seed-syllables of the letters beginning with *ka* and *bha* and ending with *ṭha* and *ḍha*.
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Sudhūmrā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. || 29 ||

One should perform sacrifice. One should sacrifice to those digits (*kalā*) of Fire; he states them: the ten digits beginning with Dhūmra are to be worshipped. For example: *dhūṃ* *namaḥ* to Dhūmrā—thus Dhūmrā; *am* *namaḥ* to Arciḥ—by this [syllable], Arciḥ; *jvaṃ* *namaḥ* to Jvalinī—thus Jvalinī; *sūṃ*...
By the mantra *sūkṣmāyai namaḥ*, [one worships] Sūkṣmā; by *jvāṃ jvālinyai namaḥ*, Jvālinī; by *viṃ viṣphuliṅginyai namaḥ*, Viṣphuliṅginī;
by *suṃ suśriye namaḥ*, Suśrī; and by *suṃ surūpāyai namaḥ*, Surūpā.
"Kaṃ, obeisance to Kapilā"—thus [one worships] Kapilā. "Haṃ, obeisance to Havyakavyavahā"—by this [formula], Havyakavyavahā is worshipped. (24–26)

"Maṃ," and so forth: having first offered "maṃ" for the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*), then offering "daśānte kalātmane," and finally offering "namaḥ" at the end of that, one should worship the fire-mandala with: *maṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane*.
The meaning is that one should worship the circle of fire (vahnimaṇḍala) in the support (ādhāra) with the mantra "namaḥ. || 27 ||

"Then," and so forth. Immediately thereafter, having brought the arghya vessel purified by the *phaṭ* syllable—that is, by the *phaṭ* mantra—and having placed it upon its support (*adhāra*), one should [visualize] there the twelve digits (*kalā*) of the Sun, with the nasalized (*sānusvāra*) syllable ending in *ṭha-ḍa*; that is, one whose ends are *ṭha* and *ḍa*.

One should worship that [deity] with the seed-syllables of the letters beginning with *ka* and *bha*, ending with *ṭha* and *ḍha*; that is, together with the name-mantra consisting of the seed-syllables in the form of the letters beginning with *ka* and *bha*, accompanied by the dative case and ending with "namaḥ. || 28 ||
He states with one verse those solar digits (*sūryakalā*) which one should worship, beginning with *Tapinī*:
for example, "Oṃ Kaṃ Bhaṃ, salutation to Tapinī" for Tapinī; "Khaṃ Baṃ, salutation to Tāpinī" for Tāpinī;
and "Gaṃ Phaṃ, salutation to Dhūmrā" for Dhūmrā.

With the mantra "aṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya" [and] "namas" at the end, one should worship the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala) in the vessel of the arghya offering, located at the dvādaśānta and consisting of the kalās.
Likewise, while reciting the *vilomamātṛkā* (the reverse alphabet) and the root mantra (*mūlamantra*),
the practitioner of mantra should fill one-third [of the vessel] with the water contained in the jar.
Having filled the remainder with special arghya water, being composed in mind,
one should worship the sixteen digits of the Moon with the seed-syllables of the sixteen vowels, using their respective names as mantras ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ. || 32 ||
"Oṃ ghaṃ paṃ, salutation to Marīci"—thus [one worships] Marīci;

"Oṃ ṅaṃ naṃ, salutation to Jvālinī"—thus [one worships] Jvālinī; "Oṃ caṃ dhaṃ, salutation to Ruci"—thus [one worships] Ruci; "Oṃ chaṃ daṃ, salutation to Sudhūmrā"—thus [one worships] Sudhūmrā; "Oṃ jaṃ thaṃ, salutation to Bhogadā."
One should worship with "Oṃ Namaḥ" to Jhāṃ Taṃ Viśvā, with "Oṃ Namaḥ" to Ñāṃ Ṇāṃ Bodhinī, with "Oṃ Namaḥ" to Ṭāṃ Ḍhāṃ Dhāriṇī,
and with "Oṃ Namaḥ" to Ṭhāṃ Ḍāṃ Kṣamā. Thus one should perform the worship.

Regarding "friendliness" and so forth: having first uttered "aṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya," one should then say "dvādaśānte kalātmane. By way of conjunction, [the mantra becomes] "aṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane. With this mantra ending in "namaḥ," [one should offer] into the arghya vessel.
One should worship the solar disc. || 30 ||
"Viloma," and so forth. Then the practitioner, the mantra-master, just as in the filling of the jar,

while reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order along with the *anusvāras*— the phonemes beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*— and while also reciting the root mantra at their conclusion, [he should act] with that which is situated in the jar.
One should fill one-third of the arghya vessel with wine as the liquid. || 31 ||
"Viśeṣa," and so forth. Being composed and attentive, one should fill the fourth part— the remainder— of the *arghya* vessel with the waters of the special *arghya* (*viśeṣārghya*),
accompanied by the seed-syllable of the sixteen vowels together with the *anusvāra*, and joined with the dative case ending followed by "namaḥ."
One should worship the sixteen digits of Soma with their respective name-mantras in the water of the arghya vessel.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā,
and Pūrṇāmṛtā— these are the digits (kalās) of the Moon that grant all desires. (33)
With the mantra "Ūṃ, obeisance to the one whose self is the sixteen [digits] at the end of the [sixteen],
to the lunar disc," the practitioner of mantras should worship the lunar disc as before.
One should place dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, red flowers, barbara grass, and aparājitā into the vessel by means of *māyā*, and likewise invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*).
One should worship those digits of Soma with the half-verse beginning with "Amṛtā" and so forth:
namely, "Aṃ, obeisance to Amṛtā," thus [worshipping] Amṛtā; "Āṃ, obeisance to Mānadā," thus [worshipping] Mānadā;
"Iṃ, obeisance to Pūṣā," thus [worshipping] Pūṣā; "Īṃ, obeisance to Tuṣṭi," thus [worshipping] Tuṣṭi.
[One should worship] Tuṣṭi with "uṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi," Puṣṭi with "ūṃ, obeisance to Rati," Rati with "ṛṃ,
obeisance to Dhṛti," Dhṛti with "ṝṃ, obeisance to Śaśinī," Śaśinī with "ḷṃ,
obeisance to Candrikā," Candrikā with "ḹṃ, obeisance to Kānti," and Kānti with "eṃ."
With "Jyotsnāyai namaḥ," [one worships] Jyotsnā; with "Aiṃ Śriyai namaḥ," Śrī; with "Oṃ Prītaye namaḥ," Prīti; with "Auṃ Aṅgadāyai namaḥ," Aṅgadā;
with "Aṃ Pūrṇāyai namaḥ," Pūrṇā; and with "Aṃḥ Pūrṇāmṛtāyai namaḥ."
One should worship Pūrṇāmṛtā. || 33 ||

"Ūṃ," and so forth. Having first uttered "Ūṃ somamaṇḍalāya," one should then say "ṣoḍaśānte kalātmane. Through this conjunction, it becomes: "Ūṃ somamaṇḍalāya ṣoḍaśakalātmane. With this mantra ending in "namaḥ," the practitioner [should worship].
The practitioner should worship the lunar mandala in the water of the arghya vessel, just as he did previously in the water of the jar. || 34 ||

"Durvā," and so forth. Then, one should cast into the vessel *durvā* grass together with unhusked rice (*akṣata*), red flowers, *barbara* grass, leaves of *barbara*, and the flower of *aparājitā*, using the *māyā* seed-syllable *hrīḥ*.
One should also invoke the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) into that very vessel. || 35 ||
Having veiled [the object] with the Kavaca mantra, one should perform protection with the Astra mudrā;
having rendered it nectar-like with the Dhenu mudrā, one should cover it with the Matsya mudrā. (36)
Having recited the root mantra ten times, one should perform the invocation of the deity.
Having invoked the beloved deity, one should worship with a handful of flowers;
immediately thereafter, one should consecrate [the offerings] with the five mantras beginning with "Akhaṇḍa. (37)
O you whose form is the Kula, place within this mine of unbroken, single-flavored bliss—the supreme nectar-soul—your own spontaneous radiance. 38.
O you whose form is the nectar of the state of the bodiless one, whose body is pure gnosis—bestow immortality upon this entity which possesses a moist, embodied form! 39.

Regarding the phrase "with the armor-mantra": then, having enveloped [the water] with the *kavaca* (armor) seed-syllable *hūṃ* using the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*, one should surround the nectar-water contained in the *arghya* vessel and perform its protection with the *astra-mudrā*.
Having rendered that very [substance] nectar-like by means of the *dhenu* and *mudrā*, one should cover it with the *matsya-mudrā*.

Regarding the word "root": then, having recited the root mantra ten times over the nectar-water contained in the arghya vessel, one should perform the invocation of the deity right there. Having invoked the chosen deity, [one should worship] with a handful of flowers.
One should worship. Immediately thereafter, one should consecrate that very nectar-water with the five mantras beginning with *Akhaṇḍa* and render it thus consecrated. || 37 ||
He shows those very five mantras, beginning with Akhaṇḍa and so forth, in their proper order: "O Kulārūpiṇī, O source of the bliss of the single undivided essence,
O producer of the bliss of full and primary passion, O self of the supreme nectar!"

In this matter, which is the very nature of the most excellent goddess, place—that is, establish—your independent, spontaneous, and radiant manifestation. (Amara states: *guṇa*, *rāga*, *drava*, and *rasa* are synonyms. 38.
"Anaṅga," and so forth: O you whose form is the nectar of the station of Anaṅga, O you whose nature is the nectar of the station of Kāma;
O you whose body is pure knowledge, O you whose form is a body of pure knowledge;
place the state of immortality within this substance in the form of wine, which is moist in form and motionless.
Establish it. || 39 ||
Having brought about a state of oneness with that form, and having become the very essence of that [offering], manifest within me as the nature of the Kula-nectar. (40)
Bring forth the nectar of immortality that fills this great vessel, which is produced from the essence of the cosmic egg and arises from the totality of all essences.

The supreme nectar of "this-ness" (idantā), filled with the vessel of "I-ness" (ahantā), is characterized by the act of offering as an oblation (homa) into the fire consisting of the Supreme I-ness (parāhantā). || 42 ||
Having thus addressed [the deity], one should then contemplate the state of aesthetic union (*sāmarasya*) of the two Śivas therein, perform worship, and also present incense and lamps.

"By that form," and so forth: O You who possess that very nature, O You who are endowed with those respective forms, having made the arghya—the wine intended for worship—of one flavor (aikarasya), characterized by the primary essence of sweetness, by means of that form which consists of the primary essence of sweetness; [having done so, offer it].
Having become the object that takes the form of the nectar of the Kula and the nature of the ambrosia, manifest your radiance and vibration within me. || 40 ||
"O Goddess, regarding the great vessel filled with wine [described] as beginning with 'the Egg of Brahmā' (*brahmāṇḍa*):

it is produced from the essence of the Egg of Brahmā— that is, it has arisen from those essences which exist within the Egg of Brahmā— and for that very reason, it is the source of all essences (*aśeṣa-rasa-sambhava*), meaning it is the origin of every single flavor."
Where such an occurrence took place, she brought forth a nectar-like essence.
"Ahantā," and so forth. *Ahantā* is the state of "I-ness. In that vessel (*pātra*), which is of the nature of that [I-ness], is contained—that is, held—this supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*) of *idantā*.
*Idantā* is the state of thinking "this is mine," "this is mine," and so on; it is of the nature of that supreme nectar. Of that [nectar]...

One should perform the act characterized by the acceptance of the oblation into the fire that consists of supreme *ahantā*— that is, the nature of the state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*). Into that fire of supreme *ahantā*, one should offer the supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*) in the form of "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is established therein together with the vessel in the form of "I-ness."
The meaning is that one should perform the oblation. || 42 ||
Thus: having addressed the liquor with these five mantras, immediately thereafter,
one should meditate upon and contemplate the *sāmarasya*— the state of essential unity— of Śiva and Śivā within that liquor, and then worship that liquor, as well as incense and lamps placed upon it.
One should show [it]. || 43 ||
Thus has the venerable consecration of the vessel (pātra-saṃskāra) been described for the worship of the Kula.
Without performing it, the practitioner of mantra incurs sin, and the worship becomes fruitless. (44)
Between the water-pot (ghaṭa) and the Śrīpātra, the wise one should place the vessels:
first the Guru-vessel, then the Bhoga-vessel, and after that the Śakti-vessel.
Then, one should place the vessel for the Yoginīs and heroes, followed by the vessel for the bali offering,
and the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamana), along with the śrīpātra; thus, in sequence,
one should perform the installation of the vessels according to the rite of the general arghya.
Having filled the vessel three-quarters full with the nectar contained within the *kalaśa*,
one should place a pure sugar-candy piece, the size of a black gram (*māṣa*), into the bowls.
Taking the nectar situated in the vessel with the left thumb and ring finger,
and using a pure cloth fragment along with the *tattva-mudrā* of the right hand,
one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) everywhere; this is proclaimed to be the ritual procedure.
Regarding "iti": the ellipsis is "without having performed the consecration of the Śrīpātra. || 44 ||
Now, one might ask: what kind of vessel should be placed between the jar (ghaṭa) and the Śrīpātra?
To this, he says "the Guru-vessel," and so forth. || 45 ||
One should place nine vessels in sequence together with the *śrīpātra*. Now, by what procedure should one place these vessels? To this he says: "Of the general *arghya*, etc. (verse 46).

"Residing in the jar," and so forth: having filled three parts of those vessels with the nectar (amṛta) residing in the jar, one should apply—that is, place—within the vessels pieces of pure sugar-candy (śuddhikhaṇḍa) and pieces of meat and so forth, each measuring the size of a black gram (māṣa). || 47 ||

"Vāma," and so forth. Taking the nectar situated in the vessel with the left thumb and ring finger and the right hand in the *tattvamudrā* together with the *śuddhikhaṇḍa*, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) everywhere. This is the procedure for the libation everywhere.
Thus it has been proclaimed. || 48 ||
Having taken the supreme *bindu* from the *śrīpātra*, conjoined with purification, one should satisfy the god Ānandabhairava and Bhairavī. (49)
One should satisfy the lineage of gurus with the nectar from the vessel of the Guru.
Having satisfied one's own guru together with his consort in the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra),
one should likewise satisfy the four preceding gurus by means of their respective names preceded by the Vāgbhava syllable.
Then, within the lotus of my own heart, I satisfy the primordial Kālī with the nectar from the vessel of enjoyment, preceded by my own seed-syllable.
The practitioner of mantra should satisfy the chosen deity three times with [offerings] ending in "svāhā";
likewise, he should perform the satisfaction of the limbs and the surrounding deities (aṅgāvaraṇa) with the nectar from the vessel of power (śaktipātra).

Regarding the phrase "from the Śrīpātra": having taken the supreme *bindu* endowed with purity from the Śrīpātra, one [worships] the deity Ānandabhairava with this mantra: "Hasakṣamalavarayūm, Vaṣaṭ to Ānandabhairava;
I satiate Ānandabhairava, obeisance. Thus, [one worships] the god Ānandabhairava.
With the mantra "sahakṣamalavarayīṃ ānandabhairavyai vauṣaṭ ānandabhairavīṃ tarpayāmi svāhā," one should likewise propitiate Ānandabhairavī. || 49 ||
"Guru," and so forth. One should satisfy the lineage of gurus—that is, the entire assembly of gurus—with the nectar from the vessel of the guru.
Now, by what mantra or in what location should one satisfy the lineage of gurus?
To this he says, "In the thousand-petaled lotus," and so forth; [one should worship] together with his consort in the thousand-petaled lotus.

Having gratified one's own guru with the first seed-syllable *vāgbhava*, namely *aiḥ*, one should likewise gratify the four gurus together with one's own guru by means of their respective names [preceded] by that same syllable; for example: *aiḥ* [to] the illustrious guru, Amukānandanātha, together with his consort.

With the mantra "I satiate, obeisance," one should satisfy one's own guru together with his consort; with "I satiate, obeisance," the supreme guru together with his consort; with "I satiate, obeisance," the supreme-and-non-supreme guru together with his consort; [and] the supreme-and-non-supreme guru together with his consort.
"I satisfy the Supreme Teacher; obeisance. Thus one should thoroughly satisfy the Supreme Teacher.

Then, etc.: immediately after that, preceded by one's own seed-syllable (bīja), in such a manner as it may be, together with the end consisting of "svāhā"—that is, accompanied by the ending in the form of "svāhā"—one should [offer] the first [oblation].

Uttering the mantra "I satiate Kālī," the practitioner, reciting the mantra, should satiate the primordial Kālikā—who is equipped with her weapons and retinue—with the nectar from the vessel of enjoyment situated in the Yoginī-vessel; then he should offer the bali-oblation to the Vaṭukas. (53)
On his own left side, the wise practitioner should fashion a general mandala;
having worshipped it, he should place there food mixed with meat and nectar.
Having worshipped with the mantra "vāṅmāyākamalāvañca vaṭukāya namaḥ" in the eastern quarter, one should offer the bali-oblation to Vaṭuka.

One should satisfy the chosen deity three times within the lotus of one's own heart. The meaning is that one should perform the libation with the mantra: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā ādyāṃ kālīṃ tarpayāmi svāhā*. Then...

In the same manner, one should perform the libation for the limbs and the enclosures (*aṅgāvaraṇa*) with the nectar from the power-vessel (*śaktipātra*). One should satisfy the deities of the limbs with the mantra "I satisfy the limb-deities,
svāhā," and the deities of the enclosures with the mantra "I satisfy the enclosure-deities, svāhā."
The meaning is that one should satisfy [them]. || 51 || 52 ||

"Yoginī," and so forth. With the mantra: "Oṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Krīḥ Parameśvari Svāhā! I satiate the primordial Kālī, together with her weapons and her retinue, with the nectar contained in the vessel of the Yoginī—Svāhā!"—one [satiates] her who is equipped with weapons, distinguished by her weaponry.
Having offered libations to the primordial Kālikā along with her equipment and retinue, one should present—that is, give—an offering (bali) to the Vaṭukas. || 53 ||
He describes the procedure for offering the *bali* to Vaṭuka and the others with the words "on his left side," and so forth.

A wise and steadfast person should draw a common square mandala on his left side. Having worshipped that mandala, [he should place offerings] there in the mandala in the four directions and in its center.
And one should place food mixed with nectar (sudhā), combined with wine (surā), and food containing meat—namely, food accompanied by flesh and the like. || 54 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "vāṅmāyā": having uttered the seed-syllables (bīja) "ai," "hrī," "śrī," and "va"—which correspond respectively to Vāc, Māyā, Kamalā, and Vañca—and then saying the phrase "vaṭukāya namaḥ," the mantra is formed by their conjunction as follows:
*ai hrī śrī va vaṭukāya namaḥ*. By means of this very mantra...

Having worshipped Vaṭuka in the eastern part of the maṇḍala, one should offer and give a bali-offering to Vaṭuka at that very spot with the mantra: "Ai Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Vaṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka," consisting of a food offering accompanied by nectar and meat. || 55 ||
Then, one should offer the bali-oblation to the south with the mantra: "Tatastu yāṃ yoginībhyaḥ svāhā. (56)
The heart-mantra for Kṣetrapāla consists of the word *saṃvarta* joined with the six long vowels;
with this, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) to Kṣetrapāla in the west.

Having extracted the seed-syllable *khāṃ* joined with the six long vowels, and having uttered "Gaṇapataye" ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), one should then utter the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*, i.e., *svāhā*). || 58 ||
In the north, one should offer an oblation to Gaṇeśa with this [mantra];
likewise, in the center, one should give an oblation to all beings according to the prescribed rule.
Having uttered *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ*, and then having spoken all the words, one should say "to those who create obstacles.
Having said "to all beings" (*sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*), the mantra is considered to be *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (60)

Regarding "tatas-tu" (then, however): immediately thereafter, he should offer this oblation (*bali*) to the Yoginīs in the southern part of the mandala, using the mantra "To the Yoginīs, Svāhā," consisting of nine items accompanied by the pretext of nectar (*sudhā*). || 56 ||

"Six," and so forth. Having uttered the *saṃvarta* [mantra], which consists of the letter *kṣa* joined with the six long vowels, and then having said "to Kṣetrapāla," one should then say "hṛt namaḥ. By joining all these words together, the mantra *kṣā kṣī kṣū kṣai kṣau kṣaḥ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ* is produced. This is it.
With this very mantra beginning with "sudhāmiṣānvitānnavalir," one should offer the bali-oblation to Kṣetrapāla in the western part of the mandala. || 57 ||

"Khānta," and so forth: having extracted the seed-syllable (bīja) ending in *kha*—which is the letter *ga*, as it is at the end of its own [alphabetical] series—and joined it with the six long vowels, one should then utter "Gaṇapataye" ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), and thereafter say "svāhā," which is the consort of fire (*vahnijāyā*). By way of this construction, [the mantras are] *gāṃ* and *gīṃ*.

The mantra "gū gai gau gaḥ gaṇapataye svāhā" is thus formed. With this very mantra—beginning with "This is an offering (bali) accompanied by nectar and meat"—one should prepare and offer the bali to Gaṇeśa in the northern part of the mandala, to the north. In the same manner...
In the center of the maṇḍala, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings according to the prescribed rule and in the proper manner. || 58 ||

He states the mantra for the offering of bali to all beings with the single syllable *hrīṃ*: having uttered *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, and the word *sarvapa* (all), one should then say *vighnakṛdbhyaḥ* (to those who create obstacles). Then, having said *sarvabhūtebhyaḥ* (to all beings), [one says] *hūṃ phaṭ*.
Then, one should duly offer a single bali-oblation to Śivā:
"Accept it, O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O Śivā, whose form is the fire of time! (61)
"Declare clearly the auspicious or inauspicious result; accept this offering for you.
This is the root offering; afterwards, say 'Salutation to Śivā.
O Śivā, this performance of the wheel has thus been described before you. (62)
Having taken with both hands, in the *karakacchapa* (tortoise) mudrā, a most enchanting flower scented with sandalwood, agallochum, and musk; || 63 ||
Having brought her into the lotus of one's own heart, one should meditate upon the Primordial Goddess, who is higher than the highest.
One should say "svāhā. Through this application, the mantra born as "hrīḥ śrīḥ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" is produced.
This very mantra, beginning with "this is the offering (bali) provided with nectar and meat," is for all beings.
It is considered [to be] in the validāna [finger]. || 60 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately after that, one should duly offer—that is, give—one *bali* offering to Śivā Phetkārikā. He states the mantra for the offering of the *bali* to Śivā in a verse and a half, beginning with: "gṛhṇa" (Accept, O Goddess, O highly fortunate one...).

One should recite the root mantra. Then, having said "This is the offering" (*eṣa baliḥ*), one should subsequently say "Salutation to Śivā" (*śivāyai namaḥ*). By joining all these words together: "Accept it, O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O Śivā, you who have the form of the fire of time; reveal the fruits of good and evil, accept the offering."
The mantra "tava hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parame svāhā, eṣa balir śivāyai namaḥ" has thus arisen; with this very mantra, one should offer the *bali* to Śivā. || 61 || 62 ||

"Candana" and so forth. Then, having taken with both hands a most enchanting flower scented with sandalwood, agallochum, and musk, and having brought it to the heart by means of the *karakacchapa* mudrā, one should meditate upon Kālī—the primordial goddess, higher than the highest—within the lotus of one's own heart. || 63 || 64 ||

Having led [the consciousness] through the *suṣumnā*, the path of Brahmā, into the great thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-mahāpadma*), and having caused it to experience bliss, one should, by means of the path of the great exhalation (*bṛhanniśvāsa*),
join it to that flower like the flame of one lamp being transferred to another. (65)
The practitioner, endowed with firm devotion, should cause [the image] to be placed upon the yantra;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he should pray to his chosen deity.
O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible through devotion and accompanied by your retinue,
remain perfectly steady for as long as I worship you.
"O Goddess Kālikā, beginning with *krīṃ*, together with your retinue and attendants, come here—reciting this twice—and stay here—reciting this again twice. (68)
Come here by the power of this sound; having arrived here by these words, stay still, address me, and accept my worship.
Having thus performed the invocation, one should establish the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the Goddess.
