Regarding the phrase "in the thousand-petalled [lotus]": having meditated upon the primordial Kālī within the lotus of one's own heart, one then leads her— by means of the *suṣumnā* channel, which serves as the path to Brahman— to the great lotus of the thousand petals, and causes her to partake of the nectar (*sudhā*).

Having made her joyful and filled with bliss, as one lamp is lit from another lamp, he brought forth from that very Kālī another primordial Kālī through the path of his broad breath— the nostril— and placed her there in his hand.

Having joined and established [the deity] upon a flower, the practitioner, endowed with firm devotion, should cause the Goddess—placed upon the flower held in his hand—to be deposited and installed within the yantra. Then, with palms joined in reverence, he should pray to his chosen deity. || 65 || 66 ||
He states what one should pray for there, beginning with the words "O Goddess of the Gods," and so forth. || 67 ||
"Krīm ādye," and so forth. Having uttered "O Goddess Kālikā, who begins with *krīṃ*, together with your retinue and the rest," and then having said twice, "Come here," and then again twice,
"Stay here."
Ā HRĪḤ KROḤ ŚRĪḤ VAHNIJĀYĀ—this is declared to be the mantra for installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
After that, [one says] "the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of this deity are here," and then immediately after, the five seed-syllables (*bījāni*). (71)
One should utter again: "The life-force of such-and-such a person resides here. Then one should recite the five seed-syllables and the name of all the sense-faculties of that person.
Then, by the command of such-and-such a person, one should again utter those five seed-syllables from the positions of speech, mind, eyes, nose, ears, and skin.
May the vital breaths come here and remain happily for a long time; *ṭha* twice.

Having first uttered "Come here" (*ehi*) from the word *śabda*, then having uttered "Be present here" (*iha sannidhehi*) from the word *sannidhi*, then having addressed the phrase "Be established here" (*iha sannīti*), and then one should say "Accept my worship" (*mama pūjāṃ gṛhāṇa*).
By joining all these words together: *krīm ādye kālike devi*.
"Come here with your retinue and so forth; come, come! Stay here, stay here! Be present here; remain concentrated here! Accept my worship!"—this is the mantra that has arisen.
In this manner, by means of this mantra, there is the invocation of the Goddess.
Having performed this, one should establish the vital breaths of that very [image]; the meaning is that one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the life-force). || 68-70 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which mantra one should use to perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (installation of the vital breaths) of the Goddess, he states the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra in four [verses], beginning with "ĀM" and so forth. Having uttered "ĀM / HRĪM / KROṂ / ŚRĪM," [one should utter] the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, SVĀHĀ).

One should utter "svāhā. Then, having said, "The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) of such-and-such a deity are here," one should thereafter pronounce the word "prāṇāḥ. Following that, one should recite the five seed-syllables beginning with "āḥ" and "hrīṃ. Immediately after that, one should utter: "The life-force (jīva) of such-and-such [a deity] is established here."

Again, one should utter those same five seed-syllables. Then, one should say, "the all-senses of such-and-such. Again, one should utter those five seed-syllables. Then, after the speaking—that is, the utterance—of "such-and-such," [one should proceed].
One should utter the words "abode of speech, mind, eyes, nose, ears, and skin. Then one should say from that word:
"May the vital breaths (prāṇas) come here and remain happily for a long time. After that, one should say "Ṭha Ṭha Svāhā. By joining all these words together, it becomes: *ā hrīḥ kroḥ śrīḥ*.

Having duly established the vital breaths (prāṇas) three times in the center of the yantra with the mudrā called Lelihānā, using the mantra "svāhā ādyā kālīdevatāyāḥ prāṇā iha prāṇā ā hrīḥ" (p. 139), one should speak with palms joined in reverence: || 75 ||
"Welcome at the very beginning; this is a most hearty welcome for you. O Supreme Goddess, here is a seat; please be seated here. (76)

Then, reciting the root mantra three times, one should sprinkle [the deity] with special *arghya* water for the sake of the purification of the god; this is the ritual of *sakalīkṛti* performed with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess with the sixteen types of offerings (*upacāra*).

KROḤ ŚRĪ SVĀHĀ! The life-force (*jīva*) of the deity Ādyakālī is established here. Ā HRĪḤ KROḤ ŚRĪ SVĀHĀ! All the sense-faculties (*sarvendriya*) of the deity Ādyakālī... Ā HRĪḤ KROḤ ŚRĪ SVĀHĀ! [Of] the deity Ādyakālī...

"Speech, mind, eyes, nose, ears, skin, and breath—having come here, may you remain happily for a long time, svāhā!"—this is declared to be the mantra for the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). || 71–74 ||

Regarding the word "iti": with this very *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, having duly established the life-breaths (*prāṇas*) of the Goddess in the center of the yantra three times (tridhā) using the mudrā called *lelihānā* as instructed by the Guru, one should speak while joining the palms in reverence (*kṛtāñjalipuṭa*).
Regarding the mudrā called *lelihānā*, as stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"One should make the index, middle, and ring fingers equal and face downward;
having made the little finger straight, one should place the thumb upon the ring finger."
This mudrā, called lelihānā, is proclaimed to be used in the practice of jīvanyāsa. || 75 ||
In response to the expectation of what he should say, he says "ādye" and so forth. "Suṣṭhu āgatam" means "a very welcome. || 76 ||
"Then," and so forth. Then, reciting the root mantra three times, one should sprinkle or consecrate the Goddess with special *arghya* water for the sake of purifying the deity.
With the six limbs: *hrāḥ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīḥ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrūḥ* to the crest-lock...

The ritual of *sakalīkṛti* (the act of making [the deity] complete) for the Goddess must be performed with the following mantras: *vaṣaṭ hraiḥ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ hrauḥ* for the three eyes (*netratraya*), and *vauṣaṭ hraḥ phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*). As for the *sakalīkaraṇa*: *Vaṣaṭ hraiḥ* for the armor; *huṃ hrauḥ* for the three eyes; *vauṣaṭ hraḥ phaṭ* for the weapon. Thus, the *sakalīkaraṇa* of the Goddess is to be performed. The *sakalīkaraṇa* is as follows:
The placement of the six limbs upon the body of the deity is known as sakalīkṛti (the act of making complete). || 77 ||
Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), the bath, clothing, and ornaments;
likewise, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and further water for sipping. (78)
One should employ nectar, betel, libations, and prostration;
these are the sixteen services to be utilized in the act of worship.
This first seed-syllable is for the water for the feet; the word "namaḥ" is for the deity.
One should offer the water for the feet at the two feet and present the water for honor (arghya) upon the head.
The wise practitioner, uttering "svāhā," should offer the water for sipping with "svadhā";
he should place the madhuparka into the lotus of the mouth.
Then, having recited "vaṃ svadhā," he should again offer the water for sipping. (81)
He demonstrates those very sixteen services with the words beginning "pādya" (verse 78).
Amṛta is wine; one should employ it, that is, offer it. || 79 ||

Now, he describes the procedure for offering the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra), beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, starting with the words "Having uttered the first seed-syllable... and so on. Having uttered the first seed-syllable, one should say the phrase: "This is the water for the feet (pādya); obeisance to the deity. By way of conjunction, [the mantra becomes]: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā idam*.

The mantra "pādyam ādyakālīdevatāyai namaḥ" is thus formed. With this mantra, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) at the Goddess's two feet. [This is done] with the word *svāhā*, that is, by employing the word *svāhā* [in the form]: *hrīṃ śrīṃ kroṃ parameśvari svāhā*.
With the mantra "Svāhā! This arghya is for the primordial Kālī; svāhā!", one should present the arghya offering upon the head of the Goddess. || 80 ||

"svāhā," etc. The phrase "by means of the word *svāhā*" connects with what precedes. The wise practitioner (*mantrin*), by means of the mantra containing the word *svadhā*—namely, *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā idam ācamanīyam ādyāyai kālyai svadhā*—[offers it] to the Goddess.

One should offer water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīyaka*) and give it. With the mantra: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā, eṣa madhuparka ādyāyai kālyai svadhā*, one should present the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) into the lotus-mouth of the Goddess. *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari*.
Having uttered, "Svāhā! This water for sipping is for the primordial Kālī; vaṃ svadhā," he should again offer the water for sipping into the mouth of the Goddess. || 81 ||
(141) "I offer bathing water for all the limbs, as well as garments and ornaments; the preceptor should present these with the mantra. (82)
One should offer perfume at the heart-lotus with the middle and ring fingers using the mantra ending in "namaḥ," and offer flowers using the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. (83)
Having placed incense and lamps before [the deity] and performed the sprinkling and other rites,
one should offer them with the mantra, and immediately thereafter release them.
Having worshipped the bell with the mantra "O Mother, Victory-Sound! Svāhā! preceded by the mantra, he should ring it with his left hand while holding it with his right.
Taking incense, the wise one should apply it below the nose;
he should wave the lamp ten times before him, reaching as far as his sight.

"Snānīyam," etc. [The mantra is: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Krīṃ Parameśvari Svāhā! I offer this bath-water, this garment, and these ornaments to the primordial Kālikā. With this mantra, one should apply these items, beginning with the bath-water, upon all the limbs of the Goddess.
The preceptor or the practitioner should give it. || 82 ||

"Madhyametyādi" and so forth. With the mantra ending in "namaḥ"— namely, *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā, eṣa gandha ādyāyai kālyai namaḥ*— one should offer perfume into the heart-lotus of the Goddess using the middle and ring fingers.
With the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Krīṃ Parameśvari Svāhā, this flower for the primordial Kālī, *vauṣaṭ*," he should offer a flower to the Goddess. || 83 ||

"Regarding 'incense' and so forth: having placed the incense and lamp before the Goddess and purified them with sprinkling and other rites, one should offer them to the Goddess by reciting the mantra: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā; etau dhūpadīpāv ādyāyai kālyai nivedayāmi* (Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Krīḥ, O Supreme Goddess Svāhā! I offer this incense and lamp to the primordial Kālī)."

Immediately after offering those scents and flowers, the wise one, having worshipped the bell with the mantra "O Mother, [accept] these scents and flowers; *jayadhvani*! *svāhā*!", and while ringing that bell with his left hand, should take up the incense with his right hand.
The practitioner should offer it by placing it below the nose of the Goddess. As for the lamp, he should wave it ten times before the Goddess, from the feet up to the eyes. (84–86)
Then, having taken up both the vessel and the purification with both hands, the practitioner of mantra, reciting the root mantra, should offer it into the center of the yantra. || 87 ||
O you who bring an end to ten million kalpas, accept this supreme ritual of Vāruṇī along with its purification; grant me imperishable liberation.
Then, according to the general procedure, one should draw a mandala in front;
upon it, one should place a vessel completely filled with food offerings (naivedya). || 89 ||

Having consecrated the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), the veiling (avaguṇṭhana), the protection (rakṣaṇa), and the transformation into nectar (amṛtīkṛta) by reciting the root mantra seven times, one should present them with the waters of the arghya offering.
This very root-offering of prepared food, accompanied by all necessary implements, I present to the beloved Goddess; O Śivā, may you partake of this oblation.

"Then," and so forth. Immediately thereafter, having taken up and grasped the drinking vessel, the purification [substance], and the meat and so on with both hands, one recites the root mantra, at the end of which one says: "I offer this liquor and this purification to Ādyā Kālī."
And reciting [the mantra], the practitioner of mantras should offer it to the Goddess in the center of the yantra. || 87 ||
Then he states the prayer beginning with "paramam" and so forth. *Vāruṇīkalpa* refers to liquor. || 88 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ": immediately thereafter, according to the general rule—that is, by means of the common procedure—one should draw a triangular or quadrangular mandala in front, before oneself.
Upon that mandala, one should place and set down a vessel completely filled with food offerings (naivedya). || 89 ||
Regarding "sprinkling" (prokṣaṇam): one should perform the sprinkling of the food offering (naivedya) contained in that vessel with the syllable *phaṭ*;
the veiling or enveloping with the seed-syllable *hūṃ*; the protection with *phaṭ* itself;
and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the *dhenumudrā* and the seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
Then, having consecrated that food offering seven times with the root mantra, one should present it to the Goddess with the waters of the arghya-offering. || 90 ||
He states the mantra for the offering of the food oblation (*naivedya*) with the single phrase "the root [mantra]": first one should recite the root mantra;

then one should say, "I offer this prepared food, accompanied by all these requisites, to the chosen deity"; then one should say, "O Śiva, may you enjoy this sacrificial offering. This is the application.
*Hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā*.
Then, with the five mudrās beginning with *prāṇa*, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the sacrificial oblation (havis). (92)
On the left, one should display the food-offering mudrā (naivedyamudrā), which resembles a full-blown blue lotus,
with the root mantra, along with water filled from a sacred ford for the purpose of drinking.
Having offered the water-pot (kalaśa), one should again offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka);
then, one should satisfy [the deity] three times with the nectar (amṛta) contained within the Śrī-vessel.
Having offered five handfuls of flowers with the root mantra upon the head, the heart, the base, the feet, and all the limbs, the preceptor— || 95 ||
Having joined his palms in reverence, he should pray to his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) and say: "I worship your attendant deities; obeisance! (96)
"Accompanied by all necessary utensils, I offer this prepared food to my chosen deity; O Śivā, may you graciously accept this oblation"—this was the mantra for the presentation of the *naivedya*.
The term "prepared food" (*siddhānna*) is also indicative of raw rice (*āmānna*). || 91 ||

"Then," and so forth. Immediately thereafter, with the five mantras taught by the Guru— namely, "Svāhā to Prāṇa," "Svāhā to Apāna," "Svāhā to Samāna," "Svāhā to Udāna," and "Svāhā to Vyāna"— one [worships] the Goddess with the five mudrās of Prāṇa and the others.
One should cause [the child] to consume the oblation; that is, one should feed [him]. || 92 ||

Regarding "on the left": on the left hand, one should show the goddess holding the *naivedya-mudrā*, which resembles a blossoming blue lotus or a fully opened water-lily. Then, with the root mantra, [one should present] a vessel filled with water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or filled with wine for the purpose of drinking.

Having offered [the oblation] to the Goddess, one should again give water for sipping (ācamanīya). Immediately thereafter, one should satisfy the Goddess three times with the nectar (amṛta) contained in the Śrī-pātra, or with wine, as before. || 93 || 94 ||
"Uttaṃmāṅga," and so forth. Then the preceptor-practitioner (deśika-sādhaka),

having offered five handfuls of flowers with the root mantra to the head (uttamāṅga), the heart, the region of the foundation (ādhāra), the two feet, and all the limbs of the Goddess, and having joined his palms in reverence, [should worship] the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
One should make a request. Whatever one requests, that is expressed by the half-verse beginning with "tava" (of you).

Having said "tava āvaraṇadevān" (the deities of your retinue), one should utter the words "pūjayāmi namaḥ" (I worship, homage). By means of this application, [the formula becomes]: "O chosen deity, I worship the deities of your retinue; homage."
There was a prayerful utterance. || 95 || 96 ||
Having worshipped the six limbs in sequence—Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Īśa, in front, and behind—one should then worship the lineages of gurus. || 97 ||
One should worship these family gurus: the Guru, the Paramādi, the Parāpara-guru, and likewise the Parameṣṭhi-guru.
One should perform the satiation three times each with the nectar from the vessel of the Guru;
then, one should worship the eight female deities (nāyikās) in the center of the eight-petaled lotus.
Maṅgalā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Jayantī, Aparājitā,
Nandinī, Nārasiṃhī, and Kaumārī are the eight Mothers.

The manner of worshipping the deities of the enclosure is shown by the words beginning with "Agni" and so forth: in front of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa, and behind the yantra— in the southeast corner, the southwest corner, the northwest corner, and the northeast corner— as well as in front, at the very beginning.

And on the back, that is, in the rear portion, one should worship the six limbs and the deities of the six limbs with the mantras: *namaḥ hrāḥ*, *namaḥ hrīḥ*, *namaḥ hrūḥ*, *namaḥ hraiḥ*, *namaḥ hrauḥ*, *namaḥ hraḥ*. Having thus worshipped them, one should worship the lineages of gurus, the series of preceptors.
Showing precisely the lineage of gurus, he says "gurum ca" and so forth: *oṃ* homage to the Guru;
*oṃ* homage to the Supreme Guru (*paramaguru*); *oṃ* homage to the Higher-Lower Guru (*parāparaguru*); *oṃ* homage to the Preceptor of the Supreme Abode (*parameṣṭhiguru*).
With these mantras, one should [worship] the Guru, beginning with the Supreme [Guru], in the center of the yantra using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should worship these lineage gurus in sequence: the Guru who has such a supreme beginning, as well as the Parāpara-guru and the Parameṣṭhi-guru. || 98 ||
"Guru," and so forth: one should perform the libation for the gurus three times, three times, and three times respectively, using the nectar from the vessel of the Guru.
Immediately thereafter, within the eight petals—that is, inside the eight leaves—in the center of the eight-petaled lotus, [one should worship] Oṃ.

One should worship the eight presiding goddesses with scents, flowers, and other offerings using their respective name-mantras, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, such as "Oṃ Maṅgalāyai namaḥ" and so forth. || 99 ||
The eight worshipful goddesses spoke with the single verse beginning with "Maṅgala" [verse 100].
On the tips of the petals, the best of practitioners should worship the eight Bhairavas. (101)
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhonmatta, Bhayaṅkara, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas. || 102 ||
One should worship Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions within the outer square (bhūpura);
one should then worship their weapons outside of that and offer libations to them.
Having worshipped with all ritual offerings, one should, with a concentrated mind, present the bali offering.
The deer, the goat, the ram, the buffalo, the boar, the porcupine, the hare, the monitor lizard, and the tortoise—these ten are recorded as the [ten-nail] animals. (105)
One may also give other sacrificial animals according to the desire of the practitioner. || 106 ||

"Daletyādi" and so forth. On the tips of the petals—that is, on the edges of the leaves—the excellent practitioner should worship the eight Bhairavas with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, using their respective name-mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, such as "Oṃ, obeisance to Asitāṅga Bhairava," and so on. || 101 ||
He speaks of the eight Bhairavas to be worshipped with the single verse beginning with "Asitāṅga. (102)

"Indra," and so forth. Then, with the name-mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings within the square enclosure (*bhūpura*). The weapons of those [guardians], Indra and the others, are the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and so forth.
One should worship with the name-mantra preceded by *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in *namaḥ*, outside that [circle], beyond the *bhūpura*.
Thereafter, one should worship with the name-mantra preceded by *praṇava* and ending with "I satiate Indra, *namaḥ*," according to the formula: *oṃ indraṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*.
One should satiate Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions.

"By all," and so forth: having worshipped the Goddess with all the ritual services (upacāras) such as water for the feet (pādya) and the rest, one should, being composed and attentive, offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) to the Goddess. || 104 ||

Now, as to which specific animal is recommended for the rite of offering a sacrifice (balidāna), he says "the deer," and so forth: the *lulāpa* is the buffalo. The ten [animals] beginning with the deer are traditionally taught to be recommended for the rite of offering a sacrifice. (105)

"Others as well": it is not only deer and the like that are prescribed for the ritual of offering oblations; rather, according to the will of the practitioner, he may offer other animals to the Goddess as well. || 106 ||

Having placed a sacrificial animal possessing auspicious marks before the Goddess, the knower of mantras, having sprinkled it with arghya water, renders it nectar-like by means of the dhenumudrā. (107)

Having worshipped the goat, the sacrificial animal, with the mantra "Obeisance to the goat," using perfume, vermilion, flowers, food offerings, and water, the wise man should mutter the Gāyatrī, which releases one from bonds, into its right ear.
After the word *paśupāśāya*, one should utter the word *vidmahe*;
then, after the word *viśvakarmaṇi*, one should say the word *dhīmahi*. (109)
Then the mantra-practitioner should utter: "Tanno jīvaḥ pracodayāt.
This is indeed the Paśu-Gāyatrī, which releases the fetters of the bound soul (paśu). || 110 ||
Then, having taken up the sword, one should worship it with the *kūrca* seed-syllable;
one should worship these [deities] at its tip, middle, and base in sequence.
Now, he describes the procedure for offering the sacrificial victim (*balidāna*) with the verses beginning with "sulakṣaṇam" and so forth.

The practitioner (*sādhaka*), who is wise, steadfast, and knowledgeable in the mantras, having placed before the Goddess an animal possessing auspicious marks and free from disease and the like, [should sprinkle it] with the water of the special *arghya* while reciting the *phaṭ* mantra.
Having sprinkled [the goat] and consecrated it with the *dhenumudrā*, having rendered it nectarine by means of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*,

and having worshipped the goat with perfumes, vermilion, flowers, food offerings, and water using the mantra "Obeisance to the goat, the sacrificial animal," [one should place it] to the right of the goat.

One should mutter the *gāyatrī* mantra for the liberation from the bonds of the Lord (*paśupāśavimocanī*) into the ear. The term "goat" (*chāga*) is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for deer and other such animals. "Water" (*pāthaḥ*) means water. || 107 || 108 ||

He states the Gāyatrī for the liberation from the bonds of the bound (paśu-pāśa-vimocanī) with the words beginning "paśupāśa" and so forth: the practitioner (mantrī), the seeker (sādhaka), should utter the word "vidmahe" at the end of the phrase "paśupāśāya. Then, after the word "viśvakarmaṇe," he should say the word "dhīmahī."

Thereafter, one should utter and recite: "May that Jīva inspire us. Through this application, the Gāyatrī is formed as follows: "We know the one who binds the fetters of the individual soul; we meditate upon Viśvakarman; may that Jīva inspire us. || 109 || 110 ||
"Then," and so forth. By means of the *kūrca* seed-syllable, namely the syllable *hūṃ*, [one should mark] at its tip, middle, and base—that is, at the tip, middle, and base of the sword. || 111 ||
The most excellent practitioner should then worship Vāgīśvarī and Brahmā, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and Umā and Maheśvara at the base. (112)
Immediately thereafter, the worship of the sword is performed with the mantra ending in "khaḍgāya namaḥ," [addressed] to the one endowed with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śakti.
Having renounced [the offering] with the Mahāvākya, one should speak with palms joined in reverence: "By the prescribed rite, may this be offered unto you. (114)
Having thus announced the sacrificial animal (paśu), one should cause it to be placed upon the ground;
then, becoming absorbed in the state of the Goddess, one should slay it with a forceful blow.
He should be cut down by himself, or by his brothers' sons, or by a brother, or even by a friend, or by a sapinda relative; he must not be allowed to take the side of women.
Regarding those whom one should worship at the tip, middle, and base of the sword, he says with a single [verse],

"Vāgīśvarīm" (to Vāgīśvarī). Thus, with the name-mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, namely *oṃ vāgīśvarībrahmabhyāṃ namaḥ*, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth at the tip of the sword.
Then the best of practitioners should worship Vāgīśvarī Sarasvatī and Brahmā; then Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in the middle of the sword; and then Umā and Maheśvara at the base of the sword. || 112 ||

Regarding the word "immediately after" (*anantaram*): immediately following that, one should perform the worship of the sword with the mantra ending in "Obeisance to the sword endowed with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śakti. || 113 ||

Regarding the phrase "by means of the Great Saying" (*mahāvākyena*): then, by means of the Great Saying, [one recites] *viṣṇuro*, *tatsat o*. Today, in such-and-such month, in such-and-such fortnight, on such-and-such lunar day, when the sun is situated in such-and-such zodiac sign, I, of such-and-such lineage and named such-and-such Śarmā, desiring the accomplishment of all desired objects, [perform this rite].

Having released the goat with the great formula, "I offer this animal to the deity," and having presented it to the Goddess, one should speak with palms joined in reverence. To the question of what one should say there, he replies with the words beginning "yathā" (verse 114).

"Thus" means: [one should sacrifice] an animal such as a goat, or even by oneself alone. One should not employ or cause others belonging to the faction of one's enemies to perform the slaughter of the animal. || 115 || 116 ||
Then one should offer lukewarm blood as a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the *vaṭukas*.
One should present the offering of a head together with a lamp, saying: "Homage to the Goddess! (117).
Thus has the ritual of the bali offering been declared for the Kaulikas in the worship of the Kula;
otherwise, the propitiation of the deity never occurs.
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice; listen, O beloved, to its procedure:
to the right of oneself, one should prepare a square mandala with sand. (119)
Having made it four cubits in measure, one should perform the inspection with the root mantra,
strike it with the weapon mantra, and perform the sprinkling with that same mantra.

Having enveloped [the site] with the *kūrca* seed-syllable, preceded by the names of the deities, the best of practitioners should worship the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with the mantra: "Salutation to the sacrificial ground. (121)
"Then" means: thereafter, with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Vaṭukas," one should present an offering of lukewarm—that is, slightly warm—blood. || 117 ||
Thus it is said; otherwise, there would be an absence of the injunction for the bali offering. || 118 ||
He states what must be done immediately thereafter with two verses beginning with "tataḥ" (then).
Next, he describes the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhāna*) with the verses beginning with "svadakṣiṇe" (on one's own right).
On the area to one's own right, one should prepare a square mandala, four cubits in measurement, consisting of four corners made of sand.
Having performed the inspection and observation of it with the root mantra,
and having struck it with kusha grass using the weapon mantra ending in *phaṭ*, one should perform the sprinkling and consecration of the mandala with that same *phaṭ* mantra. || 119 || 120 ||

"Kūrca," and so forth. Having enveloped— that is, encircled— that mandala with the *kūrca* seed-syllable, namely the syllable *hūṃ*, the most excellent of practitioners (*sādhakasattama*), while uttering "Salutation to the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) preceded by the deities," should perform worship.

The meaning is that one should worship the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the mantra: "Obeisance to the sacrificial mound of such-and-such deity. || 121 ||
(149) Three lines each, measuring one span (prādeśa), should be drawn with their tips pointing eastward and northward; there, one should worship these [deities]. 122.
On the lines pointing eastward, one should worship Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara; and on the lines pointing northward, one should worship Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu.

Then, in the middle of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the wise one should draw this supreme yantra: a triangle containing the syllables *hasauḥ*, a hexagon outside of that, a circle beyond that, then an eight-petalled lotus, and finally a square enclosure (bhūpura) outside of that. 124.
Having worshipped with a handful of flowers accompanied by the root mantra and the Praṇava,
the wise one, having sprinkled the sacrificial materials, should worship in the pericarp;
or he may worship Māyā, Ādhāraśakti, and the others individually.
"Pointing eastward" means those whose tips are directed toward the east, the eastern direction;
and "pointing northward" means those whose tips are directed toward the north, the northern direction.
Measured by a span (*prādeśa*), three lines each, equal to a span in length, are [to be drawn] upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
These [lines] are to be drawn. There, upon those lines, one should worship these [deities].
When the thumb is extended and joined with the index finger, it constitutes a *prādeśa*. Amarasiṃha says the same:
"The *prādeśa*, *tāla*, and *gokarṇa* are formed when the fingers beginning with the index finger are extended."
From the thumb to the little finger, it should be a *vitasti*, which consists of twelve *aṅgulas*. || 122 ||

Showing those whom one should worship upon those lines, he says "on the east-pointed [lines]" (*prāgagrāsu*): on the east-pointed lines, with the name-mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in *namaḥ*,
one should worship Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara— that is, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Indra— respectively, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should worship. On the lines with their tips pointing north, one should worship Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu—that is, Brahmā, Yama, and Candra. || 123 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately after that, in the center of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), there is a triangle whose interior contains the syllable *hsauḥ*—that is, one in which the letters *ha*, *sa*, *u*, and the *visarga* are combined; outside of that is a hexagon, and outside of that is a circle, [forming] the mandala. Then...
Then the wise one should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the outside, and beyond that, a square enclosure (bhūpura) with four gates. || 124 ||

"By means of the root [mantra]" means: having thus worshipped the supreme yantra that has been drawn with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while reciting the root mantra, and having consecrated the sacrificial substances (*homadravya*) with the *praṇava* (oṃ),
[one should place it] in the seed-vessel at the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the eight-petaled lotus.
Having worshipped Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in the corners beginning with the southeast, one should then worship them in the cardinal directions starting from the east in due order. (126)

The practitioner of mantras should worship Adharma as Ignorance (ajñāna), immediately followed by Non-detachment (avairāgya) and Lack of Sovereignty (anaiśvarya); and in the center, he should worship Ananta and the lotus.
One should worship these—the mandalas of the Sun accompanied by the Kalās and likewise of the Moon—within these filaments starting from the east and in the center. || 128 ||
Yellow, white, reddish-brown, black, smoky, intense, as well as spark-emitting, radiant, and flaming—thus they are in order. (129)
One should perform worship everywhere with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should worship the seat of Fire with "Raṃ, to the seat of Fire, namaḥ. (130)

The wise practitioner, while uttering the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, should worship Māyā along with the support-power (*ādhāraśakti*) and the others as they are collectively present. The meaning is that he should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the mantra: "Obeisance to the support-power and the others" (*hrīṃ ādhāraśaktyādibhyo namaḥ*). Alternatively, [he may worship] the support-power and the rest individually.
One should worship each one individually. || 125 ||

"Agni," and so forth: having worshipped Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya respectively in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni) of the yantra with perfumes, flowers, and so on, using mantras consisting of the name preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in *namaḥ*, one then proceeds in order through the directions starting from the east.

Immediately after this, the practitioner should worship Adharma, Ignorance (Ajñāna), Non-detachment (Avairāgya), and likewise Non-mastery (Anaiśvarya). In the center of the Yantra, he should worship Ananta and the Lotus (Padmaka).

"Kala," and so forth. With the very same two mantras previously mentioned, one should worship the mandalas of both the Sun accompanied by its *kalās* and the Moon accompanied by its *kalās*, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, precisely in the center of the yantra. In these filaments (kesaras), starting from the east and so on—
And one should worship these in sequence in the middle. || 128 ||

Regarding those whom one should worship, he says with the verse beginning "yellow" (*pītā*) and so forth: one should worship Jvalinī in the center among the yellow, white, and other [colored goddesses]. || 129 ||

"Beginning with *praṇava*," and so forth: in every location, one should worship the seat of Fire in the center of the yantra with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Fire (*raṃ vahnir-āsanāya namaḥ*)."
Having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and possesses eyes like blue lotuses, united with Vāgīśvara upon that very seat, the practitioner of mantra [should proceed]. (131)
Having worshipped those two with the *māyā* [syllable] according to the rules, one should then bring forth the fire;
having performed the inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) with the root mantra, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) with the syllable *phaṭ*.
Then, having uttered the Praṇava and the heart-mantra for the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) of the Fire-god,
and having worshipped the seat upon the yantra, one should worship these [deities] in the cardinal directions in due order: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā.

Then, having worshipped the sacrificial ground with the words, "Obeisance to the sacrificial ground of such-and-such a deity," one [should worship] the Goddess in her primary form in the center of it.
Having meditated upon the goddess Vāgīśvarī, preceded by the seed-syllable of fire,
one should extract the fire while reciting the *kūrca* and *astra* mantras at the end of the root mantra.
One should cast away the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters toward the wife of Vahni (the goddess Svāhā);
having gazed upon the fire with the Astra-mantra, one should veil it with the Kūrca.

Regarding the phrase "Vāgīśvarī": then, having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī— united with Brahmā as Vāgīśvara, possessing eyes like blue lotuses, with dark-lotus-like eyes, and having bathed after her menses— the practitioner, the mantra-master, [should place her] upon that seat, which is the fire-pedestal.
Having worshipped Vāgīśvarī and Brahmā with their name-mantras preceded by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should thereafter,
according to the prescribed rule, bring forth pure fire using either a shallow dish (*śarāva*) or a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), while reciting the root mantra.
Having performed the visualization of the Fire, one should perform its invocation with the mantra *phaṭ*.

Regarding the syllable *praṇava*: first one should utter the *praṇava* (oṃ), then one should say "to the Yoga-pīṭha of Fire," and then one should say "heart, salutation" (*hṛt namaḥ*). By combining these, it becomes: *oṃ vahneryogapīṭhāya namaḥ*.
Manu was born. Having worshipped the pedestal of the fire within the yantra by means of this very Manu,

one should worship these [deities] in the four directions starting from the east of the pedestal with scents, flowers, and so forth, using their name-mantras preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should worship. He states those whom one should worship in the directions starting from the east in the half-verse beginning with "vāmā" and so forth. || 133 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately thereafter, reciting the entire mantra phrase, "Obeisance to the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) of such-and-such a deity," one should worship the sacrificial ground with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
and in its center, [one should worship] the form of the root deity.
Having consecrated the cow with nectar, one should lift the fire with both hands and, while rotating it clockwise over the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), place it upon the fire. (137)
Touching the ground with the three parts of the knee and contemplating the seed-syllable of Śiva,
one should bring it facing oneself and place it within the yogic instrument (yantra) of the womb.

Then, having uttered the Māyā-bīja and the form of Fire (vahnimūrti) joined with the syllable *ṅe*, the wise one should worship it with the word "namas" at the end; thereafter, [uttering] *raṃ* followed by "of Fire," he should worship the consciousness (*caitanya*) of Fire with "namas to Consciousness. || 139 ||

Having meditated upon the goddess Vāgīśvarī, one should extract the fire [element], preceded by the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ)— that is to say, having raised the fire by means of the seed-syllable Raṃ— such that the seed-syllable of fire precedes it. At the end of the root mantra, one should add the "kūrca" weapon-syllable Hūṃ and the "astra" syllable Phaṭ.

While reciting the seed-syllable *cā*, one should recite "to the flesh-eaters" (*kravyādebhyaḥ*) at its end, and then recite "the wife of fire" (*vahnijāyā*), namely *svāhā*. By means of this application, the mantra is formed as follows: *hrīḥ śrīḥ krīḥ parameśvari svāhā hūṃ phaṭ kravyādebhyaḥ svāhā*. With this very [mantra]...

With the mantra, one should cast toward the southern direction the portion of raw flesh— the part belonging to the Rākṣasa— which is blazing from the fire in the form of a burning mass. Then, having gazed at the fire with the Astra-mantra "Phaṭ," one should [offer] with the *kūrca* [brush] while uttering "Hūṃ."
One should veil the fire with the seed-syllable itself; that is, one should encircle it. || 134–136 ||

Saying "O cow," one should consecrate [the fire] with the *dhenu* mudrā as nectar; then, with both hands, one should again raise—that is, lift up—the fire. Having raised it, and while rotating the fire three times over the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in a clockwise direction, one should [visualize] the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*).
Meditating upon the fire which is the form of Śambhu’s virility, the practitioner,
with his knees touching the ground, should bring it face-to-face with himself and fix or place it within the triangular mandala of the yoni-yantro. || 137 || 138 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately after that, having uttered the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* for Māyā, one should utter the form of Fire (*vahnimūrti*) together with the suffix *-ṅe* and ending in *namaḥ*. By this combination, the mantra *hrīṃ vahnimūrtaye namaḥ* is produced. With this mantra...

Then, having worshipped the form of Fire, the wise practitioner should subsequently utter "raṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of Fire" (caitanyāya namaḥ). Through this combination, the mantra "raṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of Fire" (raṃ vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ) is formed. With this very mantra, one should fully worship the consciousness of Fire. || 139 ||
Having conceived of the form of fire as consciousness through salutation, the knower of mantras should then kindle the fire with this mantra: (140)
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then the words "cit piṅgala," one should then utter "han dviḥ, daha daha, paca paca. (141)
"Sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā" is the mantra for kindling the fire;
then, having joined one's palms in reverence, one should perform the salutation to Agni. || 142 ||
I bow to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations; who is golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and whose faces are turned in every direction. 143.
Having thus established the fire, one should cover the sacrificial ground with *kuśa* grass;
then, having assigned the name of the fire according to one's own desired deity, one should perform the worship.

"Namasa iti": Having conceptualized the form of the fire and the consciousness of the fire by means of the mantra "namas," having mentally fashioned them, the practitioner who knows the mantras should then, immediately thereafter, ignite—that is, kindle—the fire with this mantra which is about to be described. || 140 ||
He states the mantra for igniting the fire in the verse beginning with "praṇavam" and continuing for one and a half lines:
first, having extracted and uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should then say the word "cit piṅgala"; then "hana hana," then "daha daha," and then "paca paca. After that—

One should say: "Omniscient One, command! Svāhā! [with the seed-syllable] *oṃ*. Thus the mantra is born: *oṃ citpiṅgala hana hana daha daha paca paca sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā*. This mantra is prescribed for the kindling of fire. (141–142)
He states the mantra for the worship of Agni: "I revere the blazing Agni," and so forth. 143.

Regarding the word "iti": having approached the fire for cremation with this very mantra and having paid homage, one should cover the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*). Then, having assigned a name to the fire according to one's own preferred [deity], one should perform the worship of the fire immediately thereafter with the mantra that will be described next.
(154) One should utter the syllable *tāra* (Oṃ), followed by the word *vaiśvānara*, and then the word *jātavedas*.
Having said *ihāvaha āvaha*, one should then follow with the word *lohitākṣa*. 145.
"O beloved of Agni, may you accomplish all rites from their very foundation.
Having thus worshipped, one should fully honor the seven tongues, Hiraṇyā and the others.
Uttering the word "sahasrārcis" in the dative case followed by "hṛdayāya namaḥ," the wise practitioner should worship the six limbs of Fire and then worship its forms.
The eight forms, beginning with Jātavedas, have been proclaimed. || 148 ||
Then one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmī, immediately thereafter;
having worshipped the eight treasures, such as Padma and the rest, one should worship the lords of the directions, beginning with Indra.
He states the mantra for the worship of Agni with the verse beginning with "tāra" and so forth, consisting of one and a half lines.

First, the *tāra*, which is the *praṇava* (oṃ), should be uttered; then, after the word *vaiśvānara*, one should say the word *jātaveda*. After that, having said "iha āvaha āvaha," [one should proceed].

One should utter the word *lohitākṣa* (red-eyed). Then, after the word *sarvakarmāṇi* (all actions), one should utter the word *sādhaya* (accomplish). At the end of that, the beloved of Agni (*agnivallabhā*), namely *svāhā*, should be pronounced.
By this arrangement: *oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvahāvaha lohitākṣa*.

"Accomplish all rites, svāhā"—this was the mantra. Having worshipped the fire with the name of one's own chosen deity using this very mantra, [one should worship] with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the seven tongues of fire, Hiraṇyā and the rest."
One should worship the seven tongues of fire, beginning with Hiraṇyā, with fragrances, flowers, and other offerings. || 145 || 146 ||

"Beginning with *sahasra*," etc.: pronouncing the word *sahasrārciḥ* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), and then the word *hṛdayāya namaḥ*, the practitioner, reciting the mantra "Salutation to the heart of the thousand-rayed one" (*sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ*), should worship the heart of the Fire-god. Then, [he should worship] the Fire-god's...

One should worship the six limbs of the fire with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the mantra "Oṃ, salutation to the six limbs. Then, the wise one should worship the forms of the fire with the mantra "Oṃ, salutation to the forms of the fire. || 147 ||
Indeed, in response to the inquiry as to how many forms of fire there are, he says "jātavedas," and so forth.
The eight forms of fire, beginning with Jātavedas, have been proclaimed—that is, previously mentioned. || 148 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately after that, one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmī, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the mantra "Obeisance to the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmī.
Following that, [one should worship] "Obeisance to the eight treasures, beginning with Padma."
Having fully worshipped the vajra and other weapons, one should take two blades of kuśa grass measuring a span and place them within clarified butter. (150)
One should meditate on the iḍā channel in the left and likewise on the piṅgalā in the right;
then, being composed, one should contemplate the suṣumnā in the middle, starting from the right side.
Having taken clarified butter, the wise one should offer it into the right eye of the Fire-god with this mantra, adding the word "Agni" at the end of the *praṇava*. (152)
The mantra is said to end with "svāhā"; one should take the oblation from the left side.
One should offer into the fire at the left eye [of the deity] with the mantra "oṃ somāya" (which has two 'tha' sounds). 153.
Having worshipped the eight treasures, beginning with Padma, with this mantra and with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should sacrifice to the lords of the directions, beginning with Indra.

"Vajra," and so forth. Then, having fully worshipped the weapons such as the vajra belonging to Indra and the other [deities], one should take two kuśa leaves measuring a span (prādeśa), and placing them within clarified butter, one should set them down on the left and the right. || 150 ||
"On the left," and so forth: one should meditate on the *iḍā* channel on the left side of the ghee;

one should meditate on the *piṅgalā* channel on the right side; and having contemplated the *suṣumnā* channel in the middle, being composed, [one should take] the clarified butter from the right side.

Having taken [the offering], the wise practitioner should immediately offer it into the right eye of the fire-god Agni with the mantra that will be stated hereafter. He states the mantra for the oblation in the right eye beginning with "at the end of the Praṇava," etc.; at the end of the Praṇava is the word "to Agni" (agnaye).
It should be stated: by way of application, [the syllable] *oṃ* [is added]. "To Agni"—thus Manu was born. And this Manu is declared to end with *svāhā*.
Then, from the left side, one should take—that is, seize—the sacrificial oblation, the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Having seized it, one should offer the oblation into the left eye of the Fire with the mantra to be recited hereafter.
One should perform the oblation with *hunet*. Regarding the mantra for the oblation in the left eye, he states: "Oṃ! To Soma, Dviṭhaḥ! Oṃ!
To Soma, Svāhā!"—this is declared to be the mantra. (151–153)
Having taken clarified butter from the center, one should perform the oblation on the forehead;
[the mantra] consists of Agni and Soma accompanied by the Praṇava and joined with the dual ending of the fourth case. (154)
This mantra is said to end with "svāhā"; then, having taken the oblation from the south, the practitioner, using the word "namaḥ," should first utter the syllable "oṃ. (155)
Then he should utter "to Agni Sviṣṭikṛt" followed by the beloved of Fire (Svāhā).
With this, the best of practitioners should offer oblations into the mouth of the Fire.
He should perform the homa with the Vyāhṛtis ending in "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ" and the Dviṭha syllable (Phaṭ). || 156 ||
One should utter the *tāra* (Oṃ) after the word *vaiśvānara*, and then say *jātaveda ihāvaha*. After the words *vahalo hi*, one should speak the words *tākṣasarva*.
Then, saying *karmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*, one should offer oblations three times with this mantra. || 157 ||

"From the middle," it says. Then, having brought and taken clarified butter from the middle, one should perform an oblation upon the forehead of the fire with the mantra to be stated. He states the mantra for the oblation on the forehead beginning with "Agni," etc.; [the two words] are joined with the dual ending of the musical instrument (*tūrya*).
When joined with the dative dual ending, Agni and Soma, accompanied by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the syllable *oṃ*, should be stated;
thus, the mantra "Oṃ agnīṣomābhyām" is produced.
This mantra is declared to end with *svāhā*. The practitioner (*mantrī*) or adept (*sādhaka*) [should worship] with the mantra preceded by *namaḥ*.
Again, having taken the oblation from the south, one should first utter the *praṇava* and speak;

then "to Agni," then "to Sviṣṭikṛt," and then one should speak ending with the word for fire (*vahni*). By this construction, the mantra "oṃ agnaye sviṣṭikṛte svāhā" is produced. With this mantra, the most excellent practitioner—
One should offer oblations into the mouth of the fire, that is, into the face of Agni. *Sviṣṭikṛt* refers to one who performs the *sviṣṭi*, which is an auspicious sacrifice;
[the term is formed with] the *kvip* suffix. Then, one should perform the *homa* with the syllables *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, preceded by the word *svāhā* at the end of each. (154–156)
"Oṃ," and so forth. First, the *tāra*, the *praṇava*, should be uttered.
Then, after the word "vaiśvānara," one should say "jātaveda ihāvahāvaha lohi.
At the end of that word, one should utter the phrase "tākṣasarve. Thereafter, [one should say] "sādhaya karmāṇi."

One should say "svāhā. With the [mantra] "yojanayā o," one should then invoke one's own chosen deity (iṣṭa) into the fire. Having performed worship along with the pedestal (pīṭha) and other elements, one should offer twenty-five oblations with the root mantra ending in "svāhā. (157–158)
Having offered the oblations while contemplating with his intellect the unity of the Goddess with the fire and his own self,
he should offer eleven oblations with the root mantra, and likewise for the deities of the limbs.
Having offered oblations intended for his own desire, with [materials] mixed with sesame, clarified butter, and honey. || 160 ||
One should offer oblations according to one's capacity with flowers, bilva leaves, or other prescribed substances; one should not arrange them so that they fall short by eight.
Then one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) accompanied by fruit and leaves,
using the root mantra ending with "svāhā. Then, having brought the Goddess from there by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should establish her within the lotus of the heart.
"O Āvahāva! O Lohitākṣa! Accomplish all rites, svāhā!"—this is the mantra that has arisen.
With this mantra, one should offer oblations three times, in three ways. || 157 ||

"Then," and so forth: immediately after that, having invoked one's chosen deity into the fire and performed its worship along with the pedestal and other elements using the previously mentioned mantra,
one should offer twenty-five oblations into the fire with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Having cast [the offerings] into the fire and the self, and contemplating with his intellect the oneness of the fire, the self, and the Goddess, he should offer eleven oblations with the root mantra alone; then,
having offered to the deities of the limbs by means of the mantra "Oṃ, svāhā to the deities of the limbs," he should make offerings intended for those limb-deities.
Oṃ Viṣṇur-oṃ. Tat sat oṃ.

Today, in the month of [name], in the [name] fortnight, on the [name] lunar day, when the sun is situated in the zodiac sign of [name], [name] of [gotra], desiring the accomplishment of the desired object [name].
"May the illustrious [Name] Śarmā, with flowers mixed with sesame seeds and clarified butter, or with bilva leaves and the like,

offer an oblation into the fire for the sake of my desired object, ending with 'svāhā' while reciting the root mantra"— with these words, he should offer flowers mixed with sesame, clarified butter, and honey, or else [the leaves].
One should offer oblations into the fire according to one's ability, using bilva leaves or the prescribed substances; one should not offer fewer than eight oblations. (158–161)

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately thereafter, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation) into the fire with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, accompanied by fruit and betel leaf. Following that, by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, [one should dissolve] the Goddess from that fire.
Having brought [them] together, one should establish them within the lotus of the heart. || 162 ||
With the mantra "Forgive me," the practitioner of mantras should dismiss that fire after having offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and he should then ascertain the rite's flawlessness.
The best of practitioners should hold the remains of the oblation between the eyebrows. || 164 ||
This procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) has been declared for all ritual actions according to the Āgamas.
Having thus completed the rite of the oblation, the practitioner should perform the recitation (japa). 165.
Listen, O Goddess of gods, to the procedure by which the Vidyā becomes propitious:
one should indeed contemplate with the intellect the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra. (166)
The syllables of the mantra are said to be the deity, and the deity is in the form of the guru;
for him who worships them without distinction, there is unsurpassed accomplishment.
Having visualized the Guru upon the head and the Deity within the lotus of the heart,
and having contemplated the Root-Mantra in the form of radiant light upon the tongue,
one should contemplate oneself as having become one with the radiance of these three. (168)

"Forgive me. Then, with the mantra "O Agni, forgive me," he should release that sacrificial fire; he should perform its dismissal. Then, the practitioner—the mantra-adept who has offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—having performed this, [the rite is complete].
One should resolve, "May the rite of the fire-oblation be free from defect," and then one should hold the remains of the oblation at the midpoint between the eyebrows.
Regarding the phrase "the procedure": he explains the very procedure for the practice of recitation (*japa*) with the words beginning "the deity" and so forth.
One should "conceive" it, meaning one should contemplate it correctly. || 166 ||

He demonstrates the manner of conceiving the identity with the deity today and its fruit by means of the verse beginning with "mantra," and so forth. "Mantrārṇāḥ" means the syllables of the mantra. "Abhedena" means through the state of oneness. || 167 ||
The "root-vidyā" is the vidyā consisting of the root-mantra; [it refers] to the triad of the guru, the deity, and the root-mantra. || 168 ||
Having encased the root mantra with the *tāra* [syllable] and recited it seven times,
the practitioner should thereafter contemplate it as encapsulated by the *mātṛkā*.
The wise practitioner should recite the seed-syllable of Māyā ten times over his own head;
likewise, he should recite the Praṇava at the mouth and Māyā again in the lotus of the heart. Having recited these seven times, the mantra-master should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, having taken up a rosary made of coral and other materials, [he should say]:
"O Rosary, O Rosary, O highly fortunate one, you whose nature is all powers! (171)
"The fourfold aims have been entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success.
Having thus worshipped that rosary with the nectar situated in the *śrīpātra*, [he should offer it]. (172)
Having satisfied [the deity] in three ways with the root mantra, one should perform the recitation with a steady mind,
either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.

"By means of *tāra*, etc. means that one should recite or chant the root mantra seven times, having encapsulated it with *tāra* at both the beginning and the end, and joined it with the fifty-one phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*. Regarding the phrase "having chanted," because that which is born of scripture (*āgamaja*) is impermanent, [the gerund suffix] is used here.
The augment *neṭ* is added [after the root vowel]. || 169 ||

Regarding "māyā": thereafter, the wise practitioner should mutter the *māyā-bīja*, *hrīṃ*, ten times upon his own head. Then, he should likewise mutter the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) ten times in his mouth. Furthermore, he should mutter the *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) seven times upon the lotus of his heart.
Having recited the mantra, the practitioner should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) as before; he should do so. || 170 ||

"Then" means immediately thereafter; having taken up— that is, grasped— a garland produced from coral and other materials, such as one made of *vidruma* (coral), and having worshipped that garland with the mantra beginning with "O garland, O garland" and ending with "be the bestower of accomplishment."
Having offered libations three times with the root mantra ending in "I satiate the rosary with the nectar contained in the Śrīpātra, svāhā," one should, with a steady mind,
recite the root mantra one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times.
One should perform the recitation; one should do it. || 171–173 ||
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) at the end, [one should offer] with the water and flowers from the Śrīpātra:
"O you who guard the secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us. (174)
"O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, may there be success for me through your grace"—with this mantra, the wise one [should place the flower] upon the lotus of the Goddess's left hand. (175)
Having offered the fruit of the recitation in the form of light, one should prostrate on the ground;
then, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite the hymn and the armor-verse (kavaca).
Then, having circumambulated [the deity], the practitioner should perform the self-surrender by offering a special arghya with the arghya given in reverse order.

Prior to this, one should proclaim [the nature of the Self] through the authority of the vital breath, the intellect, the body, and the qualities (dharma) within the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the state beyond. 178.
One should first express it with the mind, then with speech, and immediately thereafter with action;
then with the two hands, then with the feet, and after that with the belly. (179)
Having said, "Whatever has been done with the genitals," "whatever was spoken," and "whatever was uttered from the feet," one should declare all that as "an offering to Brahman.
At the end, one should say, "May it be so," and thereafter, "all that which is mine and myself. (180)
One should say, "I offer my feet at the lotus-like feet of Ādyākālī";
having uttered the Praṇava and the words "Tat Sat," one should perform the self-surrender.
"Prāṇāyāma," and so forth. Thereafter, having performed *prāṇāyāma*,

the wise practitioner, using the water and flowers from the *śrīpātra* and the mantra beginning with "guhyātiguhyam" and ending with "maheśvari," [offers] to the Goddess the fruit of his recitation in the form of radiant light.
Having offered [the flower] into the lotus of her left hand and prostrating on the ground like a staff, one should bow to the Goddess.
He states the mantra for the self-surrender with four and a half verses beginning with "tataḥ" (then).
One should recite: "Prior to this, by virtue of my authority over life, intellect, body, and dharma, throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Then...
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he should pray to his chosen deity:
having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, he should say, "Śrī Ādyā Kālikā. (182)
Having worshipped according to one’s ability and said, "Forgive me," one should dismiss [the deity] and,
having smelled the flower with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, place it upon the heart.

Having fashioned a well-adorned triangular mandala in the northeast, one should worship the Goddess there with the water and flowers used for her previous offerings (nirmālya). Reciting "Hrīḥ," followed by the words "nirmālya-pada" and "vāsinyai namaḥ," [one should perform the worship]. (184)
One should say: "First with the mind, then with speech, then with action, then with the two hands"; from that [one should say] "with the feet," and after that "with the belly";
and after that, having said "with the penis," one should say "whatever was done" and "whatever was remembered."

Then, one should say "all that which has been spoken after the word *padāt*. Thereafter, one should utter *brahmārpaṇam*. Then, at the end of the word *bhavatu*, one should utter *māṃ madīyaṃ sakalam*. Immediately following that, one should say *ādyākālīpadāmbhoje'rpayāmi*.
One should utter the word *pada*. Then one should utter the *praṇava* and the words *tat sat*. By joining all these words together:

"Whatever [I have done] previously, by virtue of my vital breath (*prāṇa*), intellect (*buddhi*), body (*deha*), and faculties (*adhikāra*), in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, through mind, speech, action, and the two hands..."
"Whatever has been done with the feet, the belly, or the genitals, whatever has been remembered, and whatever has been spoken—may all that become an offering to Brahman.
I offer my entire self and everything belonging to me at the lotus-feet of Ādyakālī. Thus the mantra *tatsat* is born.
Having recited this mantra, one should perform the offering of oneself to Kālī. (177–181)

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, having joined one's palms in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*), one should pray to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). To address the question of what one should pray for, he says "the seed-syllable of *māyā*," and so forth.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of *māyā*, which is *hrīṃ*, one should say "O Śrī Ādyakālikā. Then...
"You have been worshipped according to my ability; please forgive me"—this was the prayerful statement.
Having dismissed the chosen deity with this very statement, one should take up the flower with the *saṃhāramudrā*, smell it, and place it within one's own heart. (182–183)
"In the northeast" means: then, having prepared a well-adorned triangular mandala in the northeastern direction,
one should [worship] the goddess Nirmālyavāsinī in that mandala with the water of used flowers using the mantra to be described.
Afterwards, the practitioner of Śakti should offer the food offering (naivedya) to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all the other gods, and then he himself should partake of it. (185)
Having established his own power on a separate seat to the left side,
or else seated upon a single seat, he should prepare a pleasing vessel.
One should fashion a drinking vessel made of gold or silver weighing no more than five *tolakas* and no less than three *tolakas*. (187)
Alternatively, having placed either that which is made of glass or that which originates from coconut upon its support, to the right of the vessel for purification; || 188 ||
Having brought the great prasāda, the wise one should serve it into the vessels himself, or by his brothers or sons, according to the order of seniority. 189.

One should perform the worship. He states the mantra for the worship of Nirmālyavāsinī with the half-verse beginning with *hrīṃ*: "Having uttered the word *nirmālya*, one should say *vāsinyai namaḥ*. By combining these, the mantra *hrīṃ nirmālyavāsinyai namaḥ* is produced. || 184 ||
"Brahma," and so forth. *Naivedya* refers to the food and other offerings presented to the Goddess. *Vitaret* means one should give.
A *śaktisādhaka* is a practitioner who is accompanied by his consort (*śakti*). || 185 ||
He describes the procedure for receiving the offering (naivedya) for the Goddess with the verses beginning "svīyaśaktim" and so forth:
having seated his own Śakti on a separate seat to his left, or else seated together with his own Śakti on a single seat, the practitioner [proceeds] for the sake of eating and drinking.
One should make a beautiful and pleasing vessel. || 186 ||

"Regarding 'pāna' and so forth: one should not prepare a drinking vessel that is more than five *tolakas* or less than three *tolakas*. And that drinking vessel should be made of gold (*suvarṇa*), silver (*rājata*), glass (*kāca*), or coconut (*nārikela*)."
Having placed the vessel of purity upon the supporting stand in the southern region,

the wise and steadfast practitioner, having brought forth the Great Grace (mahāprasāda), should serve it into the vessels either himself or through his brothers or sons, according to the order of seniority. In this context, seniority is determined by birth.
It is not to be grasped, but rather [attained] through consecration; thus it should be understood. (187–189)
Amṛta should be placed in the drinking vessel, as well as items such as the *śauddhya* and *śuddhi*;
thereafter, one should partake of food and drink together with the members of the assembly (*sāmayika*). (190)
First, for the purpose of spreading [the seat], one should take up the highest purity;
then, with a most joyful mind, the entire family practitioner [should proceed]. (191)
Taking up each one’s own vessel filled with supreme nectar,
[one should contemplate] Kulakuṇḍalī, whose form is consciousness, extending from the Mūlādhāra to the tip of the tongue.
Having visualized that lotus-face while reciting the root mantra,
and having obtained each other’s permission, one should offer oblation into the mouth of Kuṇḍalī.
The drinking of wine is the characteristic mark of the acceptance of fragrance for noble women;
for practitioners who are householders, the five vessels are proclaimed. (194)
From excessive drinking, the loss of accomplishment arises for those of noble lineage. || 195 ||
"Drink," and so forth: nectar (sudhā) and wine (madirā) should be offered in the drinking vessel;

for the sake of purification, substances such as meat, fish, and the like should be offered in the vessel of purity (śuddhipātra). Thereafter, together with the *sāmayika*s—those persons who have attained the time of the worship of the Goddess—...
One should partake of food and drink. || 190 ||
"At the beginning" means that first of all,
for the purpose of establishing the wine and for the purpose of spreading [the seat], one should take the highest purity.
Then, with a mind exceedingly joyful, the entire assembly of *kula*-practitioners— every single one— [should proceed].
Having taken up and held one's own respective vessel filled with supreme nectar and filled with the finest wine,

one should contemplate and meditate upon Kulakuṇḍalinī, whose form is consciousness (cidrūpā) and whose nature is pure awareness (caitanyasvarūpā), as she abides pervading the space from the *mūlādhāra* to the tip of the tongue.
Uttering the root mantra (mūlamantra) at her lotus-face,
and having obtained each other’s permission, one should offer the supreme nectar (paramāmṛta) as an oblation into the mouth of Kuṇḍalī. || 191–193 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with *ali* and so forth: for women of noble family (*kulastrī*), the characteristic of accepting *gandha*—which is essentially the acceptance of the scent associated with wine—is proclaimed as *alipāna*, that is, the drinking of wine. This applies to householder practitioners (*sādhaka*).

The "five vessels" is proclaimed by household practitioners as the drinking of wine measured by five vessels; (p. 164) one should drink only that amount of wine which is measured by five vessels, so long as one does not move the gaze and so long as one does not move the mind.
One should drink as long as that; after this, it is the drinking of the animal (paśu).
How could he who is a sinner, who feels aversion toward the consumption [of wine] and is a practitioner of power (śakti-sādhaka), speak thus: "I worship the Primordial Kālī"? (197)
Just as no fault of contact exists in food and other offerings dedicated to Brahmā, so too one should avoid distinctions of caste even regarding your grace. 198.
In this very manner, one should perform the drinking and eating;
there is no need for washing the hands during the consumption of the food offering (naivedya).
One should remove the smears with a cloth or even with water. 199.
Then, having taken the remains of the offered flowers upon his head, the wise man should move about on the ground like a deity, applying the paste from the yantra to the region of the beard.
Thus, in the glorious Mahānirvāṇa Tantra— the supreme among all supreme tantras,
the essence of the determination of all dharmas— within the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva,
this is the section titled "The Description of the Installation of the Śrīpātra and the Performance of the Homa-cakra."

The sixth chapter. The meaning is that it is to be drunk. By the phrase "of householders," it is indicated that for those other than them who drink liquor exceeding the measure of five vessels, [there is no such permission].

It has been indicated that this is a fault. Now, one might ask: what fault is there for household practitioners who drink wine exceeding the measure of five vessels? To this, he says "from excessive drinking," and so forth.
"Yāvaditi" means that one should move or cause to whirl. || 196 ||
Regarding the word *pāna*: *ghṛṇī* means one who possesses disgust (*jugupsāvān*). According to Amara, *ghṛṇā* is that which causes disgust (*jugupsākaraṇe*).
"Thus" means: the removal of smearing, that is, the clearing away of the smearing on the hands. || 199 ||
Regarding the word "tataḥ": it refers to the region of the *kūrca*, which is the space between the eyebrows.
Amarasimha states: "The *kūrca* is not feminine; it is the space between the eyebrows. (200)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. The seventh chapter:
Having heard the extraction of the mantra of the goddess Ādyakālikā, which yields great fruit, [the disciple asks:]...
It produces both good fortune and liberation, and is the sole means for the knowledge of Brahman. || 1 ||

The morning duties, as well as the ritual bath, the twilight worship, the purification of consciousness, and the procedure for ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship, categorized according to their external and internal distinctions. || 2 ||
Having performed the offering of oblations, the fire sacrifice, and the ritual of the wheel,
and having accepted the *mahāprasāda*, the goddess Pārvatī, her mind filled with joy and bowed in humility, spoke to Śaṅkara.
The Goddess said:
O Sadāśiva, Lord of the World, benefactor of the worlds! Out of compassion, O God, you have explained the means for attaining the Supreme Nature (Parā-prakṛti).
It brings benefit to all living beings and is the sole cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it especially bestows swift accomplishment upon living beings in the Kali age.
Oṃ! Homage to Brahmā.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Having heard," etc.: "of great fruit" means that which possesses a great fruit; it is such as that. (1–3)
In response to the inquiry as to what Pārvatī said to Śaṅkara, he says "Sadāśiva," and so forth. || 4 || 5 ||
(166) My mind, having immersed itself in the nectar-ocean of your speech, does not wish to emerge of its own accord; rather, it soon desires [to remain there] ever again.
O Lord, the hymn and the armor (kavaca) of the Great Goddess were indicated during the ritual of worship but were not revealed; please reveal them now.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, who are adored by the world, to this unsurpassed hymn;
by reciting or hearing it, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
It pacifies misfortune, increases happiness and prosperity, removes untimely death, and wards off all calamities. || 9 ||
O Śivā, by the grace of this hymn, I am Tripurāri, the cause of the presence of bliss for the illustrious Ādyākālikā.

The seer (ṛṣi) of this hymn is declared to be the Goddess Sadāśiva; the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity (devatā) is proclaimed to be the primordial Kālikā. Its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 11 ||

"Your," and so forth: my mind, having immersed itself in the ocean of the nectar of your speech—the sea of the ambrosia consisting of your words—does not desire, nor does it wish, to rise up from there of its own accord or by its own will; rather, [it desires] further.
Furthermore, before long—and indeed very swiftly—it shall again seek the nectar of your speech. || 6 || 7 ||
Thus entreated by Pārvatī, Śrī Sadāśiva said, "Listen," and so forth. It is "anuttamam" (unsurpassed), meaning that from which nothing is superior. || 8 || 9 ||
Tripurāri: he whose enemies are the three cities—consisting of heaven, earth, and the netherworld (pātāla)—is Tripura, a specific asura; his enemy (ari) is the foe. || 10 ||
Now, he states the seer and other details of this hymn with the half-verse beginning "of the hymn" (stotrasya).
Hrī, Kālī, Śrī, Karālī, Krī, Kalyāṇī, Kalāvatī, Kamalā, she who destroys the pride of the Kali age, and she who is endowed with the compassion of Lord Kapardin. || 12 ||
She is Kālikā and Kālamātā, possessing a splendor equal to the fire of cosmic destruction;
she has matted hair, a formidable mouth, and is an ocean of the nectar of compassion.
Consisting of compassion, the support of compassion, the ocean of compassion, the source of compassion;
she is the fire, the tawny one, the dark one, and the increaser of the bliss of Kṛṣṇa. || 14 ||

She is the Night of Doom, she who assumes forms at will, and she who releases one from the noose of desire; she is the rain-cloud, the bearer of all arts, and the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age. || 15 ||
She is delighted by the worship of young maidens, she whose abode is the worshipers of young maidens;
she finds bliss in feeding young maidens, and she assumes the form of a young maiden. || 16 ||
She who wanders through the kadamba groves, she who dwells in the kadamba groves;
she who finds delight in the kadamba flowers, she who wears garlands of kadamba flowers. || 17 ||
She is a young maiden with a sweet voice, resounding with melodious notes;
she is devoted to drinking *kādambarī* wine and is fond of the *kādambarī* flower.

Now he recites the hymn of one hundred names known as the *Ādyakālīsvarūpa*, beginning with *hrīḥ kālī* and so forth. "Endowed with the compassion of Kapardīśa": *kaparda* means a mass of matted hair; one who possesses this is *kapardī*.
He is also the Lord (*īśa*), the Master of the World; thus he is *kapardīśa*. She is endowed with the compassion that resides therein.
It is logical. || 12 ||
She whose mouth—her face—is *karāla*, meaning jagged or protruding;
for Amara states: "The word *karāla* means jagged or high. (13)

"Accessible through compassion" means that which is reached or known solely by means of one's own compassion (*kṛpā*). [The root] *gam* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule "the roots *grah*, *dṛ*, *niś*, and *ci* take the accusative. (Pāṇini 3.2.17) 14–17.
She whose throat possesses a sweet, deep sound like that of a cuckoo;
she who is devoted to the skull-bowl as her vessel, who wears a garland of skeletons,
who is satisfied by the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā), and who dwells upon the Lotus-Seated One.
Dwelling in the midst of the abode of Kamalā, she delights in the fragrance of the lotus;
her gait is like that of a swan, she destroys impotence, and she can assume any form at will. || 20 ||
She dwells in Kāmarūpa, she sports in the sacred seat (pīṭha) of desire;
she is lovely, a wish-fulfilling creeper, adorned with desirable ornaments. || 21 ||
She is to be worshipped for her desirable qualities, with tender limbs and a slender waist;
she is satisfied by the nectar of the Cause and bestows the perfection of the bliss of the Cause.
She delights in the recitation of the Kāraṇa-mantra, she rejoices in the worship of the Kāraṇa, she is immersed in the ocean of the Kāraṇa, and she observes the vow of the Kāraṇa. || 23 ||
She who possesses the delightful fragrance of musk, she who is radiant with a tilaka of musk, she who delights in the worship of musk, and she who is dear to the worshipper of musk. || 24 ||
She who produces the fragrance of musk, she who delights the musk-deer;
she who is pleased by a meal of musk, she who is gladdened by the scent of camphor;
she whose ornaments are garlands of camphor, she who is anointed with camphor and sandalwood. || 25 ||
She who brings delight through the cause of camphor, she who drinks the nectar of camphor, she who has bathed in the ocean of camphor, and she whose abode is the ocean of camphor. || 26 ||

She is delighted by the recitation of the *kūrca* seed-syllable, devoted to the chanting of the *kūrca*, of noble lineage, worshipped by the followers of the *Kula*, and the one who acts for the benefit of the *Kaulikas*. || 27 ||
"Kaṅkālamālyadhāriṇī" means one whose habit is to wear a garland of the bones of the body; for Amara states that "kaṅkāla" refers to the bone of the body. (19–26)
She follows the family traditions, she is full of wonder, and she shows the way of the family path;
