she is the sovereign of Kāśī, the remover of suffering, and the bestower of boons upon the Lord of Kāśī. || 28 ||
She brings delight to the Lord of Kāśī and is enchanting to the Lord of Kāśī.
Her feet were adorned with anklets, her waist graced by the sound of tinkling girdles;
she made her dwelling upon the mountain of gold and was like moonlight upon the golden peak.
She is the bliss arising from the recitation of the seed-syllable of desire, whose essential nature is the seed-syllable of desire;
she is the destroyer of evil intellect, the noble one who destroys the suffering of her clan, and the beloved of the Kula.
"Kṛī / Hrī / Śrī / By these syllables of the mantra, she is the slayer of Kālakaṇṭaka. Thus begins the proclamation of the hundred names of the goddess Ākālikā. (32)
It is composed of the syllabic peak of the letter *ka*, and its essential nature is the form of Kālī.
Whoever recites this at the time of worship with their mind fixed on Kālikā, shall quickly attain mastery over the mantra; Kālī becomes pleased with him.
One obtains intelligence and knowledge merely by the command of the guru;
one shall become wealthy, famous, charitable in disposition, and endowed with compassion. (35)
The practitioner rejoices on earth through the happiness and sovereignty of sons and grandsons. || 36 ||
Devoted to the recitation of the *kūrca* mantra, they were intent upon the recitation of the seed-syllable *hūṃ*. || 27–29 ||
In the Kali age, she whose anklets on her feet possess a deep sound; that is, she whose two anklets on her feet are endowed with a profound resonance. || 30 ||
She whose joy consists in the recitation of the Kāmabīja; that is, she who finds bliss in the chanting of the Kāmabīja, namely "klīm. || 31 || 32 ||
It is constructed from the peak-syllable *ka*, and it is joined with the aggregate of the letter *ka*. || 33 ||
Now, he describes the fruit of reciting this hymn with the words beginning "At the time of worship" (pūjākāle), etc. (34–p. 170):
"On the night of the new moon of the month of Bhādra, accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), having worshipped Mahākālī, the primordial Mistress of the three worlds," (37)
Having recited the hundred names, one becomes manifest as Kālī herself;
for such a person, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unattainable within the three worlds. (38)
In knowledge he would be Vākpati himself, and in wealth he would be the Lord of Wealth;
in depth he would be like the ocean, and in strength he would be comparable to the wind. (39)
Difficult to behold like the sun of piercing rays, yet beautiful to look upon like the moon; he was Kāma incarnate in form, captivating the hearts of women. || 40 ||
By the grace of this hymn, one attains victory everywhere;
whatever desire one may set before oneself while reciting this praise, [that shall be fulfilled]. 41.
By the grace of the Primordial Goddess Śrī, one attains whatever desire one may have,
whether in battle, in the royal court, at a gambling match, in a dispute, or in a life-threatening crisis.
Likewise, when one is seized by bandits, during a village fire, or surrounded by lions and tigers; || 43 ||
In the forest, in the wilderness, in difficult terrain, or even in fear of the king of planets;
in the burning heat of fever, in long-standing illness, or when crowded with great diseases and the like—44.
In cases of diseases caused by child-seizing spirits and the like, as well as upon seeing evil dreams, or when in treacherous waters, or when a ship has met with disaster due to the wind; 45.
Regarding "bhauma" and so forth: the meaning is "during the great night (mahāniśā) connected with the new moon day (amāvāsyā) on Tuesday.
In the compound *bhaumāvāsyā*, the vowel *mā* is elided due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
Endowed with the five *māpakas*, that is, possessed of the five beginning with wine. || 37–39 ||
Like the sun of piercing rays, he is difficult to behold, to be seen only with great difficulty.
(40, p. 171) Having meditated upon the supreme Māyā, the primordial Kālī who is higher than the highest, whoever recites these hundred names endowed with firm devotion—(46)
O Goddess, one shall be liberated from all calamities; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
For such a person, there is no fear of sins, nor is there ever any fear of diseases.
He is victorious everywhere; nowhere does he suffer defeat.
Merely by the sight of him, multitudes of calamities flee away. 48.
He is the speaker of all scriptures, the enjoyer of all prosperity, the performer of the duties of his caste, and indeed the lord of his kinsmen. (49)
His speech shall dwell in his mouth, and Kamalā shall reside permanently in his home;
all men shall bow down with great reverence at his name.
In his sight, the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman* are indeed regarded as mere blades of grass;
thus, the hymn of one hundred names known as the *Ādyakālīsvarūpa* has been proclaimed. (51)
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for this [hymn] is said to consist of one hundred and eight recitations;
when accompanied by this preparatory ritual, the hymn bestows the fruit of all desired objects. (52)
One should recite this hymn of one hundred names, which is the primordial nature of Kālī,
or cause it to be recited, or hear it, or cause it to be heard.
Freed from all sins, he shall attain union with Brahman. || 54 ||
In a wilderness devoid of trees, water, and the like, on a road far from a village. || 44–49 ||
Whether they are agitated, fearful, or respectful. || 50 || 51 ||
Of this hymn of one hundred names, verses 52–54.
The venerable Sadāśiva said: The great hymn of praise to the Supreme Brahman, the primordial Prakṛti, has been told;
now hear the armor-verse (kavaca) of the primordial Śrī Kālikā. (55)
The seer of this armor-mantra, Trailokyavijaya, is Śiva;
the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is proclaimed to be the primordial Kālī. (56)
The seed-syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) is declared to be the "seed" (*bīja*), while *ramā* (śrīṃ) is proclaimed as the "power" (*śakti*).
*Krīṃ* is the "pin" (*kīlaka*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is celebrated for the attainment of desired goals. || 57 ||
May Hrīmā and the others protect my head; may Śrī Kālī protect my face;
may Krīṃ, the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), protect my heart; and may Parātparā protect my throat. 58.
May the Sustainer of the World protect my eyes; may Śaṅkarī protect my ears;
may Mahāmāyā protect my nose; and may Sarvamaṅgalā protect my tongue.
May Kaumārī protect the teeth; may Kamalālayā protect the cheeks; may Kṣamā protect the upper and lower lips; and may Cāruhāsinī protect the chin.
May Kuleśānī protect the neck; may Kṛpāmayī protect the hump. May Bāhudā protect the two arms, and Kaivalyadāyinī protect the hands.
May Kapardinī protect my shoulders; may Trailokyatāriṇī protect my back;
may Aparṇā protect my sides; and may Kamaṭhāsanā protect my hips.
Having been previously urged by Pārvatī to speak of the armor (kavaca), Śrī Sadāśiva said, "It has been told," and so forth. || 55 || 56 ||
The seed-syllable of Māyā is *hrīṃ*; the seed-syllable of Ramā is *śrīṃ*. (57–59)
The chin is the lower portion of the lower lip. (60–62)
May Viśālākṣī protect my navel, the seat of progeny; may Prabhāvatī protect my thighs; may Kalyāṇī protect my hips; and may Pārvatī protect my feet. (63)
May Jayadurgā, the bestower of all perfections, protect my life-breaths and my entire body;
for whatever place is devoid of protection and abandoned by the armor-mantra, [may she protect that as well].
"May that primordial, eternal Kālī always protect all of that for me.
Thus has been told to you this divine [mantra] named Trailokyavijayā. (65)
This is the most wonderful armor of the primordial goddess Kālikā.
Whoever recites this at the time of worship with a mind focused on the Primordial Goddess (Ādyā) attains all desires; Ādyā becomes well-pleased with him.
There shall be swift accomplishment of the mantra, and the servants—the minor supernatural powers—will be his.
One without a son obtains a son; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth; one seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; and one desiring pleasures shall attain their desires. 68.
By reciting this armor-mantra one thousand times, its preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is accomplished; thus perfected, it shall bestow the fruits as described.
If one writes [the mantra] on birch bark with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, and red sandalwood, and wears it as a pill placed within gold; || 70 ||
The generative organ is the place of progeny. 63–66.
Now, he describes the fruit of reciting the armor-armor (*kavaca*) named *Trailokyavijaya* with the verses beginning "At the time of worship" (*pūjākāle*), etc. (vv. 67–68).
Of the armor, that is, the breastplate. || 69 || 70 ||
Whether on the crest-lock, the right arm, the throat, or the waist, the practitioner’s primordial Kālikā, once brought under control, bestows his desired object. (71)
Nowhere shall he have fear; the poet shall be victorious everywhere.
He shall be free from disease, long-lived, strong, and capable of retaining [what he has learned]. (72)
Skilled in all branches of knowledge and knowing the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures,
the protectors of the earth remain under his control, and both worldly enjoyment and liberation are held within the palm of his hand.
It is the supreme means for bringing about the highest good for those joined with the impurities of the Kali age.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, you have graciously told me the hymn and the armor (kavaca);
now, O All-pervading One, I desire to hear the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
Śrī Sadāśiva said: Whatever procedure is prescribed for the *puraścaraṇa* rite of the Brahma-mantras,
that very same procedure is desired for the mantras of Adyākālī.
O Goddess, when the practitioner is incapable of performing recitation, worship, oblations, and so forth, the worship and the *puraścaraṇa* must be performed in an abbreviated manner. (77)
He bestows; he gives. || 71 || 72 ||
"Nipuṇa" means skilled or proficient. || 73 || 74 ||
Then, desiring to hear the procedure for the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) of the mantras of Ādyakālī, the Goddess spoke, beginning with "It has been told," and so forth. (75)
Thus impelled by the Śrīdevī, the venerable Sadāśiva spoke, beginning with the words "The procedure," and so forth.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) indeed, and the preliminary rite also, should be performed in brief.
(175) For indeed, compared to non-performance, even a very slight performance is superior;
O auspicious lady, listen first as the abbreviated worship is described therein. (78)
Having sipped water (ācamana) with the root mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages (ṛṣi).
Then one should perform the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), as well as the ritual placement on the hands and the body.
Having pervaded all the limbs, the wise one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
meditation, worship, and recitation—this is the procedure for the abbreviated rite of worship.
In the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of mantras, where a specific number of recitations has been prescribed, the puraścaryā is ordained by means of four times that number of recitations.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, or on a Tuesday or a Saturday,
one should procure the five elements (*pañcatattva*), perform worship, and [worship] the Goddess who consists of the universe.
During the dead of night, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times with undistracted mind;
having fed those established in Brahman, one becomes one who has performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Starting from Saturday until Tuesday,
one should recite the mantra every day with a count of one thousand.
He states the reason for performing the abbreviated worship and so forth with the words "yato hi" (for since). || 78 ||
He explains the abbreviated worship itself with the words beginning with "having sipped water" (ācamya).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) that pervades all limbs. || 80 ||
Now, he describes the abbreviated preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) with the words beginning "In the preliminary practice" (*puraskriyāyām*).
Wherever a specific recitation (*japa*) is prescribed for the preliminary practice of mantras,
the preliminary practice is accomplished by a recitation four times that amount, even without performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other such rites.
It is prescribed. || 81 || 82 ||
Ten thousand is an ayuta. || 83 ||
By reciting [the mantra] exactly eight times, the preliminary service (puraskriyā) of the mantra is accomplished. || 85 ||
O Goddess, the mantras of the primordial Kālī are perfected mantras that grant excellent accomplishment at all times in every age, especially in the Kali age. (86)
O Pārvatī, in the Kali age, many forms of Kālī manifest in various ways;
yet in this powerful Kali age, this particular form is for the welfare of the world.

In this matter, there is no requirement for the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) and the like, nor is there any fault regarding enemies, friends, and so forth; whether by following rules or without them, one should propitiate the First Goddess while reciting [the mantra]. 88.
One attains the knowledge of Brahman through the grace of the illustrious Primordial Goddess;
a mortal endowed with the knowledge of Brahman is liberated while living, without a doubt. (89)
There is no great exertion, nor even physical hardship, O beloved;
for the practitioners of the primordial Kālī, the sādhana is a means of attaining happiness.
In this matter, the purification of the mind alone bestows the fruit upon practitioners of mantra.
As long as the practitioner is not able to abandon the turbidity of the mind,
so long should he perform ritual action, endowed with devotion to his lineage.
For action performed according to the rules is indeed the cause of mental purification;
at the outset, one should receive the mantra from the mouth of the Guru, just like the Brahma-mantra.
Now, he describes the third *puraścaraṇa* with the verse beginning "Kujeti" and continuing for half a verse.
"Until Tuesday" means up to the second Tuesday.
|| 84 || "This form" refers to the form of the primordial Kālī. || 87 ||
Here, regarding the mantra of Ādyākālī (verses 88–91):

"As long as" means: for as long as one is unable or incapable of abandoning—that is, casting off—the turbidity of the mind, which is its impurity; for that long, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), being endowed with devotion to his lineage and possessing vows and observances (*vratin*), [should remain].
Having performed the daily observances such as the morning rites, one should perform the preliminary worship (puraskriyā).
O Great Goddess, when the mind is purified, the knowledge of Brahman arises;
once the knowledge of Brahman has arisen, there is neither duty nor non-duty. (94)
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Supreme Lord, what is Kula? And what, O All-pervading One, is Kulācāra?
I wish to hear the true definition of the five principles (pañcatattva) according to reality. (95)
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
O Mistress of the Kula, you who desire the welfare of practitioners, you have asked well.
For your pleasure, I shall speak; listen attentively as it truly is. 96.
The individual soul (jīva), the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti), space, time, and ether, as well as earth, water, fire, and air—this is designated as the Kula. (97)

And whatever conduct one practices toward these [objects] with a non-conceptualizing mind, perceiving them as Brahman—that alone is the primordial Kula practice, which bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation. (98)
One should perform the ritual action, but not beyond that. He states the reason for this as "properly" (*yathāvat*); for (*hi*) because... [92–94]
Desiring to know the traditional conduct of the Kula and other such matters, the venerable Pārvatī spoke, beginning with the words, "What is the Kula? (verse 95).
Thus impelled, Śrī Sadāśiva said: "It has been well asked," and so forth.
First, he defines "Kula" there with one verse beginning with "jīva": "The nine, beginning with the individual soul (jīva), are designated—that is, called—'Kula'. (97)
Now, with the words "by perceiving as Brahman," he explains family custom (*kulācāra*) through one [verse]: O first ones, that conduct which consists of perceiving these—

such as the individual soul (*jīva*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and so forth— as Brahman, being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), meaning devoid of various kinds of mental constructions (*kalpanā*), that alone is [family custom].
The family tradition (kulācāra) is said to bestow dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. || 98 ||

Through merits accumulated over many births, by means of austerity, charity, and firm vows, the minds of practitioners whose sins have been exhausted shall be directed toward the family tradition (kulācāra). 99.
When the intellect, having entered into the conduct of the family, becomes quickly and perfectly pure, then their mind is born within the lotus-feet of those [teachers]. 100.
Having obtained this supreme knowledge through service to the true guru,
and becoming devoted to the Kula practice, one should worship the Mistress of the Kula (Kuleśvarī) by means of the five elements.
Worshipping Kālikā, the Primordial One, those best of practitioners who know the Kula,
having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, go at the end to the state free from suffering.
That which is the great medicine for living beings, which causes the forgetting of suffering and generates bliss—that is the defining characteristic of the primordial reality (ādyatattva). || 103 ||
O Beloved, that which is the unconditioned reality, which bestows delusion and causes wandering, and which generates the disease of dispute—this must always be abandoned by the Kaulas. (104)

That which is produced from village, wind, and forest [products], which increases nourishment, and which bestows intelligence, splendor, and strength, is characterized by the second principle (tattva). || 105 ||
Now, he describes the extreme difficulty of attaining the conduct of a noble family with the verse beginning "by [merits] acquired over many births," and so forth.

Now, he describes the supreme fruitfulness of the family tradition (kulācāra) with the verses beginning "one who has entered the family tradition" and so forth. This is the Vidyā, which consists of mantras. 100–101.
The state of liberation is free from affliction and devoid of all calamities. || 102 ||
Next, he describes the characteristics of the five principles (tattvas), beginning with wine and so forth, starting with the words "mahauṣadham" and so on. || 103 ||
Reality is the primordial reality. || 104 ||
"Grāmya," and so forth: domestic animals (*grāmya*) are those produced in villages, such as goats and the like;

wild birds (*vāyavya*) are those produced from the wind, such as partridges (*tittiri*) and hārīta birds and the like; and forest animals (*vanya*) are those produced in the forest, such as deer and the like—of these [various kinds]. || 105 ||
O auspicious lady, that which arises from water is desirable, bestows happiness, increases progeny, and is characterized by the third principle. (106)

That which is born from the earth and is easily obtained, which is the very life of living beings, the root of the lifespan of the three worlds, and characterized as the fourth principle (tattva). || 107 ||
O Goddess, it brings great bliss to living beings and is the cause of creation;
it is the root of the world without beginning or end, and the defining characteristic of the Śeṣa-tattva.
Know that the first principle is fire, O beloved; the second is wind.
Know water to be the third, and earth the fourth, O Śivā. (109)
O fair-faced one, know that the fifth is space (viyat), the support of the world. 110.
Having thus understood the five principles of the Kula, O Mistress of the Kula,
as well as the conduct of the Kula-dharma, a man shall become liberated while living.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Hymns, Armor, and the Principles of the Kula," in the *Śrī Mahānirvāṇatantra*, the most excellent among all tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas, within the dialogue between the venerable Primordial Goddess and Sadāśiva.
Desirable means that which is to be longed for. || 106–111 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. The eighth chapter:
Having heard the various kinds of teachings, Bhavānī, the liberator from worldly existence, [spoke].
For the welfare of the worlds, the Mother spoke again to Śaṅkara.
The Goddess said: I have heard many kinds of dharma that bestow happiness here and in the hereafter, which grant virtue, wealth, and desire, remove obstacles, and are the cause of liberation.
Now I wish to hear; O Lord, speak of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramas), and out of compassion, tell me also those prescribed duties that pertain to them. (3)
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
O lady of virtuous vows, the four castes and the stages of life have been described,
as well as the specific codes of conduct for each caste and stage of life.
Ā / Homage to Brahman.
"Having heard," and so forth. She is the liberator from existence (*bhavamocanī*), whose nature is to shatter the saṃsāra of her devotees.
The term "of the worlds" (*jagatām*) is connected by way of the maxim of the eyeball of a crow (simultaneously with both preceding and following words).
It is connected. || 1 ||
In response to the expectation of what he said, he says "It was heard," and so forth. || 2 ||
In that regard, among the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramas). || 3 ||

Thus impelled, Śrī Sadāśiva said, beginning with "The four," and so forth: "O you of good vows, in the Kṛta age and others— namely Satya, Tretā, and so on— the castes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas) were declared to be four,
as were the conducts (ācāras) of those castes and stages."
In the Kṛta and other ages, up to the Kali age, five castes are proclaimed:
the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, the Śūdra, and the Sāmānya (commoner). (5)
O Maheśvarī, among all these castes there are two stages of life;
O Primordial One, listen as I tell you their rules of conduct and duties.
The conduct arising from the Kali age has already been described:
for men who are devoid of austerity and Vedic study, whose lifespans are short, and who are incapable of exertion and toil, how could there be any physical fatigue? (7)
In the Kali age, O beloved, there is no stage of life for the student (brahmacarya) nor even for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha);
there are only two stages of life: that of the householder and that of the mendicant.
They have been described individually. However, in the Kali age, the castes (*varṇas*) are proclaimed to be of five kinds.
He shows these with the half-verse beginning with "brāhmaṇa," etc. This is the general mixing of castes (*varṇasaṅkara*).
(4–5) Regarding the phrase "of these": O primordial Maheśvarī, of these [groups] beginning with the Brāhmaṇas...
The grammatical connection is as follows: "I shall speak before you of the two stages of life for all castes, as well as the duties consisting of the conduct of those castes and stages; listen. (6)

Intending to describe the two stages of life (āśramas) that exist in the Kali age, Mahādeva first demonstrates the reason for the absence of the previous two stages with the verse beginning "puraiva" and so forth, consisting of one and a half verses.
Those whose birth or origin (*sambhava*) is in the Kali age are called *kalisambhavāḥ*; of them...
The intended meaning has already been stated. The word "tāvat" is used here as a particle of emphasis. Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "tapaḥ":

for those devoid of austerity (*tapas*) and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*)—where "austerity" refers to practices such as the *kṛcchra* penance and "Vedic study" refers to the recitation of the Vedas—for those who are incapable of the exertion and labor required by these two.
Affliction (*kleśa*), distress (*upatāpa*), exertion (*prayāsa*), and fatigue (*pariśrama*)—because these two [affliction and distress] have ceased for them, they are incapable [of such things].
This applies not only to those of this kind, but also to those of short lifespan. For such persons, how could there be physical exhaustion? Not by any means whatsoever.
The meaning is "it would be. || 7 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "brahmacarya" and so forth: O beloved, therefore in the Kali age there is no stage of life (āśrama) of celibate studentship, nor is there the stage of forest-dwellers; rather, in the Kali age, only two stages of life remain, namely those of the householder and the mendicant. || 8 ||
O Śivā, in the Kali age, all the rites for the householder are declared in the Āgamas;
for householders, the accomplishment of rites never occurs through other paths. (9)
O Goddess, even in the stage of life of a mendicant, the carrying of the staff prescribed by the Vedas does not exist at all in the Kali age, O knower of truth, because that is a Vedic refinement.
O auspicious lady, the assumption of the Avadhūta stage of life according to the Śaiva ritual procedure is declared to be the very act of taking up renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in the Kali age.
O Goddess, in the powerful Kali age, everyone— both Brahmins and members of the other castes— is entitled to both [the practice] and the stages of life (āśramas).
The purificatory rites and rituals for all [castes] follow the path of Śiva; however, the ritual emblems (karmaliṅga) for Brahmins and others are distinct from one another.
He states with the words "of the householder," etc., that it is not only the absence of the two [other] stages of life in the Kali age, but rather the absence of all Vedic rites as well.
"Of householders" (gṛhamedhinām) means of those who possess attachment to the home, i.e., of householders. || 9 ||

In the Kali age, all Vedic rites are prohibited not only in the householder stage of life (*gārhasthyāśrama*), but even in the mendicant stage (*bhaikṣukāśrama*); thus he says, "even in the mendicant stage," and so forth. That refers to the carrying of the staff (*daṇḍadhāraṇa*) as prescribed in the Vedas. *Śrautasaṃskṛtiḥ* means Vedic refinement.
Formative force. || 10 ||
If this is so, then what indeed is the purpose of taking up the renunciant life (saṃnyāsa) in the Kali age?

To this he says "Śaiva," and so forth: O blessed lady, that which is the maintenance of the Avadhūta stage of life according to the rite of purification (saṃskāra) proclaimed by Śiva—that alone [is the true renunciation] in the Kali age.
The undertaking of renunciation has been described. || 11 ||

Now, one might object: "In the Kali age, does the eligibility for the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa-āśrama) belong to all castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as it did in the Satya and other ages, or is it restricted only to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas? To this, he says: "Of the Brāhmaṇas," and so forth. (Verse 12)

Now, one might ask: in this powerful Kali age, will all the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, come to have a single uniform conduct, or shall they each have their own distinct conduct? To this, he says: "Of all," and so forth.
[The meaning is: of all the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, all...

(183) As soon as he is born, he shall be a householder; through the performance of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra), he becomes an inhabitant of a religious order (āśramin). O Maheśvarī, one should first undertake the life of a householder according to the prescribed rule.
When dispassion arises once the knowledge of reality has been produced, then, having renounced everything, one should enter the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). || 15 ||
A wise man should acquire knowledge in childhood, wealth and a wife in youth, perform righteous deeds in middle age, and in the fourth stage of life, he should renounce the world.
Having abandoned one's mother, father, aged [parents], a devoted wife, and an infant son, one should not enter the stage of the wandering ascetic (avadhūta). || 17 ||
He who goes forth into homelessness having abandoned his mother, father, children, wife, kinsmen, and even his relatives, shall become a perpetrator of a great sin.

All ritual acts (*saṃskāras*) and all other actions are to be accomplished by the single path of Śiva alone. The meaning is that because they are to be accomplished by the unique path of Śambhu, all actions for all castes (*varṇas*) are indeed equal in the Kali age. However,
Even in the Kali age, the ritual emblems and ritual marks of the Brahmins, of others, and of those distinct from the Brahmins, each remain indeed separate. || 13 ||
Now, does the state of belonging to the householder stage of life (gārhasthyāśrama) arise by mere birth or by means of a sacramental rite (saṃskāra)? To this he says, "As soon as born," and so forth.
Now, between the stages of the householder and the mendicant, which comes first?
Regarding which stage of life one should resort to, he says here: "The state of the householder," and so forth. 14.
In the knowledge of reality, that is, in the knowledge of Brahman. || 15 ||

Now, at what stage of life should the householder’s stage (gārhasthya-āśrama) be resorted to, and at what stage should renunciation (saṃnyāsa) be undertaken? To this he says, beginning with "vidyām" (knowledge), etc.:
one should acquire knowledge in childhood, i.e., during infancy; and in youth, wealth, property, and a wife.

And he should acquire a wife. In the third stage of life, when he has reached maturity, he should perform righteous deeds—deeds not departing from dharma. A wise and learned man should renounce and enter the life of a wandering mendicant (saṃnyāsa) in the fourth stage of life. || 16 || 17 ||
(184) He who would go to the stage of a mendicant without having gratified his own ancestors and others would be a matricide, a patricide, a killer of women, and a slayer of a Brahmin. (19)
A Brāhmaṇa who has deviated from the Vedic path should perform the sacraments prescribed for his own caste according to the Śaiva way; this is the dharma in the Kali age.
The Goddess said:
O All-pervading Lord, what is the duty of a householder and what is that of a mendicant?
Tell me of the duties of a Brahmin and those distinct from him, as well as the purificatory rites and so forth. (21)
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
Householdership is the primary duty for all those born as human beings;
I shall first describe that very thing according to its true nature—listen, O Kaulinī. (22)
A householder should be devoted to Brahman and intent upon the knowledge of Brahman;
whatever action he may perform, he should offer that unto Brahman.

He states, in the two verses beginning with "mātṝḥ," that for a man who renounces [the world] after abandoning his mother and others, there would be a great sin (mahāpātaka). Because the plural number indicates a plurality of instances, "pitṝn" means fathers and so forth. "Svajanān" means those related by oneself.
Those who must be supported are one's own dependents; "relatives" refers to those such as brothers and others who are incapable [of supporting themselves].

Having heard [the rules for] the five castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—their two stages of life (āśrama) and their common duty—it is now [the turn to hear] all their specific duties in their entirety.
Desiring to hear the teachings, the Goddess Śrī said: "Who indeed," and so forth. What is the teaching?
Thus impelled by the Goddess, Śrī Sadāśiva said,
beginning with "The state of the householder," and so forth: "O Kaulinī, since for all those born as humans—
that is, for men— the duty of the householder is the primary dharma."
Therefore, that very dharma exists; I shall first declare it, so listen to it in its true essence—this is the syntactical connection. || 22 ||
By the words "one who is established in Brahman" (brahmaniṣṭha) and so forth, he indeed declares the dharma of the householder (gārhasthya).
One whose steadfastness (niṣṭhā) is in Brahman is "established in Brahman. || 23 ||
One should not engage in false speech, nor should one practice deceit;
a householder should be devoted to the worship of the deities and guests. (24)
A householder, regarding his mother and father as the manifest, perceptible deities themselves, should always serve them with every effort. (25)
O Pārvatī, when the auspicious mother is satisfied and the father is satisfied, O Goddess, your own pleasure arises and the Supreme Brahman is propitiated. (26)
You are the primordial mother of the worlds, and Brahmā is the father, higher than the highest;
since their mutual pleasure is the goal, what other austerity can there be for householders? (27)
Having understood the specific requirements for each occasion, one should provide a seat, a bed, clothing, drink, and food to the mother and the father.
He should speak with gentle words and always act in a pleasing manner; a son who follows the commands of his parents is a true son and a sanctifier of the lineage. (29)
One who desires his own welfare should not engage in levity, jesting, threatening, or reproaching in the presence of his parents. (30)
Upon seeing his mother or father, he should rise with haste and bow;
he should not sit down without permission, remaining ever obedient to his father's command.
Deceit is lack of straightforwardness. 24–26.
Because [it arises] from pleasing both the mother and the father. || 27 ||

"Seat," and so forth. That upon which one lies is a "bed" (*śayana*), meaning a couch. That which is drunk is a "drink" (*pāna*), meaning water and so on. "Food" (*bhojana*) refers to edible substances.
"At those respective times" means at the time of offering the seat and the other items. "One should employ" means one should offer them. || 28 ||
Excitement is lack of discipline; threatening is the intimidation of servants and others. || 30 ||
Full of agitation and full of respect. || 31 ||
He who, intoxicated by the pride of knowledge and wealth, should treat his father with contempt, goes to a terrible hell, having been cast out from all dharma. (32)
A householder should not eat while neglecting his mother, father, son, wife, guests, and siblings, even if his life-breaths have reached his throat.
He who, having deceived his teachers and kinsmen, eats merely to fill his own belly, is censured by the world in this life and shall become a denizen of hell in the next.
A householder should protect his wife, practice learning, and nourish his children, kinsmen, and relatives; this is the eternal dharma.
The body was nurtured by the mother, nourished by the father, and affectionately instructed by one's own kinsmen; yet that lowest of men would abandon them. (36)
O Great Goddess, for their sake one should constantly satisfy them with one's power, even by undergoing hundreds of hardships; for this is the eternal dharma. (37)

That man on earth who is devoted to Brahman, true to his word, and established in the ultimate truth—he is the blessed man in the world, he is the successful one, and he is the knower of the supreme goal. || 38 ||
One should never strike one's wife, but should always protect her like a mother;
even in the midst of terrible distress, one should not abandon her if she is a virtuous, devoted wife.
Offense against the father means disrespect toward one's mother and father. || 32 || 33 ||
"Gurus" refers to parents and others; "despised by the world" means censured by people. || 34 || 35 ||
By one's own people and kinsmen. || 36 ||
Of these, [namely] the mother and the others; he should gratify them, he should satisfy the mother and the others. || 37 ||

Fortunate is the one who has performed good deeds; he is accomplished and discerning. One who is true to his word and faithful to his promise should not touch another woman while staying with his own wife.
A wise man who does otherwise with a wicked mind shall become a denizen of hell. (40)
A wise man should avoid sharing a bed or a dwelling with another's wife, as well as improper conversation; he should not display his prowess before her. (41)
One should constantly please one's wife with wealth, clothing, affection, faith, and gentle speech; one should never act in a way that is disagreeable to her.
During a festival, on a journey, at sacred fords, or in another's house,
a wise man should not send his wife alone, unless she is accompanied by a male relative or a servant.
O Maheśānī, that man with whom a devoted wife is pleased has performed every duty; he is indeed dear to you.
For a period of four years, the father should fondle and protect his sons;
thereafter, until they reach sixteen, he should instruct them in virtues and knowledge.
One should employ sons who are more than twenty years of age in the household duties;
thereafter, regarding them as equals, one should manifest affection toward them. (46)
A daughter should likewise be protected and instructed with great care;
she should be given in marriage to a learned groom, accompanied by wealth and jewels.
With a wicked heart and a corrupted mind. || 40 ||
In a rarefied, uninhabited place. || 41 || 42 ||
In another dwelling, that is, in a house belonging to another. || 43 || 44 ||
Then, after four years have passed. || 45 ||
He should impel, that is, cause them to proceed—those sons who are more than twenty years of age. || 46 ||
The same applies as in the case of a son. || 47 ||
In this manner, by following the proper sequence, the householder should protect and satisfy his brothers, as well as his sisters, nephews, kinsmen, friends, and servants. (48)
Then, the householder should protect those who dwell in his village, who are devoted to their own duties, as well as guests and neutral strangers. 49.
O Goddess, if a householder who possesses wealth does not practice in this way, he should be known as nothing but a beast; he is a sinner and despised by the world.
One should not indulge in excessive sleep, laziness, bodily exertion, the arranging of hair, nor attachment to food and clothing. (51)
Moderate in food, moderate in sleep, restrained in speech, and restrained in sexual intercourse—clear-sighted, humble, pure, and skillful—one should be disciplined in all actions. (52)
A hero should be humble toward his enemy, his kinsman, and in the presence of his elders;
he should not feel contempt for those who are despised, nor should he disparage those who are proud.
Having ascertained through living together and through reasoning their goodwill, their dealings, their conduct, and their innate nature, one may then place trust in them.
Then, after the protection and pleasing of his brothers and others, [he considers] those who are neutral, being neither friends nor enemies. || 48 || 49 ||
He states with the words "If... and so forth that for a householder who does not act in this manner while possessing wealth, there would be both a basis for sin and contempt from the world. || 50 ||
Attachment (*āsakti*) means clinging (*āsaṅga*); "excessive" (*atirikta*) means more than required (*adhika*). || 51 ||
One who is moderate in diet eats in measured quantity; one who is pure is free from deceit and the like;
one who is clean is endowed with external and internal purity; one who is skillful is free from laziness; and one who is disciplined is possessed of industry. || 52 ||
He is a hero, full of prowess; one should not despise him nor disregard him. || 53 ||
By means of reasonings and thorough investigations. || 54 ||
Even toward a petty person who causes fear or hatred, a wise man, observing the proper occasion, should manifest his true nature; he must never transgress the Dharma. (55)
One who knows the Dharma should not disclose his own fame or prowess, nor that which was spoken for the sake of protection, nor that which was done for the benefit of others.
Even when defeat is certain and the course of action is loathsome, one who desires fame should not engage in a lawsuit, whether the claim is large or small.
Exerting himself, he should acquire knowledge, wealth, fame, and dharma;
and he should abandon vice, association with the wicked, and false malice. (58)
Activities follow the state [of the practitioner], and ritual actions follow the convention; therefore, having observed both the state and the convention, one should perform the rite. (59)

Devoted to the security and well-being [of others], skillful, righteous, and affectionate toward kinsmen, he should be moderate in speech and moderate in laughter, especially in the presence of those worthy of honor. (60)
One who has conquered the senses, whose self is serene, who is well-reflected, and firm in his vows,
being vigilant and far-sighted, should contemplate the contacts of the senses with their objects.

He should cause [the enemy] to tremble and be terrified. From the hater, that is, from the enemy; from the mean, that is, from the insignificant. From his own being, that is, from his own power—the splendors born of his treasury and army.
Regarding this, Amara states: "That which is born of the treasury and the army is called *pratāpa* (majesty), *prabhāva* (power), and *tejas* (splendor). (55–57)
Exerting himself means making an effort. || 58 || 59 ||
Delighting in yoga and kṣema; yoga is the acquisition of what has not been obtained, while kṣema is the preservation of what has been obtained; he is devoted to both of these. 60.

"Having conquered the senses," and so forth. "One whose thoughts are well-considered" (sucintya) means one for whom the scriptures and other objects of reflection are properly contemplated. "The contacts of the senses" (mātrāsparśān):
the *mātrās* are the functions of the senses, by which objects are measured; their "contacts" (*sparśān*) are the connections with sense-objects. || 61 ||
A wise person should speak words that are true, gentle, pleasant, and beneficial;
likewise, they should avoid self-exaltation as well as the disparagement of others. (62)
He by whom a reservoir, trees, a resting house on the road, or a bridge has been established, has conquered the three worlds. (63)
In whom his parents find contentment and whose circle of friends is devoted;
he whose fame the worlds sing—by him the three worlds are conquered. (64)
He whose vow is truth alone, who has compassion for the distressed in every way,
and who has brought desire and anger under control— by him the three worlds have been conquered.
He who is detached from the wives of others, free from desire for the possessions of others,
and devoid of hypocrisy and envy— he has conquered the three worlds.
He who does not fear battle and does not turn his back even in the midst of combat—whether he dies in a righteous war or not—by him the three worlds have been conquered. (67)
He who is free from doubt, possessed of great faith, intent upon the conduct of Śambhu, and devoted to my teaching—he has conquered the three worlds. (68)
By that knower who performs actions for the sake of the world's journey with an even gaze toward all things, the three worlds are conquered.
O Goddess, purity is indeed twofold, distinguished as external and internal;
that which consists of the surrender of the self to Brahman is known as internal purity. (70)
Free from desire and free from longing. 66–68.
In all cases, such as with enemies, friends, and so forth. || 69 || 70 ||
The removal of impurities by means of water or even ashes, whereby the purification of the body occurs—that is called external purity. (71)
The Gaṅgā, rivers, lakes, ponds, as well as small wells—
all these produce purity in succession, O beloved, with the celestial river (Gaṅgā) being the foremost.

O lady of excellent vows, know that the ash here is the best kind used for sacrifice, while the clay is free from impurities; likewise, garments made of antelope skin, grass, and so forth, are to be understood as being like the clay.
What is the use of saying much more here regarding the auspicious rules for purity and impurity?
A householder should perform whatever action ensures that his mind remains pure. 74.
At the end of sleep, at the end of sexual intercourse, at the end of evacuation,
after voiding feces or urine, at the end of a meal, and when touched by impurity, external purification is prescribed.

The three daily twilight rites (saṃdhyā) should be performed, both Vedic and Tantric, in their proper sequence; according to the specific distinctions of one's practice, one should perform worship in accordance with the rules.
O Dear One, for those who worship the Brahma-mantra, through the recitation of the Gāyatrī and through knowledge, that which is expressed as "Brahman" becomes the Vedic Sandhyā. (77)

Regarding the phrase "with water": external purification (*bahiḥśauca*) is said to be the removal— that is, the clearing away— of impurities by means of water, or ashes, or whatever substance such as clay, cloth, leather, or grass brings about the purification of the body.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya). || 71 ||
*Kṣullakāḥ* refers to small reservoirs of water. According to Amara, *kṣullaka* is used in three genders even when referring to something very small.
*Sarvam* refers to everything, such as the waters of the Gaṅgā and so forth. || 72 ||

"Regarding the words *bhasma* and so forth: here, in the rule for external purification, O lady of good vows (*suvrate*), know that even garments, deerskins, grass, and the like are superior only when they are free from impurity, just as clay is. (73–76)

Having first shown the differences in worship, he demonstrates the differences in the *sandhyā* rites with two verses beginning with "Brahman," etc. This is because for those who worship the Brahman-mantra,
through the recitation of the Gāyatrī and by means of the knowledge that "the Brahman expressed by her is the very Brahman propounded by the Gāyatrī," [the result is attained].
The Vedic twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) takes place. || 77 ||

p. 192) For others, the Vedic *sandhyā* consists of the worship of the sun (*sūryopasthāna*) preceded by the offering of water (*arghyadāna*) to the Lord of Day, as well as the recitation of the *gāyatrī*. (78)
O auspicious lady, the rule for recitations in all daily rites is one thousand and eight, or one hundred, or even ten times.
O Goddess, Śūdras and those of common castes alone possess the right to perform the rites prescribed in the Āgamas; from that, all spiritual accomplishments shall arise.
Morning is the time of sunrise, midday follows thereafter, and evening is the time of sunset; such is the sequence of the three periods of the day.
The illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord, you yourself have explained that the Tantric ritual is prescribed for all castes, beginning with the Brahmins, now that the powerful Kali age has arrived. (82)

Regarding the phrase "of others": for others—those distinct from the worshippers of the Brahma-mantra—the Vedic *sandhyā* consists of offering *arghya* to the Sun, the Lord of Day, preceded by the worship of the Sun, as well as the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī*. || 78 ||

Now, with the words beginning "aṣṭottaram," he states the rule for the recitation of mantras during the daily rites (*āhnika-karma*): even a hundred [recitations] must be exactly eight more than that (one hundred and eight). This applies everywhere, both in Vedic and Tantric practice. (79)
Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. || 80 ||
Now, he describes the sequence of the three times required for the ritual of *sandhyā* with the words beginning "at dawn" (*prātaḥ*).
That time in which the sun rises is the time of sunrise. || 81 ||

Previously, it was stated by Śrī Sadāśiva that in the powerful Kali age, all castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, have the right only to Tantric rites; however, at present, even for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, [the right exists] to Vedic rites as well.
Thinking it improper that there should be eligibility for the twilight worship (sandhyā), the venerable Goddess said, beginning with "viprādī" and so forth. 82.
(193) Therefore, O Lord, how is it that you now employ the Brahmins in Vedic rites? You ought to explain all of that in detail.
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
O knower of reality, you speak the truth; the Tantric ritual for all people grants success in all actions for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation. (84)
Just as this Brahmasāvitrī is Vedic, so too should the Tantric one be known; it is praised for both types of ritual action.
Therefore, O Goddess, it is said here that in this powerful Kali age, the twice-born have the right to Gāyatrī alone, and never to any other mantra. (86)
Tārādyā, Kamalādyā, and Vāgbhavādyā are, in their respective order, declared to be the Sāvitrī for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas in the Kali age. (87)
O Supreme Goddess, for the purpose of distinguishing the twice-born and others from the Śūdras,
this Vedic Sandhyā was proclaimed even prior to the daily rites (āhnika-karma).
Otherwise, one may become a possessor of supernatural powers (siddhi) through the Śāmbhava paths alone.
This is the truth, the truth, again the truth; this is the truth, there is no doubt about it. (89)
You enjoin; you set in motion. || 83 ||
To this, the venerable Sadāśiva replied with the words beginning "It is true," and so forth. (84–86)

"Beginning with Tārā," and so forth. In the Kali age, according to the sequence—that is, in due order—the [goddesses] beginning with Tārā for the Brāhmaṇas, those beginning with Praṇava (Oṃ) for the Kṣatriyas, those beginning with Kamalā (Śrī) for the Vaiśyas, those beginning with the Śrī-bīja for the [Brāhmaṇas], those beginning with Vāgbhava (Ai) for the [Kṣatriyas], and those beginning with the Sāvitrī-bīja for the [Vaiśyas]—are declared to be Gāyatrīs. || 87 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the twice-born and others": O Supreme Goddess, for the sake of distinguishing the twice-born— namely the Brāhmaṇas and so forth— from the Śūdras, this Vedic [practice] must indeed precede the daily rites of the Tantrikas.
It is declared that the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) must be performed. 88 || 89 ||

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, even when the [proper] time has passed, this twilight rite (saṃdhyā) must be performed by those seeking liberation who are not afflicted by illness, after having uttered "Oṃ Tat Sat Brahma. (90)
A seat, clothing, a bowl, a bed, a vehicle, a dwelling, and all types of household articles—when they are pure, they are praised as being pure. (91)
Having completed his daily rites, a householder should regularly perform his private Vedic study or domestic duties; he must never remain idle.
Performing recitation and giving gifts at a sacred pilgrimage site on an auspicious lunar day, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one shall become an abode of all blessings.
In the Kali age, those whose vital breaths depend upon food do not find fasting praised;
instead, a single gift is prescribed as a substitute for fasting.
In the Kali age, O Maheśānī, charity becomes the means for attaining all perfections;
its only worthy recipient is known to be a poor man endowed with virtuous conduct.
O Mother, the days on which the months, years,
and fortnights begin are the fourteenth, the eighth, the bright eleventh, and likewise the new moon day (Kuhū).
One's own birthday, the day of the death of one's parents, and the day of a Vedic festival are proclaimed to be auspicious times. || 97 ||
"Kāla" and so forth: O Goddess worshipped by the gods, even when there is a lapse of time—
that is, even when there is a transgression of the prescribed time for the twilight ritual—
those who are not afflicted by the incapacity caused by old age and other such factors [should perform it].
O people who desire liberation through emptiness and long for liberation, having uttered "Tat Sad Brahma," this Vedic and Tantric twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) should be performed. || 90 ||
"Household goods" refers to every object related to the home. || 91 ||
Svādhyāya is the study of the Vedas. (92–95)
The Gaṅgā river, the great rivers, the abode of the Guru himself, and the renowned sacred field of the deities are proclaimed as meritorious tīrthas. (98)

For men traveling to a sacred pilgrimage site, neglecting their Vedic study, service to their parents, and protection of their wife would lead them to hell rather than to the merit of the pilgrimage. (99)
For women, there is no service at sacred fords, nor rites such as fasting and the like;
indeed, there is no observance of vows whatsoever apart from service to the husband. (100)
For women, the husband alone is their sacred ford, their austerity, their charity, their vow, and their teacher; therefore, a woman should perform service to her husband with her whole being. (101)
She should always do what is pleasing to her husband through her speech and her service;
following his commands, she should satisfy his kinsmen. 102.
A devoted wife should not look at her husband with a cruel gaze, nor should she ever cause him to hear harsh words; she should not even mentally harbor anything unpleasant toward her husband. 103.
She who always gladdens her husband with agreeable deeds through body, mind, and speech, she alone shall attain the state of Brahmā. 104.
She should not look at the face of another, nor should she engage in conversation with others; following her husband’s command, she should not display her limbs to others. 105.

Now, he describes in sequence the auspicious time and the sacred bathing place required for the rite of offering recitations (japadāna), beginning with the words "In the month" and so forth. *Kuhū* is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), when the digit of the moon has vanished.
Now, he describes the duties of women with seven verses beginning with "not at a sacred ford" (na tīrthe). 100.
With one's whole being and with every effort. || 101 ||
By means of attendance and service. || 102–105 ||

In childhood she should remain under the authority of her parents; upon reaching youth, under her husband; and in old age, under the relatives of her husband. She should never be independent at any time. (106)

A father should not marry off a young girl who does not know the bounds of propriety toward her husband, who does not know how to serve her husband, and who is ignorant of the teachings of the Dharma.
One should not eat human flesh, nor the flesh of animals in human form;
nor should one eat the flesh of cows, which provide many benefits, for they are devoid of [desirable] flavor.
O Śivā, all fruits— both cultivated and wild— and various kinds of roots growing from the earth may be eaten at one's own will.
Teaching and officiating at sacrifices are the supreme duties for Brahmins;
in the event of inability, one should maintain oneself through the livelihoods of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
For kṣatriyas, the virtuous conduct consists of warfare and the governance of the land;
if unable to do so, they may resort to the conduct of a merchant, or otherwise, the conduct of a śūdra.
O Supreme Goddess, for Vaiśyas who are incapable of trade, there is no fault in following the livelihood of a Śūdra; for Śūdras, however, service is prescribed as their livelihood.
Independent and self-dependent. || 106 || 107 ||
By the qualification "of great benefit" applied to the cows, the reason for the prohibition of feeding them is shown. "Meat-eaters" refers to carnivorous creatures such as vultures and the like;
"devoid of flavor" means lacking any sense of taste. || 108 || 109 ||
Now, he states the conduct of a Brahmin, beginning with "teaching," and so forth. || 110 ||
Next, he describes the conduct of the Kṣatriyas with the single verse beginning "Of the Rājanyas" (111). Here, it concerns the virtuous conduct consisting of governing and [engaging in] battle.

Now, he describes the livelihood of Vaiśyas and Śūdras with the single verse beginning with "vāṇijya" (112, p. 1197): "For Vaiśyas, moreover, trade is the highest livelihood; for the common castes, however, [it is] the livelihood other than that of the Brāhmaṇas."
O Goddess of gods, there is authority for the sake of accomplishing the journey of the body. || 113 ||
Free from hatred, devoid of possessiveness, peaceful, truthful in speech, with senses conquered, free from envy, and without guile—such a one shall be a Brāhmaṇa established in his own duty. 114.
One should teach disciples who abide on the path of truth with the mindset of a father toward a son;
one should be a seeker of the welfare of all the world, free from partiality. (115)
A Brahmin should avoid, under all circumstances, false speech, envy, addiction to vices, speaking unpleasant words, intimacy with the base, and hypocrisy. (116)
The desire for combat is censured in the context of peace; peace is the highest good through honors.
For kṣatriyas, O lovely-faced one, there is either death or victory in battles. (117)
He should be free from greed regarding the wealth of his subjects and should collect a moderate tax;
protecting the dharma he has undertaken, he should cherish his subjects like his own children. (118)
The king should always carry out justice, war, peace, and whatever other actions there may be, after having deliberated upon them together with his ministers. (119)
Now, he describes the livelihood of those of mixed castes (*varṇasaṅkara*) with the single verse beginning with "sāmānyānām" (113).

Now he describes the duties of a Brahmin with the verses beginning with "adveṣṭā" and so forth. "Nirmama" means one who is devoid of the sense of "mine-ness" regarding the body and other such things. "Śānta" means one whose mind is restrained. || 114 ||

"Falsehood," and so forth. Envy (*asūyā*) is the attribution of faults to another, even when they possess virtues. Addiction (*vyasana*) refers to activities such as gambling. Deceit (*dambha*) is the inflation of the mind caused by a desire for self-regard and honor. (116)

Now, he describes the duties of the royalty (rājanya) with the words beginning "yuyutsu" and so forth: O Varānane, O lady of most praiseworthy countenance, when there is a *sandhi*— that is, a reconciliation or alliance— between *rājanyas*, i.e., Kṣatriyas, the desire to fight (*yuyutsā*) is censurable and condemned.

One should fight with a righteous war, and punishments and honors should be administered according to justice and in accordance with the scriptures; one should make peace according to one's strength. (120)
One should accomplish one's purpose with enemies through strategic means, whether by war or by peace;
for all prosperities, including victory and security, are dependent upon such means.
May he always refrain from associating with the base, be dear to the wise, steadfast in adversity, skillful, virtuous, and moderate in his expenditures. (122)
Skilled in the fortification of strongholds and proficient in the training of weapons,
he should seek out the disposition of his own army and instruct them in the art of warfare.

O Goddess, one should not slay enemies who have fainted in battle, those who have cast away their weapons, those who have turned their backs, those brought in by force, nor even the wives and children of enemies. (124)
Whatever objects have been acquired through victory and whatever have been obtained through treaties, he should bestow them upon his troops according to their respective merit. || 125 ||
A king should individually ascertain the valor and conduct of his warriors;
intent on his own welfare, he should not appoint a single person as the commander of a vast army. 126.

[This] would be so. However, for them, peace through honors alone would be best. In their battles, however, either death or victory would be best; the meaning is that flight and the like are not [acceptable]. (117–119)

"Honoring" (puraskriyā) means respectful treatment (satkāra). "According to one's strength" (yathābalam) means not exceeding one's strength; that is to say, preceded by [an assessment of] one's strength. || 120 || 121 ||
Vīrata means dispassionate; dhīra means courageous; dakṣa means industrious. || 122 ||

"Skilled," and so forth. Regarding "the fortification of a stronghold": a *durga* is that which the enemy finds difficult to traverse due to mountains, moats, ramparts, and the like; it refers to a city that is difficult to access.
It is the fortification (*saṃskāra*) of such a city. || 123 || 124 ||
A king should not place his trust in a single person, nor should he entrust a single individual with the administration of justice.
He should avoid equality, play, and mockery with those who are lowly. (127)
One who is learned yet speaks little, who desires knowledge and possesses it, who is highly esteemed yet free from deceit, and who is steadfast in both punishment and favor. (128)

Whether by himself or through the observation of spies, the lord of men should examine the dispositions of his subjects; in this same manner, he should observe the intentions of his kinsmen and servants.
Out of anger, deceit, or negligence, a master who perceives the truth must never hastily bestow honor or punishment.

The army, the commander-in-chief, ministers, women, children, and servants—if they are at fault, they must be protected; if they are guilty, they must be punished by the king according to the law. (131)
The king should protect like a father those who are insane, those incapable of self-care, children, those whose kinsmen have died, those overcome by fever, and the elderly. (132)
Know that agriculture and commerce are the eternal livelihood of Vaiśyas, by which means the maintenance of the bodies of people is accomplished. (133)
He should cross over; he should give. || 125–127 ||

"Though he be learned," and so forth. Even though he possesses great honor—that is, abundant respect—the king should be free from hypocrisy, meaning he should be devoid of mental inflation caused by that abundant honor. || 128 ||

"By himself," and so forth. A "spy" (*cara*) is an undercover agent skilled in investigating other principles; "by that vision" means by means of his mode of observation. "The dispositions of the subjects" refers to the intentions or activities of the people. || 129 ||
From hypocrisy—that is, from the mental agitation caused by motives such as sovereignty and the like. || 130 || 131 ||
Those whose kinsmen have died; that is, those who are such that their relatives are deceased.
Now he begins to describe the conduct of Vaiśyas with the words "of the Vaiśyas," and so forth.
By which means—namely, the activities of agriculture and trade—the maintenance of the body, that is, the sustenance of the physical frame, [is achieved].
Therefore, O Goddess, in all respects regarding the activities of trade and agriculture, one should utterly avoid negligence, addiction, laziness, falsehood, and deceit. (134)
O Auspicious One, having determined the value of the object with the agreement of both parties, there shall be mutual acceptance, and from that, the completion of the purchase occurs. (135)

O beloved, for those who are intoxicated, deranged, or childish, for men seized by enemies, and for those whose intellects are bewildered by disease, giving and selling are not accomplished [if done] at improper times. 136.
The successful purchase of unperceived [substances] occurs through hearing of their qualities;
in the opposite case, if those qualities are otherwise, the purchase is likewise otherwise. (137)
Because of the disclosure of hidden defects in elephants, camels, and horses, one may rescind that purchase even after a year has passed; otherwise, one ought not to do so. (138)
The human body is the vessel for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, by my command, that [body] must not be sold. 139.
O beloved, when the year has passed, there will be a gain of barley, wheat, and grains;
this is declared to be the fourth yoga, the eighth among the elements.
In matters of debt, agriculture, trade, and likewise in all undertakings, whatever has been undertaken by mortals must be carried out in accordance with the scriptures. (141)
In every respect and in every way. || 134 ||

"Having ascertained," and so forth. "Having ascertained" means having determined. "Its price" means having also determined the price of the object that was determined. "Of both" refers to the seller and the purchaser.
Of things not seen; in the case of their reversal, that is, their opposite. || 137 || 138 ||
That which is to be purchased is the human body to be purchased. || 139 ||
The creditor may take more than the principal capital as profit.

(140–141) A man engaged in the occupation of service should be skillful, pure, truthful in speech, one who has conquered sleep, one who has conquered his senses, vigilant, and free from laziness. (142)
The master is to be honored like Viṣṇu, and his wife like one's own mother;
likewise, his kinsmen are to be honored by servants who desire happiness both in this world and the next. (143)
One should recognize the master’s friends as one’s own friends and his enemies as one’s own enemies;
always remaining apprehensive, one should abide awaiting the command of the lord. (144)
She should guard with extreme effort any instance of disrespect, any flaw in the household, anything said for the sake of protection, and anything that causes dishonor to her husband. || 145 ||
He should be free from greed regarding his master's wealth and always devoted to his master's welfare;
in his presence, he should renounce improper speech, play, and laughter. (146)
One should not look even at the female servants of that house with an evil mind;
one should avoid a secluded bed and laughter together with them. (147)
One should not employ the bed, seat, vehicle, clothing, vessels, sandals, ornaments, or weapons of the Lord for one's own sake. (148)
If one who has committed an offense should earnestly seek forgiveness from his lord, he should avoid boldness, arrogant speech, and equality in conduct. (149)

Now, he describes the duties of a servant with the verses beginning with "dakṣa" and so forth. *Dakṣa* means clever or skillful in one's own tasks. *Śuci* means pure or clean. *Apramatta* means attentive or careful regarding one's own duties. (142–146)

"Na pāpa... and so forth. With a sinful mind, he should not even look at the female servants of that master; what need is there to mention his wife, daughters, and others? "Vivikta-śayyām" means a private bed or a secluded place for sleeping. "Tābhiḥ" refers to those female servants of the master's house. || 147 || 148 ||
Boldness is audacity. || 149 ||
O Śivā, all castes, according to their respective castes, may perform the Brāhma marriage and likewise take food from the circle of Bhairavīs, provided it is not from the circle of the Tattvas. (150)
O Great Goddess, in both cases the Śaiva marriage is proclaimed;
likewise, in giving and in drinking, no distinction of caste exists. (151)
The Śrī Devī said:
What is this Bhairavī-cakra, and of what nature is the Tattva-cakra? I desire to hear all of that; you should deign to speak it out of compassion. (152)
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
O Goddess, in the ritual procedure for the Kula worship, the practice of the Cakra has been proclaimed;
it should be performed by the most excellent practitioners at the time of the special worship. 153.
O Dear One, regarding the Bhairavīcakra there is no such restrictive rule;
having reached it according to the proper occasion, one should perform this auspicious cakra. 154.
I shall describe the ritual procedure for practitioners which brings about auspiciousness;
by means of this, the Goddess, when propitiated, swiftly grants whatever is desired. (155)
*Aśana* means eating; *ṛte* means without. || 150 ||
In both cases, namely in the Bhairavīcakra and the Tattvacakra. || 151 ||
Then, desiring to hear the procedure for the Bhairavīcakra and the Tattvacakra, the venerable Goddess said: "What is this? and so forth. (152)
Being thus entreated, Śrī Sadāśiva said, "The Kula-worship," and so forth.
The performance of the *cakra* is that which has been described in the procedure for that Kula-worship. (153–154)
Of this Bhairavīcakra; by which [means], namely by the ritual procedure of the Bhairavīcakra;
he bestows, that is, he gives. || 155 ||
The family preceptor, having spread out an excellent seat on a beautiful spot and having purified it with the seed-syllable of the weapon beginning with *kāma*, should then sit down. (156)
With vermilion, or with saffron, or with water alone, the wise man should fashion a triangular or square mandala. (157)
Having brought a variegated jar, smeared with curd and unbroken grains of rice, joined with fruits and sprouts, and adorned with a tilaka mark of vermilion; 158.
Having established [the vessel] in that mandala with the syllable Om (praṇava), the practitioner, having filled it with well-perfumed waters, should present incense and lamps. || 159 ||
Having worshipped with perfume and flowers, one should contemplate one's chosen deity;
there, one should perform the worship according to the abbreviated ritual procedure.
I shall state the specific distinction here; listen, O goddess worshipped by the immortals!
For the nine vessels beginning with that of the Guru, their installation is not required here. (161)
He describes the performance of the Bhairavī-cakra with the words beginning "the Kulācārya" and so forth.

The Kulācārya is the teacher of the Kula. On a delightful ground—that is, on a beautiful site—having spread out and covered an excellent seat with the syllable *klīṃ*, which begins with *kāma* (desire).

Having purified [the seat] with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja) ending in *phaṭ*, he should then sit there upon that seat using vermilion (*sindūra*). Then, the wise and learned one should draw a triangular mandala with vermilion, or with *kusīda*, or with pure red sandalwood, or even with water alone.
Outside of that, one should construct a square mandala with four corners. || 157 ||
"Variegated," and so forth. After that, having brought a jar that is "variegated"— meaning one upon which various paintings (*citrāṇi*) have been drawn—
and which has been smeared with curd and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and joined with fruits and sprouts;

Having prepared [the vessel] adorned with vermilion tilakas and filled with water well-scented with camphor and other fragrances, and having established it within that mandala with the Praṇava (the syllable *oṃ*), the practitioner should present incense and lamps before it. || 158 || 159 ||

"Having worshipped" means: then, having fully worshipped the jar with scents and flowers, one should contemplate one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) therein. Having so contemplated, one should perform the worship of the chosen deity in that water-pot according to the previously mentioned abbreviated ritual procedure (*saṃkṣepapūjāvidhi*).
One should practice; one should perform. || 160 || 161 ||
Having taken up the reality as desired and established it before him, the practitioner, observing the vow, should sprinkle it with the weapon-mantra and gaze upon it with divine vision. || 162 ||
Having offered fragrant flowers upon the *aliyantra*, one should meditate there upon the goddess Ānandabhairavī as well as Ānandabhairava. 163.
Endowed with fresh youth, her body was as ruddy as the morning sun;
her lotus-face shone with a beautiful smile and nectar-like speech. || 164 ||
One should meditate upon her who delights in dance and song, adorned with various ornaments, wearing diverse garments, and whose lotus-like hands grant boons and fearlessness. 165.
Having thus meditated upon the one consisting of bliss (Ānandamayi), one should remember Ānandabhairava.

"As desired": then the practitioner observing the vow (vratī), having taken the substance as desired—such as wine and so forth—and having placed it before him in front, should sprinkle it with water while reciting the Astra-mantra ending in *phaṭ*, and he should gaze upon it with the divine vision (*divyadṛṣṭi*). || 162 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the *aliyantra*": then, having placed fragrant flowers in the *aliyantra*, which is a vessel for wine, one should meditate upon the goddess Ānandabhairavī and likewise the god Ānandabhairava within that very *aliyantra*. || 163 ||

He describes the meditation on Ānandabhairavī herself with the words "endowed with fresh youth" (*navayauvanasampannām*). "Endowed with fresh youth" means having attained new adolescence. "With a body like the young sun" (*taruṇāruṇavigrahām*) means having a form resembling the newly risen sun.
Her lotus-face, which is radiant and shining with a beautiful smile and nectar-like speech— that is,
with a charming laugh and speech as sweet as ambrosia— is a blooming lotus-mouth.
She who was thus: she by whom joy and delight were produced through dance and song; she adorned with various ornaments, decorated with many kinds of finery;
wearing wonderful and marvelous garments.

One should meditate upon Ānandabhairavī, who is clothed in garments (*vasana*) and whose lotus-hands display the gestures of boon (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*). Thus [is described] Ānandabhairavī.
Having meditated [upon this], one should remember Ānandabhairava. (164–166)
White as a mass of camphor, with eyes as broad as lotuses,
the beauty of his body adorned with divine garments and ornaments;
with his left lotus-hand holding a vessel filled with nectar—
I meditate upon him holding a purifying pill in his right hand. || 167 ||
Having meditated thus and contemplating the state of aesthetic union (*sāmarasya*) of both there,
the preceptor, having worshipped with the name-mantra beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, using fragrance and flowers, should then purify the causal principle (*kāraṇa*). || 168 ||
The worshiper of the Kula, reciting the mantra of the three syllables beginning with *pāśa* and ending with *svāhā* one hundred and eight times, should purify the cause (*hetu*).
In this powerful Kali age, for householders whose minds are solely intent on domestic desires,
the three sweets (madhuratraya) should be employed as a substitute for the primary [Vedic] principles.
He describes the meditation on Ānandabhairava with a single verse, beginning with "white as a mass of camphor. "White as a mass of camphor" means as brilliant as a stream of camphor.
"Lotus-eyed" means one whose two eyes are as long and wide as lotuses.

One whose bodily splendor is adorned with divine garments and ornaments— that is, one whose body is embellished and decorated with divine clothes, ornaments, raiment, and finery, and who possesses such superior radiance and luster— [with his] left [hand].

I remember and meditate upon Ānandabhairava, who holds with his left lotus-hand a vessel rich in nectar and a vessel accompanied by wine, and who holds the pill of purification with his right lotus-hand. || 167 ||
Having meditated thus— having meditated on both in this manner—

the teacher or practitioner, contemplating the state of *sāmarasya* (equilibrium) or *aikarasya* (oneness) of both Bhairavī and Bhairava within that *aliyantra*, [should worship] with the name-mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Having worshipped those two with perfumes and flowers, one should then purify the causal substance, the liquor.

Now, by what mantra should one purify the liquor? To this he says "pāśādi" and so forth. With that which ends in *svāhā*—that is, with such [a mantra] consisting of the three seed-syllables beginning with *pāśa*, namely *āḥ*, *hrīḥ*, and *kroṃ*—while reciting this very mantra one hundred and eight times.
The family priest should purify the cause, which is the wine. || 169 || 170 ||
Milk, sugar, and honey are to be known as the "triple sweet" (madhuratra).
Having perceived this as the form of the bee, one should offer it to the deity. (171)
Those born in the Kali age, by their very nature, have minds bewildered by desire;
possessing ordinary intellects, they do not recognize Śakti in that form.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, in their stead, for the sake of the remaining reality, there is meditation upon the lotus feet of the Goddess as well as the recitation of one's own chosen mantra. (173)
Then, one should consecrate each of those items, such as the meat and others, which have attained their true essence, by reciting this mantra a hundred times.
Having meditated upon everything as consisting of Brahman and closed both eyes,
one should offer the food and drink to Kālī as before and then partake of them.
He describes the three sweets as "milk" and so forth; the form of the bee is the nature of the wine.
This is the apparatus of sweetness (madhurayantra). || 171 ||
Śakti is the woman. || 172 ||

"From this," and so forth. O Pārvatī, for this reason, in place of sexual union—which is the residual reality (śeṣatattva) for those born in the Kali age—meditation upon the lotus-feet of the Goddess must be performed;
likewise, the recitation of one's own chosen mantra must be performed. || 173 ||

Regarding "tatastviti": thereafter, one should consecrate and purify the various substances such as *palala* (sesame paste) and *māṃsa* (meat), which have attained their essential nature (*prāptatattva*), by reciting this mantra—*ā hrīḥ kroḥ svāhā*—one hundred times for each. This is the meaning. || 174 ||

"Everything. Then, having closed both eyes and meditated upon all reality—including wine and other substances—as consisting of Brahman and being of the nature of Brahman, one should offer it to Kālī as before and partake of the food and drink just as previously. || 175 ||
(207) But this Bhairavī-cakra, hidden in all the tantras, has been declared before you, O auspicious lady, as the essence of essences, higher than the highest. (176)
O Pārvatī, marriage must by all means be performed by the preeminent practitioner according to the Śaiva path, both within the Bhairavī-cakra and within the Tattva-cakra. (177)
Without marriage, O hero, by performing service to Śakti, one would incur the sin of those who go to another's wife; of this there is no doubt. (178)
When the Bhairavī-cakra has arrived, all castes are the best of the twice-born;
when the Bhairavī-cakra has ceased, all castes are distinct once again. (179)
In this matter, there is no consideration of caste, nor any discrimination regarding leftovers and the like; the heroes situated within the circle are my own forms, designated by the name "men. (180)
There is no restriction of place or time, nor any deliberation regarding the recipient;
whatever substance has been brought by anyone should be employed in this wheel. || 181 ||
Whether brought from a distant land, cooked or even uncooked,
or even [offered] by a hero or a beast, it is pure when situated in the center of the discus.
O Great Goddess, at the commencement of the wheel, all obstacles become overwhelmed with fear;
terrified by the Brahmanic splendor of the heroes, they flee. 183.
Now, he begins to describe the majesty of the Bhairavīcakra with the words "This, however," and so forth. || 176 || 177 ||
Pariṇaya means marriage. || 178 || 179 ||
Here, in the Bhairavīcakra. || 180 ||
The substance refers to intoxicants and the like. || 181–183 ||
Piśācas, guhyakas, yakṣas, vetālas, and those of cruel species, having heard of this Bhairavī-cakra here, flee far away in terror. (184)
There, all the sacred fords (tīrthas), including the great tīrthas and others, as well as all the hosts of gods led by Indra, come with reverence. (185)
