O Śivā, the site of the Cakra is a great sacred ford, superior to all other holy places;
it is there that the thirty gods long for your supreme food offering.
Whether brought by a Mleccha, a Śvapaca, a Kirāta, or a Hūṇa, food—whether raw or cooked—that is placed into the hand of a hero is pure. (187)

But having seen the circle of Bhairavīs and my own forms as well as the practitioners, even those defiled by the impurities of the Kali age are liberated from the bonds of the bound souls (paśu-pāśa). || 188 ||
In this powerful age of Kali, however, one should not conceal the wheel;
everywhere and at all times, the hero should accomplish the Kula practice. 189.
In the center of the disc, one should avoid idle chatter, restlessness, speaking too much, spitting, passing wind, and changing the color of the lips.
One should abandon from afar the cruel, the wicked, the beasts, the sinful, the atheists, those who defile their lineage, and those who revile the family scriptures. || 191 ||
Whether out of affection, fear, or attachment, by causing animals to enter [the fire], even a hero who has fallen away from the family dharma shall go to hell. (192)
"Sādhvasam" means with fear. || 184 ||
There, at the location of the wheel. || 185 || 186 ||
By the Hūṇu, a specific caste; raw, meaning uncooked. 187–191.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of common birth—whoever indeed rely upon the dharma of their own lineage—those are always to be honored like gods. (193)
But he who, out of pride regarding caste, creates a distinction of castes within the *cakra*,
goes to a terrible hell— even if he has reached the further shore of the Vedānta.
For those virtuous Kaulas within the circle who possess pure minds and whose very nature is manifest Śiva, how could there be any suspicion of sin? (195)
As long as the Brahmins and others who follow the path of Śiva reside within the [sacred] circles (cakras),
they shall practice the conduct of Śambhu according to the teaching of Śiva.

All those who have emerged from the wheel should perform their respective duties, as prescribed for their particular caste and stage of life, individually, for the sake of establishing the course of worldly existence. (197)

Even by performing a hundred preliminary rites (puraścaryā), a wise person obtains that same fruit by reciting [the mantra] but once in the center of the wheel while seated upon a corpse, a skull, or a funeral pyre. 198.
Who indeed would be capable of describing the greatness of the Bhairavīcakra?
One who performs this even once is liberated from all sins. (199)
By practicing this constantly, a mortal shall become a protector of the earth for six months, and himself a conqueror of death for a year; he shall attain the liberation of Brahman.
Out of fear or out of affection—that is, out of attachment caused by fear. || 192–195 ||
They should look after [them]; they should perform [these duties]. || 196 || 197 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "puraścaryā" and so forth: whatever fruit one obtains from the corpse-seat (*śavāsana*), the skull-seat (*muṇḍāsana*), and the funeral-pyre-seat (*citāsana*). || 198 || 199 ||
(210) What is the use of saying more here? Know this to be the truth, O Kālikā:
for there is no path other than the family way (*kulamārga*) for attaining happiness in this world and the next. 201.
In this age of Kali, when the power of the age is predominant and all [other] dharmas have fallen away,
even a Kaula who fails to conceal the Kula-dharma will become a denizen of hell.
The wheel of Bhairavī, the sole means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been described.
O Mistress of Kula, I shall now speak of the wheel of the principles (tattva); listen to that. 203.
The wheel of reality (*tattvacakra*), the king of wheels, is called the divine wheel;
no one has authority over it except for those practitioners who possess knowledge of Brahman. (204)
Those who worship the Supreme Brahman, who know Brahman and are devoted to Brahman, whose inner selves are pure, who are tranquil, and who delight in the welfare of all living beings; || 205 ||
Those who are changeless, free from conceptual construction, compassionate by nature, firm in their vows,
and whose resolutions are true— such Brahmins alone are qualified for this.
Those who perceive the moving and the unmoving through the state of Brahman—
those men who know reality possess the authority within the wheel of reality.

O Goddess, for those in whom the realization that "all existence is composed of Brahman" arises within this wheel known as the *tattva*, they alone are the masters of the wheel of reality (*tattvacakrin*).
Regarding "for six months": the grammatical construction is that a mortal who practices the Bhairavī-cakra for six months shall become a protector of the earth (a king). || 200–203 ||
Here, in this sovereign wheel, the wheel of reality (tattvacakra). || 204 ||
They are peaceful, being empty of passion, hatred, and the like. || 205 ||
There, in the wheel of reality (tattvacakra). || 206 || 207 ||
"Bhāva" means cultivation (*bhāvanā*), that is to say, reflection (*vicintana*). || 208 ||
(211) There is no need for placing a water-jar here, nor for elaborate worship;
one should accomplish the practice of reality everywhere through the state of Brahman. (209)
O Dear One, the master of the wheel (cakreśvara) should be a counselor of Brahman and one established in Brahman;
together with practitioners who know Brahman, he should commence the wheel of reality (tattvacakra).
In a delightful and perfectly pure place that brings happiness to practitioners,
one should bring a variegated seat and prepare a stainless seat.
Having sat there together with the practitioners of Brahman, the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) should attain the principles (tattvas) and establish them before Śivā.
Reciting the mantra one hundred times, beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with the vital seed-syllable (*prāṇabīja*),
he should utter this mantra as the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*) over all the principles (*tattva*).
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is thus absorbed in action that is Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained. 214.
The means for accomplishing reality; the means for accomplishing the wheel of reality. || 209 || 210 ||
Now, he describes the procedure for the wheel of reality (tattvacakra) with the verses beginning with "ramye" and so forth. || 211 ||
There, upon the imagined pure seat, one should cause the principles—wine and so forth—to be seated, that is, brought there.
"Tārādi" and so forth: then, regarding all the principles (tattvas) such as wine and the rest, "beginning with Tāra" means that which has Tāra—the Praṇava—as its beginning;
"ending with the Prāṇabīja" means that which has the seed-syllable "Haṃsa"—the Prāṇabīja—as its end.

Having recited one hundred times the mantra "oṃ haṃsaḥ," which begins with *tāra* (oṃ) and ends with the seed-syllable of breath (*prāṇabīja*), the Lord of the Wheel should utter this mantra that is about to be described. || 213 ||
He states the mantra itself: "The offering is Brahman," and so forth. || 214 ||
Having recited [the mantra] seven times or three times, one should purify all of those. || 215 ||
Then, having offered it to the Supreme Self with a sacred mantra, he should partake of food and drink together with practitioners who are knowers of Brahman.
O Great Goddess, in the Wheel of Brahman one should avoid distinctions of caste;
there is no restriction of place or time, nor likewise any restriction regarding the recipient.
Those foolish men who, out of negligence, cause a division of the lineage or a division of the caste within the divine wheel, go to the lowest state. || 218 ||
Therefore, with every effort, the best of practitioners who know Brahman should perform the wheel of principles for the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation. 219.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, you have described the duties of householders in their entirety;
out of compassion, you should now speak of the duties prescribed for renunciants.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said: O Goddess, in the Kali age, the stage of the Avadhūta is called renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
Listen now to all that regarding the procedure by which it must be performed.
"Sevenfold": having recited this mantra seven times or three times, one should purify all those [substances], such as wine and the rest. || 215 ||
With the Brāhmaṇa mantra "Saccidekaṃ brahma" (Brahman is Being-Consciousness-Bliss), [he should perform the rite]. || 216 ||
In the Brahma-wheel, that is, in the wheel of reality. || 217–219 ||
Having thus heard all the duties of householders without exception, the venerable Goddess, desiring now to hear the duties of renunciants, said:
"Of householders," and so forth. (220)
Thus impelled, the venerable Sadāśiva spoke, beginning with "O Avadhūta," and so forth;
that procedure is now, at this present time, [being explained]. || 221 ||

When the knowledge of Brahman has arisen and all ritual action has ceased, one who is proficient in the science of the inner self should take recourse to the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). || 222 ||
Having abandoned his aged parents, his devoted wife,
and his dependent kinsmen, one who goes forth into the wandering life shall become a denizen of hell.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, and even a commoner—
these five have the eligibility for the purificatory rite of the Kulāvadhūta.
Having completed his domestic duties and having satisfied others as well, he should depart from his dwelling free from possessiveness, devoid of desire, and with his senses conquered. (225)
A person desiring to depart from home should affectionately seek the consent of his kinsmen, relatives, villagers, and neighbors after having summoned them. (226)
Having obtained their permission and bowed to the Supreme Deity,
he should circumambulate the village and depart from his home without looking back.
Freed from the bonds of saṃsāra and blissful with supreme joy, one should approach a Kula-avadhūta who knows Brahman and make this request: || 228 ||
He states the very procedure for taking up renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) with the words beginning "In the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmajñāne*), etc.
One who is skilled in the science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*) is one who is proficient in the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). (222–224)

Having completed and accomplished [his duties], free from the sense of "mine" (nirmama)—that is, devoid of attachment to objects such as his home—he [should depart] from his dwelling, that is, from his house. || 225 ||
One should seek consent; one should obtain permission. || 226 ||
Indifferent and free from desire, he should go. || 227 ||
He is one who has emerged from supreme bliss and is immersed in supreme bliss. || 228 ||
"O Supreme Brahman, these years of mine have passed in the householder stage of life.
O Lord, grant me your favor regarding the undertaking of renunciation. (229)
Having observed that he has ceased his household duties and, seeing him to be tranquil and discerning, the teacher should duly direct him toward the second stage of life.
Then the disciple, having bathed, with self-restraint, and having performed his daily rites,
should worship the divine sages and the ancestors for the sake of liberation from the three debts.
The gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—along with their respective hosts, as well as the sages beginning with Sanaka, and likewise the celestial and brahminical rishis; || 232 ||
In this regard, I shall also declare those ancestors who are worthy of worship; listen to them as well. || 233 ||
The father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather;
the mother, the grandmother, O Goddess, and likewise the great-grandmother;
and similarly the maternal grandfathers and so forth, as well as the maternal grandmothers and so forth. (234)
He states what one should pray for with the words beginning "in the stage of the householder" (gṛhāśrame), etc. (verse 229).
Peaceful, with a mind that has ceased [its activity]. || 230 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): thereafter, the disciple, having become self-restrained with a controlled mind, and having performed his bath and daily rites, should worship and honor the divine sages (*devarṣis*), the gods (*devas*), and the ancestral sages (*pitṛs*) for the sake of liberation from the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*). || 231 ||
He states with the words "the gods," etc., those gods and sages who are to be worshipped for the sake of liberation from debt:

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, together with their respective retinues—these are the gods to be worshipped in the rite of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Those of whom Sanaka is the first are called "Sanakādyas" (those headed by Sanaka).

The sages Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, and others who are of the same lineage as Sanaka, as well as the celestial sages (devarṣis) such as Nārada and others, and the brahminical sages (brahmarṣis) such as Bhṛgu and others, are worthy of worship. || 232 ||
In this matter of renunciation and action. || 233 ||
For the sake of liberation from debt, he speaks of the venerable ancestors themselves with the verse beginning "the father" and so forth, consisting of one and a half [stanzas].

In this way, just like the father and others, the maternal grandfathers and so forth are also to be worshipped; such is the lineage. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the paternal great-grandfather and the paternal great-great-grandfather are included.
And there is the inclusion of the paternal great-grandmother and the paternal great-great-grandmother. || 234 ||

In the east one should worship the sages, in the south one should worship the gods, and in the west one should worship the paternal grandfathers; thus one should perform the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (235)
One should provide two seats each in the sequence starting from the east;
having invoked the deities and others there in order, one should perform the worship.
Having worshipped them according to the prescribed rule, one should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to each individually.
Having offered the rice-balls in due order according to the ritual for offering piṇḍas,
one should, with palms joined in reverence, pray to the ancestral deities.
Be satisfied, O ancestors, gods, divine sages, and the hosts of mother-goddesses;
may you soon discharge me from my debt regarding the state that transcends all qualities.
Having thus sought freedom from debt and having bowed down again and again,
one who is liberated from the three debts should perform the ancestral rite for oneself (ātma-śrāddha).

Now, in response to the inquiry as to in which direction one should worship the gods, the sages, and the ancestors, he says "in the east," and so forth. In the rite of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), one should worship the gods and the sages in the east, that is, in the eastern direction; [and] in the south...

One should worship the ancestors, beginning with the father, in the eastern direction; one should worship and honor the maternal grandfathers, beginning with the maternal grandfather, in the western direction. || 235 ||

Now, he describes the procedure for the worship of the gods and others in brief, beginning with the words "in the order starting from the east" and so forth. In the order starting from the east—that is, according to the sequence beginning with the east—one should provide two seats each in the three directions. Regarding those seats:
Having invoked the gods and others in pairs, one should perform—that is, carry out—their worship in due order. || 236 ||
"Having worshipped," and so forth: having worshipped the gods, sages, and ancestors according to the rule,
one should offer separate *piṇḍas* to those gods, sages, and ancestors individually, according to the rule,
to the gods and others in their proper sequence by means of the procedure for offering *piṇḍas* that will be described hereafter.
Having offered the piṇḍa and joined his palms in reverence, he should pray to the ancestral deities (pitṛdevatās).

Regarding what he should pray for there, [the text] says "be satisfied" (tṛpyadhvam) and so forth: "O fathers, O gods, O divine sages (devarṣis), and O hosts of mothers, may you be satisfied in the state that transcends all qualities (guṇātītapada)."
Make me free from debt very soon, indeed very quickly, as I proceed toward that state which transcends all qualities. || 238 || 239 ||
For the father is indeed the self of all; he is their father and their great-grandfather.
Therefore, for the sake of surrendering the self into the Self, the wise man should perform the rites of the self. (240)
Facing north and seated upon the prepared seat as before,
O Goddess, one should invoke one's own ancestors and offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) while performing worship.

For the purpose of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one should spread darbha grass with their tips pointing eastward, southward, and westward in due order; for one's own ritual action, they should have their tips pointing northward. 242.
Having completed the śrāddha rites according to the path shown by the guru,
one who desires to practice yoga should recite this mantra one hundred times for the sake of purifying the mind.
Hrīḥ! We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant one who increases prosperity.
May he deliver me from death, even as a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality. 244.
According to the method of worship, the Guru, having placed a water-pot upon the altar preceded by the drawing of a mandala, should commence the ritual worship there. (245)
Showing the reason for placing faith in the Self, he says "for the father," and so forth.
For since the Self alone is the father of all, it would also be their father, grandfather, and great-grandfather;
therefore, for the sake of offering oneself to the Supreme Self, the wise one—the learned person—[should act].
One should perform the ritual action for oneself. || 240 ||

In brief, he states the procedure for himself and for the *śrāddha* with the words "facing north" and so forth. "His own ancestors" refers to the ancestors, such as the father and others, who are of the nature of his own self. Regarding "with the tips pointing east," this is for the sake of the *piṇḍas*.
For the purpose of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) intended for the gods, sages, and ancestors, one should first, in due order and sequence, spread— that is, cover—
the darbha grasses with their tips pointing eastward, southward, and westward, respectively, during one's own ritual.
But in the rite for one's own ancestors, he should spread such darbha grasses as have their tips pointing toward the north. || 242 || 243 ||
He states that very mantra beginning with "hrīḥ" and "tryambakam," and so forth. || 244 ||
"Upāsanā," and so forth.

Then, having established a water-pot (kalaśa) preceded by a mandala upon the altar constructed according to the rules of worship, the Guru should commence the worship of the disciple’s chosen deity within that pot. || 245 ||
Then, having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman by way of the Śāmbhava path and having performed worship, the knower of Brahman should carry out the installation of the fire (vahnisthāpana). (246)
Having offered the oblations prescribed for his own ritual manual into the fire previously consecrated, the Guru should summon the disciple and cause him to be offered as a complete sacrifice.
Having first offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should perform the *prāṇahoma*.
The vital airs are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. (248)
Then one should perform the *tattva-homa* for the sake of liberation from the superimposition of the body upon the Self:
earth, water, fire, air, and space. (249)
Smell, taste, form, touch, and sound follow in due order;
then speech, hands, feet, the anus, and after that the generative organ. (250)

"Then, indeed": then, following the worship of the disciple's chosen deity, the Guru who knows Brahman, having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman and performed its worship by way of the Śāmbhava path, should perform the installation of the fire upon the altar. || 246 ||

"Prāgukta" and so forth: Then, having offered the oblation prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*) into the fire consecrated by the previously mentioned procedure, the Guru should summon that disciple and cause him to offer [the remainder] entirely into the fire. || 247 ||

"At the beginning" means: first, having offered the totality with the *vyāhṛtis* such as *bhūḥ* and so forth, one should then perform the *prāṇahoma*, that is, the offering to the five winds (*pañcavāyu*) residing in the body, such as *prāṇa* and the rest. He states the five winds, beginning with *prāṇa*, which are to be offered:
By the half-verse beginning with "prāṇa," etc. (248).

Regarding the word "tattva": thereafter, for the sake of liberating oneself from the superimposition of the body as the self—that is, for the purpose of freeing oneself from the cognition of the self residing in the body—one should perform the *tattva-homa*, the oblation of the twenty-four principles beginning with earth and water, in their proper sequence. Indeed, it must be done in due order.

He states that the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) which are to be offered in the oblation by means of slightly more than two and a quarter verses, beginning with "earth" and ending with "egoity" (*ahaṅkāra*). (249)
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the organs of cognition;
the mind, intellect, consciousness, and ego are the functions born of the body. (251)
All the functions of the sense organs and those which are the functions of the vital breaths.
At the end of these words, one should utter the word "śuddhyantām" (may they be purified).
Also: "Hrīḥ! May I become light, stainless, and free from evil. (253)
Having offered the twenty-four principles and the bodily actions into the fire, one should then contemplate the body as being like a corpse, free from all activity.

"Smell," and so forth. After the oblation of the five principles beginning with earth, the five principles beginning with smell are to be offered in their respective order. Following that, the five organs of action beginning with speech are to be offered. After that, the [organs] beginning with hearing.

The five sense organs of cognition are to be offered as oblations. Then, the four principles beginning with the mind (manas) are to be offered. Finally, the activities born of the body are to be offered as oblations. || 250 || 251 ||
"All" means that, therefore, all the functions of the senses as well as the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) are also to be offered as oblations. || 252 ||
He states the mantra for the oblation (*homa*) of the five vital airs beginning with *prāṇa*, the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth,
the bodily activities, the functions of all the sense organs, and the actions of the vital airs such as *prāṇa*,
starting with the words "etāni" and so forth. First, one should recite "etāni me."

At the end of that word, one should utter the word "śuddhyantām" (may they be purified). Then one should utter: "hrīḥ jyotirahaṃ virajā vipāpmā bhūyāsam" (Oṃ Hrīḥ, may I become light, stainless, and free from sin). Then one should also utter "dviṭhaḥ svāhā". By way of this application, [the mantra becomes]: "etāni me śuddhyantāṃ hrīḥ jyotirahaṃ virajā vipāpmā" (may these be purified for me; Oṃ Hrīḥ, may I become light, stainless, and free from sin).
The mantra "bhūyāsaṃ svāhā" is produced. By this very [mantra], one should offer all [the vital functions], beginning with prāṇa and ending with the activities of prāṇa. Just as [one says]:
"May my prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna be purified; hrīṃ! I am light."

"May I become free from passion and free from evil, svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the others. This same application is to be understood everywhere. || 253 ||

"Twenty-four," and so forth. Thus, having offered the twenty-four bodily principles (*tattva*) and the actions of the body as oblations into the fire, and having become inactive—having emerged from all activities—one should then contemplate the body as if it were dead. || 254 ||
Having visualized the body as being like a corpse, devoid of all activity, and recollecting the Supreme Brahman, one should remove the sacrificial thread. (255)

Having removed the sacrificial thread from the shoulder with the mantra "ai/ klī/ hū/", the knower of reality should place it in his hand, recite the three *vyāhṛtis*, utter the wife of fire (*svāhā*), and cast it, smeared with ghee, into the fire. || 256 ||
Having thus offered the sacred thread while reciting the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja),
and having cut the top-knot and placed it in his hand, he should immerse it in the midst of the clarified butter.
O Brahmaputrī, O Śikhā, you are indeed a young ascetic maiden;
a place is being given to you in the fire—go, O Goddess, salutations be to you! (258)
Uttering the *kāma*, *māyā*, and *kūrca* mantras along with the *vahnijāyā*,
one should perform the *śikhā-homa* in that well-consecrated fire.

"Having meditated" means: having meditated upon—that is, having contemplated—the body, the physical frame, as being devoid of all activity and like one who is dead; and while remembering the Supreme Brahman, which is renowned as the cause of the universe, he should remove the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), from his chest.
One should lead the shoulder. || 255 ||

"AIM," and so forth. Then, the knower of reality— the one who knows Brahman— having removed the sacrificial thread from his shoulder with the mantra "AIḤ KLĪṂ IM," having placed it in his hand, and having recited the three *vyāhṛtis*,
at the conclusion of the three *vyāhṛtis*, he should utter the word "svāhā," which is the consort of Fire (*vahnijāyā*).
One should cast the sacrificial thread, smeared with and mixed with clarified butter, into the fire. || 256 ||

"Having offered," it is said: having thus offered the *upavīta* (sacrificial thread) into the fire while reciting the seed-syllable of desire, *klīm*, and having cut off his topknot (*śikhā*) and placed it in his hand, he should join it—that is, establish it—in the middle of the eighth [finger]. || 257 ||

"Brahmā. Then, while reciting the mantra beginning with "O Daughter of Brahmā" and ending with "Salutations to You," at the conclusion of this mantra, he should utter Kāma (klīm), Māyā (hrīm), Kūrca (hūm), Astra (phaṭ), and Vahnijāyā (svāhā).
(220) Taking refuge in the crest-lock (śikhā), the ancestors, the gods, and likewise the divine sages—all the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karmāṇi)—dwell upon the crest-lock. || 260 ||
Therefore, having gratified all those gods, sages, ancestors, and deities,
an embodied being becomes one with Brahman by the renunciation of the topknot and the sacred thread.
For the twice-born, renunciation occurs through the abandonment of the sacrificial thread and the topknot;
for Śūdras and others, however, the rite of consecration is performed by offering the topknot into the fire.
Then, having loosened his topknot and sacred thread, he should prostrate like a staff before the guru.
The guru, having raised that disciple up, should say this into his right ear: || 263 ||
"Thou art That, O one of great wisdom; contemplate 'I am He,' the Swan.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, conduct yourself happily according to your true nature. (264)
Uttering the seed-syllable "svāhā," one should perform the *śikhā-homa* (the oblation for the crest-lock) in that well-consecrated fire. || 258–260 ||
Consisting of Brahman, having the nature of Brahman. || 261 ||
Of the twice-born—namely Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—and of others belonging to the mixed castes. || 262 || 263 ||

Now, in response to the question of what the teacher should say into the right ear of the disciple, he says: "That thou art," and so forth. O you of great wisdom, O you of great intelligence! "That" refers to the Supreme Brahman, which is universally renowned as the cause of the universe.

You alone are He; therefore, contemplate and reflect: "I am indeed that Supreme Self; He alone am I. Furthermore, being free from possessiveness—devoid of the sense of "mine" regarding sons and other objects—and free from egoism—devoid of mental inflation caused by learning and other such things.
"Move about here and there so that there may be happiness by its very nature";
the elision of "aham" (I) and so forth is an archaic Vedic usage. || 264 ||
Then, having set aside both the jar and the fire, the Guru, who knows the reality of Brahman, recognizing him as the very nature of the Self, should bow with his head. (265)
Salutation to you, salutation to me; salutation to you, salutation to me, salutation, salutation!
You alone are that, you alone are the reality; O you whose form is the universe, let there be salutation to you.

For those who worship the Brahma-mantra, who possess knowledge of reality, and whose selves are conquered, the taking of renunciation occurs through the cutting of the topknot with their own mantra. || 267 ||
For those purified by the knowledge of Brahman, what is the use of sacrifices, ancestral rites, or worship?
For those devoted to acting according to their own will, no transgression exists.
Then, free from the pairs of opposites, desireless, and steady-minded,
that disciple may wander at his own will upon the earth, being truly one with Brahman.
Contemplating everything from Brahma down to a blade of grass as being of the nature of Reality (Sat),
forgetting names and forms, one should meditate upon the Self within the self.

Regarding the word "tataḥ": thereafter, having discarded the pitcher and the fire, the guru, who knows the reality of Brahman, considering that disciple to be his own self-nature, should bow with his head using the mantra to be described hereafter. || 265 ||
He states that very mantra with which one should prostrate—
beginning with "Homage to you" (namas tubhyam)— in verse 266.

Regarding those who worship the Brahma-mantra, he states a specific rule for the taking of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) with the words beginning "brahmamantra... [and so forth]. For those who possess knowledge of reality—the knowers of Brahman—whose selves are conquered and whose minds are subdued...
For those who worship the Brahma-mantra, the taking of renunciation occurs simply by the cutting of the topknot with their own mantra. || 267 ||

Now, one might object that those who take up renunciation (saṃnyāsa) without having performed sacrifices, ancestral rites (śrāddha), and so forth—being practitioners of the Brahma-mantra—would incur sin; to this, he says "brahmajñāna" and so on. || 268 ||
"Of a nature free from duality": "dualities" (dvandva) are pairs such as pleasure and pain;
one who is devoid of these is "free from duality" (nirdvandva), and his essential nature is that [freedom]. || 269 ||
Contemplating and reflecting upon everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— a cluster of grass— perceiving it as being of the nature of existence, that is, as the nature of reality. || 270 ||
Without a fixed abode, acting with patience, free from fear and devoid of attachment, without the sense of "mine" and without egoism, the renunciant should wander upon the earth. (271)

Freed from injunctions and prohibitions, without concern for acquisition or preservation, the knower of the Self is equanimous toward pleasure and pain; steadfast, self-conquered, and free from longing.
Steadfast in soul, though he has encountered suffering, he remains free from desire even when pleasure is attained;
ever blissful, pure, peaceful, indifferent, and undisturbed. || 273 ||
He should not cause distress to living beings, but should always be devoted to the welfare of all creatures;
free from anger and fear, self-controlled, devoid of mental constructs, and free from worldly exertion. (274)
One should be free from sorrow and hatred, and remain equal toward enemy and friend; enduring cold, wind, and heat, one should be the same in honor and dishonor.

"Without a dwelling," and so forth. "Without a dwelling" means devoid of a fixed residence. "Of patient conduct" means one for whom patience itself is the conduct. "Free from apprehension" means devoid of anxiety. "Devoid of attachment" means unattached to anything whatsoever. || 271 ||
"Free," and so forth. "Without acquisition or preservation" (*niryogakṣema*): *yoga* is the taking up of what has not been obtained;

*kṣema* is the protection of what has been obtained; he is devoid of both. "Equal toward pleasure and pain" (*sukhaduḥkhasama*): he for whom pleasure and pain are equal. "One who has conquered the self" (*jitātmā*): one who has mastered the body. "Free from longing" (*vigataspṛha*).
One whose longing—the desire to grasp this or that object as soon as various high and low things are seen—has vanished. || 272 ||

"Stable," and so forth: "stable-souled" means one whose mind is steady or whose nature is firm; "free from desire" means devoid of longing for enjoyments; "pure" means endowed with both external and internal purity; "tranquil" means one whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is restrained; and "independent" means free from reliance on others.
Unagitated, meaning devoid of agitation. || 273 ||
"Not," and so forth. "Not causing agitation" means not generating fear.

"Free from indignation and fear" means having abandoned anger and dread. "Self-controlled" means having restrained the external sense organs. "Devoid of exertion" means being free from activity for the sake of maintaining one's own body. || 274 ||
"Śoka" and so forth: equal toward enemy and friend, meaning uniform in nature; likewise equal toward honor and dishonor, meaning devoid of joy and dejection. || 275 ||

Equanimous toward the auspicious and the inauspicious, content with whatever object is obtained by chance, he should be free from the three qualities (*guṇa*), free from conceptual construction, free from greed, and without accumulation. (276)
Just as the entire world of falsehood rests upon truth, so too does the body rest upon the Self; knowing this, one becomes happy. (277)
The sense organs alone perform their respective functions individually; the Self is a witness, untainted. Knowing this, one becomes a partaker of liberation. || 278 ||
A renunciant should avoid accepting alms for his own sake, censuring others, speaking untruths, sexual play with women, the emission of semen, and malice. (279)
One should maintain an equal vision toward all—whether toward an insect, a god, or a human—and as a wandering mendicant, one should recognize everything as Brahman in all activities. (280)
Whether it be the food of a Brahmin or the food of a dog-eater, from whatever source it may have come,
one should eat it without hesitation, considering the place, the time, and the recipient.

"Equanimous," and so forth. "Beyond the three qualities" (*nistraiguṇya*): that which possesses the three qualities (*triguṇa*) is one who has desires; the state of such a person is "the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*). One who has emerged from that is "beyond the three qualities" (*nistraiguṇya*), meaning free from desire. "Free from conceptual construction" (*nirvikalpa*): devoid of various kinds of mental fabrications.

Free from greed (*nirlobhaḥ*): even when the acquisition of wealth and other things occurs in many ways, greed (*lobhaḥ*) is the ever-increasing desire; one who is devoid of that is free from greed. Not hoarding (*asañcayī*): one who lacks the accumulation of various objects. (276)

"Yathā" and so forth: Just as the universe, though false and illusory (*mṛṣā*), stands and exists as if it were real by relying upon and taking support from the True Supreme Self (*paramātman*), even so, that which is illusory [rests] having taken refuge in the Self.
In this way the body remains stable; knowing this, the renunciant shall be happy. || 277 ||
Regarding "the senses": the senses alone perform their respective individual functions. The Self, however, is merely a witness, the observer of both auspicious and inauspicious actions.
For this very reason, it is untainted and is not bound by those various actions. Thus...
Only by knowing this does the renunciant become a partaker of liberation. || 278 ||
Falsehood is speaking that which is not in accordance with reality; envy is the attribution of faults even where virtues exist. (279–281)
Devoted to the study of inner sciences and the constant investigation of reality, the Avadhūta should pass his time, intent upon acting according to his own will. (282)
One should never cremate the dead body of renunciants (saṃnyāsins);
rather, after honoring it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should either bury it or immerse it in water.
O Goddess, for mortals who have not attained yoga and who always long for objects of desire, worldly engagement arises naturally within the turmoil of karma. (284)
Even there, let them remain devoted to meditation, worship, recitation, and spiritual practice;
let them know that alone to be the highest good where their resolve is firm. (285)
Therefore, the prescriptions for ritual action have been proclaimed for the sake of purifying the mind;
for that purpose, manifold names and forms have been fashioned by me. (286)
O Goddess, without the knowledge of Brahman and without the renunciation of ritual action, a person performing rituals for a hundred kalpas shall not become a partaker of liberation. || 287 ||
One who knows the reality, a liberated soul while living, a Kulāvadhūta in human form—one should regard him as Nārāyaṇa manifest and worship him even if he is a householder. || 288 ||
Through the study of the inner sciences (adhyātmaśāstra), the recitation of the Vedānta scriptures, the investigation of reality (tattva), and the discernment of the principle of Brahman; || 282 ||
Having prepared a pit in pure ground, one should bury it right there; or [place it] in water, in the waters. || 283 ||

"Of mortals who have not attained yoga"—that is, of those by whom yoga, the connection with the knowledge of Brahman, has not been attained; "in the mass of karma," that is, in the multitude of ritual actions. || 284 ||

Even there, even in that very place; mortals who have not attained yoga; being "full of attachment" means possessing devotion; "that very thing" refers to the ritual of worship and so forth. || 285 ||
By the mere sight of an ascetic, one is liberated from all sins;
one obtains the fruit of visiting sacred fords, observing vows, performing austerities, giving gifts, and offering all sacrifices. (289)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties and Conduct of the Castes and Stages of Life," in the glorious Mahānirvāṇa Tantra— the most excellent among all Tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas— within the dialogue between the venerable Primordial Goddess and Sadāśiva.
For that purpose, for the sake of mortals who have not yet attained yoga. || 286–289 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. In the ninth chapter,
the venerable Sadāśiva said:
O lady of virtuous vows, the duties pertaining to the conduct of the castes and stages of life have been described to you; now listen as I speak of the sacraments for all the castes. 1.
O Goddess, without the purificatory rite (saṃskāra), purification of the body does not arise;
one who has not undergone the rites is not qualified for rites pertaining to the gods or the ancestors.

Therefore, the castes beginning with the Brahmins, desiring their own welfare in this world and the next, must by all means perform the sacraments prescribed for their respective castes with diligent effort. (3)

The sprinkling for life (jīvaseka), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), as well as the birth ceremony (jāta), naming (nāma), the first outing (niṣkramaṇa), the first feeding of solid food (annāśana), and thereafter the tonsure (cūḍā), the initiation (upanayana), and marriage (udvāha)— these are declared to be the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Oṃ, salutations to Brahman!
May my mind be constantly fixed upon the lotus feet of Śrī Śrīnātha.
Having thus explained all the duties and practices pertaining to the castes and stages of life, [the author] now...

Desiring to explain all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for all castes (*varṇa*), Śrī Sadāśiva said: "O [beings] of the castes and stages of life," and so forth. "From me" means from me as I speak—that is, as I am telling it. (1–3)
For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, there are ten sacraments beginning with *jīvasēka* and ending with marriage; for Śūdras and those of mixed castes (*varṇasaṅkara*),
there are only nine sacraments, beginning with *jīvasēka*, excluding the sacrament known as the initiation (*upanayana*).
He says "they exist" and so forth, with the two and a half verses beginning with "the single life-force" (jīvaseka). || 4 ||
For Śūdras—those distinct from the Śūdra [caste]—the sacred thread (*upavīta*) does not exist.
For them, there are only nine sacraments (*saṃskāra*); for the twice-born (*dvijāti*), ten are traditionally prescribed. (5)
O lady of excellent hips, one should perform all obligatory rites, as well as occasional and optional ones, according to the path of Śambhu.
O beloved, whatever rites and whatever specific actions there may be, those have already been explained by me in the form of Brahmā.

And likewise, for all the sacramental rites (saṃskāras) as well as other rituals, the mantras have been shown in their proper sequence according to the distinctions of the castes, such as the Brahmins and others. || 8 ||
In the Satya, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, one should employ those mantras beginning with the Praṇava in their respective ritual applications according to the time.
But in the Kali age, O Supreme Goddess, by the command of Śaṅkara, men shall perform all rites with those very mantras beginning with Māyā.
In the Nigamas, Āgamas, Tantras, Vedas, and Saṃhitās, all mantras were spoken by me alone; their application varies according to the different ages.
In this age, O auspicious lady, human beings have their life-breaths dependent on food and are diminished in luster;
for their welfare, the family dharma has been prescribed.
For those whose lives are weakened by the Kali age and whose minds are incapable of exertion, I shall describe to you their rites, such as the funeral consecration (saṃskāra), even in brief.
Of those born from the intermixture of castes who are distinct from Śūdras;
that is, of those Śūdras and those distinct from Śūdras. Of the twice-born—namely, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. || 5 || 6 ||
The ritual procedures are what are required; this is the ellipsis. (7–9)
"By those beginning with Māyā": those mantras whose first [syllable] is the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*;
by them. (10–13)
(228) Kuśaṇḍikā is the beginning of all auspicious rites;
therefore, O Goddess praised by the gods, I shall first explain it—listen to it! 14.
In a delightful and well-prepared place, free from husks, charcoal, and the like,
the wise man should fashion a sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit in size.
Three lines should be drawn there in that mandala with their tips pointing eastward;
having sprinkled them all with water using a *kūrca* brush, one should bring forth the fire by means of fire-sticks.
Having brought the fire, he should place it at its side while recollecting the Vāgbhava mantra.

Then, having taken a burning piece of wood from that [fire] with his right hand, he should offer it with the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the flesh-eaters, Svāhā! and thus relinquish the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters.
Having thus lifted the fire, which is established there, with both hands toward oneself,
one should remember the Vyāhṛtis beginning with Māyā over those lines.
That Kuśaṇḍikā rite. || 14 ||
He speaks of the *kuśaṇḍikā* itself with the words beginning "in a delightful [place]," and so forth. A *sthaṇḍila* is a leveled square.

Regarding the passage beginning "three," one should draw three lines on the *sthaṇḍila*—a leveled area fashioned within that mandala with a measurement of one cubit (*hasta*)—with their tips pointing eastward. Then, with a bundle of *kūrca* grass and the mantra "HŪM,"...
Having sprinkled those lines with water and consecrated them by means of fire, one should bring forth or summon the fire with the mantra "raṃ". || 16 ||

"Having brought," and so forth. Having brought fire while recollecting the mantra "aim," which is the Vāgbhava [bīja], one should place it at its side—that is, at the side of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 17 ||

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, having taken from that fire a single piece of burning wood—a blazing log—with the right hand, one should offer the portion for the *kravyādas* (the flesh-eating *rākṣasas*) in the southern direction with the mantra: "Hrīḥ! Svāhā! Salutation to the *kravyādas*."
One should abandon [the practice] in that direction. || 18 ||

"Thus," and so forth. In this manner, having lifted up— that is, raised— the consecrated fire established in this way with both hands, while recollecting the *māyā* seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and the *vyāhṛti* beginning with that seed-syllable, [he should perform the rite] for himself.
Having established the fire by means of grass and wood and having strengthened it,
and having offered two fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter into that sacrificial fire, one should perform the naming rite according to one's own ritual manual and meditate upon Dhanañjaya. (20)
Resembling the reddish glow of the rising sun, with seven tongues and two heads,
mounted upon a goat, bearing a spear, and adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Having meditated thus and joined his palms in reverence, he should invoke the Fire-god.
"O Māyā, come, come from every quarter," one should say, "O beloved of all the immortals.
Then, at the end of the word *havyavāha* (bearer of oblations), one should say with the sages and their own attendants:
"Protect the sacrifice, protect it! Namaḥ svāhā!"—thus one should speak thereafter. (23)
Having established [the fire] upon those lines so that it is directly in front,
and having strengthened the fire with grass and wood,
he should offer two pieces of wood (samidhs) smeared with ghee into that sacrificial fire.
Having cast [the oblation] into the fire and assigned it the name prescribed by his own ritual manual, he should meditate upon Agni as Dhanañjaya. || 19 || 20 ||

He describes the meditation on Fire itself with the words "resembling the redness of the young sun," and so forth. It is that which has a luster—meaning a radiance—red like the young sun, that is, the sun;
thus it is of such a nature. || 21 ||

"Having meditated," and so forth. Having thus meditated upon the fire Havyavāhana, one should then, with palms joined in reverence (*prāñjali*), invoke Havyavāhana with the mantra to be recited hereafter.

He states the mantra for the invocation of Fire (Vahnyāvāhana) with the half-verse beginning with "māyām" and so forth: "O Dear One, first one should utter the seed-syllable *māyā*, namely *hrīṃ*; then, having said 'come, come' (*ehy ehi*), after that word one should utter the word 'sarvāmara'; then [the word] 'havyavāha'."

At the end of each word, one should say with the sages and their own retinues, "Protect the sacrifice! Protect! Then one should say, "Obeisance! Svāhā! By joining all the words together: *Hrīḥ! Come, come, O carrier of the oblations for all the immortals, along with the sages and your own retinues; protect the sacrifice, protect!*
The mantra "namaḥ svāhā" was thus born. || 23 ||
Having thus invoked [the deity] while reciting "This is your source" (*ayaṃ te yoniḥ*) to the bearer of oblations,
and having worshipped him with the ritual services (*upacāra*), one should worship the seven tongues of flame.
Kālī, Karālī, Manojava, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā,
Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarūpiṇī.
And there are seven flickering tongues of flame. || 25 ||
Then, O Maheśānī, beginning from the east of the fire and together with Kīlālapāṇi, one should perform the sprinkling three times, ending at the north.

In the same manner, one should perform the threefold sprinkling around the fire, starting from the southern direction and ending at the northern direction, and then [sprinkle] the sacrificial materials.
Thus: having invoked the fire-god Havyavāhana with this mantra, and while reciting "O Fire,
this is your womb," one should duly worship the fire with offerings such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, using the name-mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should worship the seven tongues of the fire with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, using the name-mantras preceded by *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in *namas*. || 24 ||
The seven tongues of fire are indeed described by the single verse beginning with "Kālī" and so forth.
These seven tongues—beginning with Kālī and ending with Viśvanirūpiṇī—are flickering and serve to receive the oblation for the fire. || 25 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ": O Maheśānī, thereafter, together with *kīlālapāṇi*—that is, with a hand holding water—one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) over the fire three times, starting from the east and ending in the north, reaching as far as the north. || 26 ||

"Likewise," and so forth. Then, in that very manner, together with Kīlālapāṇi himself, one should perform the threefold sprinkling and consecration (*paryukṣaṇa-abhiṣecana*) of the consumer of oblations, Agni, starting from the southern direction (the south) up to the northern limit, ending at the north, which belongs to Kubera. After that, [one should likewise perform it] for the sacrificial materials as well.
One should perform the sprinkling around in exactly three ways. || 27 ||
Then one should spread darbha grass starting from the east up to the north, with the blades directed toward the north, then toward the north-east, and then toward the other directions. (28)
Having placed the fire to the south and having gone near the seat of the Brahman priest, [he should release the cord] from the prepared seat of the Brahman with his left thumb and little finger. (29)
Having taken a single blade of *kuśa* grass and saying, "Hrīṃ! Parāvasu has been expelled," he should cast it toward the south of the fire using the *utkara* or similar means. || 30 ||
"Sit, O Lord of Sacrifice; O Brahman, here is the seat prepared for you.
Saying "I sit," the Brahman priest should enter there, facing north. || 31 ||
Having worshipped Brahmā with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should pray as follows: || 32 ||
Protect the sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice; protect the sacrifice, O Great Lord of Heat!
Protect me, the master of the sacrifice, O Witness of all actions; salutations be unto You.

"One should spread [the grass]": thereafter, starting from the east toward the west, one should spread it with the tips pointing north— situated in the northern direction— with the tips directed toward the north and positioned away from other directions.
One should strew—that is, cover—the sacrificial ground with *darbha* grass blades whose tips point toward the east. || 28 ||
"Then, having placed the fire to the south, one approaches the seat of the Brahmā priest;
with the left thumb and little finger, one takes a single blade of *kuśa* grass from each of the blades prepared for the Brahmā’s seat, [reciting] *hrīḥ*."

Having recited the mantra "Nirastaḥ parāvasuḥ," he should discard that same blade of *kuśa* grass toward the southern direction of the fire, along with the *utkara* (the heap of earth) and other materials. || 29 || 30 ||
"Sīda" (sit down). The performer of the sacrifice should say to the Brahman priest: "O Lord of the Sacrifice, O Brahman, here is the seat prepared for you; sit down, take your place here.
Then, saying "I sit," the Brahman priest, having turned to face the north, sits upon that seat.
One should enter. || 31 ||
"Having worshipped," and so forth: then, having fully worshipped Brahmā with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should pray to him as follows. || 32 ||
In response to the expectation of what one should pray for here, he says, "Protect the sacrifice," and so forth.
"Gopāya" means protect. || 33 ||
Brahmā should say, "I shall protect [it]," or in the absence of Brahmā, he himself should say so.
For the success of the sacrifice, one should there imagine a Brahmin made of *darbha* grass. (34)

Then, having invoked [the deity] with the words, "O Brahman, come here, come here," and having worshipped [him] with water for the feet and other offerings until the completion of the sacrifice, the practitioner should pray, "You must remain [here]," and thereafter bow down. (35)
Having sprinkled water three times around the fire from the northeast toward the southeast with the hand, and having subsequently sprinkled it over the fire three times; || 36 ||
Having arrived by that path and seated himself comfortably on his own seat,
he should spread darbha grass with their tips pointing north upon the northern part of the sacrificial mound.
The wise one should place all the sacrificial materials upon them:
the vessel for sprinkling water with its water, the vessel for clarified butter, the fuel sticks, and the kuśa grass.
"I shall protect. When thus requested by the performer of the sacrifice, the Brahman priest should say, "I shall protect.

However, in the absence of a Brahman priest, he himself should say, "I shall protect. In that case, when there is no Brahman priest, one should fashion a Brahmin made of *darbha* grass for the successful completion of the sacrifice. || 34 ||

"Then," and so forth: thereafter, the practitioner, as the performer of the sacrifice, having invoked Brahmā with the mantra "O Brahmā, come here, come here! and having worshipped him with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, [should attend to him] until the completion of the sacrifice.
Having requested, "May you remain here for the time being," one should then bow to Brahmā. || 35 ||

"With water" means: then, with a hand holding water— that is, with a wet hand— one should sprinkle and consecrate [the area] three times, starting from the northeast corner (Īśāna) of the fire and proceeding as far as the vicinity of Brahmā.
Having sprinkled the fire three times, the performer of the sacrifice should then return by the same path by which he had gone to the vicinity of the Brahmā-seat, sit comfortably upon his own seat,
and [spread] darbha grass with tips pointing north on the northern part of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should spread out *kuśa* grass. || 36 || 37 ||

Regarding the phrase "in them": the wise performer of the sacrifice should place—that is, arrange—all sacrificial materials upon those *darbha* grasses. He states which sacrificial materials are to be placed upon the *darbha* grasses with the words beginning "with water," and so forth. (38)
Having brought forth the *sruk*, *sruva*, and other implements with the mantras *hrāḥ*, *hrīḥ*, and *hrūm*,
and having consecrated them by sprinkling [them] with divine vision, immediately thereafter— (39)
Having placed his right knee upon the ground,
the wise man, taking clarified butter with the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles while contemplating his own welfare,
should offer three oblations ending with the *dviṭha* (svāhā) mantra, saying "Oṃ Hrīṃ Viṣṇave Svāhā."
In the same manner, taking clarified butter and meditating upon the god Prajāpati,
one should offer it with a stream of ghee from the northwest corner to the southeast corner.
Taking up clarified butter once more and meditating upon the god Purandara,
he should offer it with a stream of ghee from the southwest corner to the northeast corner.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, having inscribed Agni, Soma, and Agni-Soma respectively in the north, the south, and the center of the fire-altar (agni-kunda), || 43 ||

"Having placed" means: having placed—that is, having set out and arranged—the items such as the water-vessel and the *prokṣaṇī* vessel upon the *darbha* grass, as well as the sacrificial vessels such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; and having consecrated them with divine vision and sprinkling while reciting the mantras "Hrāḥ Hrīḥ Hrūm."
Immediately after that, having placed his right knee upon the ground and having taken up clarified butter with the *sruk* and *sruva* sacrificial ladles, the wise performer of the sacrifice,
contemplating his own welfare, [should offer it] with the mantra ending in *dviṭha* (namas) and ending in *svāhā*: "Hrīḥ, to Viṣṇu."
With the mantra, one should offer three oblations dedicated to Viṣṇu. || 39 || 40 ||

"Likewise," and so forth. In the same manner, having taken clarified butter with the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, while meditating upon the god Prajāpati, one should offer it toward the northwest (vāyavya) for his sake, using the name-mantra preceded by the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, followed by the fourth case ending and ending in *svāhā*.
Beginning from the southwest corner and ending at the southeast corner, one should offer oblations with a stream of clarified butter.

"Again," and so forth. Again, having taken clarified butter (ājya) with the *sruva* ladle from the *sruc*, while meditating upon the god Purandara, one should offer it to him with the name-mantra beginning with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, followed by the fourth case ending and ending in *svāhā*. [One offers] to Nairṛta among the Nairṛtas.
Beginning from the southeast corner and ending at the northeast corner—that is, up to the northeast corner—one should offer oblations with a stream of clarified butter. || 42 ||
"Then," and so forth. O Supreme Goddess, thereafter— on the northern side of the fire,
on the southern side (the right), and in the middle— one should, in due order and sequence, address the fire, Soma, and Agni-Soma, beginning with *māyā*.
Having offered three oblations with the mantra beginning with *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and ending with the fourth case and *namaḥ*,
the wise practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) as prescribed for the rite to be accomplished.
They declare that the *dhārā-homa* (continuous stream oblation) concludes with the offering of three oblations.
Whatever [deity] one has in mind for whom one should offer the oblation, that recipient must also be designated for its sake.
Having completed the primary rite, one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation. (46)
O fair-faced one, in the Kali age, there is no expiatory fire-offering (homa) consisting of specific penances;
rather, expiation is prescribed by means of the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and the *vyāhṛti* mantras. (47)
Taking the sacrificial oblation as before while mentally recollecting Brahmā, [he should pray]:
"O Lord of Gods, in this rite, whether through negligence or even by wandering astray... (48)
Having offered three oblations with the name-mantra preceded by the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* and ending with *namaḥ* along with the dative case,

the wise and intelligent performer of the sacrifice should perform the fire-offering (*homa*) as prescribed for the ritual to be performed, such as the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the seasons. || 43 || 44 ||

"Āhutītyādi" and so forth: they declare—that is, they speak of—the *dhārāhoma* as that which begins with the offering of three oblations dedicated to Viṣṇu and ends with the offering of three oblations dedicated to Agni and the others. || 45 ||

"Yadityādi" and so forth: for whichever deity one intends to offer an oblation (*āhuti*), for that [deity]—for its sake—the designation of the object to be given must also be made; that is, the mention or specification of the substance to be given must be performed. For example: *hrīṃ viṣṇave svāhā, idaṃ haviḥ viṣṇave* (Hrīṃ! Svāhā to Viṣṇu; this oblation is for Viṣṇu). It is exactly like this.

Having thus completed the primary rite of oblation—which is the very action under discussion and constitutes a constituent part of the ritual to be performed—one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, the sacrifice that brings about auspiciously desired results. || 46 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "prāyaścitta": since in the Kali age there is an absence of the fire-oblation consisting of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), expiation is prescribed here by means of the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and the oblation of the *vyāhṛti* mantras.
(47) Now, he describes the procedure for performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the verses beginning with "pūrvavat."

As before, having taken the oblation of clarified butter with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles while mentally recollecting Prajāpati, the Brahman, one should offer it to him with the mantra beginning with *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and ending with *svāhā*.
Whatever has been done deficiently or in excess, make all of it well-offered (sviṣṭakṛt).
O Goddess, one should offer the oblation with this mantra beginning with *māyā* and ending with *svāhā*.

"O Agni, you are the purifier of all worlds, the lord who performs the perfect sacrifice (Sviṣṭakṛt), the witness of the sacrifice, and the bringer of well-being; fulfill all desires. With this [mantra], one should perform the oblation using the *māyā* syllable (*hrīṃ*) as the wife of Fire (*vahnijāyā*). || 50 ||
Having thus completed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, the performer of the sacrifice [said]: "O Supreme Brahman, whatever in this rite was improperly performed or what was prescribed [correctly]," (51)
O All-pervading Lord, for the sake of that pacification and for the perfection of the sacrifice, an oblation is offered with the three *vyāhṛtis*—
*bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*— beginning with *māyā* (the seed-syllable) and ending with the fire-born wife (*svāhā*).
O Lord of Gods, whatever has been done deficiently or excessively in this rite, whether through negligence or by mistake, please make it all well-offered (sviṣṭakṛt).
With this mantra, one should offer an oblation; one should give [it]. || 48 || 49 ||

"Tvam" and so forth: Then, addressing Agni with [the mantra] joined by the *māyā* (hrīṃ) as the initial element and the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā) as the final element—namely: "O Agni, you are the purifier of all worlds, the lord who makes the sacrifice well-offered (*sviṣṭakṛt*).”
Witness of the sacrifice, bringer of well-being, fulfill all desires.
With this mantra, one should perform the oblation. || 50 ||
"Thus," and so forth. Having thus—in this manner—completed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, the performer of the sacrifice, who accomplishes the rite, [reflects]:
"Of this ritual, O Supreme Brahman, whatever was improper and whatever was prescribed..."
O All-pervading Lord, for the sake of its pacification and for the successful completion of the sacrifice, an oblation is offered with the Vyāhṛtis.

Having thus prayed to the Supreme Brahman and directed [the offering] toward the Supreme Brahman alone, one should offer three oblations with the three mantras "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," preceded by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, along with the mantras beginning with *māyā* and ending with *vahnijāyā*.
In the same manner, one should offer three oblations with the *hrīḥ* mantra, and likewise with the triad [of mantras].
Having offered them into the fire, the wise practitioner should, together with the patron, offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). || 53 ||
If one is the performer of the ritual oneself, one should personally offer the oblation;
this very procedure is prescribed for the beginning of the consecration rite (abhiṣeka).
First, having uttered *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), one should then say:
"O Lord of Sacrifice (*yajñapati*), may my sacrifice be complete; may the deities of the sacrifice rejoice;
may they grant the fruits [of the rite] perfectly, ending with the beloved of Agni (*vahnikāntā*, i.e., *svāhā*). This is the mantra. || 55 ||
Having arisen with this mantra, the wise one, being well-composed,
should offer an oblation consisting of fruit and betel-leaf into the sacrificial fire.
Having offered the final oblation, the wise one should perform the rite of pacification (śāntikarma);
he should sprinkle his head with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using *kuśa* grass.
The wise performer of the sacrifice should offer a single oblation with the three worlds beginning with *bhūḥ*, starting with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and ending with *svāhā*.

Having thus offered the oblations, he should, together with the patron of the sacrifice, offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire for the sake of Viṣṇu, using the mantra that will be described hereafter. (51–53)
The verse beginning with "If [he] himself," etc., however, has a clear meaning. || 54 ||

He states that very mantra with which one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* by means of the verse beginning with "At the start," etc., consisting of one and a half lines: first, having uttered the seed-syllable *māyā*, *hrīḥ*, then one should say "O Lord of Sacrifice" (*yajñapate*), and then "May my sacrifice be complete; may [the gods] rejoice."

One should say: "May the deities of the sacrifice duly bestow the fruits. With the application [of the mantra]: *hrīṃ*, "O Lord of the Sacrifice, may my sacrifice be complete; may the deities of the sacrifice rejoice; may they duly bestow the fruits, svāhā! This is the Manu born [from the syllable]; this Manu extends up to the beloved of Agni (the letter *ra*).
It is taught that [the mantra] ends with *svāhā*. || 55 ||

"With the mantra," and so forth. The wise performer of the sacrifice, having risen together with the patron (yajamāna), being well-composed and extremely attentive, should offer an oblation accompanied by fruit and betel-leaf into the sacrificial fire (hutāśana) with this mantra. || 56 ||

"Having given," and so forth. Thus, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the wise practitioner who accomplishes the sacrifice should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*). He states the very procedure for performing the rite of pacification with the words beginning "In the *prokṣaṇī* vessel," and so on. (57)
May the waters be auspicious and friendly to me; may the plants be so as well. May the waters protect me always; the waters themselves are Nārāyaṇa. (58)
Having performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with these two verses, "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss; grant us strength," one should cast drops [of water] upon the ground. || 59 ||
May the waters be ill-disposed toward those who always hate me and those men whom we hate; may they consume them as well.
Having cast drops [of water] in this direction toward the north-east and having set aside those kuśa grasses, one should, with palms joined in reverence, pray to the bearer of oblations (Agni).
O Carrier of Oblations, grant me intelligence, knowledge, strength, memory, wisdom, faith, fame, prosperity, health, splendor, and long life.
Having thus prayed to Vītihotra, one should dismiss him with this [mantra], O Śivā.

He recites the two mantras beginning with "āpaḥ" for the purpose of wiping the head, etc.: "O waters, may you be well-disposed toward me, and may the plants be so"—this is the grammatical construction (*anvaya*). *Sumitriyāḥ* means those who are indeed good friends (*sumitrāṇi*); the suffix *ṣṇya* is used here in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
This is its injunction. || 58 ||

The meaning of the verse beginning with "āpaḥ" will be explained later. Having performed the sprinkling of the head with these two mantras, one should cast the drops upon the ground with *kuśa* grass. (59)
He states the mantra for the deposition of drops upon the ground with the words beginning, "Those who hate... (ye dviṣanti).

"By this," and so forth. With this mantra, having sprinkled drops of water with *kuśa* grass in the northeastern direction and having cast those *kuśa* blades away in that very same place, one should, with palms joined in reverence, pray to Havyavāhana, the Fire-god. || 61 ||
In response to the expectation of what one should pray for from Agni, he says "buddhim" and so forth.

*Buddhi* is the knowledge of the true principles of the scriptures and other sciences; *vidyā* is the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*); *medhā* is the intellect endowed with the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*); and *prajñā* is skill in discerning between the essential and the non-essential. || 62 ||
Regarding the word "iti": O Śivā, having addressed Agni Vītihotra with the mantra about to be recited, one should dismiss him with that very [mantra]. || 63 ||
O Sacrifice, go to the Lord of Sacrifice; go to the Sacrifice, O Consumer of Oblations!
Go to your own source, O Lord of Sacrifice, and fulfill our heart's desire. (64)
Having offered an oblation of curd to the fire in the northern direction with the mantra "agne kṣamasva svāhā," one should move the fire to the south.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin and having bowed with devotion, he should dismiss him;
thereafter, he should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) with the ashes adhering to the sacrificial ladle (sruva).
Having uttered "māyāṃ kāmaṃ," the performer of the sacrifice should apply a tilaka on the forehead with this mantra, saying: "Be the bringer of peace for all. (67)
May there be peace and may there be auspiciousness through the grace of Vāsava and Agni, as well as that of the Maruts, Brahmā, the Vasus, Rudra, and Prajāpati. (68)

He states the mantra for the dismissal of the fire as follows: "O Sacrifice (Yajña), go to the Lord of Sacrifice, Viṣṇu; O Consumer of Oblations (Hutāśana), you go to the Sacrifice; O Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñeśa), you who perform the sacrifice, go to your own womb, your own place."

Go! O Yajñādika, fulfill our desire, our wish. Having offered an oblation of curd into the northern direction of the fire with this mantra beginning with "yajñayajñapate" and ending with "agne kṣamasva svāhā," [one should proceed].
One should move the fire in the southern direction with this very mantra. || 64 || 65 ||
The passage beginning with "To Brahmā" (brahmaṇe) has a clear meaning. || 66 ||

Now, by which mantra should the tilaka be applied to the forehead? To this he says "māyām" and so forth. Having uttered the seed-syllable *māyā* (hrīḥ) and the seed-syllable *kāma* (klī), one should say: "Become the bringer of all peace. By way of application: *hrīḥ klīḥ sarvaśāntikaraḥ*.
The mantra "bhava" has arisen; with this mantra, the sacrificial priest, the performer of the sacrifice, should apply a tilaka on the forehead. || 67 ||
"Peace," and so forth. "Śiva" means auspiciousness. In the passage beginning with "of the Maruts" as well, the word "by grace" (prasādataḥ) must be supplied. || 68 ||
With this mantra, one should place a flower upon the head;
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability for the primary rite and the fire-oblation (homa). (69)
Thus, O Goddess, this *kuśaṇḍikā* for all rites has been described to you;
it should be diligently employed at the beginning of auspicious acts by the practitioners of the Kula.

For those whose family tradition (kulāgama) prescribes the *caru* offering for the auspicious rite at hand, the procedure for the *caru* is now declared for the sake of accomplishing their ritual action. (71)
The vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru) should be made either of copper or of clay. || 72 ||
Having performed the rites up to the consecration of the materials according to the procedure taught in the Kuśaṇḍikā, he should bring the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru) before himself.
Having seen a single blade of *kuśa* grass for the purifier (*pavitra*) that is unbroken, without a wound, and measuring one span (*prādeśa*), one should place it within the vessel.

"By this"—meaning, with this mantra beginning with "May there be peace" (*śāntir astu*) and ending with "of Prajāpati" (*prajāpateḥ*), one should hold a flower over the head. Then, according to one's own ability, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brāhmaṇa who has assisted in the sacrifice for both the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the primary rite. || 69 || 70 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the context," and so forth: "in the context" refers to the ritual action, such as the seasonal consecrations (*ṛtusaṃskāra*) and the like.
"Caru" is the supreme food intended for the deity. That *caru* which has its arrival (*āgama*) within the lineage (*kula*) is called "the lineage-arrival" (*kulāgama*). || 71 ||
He describes the rite of *caru* with the words beginning "the *caru*-pot" and so forth.

"Kuśaṇḍikā," and so forth. Having performed all the rites up to the preparation of the substances—that is, until the end of the purification of the materials—according to the procedure taught in the Kuśaṇḍikā, one should bring the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (carusthālī) to a place in front of oneself. || 73 ||

"Unbroken" means: then, having seen the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (*carusthālī*) to be unbroken, undamaged, without wounds, and without cracks, one should place—that is, set down—a single *pavitra* blade of *kuśa* grass, measuring a span (*prādeśa*), in the middle of the vessel. || 74 ||

Having brought rice and placed it there near the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), O worshiper of the gods, those deities who are to be honored in whichever rite is being performed [should be worshipped]. (75)
Having uttered each respective name in the dative case, pronouncing the word "ājuṣṭam" (enjoyed),
and speaking in sequence the words "gṛhṇāmi" (I take), "nirvapāmi" (I offer), and "prokṣāmi" (I sprinkle), [he should perform the rites].
Having taken four handfuls of rice for each deity, one should pour them into the cooking pot and sprinkle them with drops of water. (77)
Then, having added milk and sugar according to the rules of cooking, one should cook it well in a consecrated fire with great care, O lady of virtuous vows. (78)
Knowing it to be well-cooked and tender, one should pour a ladle of clarified butter (ghṛta) into it.

"Having brought," and so forth. Then, having brought rice grains to that sacrificial site and having placed them near the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should state the name of whichever deities are to be worshipped in whatever rite— such as the seasonal consecration (*ṛtusaṃskāra*)— ending with the dative case, and thereafter...
Uttering "tvājuṣṭam" (what is dear to you), and thereafter saying in succession "I take," "I offer," and "I sprinkle," while addressing each deity individually, he should take four handfuls—
that is, a quantity measured by four handfuls— of rice grains and pour them into the vessel.

One should sprinkle with a drop of water. Taking rice grains with the mantra, "I accept what is pleasing to [Name] Deva," one should place them in the cooking pot with the mantra, "I offer what is pleasing to [Name] Deva. [To] [Name] Deva, what is pleasing...

The meaning is that one should sprinkle them with drops of water while reciting the mantra "I sprinkle" (*prokṣāmi*). Furthermore, there is a word division as *ā-juṣṭam*. *Ājuṣṭam* means "pleasure" (*prīti*); thus, *ājuṣṭam* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

"Then," [it says]. O observer of good vows, thereafter, having placed milk and sugar in a vessel in due order, one should cook the *caru* well according to the rules of preparation over a consecrated fire with a mind full of vigilance. || 78 ||
"Supakvam" means: then, having recognized that the sacrificial porridge (caru) is well-cooked and tender, one should offer a sruva-spoon filled with clarified butter (ghṛta) into it. || 79 ||
Having placed the vessel upon the kuśa grass to the north of the fire,
and having again poured ghee three times, one should cover the pot with kuśa grass.
Then, having first taken some ghee from the vessel for the sacrificial ladle and the pot for the *caru* offering,
and having taken a small portion of the *caru*, one should perform the knee-oblation (*jānu-homa*).
Then, having performed the *dhārā-homa* (continuous stream oblation) during the principal rite,
one should offer oblations with the mantras prescribed for whichever deities are enjoined therein.
Having completed the primary oblation preceded by the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering,
and having performed the oblations consisting of expiations, one should perform the conclusion of the rite.
This procedure is proclaimed for the consecrations of conditioned things;
it should be performed at the beginning of auspicious rites for the sake of the successful accomplishment of those actions. (84)
Now it is said: O Mahāmāyā, the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) are to be performed. First among them, the rite of the menses (ṛtusaṃskāra) is described; listen to it in due order. 85.

Regarding the word "of Agni": then, having removed the vessel of cooked rice (caru) from the fire and placed it upon *kuśa* grass in a location to the north of the fire, having established it there, and having again poured clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into it three times, one should cover the pot with *kuśa* grass. || 80 ||
"Then" means: thereafter, having first held the clarified butter and first poured the clarified butter, one should take a small portion of the *caru* from the *caru*-pot with the *sruva* ladle,
and having taken it, perform the *jānu-homa* (knee-oblation) upon the earth.
That oblation which is prescribed after having lowered the right knee is to be understood as the *jānuhoma*. || 81 ||

"Having maintained," and so forth: then, having performed the *dhārā-homa* (continuous stream oblation), one should offer oblations—that is, give them—with the mantras of those deities who have been prescribed as the objects of worship in whichever primary rite (*pradhāna-karman*) is being performed. || 82 ||

"Having completed," etc. Thus, having completed the primary oblation (*prakṛtahoma*), and having performed the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*) preceded by the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should perform the conclusion of the rite, which is the completion of the act of offering. || 83–85 ||
Having performed his daily obligatory rites and being purified, he should worship the five deities:
Brahmā, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, the planets, and likewise the guardians of the directions. (86)
One should worship these [deities] in the jars located in the eastern direction of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Then, the sixteen Mothers, beginning with Gaurī, should be worshipped in their proper sequence. (87)
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā,
Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Kṣamā,
as well as one’s own personal deity and likewise the family deity. (88)
May all the Mothers come, who bring joy to the thirty gods;
may they grant every desired object for this marriage, vow, and sacrifice. (89)
Mounted upon the power of their vehicles and always assuming gentle forms, may all the Mothers come for the prosperity of this sacrificial festival. (90)
Having thus invoked the groups of Mothers and worshipped them according to one's capacity,
one should offer seven or five drops of vermilion and sandalwood paste upon the threshold, which is one span in measure and reaches to the level of the navel.
He states the ritual procedure for the seasonal consecration (*ṛtusaṃskāra*) with the words beginning "having performed the daily rites" (*kṛtanityakriya*).
