Now, in response to the expectation of which five deities one should worship, he says "Brahmā," and so forth. (86)

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the sthaṇḍila": on the eastern side—that is, the front part—of the sthaṇḍila or quadrangle, one should worship these deities, Brahmā and the others, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in the five jars that have been placed there. || 87 ||
He shows that the sixteen Mothers, beginning with Gaurī, are indeed to be worshipped, by means of the verse beginning with "Gaurī" and so forth, consisting of one and a half [stanzas]. (88)
Now, he states two mantras for the purpose of invoking the sixteen Mothers, beginning with Gaurī, starting with "May all the Mothers come," and so forth. (89–90)

"Thus," and so forth. Having invoked the groups of Mothers with these two mantras and having worshipped them according to one's capacity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, [one should do so] at the threshold (dehalī) measured by the navel— that is, reaching up to the navel— in the dimension of a span (prādeśa).
The wise one, recollecting Kāma, Māyā, and Ramā for each individual drop, should offer an unbroken stream of clarified butter and there worship Vasu. (92)
Having thus performed the rite of Vasudhārā according to the very path described by me,
the wise practitioner, having prepared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) preceded by the installation of the fire,
and having consecrated the oblation materials, should cook the most excellent caru.
In this rite, there is a *caru* offering to Prajāpati, and the fire is named Vāyu;
having completed the ritual up to the end of the continuous stream of oblations (*dhārāhoma*), one should commence the seasonal rites (*ārtava*).
Hrīḥ! Having offered three oblations of cooked rice (caru) to Prajāpati with the mantra "Svāhā," one should offer a single oblation while reciting this mantra: || 95 ||
As for its extent, one should apply seven or five drops of vermilion and sandalwood paste within a space measuring one span (prādeśa). || 91 ||
"Pratyeka," and so forth: the wise practitioner who accomplishes the rite, while recollecting the seed-syllables *klīm* for desire, *māyā* as *hrīm*, and *ramā* as *śrīm*,
having offered an uninterrupted stream of ghee drop by drop, [places] the Vasu (the letter *va*) right there.
One should worship the deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 92 ||
"Vasudhārām," and so forth. Having prepared and accomplished the Vasudhārā rite in this manner by the very path taught by me, the wise and discerning practitioner of rites,
having fashioned a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or a quadrangle (*catvara*), [should perform the rite] there, preceded by the installation of the fire.
Having consecrated the materials for the oblation, one should cook the *caru* which is unsurpassed—that is, of which nothing superior exists. || 93 ||

"Prājāpatya," and so forth. Here, in this rite of seasonal consecration (*ṛtusaṃskārakarma*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) that is cooked belongs to Prajāpati—that is, it has Prajāpati as its deity. And Hutāśana, the fire, becomes Vāyu by name. Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, up to the end of the *dhārāhoma* (stream-offering),...
Having completed the ritual action that must be performed, one should begin the seasonal rite of consecration (*ṛtusaṃskārakarman*).

"Hrīm," and so forth. Having offered three oblations of *caru* to Prajāpati with the mantra "Hrīḥ! To Prajāpati, svāhā!", he should offer one oblation while uttering this mantra which is about to be stated. || 95 ||
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms.
May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you. (96)
Meditating upon Sūrya, Prajāpati, and Viṣṇu, one should offer an oblation with clarified butter, or with cooked rice (caru), or even with cooked rice mixed with clarified butter.
May Śinīvālī bestow a fetus; may Sarasvatī bestow a fetus.
May the two divine Aśvins, adorned with lotus garlands, place a fetus within you. 98.
Having meditated upon the goddess Śinīvālī, as well as Sarasvatī and the two Aśvins, one should offer the supreme oblation with this mantra ending in "svāhā. (99)
Then, reciting "Kāma, Badhū, Māyā, Ramā,
Kūrca," and saying, "Place a virtuous embryo in this woman who desires a son," he should meditate upon Ravi and Viṣṇu and offer oblations into the consecrated fire.
He recites the mantra, "Viṣṇur yonim," for the purpose of offering a single oblation; [the word] *piṃśatu* means "may he illuminate" or "may he adorn. || 96 ||

"With clarified butter," and so forth. With the mantra beginning with "Viṣṇur yoniḥ," while meditating upon Sūrya, Prajāpati, and Viṣṇu, one should offer—that is, give—a single oblation (āhuti) intended for them alone, using either clarified butter (ājya), ghee (ghṛta), or sacrificial porridge (caru), or indeed sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter or ghee. || 97 ||

"Having meditated," and so forth. Having meditated upon the goddess Śinīvālī with this mantra ending in *svāhā*, beginning with "O Śinīvālī, bestow the womb," and likewise upon the two Aśvins together with Sarasvatī—
the two gods Aśvins accompanied by Sarasvatī— one should offer the supreme oblation.

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, while reciting the seed-syllables *kāmaṃ* (the syllable *klīm*), *badhūm* (the syllable *strīm*), *māyām* (the syllable *hrīm*), *ramām* (the syllable *śrīm*), and *kūrcam* (the syllable *hūm*), together with *sadviṭham* (*phaṭ*) and *svāhā*, [one should address] "this woman who desires a son."

Having said, "Place the embryo," and having uttered the mantra: *klīṃ strīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ, place the embryo for this woman who desires a son, svāhā*, one should meditate upon Ravi and Viṣṇu and offer oblations into the consecrated fire. || 100 ||

"Just as this goddess Earth, lying on her back, has conceived a fetus, so may you conceive a fetus for birth in the tenth month. With this mantra ending in *svāhā*, while meditating upon Viṣṇu, he should offer the oblation. (101)
Again, taking clarified butter and meditating upon Viṣṇu, the supreme beyond the supreme,
he should offer the oblation into the fire while reciting: "O Viṣṇu, through your most excellent form, bestow upon this woman a most noble son," ending with the two syllables *ṭha-ṭha*.
Having recited the *kāma* mantra enveloped by the *māyā* mantra, and the *vadhū* mantra enveloped by the *māyā* mantra,
he should again recite both the *kāma* and *māyā* mantras and touch her head.
Surrounded by women who had sons living,
the husband touched her head with both hands and placed it upon the hem of his garment.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu, Durgā, Brahmā, and Sūrya, one should offer three fruits;
then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should conclude with the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitti*).

"Yatheyam iti": for the sake of procreation (*sūtaye*), with this mantra ending in *svāhā*—namely, "Just as this earth... and so forth—one should offer an oblation into the fire, meditating upon Viṣṇu and dedicating it specifically to Him. || 101 ||

"Again," and so forth: having again taken up clarified butter (*ājya*), that is, *ghṛta*, and having meditated upon Viṣṇu, who is superior even to the supreme, and having directed [the offering] toward Him alone, [one recites]: "O Viṣṇu, through Your eldest form, bestow upon this woman a most excellent son, Svāhā!"

The grammatical connection is that, having uttered the mantra, one should cast the oblation of clarified butter into the fire. "Distinguished by the most excellent form" means superior; "varīyasam" means most excellent or pre-eminent.
[The mantra is: *ṭha-dvandvaṃ svāhā*. 102.

"By means of Kāma": then, one should take the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), which is encased at the beginning and end by *kāma*, the seed-syllable *klīṃ*; likewise, one should take the seed-syllable *vadhū* (*strīṃ*), which is similarly encased by *māyā*, the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*; and again, the seed-syllable *kāma*, the seed-syllable *klīṃ*.

Having recited the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) and the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, and having recited the mantra *yojanayā klīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ*, one should touch the head of this wife. || 103 ||
"Patītyādi" and so forth. Surrounded by women who have husbands and sons,
the husband, having touched and stroked the head of his wife with both hands,
[should place] Viṣṇu, Durgā, and Brahmā with both hands upon the edge of her lap.
Alternatively, by worshipping Gaurī and Śaṅkara at the time of dusk and by offering an arghya oblation to the Sun, the purification of the couple shall come to pass. (106)
The rite regarding the menstrual period has been explained; now hear concerning the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).
On that night or on another night, during the even-numbered nights, having entered the interior of his dwelling with his wife and meditated upon the god Prajāpati; || 108 ||
Touching his wife, the husband should recite, preceded by the seed-syllable of Māyā:
"O Bed, for the sake of our noble offspring, be auspicious to us both. (109)
Having ascended the bed with his wife, facing either the east or the north,
he should sit down, look at the woman, place his hand upon her head,
embrace her with his left hand, and recite the mantra at various points.

Having meditated upon Prajāpati and Sūrya, one should offer three fruits; the remainder of the instruction is that one should thus conclude the rite pertaining to the menses (ārtava). || 104 || 105 ||

Now, with the verse beginning "Or else" (yadvā), he states the procedure for another seasonal consecration (*ṛtusaṃskāra*). "At the time of *pradoṣa*" means at the commencement of the night. || 106 || 107 ||
Now, he describes the procedure for the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) with the words beginning "on that night" (*tadrātrau*).

On that night— the night of the seasonal rite (*ṛtu-saṃskāra*)— or on another night, having gone into the interior of the house with his wife during an even-numbered night, he should meditate upon the deity Prajāpati.

And the husband, touching his wife, preceded by the *māyābīja*—that is, with the *māyābīja* "hrīṃ" placed at the beginning—should recite this mantra: "For the sake of our noble offspring, may you be a bringer of auspiciousness upon this bed. || 108 || 109 ||
"Having ascended": then, having ascended the bed together with his wife, the husband, facing either east or north, sits there and, looking at the woman,
places his right hand upon her head and embraces her with his left hand.
One should mutter the *mantra* at each respective place. || 110 ||

Having recited the *Kāma* syllable (*kām*) one hundred times on the head, the *Vāgbhava* syllable (*aiṃ*) one hundred times on the chin, the *Ramā* syllable (*hrīṃ*) twenty times on the throat, and [the same] one hundred times on each of the two breasts; (111)
Having recited the Māyā-bīja ten times at the heart and twenty-five times at the navel,
one should place the hand upon the yoni together with the Vāgbhava-bīja and Kāma.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, and performing likewise upon the linga,
he should approach a woman after manifesting her womb through *māyā*, for the sake of obtaining a son.
At the moment of the emission of semen, the Lord, having meditated upon the Creator of the Universe,
should cause it to fall into the *cit-kuṇḍa* below the navel, within the *raktikā*.
Immediately after the emission of semen, the wise one should recite this mantra: || 115 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which mantra should be recited at which specific location, he says: "At the head, Kāma," and so forth. Having recited the mantra *klīm* (Kāma) one hundred times at the head—that is, on the crown—and [then] at the chin...
Having recited the *vāgbhava* mantra, *aim*, one hundred times on the lower part of the lower lip,
and having recited the *ramā* mantra, *śrīm*, twenty times at the throat,
and [recited] the *śrīm* mantra one hundred times on the pair of breasts;
One should recite it one hundred times. || 111 ||

"In the heart," and so forth. Then, having recited the *māyā* mantra *hrīḥ* ten times over the wife's heart, and having recited that same *māyā* mantra *hrīḥ* twenty-five times over her navel, and having placed his hand upon her vulva with desire, [he should recite] *klīm*.

Having recited the mantra "aim" (Vāgbhava), together with the seed-syllable, one hundred and eight times upon the linga; likewise, performing the recitation of the mantra "klīm aim" upon the [female organ], the husband, by means of his power of illusion (*māyā*) and the mantra "hrīm," causes the vulva to expand and open for the sake of obtaining a son— that is, for the attainment of a son.
He should approach a woman. || 112 || 113 ||
"At the time of the emission of semen," and so forth.

At the moment of the emission of semen, at the time of the discharge of the seed, the husband, having meditated upon Prajāpati Viśvakṛt, should cause the seed to fall into the *cit-kuṇḍa* below the navel, into the *raktikā* channel. || 114 || 115 ||
Just as the earth is pregnant with fire, as the sky with the wielder of the thunderbolt, and as the quarters of space are pregnant with the wind, so may you become pregnant. 116.
O Maheśvarī, when the embryo has been conceived— whether during that very menstrual period or at another time—
the householder should perform the Puṃsavana rite in the third month of pregnancy.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites, the husband should worship the five deities and the Mothers beginning with Gaurī, and he should arrange the stream of wealth (vasordhārā).
Then, having performed the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* according to the previously mentioned procedure, the wise man,
having completed the rites up to the *dhārā-homa*, should perform the *puṃsavana* ceremony.
There is a sacrificial oblation (caru) for Prajāpati, and the fire there is named Candra.
One should place one barley grain and two māṣa beans into cow's curd;
then the husband should ask the woman three times: "O blessed lady, what are you drinking? || 121 ||
Then the woman should say: "The illusion of the male-child-conception is threefold;
the woman should drink three handfuls of curd mixed with barley and black gram. (122)

Regarding the mantra that the Lord recites immediately after the sprinkling of the seed-syllable, he states it as "yathāgninā" and so forth. *Bhūḥ* is the earth; *dyauḥ* is heaven; and by *vajradhāriṇā* is meant Indra.
He describes the very procedure for the *puṃsavana* rite with the words beginning "having performed his daily duties" (*kṛtanityakriya*).
Having performed his daily duties, the husband should worship the five previously mentioned deities, beginning with Brahmā, in that *puṃsavana* rite. (120)

"Regarding the phrase *gavye* and so forth: one should place one barley grain and two beans into the *gavya*—that is, into the curd produced from a cow. Then, O auspicious wife, the husband should ask the woman three times, saying, 'What are you drinking? || 121 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): thereafter, [the mantra] *hrīṃ* is the *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child). The term *puṃsavana* means that a woman with a parting in her hair (*sīmantinī*) should say it three times, in three ways. Then, having gone from the place of sacrifice to another location, the woman should drink three handfuls (*prasṛti*) of curd mixed with barley and black gram.
One should bring the woman, whose sons are living, to the place of sacrifice;
having established her on the left side, one should perform the oblation of sacrificial porridge (*caru*). (123)
Taking the sacrificial porridge (caru) as before, while reciting the *māyā* mantra and the *kūrca* mantra:
"Those who create obstacles to the embryo, and those who destroy the embryo... (124)
O Dviṭha, destroy all those spirits, ghosts, piśācas, vetālas, and child-killers; effect a pair [of protections] and provide guardianship for the fetus. 125.
Having meditated upon the fire as a slayer of demons by means of this mantra,
and repeatedly visualizing Rudra and Prajāpati, one should offer twelve oblations.
Then, having offered five oblations with the mantra "Māyā candramase svāhā," and having touched the heart of his wife, he should recite the Māyā-Lakṣmī mantra one hundred times.

"Jīvadityādi" and so forth. Then, together with those women who have living sons—meaning those whose children are alive—one should bring a woman (*vanitā*) to the place of sacrifice. Having seated that woman on one's left side, [one should perform] the *caru* oblation.
One should practice. || 123 ||

"As before" means: as previously [stated], having taken the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in the *sruva* ladle and grasped it while reciting the *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), the *kūrca* (*hūṃ*), and the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should utter the sentence beginning with "those who are in the womb...
and ending with "...all of them. Then, one should utter "destroy the pair" (*nāśaya dvaṃdva*). Then...

One should say, "Perform the protection of the womb. Then one should say, "Dviṭhaḥ svāhā. By joining all the words together: *hrīḥ hūḥ ye garbhavighnakartāro ye ca garbhavināśakā bhūtāḥ pretāḥ piśācāśca vetālāḥ*.

The mantra that has arisen is: "O slayers of hair, destroy them all, destroy them! Protect the fetus! Svāhā! With this mantra, one should meditate upon Rudra as the fire-god Hutāśana, the destroyer of demons, known by the name Rakṣoghna.
And meditating upon Prajāpati, one should offer twelve oblations. || 124 || 126 ||

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, having offered five oblations with the mantra "Hrīḥ, svāhā to the Moon," and having touched the heart of his wife, he should mutter the mantra "Māyā Lakṣmī, Hrīḥ Śrīḥ" one hundred times. || 127 ||
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭikṛt* oblation, he should conclude with the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitti*).
Thereafter, in the fifth month, he should give the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) to the woman. (128)
Sugar, honey, milk, ghee, and curd, taken in equal parts—
this is declared to be the "five nectars" (pañcāmṛta), which is prescribed for the purification of the body.
O Śivā, having recited Vāgbhava, Madana, Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kūrca,
and Purandara five times each over the five substances,
the husband should unify them and have his beloved consume the nectars therein. (130)
One should perform the Sīmantonnayana rite in the sixth or even the eighth month;
this ceremony for parting the hair continues as long as offspring has not been born. (131)
Having performed the ritual up to the end of the previously mentioned *dhārāhoma* (continuous stream oblation) together with his wife,
the wise man, seated upon his seat, should offer three oblations while pronouncing the word *vahnijāyā* (the wife of fire, i.e., *svāhā*) after [the names of] Viṣṇu, Bhāsvat, and Dhātṛ.
Then, having meditated upon the Moon within the fire of Śiva’s mouth,
a person should perform the oblation seven times, dedicating it to Soma.
One should complete the *puṃsavana* rite; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 128 ||
Now, what indeed is this "five nectars"? To this he says, "sugar" and so forth. "Equal parts" means having identical proportions. || 129 ||
"Vāgbhava," and so forth. Vāgbhava is *aiṃ*; Madana is *klīṃ*; Lakṣmī is *śrīṃ*; Māyā is *hrīṃ*; Kūrca is *hūṃ*; and Purandara is *laṃ*.
These five seed-syllables (*bīja*) are [to be placed] five times each upon the five substances, such as sugar and the rest.

Having recited [the mantra] five times and having combined the sugar and other [ingredients] into an elixir of immortality (*amṛta*), the husband should have his beloved wife consume it here in the fifth month. || 130 || 131 ||
He explains the very procedure for the *sīmantonnayana* rite with the words beginning "the aforementioned," etc. A wise,
learned man, having sat on a seat together with his wife and having performed the ritual up to the end of the previously mentioned *dhārā-homa*, [should first offer] to Viṣṇu.
Having meditated upon the Aśvins, Vāsava, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, and Prajāpati, one should offer oblations five times each to Śivā. (134)
The husband, taking a golden comb in his right hand,
should place it within the mass of hair at the parting of the hair.
Meditating upon Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, while reciting the seed-syllable of Māyā.
O auspicious and fortunate wife, O lady of excellent vows, in the tenth month,
may you give birth with ease and joy through the grace of Viśvakarman.
"O long-lived Kaṅkatikā, you who are radiant, grant me auspiciousness.
Then one should complete the rite with the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation and other concluding elements. || 138 ||

Uttering "to Bhāsvat" and "to Dhātṛ," and then pronouncing the fire-born wife "svāhā," while reciting the mantra "svāhā to Viṣṇu, svāhā to Sūrya, svāhā to Prajāpati," he offers three oblations intended for Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati.
One should give [it]. || 132 – 134 ||
"Gold," and so forth. Then the husband, taking a golden comb—
a grooming instrument made of gold— in his right hand, first reciting the seed-syllable of Māyā, "hrīḥ," and then...
O auspicious, fortunate, and virtuous wife, in the tenth month,
may you give birth with joy through the grace of Viśvakarman;
may this long-lived comb bring you splendor and grant you well-being.
Reciting this mantra and meditating upon Śiva, Viṣṇu, Vidhi, and Prajāpati,
he should place [the hair] from the parting of the hair (sīmanta) into the mass of hair (keśapāśa), that is, into the interior of the bound hair. [This is for the verse beginning with] "āyuṣmatī."
The word *bhava* should be construed with *anena*; the word *te* is to be construed with *kaṅkatikā*.
Having seen his newborn son and having given gold within the house, the wise man should complete the *dhārā-homa* according to the previously mentioned procedure. (139)
Then one should offer five oblations, dedicating them to Agni, Indra, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, and Brahmā immediately thereafter. (140)
Having placed equal portions of honey and clarified butter in a bronze vessel,
the father, having recited the Vāgbhava mantra a hundred times, should cause his son to consume it.
Uttering this mantra with the ring finger of the right hand:
"O child, may your lifespan, luster, strength, and intelligence always increase. (142)
Having thus performed the rite for generating longevity, he should assign a secret name;
when his son has undergone the initiation ceremony, he should address him by that name.
Having performed the expiatory rites and other ceremonies, one should complete the birth-rite (jātakarma).
Thereafter, the nurse should perform the cutting of the umbilical cord with great enthusiasm. || 144 ||
As long as the umbilical cord is not severed, ritual impurity does not apply; indeed, before the cutting of the cord, one may perform rites for the gods and the ancestors. 145.

Now, he describes the procedure for the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) with the verses beginning "immediately upon birth" (*jātamātram*), etc. The word "having given" (*dattvā*) implies "to the son" (*sutāya*). "In another house" (*gṛhāntare*) means in a house other than the lying-in chamber (*sūtikāgṛha*). The portion beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*) is of clear meaning. || 139 || 140 ||
"Madhu" (honey). Immediately after that, following the offering of the five oblations, one should bring honey and clarified butter in equal portions into a bronze vessel;
having recited the *vāgbhava* mantra, "aim," over it a hundred times, [one attains] longevity, luster, strength, and intelligence.
Reciting the mantra, "May you always grow, O child," the father should cause his son to eat honey and clarified butter with the ring finger of his right hand. || 141 ||
The phrases "thus [is] the production of life" and so forth, however, have clear meanings. (143–145)
In this very same manner, but without mantras, the rite should be performed for a girl as well;
one should give her a name publicly in the sixth or eighth month. (146)
Having bathed the infant and clothed him in two auspicious garments, the mother,
having approached her husband’s side, should place the son facing the east.
One should sprinkle the head of the child with water containing gold and *kuśa* grass;
[for these are] the Jāhnavī, Yamunā, Revā, and the most pure Sarasvatī. (148)
May the Narmadā, the Varadā, the Kuntī, the oceans, and the lakes—may these all consecrate you for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha. (149)
Hrīḥ! O Waters, you who are indeed sources of bliss, grant us strength for great joy and for the sake of vision. 150.
"Of the maiden," and so forth. For the maiden as well, the birth-rite (jātakarman) must be performed in this very same way, even without mantras—that is, entirely devoid of mantras. || 146 ||

Now, the procedure for the naming ceremony is as follows: having bathed [the child] with the verses beginning "snāpayitvā" and so forth, the mother, after having the infant bathed and dressed in two auspicious garments, approaches her husband and places the son facing the east. || 147 ||

"He should consecrate," and so forth. Then the father should consecrate the head of the child with water mixed with gold and *kuśa* grass, using the mantras beginning with "O Jāhnavī" (the Ganges). || 148 || 149 ||

"O Waters," and so forth: O Waters, since you indeed are *mayobhuvaḥ*—*mayaḥ* meaning happiness, and you are the bringers or bestowers of that—therefore, establish us (*naḥ*) for *ūrja*, that is, for food. Furthermore, [establish us] for great joy (*mahe raṇāya*).

"Bestow [this] for the sake of delightful vision, for the sake of beautiful sight. This is the meaning: O Waters, since you bring us happiness, therefore grant us this-worldly food and the like, as well as that which belongs to the hereafter, which is greatly delightful and beautiful to behold.

"Join with Brahman. The form *hiṣṭhā* is the second person plural imperative of the root *as* (to be). The form *dadhātana* is also the second person plural imperative of the root *dhā* (to place); this is established by the rule *chandasi bahulam* (in Vedic usage [these forms] occur frequently). *Maha*... [text fragment ends].
Thus, because the word *mahate* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), there is the elision of the vowels *a* and *ta*;
[the result is] *hrī*. "O Waters, may you grant us a share here of that most auspicious essence (*rasa*) of yours, like longing mothers. (151)
Hrī! To you, for whose abode you quicken us, O Waters, we come gladly; and do you give birth to us. 152.

Having consecrated [the fire] with the three mantras and performed the purification of the fire as before, the wise practitioner, having completed the rites up to the final stream, should offer five oblations.
The word *sati* occurs as *mahe*. In the sense of "for delight" (*raṇāya*), there is a substitution of *raṇa* for the word *ramaṇīya* in Vedic usage.
In the form *cakṣuṣe*, the dative case ending is applied to a stem ending in the suffix *us*. || 150 ||

"Yo vā" and so forth: O Waters (*āpaḥ*), that most auspicious (*śivatamaḥ*)—meaning of an extremely beneficial nature—essence (*rasaḥ*) or extract of yours which is sweet, with that essence make us here partakers (*bhājayata*); that is, make us possessors of a share, connected with that essence.
The meaning is "make [us so]. Of what nature are you? "Ūśatīḥ," meaning full of desire, like mothers through affection.
This is the sense: just as mothers through affection make their sons partakers of the same essence, so too do you [make] us [so].
"Perform the connection with the essence that brings about auspiciousness. Regarding the word *ūśatīḥ*: the root *vaś* means "to desire";

from it, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied, followed by the suffix *īp*. Then, when the case-ending *jas* is applied, the long vowel of the preceding class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). O Waters (*āpaḥ*), for you (*vaḥ*), unto him (*tasmai*), in him (*tasmin*)...
"Rase'ramalam paryāptam" means "let us go, let us go to that essence"—that is the sense. Furthermore, "vaḥ tatra rase naḥ bhogam yūyam janayatha": you produce enjoyment for us in that essence.
And for the sake of the exhaustion—that is, in the place of the exhaustion—of that essence, "jinvatha," meaning you satisfy or delight [all beings] from Brahma down to a blade of grass.

The word "jagat" (the world) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. This is the meaning: O Waters, in the place of that essence of yours in which the world delights, may we attain satisfaction regarding that;
and may you produce enjoyment for us therein. To him—

In both instances, "kṣayāya" is the dative case used in the sense of the locative. "Gamāma" is the first person plural of the imperative; the absence of the substitute "gaccha" is a Vedic anomaly (chāndasa).
In "janayathā," the lengthening of the vowel occurs in Vedic usage. "Jinvatha" is established as correct in Vedic usage. 151, 152.

"Having consecrated," and so forth: having consecrated the head of the child with these three mantras, and having performed the purification of the fire as before, the wise father, having completed the ritual up to the end of the stream—that is, up to the end of the stream-offering—should offer five oblations. || 153 ||
Having offered the first oblation to Agni, then to Vāsava,
then to Prajāpati, and also to the Viśvedevas,
one should offer an oblation to Brahmā in the fire known as pārthiva. (154)
Then, taking the son onto his lap, the wise man should cause him to hear an auspicious name—consisting of few syllables and easy to pronounce—in his right ear. (155)
Having caused the name to be heard three times and having announced it to the Brahmins,
he should then complete the rite by performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the subsequent ceremonies.
For a girl, there is no formal exit from the womb, nor does the Vṛddhi-śrāddha exist;
however, the wise man should perform the naming, the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony without mantras.
One should perform the rite of the infant's first outing in the fourth or the sixth month. || 158 ||
Having performed his daily rites, O dear one, and having worshipped Gaṇanāyaka,
the wise father, after bathing his son and adorning him with garments and ornaments, should place him before himself and utter this mantra: || 159 ||
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, and likewise Bhāskara;
Indra, Vāyu, Kuvera, Varuṇa, Agni, and Bṛhaspati—grant welfare to the child and protect him always upon his path. (160)
Now, in response to the expectation of for which deities one should offer the five oblations, he says "To Agni," and so forth. || 154 ||

"Then," and so forth. Then, having taken the son onto his lap—that is, holding him in his embrace—the wise father should cause the son's auspicious name, which consists of few syllables, is easy to pronounce, and signifies good fortune, to be heard in the right ear—that is, the right side of the head. || 155 ||
Now, he describes the ritual procedure for the child's first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*) with the words beginning "having performed the daily rites" (*kṛtanityakriya*).

He states the very mantra that one should recite: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu... (160). Having spoken thus, and having taken [the child] onto his lap accompanied by song and instrumental music, [he should proceed].
One should lead the child outside together with his joyful kinsmen.
Having gone some distance on the path, one should have the child look at the sun.
Hrī! May that eye, beneficial to the gods, rise up before us, brilliant and clear.
May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns. 163.
Having thus shown the sun and returned to his own home, the father should offer the *arghya* oblation to the Lord of Day and then feed his own kinsmen. (164)
In the sixth month of the prince, or even in the auspicious eighth month,
the father’s brother or the father himself should perform the rite of first feeding with solid food.
As before, the father should perform the worship of the deities and likewise the consecration of the fire; having thus duly completed the rites ending with the pouring of water, he should proceed.
There, one should offer five oblations into the pure fire;
the first directed toward Agni, and the second while recollecting Vāsava.
Then, having dedicated [the offerings] to Prajāpati, the god, and then to the Viśvedevas,
one should offer the fifth oblation intended for Brahmā.

"Thus," and so forth. Having uttered this mantra, and having taken the child onto his lap—that is, holding him—he should bring the child outside accompanied by joyful kinsmen, preceded by songs and instrumental music. || 161 ||
"Having gone," and so forth: having traveled some distance on the road or path, the father should cause the child, the infant, to behold—that is, show—the sun. || 162 ||
He states the mantra with which one should show the sun to the child: *hrīṃ;
tac cakṣuḥ*. That eye, beneficial to the gods, which rises pure in the east—rising above the pure, it moves—that form of the sun exists so that we may [see] for a hundred autumns.
"May we see many years, and while seeing them, may we live for a hundred autumns.
(163) He describes the ritual procedure for the first feeding of solid food with the words beginning "as before," etc. (166).

In that regard, concerning the rite of the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*): indeed, when the expectation arises as to which deities one should offer the five oblations (*pañcāhuti*), he says "Agni," and so forth. || 167 || 168 ||
Then, having meditated upon the giver of food within the fire and offered five oblations, the father—
either there at the cremation ground or in another house— having placed his son on his lap adorned with clothes and ornaments, should feed him the nectar of milk-rice (*pāyasa*). (169)
Having fed [the child] five times with the mantras of the five *prāṇāhuti* offerings, one should then place a little of the food, condiments, and so forth, into the mouth of the child.
One should conclude the rite with the sound of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, followed by the expiatory ceremony (prāyaścitti).
Thus has the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) been described; now hear the procedure for the tonsure ceremony (cūḍāvidhi). || 171 ||
In the third or fifth year, according to family custom,
one should perform the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma) for the child to accomplish the purification rite of infancy.
Having completed the ritual actions beginning with the worship of the deity and ending with the final oblation,
the practitioner [should prepare] a place to the north of the true fire, filled with the dung of a bull.
The wise man should place a shallow bowl containing sesame seeds and wheat, along with lukewarm water and a single razor well-sharpened. (174)
"Then," and so forth. Then, having meditated upon the Goddess Paramānnadā and offered five oblations (pañcāhuti) into the fire dedicated to her, the father— having thus offered the five oblations—
[places] his son, adorned with garments and ornaments, upon his lap either there or in another house.

Having placed and established the nectar of milk-rice (pāyasa), which is the supreme food in the form of ambrosia, one should cause [the recipient] to consume it; that is, one should feed them. || 169 ||

"Five," and so forth: having fed the son five times with milk-rice using the mantras consisting of the five oblations to the vital breaths— *prāṇāya svāhā*, *apānāya svāhā*, *samānāya svāhā*, *udānāya svāhā*, and *vyānāya svāhā*.

Then, having placed a little of the food, condiments, and so forth into the child’s mouth, one should complete the rite of the first feeding (annaprāśana) with the sounding of conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments, and by means of an expiation (prāyaścitti). || 170 || 171 ||

Now, he describes the procedure for the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) with the words beginning "In the third [year]," and so forth. The wise, discerning practitioner— the father who accomplishes the rite—
having performed the ritual from the worship of the deity as before up to the *dhārā* (consecration stream), [proceeds] from the true fire...

To the north of the fire named Satya, one should place a shallow bowl filled with bull-dung and mixed with sesame and wheat, along with lukewarm water— slightly warm— and a single well-sharpened razor. || 172–174 ||
Having approached his son there, Janaka placed him on his own left side and, with those lukewarm waters, [bathed him] upon his mother’s lap. (175)
Having recited the Vāruṇa mantra ten times and having wiped the hair on the child’s head,
one should fashion a single *juṣṭi* offering with two blades of *kuśa* grass through the power of *māyā*.
Having recited the Māyā and Lakṣmī mantras three times and taken an iron razor,
he should cut the root of the juṣṭikā plant and place it into the hand of the Mother.
The mother of the boy, taking [the hair] with both hands, should place it in a shallow bowl containing cow dung; the father should say, "May there be satisfaction for the barber. (178)
Having recited "O razor-shorn child, accomplish the shaving comfortably," [the priest],
looking at the barber while facing the fire named Satya,
should offer three oblations dedicated to Prajāpati. (179)
"Having approached," and so forth: Then the father Janaka, having approached— that is, brought— his son, the child,
to the vicinity of that fire named Satya, and having placed him on his own left,
in the lap of his mother on the left side of himself, [he performed the rite] with those [materials] which had been placed by them to the north of the fire.

Having recited the *vāruṇa* seed-syllable *vaṃ*, which pertains to Varuṇa, ten times over lukewarm water, one should wipe the hair of the child— the locks of the boy— with the *māyā* seed-syllable *hrīṃ* while using two *kuśa* blades, and thus perform a single act of purification (*juṣṭi*). || 175 || 176 ||

"Mayām" and so forth: Then, having recited three times the seed-syllable of Māyā (hrīḥ), the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī (śrīḥ), and [the other syllables], one should take an iron razor, cut the root of the *juṣṭikā* plant, and place—that is, set down—the *juṣṭikā* in the hand of the Mother. || 177 ||

"O Prince," and so forth. The mother of the prince, having taken and grasped the *juṣṭikā* with both hands, should place it in a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) smeared with cow dung. Then the father—the child’s progenitor—should speak to the barber. || 178 ||
In response to the expectation of what the child’s father should say to the barber, he says:
“O barber, O you who shave with a razor, perform the shaving of the child so that it may be pleasant; *ṭha* *ṭha* *svāhā*.”
Then, having had the child shaved by a barber and bathed, and having adorned him with garments, ornaments, and garlands, [he should place him] in the presence of the fire. (180)
Having placed [the vessel] on his own left side, he should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation;
then, having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the father should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
"O child, may Māyā and the all-pervading Creator of the Universe grant you well-being.
Having recited this into the ear of the child with a golden or iron probe, one should perform the piercing of the ear. (182)
Then, having consecrated the son with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having performed the rites for peace and the giving of the sacrificial fee, one should complete the rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma).
From conception until the tonsure ceremony, the rites are the same for all castes;
however, for Śūdras and those of common birth, all of these are performed without mantras.

The rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) and ending with the tonsure (cūḍā) should be performed by members of all five castes without mantras, except for the single rite of the first outing (niṣkramaṇa), even in the case of a girl. 185.

Having recited the mantra beginning with "kṣuramuṇḍin" and ending with "sādhaya svāhā," the father of the child, looking at the barber, should offer three oblations into the fire named Satya while addressing Prajāpati. || 179 ||
"By the barber": then,
having bathed the infant who has had his head shaved by the barber, and having adorned him with garments, ornaments, and garlands, he should place him near the fire on his own left side.
One should perform, that is, carry out, the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation. || 180 || 181 ||

"Mayā" and so forth: "Māyā" is the syllable *hrīḥ*. Having recited this mantra—beginning with "O child, *hrīḥ*" and ending with "the Lord who creates the universe"—into the ear of the child, [one should offer it] with a golden vessel, that is, one made of gold, or a shining one, that is, one produced from silver.
Or one should perform the piercing of the child's ear using a needle made of iron.

Now, it is said that there is a prescribed rule for the investiture with the sacred thread (*upavīta*) for the twice-born; once this has been performed, the twice-born become entitled to perform rites for the gods and the ancestors. (186)
One should perform the initiation (upanayana) of the child in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [after birth];
however, one who has exceeded the sixteenth year should not be initiated, even if he is devoid of sacred rites.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites, the learned man should worship the five deities,
as well as the Mothers beginning with Gaurī, and he should arrange for the offering of Vasudhārā.
Thereafter, one should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* for the satisfaction of the deities and the ancestors;
one should carry out the rite according to the procedure prescribed for the *kuśaṇḍikā*, up to the end of the *dhārā-homa*.
In the morning, the boy— having eaten his meal, well-bathed, and beautifully adorned—
should have his head shaved except for the *śikhā* (top-knot) and be dressed in silken garments.
Having brought [the disciple] to the pavilion of shade and having seated him upon a pure seat to his own left, near the fire that has arisen.
"Then," and so forth. "Of the twice-born" refers to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. || 186 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "garbha": one should perform the *upanayana* (sacred thread ceremony) for a child (*śiśu*) in the eighth year from conception or from birth. A child who has exceeded sixteen years—that is, one who has passed the age of sixteen—should not be initiated. Such a child is devoid of religious duties (*niṣkriya*).
He also becomes one who is devoid of rites for the gods and the ancestors. || 187 ||

Next, he describes the procedure for the rite of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) with the verses beginning "having performed the daily rites" (*kṛtanityakriya*), etc., [referring to] the five deities, Brahmā and the others. || 188 || 189 ||

"Prātar" and so forth: then, in the morning, he who has performed his meal— that is, one by whom eating has been done— and he whose shaving was performed without the topknot (*śikhā*), and who is well-bathed— that is, one who has properly performed his ablutions— [and adorned] with ornaments and the like.
Having brought the boy— who was well-adorned, embellished with silken garments,
and further graced by two fine *dukūla* cloths— to a shaded pavilion near the fire named Samudbhava, he [placed him] before his own...
On the left side, on a pure seat, he should say to the disciple: "O child, observe celibacy. Then the disciple should inform the guru: "I shall observe celibacy. || 192 ||
Then the preceptor, with a serene mind, should give two saffron-colored garments to the disciple whose heart is tranquil, for the sake of long life and splendor. (193)
One should silently give a triple-stranded girdle made of muñja grass or kuśa grass, joined with knots, to one who wears saffron-colored garments.
Having uttered the *māyā* [syllable], the auspicious girdle (*mekhalā*) shall be the bestower of welfare;
having spoken thus and fastened the girdle, he should remain silent before the Guru. (195)
"The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is the supreme purifier; that which Bṛhaspati bestowed from of old is innate.
Put on this auspicious, foremost, life-prolonging *yajñopavīta*; may there be strength and splendor for you.
With this mantra, one should give it to the child together with a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*).
One should give a sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and a staff made of bamboo, or of khadira wood, or of palāśa, or produced from a milky tree. || 197 ||

Having established him in the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the teacher should say to the disciple, "Practice it, my son. Thereafter, the student should inform the teacher, "I shall practice the life of celibacy. (190–192)

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, the Guru, with a serene self— that is, a tranquil mind— [bestows the initiation] upon the disciple whose mind is peaceful, for the sake of long-livedness (dīrghāyuṣṭva)—
meaning the state of one who possesses long life— and for the sake of splendor (varcas) and vital energy (tejas).
One should give two garments dyed with a reddish-brown color, namely, clothes colored with kaṣāya. || 193 ||

Regarding the phrase "the mauñjī": one should silently give a girdle (*mekhalā*) made of *muñja* grass or *kuśa* grass, triple-stranded and provided with a knot, even to a child who is wearing saffron-colored garments. || 194 ||

Regarding "māyām": having first uttered the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* for *māyā*, and then having recited the mantra, "May the auspicious girdle be the bestower of welfare," one should tie the girdle around the waist and stand before the Guru in silence. || 195 || 196 ||

"By means of the mantra," and so forth. With this mantra beginning with "yajñopavītam" and ending with "balam astu tejaḥ," one should give the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*)— accompanied by a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), that is, joined with the skin of a black-colored deer— to the child.

Having sprinkled [the disciple], who holds a staff and wears the sacred thread, three times with water from kusa grass using the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which is encased by the Māyā [syllable], he should then fill the child's cupped palms with water. (198)
Then, the preceptor should cause the student—who has offered his joined palms to the Lord of Day—to behold the Sun with the mantra "taccakṣuḥ. (199)
Then, having seen the sun, the teacher should say to the young student:
"Fix your mind upon my vow; I give my heart to you.
Be of one mind, my child; may your speech be auspicious for me. (200)
Having touched [the disciple] on the heart and recited this, he should ask him: "What is your name?
The disciple should say: "I am so-and-so Śarmā; I salute you. (201)
One should also give a staff made of bamboo, or one produced from the Khadira tree, or one produced from the Palāśa tree, or one produced from a milk-exuding tree, to the child. || 197 ||

"Āpo hi ṣṭhā," and so forth. Then, with the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā" enclosed and joined at the beginning and end by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* through *māyā*, one should [sprinkle] water from *kuśa* grass upon him who holds a staff and wears the sacred thread (*upavītin*). That is, he holds a staff and possesses the sacred thread.
Having consecrated the child by repeating [the mantra] three times, he should thereafter fill the child's joined palms with water or other liquids. || 198 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadañjalim" (that añjali): the preceptor should cause the young *brahmacārī*, who is offering that *añjali* to Dineśa—that is, to Sūrya—to behold Bhāskara with the mantra "taccakṣuḥ. In the word "dātāram," the suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of habitual action (*śīla*). For this very reason—

In the phrase *tadañjaliṃ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which would have been required for the object by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛn*. || 199 ||

"Having seen the sun," and so forth. Thereafter, the supreme teacher, the Guru, should speak to the young boy (*māṇavaka*), who is one by whom the sun has been seen—that is, one for whom the sun has appeared. In response to the expectation of what the teacher should say to the child, he says: "Mine... [and so on].
Regarding the passage beginning with "vrate": "juṣasva" means "accept," that is, "practice" my vow; "śivam" means "auspicious. || 200 ||

Regarding the word "in the heart" (*hṛdi*): the Guru, having recited the mantra beginning with "This is my vow" (*mamavrataṃ*) and ending with "Śiva," and having touched the disciple's heart, should say to that disciple, "Child, what is your name? Thus addressed by the Guru, the disciple replies, "I am [Name] Devaśarman."
One should say, "I salute you. || 201 ||
(263) When the Guru asks, "Whose brahmacārin are you? O Pārvatī, the disciple should answer attentively: "I am your brahmacārin. (202)
"O Agni, you are the student of Indra; you are devoted to your preceptor.
Having spoken thus, the true guru should thereafter entrust him to the gods.
I entrust you to Prajāpati, to Vatsa, to Savitṛ, and to Varuṇa; to the Earth, to the Viśvedevas, and indeed to all the gods. May they all protect you constantly. (204)
Then the young brahmin, having circumambulated the fire by turning to the right and having circumambulated the Guru, should again take his seat.
O Dear One, when the teacher has been touched by the disciple in the fire of emergence,
he should offer five oblations, intending them for the five deities.
"Of whom," and so forth. When the preceptor asks, "O child, whose student (*brahmacārin*) are you?", the disciple, being attentive and careful, should say, "I am your student. || 202 ||
"Of Indra," and so forth. "O child, you are the religious student (brahmacārī) of Indra;
Agni, the consumer of oblations, shall be your teacher (ācārya), your guru. Having thus addressed the disciple, the true guru should thereafter entrust that disciple to the gods. || 203 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to which deities the Guru should entrust the disciple to, he says: "O child, [I entrust] you to Prajāpati," and so forth.
Then, and so on: thereafter, the young boy (*māṇavaka*), by means of the practice of circumambulation to the right...
Having circumambulated the fire and the Guru, one should again take one's seat. || 205 ||
Regarding the word "guru": the preceptor, having been touched by the disciple, should offer five oblations into the fire known as Samudbhava, while dedicating them to the five deities. || 206 ||
Prajāpati, as well as Śakra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and likewise Śiva. || 207 ||
One should offer oblations with [the names] beginning with "māyā" (hrīṃ) and ending with the "wife of fire" (svāhā), using their respective names.
This rule is proclaimed for all cases where no specific mantra is mentioned.
Then there were Durgā, Mahālakṣmī, Sundarī, and Bhuvaneśvarī; the ten guardians of the directions beginning with Indra, and the nine planets beginning with the Sun.
Having offered oblations to each by name and having covered the boy with a garment, the wise man should question the young student who takes pride in his celibate life:
"O son, what is your stage of life? Tell me, what is in your mind? (210)
Then the disciple, with full attention, having taken hold of the two feet of the Guru, should say:
"By means of the instruction in the knowledge of Brahman, please make me an inhabitant of the [spiritual] stage. (211)

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which five deities one should offer the five oblations (āhuti) with reference to, the author indicates those five deities in the second half-verse beginning with "Prajāpati. || 207 ||
Now, with which mantras should one offer oblations intended for the five deities?

To this he says "māyādi" and so forth. Intending the five deities beginning with Prajāpati, one should [offer] with their respective names preceded by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, starting from *māyā* (the *hrīṃ*) up to *vahnijāyā* (the *svāhā*).

One should offer oblations. Now, one might ask: must the oblation be performed with the names of each deity, beginning with *māyā* and ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), specifically intended for the five deities starting with Prajāpati, or may it also be intended for other deities? To this, he says:
"In a mantra that has not been stated," and so forth. || 208 ||

"Then," and so forth. Then, having offered oblations to these [goddesses] such as Durgā and Mahālakṣmī by reciting their individual names beginning with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, and having covered the boy with a garment (*vāsas*), [the father asks]: "O son, what is your hermitage? Or what is in your mind?"
"What is it? Tell me," thus should the wise and intelligent teacher ask the young student who takes pride in his religious studentship (brahmacarya). || 209 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "tataḥ" and so forth: thereafter, the disciple, being attentive and vigilant, should take hold of the two feet of the guru and pray: "O Guru, by means of the instruction in the knowledge of Brahman—that is, through the instruction in the Sāvitrī—may you make me an inhabitant of the [spiritual] stages of life (āśramin). || 211 ||

When the child has thus made this prayer, O Śivā, the Guru, having caused the threefold *tāra*— which consists of all mantras— to be heard in the child’s right ear, and having uttered the three *vyāhṛtis*, should cause the *Sāvitrī* to be heard. (212)
The seer (ṛṣi) is declared to be Sadāśiva; the meter (chandas) is said to be Triṣṭubh;
and the presiding deity (adhiṣṭhātrī) is Sāvitrī, who is employed for the sake of liberation (mokṣa). || 213 ||
First one should utter "tat savituḥ," and after that the word "vareṇyam";
at the end of the word "bhargaḥ," one should say the word "devasya," and then the word "dhīmahi. (214)
Then, O Supreme Goddess, having again uttered the *praṇava*, the Guru should explain the meaning of the *sāvitrī* with the words: "May He who impels our intellects... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.6.4).

"Thus," and so forth. At that time, while the child is being petitioned in this manner, one should [place] the *tāra*, the *praṇava*— which consists of all mantras, has the nature of all mantras, or is the principal of all mantras— three times, i.e., three repetitions, into the right ear of the child.
Having caused [the student] to hear it, and then having uttered the three vyāhṛtis beginning with bhūḥ, the teacher should cause him to hear the Sāvitrī, that is, the Gāyatrī. || 212 ||

Now, he states the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details of the *gāyatrī* with the words beginning "The seer" (*ṛṣiḥ*). For this *gāyatrī*, Sadāśiva is the seer, *triṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*), Sāvitrī is the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātrī devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*). One should offer salutation to Sadāśiva, the seer, on the head; to the *triṣṭubh* meter, on the mouth.
Having performed the *ṛṣinyāsa* with the words, "Salutation to Sāvitrī in the heart; salutation to the presiding deity," the recitation (*japa*) of the Sāvitrī mantra should be performed. || 213 ||

He speaks of the Sāvitrī itself in the first half-verse beginning with "at the outset," and so forth. At the outset, one should say "tat savituḥ"; thereafter, one should utter and extract the word "vareṇyam"; then one should say the word "bhargaḥ";
at the end of that word, one should say the word "devasya"; and at the end of that, one should say the word "dhīmahi."

Then one should say, "May he who impels our intellects. Through the conjunction of all these words, the Sāvitrī mantra arises in this form: "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. At the end of the Sāvitrī, again—
Having uttered the *praṇava* as the syllable *oṃ*, the teacher should explain the meaning of the *Sāvitrī*.
The phrase "the meaning of the *Sāvitrī*" is an elliptical expression that includes the meaning of the *praṇava* and the meaning of the *vyāhṛtis* as well.

By means of the *Tārā* mantra consisting of three syllables, the Supreme Lord is revealed—the God who is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and who is the protector, the destroyer, and the creator. (216)
That god, the soul of the three worlds, remains pervading the three qualities (guṇas);
therefore, Brahman, who consists of the universe, is to be expressed by the three vyāhṛtis.
He who is expressed by the *tāra* (Om) and the *vyāhṛtis*, he alone is to be known through the *Sāvitrī*—the Lord Savitṛ, the creator of the universe, who sports as the world itself. (218)
May we meditate upon that supreme reality, the eternal and all-pervading, which contains within it great splendor and is to be sought by those of self-restraint. 219.
May He who is the effulgent Lord, the witness of all, impel and direct our mind, intellect, and senses toward virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. || 220 ||

First, he explains the meaning of the *praṇava* (Om) and the meaning of the *vyāhṛtis* (Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ) with two verses beginning with "consisting of three syllables," and so forth. He is the *pātā*, the protector of the world;
the *hartā*, its destroyer; and the *saṃsraṣṭā*, its creator—yet he is beyond (*para*) and far removed from *prakṛti*.
Or, that Supreme Lord, the Paramātman, the God who is the substratum of activities such as radiance and so forth—

this Supreme Lord, the God, is propounded and made known by the *Tāra*, which consists of three syllables, namely the *Praṇava* composed of the three letters beginning with 'A'. That God who is propounded by the *Praṇava* is he.

Since the Divine is the self of the three worlds and possesses the nature of the three worlds, and since He abides pervading the three qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest, for that reason Brahman— who consists of the universe and has the universe as His very form— is expressed by the three vyāhṛtis, Bhūr and the others, which denote the three worlds.

Having thus explained the meaning of the *praṇava* and the meaning of the *vyāhṛtis* by means of two [verses], he now explains the meaning of the *sāvitrī* by means of the three verses beginning with "tāra," starting with "tāra" and so forth.
That which is denoted by the *tāra* and the *vyāhṛtis*...

That very Supreme Self is what is expressed by the *Sāvitrī* and is to be known as such. He explains how the Supreme Self alone can be the referent of the *Sāvitrī* with the words "of the one whose form is the world," and so forth. The term "of Savitṛ" is explained as "of the one whose form is the world."
Regarding the word *saṃsraṣṭuḥ*: it is an elaboration of *devasya*, meaning "of the shining, all-pervading Lord. He states the meaning of the word *bharga* as "the great splendor residing within.
He states the meaning of *vareṇyam* as "that which is to be chosen by those who have restrained their selves. Regarding *dhīmahi*...

(O Commentary, p. 267: O Goddess, having thus instructed the disciple in the Brahma-vidyā endowed with its meaning, the true guru should enjoin him to the duties of the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama). || 221 ||
My child, now abandon this attire appropriate for the life of a celibate student;
worship the gods and the ancestors according to the path proclaimed by Śambhu.
Your body has been purified by the instruction in the knowledge of Brahman;
you have attained the stage of a householder, so perform the duties prescribed for that state.
"Let us meditate. He states the meaning of that word as "the supreme truth, all-pervading, and eternal.
The explanation of "who" is "the Lord, the witness of all. The explanation of "of the intellects" is "mind, intellect, and senses. The explanation of "may [He] impel" is...

"One should impel [the person] toward virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). And the explanation of "should impel" is "one should employ. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: [one should employ] that which is most excellent (*vareṇya*) of the Sun—the divine, all-pervading creator of the world, the reality whose nature is the universe—by those who have restrained their selves.
With restrained internal organs, we [seek] that which is to be chosen, to be worshipped— that supreme,
most excellent Truth, which is real, all-pervasive, having the nature of permeating all objects,
eternal, devoid of beginning or end, and the great, internal splendor and light.
Let us meditate; let us contemplate Him who is the Lord, the witness of all,

the observer and director of the auspicious and inauspicious actions of all beings— may He impel our thoughts, that is, our minds, intellects, and senses, toward virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

"One should impel" means one should apply [the mantra]. Here, although a distinction between Savitṛ and Bharga appears from the phrase "the splendor of Savitṛ," nevertheless, it should be understood that in ultimate reality there is indeed non-difference. (218–220)

"Thus," and so forth. O Goddess, having thus instructed the disciple in the Gāyatrī—the Brahma-vidyā endowed with meaning—and having sent him here and there for the purpose of begging alms, the true Guru should engage and direct the disciple toward the duties of the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama). || 221 ||

He describes the initiation of the disciple into the duties of the householder stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*) with the words beginning "brahmacarya": "O child, you must now abandon the attire appropriate for celibacy and proceed by the path proclaimed by Śambhu, according to the way taught by Śambhu."
Worship and duly honor both the gods and the ancestors. || 222 ||

"Brahman," and so forth. O child, by the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, your physical body has become purified. Now that you have entered the stage of a householder, perform the duties prescribed for it. || 223 ||
(268) "Accept these two sacred threads, divine garments and ornaments, the sandals, the parasol, perfumes, garlands, and ointments. (224)
Then [he gave him] ochre-colored garments, a black antelope skin,
a sacred thread, a girdle, a staff, and an alms-bowl.
O Śivā, having offered to the Guru alms obtained through proper conduct, and having put on a pair of pure sacred threads and auspicious garments; 226.
Wearing perfumes and garlands, he should remain silent in the presence of the teacher;
then the guru should say this to the disciple who belongs to the householder stage of life: ||| 227 ||
With your senses conquered and speaking the truth, be devoted to the knowledge of Brahman;
perform the duties of Vedic study and the stages of life according to dharma.
Having thus instructed the twice-born, he [then] [performed the rite] in the fire produced from the ocean,
with the three worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ— preceded by Māyā and ending with the Praṇava.

"Upavīta," and so forth: O child, you should now take two sacred threads (upavītas), two divine garments and ornaments, sandals, an umbrella, and shoes, as well as perfumes, garlands, and ointments. || 224 ||
"Then," and so forth. Having been thus commanded by the Guru, the disciple thereafter [takes] the saffron-colored garment— clothing dyed with *kaṣāya*— along with a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*),
a sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*), a girdle (*mekhalā*), a staff (*daṇḍa*), and an alms-bowl (*bhikṣākaraṇḍaka*).
Having offered the alms-bowl and the alms-food obtained according to custom to the Guru,
and having presented him with a pair of pure sacred threads and put on two auspicious garments,
he, wearing perfumes and garlands, should stand silently in the presence of the preceptor, near the Guru.
Then the Guru should say this to the disciple who is in the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśramin): [225–227]
Now, in response to the inquiry, "What should the teacher say to a disciple who is a householder? he says, "One who has conquered the senses," and so forth. || 228 ||

Having offered the oblation in three ways, the preceptor, performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), O auspicious lady, should bring the rite of the vow to completion. (230)
The nine sacraments beginning with the sprinkling for life (jīvasēka) and ending with the vows (vrata) are derived from the father;
however, O beloved, marriage may be accomplished either through the father or through oneself.
On the day of the wedding, having bathed, performed his daily rites, and being accomplished in his duties,
he should worship the five deities as well as Gaurī and the other Mother-goddesses;
then, having prepared the stream of wealth (vasordhārā), he should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha.
At night, having brought a promised bowl accompanied by song and instrumental music,
he led him to a pavilion of shade and seated him upon an excellent seat.
The donor, facing east, should enter while facing west;
having sipped water (ācamana), he should pronounce blessings and prosperity together with the Brahmins.

"Thus," and so forth. Having instructed— that is, commanded— the twice-born disciple, one who possesses the status of a *dvija*, [the teacher] subsequently [offers oblations] into the fire named Samudbhava, using [mantras] beginning with *hrīṃ* (the seed-syllable of Māyā) and ending with *oṃ* (the *praṇava*), and [the vyāhṛtis] *bhūr bhuvaḥ*.

Having caused the disciple to offer oblations three times with the *svāhākāra* mantra, the preceptor, performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and offering the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), should complete the ritual of the vow, namely the act of donning the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). || 229–231 ||
Now, he describes the ritual procedure for the marriage ceremony with the verses beginning "on the day of the wedding" (vivāhāhni) and so forth. || 232 ||
"At night," and so forth. Then, having brought the bride— who had accepted the proposal and become the chosen bride (*vara*)— accompanied by song and instrumental music,
to the pavilion of shadows at night, he should place her upon an excellent seat or a superior throne, facing Indra (the east).
Having seated the girl facing the east, the giver, turning toward the west, should enter. Seated facing the west, the giver, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), should say:
"In this auspicious marriage rite which is to be performed, may you grant your blessing."

Having said, "Let them speak," he should recite blessings such as "May Indra of great fame grant us well-being," together with the Brahmins. Then, having said, "In this auspicious marriage rite which is to be performed,
may you all declare its success," [he should proceed].

One should ask the excellent question regarding the practitioner and the question regarding the worship; having received the answer to the question from the boon-granting deity, one should worship the deity with water for the feet and other offerings. (235)
One should offer the gift to be given with words;
one should present the water for the feet at the feet, and offer the water of honor (arghya) upon the head. || 236 ||
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) into the mouth, as well as fragrance, garlands, and fine garments;
one should also present divine ornaments, jewels, and a sacred thread (yajñasūtra). || 237 ||
Then, having placed curd, ghee, and honey in a bronze vessel,
one should offer the *madhuparka* with these words and place it in [the guest's] hand.
The bridegroom, having taken the vessel and placed it in his left hand,
[should offer oblations] with the right thumb and ring finger while reciting the mantras prescribed for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings.

Together with them, one should say "May there be success! May there be success! May there be success! and one should explain and cause [them] to recite the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). || 233 || 234 ||
"Excellent," and so forth. Then the donor should ask for permission to give with "Excellent!
May you be seated," and he should ask for permission to perform the worship with "I shall honor you.
Then, having received and accepted the responses from the bridegroom—"Yes, I am seated" and "O, please worship"—he should proceed.
One should worship the bridegroom with water for the feet and other offerings; that is to say, one should present the water for the feet and so forth to the bridegroom. || 235 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which mantra should be used and at which specific parts of the body one should offer the water for the feet (pādya) and other articles, he says: "I offer," and so forth.
With the mantra, "I offer this to you," one should present the substances to be given, such as the water for the feet, to the bridegroom.

Then, with the words beginning "tatas tu" and so forth: then, having placed curd, ghee, and honey in a bronze vessel, he should offer the *madhuparka* into the right hand of the bridegroom with the formula, "I offer this to you. || 238 ||
"Even the bridegroom," and so forth. Even the bridegroom, having taken the vessel of *madhuparka* and placed it—
having set it down— in his left hand, [should offer it] for *prāṇa* with his right thumb and ring finger.
Having smelled that vessel five times with the mantras beginning with "svāhā," one should place it in the northern direction.
Having thus offered the madhuparka, one should again cause the bridegroom to sip water for purification (ācamana). || 240 ||
Having supported the bridegroom’s right knee with durvā grass and unbroken rice grains,
and having remembered Viṣṇu, he should then [utter] "Tatsat" followed by the month, fortnight, and lunar day.
Having observed the auspicious signs, he should choose an excellent bridegroom, [inquiring] about each one's lineage, ancestral invocation, and name, starting from the great-grandfather.

Having recited the names ending in the sixth case up to the father of the bridegroom, one should state the name of the bridegroom in the second case, together with his *gotra*, *pravara*, and personal name. (243)
In the same manner, having mentioned the maiden, the learned man, saying "I choose you for the purpose of giving [her] through the Brāhma marriage," should proclaim, "I choose [you]. (244)
Having smelled the madhuparka five times with the mantras prescribed for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings, he should place that vessel—
the madhuparka vessel— in the north, the northern direction. Thus for the bridegroom.
Having offered the madhuparka, he should again cause [the guest] to sip water for the sake of purification. || 239 || 240 ||
"Durvā," and so forth. Then, having supported the right knee of the bridegroom (the son-in-law),
first recollecting Viṣṇu, then uttering "Tatsat," and then enumerating the causes beginning with the month, [one should proceed] from the bridegroom's great-grandfather.

Having recited the names of the lineage (*gotra*) and the ancestral priests (*pravara*) for each of the three generations— beginning from the great-grandfather and ending with the father, up to the limit of the father—
one should then address the bridegroom, distinguished by those names of lineage and ancestral priests, using the accusative case.

Then, having likewise recited the names of the lineage (*gotra*) and the ancestral sages (*pravara*) of three generations of the girl— beginning with her great-great-grandfather and ending with her father—
in the genitive case, and then having recited the name of the girl, distinguished by those *gotra* and *pravara* names, in the accusative case; thereafter—

Having said, "I shall give you [my daughter] through the Brāhma form of marriage," the learned giver should proclaim, "I choose [you]. Through this conjunction, [the mantra] is: *viṣṇurāpaḥ* / *tatsat* / *oṃ*. Today, in such-and-such month, in such-and-such fortnight, on such-and-such lunar day, while the sun is situated in such-and-such zodiac sign...

On this day, [the sun] being in Bhāskara, the illustrious Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra, the great-grandson of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such pravara,
and the grandson of [the illustrious Amukadevaśarman] of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such pravara...
"I am chosen," the groom should say; then the giver of the bride should speak to the groom, saying, "Having said 'as prescribed,' perform the marriage rite.
The groom should reply to that with, "I shall do so according to my knowledge. (245)
Then, having brought forward the maiden adorned with garments and ornaments,
and having covered her with another cloth, he should place her facing the bridegroom.
Having again honored the groom with garments, ornaments, and other gifts,
he should place the bride’s hand upon the groom’s right hand.
In the midst of that, having offered the five jewels, or indeed fruit and betel,
and having performed worship, he should bestow his daughter upon the learned groom.
The bridegroom is the illustrious Amukadevaśarman, belonging to the [Amuka] gotra and [Amuka] pravara,
the son of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman of the [Amuka] gotra and [Amuka] pravara,
and the grandson of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman.

The great-granddaughter of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such pravaras; the granddaughter of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such pravaras; [the daughter] of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such pravaras...

The formal statement was made as follows: "I choose you to give your daughter, the lady named [Name], of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such pravaras, to me, the son of the illustrious [Name] Devaśarman, according to the Brāhma form of marriage."
With this statement, he should choose the most excellent boon with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
"He is chosen," and so forth: then the groom should say, "I am chosen. Then the giver, having said "as prescribed," should tell the groom, "Perform the marriage rite as prescribed. As prescribed...

The meaning is that one should say to the son-in-law, "Perform the marriage rite. Thereupon, the groom should reply, "I shall perform the marriage rite according to my knowledge. Regarding the phrase "Thereupon" (*tataḥ*) and so forth: after that, [one should present] the maiden adorned with garments and ornaments.
Having brought her from the house while she is covered with another garment, he should place her before the bridegroom. || 246 ||

"Again," and so forth. Then the giver, having again honored the bridegroom with garments, ornaments, and other such gifts, should place—the hand of the girl, that is, her right hand—into the right hand of the bridegroom; he should set it there. || 247 ||

"In the midst of that," and so forth. Then, having placed five jewels, or even just fruits and roots, in the middle of her hand, and having honored his daughter, he should bestow or give her to a wise and learned groom. || 248 ||
As before, one should recount the story of the three persons as well as the account of the cause;
then, aiming for the desire of the self, one should state the boon in the dative case. (249)
He should utter the name of the maiden, ending in the accusative case, while pronouncing her as one who has been honored and adorned, provided with a covering, and having Prajāpati as her deity.
Having said "I give this to you," the giver should say "I bestow it";
the bridegroom should accept by saying "May there be well-being," and the giver should address the bridegroom.
"You must conduct yourself in accordance with dharma, artha, and kāma together with your wife.
Having said "So be it," the groom should recite the praise of Kāma.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what statement the girl is to be offered to the groom, he says "as before" and so forth.
As before— that is, as previously— having performed the narration of the three lineages (*tripuruṣākhyāna*) and the narration of the occasion (*nimittākhyāna*), [he offers] himself.
Then, having mentioned even a desire (*kāma*), he should utter the name of the bridegroom in the dative case;

thereafter, pronouncing the name of the maiden in the accusative case— referring to her as "the maiden" (*kanyā*), with Prajāpati as the deity, and describing her as worshipped, well-adorned, and provided with a covering— he should say, "To you, I [give her]."
Then, saying "I bestow," he should give his daughter. [With the formula: "By this application, may Viṣṇu be pleased; *tatsat*!

Oṃ! Today, in the month of [name], in the fortnight of [name], on the lunar day of [name], when the sun is situated in the zodiac sign of [name], [he], of the [name] lineage, desiring the attainment of his desired goal [named] [name]..."
To the great-grandson of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such pravaras, [namely] the illustrious Amukaśarman;
and of the illustrious Amukadevaśarman, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such pravaras.

To the grandson of the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such lineage (gotra) and such-and-such ancestral line (pravara), the son of the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such ancestral line; to the bridegroom, the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such ancestral line; [and] to the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such ancestral line.

The great-granddaughter of the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such pravara; the granddaughter of the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such pravara;
the daughter of the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such pravara—[I give] her, who has been worshipped and fully adorned.

The meaning is that she should hand over her daughter to the learned groom with the formula: "I give this maiden, Enā, who is clothed, whose deity is Prajāpati, and who is desirous [of union], to you. The groom, having said "May it be well," should accept his wife. Then—
The giver should pronounce a blessing. 249–251.
In response to the expectation of what the giver should say regarding the bridegroom, he says "In dharma," and so forth:
"O son-in-law, you must conduct yourself together with your wife in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma. Thereupon, the bridegroom—
The giver is desire, and the receiver is also desire; he gave me, who am full of desire, to you, who are full of desire.
With desire I accept you; may the desire of both of us be fulfilled. (253)
Then the giver should say to the son-in-law regarding the daughter:
"By the grace of Prajāpati, may your mutual desire be fulfilled;
may it be auspicious; and may you both protect righteousness. (254)
Then, having covered them with a cloth, the giver, amidst auspicious rites,
should cause the bridegroom and the bride to look at each other's auspicious faces.
Then, one should give gold and jewels as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the son-in-law according to one's capacity; one should ensure that the rite is performed without flaw.
Having said "bāḍham," one should recite the hymn to Kāma. "Bāḍham" signifies acceptance; according to Amarasimha, "bāḍham" is used for both "intense" and "a solemn promise. || 252 ||
He speaks specifically in praise of desire: "The giver is desire. Desire becomes the giver; desire itself becomes the receiver.
"Desire has given the desiring woman to desire. O wife, "I receive you through desire; may the desire of us both be fulfilled. (253)
