"Then," and so forth. After that—that is, following the recitation of the praise of Kāma—the giver should speak to the daughter, the son-in-law, and the bridegroom.
To the question of what he should say, he says: "By the grace of Prajāpati," and so on. || 254 ||

"Then," and so forth. Thereupon, the giver, having covered the bride and groom with a cloth, should cause the bride and groom to gaze auspiciously at one another amidst highly auspicious songs, instrumental music, and the like. || 255 ||

"Then," and so forth. Then, for the sake of the completion of this auspicious marriage rite performed today, [I offer] a gift of gold and other items to the bridegroom, [named] Amuka-devaśarman, of the [Amuka] gotra.
With the words, "I bestow these upon you," the giver should present gold, jewels, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the son-in-law according to his capacity. Thereafter, he should resolve:
"May this auspicious marriage rite that has been performed be free from defects. || 256 ||
The bridegroom, together with his wife, whether at night or during the day, should perform the installation of the fire according to the procedure prescribed for the *kuśaṇḍikā* rite. (257)
In this rite, the fire is named Yojaka, and a caru-oblation for Prajāpati is prescribed;
having completed the rites up to the end of the pouring of the stream, the excellent performer should offer five oblations.
Having meditated upon Śiva, Durgā, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) one by one, he should offer oblations, aiming at each individually, into the consecrated fire.
Saying, "I shall take the two hands of my wife," he should grasp her hand, [reciting]: "O fortunate one, I take your hand; be devoted to your elders and husband.
Practice the duties of the householder's life according to dharma as prescribed. (260)
O auspicious lady, the bride should offer eight oblations into the fire with clarified butter provided by her husband and parched grains brought by her brother,
dedicating them to Prajāpati.
Having circumambulated the fire and risen together with his wife,
he should perform the oblation three times over for each pair— namely Durgā and Śiva, Ramā and Viṣṇu, and Brāhmī and Brahmā. 262.

"Let him choose," and so forth; the words "immediately thereafter" are to be understood as the ellipsis. Or even during the day—that is, on the day following that very night—in this marriage ceremony. (257, 258)

Now, in response to the expectation of the question—"With reference to which deities should the bridegroom, together with his wife, offer the five oblations?"—the author says "Śiva," and so forth. || 259 ||

"Of the wife": then, reciting and proclaiming the mantra to be spoken next, "O fortunate one, I take your hand," and so forth, he should grasp the pair of hands of his wife. He states that very mantra beginning with "I take your hand, O fortunate one. || 260 ||

"By ghee," and so forth. O Śivā, then the bride—the wife—should offer four Vedic oblations (vedāhutīḥ) dedicated to Prajāpati, using the ghee provided by her husband and the parched grains (lājāḥ) brought and offered by her brother. || 261 ||

"Having circumambulated," and so forth: Then the groom, together with his bride, having risen and circumambulated the fire, should recite the names of Durgā and Śiva, Ramā and Viṣṇu, and Brāhmī and Brahmā— pairing them two by two— three times each, that is, three rounds.
One should perform the oblation three times; one should do so. || 262 ||
One should perform seven ascents upon a stone circle without reciting mantras;
if this is done at night, one will certainly see Arundhatī along with the women. (263)
Then the excellent [officiant], having returned and sat down properly upon his seat,
should bring the rite to completion with everything from the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation up to the final *pūrṇāhuti*.

The Brāhma marriage is ordained as faultless when contracted with a woman of the same caste (savarṇā) who belongs to a different lineage (gotra) and is not a sapinda relative, in accordance with the family dharma.
She who is to be taken in the Brāhma marriage alone is the true wife and mistress of the household;
without her permission, one should not perform the Brāhma marriage again. (266)
O Goddess of the Family, as long as her offspring or her lineage exists within the family,
the children born of Śiva are not entitled to the inheritance.
The Śaivas and those belonging to their lineage shall receive shares of the wealth, as well as clothing and food according to their means, O Supreme Goddess. (268)
The Śaiva marriage is of two kinds, prescribed for the *kulacakra*:
one is according to the rule of the *cakra*, and the second lasts for the duration of life. (269)

"A stone-circle," and so forth. Then the groom, together with his wife, should perform the seven ascents of the stone-circle and the ascent of the seven circles without mantras—that is, entirely devoid of mantras. If those ascents take place at night, then...
Then, surrounded by women and accompanied by his wife, the bridegroom shall certainly behold Arundhatī. || 263 ||
One should complete the marriage rite; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 264–266 ||
"Of her," and so forth: of that wife who has been taken through the Brāhma form of marriage, regarding her offspring—whether a son or a daughter. || 267 ||
From people who share in wealth. || 268 || 269 ||
At the time of the performance of the *cakra*, the composed hero should perform a marriage with his own attendants and practitioners of *śakti* through mutual desire. (270)
One should announce one's intention to the hosts of Bhairavīs and Vīras:
"May you grant your consent for the Śāmbhava marriage of us two. (271)
Having obtained their permission and having recited the seven-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times, he should prostrate before the supreme Kālikā.
Then, O Śivā, in the presence of the Kaulas, he should say to that lovely woman:
"With a sincere heart and with the feeling of a husband, choose me. (273)
Then, O Goddess, having covered her beloved with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
that faithful Kaula woman should place her hands upon his hands.
Now, he explains the ritual procedure for the marriage of Śambhu with the verses beginning with "cakrānuṣṭhāna":
at the time of the performance of the *cakra*, together with his own attendants who are practitioners of the *śakti*,
by mutual desire— that is, by the longing of the Vīra for Bhairavī and vice versa.
Being composed and attentive, the hero should perform the marriage ceremony. || 270 || 271 ||
"Of them," and so forth.
Having obtained the permission and consent of those hosts of Bhairavīs and Vīras,
and having recited one hundred and eight times the seven-syllable mantra "parameśvari svāhā," O Supreme Goddess...
The hero should prostrate before the supreme and most excellent Kālikā. || 272 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "tata" and so forth: O Śivā Pārvatī, then the Vīra, in the presence—that is, near—the Kaulas, should say to that woman, "O Ramanī, choose me as your husband with a sincere mind, free from deceit (kaitava). || 273 ||

"O Goddess, then that Kaulā, being full of faith, having chosen her beloved— the one dear to her— with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), should place her own two hands upon his hands. || 274 ||
Then the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) should consecrate the couple with this mantra.
At that time, the Kaulas situated within the wheel should respectfully say, "May it be well! (svasti).
May Kālī, Rājarājeśvarī, Tāriṇī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Bagalā, Kamalā, Nityā, and Bhairavī protect you both.
One should consecrate them twelve times with honey or with the water of the *arghya* offering;
then, once they have prostrated, the wise one should cause them to hear the syllable *Vāgbhava* and *Ramā*.
O Kuleśvarī, whatever has been accepted therein must be diligently observed by those two of noble lineage, according to the procedure taught by Śambhu.
In this marriage according to the Śaiva tradition, no consideration of age or caste is required;
by the command of Śambhu, one may marry a woman who is not a sapinda relative and who has lost her husband. (279)

She who has been married according to the Śaiva dharma by means of the determination of the *cakra*—if he desires offspring, he may approach her when she sees her season; however, once the *cakra* has passed, he should abandon her. || 280 ||

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśa) should consecrate that couple—the husband and wife—with the mantra to be described hereafter. At that time, the Kaulas situated within the wheel should say "Svasti! (May there be well-being!), doing so with full reverence. || 275 ||
Now, in response to the expectation of asking by which mantra the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) should consecrate the couple, he says "Rājarājeśvarī," and so forth. || 276 ||

"One should consecrate," and so forth. The Lord of the Mandala (cakreśa), by means of this very mantra, should consecrate the couple twelve times—either with honey, or with wine (madya), or with arghya water—that is, the water for the guest-offering. Then, toward the couple who have prostrated, the wise Lord of the Mandala...
One should cause [the disciple] to hear the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava, namely *aim*, and the seed-syllable of Ramā, namely *śrīm*. || 277 ||
In that regard, concerning the Śāmbhava marriage rite, by those two, the husband and wife.

Regarding the phrase "pariṇītā" and so forth: if a woman has been married according to the *cakra-nirdhāraṇa* (the determination of the *cakra*) within the Śaiva dharma, a hero seeking offspring should abandon her once she has passed beyond the *cakra*, upon seeing her second menstrual period. || 280 ||

(279) A child born from a Śaiva wife through the natural order (anuloma) should be treated like a mother; however, one born through the inverse order (viloma) should be treated according to the common caste rules. || 281 ||
In all ancestral rites (pitṛkarma) for these mixed castes,
the offering of food to the Kaulas is prescribed as their meal.
O Goddess, eating and sexual union—which are dear to humans by their very nature—have been prescribed in the Śaiva dharma for the sake of its summary and for the benefit [of practitioners]. (283)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, by practicing the Śaiva dharma, one becomes the master of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation; it is not otherwise.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Kuśaṇḍikā and the Tenfold Saṃskāras," in the glorious Mahānirvāṇatantra— the supreme among all supreme tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas— within the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva.

Regarding the passage beginning with "śaivabhāryā" (the wife of a Śaiva): offspring born from a woman of a lower caste who is the wife of a Śaiva should perform their duties just like their mother. For example, the offspring born to a Kṣatriya woman—who is a Śaiva wife—from a Brāhmaṇa [should act accordingly].

One should perform the duties of a Kṣatriya; thus, in reverse order of the castes, the offspring born from a Śaiva wife should perform the duties like those of a common caste, that is, like a fifth caste. (281–284)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. The tenth chapter:
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord, the procedure for the *kuśaṇḍikā* and the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have been heard;
O God, please graciously reveal to me the procedure for the *vṛddhiśrāddha*.
O Śaṅkara, [tell me] regarding which specific ritual action and upon which foundations the procedure for the *kuśaṇḍikā* and the *vṛddhiśrāddha* are performed.
"O Maheśāna, tell me truly what is to be done and what is not to be done, for my own pleasure and for the welfare of all living beings. (3)

Śrī Sadāśiva said: O auspicious lady, regarding the ten purificatory rites beginning with the sprinkling of the vital breath (jīva-seka) and ending with marriage, that which is prescribed for each is proclaimed here with its specific details.
That very same task should be performed by men who know reality and desire their own welfare;
hear now, O fair-faced one, what else must be done.
Oṃ! Homage to Brahmā.

Having heard the procedure for the ten types of sacraments (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the sprinkling for life (*jīvaseka*) and ending with marriage (*vivāha*) according to the *Kuśaṇḍikā* rite, [the following is now presented].

Desiring to hear the procedure for the *vṛddhiśrāddha* and the *kuśaṇḍikā*, as well as in which specific rites the *vṛddhiśrāddha* is to be performed and in which it is not, the venerable Goddess said: "The procedure for the *kuśaṇḍikā*, etc.; please explain."
Being thus entreated by the Goddess, Śrī Sadāśiva said:
"From the initiation of life (*jīvaseka*), etc. That is, beginning with the initiation of life. (4–5)
O Dear One, [this applies] to the rites of consecration for ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as for images of deities, houses, gardens, vows, and so forth. (6)
In all cases, the worship of the five deities and the Mothers must be performed,
as well as the Vasordhārā, during the Vṛddhiśrāddha and the Kuśaṇḍikā rites.
In the ritual duties pertaining to women, there is no *vṛddhi-śrāddha*;
for the sake of satisfying the deities and the ancestors, one should simply offer a single meal.
O lotus-faced one, the worship of Devamātrā, the Vasudhārā rite, and the Kuśaṇḍikā ceremony should be performed there with devotion by the officiating priest on behalf of the woman.
A son, grandson, daughter’s son, kinsmen, sister’s son,
son-in-law, officiating priest, and father-in-law are prescribed as substitutes for Śiva.
I shall explain the Vṛddhi-śrāddha according to its true nature; listen, O Kālikā. (11)
Having performed his daily obligatory rites with a well-composed mind,
a person should worship Gaṅgā, Viṣṇu the Lord of Sacrifice, Vāstveśa, and Bhūpati.
"Vāpī" and so forth; "devapratikṛteḥ" means of the image of a deity. || 6 ||
"Of the five deities," such as Brahmā and the others; "of the Mothers," such as Gaurī and the others;
"of women," and so forth. In the word "strīṇām" (of women), the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*.
The ellipsis to be supplied is "one should abandon a woman. (8)

In that regard, regarding the duties to be performed by women, [the ritual] was carried out by the officiating priest (ṛtvij), acting as a substitute for himself, namely the domestic chaplain (purohita). || 9 ||
Now, is it not the case that only the family priest is praised as a representative, or could anyone else also serve? To this he replies with the words "the son," and so forth. || 10 || 11 ||

Now, he describes the procedure for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* with the words beginning "having performed" (*kṛtvā*). Having performed the daily obligatory rite (*nityodita-karma*), a man, facing east and being well-composed— that is, extremely attentive—
[should worship] with the name-mantra preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should worship and honor, in sequence, Gaṅgā, Yajñeśvara, Viṣṇu, Vāstvīśa, Bhūpati, Bhūmisvāmin, and Puruṣa with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 12 ||
Then, while recollecting the *praṇava*, one should fashion the Brahmins out of *darbha* grass, using five, nine, seven, or three [stalks] each. (13)
With *kuśa* grass that is hollow-free, possesses tips, and is turned to the right,
he should honor the twice-born with two and a half coils, having the tips pointing upwards.
In the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, the Pārvaṇa, and other rites, six Brahmins are prescribed;
however, O Śivā, in the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, it is said that there is only one twice-born man.
Then, having placed the Brahmins made of *kuśa* grass in a single vessel and facing them toward the direction of Kubera, the wise man should bathe them with this [mantra].
Hrīḥ! May the goddesses be auspicious for our desired welfare; may they be auspicious for our drinking;
may they flow toward us with peace and prosperity. 17.
Then, one should worship the kusha grass and the brahmins with fragrances and flowers.
"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, while recollecting the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), the person should fashion—that is, construct—the Brahmins made of *darbha* grass.
He states the procedure for the construction of these *darbha*-Brahmins with the verse beginning "with five," and so on.

With nine, seven, five, or even three blades of *kuśa* grass that are without a hollow interior (i.e., solid), devoid of a central core, with their tips intact, and pointing upwards— arranged in a clockwise direction by winding them two and a half times— one should [place] the *dvijas*.
One should compose [the hymns] for the Brahmins. || 13 || 14 ||
Now, in response to the expectation of how many Brāhmaṇas made of Darbha grass are to be imagined, he says: "In the Vṛddhi-śrāddha," and so forth. || 15 ||

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, the wise performer of the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, having placed the *kuśa*-grass Brahmins in a single vessel or bowl facing north (toward the direction of Kubera), should bathe them with the mantra to be recited hereafter. || 16 ||
He states the mantra itself for the purpose of bathing the brahmin made of kuśa grass: "Hrīḥ! Śannaḥ," and so forth. || 17 ||

Then, with the words "tatastu" and so forth: thereafter, the wise one should worship the *kuśa*-made Brahmins (*brāhmaṇas*) with scents and flowers using their name-mantras (*nāma-mantra*), beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *namaḥ*, in pairs on the west and the south respectively. (p. 283)
One should place six bowls containing darbha grass, together with tulasī and sesame seeds.
In two vessels in the west and four vessels in the south,
he should seat six Brahmins facing east and facing north respectively.
Know, O Pārvatī, that the side of the gods is in the west; the two sides of the father and the maternal grandfather are in the south and the north, respectively.

O fair-faced one, in the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha performed for auspicious occasions, the Nāndīmukha ancestors and Nāndīmukha mothers, as well as the maternal grandfathers and so forth, and the maternal grandmothers and so forth, should likewise be mentioned by name.

"In the west," and so forth. Then the wise practitioner of the rite should, in due order, place pairs of vessels in the west and the south; these should be accompanied by *darbha* grass and *kuśa*, and joined with *tulasī* and sesame seeds—six vessels in total. || 19 ||

"In two vessels," and so forth. Then, in the two vessels placed in the western direction and the four vessels placed in the south (the southern direction), one should [place] those made of *kuśa* grass, facing east and facing north, respectively.
He should cause six Brahmins to be seated.

"Daivapakṣam," and so forth: O Pārvatī, know—that is, understand—that the divine side (*daivapakṣa*) is in the western direction. But on the right—meaning respectively in the left and right portions of the south—you should know the two sides of the father and the maternal grandfather as well.

"Those with joyful faces (nāndīmukha)," and so forth. O Goddess of beautiful countenance, in the *śrāddha* known as the *ābhyudayika*, the ancestors—the father and others—are to be designated as "those with joyful faces" (*nāndīmukha*), and the mothers—the mother and others—as "those with joyful faces" (*nāndīmukhī*); they are to be mentioned and invoked in this manner. Thus...
The maternal grandfathers and others, as well as the maternal grandmothers and others, should also be mentioned as being "nāndīmukha" (joyful-faced). || 22 ||
Facing north with a clockwise rotation, one should perform rites for the gods;
facing south with a counter-clockwise rotation, one should accomplish rites for the ancestors. (23)
O Śivā, one should perform all rites according to the sequence beginning with the deities;
if one bypasses the Mothers and their Mothers, that Śrāddha becomes fruitless.
Facing north (toward Kubera), one should formulate the formula for the rite for the gods;
facing south, one should formulate the formula for the rite for the ancestors and likewise for the maternal ancestors.
In that regard, first listen to the formula for the side of the gods, O lady of pure smiles. (25)
Having first mentioned the signs such as time and so forth,
and thereafter having stated [the purpose] for the success of each respective rite, the best of practitioners— || 26 ||

"By turning to the right," and so forth: by turning to the right, facing north—that is, with his face toward the north—one should perform or carry out divine rites (*daivakarma*). By turning to the left, facing south—that is, with his face toward the south—one should accomplish the ancestral rites (*pitṛkarma*). || 23 ||

"Everything," and so forth. O Śivā, one should perform all ritual action precisely according to the sequence beginning with the divine (daiva). Now, one might ask: what fault is there in performing rites for the ancestors (pitṛ) by turning toward the south and facing southward? To this, he says "by transgressing," and so forth.

If one omits the mothers of one's mother—the mother’s father and so forth—that śrāddha becomes fruitless. The phrase "the mothers of one's mother" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes the father of one's mother and others as well. || 24 ||

"Facing Kaubera," and so forth: having turned toward Kaubera—that is, facing north—one should formulate and compose the words of permission for the divine side (daivapakṣa). Having turned toward Yama—that is, facing south—one [should do so] for the ancestral side (pitryapakṣa) and also for the maternal grandfather's side.
One should formulate the sentence of authorization.

He states that very sentence of authorization which is to be formulated on behalf of the divine party by means of the words beginning with "kālādīni" and so forth. First, having enumerated the causal factors such as time and the rest,
and subsequently having stated [the purpose] for the success of each respective rite, the most excellent practitioner—

Having first uttered the names of the lineages (*gotra*), one should proclaim the name in the genitive case for the three ancestors beginning with the father, likewise for the three beginning with the mother, and similarly for the three beginning with the maternal grandfather and the three beginning with the maternal grandmother. Then—

One should utter and pronounce the word "viśveṣāṃ devānām" (of all the gods). Thereafter, one should utter the word "śrāddha. [Then for] the three beginning with the father, and likewise for the three beginning with the mother: (p. 285) [one should utter their names].
And also for one's maternal grandfathers, maternal grandmothers, and so forth, O beloved.
One should pronounce the name ending in the genitive case, preceded by the recitation of the lineage (gotra);
then one should utter the word "śrāddham" for all the Viśvedevas.
"After the two Kuśas have been fashioned, I shall also act as their wife;
O Supreme Lord, I shall do so"—this was the statement of her request for permission. (29)
O Pārvatī, having set aside all the gods,
permission is proclaimed for the paternal side as well as for the maternal grandfather's side.
Afterwards, one should also utter "I am" regarding the two Brahmins fashioned from *kuśa* grass. Then, one should utter "I shall perform. By joining all the words together: *Viṣṇur oṃ tat sat. Oṃ.
Today, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight, on such-and-such a lunar day, for the sake of the prosperity of such-and-such a rite.*

To the Nāndīmukha ancestors— father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, named so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so Devaśarman, belonging to such-and-such gotra; and to the Nāndīmukha female ancestors belonging to such-and-such gotra.

And for [the names] of my mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother, such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such, the goddesses of such-and-such lineage, who are Nāndīmukha; and for my maternal grandfather,
maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather, such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such.
And for the non-god-like [ancestors] of such-and-such lineage, the Nāndīmukha maternal grandmothers,
great-grandmothers, and great-great-grandmothers, named so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so,
and for the goddesses and all the Viśvedevas, this is the *ābhyudayika* [offering].
The statement "I shall perform the *śrāddha* for two Brahmins made of *kuśa* grass" arose.
O Supreme Goddess, regarding the divine side (*daivapakṣa*), this very [statement] is declared to be the formula of permission.
As for the formula of permission regarding the paternal side (*pitṛpakṣa*) and the maternal grandfather's side (*mātāmahapakṣa*)...

He states that which is to be formulated with the words beginning with "viśvān" and so forth: O Pārvatī, in the case of the paternal side as well as in the case of the maternal grandfather's side, it is proclaimed that permission is granted by setting aside the Viśvedevas;
thus the formula for permission is declared. This is the formula for permission in the case of the paternal side.

Just as: Oṃ! Today, in the month of [name], in the fortnight of [name], on the lunar day of [name], for the sake of the prosperity of such-and-such rites, [for the sake of] those of [such-and-such] lineage, the Nāndīmukhas...
Of my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, named so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so Devaśarman,
belonging to such-and-such gotras, who are Nāndīmukha; and of my mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, named so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so, who are goddesses.
"I shall perform the *abhyudayika* śrāddha for two Brahmins made of *kuśa* grass.
In the same way, this formula of authorization should be formulated for the maternal grandfather's side as well. (30)
Then, O Śivā, one should recite the Gāyatrī, the knowledge of Brahman, ten times.
"Salutations to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis;
may Puṣṭi and Svāhā always be present. (32)
Having recited this three times, the excellent practitioner should take water in his hand and purify the śrāddha materials with the mantra "vaḥ hūṃ phaṭ."

O Mistress of the Family, having placed a single vessel in the southeast and having recited the mantra for the destruction of demons and the nectar: "Perform protection for my sacrifice," one should place [the offering] in that vessel together with a tulasī leaf.
O Goddess, having placed water before the deities and others in the proper order, the wise man,
after giving a mouthful of water to the Brahmins, should offer them seats of Kuśa grass.
Then, immediately after the formulation of the sentence of permission. || 31 || 32 ||

"Having recited this," and so forth: having recited three times— three rounds— the mantra beginning with "devatābhyaḥ" and ending with "bhavantu," then the excellent performer of the śrāddha, taking water in his hand, [should recite] the mantra "vaḥ hūṃ phaṭ."
One should purify the materials for the śrāddha rite. || 33 ||

"In the southeast," and so forth. Then, having placed one vessel in the southeastern direction, he should first consecrate it with the *rakṣoghna* (demon-destroying) nectar, and then say, "Protect my sacrifice for me. By way of application: "You are the demon-destroying nectar; [protect] mine."

"Perform the protection of the sacrifice"— thus the mantra was produced. Having spoken this mantra and having placed water mixed with *tulasī* and barley in that vessel established in the south-eastern direction, the wise performer of the *śrāddha* then [proceeded].

Having given a mouthful of water to the Brahmins made of *kuśa* grass according to the sequence beginning with the gods (*daivādi*), one should address the Viśvedevas with the formula: "O Viśvedevas, this seat is for you; salutations. Then [one addresses] the ancestors: "O [Name], of such-and-such gotra, Nāndīmukha father, [Name] Devaśarman, of such-and-such gotra..."

"O Nāndīmukha grandfather, [Name] Devaśarman, of such-and-such gotra; O Nāndīmukha great-grandfather, [Name] Devaśarman, of such-and-such gotra—this seat is for you, svadhā! With this formula, [one offers] to the ancestors and others, and to the mother: "O Nāndīmukhī mother, [Name] Devī, of such-and-such gotra..."
O auspicious one, the wise man should then invoke Nāndīmukhī, Grandmother [Name], O Goddess, as well as the Viśvedevas and the Pitṛs,
the Mothers, the maternal grandfathers, and likewise the maternal grandmothers. (36)
Having first invoked them, one should worship the Viśvedevas;
thereafter, one should sacrifice to the three paternal ancestors, the three maternal ancestors, and the three maternal grandfathers.
O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukhī great-grandmother, O Goddess [Name], this seat is for you;

*svadhā*. With this formula, [the offering] is made to the mother and others: O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha maternal grandfather, [Name] Devaśarman; O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha...

"O great paternal great-grandfather, Devaśarman of such-and-such a lineage, Nāndīmukha; O paternal great-grandmother, Devaśarman of such-and-such a lineage, Nāndīmukha—this seat is for you, Svadhā!"—with this formula, [one offers] to the maternal grandfather and others, [saying]: "O maternal grandmother of such-and-such a lineage, Nāndīmukhī..."

"O Goddess [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukhī; O Grandmother [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukhī; O Great-Grandmother [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukhī; this seat is for you—svadhā. With these words, one should offer a seat of *kuśa* grass even to the grandmothers and the others. || 34 || 35 ||

"Then," and so forth. Thereupon, the learned performer of the *śrāddha* [invokes] the Viśvedevas with the formula: "Come here, stay here, be present here, accept my worship!"—and likewise the Viśvedevas, those of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), the *nāndīmukha* ancestors: father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.

"O Devaśarman, [son of] such-and-such and such-and-such, come here, stay here, be present here; accept my worship"— with these words [he addresses] the ancestors, beginning with the father, as well as those of such-and-such lineage (gotra), the Nāndīmukhīs, namely the mother,
paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother, [addressing them as] such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such goddesses.

"Come here, stay here, be present here, accept my worship"— with these words, [he addresses] the Mothers, as well as the maternal grandfather and others, specifically: [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha maternal grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather.
"O such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such Devaśarman, come here, stay here, be present here,
and accept my worship"— with these words [he addresses] the maternal grandfathers (mātāmaha) and others, such as the maternal great-grandfathers,
who belong to such-and-such gotra and are Nāndīmukhas.

With the formula, "O Mother, Grandmother, and Great-Grandmother, [named] so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so, O Goddesses, come here, stay here, be present here, and accept my worship," he should invoke the Mothers— the Mother, Grandmother, and so forth— upon seats of kusha grass. || 36 ||

"Having invoked," and so forth. Having thus invoked the Viśvedevas and the others, one should first offer the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and so on, along with incense, lamps, and garments, using the formula: "O Viśvedevas, these [offerings]—the water for the feet, the arghya, the ācamana, etc.—are for you; obeisance."

O fair-faced Śivā, having worshipped the three maternal grandmothers with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, incense, lamps, and garments, one should perform the inquiry regarding the overturning of the vessels according to the sequence of the deities. (38)
One should fashion a single square mandala by means of illusion;
likewise, one should fashion two mandalas on each of the two sides as well. (39)
Having set out the vessels upon these [seats] consecrated by the Vāruṇa-sprinkling, the practitioner,
with those [vessels] washed, should serve all the utensils along with the water for drinking and the foods in due order. || 40 ||

One should worship all the gods (*viśvedevāḥ*). Then, with the formula: "O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha ancestors—father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, [Name], [Name], and [Name] Devaśarman—may these perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth be *svadhā* unto you," one worships the three paternal ancestors.

In the same manner, one should offer to the three maternal ancestors—the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother—belonging to such-and-such gotra and named such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such goddesses, with the formula: "Obeisance to you; may these water for the feet and other offerings be *svadhā*. This is done using the prescribed ritual formulation.

One should worship— that is, honor— with water for the feet and other offerings the three maternal grandfathers by means of the prescribed formula, and likewise the three maternal grandmothers by means of the formulated formula, in due order. O Śivā of beautiful countenance,
having thus worshipped the Viśvedevas and the others, one should then proceed according to the divine order, that is, starting from the side of the gods.
Thinking, "I shall cause the vessels to fall," he should pose the question regarding the falling of the vessels to the Brāhmaṇa. || 37 || 38 ||

"Maṇḍalam" and so forth. Then, having received from the Brāhmaṇa the command "O, cause [it] to fall," one should subsequently, on the side of the deities (*daivapakṣe*), fashion a single square (*caturasraka*) four-cornered mandala by means of the *māyā* seed-syllable *hrīḥ*. This applies to both sides as well.
Likewise for the paternal and maternal grandfathers' sides, one should draw two mandalas each in the four corners using the seed-syllable HRĪḤ. || 39 ||

"Vāruṇa," and so forth. Then the practitioner, having arranged and placed the vessels in sequence upon these mandalas which have been sprinkled with water and consecrated by the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, [should fill] those vessels washed with that same seed-syllable *vaṃ* with all the ritual implements.
One should serve the foods, along with the drinking water intended for sipping and the water for drinking, in sequence, following the order beginning with the deities. || 40 ||
Then, having offered honey and barley, and having sprinkled all the foods with the mantras *hrāḥ*, *hrūḥ*, and *phaṭ*, [he should offer them] to the Viśvedevas as well as to the ancestors. (41)
Having mentioned his mothers, maternal grandfathers, and maternal grandmothers, the knower of reality should offer salutation to Goddess Gāyatrī and recite [the mantra] three times for the deities.
After that, one should ask questions regarding the remaining rice-ball and the piṇḍa.

"Then," and so forth. Thereafter, having placed honey and barley-grains upon the foods, the knower of reality (tattvavid), having consecrated and sprinkled all the foods with the mantras *hrāḥ*, *hrūḥ*, and *phaṭ*, [should offer them] to the Viśvedevas, as well as to the ancestors (pitṛs) beginning with the father, and likewise to the mothers beginning with the mother.

Having mentioned and named the maternal grandfathers, such as the maternal grandfather and so forth, as well as the maternal grandmothers, such as the maternal grandmother and so forth, and having offered all the foods to the Viśvedevas and the others, [one says] "O Viśvedevas..."

With the formula, "This food, together with water for drinking, honey, barley, and all necessary utensils, is offered as *namaḥ* to you," [he offers] to the Viśvedevas and to the Nāndīmukha ancestors— the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, named so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so Devaśarman, belonging to such-and-such a *gotra*.

Accompanied by water for drinking, honey, barley, and all necessary utensils, [one offers] this food with the formula "May it be savory for you" (svadheti) to the ancestors and others, namely: the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother of such-and-such gotra, the Nāndīmukhīs, O Goddesses, named so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so.

"May this food, accompanied by water for drinking, honey, barley, and all necessary utensils, be *svadhā* to you"— with these words, [he offers] to the mother and others, saying: "O [Name], of such-and-such gotra, Nāndīmukha mother, maternal great-grandmother, and maternal great-great-grandmother."
"O Devaśarman, [son of] such-and-such,

such-and-such, and such-and-such, may this food— accompanied by water for drinking, honey, barley, and all necessary utensils— be *svadhā* to you," with these words, [the offering is made] to the mother and others, who belong to the [such-and-such] *gotra* and are *nāndīmukhī*.

With the formula, "O Goddesses— [Name], [Name], and [Name]— the maternal grandmother, the great-grandmother, and the great-great-grandmother; may this food, accompanied by water for drinking, honey, barley, and all necessary utensils,
be *svadhā* unto you," he offers the food along with the utensils to the maternal grandmothers and the others as well.

Having offered [the portions] in sequence, one should recite the goddess Gāyatrī ten times. Then, one should recite three times the mantra beginning with "devatābhyaḥ" and ending with "bhavantu. O first [wife], thereafter [one should ask]: "There is this remaining food; where should it be given? and [declare]: "I shall perform the offering of the piṇḍas."
One should pose questions regarding the remaining food and the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the Brahmin. (41–43)

O Dear One, having received the response from the twice-born, one should fashion twelve *piṇḍas* resembling the fruit of the *mālūra* tree using the remaining unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and other materials. (44)
But one should fashion another single pinda equal to that, O Ambika;
one should spread darbha grass mixed with barley upon a mandala in the southwest (Nairṛta) direction.

Those in my family for whom the funeral rice-offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives, those who were consumed by fire, and those who were killed by serpents or tigers; [may they all attain peace].
May those who were my kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and those who were my kinsmen in another birth, attain inexhaustible satisfaction through the funeral rice-balls and water offered by me. (47)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having offered the *piṇḍa* to those who have no *piṇḍa* with the two mantras,
and having washed his hands and sipped water (*ācānta*), he should then mutter the *Sāvitrī*.
Having recited [the mantra] three times for the deities, he should then arrange the mandalas.

"By the remnants of what has been given," and so forth. Thereafter, having received the response from the twice-born, "Let it be given to those you desire; do so," he [should fashion] objects resembling the wood-apple fruit (*bilva*) out of the *akṣata* grains and other materials remaining after what has been given.
One should fashion twelve pindas equal in size to bilva fruits.

"Anyat tu," and so forth: then, one should fashion another single *piṇḍa* (ball of food), equal to those [others] and like a *bilva* fruit. Then, in the southwest corner (*nairṛta*), upon a prepared square mandala, [one should place] *darbha* grass mixed with barley.
One should spread out and cover [the ground] with *kuśa* grass. || 45 ||

"Having given," and so forth: with these two mantras beginning with "O you who are worshipped by the gods, those in my lineage... and ending with "...may they attain imperishable satisfaction," [the offering] is made from the *piṇḍas*—or even from those devoid of *piṇḍas*—in the south-west corner (nairṛtakoṇa) which has been prepared.
Having offered the thirteenth ball of rice— prepared after the twelve previously arranged balls— upon the darbha grass covering the square mandala,
he should wash his hands; then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he remains with his mouth cleansed.
Having recited the Sāvitrī Gāyatrī twelve times and having recited the mantra "devatābhyaḥ" three times, he should arrange the mandalas. || 46–48 ||

O Goddess, in front of the vessel containing the remnants, the wise practitioner should, according to the previously mentioned procedure, draw two mandalas each, starting from the ancestors in due order. (49)
Having sprinkled [the ground] with the previous mantra, the skillful one should spread kuśa grass upon it;
having sprinkled the darbha blades with air in the auspicious manner of the ancestral darbhas,
he should offer three balls of rice each at the top, the root, and the middle.
O Maheśvarī, having addressed each one by name individually,
one should offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) mixed with barley and honey along with the *svadhā* invocation.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what rite, in what place, or how many mandalas should be fashioned, he says "ucchiṣṭa" and so forth: O Goddess,
the wise and learned performer of the śrāddha [should fashion them] from the ancestors according to the previously mentioned rite.
Gradually, one should fashion two square mandalas in front of each of the vessels containing the remnants. || 49 ||

"By the previous mantra," and so forth. O Śivā, then, having sprinkled and consecrated the mandalas with the previous mantra in the form of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, the performer of the *śrāddha*, being accomplished and discerning, should spread *kuśa* grass upon those mandalas. Then, by means of the wind [mantra], *yaṃ*.

Having sprinkled the *darbha* grass with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and consecrated it, one should place three [stalks] each for the fathers and so forth, the mothers and so forth, the maternal grandfathers and so forth, and the maternal grandmothers and so forth, in order, at the root, the middle, and the top of the *pitṛ-darbha* grass.
One should offer and give the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa). || 50 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to by which specific words the *piṇḍas* should be offered to the father and the others, he says: "By means of the address," and so forth. O Maheśvarī, having uttered the name of each of the ancestors individually, distinguished by the vocative case—the form used for addressing—[one should offer them].

One should offer a *piṇḍa* mixed with honey and barley, joined with honey and barley, accompanied by the exclamation *svadhā*. With the formula: "O Father, of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha, Amukadevaśarman, this *piṇḍa* mixed with honey and barley is for you; *svadhā*," one should offer it at the base of the *darbha* grass to the father.

"O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha grandfather, [Name] Devaśarman, this ball of rice mixed with honey and barley is for you; svadhā!"—with these words, [he offers it] into the middle of the *darbha* grass for the grandfather.
"O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha great-grandfather, [Name] Devaśarman, this..."

Having scattered the remnants of the rice-ball at the end of the ball-offering for the great-grandfather— [addressing him] by his [gotra] name, O [Name], with the formula "This rice-ball, joined with honey and barley, is for you; Svadhā!"— over the upper portion of the *darbha* grass, he [scatters] the remnants of the balls for those who partake of the smears.
One should gratify [the deity] with an application of oil; this is the rule for the rites dedicated to a single ancestor (naikoddiṣṭa). || 52 ||
For the sake of satisfying the deities and the ancestors, one should recite the Sāvitrī mantra ten times;
having recited it three times for the deities, one should then worship the rice-balls (piṇḍas).

With the formula, "O [Name], belonging to the [Gotra] lineage, O Nāndīmukhī mother, O [Name] goddess; this ball of rice (piṇḍa) accompanied by honey and barley is for you; svadhā!"—one offers it at the root of the *darbha* grass to the mother. With the formula, "O [Name], belonging to the [Gotra] lineage, O Nāndīmukhī paternal grandmother, O [Name] goddess; this ball of rice accompanied by honey and barley is for you; svadhā!"—[one offers it to the paternal grandmother].

In the middle of the *darbha* grass, [one offers] to the paternal grandmother: "O *nāndīmukhī* [grandmother], belonging to the *gotra* of such-and-such, O goddess [name of the great-grandmother], this *piṇḍa* accompanied by honey and barley is for you; *svadhā*! With this formula, [one offers] to the paternal great-grandmother on the tip of the *darbha* grass: "O *nāndīmukha* [great-grandfather], belonging to the *gotra* of such-and-such..."
With this formula, "O maternal grandfather, Amukadevaśarman, this ball of rice (piṇḍa) accompanied by honey and barley is for you;

Svadhā! [he offers it] at the root of the darbha grass to the maternal grandfather, saying: "O [maternal] great-grandfather, of such-and-such gotra, Nāndīmukha, Amukadevaśarman, this [ball of rice] accompanied by honey and barley..."
With the formula "This ball for you, svadhā," he offers it in the middle of the *darbha* grass to the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), saying:

"O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, Nāndīmukha, Great-grandfather [Name] Devaśarman, this ball accompanied by honey and barley is for you, svadhā"; and with the same formula, he offers it on the tip of the *darbha* grass.

"To the great paternal grandmother, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, O Nāndīmukhī; to the maternal grandmother, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, O Goddess, this rice-ball accompanied by honey and barley is for you—svadhā! With these words, [he offers it] at the root of the *darbha* grass to the maternal grandmother, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, O Nāndīmukhī, and to the maternal great-grandmother, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, O Goddess.

With the formula, "This ball of rice mixed with honey and barley is for you, Svadhā," he offers it in the middle of the *darbha* grass to the maternal great-grandmother (*pramātāmaha*). Then, with the sentence, "O [Name] of such-and-such lineage, O Nāndīmukhī, O [Name] Goddess, this ball of rice mixed with honey and barley is for you, Svadhā," he offers it on the tip of the *darbha* grass to the maternal great-great-grandmother (*vṛddhapramātāmaha*).
The meaning is that one should offer the pinda to the great-grandmother (vṛddhapramātāmahī). || 51 ||

"At the end of the *piṇḍas*, etc. means: at the end of the *piṇḍas*, that is, at the conclusion of the offering of the *piṇḍas*, having scattered—that is, having strewn—the remains of the *piṇḍas* all around the *piṇḍas* with the formula "May the ancestors who partake of the smearing be pleased," [he offers] with the hand-smearing, that is, with the food adhering to the hand, to those who partake of the smearing, beginning with the fourth ancestor.
One should gratify the ancestors. This rule applies to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites; however, this procedure for gratifying the ancestors who partake of the scrapings does not exist there.

"Devatā" and so forth: Then, for the sake of satisfying the deities and the ancestors, one should mutter the Sāvitrī-Gāyatrī ten times. Then, having muttered the mantra "To the deities" three times, one should worship the rice-balls (piṇḍas) with perfumes and flowers. || 53 ||
Having kindled incense and a lamp, and having closed both eyes,
the wise one, visualizing the ancestors— who possess divine bodies— consuming the *kavya* offerings at the sacrifice, should bow down while uttering this mantra: 54.
My father is my supreme dharma; my father is my supreme austerity. My father is heaven itself; when he is satisfied, the entire world is satisfied.
Then, taking the remains of the offerings (nirmālya), one should pray for blessings from the ancestors.
O compassionate ancestors, may blessings be bestowed upon me;
may the Vedas and my progeny increase eternally, as may my kinsmen. (57)
May those who give to me increase; may I have abundant food.
May there always be those who ask of me, and may I never have to ask anything of anyone.
Immediately after that, the knower of reality should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the twice-born starting with the one for the gods;
likewise, he should perform the rite of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) during the three fortnights.

"Having kindled," and so forth: then, having kindled incense and a lamp, and having closed both eyes, one should visualize and contemplate the ancestors—who possess divine bodies and are consuming (*aśnataḥ*) the *kavya*, the food for the ancestors, at the sacrifice (*adhvare*); [one should contemplate] this...
Uttering and reciting the mantra that is about to be stated, the wise person should bow down to them; he states that very mantra beginning with "My father," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tataḥ" and so forth: thereafter, having taken up the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering), such as flowers and the like,

the practitioner of the rite (*karmasādhaka*), while reciting the two mantras beginning with "May blessings be granted to me" and ending with "And may I not beg for anything from anyone," [offers] the blessings and desired objects to the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
One should pray and entreat. || 56–58 ||

"Daivāditaḥ," and so forth. Immediately thereafter, reciting the words "O Brahman, forgive me" and "Go to Gayā for the sake of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas)," the practitioner who knows the reality should release the darbha-grass "brāhmaṇas" and the funeral cakes according to the sequence beginning with the divine side (daivapakṣa). In that very same manner...

In all three cases, following the sequence beginning with the divine (daivādika), having recited the Gāyatrī ten times with "Oṃ" and "Tatsat," and having likewise [recited it] five times for the deities,
one should look upon the fire, the sun, and a Brahmin, and with palms joined in reverence, ask this: || 60 ||

Having recited this Śrāddha formula, he should declare, "It has been performed with all its constituent parts. The twice-born should likewise say correctly, "It has been performed with all its constituent parts according to the injunctions. (61)

For the sake of pacifying any deficiency in the constituent parts [of the rite], one should recite the *praṇava* ten times and complete the ritual by means of the "sealing of the absence of defects" (*acchidrābhividhāna*). One should then offer the food from the vessel and the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to a Brāhmaṇa.
In the absence of Brahmins, one should cast [the offerings] into cows, goats, or into water;
this is declared to be the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* performed during the rites of obligatory consecration (*nitya-saṃskāra*).
When a Śrāddha is to be performed on a Parvan day, one should designate it as a Pārvaṇa rite.

Reciting the formula beginning with "Today," etc., one should offer gold and other items according to one's capacity with the words: "I relinquish this gold and so forth as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sake of the establishment of this *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*, to the Brāhmaṇa named Devaśarman of such-and-such a lineage (*gotra*). Thus, one gives gold and the like according to one's means.
One should offer the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 59 ||

"Beginning with 'gāyatrīm' and so forth: then, having recited the Gāyatrī ten times and also having recited the mantra 'devatābhyaḥ' five times, and having looked at the fire and the sun, he, with palms joined in reverence, should ask the Brahmin this. (60)
In response to the expectation of what one should ask the Brahmin, he says "this," and so forth.

Having recited, "This *śrāddha* has become complete with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*)," one should utter it. By way of application, one should ask the Brahmin: "Has this *śrāddha* become complete with all its constituent parts? Then, according to the prescribed rule...
"The twice-born should declare that it has indeed arisen correctly with all its constituent parts. || 61 ||
By means of the formula for making [the rite] flawless, "This śrāddha rite has been performed; may it be flawless," [the performer ensures its perfection]. || 62 || 63 ||

Having thus explained the procedure for the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*, he now states [the following] with the words beginning "In the śrāddha," etc., that by that very same procedure, the *pārvaṇa* and other types of śrāddhas should also be performed, specifically when they are to be performed on a festival day (*parvan*) such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).
In the permissive statements regarding those things that may be optionally performed, one should proclaim—that is, utter—the *śrāddha* as being of the *pārvaṇa* type. || 64 ||
At the consecration of deities and the like, during pilgrimages, and upon entering [a new home], one should perform this Śrāddha according to the Pārvaṇa rite. (65)
In these śrāddha rites, one should not address the ancestors as "nāndīmukha";
rather, in the place of the word "svadhā," one should utter the phrase "namo 'nta puṣṭyāya."
O fair-faced one, among the triad beginning with the father, the wise man should perform the Śrāddha after marking the deceased as being above those who are still living.
While Janaka and the other three are alive, one should avoid performing the Śrāddha;
O Goddess of the gods, when they are pleased, one obtains the fruit of the Śrāddha sacrifice.
O auspicious lady, while the father is living, no one else has the authority to perform a śrāddha;
likewise, there is no authority for a wife to perform a śrāddha for her mother, except for the Nāndīmukha rite.
But in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, O Mistress of the Kaulas, one should not worship the Viśvedevas;
one should formulate the formula of authorization (*anujñāvākya*) by designating only a single [deity]. (70)
A person should offer food and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) facing the south;
in place of barley, sesame seeds should be offered, and everything else is as previously described.

"Devatādīti," and so forth. When a *śrāddha* is to be performed for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of deities and the like, or upon entering on a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), one should declare, "This *śrāddha* is to be done according to the *pārvaṇa* rite," within the permissive formulas (*anujñāvākya*) that are to be employed. || 65 ||

"Regarding these," and so forth: in these *śrāddha* rites, one should not address the *pitṛs* as *nāndīmukhas*. Furthermore, in the mantra "to the deities and to the *pitṛs*," at the end of the word "namas," one should utter the word "svadhāyai" instead of "puṣṭyai. Everything else is to be performed exactly as before.
"Upper realm" means existence in the upper [realms]. || 67 || 68 ||

"Jīvat" and so forth: O auspicious lady, while the father is alive, there is no eligibility for other śrāddhas for the son, the mother, or the wife, without performing the śrāddha [for the father], nor likewise the *nāndīmukha* or *ābhyudayika* śrāddha; such is the grammatical connection. || 69 ||
In the case of an Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha. || 70 || 71 ||
p. 296) This is the specific rule for the *śrāddha* for a *preta*: one should avoid the worship of the Gaṅgā and other deities;
in the speech, the gift, and the offering of food and rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), one should mention the deceased as a *preta*. (72)
That śrāddha which is performed with reference to a single individual is called ekoddiṣṭa;
in the food and the rice-ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased, one should provide fish and meat.
O leader of the family, know that the śrāddha which a man performs on the second day after the end of the period of impurity is indeed the preta-śrāddha. (74)
Except in the cases of miscarriage or stillbirth, a person should observe the period of impurity for those born dead or born alive according to the customs of their family. (75)
O Goddess, for the twice-born, the determination of impurity is ten days; for the Śūdra and commoners, it is twelve days or a fortnight; and for others, it is a month.

Regarding the passage beginning with "pretaśrāddhe" and so forth: in a *śrāddha* for the deceased (*pretaśrāddha*), one should avoid and not perform the worship of Gaṅgā and other deities. In the formula of permission (*anujñāvākya*) and in the offering of the food-ball (*annapiṇḍa*), one should mention—that is, utter—the name of the deceased person as a *preta*. This specific rule is to be understood as applying to the *pretaśrāddha*. || 72 ||
Now, what indeed is this *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha? To that he says: "aiming at one," and so forth. One should "assign" it, meaning one should offer it. || 73 ||
Now, what indeed is this *preta-śrāddha*? To that he says: "At the end of impurity," and so forth.
"At the end of impurity" (*aśaucāntāt*) means that where there is an end (*anta*) to impurity (*aśauca*), that is the "end of impurity"; from that. || 74 ||

Now, as a digression, he explains the rules regarding impurity (*aśauca*) and so forth with the verses beginning with "from miscarriage" (*garbhasrāvāt*). From miscarriage (*garbhasrāva*), from the falling of the fetus (*garbhapāta*), and from a "born-dead" child (*jātamṛta*—one who has been born but died immediately); and other than those, in the case of the other two: the dead-born (*mṛtajāta*) and the born-dead.
A person, being conscious, should observe the period of impurity and perform the rites pertaining to impurity according to the customs of his own family. || 75 ||
"Of the twice-born," and so forth. In the event of the death of a *sapiṇḍa* who has been initiated (*upanīta*), or in the case of the birth of a child,

the calculation of the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for the twice-born— the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas— should be understood as being respectively ten days, twelve days, and a fortnight (*pakṣa*).
However, for a Śūdra and for one of equal caste, the determination of impurity should be understood as lasting one month;
for a Śūdra and one of equal caste, marriage is to be known as the substitute for the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana). || 76 ||

O Śivā, when a kinsman who is not a *sapiṇḍa* has died, a three-night period of impurity is prescribed; likewise, O Śivā, even for one who hears of the death of a *sapiṇḍa* while his own period of impurity has already passed, [the same applies]. (77)
One who is impure shall not be entitled to rites for the gods or for the ancestors, except for the primary worship of one's own lineage and for rites already commenced. (78)
One should cremate mortals older than five years in the cremation ground;
however, O Mistress of the Family, one should not cremate a woman who desires her family lineage along with her husband. (79)
A wife who is of the same nature as you, yet whose form is concealed in this world, may go to hell due to delusion if she ascends the funeral pyre of her husband. (80)
But as for those who worship the Brahma-mantras,
O Kālikā, one should cause them to be carried away, buried, or burned, according to their specific injunctions.
O Mother, death is recommended in a field of merit, at a sacred ford, especially in the presence of the Goddess, or in the vicinity of those of noble lineage.
He who, contemplating the one Truth and forgetting the three worlds, gives up his life-breaths, becomes established in his own true nature. (83)

Regarding the passage beginning with *asapiṇḍa*: when a kinsman who is not a *sapiṇḍa*—that is, a member of one's lineage (*gotra*) other than a *sapiṇḍa*—has died, a period of impurity (*aśauca*) of three nights is prescribed. This applies even to a person who hears of the death (*mṛti*, *maraṇa*) of a *sapiṇḍa* once their own period of impurity has already passed.
Impurity for three nights is prescribed.

"Impure," and so forth. O First One, apart from the worship of the Kula and the karma that has already begun, a person who is impure would not be qualified for any other rite, whether directed toward the gods (daiva) or the ancestors (pitrya), except for the worship of the Kula and the karma that has already begun. || 78 ||
In the cremation ground, the forest of the ancestors. || 79–82 ||
"Vibhāvayan" means contemplating or reflecting upon his own nature, which is the Supreme Self.
Having brought the corpse to the cremation ground and bathed it, one should sprinkle it with ghee, place it facing north, and lay it upon the funeral pyre. (84)

Uttering the name of the deceased preceded by their lineage and ending in the vocative case, and having offered the rice-ball (piṇḍa) into the mouth of the deceased, one should kindle the fire while recollecting the mantra. 85.
O beloved, one should fashion a *piṇḍa* there using prepared food, or rice,
or the flour of barley and wheat, making it the size of an *āmalaka* fruit.
When the sons of the deceased are present, the eldest son has the entitlement to perform the śrāddha;
in his absence, it shall belong to another son or others, according to the order of seniority.
On the final day of the period of impurity, having bathed and become pure,
a man should offer sesame seeds and gold for the sake of liberating the deceased from the state of being a *mṛtapreta*.

"Upon the plane of the hungry ghosts," and so forth: having brought the corpse to the plane of the hungry ghosts, having sprinkled it with ghee—that is, having anointed it with ghee—and having bathed it, one should place that corpse upon the funeral pyre facing north. || 84 ||
"Ending with the vocative," and so forth.

Reciting the name of the deceased (preta), his lineage (gotra), and his family name (nāma)—all ending in the vocative case—one says: "O! Today, O deceased [name], of such-and-such lineage, father [name] Devaśarman, this..."

Uttering the words "This ball of rice is for you, Svadhā," and having offered the ball of rice into the mouth of the deceased while recollecting the fire-mantra *ram*, he should burn the corpse— provided that his eldest son is present.

Regarding the phrase "at the end of the period of impurity" (aśaucānta) and so forth: on the day following the final day of the period of impurity (aśaucāntādvāsarāt), having performed his bath and being pure, a man [should say]: "Today," etc., for the deceased father named Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such lineage (gotra).

With the formula, "For the sake of liberation from the state of a preta, I relinquish sesame seeds together with gold to give to the Brāhmaṇa named Devaśarman of such-and-such a lineage," one should relinquish sesame seeds and gold for the purpose of liberating the deceased from the state of a preta. || 88 ||
A virtuous son should offer land, clothing, vehicles, bowls fashioned from precious substances, and various kinds of food for the sake of the deceased’s rebirth in heaven. (89)
One should offer for the sake of heaven whatever substance is dear to the deceased—be it perfume, garlands, fruit, water, or even a comfortable bed. (90)
Then, having adorned a single bull with a golden [ornament] marked by the sign of the trident, one should release it for the attainment of one's own voice. 91.
Having performed the śrāddha with great devotion according to the procedure prescribed for the śrāddha of a deceased person,
one should feed Kaula Brahmins who possess knowledge of Brahman, even if they are hungry.
A person who is unable to give extensive gifts, by performing a śrāddha according to his own capacity and feeding those who are hungry, may liberate his father from the state of being a preta.
This first *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is the cause of liberation from the state of being a *preta*;
year after year, on the anniversary of death, one should offer food to the one whose life-force has departed.
What is the use of numerous rituals or what use are many rites?
Through the worship of the Kaulika, a human being attains all perfections.
Without fire-offerings, recitations, ancestral rites, or purificatory ceremonies,
the complete accomplishment of all tasks shall come about through a single act of Kaulika worship.

"Oṃ! To the Brāhmaṇa named Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra, for the sake of the deceased father named Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra, for the purpose of [his] attainment of heaven. [The word] "gām" and so forth [is used].

Oṃ! Today, for the sake of the deceased father named Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra, for the purpose of [his] attainment of heaven, [this is offered] to the Brāhmaṇa named Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such gotra.

With the words, "I give this cow," the virtuous son should present a cow for the sake of the deceased's ascent to heaven; in the same manner, by means of appropriately formulated statements, he should also give land and other gifts for the sake of the deceased's ascent to heaven. || 89 || 90 ||
For the attainment of that very state, for the attainment of heaven by the deceased. || 91 || 92 ||
Those who are hungry and famished. || 93 ||

"Ādyā" and so forth: this first *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is the cause for the deceased's liberation from the state of being a *preta*. It should be understood that thereafter, in the *ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha* performed every year on the anniversary of death, one should not utter the word "deceased *preta*" (*mṛtaṃ pretaṃ*).
To the one whose vital breath has departed, to the one from whom life-force has vanished. || 94–96 ||
Starting from the fourth day of the bright fortnight, one should accomplish auspicious rites until the fifth day of the dark fortnight; this is the procedure declared by Śiva. (97)
Even on another prohibited day, one who desires to perform the rite may perform those unavoidable rituals with the permission of the preceptor, the officiating priest, and the guild-leader. || 98 ||

Having worshipped the Primordial Goddess with the five elements (pañcatattva), the Kaulika should perform these acts: the commencement of building a house, its consecration, setting out on a journey, and the wearing of jewels and other ornaments. (99)
Alternatively, the best of practitioners may perform a brief journey;
meditating on the Goddess, reciting the mantra, and bowing, he should proceed according to his capacity. (100)
In all worship of the deities, such as during the autumnal festivals and other occasions,
one should perform meditation and worship according to the procedure prescribed in the respective ritual manuals (kalpa).

One should perform the bali-offering and the fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure prescribed for the initial worship; having performed the Kaula worship and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should bring the rite to completion. || 102 ||
Having fully worshipped Gaṅgā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, and Brahmā, one should worship the deity who is the intended object; this is declared to be the general procedure.
The Kaulika is the supreme Dharma; the Kaulika is the supreme deity; the Kaulika is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha); therefore, one should always worship the Kaula. 104.
Three and a half crore sacred sites and all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, reside within the body of the Kaulika; what, then, could not be attained through the worship of the Kaulika? 105.
The land in which a true Kaula, consecrated by the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), shines forth, is blessed, honored, and most meritorious; that land is sought after even by the gods. (106)
Who on earth can know the power of that practitioner who has received the full consecration, whose self is Śiva, and who is free from merit and sin? (107)
"White," and so forth; "black" means dark. "As far as" (*yāvat*) indicates a limit. (97–108)
Merely in human form, delivering the entire world and teaching the way of worldly conduct, the Kaula wanders upon the earth. (108)
The Śrīdevī said:
O Lord, you have described the greatness of the Kaula who has received the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka). Out of compassion, please cause me to hear the procedure for that initiation. 109.
Śrī Sadāśiva said: This supreme rite was kept secret throughout the three ages;
in former times, men who performed it with a sense of secrecy attained liberation.
In this formidable Kali age, however, when the path of the Kula is revealed,
one should perform the consecration with light either by night or during the day.
One does not become a Kaula merely by the consumption of wine without consecration;
through the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), one becomes a Kaula, a lord of the circle (cakrādhīśa), and a worshiper of the Kula.
On the day preceding the consecration, for the pacification of all obstacles, the Guru should worship Vighneśa with offerings according to his capacity. (113)
Desiring to hear the ritual procedure for the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), the Śrī Devī said:
"Of the Kaula who has been fully consecrated," and so forth. (109)
Being thus entreated, the illustrious Sadāśiva spoke: "The procedure," and so forth.
*Naktaṃ* means at night. || 111 || 112 ||
Now, he explains the procedure for the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) with the words beginning "Therein" (*tatra*), etc.;
[he refers to] Vighneśa as Gaṇapati. || 113 ||
(302) O Dear One, if the Guru should not be authorized for the auspicious and complete consecration, then one who has been consecrated as a Kaula should perform the rite of purification. 114.
The seed-syllable of this [deity] is proclaimed to be the letter *kha* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*). || 115 ||
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Gaṇaka, the metre (chandas) is Nivṛt, and the deity (devatā) is Vighna;
it is employed for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the rite to be performed. || 116 ||
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the root mantra joined with the six long vowels;
then, O Śivā, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate upon Gaṇapati.

"Regarding the words 'the guru' and so forth: if, due to not having been consecrated, the guru were not authorized for the auspicious full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣecana), then a person should accomplish that purificatory rite of the full consecration by means of a consecrated Kaula. || 114 ||

Now, he describes the procedure for the worship of Gaṇapati with the verses beginning with "khāntārṇam": "The letter at the end of 'kha' (khāntārṇa), joined with the bindu (the anusvāra)—that is, the final letter of 'kha', which is the syllable *ga*—is proclaimed to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of this Lord of Obstacles. (115)

Now, in order to prescribe the *ṛṣinyāsa*, he states the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details of the *gaṇapatibījamantra* with the words beginning "the calculator" (*gaṇaka*), etc. For this *gaṇapatibījamantra*, the seer is Gaṇaka, the meter is *nivṛt*, and the deity is Vighna, who is to be performed.

The application is for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the rite of the auspicious full consecration (*śubhapūrṇābhiṣeka*). Homage to Gaṇaka, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head. Homage to the Nivṛt-chandas, on the mouth. Homage to Vighna, the deity (*devatā*), at the heart.
Thus one should perform the Ṛṣinyāsa. || 116 ||

"Six," and so forth. Then, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by applying the six limbs—the thumbs and so forth, as well as the heart and so forth—using the root mantra of Gaṇapati joined with the six long vowels. *Gāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Gīṃ*...

*Tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā* | *Gūṃ madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ* | *Gaiṃ anāmikābhyāṃ hūṃ* | *Gauṃ kaniṣṭhābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ* | *Gaḥ karatalapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with the thumbs. *Gāṃ*.

"Hṛdayāya namaḥ" (Salutation to the heart). "Gīṃ śirase svāhā" (Svāhā to the head). "Gūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ" (Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock). "Gauṃ kavacāya huṃ" (Huṃ to the armor). "Gauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ" (Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes). "Gaḥ karatalapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ phaṭ" (Phaṭ to the palms and backs of the hands). The meaning is that one should thus perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs, beginning with the heart. Then, "Gam... [and so forth].
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the mantra, one should meditate upon Gaṇapati. || 117 ||
Having the luster of vermilion, three-eyed, with a broad belly,
and holding a sword in his lotus-like hands;
Worship Gaṇapati, who holds a noose, a goad, and a lotus in his broad hands, and carries a water-pot filled with wine;
whose crown is illuminated by the crescent moon, whose face is that of a lordly elephant, whose cheeks are moistened by the juice of the citron fruit,
who is adorned with the king of serpents, and who is clothed in red garments and smeared with red unguents.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis):
Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, and Kāmarūpiṇī. (119)
Ugrā, Tejasvatī, Satyā, and Vighnavināśinī—
having worshipped these starting from the east, one should then worship the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā).
He describes the meditation on Gaṇapati with the verse beginning "sindūrābham" (red as vermilion), and so forth.

The syntactical connection is: "O devotees, you should worship Gaṇapati, the Lord of the Gaṇas. Of what nature is Gaṇapati? He is "sindūrābham"—one whose luster or radiance (*ābhā*) is like that of vermilion (*sindūra*), or one in whom it resides.
Of such a nature; furthermore, of what kind? Three-eyed, meaning having three eyes. Furthermore, of what kind?

With a very broad belly, meaning an exceedingly expansive abdomen. Furthermore, of what kind? With lotus-hands—meaning with hands that are like lotuses—holding a sword, a noose, a goad, and the *iṣṭa* (the desired object), namely the noose and the goad.

And bearing a boon, holding it; furthermore, of what kind? One whose trunk, a large and expansive hand, shines with a jar full of *vāruṇī* liquor—that is, a jar filled with the intoxicating drink *vāruṇī* that gleams upon his broad trunk.

Such was he. Furthermore, of what nature was he? One whose crest—the crown upon his head—is illuminated by the crescent moon; that is, one whose diadem is made radiant by the young moon. Furthermore, of what nature was he?
One whose face is like that of the lord of elephants, the king of elephants.

Whose [face] was thus; furthermore, of what kind? With cheeks moistened by the flow of rut from a citron-like [elephant], meaning one whose two temples or cheeks were wet with the stream of ichor (*madapravāha*) like a citron;
furthermore, of what kind? Adorned by the lord of serpents, meaning by the king of snakes.

[He] whose ornaments were bound [on him], or by whom [they were bound], was thus; furthermore, of what kind? "Red garments and body-unguents"—one whose coloring (rāga) of the limbs was red due to red garments, being thus. || 118 ||

"Having meditated thus," and so forth. Having thus meditated upon Gaṇapati, and having worshipped and honored him with mental offerings, one should worship the Śaktis of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) with perfumes, flowers, and so on, using their name-mantras preceded by the Praṇava and ending in "namaḥ. As for those [Śaktis]:
Having meditated again upon Gaṇeśāna and worshipped him with the fivefold offerings (pañcatattva-upacāra),
one should likewise worship Gaṇeśa, the leader of the hosts (gaṇanāyaka), in the four directions surrounding him.
The best of Kaulas should worship Gaṇanātha, who sports with his attendants, as well as Ekadanta, Raktatuṇḍa, Lambodara, and Gajānana. 122.
And Mahodara, Vikaṭa, Dhūmrābha, and Vighnanāśana. || 123 ||
Then, having worshipped the Śaktis headed by Brāhmī and the guardians of the quarters (Dikpālas),
and having fully worshipped their weapons, one should bid farewell to Vighnarāja.
Having thus worshipped Vighneśa,
one should perform the ritual of consecration (adhivāsana) and feed the knowers of Brahman and the Kula practitioners with the five elements (pañcatattva).
One should worship the powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktis). He states this in the single verse beginning with "tībrā ca" and so forth.

Having worshipped these, starting from the east and proceeding in order, as Tībrā and the others, with their respective name-mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should worship Kamalāsana. || 119 || 120 ||
"Again," and so forth. Furthermore, the best of Kaulas, having meditated upon Gaṇeśāna,
[should worship] with the five principles (*pañcatattva*) consisting of wine and the rest— which have been purified by the previously mentioned mantras— as well as other [offerings].

Having worshipped with services such as water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), one should then worship Gaṇeśa and the others in due order in the four directions with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using their respective mantras ending in "namaḥ. Then, following that, [one should worship] with the name-mantras beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending in "namaḥ."
Having worshipped the eight Śaktis beginning with Brāhmī, headed by Brāhmī, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as the world-protectors (dikpālas) beginning with Indra,
and having fully worshipped the weapons of those world-protectors, [one should say]: "O King of Obstacles, forgive me."
One should dismiss Vighnarāja with this verse. || 124 ||
"Thus," and so forth. Having thus fully worshipped Vighneśa, one should perform the preparatory consecration (adhivāsana) according to the procedure to be described hereafter. || 125 ||
Then, on the following day, having bathed and performed the daily obligatory rites,
one should offer gold with sesame seeds for the sake of destroying sins committed since birth,
and also at least one meal for the satisfaction of the Kaulas, O beloved. (126)
Having offered the *arghya* to the Sun, and having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, the planets, and the groups of Mothers, one should perform the pouring of the stream of wealth (*vasudhārā*).
For the sake of the success of his ritual action, he should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha;
then, having gone to the presence of the Guru and prostrated, he should make this request: || 128 ||
Save me, O Lord, beloved of the lotus-like family tradition;
O treasure of compassion, place the shade of your lotus feet upon my head.
"O illustrious one, grant me your command for this auspicious and complete consecration;
by your grace, may I attain the successful accomplishment of this rite without obstacle. (130)
"O child, by the command of Śiva and Śakti, perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
By the decree of Śiva, may the accomplishment consisting of your heart's desire arise."

Having thus received the command of the Guru for the pacification of all calamities, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the attainment of longevity, prosperity, strength, and health. (132)
"Then," and so forth. Then, on the day following that [first] day, having bathed and performed the daily obligatory rites (*nitya-kriyā*), [the performer says]:

"O! Today, I, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and named Śrīmat Amuka-devaśarman, desiring the destruction of all misdeeds committed since birth, [offer this to] Amuka-devaśarman of such-and-such lineage."

With the statement, "I do not give sesame seeds together with gold to a Brāhmaṇa," one should offer sesame seeds and gold for the sake of destroying sins committed throughout one's life.
