Likewise, by means of an imagined formula, one should also offer even a single meal for the satisfaction of the Kaulas.
That which one should pray for is stated by the two verses beginning with "Save me, O Lord" (trāhi nātha).

129. "In this way," and so forth: having thus received the command of the Guru, for the pacification of all calamities and for the attainment of longevity, prosperity, strength, and health—Oṃ! Today, [I,] of such-and-such lineage...
Then, the illustrious Mukadevaśarman, desiring the destruction of all afflictions without exception,
having made his resolve and having honored the Guru with garments, ornaments, and decorations— these being the requisite means accompanied by ritual purity— should choose him as his preceptor. (133)
The Guru [should reside] in a charming house, variegated with red chalk and other pigments, adorned with colorful banners and flags, and beautified by fruits and sprouts. || 134 ||
Adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells, it was illuminated by the moonlight;
it was entirely free from even a trace of darkness due to rows of ghee lamps.
In a place well-perfumed with incense containing camphor and yakṣa-dhūpa, and adorned with fans, chowries, peacock feathers, mirrors, and other ornaments; || 136 ||
One should construct there a raised earthen altar, measuring one and a half cubits in height and four finger-breadths in width, using powders made from unbroken grains.
One should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), thinking: "Desiring long life, prosperity, strength, and health, I shall perform the auspicious and complete consecration ceremony. || 132 ||

Then, "tatastu" and so forth. Then, having made his resolve, the disciple, having worshipped the Guru with garments, ornaments, and decorations accompanied by purificatory substances, as well as meat and other offerings and intoxicants, [says]: "Oṃ! Today, I, of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious..."
With the words, "I, Amukadevaśarman, choose you, the illustrious Amukānandanātha of such-and-such a lineage, as my Guru," one should choose the Guru by offering garments and other gifts. || 133 ||
"Then the Guru," and so forth. Then, in the guru's house,
he should construct— that is, fashion— a clay altar measuring one and a half cubits in height and four finger-breadths in width.

The grammatical connection is with the words contained in the fourth verse. It should be understood that the words beginning with *manohare* ending in the locative case function as adjectives qualifying the house (*gehasya*).
[It is] "adorned with variegated banners and flags" (134).
Adorned with networks of small bells and garlands of clusters of tiny tinkling bells,
[it was scented] with yakṣa-incenses and the resin of the śāla tree, and decorated with barhis— peacock feathers.
Then the venerable Guru should fashion the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is most beautiful with yellow, red, black, white, and dark-green colors. (138)
Having performed the ritual procedure beginning with mental worship according to the rules prescribed for one's own specific Kalpa,
one should purify the five elements (pañcatattva) using the previously mentioned mantra.
Having purified the five elements within the mandala prepared beforehand,
[one should place] either a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even one made of clay.
Having washed it with the seed-mantra of the weapon (astra-bīja) and adorned it with curd and unbroken rice-grains (akṣata),
one should establish it with the seed-mantra of Brahma and mark it with vermilion (sindūra) by means of the Śrī-mantra.
One should fill that causal [element] by means of the root mantra recited three times, using the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, adorned with the nasal bindu.
Alternatively, one should place the nine gems or gold into the middle of the jar with either pure water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) or with ordinary water.

Thereafter, the venerable Guru should fashion and draw upon the altar prepared there a most beautiful *sarvatobhadra* mandala using powders made from unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) of yellow, red, white, pale-white, and dark-blue colors; "dark" meaning blue in color.
With dark, greenish-yellow colors. || 137 || 138 ||
"By their respective [methods]," and so forth.

Then, having performed the ritual actions up to the mental worship—according to the procedure prescribed in the specific *kalpa* for each—one should purify the five principles (*pañcatattva*), such as wine and the rest, with the previously mentioned mantra. || 139 ||

"Having purified," and so forth: having purified the five principles (*pañcatattva*) with the previously mentioned mantra, [one places] upon the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala prepared beforehand that which has been washed and rinsed with the weapon-seed mantra (*astrabīja*) "phaṭ," and smeared with curd and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
One should establish a jar— whether made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay— which has been smeared with curd and unbroken rice,
using the Brahma-bīja, which is the Praṇava (Om), and the Śrī-bīja (Śrīm).
And one should mark it with vermilion. || 140 || 141 ||

"By those beginning with the letter *kṣa*, etc. means: then, by means of the threefold recitation of the root mantra together with the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, adorned with the *bindu* (the nasal *anusvāra*), [one should perform the rite] with wine or with pure water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
The Treasure of Compassion should place a sprout derived from the *panasa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vakula*, or *āmra* trees into his mouth with the *vāgbhava* mantra. (144)
Having recited the *rāmā* and *māyā* mantras, one should place either a clay bowl or a vessel filled with fruits and unbroken rice upon sprouts.
O fair-faced one, one should bind his neck with a pair of garments;
for Śakti they are red, while for Śiva and Viṣṇu white clothing is prescribed. (146)
Having recollected and stabilized the syllables *sthāṃ*, *sthīṃ*, *māyā*, *ramā* within the interior of the jar,
and having cast the five principles (*pañcatattva*) therein, one should arrange the nine vessels.
The vessel for the spear (śakti) should be made of silver, the vessel for the Guru of gold;
the Śrīpātra should be a great conch, while the others may be fashioned from copper.
One should fill that jar with water from another pure source or even with ordinary water; then, one should place the nine gems or gold inside the jar. (142-143)
"Into its mouth" means into the mouth of the jar; "with the Vāgbhava" means with the mantra *aim*. || 144 ||

"Śarāvam," and so forth. Then, having recited the seed-syllables *ramā* (śrīṃ), *māyā* (hrīṃ), and *hrīṃ*, one should place upon the sprouts a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) made of gold or other materials, or even one made of clay or earth, provided it is accompanied by fruit and unbroken rice grains.
One should establish [it]. || 145 ||

Regarding that jar: [one might ask], "Should one tie the neck of the jar with a pair of garments of what color? In response to this expectation, he says: "Red, when [the jar] is capable," and so forth. || 146 ||

"Sthāṃ sthīm," and so forth. Then, having recollected *sthāṃ*, *sthīṃ*, *māyā* (hrīṃ), and *ramā* (śrīṃ), and having recited the mantra "O *sthāṃ*, *sthīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, become firm (*sthirībhava*)," one should deposit the five principles (*pañcatattva*) into the interior of the jar that has been made stable, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should arrange and place nine vessels. || 147 ||
Now, one might ask: "Should one place new vessels made of various substances there?
To this he says, "silver," and so forth. A *mahāśaṅkha* is a human skull. 148–149.
One should avoid vessels made of stone, wood, or metal;
rather, one should provide a vessel according to one's ability for the worship of the Great Goddess. (149)
Having arranged the vessels, one should satisfy the gurus and the Goddess;
thereafter, the wise practitioner should worship the jar filled with nectar.
Having displayed incense and lamps, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings;
having worshipped the deities of the seat, one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). || 151 ||
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and meditated, he should invoke Maheśvarī and worship the desired deity according to his capacity, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
O Śivā, having completed the concluding rites of the fire-oblation, the true Guru should honor the young maidens, the Śaktis, and the practitioners with flowers, sandalwood paste, and garments. (153)
May you Kaulas, who observe the Kula vows, show favor toward my disciple;
may you grant your consent for the consecration of the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
When the Lord of the Maṇḍala asks thus, they should say to that Guru with reverence:
"By the grace of Mahāmāyā and through the power of the Supreme Self, let this disciple become complete for you, being devoted to the highest reality. (155)
"Gurus and the Goddess" is an elliptical expression that includes Ānandabhairava and the others as well;
one should satisfy them with their respective mantras as previously described. || 150 ||

"Having shown," and so forth: then, having shown incense and lamps toward the jar, one should offer—that is, give—the bali-offering for all spirits (sarvabhūtabali) with the previously mentioned mantra. 151–152.

Having performed and accomplished the ritual duties up to the end of the fire-oblation—that is, having completed the rites extending to the conclusion of the *homa*—[one should proceed]. || 153 || 154 ||
Devoted to the supreme reality, he was intent upon the Supreme Brahman.
(310) And the disciple, having had the Guru worship the Goddess, should—after reciting *kāma*, *māyā*, and *ramā* over the worshipped jar—move the pure jar. (156)
Arise, O Brahma-vessel, whose essence is the deity, bestower of perfection! Sprinkled with your water and twigs, may my disciple be devoted to Brahman. 157.
Having thus moved the water-pot facing northward, the Guru, filled with compassion, should perform the consecration with these mantras that are about to be described. (158)

Sadāśiva is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the Śubhapūrṇābhiṣeka; the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, the deity (devatā) is the Primordial One (Ādyā), and the seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be the Praṇava.
Its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the purpose of the Śubhapūrṇābhiṣeka. || 159 ||

"By the disciple," and so forth. Then the Guru, having had the Goddess worshipped by the disciple, and having recited the mantra *kāmaṃ māyāṃ ramāṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* over the worshipped jar, should move the pure jar with the mantra to be mentioned hereafter. || 156 ||
He states the mantra for moving the jar itself, beginning with "uttiṣṭha" (arise), etc. 157.
"Thus," and so forth. Having thus moved the *kalaśa* (vase), the compassionate Guru should consecrate (*abhiṣiñcet*) the disciple, who is facing north, with these mantras to be recited hereafter.
Next, he states the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details for the mantras of the auspicious full consecration (*śubhapūrṇābhiṣeka*).

By the half-verse beginning with "of the auspicious full consecration" (śubhapūrṇābhiṣekasya), [it is stated]: for these mantras of the auspicious full consecration, Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas),
Ādyā Kālī is the deity (devatā), and Oṃ (praṇava) is the seed-syllable (bīja), for the purpose of the auspicious full consecration.

The application (viniyoga): Salutation to Sadāśiva, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh meter (chandas) on the mouth; salutation to the deity Ādyā Kālikā on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable (bīja) Oṃ (praṇava) on the private parts; this is the application for the purpose of the auspicious full consecration.
The placement of the Ṛṣis (ṛṣinyāsa) should be performed. || 159 ||
May the Gurus—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—consecrate you; may the Mothers—Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Bhavānī—consecrate you. (160)
May Ṣoḍaśī, Tāriṇī, Nityā, Svāhā, and Mahiṣamardinī consecrate you with water purified by mantra. || 161 ||
May Jayadurgā, Viśālākṣī, Brahmāṇī, Sarasvatī, Vagalā, Varadā, and Śivā—may these all consecrate you. 162.
May the Śaktis—Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vanamālinī, Indrāṇī, Vāruṇī, and Raudrī—consecrate you. || 163 ||
May Bhairavī, Bhadrakālī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Umā, Kṣamā, Śraddhā, Kānti, Dayā, and Śānti always consecrate you. 164.
May Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahānīlasarasvatī, Ugracaṇḍā, and Pracaṇḍā consecrate you at all times. (165)
May Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, and Rāma Bhārgava consecrate you with water. 166.
May Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhonmatta, Bhayaṅkara, Kapālī, and Bhīṣaṇa consecrate you with water. 167.
May Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, Vipracittā, and Mahogrā always consecrate you. (168)
Then he recites the initiation mantras beginning with "May the gurus initiate you," using the word *tvā* (you). 160–162.
"tvā" means "you. || 163 ||
The genitive case is used for "them" (te) because they are intended to be expressed as the residual factor (śeṣatva) of the action. 164–169.
May Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, Kubera, and Maheśāna—the lords of the directions—sprinkle you with blessings. (169)
May the planets—the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—along with the lunar mansions, consecrate you. (170)
May the lunar mansion, the karana, the yoga, the days of the week, the fortnights, the days, the seasons, the months, and the years always consecrate you. (171)
May the oceans— the salt, sugarcane, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk,
and the final ocean of fresh water— consecrate you with water purified by mantras.
May the Gaṅgā, Yamunā (Sūryasutā), Revā, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī, Sarayū,
Gaṇḍakī, Kuntī, Śvetagaṅgā, and Kauśikī consecrate you with water purified by mantras. 173.
May the great nāgas beginning with Ananta, the winged birds beginning with Suparṇa, the trees beginning with the Kalpavṛkṣa, and the mountains sprinkle you. 174.
May those who move through the netherworld, the earth, and the sky, who bring about well-being,
and who are satisfied by the full consecration, consecrate you with water.
May misfortune, ill-repute, diseases, dejection,
and likewise sorrows perish through this consecration by means of the supreme splendor of Brahman.
Jīva is Bṛhaspati; Sita is Śukra. || 170–172 ||
The daughter of the Sun, the daughter of Sūrya, is Yamunā. || 173 ||
Anantādyāḥ refers to Śeṣa and others; suparṇādyāḥ refers to Garuḍa and others; patatriṇaḥ refers to birds. || 174 || 175 ||
May Alakṣmī, Kālakarṇī, the Ḍākinīs, and the hosts of Yoginīs perish, struck by the consecration with the seed-syllable of Kālī. (177)
May the spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and seizing demons who cause misfortune flee and perish, struck by the seed-syllable of Ramā. || 178 ||
May the defects caused by malevolent magic and those arising from hostile mantras, as well as the defects born of mind, speech, and body, be destroyed through this consecration. (179)
May all calamities perish; may prosperity be firmly established;
through this complete consecration, may all desires be fulfilled. (180)
Having thus sprinkled the practitioner with twenty-one mantras,
the Guru should cause him to hear again the mantra obtained from the mouth of the sacrificial animal (paśu).
Having addressed them by the previously mentioned names and making the practitioners of power aware, the Kaula Guru should impart the narrative ending with Ānandanātha. (182)
Having heard the mantra and worshipped one's own deity within the guru’s yantra,
one should then honor the guru with the fivefold offering of the *pañcatattva*.
Having given cows, land, gold, garments, drinks, and ornaments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, one should worship the Kaulas who are identical with Śiva.
Śucaḥ means sorrows. || 176 || 177 ||
They are the bringers of misfortune and the producers of inauspiciousness. || 178–181 ||

"Previously mentioned," and so forth. Then the Kaulika Guru, while instructing the practitioners of Śakti, should address the disciple by the previously mentioned name and bestow upon him a name ending in Ānandanātha. For example:
"O Amukadevaśarman, from this day forward, you shall be known by the name Amukānandanātha. || 182 || 183 ||

"Go-bhū-hiraṇya," etc. Oṃ! Today, etc., for the sake of making complete the rite of this auspicious full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) that has been performed, [I offer] a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of cattle, land, gold, and so forth, to [the recipient], whose lineage is such-and-such (*amuka-gotra*) and whose name is such-and-such Ānandanātha.

Having performed the Kaula worship, being steadfast, tranquil, and endowed with great humility, one should touch the feet of the venerable Guru, bow with devotion, and make this request: (185) p. 314)
O Śrīnātha, Lord of the worlds, my own Lord, O ocean of compassion!
By bestowing the supreme nectar, fulfill our heart’s desire. (186)
O Kaulas, who are the very embodiment of Śiva before one's eyes, let my command be given:
to this humble and worthy disciple, I shall bestow the supreme nectar.
O Lord of the Wheel, Supreme Sovereign, Sun to the Lotus of the Kaula lineage!
Make this true disciple one who has attained his purpose; grant him the nectar of the Kula.
Having received the command of the Kaulas, he should place the drinking vessel, filled with supreme nectar and purified, into the hand of the disciple. || 189 ||
Having drawn the Goddess into his heart, the Guru should apply a tilaka with the ashes clinging to the *sruva* ladle upon himself, upon his disciple, and upon the *kūrca* of the Kaulas.
Then, distributing the principles of grace (*prasāda*) to those belonging to the *Kaula* tradition,
one should partake of food and drink according to the ritual procedure for the worship of the *cakras*.
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the auspicious and complete consecration, which alone generates the knowledge of Brahman and is the means for attaining the fruit of Śiva-hood. (192)
One should perform the full consecration for nine nights, seven nights, five nights, three nights, or even for a single night. || 193 ||

With the words "I have bestowed," having given to the Guru as much of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as he can afford—such as cows, land, gold, and so forth—he should worship the Kaulas, who are identical with Śiva and whose very nature is Śiva. || 184 ||
One should entreat; one should beg. || 185 ||
That which one should pray for is stated in the single verse beginning with "Śrīnātha" (186–190).
O Mistress of the Kula, five ritual procedures (pañcakalpa) are proclaimed for this consecration (saṃskāra).
During the nine nights, the Sarvatobhadra mandala must be constructed. (194)
O beloved, in the seven-night rite there is a lotus with nine pericarp-segments; in the five-night rite, a five-petaled lotus; and in the three-night and one-night rites, an eight-petaled lotus.
In the Sarvatobhadra mandala, or even in one with nine centers, nine jars should be placed by the practitioners;
or five jars, numbering five, in a mandala with five lotuses.
O Goddess, on an eight-petaled lotus, one jar is prescribed;
one should worship the deities of the limb-enclosures (aṅgāvaraṇa) upon the filaments and other parts. || 197 ||

For the Kaulas who have attained perfection through the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) and whose souls are stainless, the purification of substances is ordained by seeing, touching, or smelling them. (198)
A virtuous person who has taken refuge in the Kaula dharma should be worshipped with great effort by those of the Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Saura, and Gāṇapatya traditions as well.
In the Śākta tradition, a Śākta guru is recommended; in the Śaiva tradition, a Śaiva guru is considered appropriate;
in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, a Vaiṣṇava, and in the Saura tradition, a Saura guru is declared to be the best.
In the Gāṇapa [tradition], the Gāṇapa himself is the true guru everywhere;
therefore, the wise one should, with his whole being, receive initiation from a Kaula. 201.
Those who worship the Kaulas with effort and devotion through the five principles (pañcatattva), having delivered all men, go to the supreme goal. 202.
"Tataḥ" means he should perform or do [it]. (191–196)
In the lotus, in the water-lily. || 197–200 ||
One who receives a mantra from the mouth of a bound soul (paśu) remains a bound soul himself, without a doubt;
one who receives a mantra from a hero (vīra) becomes a hero; and from a Kaula, one becomes a knower of Brahman. (203)

A hero consecrated by the Śakti should purify the five principles (tattvas) solely within the ritual procedure for worshipping his own chosen deity; however, he shall not become a Lord of the Cakra (cakreśvara).
The slayer of a hero, the drinker of intoxicants in vain, one who has sexual intercourse with the wives of heroes, the thief, and the fifth, the associate of these great sinners. 205.
Those evil-minded ones who revile the path of the Kula, the Kula-substance, and the Kula-practitioner go to the lowest state. (206)
The Rudra-Ḍākinīs dance, and the Rudra-Bhairavas dance, finding bliss in chewing flesh and bone for those men who hate the Kaula wine. 207.
Those who revile compassionate ones who are truthful in character and always desirous of the welfare of others do not attain liberation from hell anywhere. 208.
Many applications and various ritual actions have been described;
for the Kaula who is solely devoted to Brahman, renunciation and performance are equal.
The one supreme Brahman alone exists, pervading the entire universe;
therefore, the worship of the universe constitutes the worship of Him, since everything is permeated by Him. (210)
With one's whole being and with every effort. || 201–204 ||
Now, he speaks of those who have committed the five great sins (*pañcamahāpātakin*) with the single verse beginning "the slayer of a hero" (*vīraghātī*), etc. (vv. 205–207).
[The term] *garhayantaḥ* means censuring or reviling. (vv. 208–209).
"One" refers to that; its worship is the worship of the Supreme Brahman. Endowed with That—endowed with the Supreme Brahman—[they attain it].
O Dear One, even those who, attached to fruits, devoted to desires, and delighting in the web of ritual acts, worship [the deity] as if it were separate, they nevertheless go to and enter That. (211)
He who perceives everything as Brahman and sees Brahman alone everywhere—he alone should be known as a true Kaula and is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (212)
Thus, in the venerable Mahānirvāṇa Tantra— the supreme among all supreme tantras,
the essence of the determination of all dharmas— in the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva,
this is the [chapter] titled "The Description of the Vṛddhi-Śrāddha and Other Rites for the Deceased, and the Full Consecration."
The Tenth Chapter (Ullāsa).

"Attached to fruits," and so forth. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Delighting in the web of karma" means those who are devoted to the multitude of ritual actions. "That" refers to the Supreme Brahman. || 211 || 212 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. The eleventh chapter begins:
Having heard the Śāmbhava doctrines according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life...
Aparṇā, with supreme affection, questioned Śaṅkara.

The Goddess said: O Lord, by your grace, all-knowing one, you have out of compassion explained to me the duties of the castes and stages of life, as well as the purificatory rites, for the sake of the world's success.
Oṃ. Homage to Brahmā!
In this Kali age, because people for the most part are nihilistic, their minds are filled with doubt, and they are overcome by desire, anger, and other such passions.
Furthermore, because they desire the pleasure of all the senses,
fail to practice the true path proclaimed by Sadāśiva, and instead resort to the wicked ways forbidden therein,
manifold sins arise. Consequently, how can there be [liberation] for them?
Having heard this, Pārvatī, possessing the intention that [liberation] is indeed emancipation (vimukti), questioned Śaṅkara;

thus it is said, beginning with "having heard," etc. Due to the distinctions among the castes (varṇas)—Brāhmaṇas and so forth—and the stages of life (āśramas)—the householder and the mendicant—the religious duties of Śambhu [are differentiated].
Having heard the dharmas proclaimed by Śambhu, Aparṇā Pārvatī, who had abandoned leaves as part of her vow,
questioned Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the performer of auspiciousness, with supreme and most excellent affection. || 1 ||
In response to the expectation of what was asked,
[the author] begins to state the very subject of inquiry with these three verses beginning with "varṇāśrama" and ending with "vaktumarhasi. O Lord, O Master, although...

For the sake of the world’s welfare and for the accomplishment of the world’s liberation, the conduct, duties, and purificatory rites of the social classes and stages of life have been told and spoken by you— the omniscient one who knows all— out of compassion, directed toward me. || 2 ||
In the Kali age, people will be of evil conduct, their minds blinded by desire and anger;
they will be atheists, full of doubt, and ever-seeking the pleasures of the senses. (3)
O Lord, those of wicked intellect will not follow the path spoken by you; O Sovereign, you should especially explain what their destiny shall be. (4)
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
"Well asked by you, O Goddess, who acts for the welfare of the worlds!
You are Durgā, the mother of the universe, who liberates one from the cycle of birth and worldly existence."
Nevertheless, the connection with the second [verse] is as follows: "In the Kali age, people will not follow—that is, they will not practice—the path taught by you, spoken by you.
He qualifies the people while showing the reason for their failure to follow the path spoken by Śiva: "in the Kali age."
By the words "of evil conduct" (*durvṛttayaḥ*) and so forth: of what nature are these people?

They are those whose conduct (*vṛttiḥ*) is directed toward wicked action, or whose conduct itself is wicked. The meaning is that they persist in wicked deeds. Furthermore, their minds are blinded by desire and anger (*kāmakrodhāndhacetasah*).

Those whose minds are blinded by desire and anger are of such a nature; the nihilists (*nāstikas*) are those possessed of the conviction that the next world and so forth do not exist; and those of a doubting nature (*saṃśayātman*) are those whose minds are filled with uncertainty as to whether the next world and so forth exist or do not exist.
"Always desiring the pleasures of the six senses," meaning they constantly long for the pleasures of the tongue and the other senses;

"of evil intellect," meaning those of corrupt understanding. O Īśāna, O possessor of sovereignty, what is the destiny of those people? What would be the means for their liberation? Thus [the Lord] spoke specifically.
"You ought to speak; you are worthy [of it]. According to the lexicon, *gati* means 'knowledge,' 'condition,' 'path,' 'journey,' and 'means'. || 4 ||
Now Śambhu praises Aparṇā’s question with the words "Well asked" and so forth:

"O Goddess, O radiant one, you have well asked what is delightful to the mind. Showing the reason for the excellence of the question, he says: "Of the worlds. Of what kind is the Goddess? One who acts for the benefit of the worlds (*hitakāriṇī*).
O producer of the desires of people! Demonstrating the seed of her being the benefactor of the worlds, he says "you," and so forth: you are the mother of the world, the progenitor of the worlds;
because you are the mother of the world, you are the benefactor of the worlds, and because you are the benefactor of the worlds, [you are the mother of the world].
"It is well asked," should be supplied [to complete the sense]. (p.
320) "You are the primordial mother of the worlds, the protectress, higher than the highest.
By you alone, O Goddess, is this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, sustained. (6)
You alone are the earth, you are the water, you are the wind, and you are the fire;
you are the ether, you are the ego, and you are the one whose form is the principle of the Great (Mahat-tattva).
You alone are the individual soul in this world; you are knowledge and the supreme deity.
You are the senses, the mind, and the intellect; you are the goal and the abiding state of all beings.
You alone are the Vedas, the Praṇava, and the Smṛtis; you indeed are the Saṃhitās, the Nigamas, Āgamas, and Tantras—the auspicious Śivā who consists of all the scriptures.

You are the liberator from birth and from saṃsāra—that is, from the cycle of repeated coming and going consisting of birth, worldly existence, and [attachment to] wife, children, and so forth. For this very reason, you are Durgā, she who is difficult to approach and difficult to know. (5)
"You" means: You are the primordial source, the first-born of all worlds; you are the sustainer and nourisher of the worlds;
you alone are the protector and guardian of the worlds;
and you are superior even to the most excellent. O radiant Goddess, [you pervade] the moving and the unmoving.
This entire universe, both moving and stationary, is sustained by you alone.

"You alone" means: you alone are the earth, the ground; you are the water; you alone are the wind, the air; you are the fire, the consumer of oblations; you are the sky, the ether; and you are the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). You alone are also that which has the nature of the Great Principle (mahattattva). || 7 ||

"You alone" means: you alone are that which is the individual soul (*jīva*) in this world; you alone are knowledge (*vidyā*) in the form of self-knowledge; you alone are the supreme deity (*paradevatā*), the most excellent divinity;
and you are the senses, such as the eyes, as well as the mind (*manas*), the heart, and the intellect (*buddhi*).

You alone are the knowledge of the reality of the scriptures and so forth, and you are of their very form; you alone are the goal and the state of existence of all things, and you are of their very form. (8)

"You alone" means that you are indeed the Vedas, such as the Yajurveda and others, and you possess their very form; you are the Praṇava, having the form of the syllable Om; and you possess the form of the Smṛtis, which are the treatises on Dharma spoken by Manu and others.
Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahānīlasarasvatī, Mahodarī, Mahāmāyā, Mahāraudrī, and Maheśvarī. || 10 ||
You are omniscient and composed of knowledge; there is nothing unknown in your presence.
Nevertheless, O wise one, you ask; for my pleasure, I shall tell it to you.
"O Goddess, you have spoken the truth regarding the conduct of human beings;
though they know what is beneficial, they are intoxicated by sins that quickly yield pleasure. (12)

You are the *saṃhitās*, such as the *Mahābhārata* and others; you alone are that which takes their form. The *nigama* is a specific work in verse-form originating from the mouth of Pārvatī at the request of Śambhu; and you are the *āgama*.

It is indeed a specific work in the form of verses concerning Vāsudeva, spoken by Śiva from his own mouth and transmitted through the face of Girijā. Furthermore, Tantra is specifically a particular work composed by Gaṇeśa and addressed to Ambikā;
and you alone are that very form, embodying all the scriptures.
And you are the embodiment of all the scriptures, such as the Vedānta; and you, O Śivā, are the sole abode of auspiciousness. || 9 ||
"Mahā" means: because you are the destroyer of the universe, you are Mahākālī;
because you are the cause of the increase of prosperity, you alone are Mahālakṣmī;
and because you are the bestower of knowledge, you alone are Mahānīlasarasvatī—at the time of dissolution.
Because you contain the belly of the entire world without exception, you are Mahodarī; because you delude the world, you are Mahāmāyā;
you are Mahāraudrī and exceedingly fierce; and you are Maheśvarī, distinguished by great sovereignty. || 10 ||

"O Omniscient One": You are the omniscient one, the knower of all objects without exception, consisting of pure knowledge, and whose very nature is the wisdom regarding liberation. Therefore, in your presence—that is, in your proximity—there is nothing whatsoever that is unknowable or beyond the reach of your wisdom. [The opponent asks: "But is there not even something unknowable to me?"
Anticipating the doubt, "If it does not exist, why do you ask?", he replies with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*).

Although this is the case, nevertheless, O wise one (*prājña*), meaning O possessor of excellent knowledge, you ask for my pleasure—the word "my" being understood as the ellipsis—and I too shall speak for your pleasure; "before you" (*te*) means in your presence.

Or [it may be read as] "to you. By the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*), the word "for the sake of pleasure" (*prītaye*) is connected with both the preceding and the following actions. || 11 ||

Now, repeating what was previously stated, he begins to give the answer with the words "What you have said is true," and so forth. O Goddess, what you have said regarding the contradictory conduct (*viceṣṭita*) of human beings (*manuja*) is indeed true. He describes that very conduct as follows: "knowing..."

By these and other such [statements], it is said: "Even though men know what is beneficial for themselves, they will not follow the path of the virtuous; for those who have cast both the beneficial and the harmful aside from the path of the virtuous, that which must be done for the sake of their ultimate liberation (niḥśreyasa) is now declared. (13)
The performance of what is forbidden and the abandonment of prescribed duties produce sin for men, which brings about suffering, grief, and disease. (14)
O Mistress of the Clan, know that very sin to be of two kinds: from producing merely what is undesirable for oneself, and from bringing about what is undesirable for others. (15)
A mortal is released from the sin that causes harm to others by means of royal decree;
he is released from other [sins] through expiatory rites and meditative concentration. (16)

They will not practice nor follow the path of the virtuous. Stating the reason for their failure to follow the true path, he qualifies those people as follows: what kind of people? Those who, by means of illicit sexual intercourse with women, the drinking of liquor, and so forth—which quickly bestow pleasure, that is, which bring about immediate gratification—[neglect the true path].

The sense is that they are intoxicated by evil deeds and, for that very reason, excluded from both the beneficial and the harmful; therefore, they will not practice [virtue]. For the sake of the supreme good—that is, for the liberation—of those people, that which is to be done, that which is to be prescribed, is now stated. || 12 || 13 ||
First,
he states with the words "anuṣṭhānam" and so forth that sin arises from the performance of prohibited actions and the non-performance of prescribed actions; [this refers to] the prohibited.

The performance—that is, the practice—of prescribed action and the abandonment—that is, the non-performance—of such action produce sin for men, which brings about affliction, grief, and disease; that is, it generates suffering, sorrow, and sickness. || 14 ||

Now, with the words beginning "svāniṣṭa," he establishes the twofold nature of the previously mentioned sin along with its cause: "O Kulānāyikā, O Kuleśvarī, because it produces only what is undesirable to oneself— that is,
because it brings about for the self that which is not desired— and likewise..."

Because it brings about the undesirable for others and because it produces even that which is not desired by others, know and understand that very aforementioned sin to be twofold, of two kinds. || 15 ||
Having thus demonstrated the arising of the two kinds of evil, he now states the means for liberation from them with the words beginning "parāniṣṭa" (undesirable to others), etc.:
from evil that produces what is undesirable to others, and even from that which produces what is unintended [by oneself].

Those who have committed sins and are not purified—either by royal decree (p. 323), or by penance, or by punishments—do not return from hell; they are censured both in this world and the next. || 17 ||
In this regard, I shall first declare the determination regarding the king's command;
by transgressing which, O Maheśānī, a king goes to the lowest state. (18)
One should look upon servants, sons, neutrals, as well as those who are dear and those who are not dear, with an equal eye regarding both their governance and their justice.
If one has committed a sin oneself, yet causes those who have not committed any offense to suffer,
one becomes purified by satisfying them with fasts and gifts.
A mortal person is released from royal punishment; that is, he becomes free. [This is expressed] in the *laṭ* (present) tense with the agentive-reflexive (*karmakartari*) construction.

However, one is released from other sins—which merely produce what is undesirable to oneself—through expiation (*prāyaścitti*), that is, through the performance of penance (*prāyaścitta*), and through meditative composure (*samādhi*), which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*). || 16 ||

In order to demonstrate that those who have committed the two kinds of sins will remain eternally in hell if they are not purified by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and punishment (*daṇḍa*), he says:
"By expiation... Those people who have committed transgressions—those who have performed sinful acts—if [they do not purify themselves] by expiation...
Even when purified by punishments, they did not become pure; being censured and reviled in this world and the next, they do not return from hell—they remain right there—this is the meaning. || 17 ||

Now, while declaring the determination of the royal decree, [the text] states that the king who transgresses it goes to hell, beginning with the words "There, first," and so forth. O Ādyā, O Maheśānī, "there" means between the expiation and the royal decree; "first" means at the very beginning.
I shall declare the determination of royal commands; by the transgression of which a king goes to an inferior state.
He states the king’s decision regarding governance with the words beginning "the servants," and so forth:

[he should govern] the servants (bhṛtyān) who are to be supported, such as ministers and others; his sons (putrān), his own offspring; the neutral (udāsīnān), those distinct from both enemies and friends; the beloved (priyān), those who are beneficial; and likewise the unloved (apriyān), those who are harmful—in all these matters of governance.
Likewise, the king should look upon justice with an even gaze, that is, with an impartial view.

(19) Now, one might ask: how can there be purification for a king who himself commits a sin by punishing men who have not committed any offense? To this, he says "If [the king] himself," and so forth. If the king...
If he himself has committed a sin,
then considering himself worthy of death for the evil he has done, the lord of men should abandon his kingdom, go to the forest, and uplift his soul through austerity. (21)
A king should never inflict a heavy punishment on those whose offenses are minor,
nor a light one on those whose crimes are grave, except when there is a specific reason for such a reversal.
In that teaching, those who are to be disciplined travel many wrong paths; therefore, in a state free from fear toward evil, a light punishment for a minor offense is a severe restraint.
For one who feels shame because of a single committed offense, for one who is highly respectful, and for one who fears sin, a mild punishment is appropriate even for a grave crime. (24)

One is purified by fasts and gifts. If one should afflict or punish others who have committed no sin—that is, who have done no evil—then, having gratified those sinless ones with gifts, one is purified by fasts and gifts. In this regard:
The gradation between fasting and giving gifts should be understood according to the relative gravity of the sin. || 20 ||
Now, [the author] states the expiation for a king who has committed an evil deed and considers himself deserving of death, beginning with the words "deserving of death" (*vadhārham*). A lord of men,
having committed a sin and considering his own self to be deserving of death— that is, worthy of being slain— [should relinquish] his kingdom...
Having abandoned [worldly life] and reached the forest, one should uplift the self through austerity; that is, one should purify it. || 21 ||

Now, [the author] prohibits a heavy punishment for a minor offense and a light punishment for a grave offense when there is no cause for such a reversal of the standard penalty, by means of the verse beginning with "guru" and so forth. In the case of a reversal— that is,
a deviation from the standard penalty— without a cause, the king [should not impose] a heavy punishment upon people who have committed minor offenses.
He should not ordain, nor should he carry out; he should not impose a light punishment upon people who have committed grave offenses. || 22 ||

By the phrase "without cause, in the case of a reversal," it is implied that one should indeed impose a contrary punishment when there is a cause for the opposite [situation]; therefore, with the two verses beginning with "in that case" (*tasmin*), he prescribes a contrary punishment preceded by the observation of the cause.
In whose teaching— that is, in the teaching of which person— many people who follow various wrong paths and abide on improper courses are to be disciplined; in that [teaching],
even though the people are free from fear regarding many sins and misdeeds, they remain without dread.
Even for a minor offense, a severe punishment is recommended. || 23 ||

"Once" means: for a person who is ashamed because of an offense committed only once, who is modest, who possesses great respect [for others], who fears even a single sin, and who is by nature timid—even if the crime is a grave one, a light punishment is recommended. || 24 ||

If a Kaula who has committed only a slight offense, or a Brahmin who has performed a minor transgression, should be highly esteemed even so, he must still be punished with words by the ruler of the earth. (25)
Having deliberated with his ministers upon what is just, punishment, and favor,
that protector of the earth who does not act accordingly shall become a perpetrator of a great sin.
A son should not abandon his parents, subjects should not abandon their king,
and a wife should not abandon her husband— except in the case of those who are extreme sinners.
The subjects should protect with effort the kingdom, wealth, and life of a righteous lord of the earth; otherwise, they fall into a downward state.
O Śivā, those who knowingly approach their mother, sister, or daughter, as well as those who strike down their great preceptors, [shall go to hell]. (29)
Now, he describes the punishment for a Kaula and a Brāhmaṇa who have committed only a slight offense, even though they are highly respected, with the verse beginning "svalpāparādhi" and so forth:
"If a Kaula, though highly respected, should commit a slight offense, such would also be the case for a Brāhmaṇa."
If he is a perpetrator of minor sins, then he should be punished by the king with words alone.

Now, [the author] states that a ruler who inflicts punishment and so forth without first conducting an inquiry together with his ministers incurs the state of being a great sinner, beginning with the verse "nyāyam" (justice).
That protector of the earth who, having deliberated with his ministers and counselors, does not administer justice, punishment, or grace, shall become a perpetrator of a great sin. || 26 ||
Now, he states the duty regarding women, sons, and subjects with the words "one should not abandon," and so forth.
A son should not abandon his parents—that is, both mother and father. Subjects should not abandon their king—that is, the monarch.
A wife should not abandon her husband—that is, her lord. [Objection: But even if fathers and others have committed mortal sins (atipātaka), they should not...
Regarding this, he says "excepting them": excepting those most sinful ancestors and others; the meaning is that such extreme sinners must indeed be abandoned. || 27 ||

He describes the fault of subjects who do not protect the kingdom and so forth of a righteous king with the verse beginning "rājyam" and so on: the subjects should protect with effort the kingdom, wealth, and life of a righteous lord of the earth; otherwise—
Those who do not protect the kingdom and so forth go to a lower rebirth. || 28 ||

(326) Those people who, having relied upon their family dharma, subsequently abandon the duties of their lineage, are considered betrayers of trust and perpetrators of extreme transgressions. || 30 ||
For one who approaches his mother, sister, or daughter, the punishment is death;
O Śivā, the same is ordained for those women as well, if they were willing participants.
The bed of one's mother, father, or sister; a daughter-in-law, a mother-in-law, or the wife of a guru;
as well as the wife of one's paternal grandfather and maternal grandfather—[these are forbidden]. (32)
The daughter of one's father or mother, the sister of one's brother, the wife of a brother, or even his daughter;
the daughter of a sister, the wife of a master, and a maiden who is one's own daughter—[these are forbidden]. || 33 ||

It has been stated that those who commit extreme sins (atipātakin), such as one's father and others, are to be abandoned; and in response to the inquiry as to who these are, he defines the committers of extreme sins with the following two verses beginning with "mātaram": "O Śivā, [one should abandon] one's mother, the progenitress, as well as one's sister."
Those who, out of ignorance, approach their own daughters or daughters-in-law; likewise, those who, out of ignorance, are destroyers or killers of their great gurus, such as mothers and others;
those who, while relying on family tradition, have nevertheless abandoned the prescribed duties of their lineage; and those who...
Those people who betray trust are remembered as the most grievous sinners. (29-30)

Now, regarding the punishment for a man who approaches his mother and others, as well as for those women who desire him, [the author] says: "The mother," etc. O Śivā, for the man who approaches his mother—the one who gave birth—likewise his sister, and likewise his daughter, death is the penalty.
Death itself is the discipline, death itself is the punishment; for those women who were filled with desire, that very death was ordained as their subduing. || 31 ||

Now, with three and a half verses beginning with *mātāpitroḥ* and ending with *vimuktaye*, [the author] states the punishment for men who have sexual intercourse with their mother’s sister and others, as well as for those women who are likewise lustful, so that they may be liberated from this sin. Regarding the mother and father...
Likewise, for those who approach their own daughter’s bed— meaning their own daughter— with the desire for sexual intercourse,
as well as their daughter-in-law (the wife of their son), their mother-in-law (the wife of their father-in-law), the wife of their preceptor,
and the women of their paternal grandfather and maternal grandfather; likewise, [for those who approach] their own sister...

For those sinners who approach the daughter of their father or mother, the daughter of their maternal uncle or paternal uncle, the wife of those two, or likewise the wife of a brother, the punishment prescribed is the excision of the penis.
For these women who possess desire, neither corporal punishment nor the cutting off of their noses is prescribed;
rather, their expulsion from the home is the means for liberation from this sin. (34)
For one who goes away abandoning his sapindas, wife, sons, women, or even those who trust him, the punishment is the forfeiture of all property and the shaving of the head. (35)
If a marriage should take place with these women through ignorance—
whether by the Brāhma or Śaiva rite— one should recognize them for what they are and abandon them at that very moment.
If one should approach a wife of the same caste or the woman of a higher caste, his punishment shall be the confiscation of his wealth and subsisting on broken grains for one month. || 37 ||

For those sinners who approach his daughter, as well as his sister’s daughter, his paternal aunt’s daughter, his lord’s wife, his own daughter, or an unmarried maiden, the punishment is the excision of the linga, that is, the cutting off of the penis.

For these women who act out of desire, the punishment (dama) is ordained: the cutting off of the nose (nāsānikṛntana), the amputation of the nose (nāsikācchedana), and expulsion from the house, for the sake of their liberation from this sin. || 32–34 ||

Now, with the words beginning "sapiṇḍa," the author states the punishment for one who approaches the wives of sapindas, as well as sons, and for one who approaches the women of those who trust him: for a person who approaches the wives of sapindas, their sons, or even the women of those who place trust in him, there shall be the confiscation of all his property.
The forfeiture of all wealth, the shaving of the hair, and the tonsure of the head shall constitute the punishment.
Now, he describes what must be done regarding a marriage contracted through ignorance by means of the rites prescribed in the Vedas and the Śiva-śāstras, involving sapindas, sons, and others.

By the words "by women" and so forth: if, through ignorance, a marriage (vivāha) should take place with these women—such as female sapindas, daughters, and others—either according to the Brāhma rite prescribed in the Vedas or according to the Śaiva rite prescribed by Śiva, then, having realized this, one should abandon those women at that very moment. || 36 ||

Now, one might ask: how is there purification for one who approaches a wife of his own caste as well as wives of other castes? To this, he says "savarṇa" and so forth. A man who approaches a wife of his own caste, and likewise one who approaches a woman of a lower caste (anuloma)—for example, a Brāhmaṇa [approaching a Śūdra woman].

A Kṣatriya [committing adultery] with a Kṣatriya woman, and likewise with a Vaiśya woman—his seizure of her wealth, one month of subsisting on grain-particles (kaṇa), and the fine are to be known as the punishment. || 37 ||
O fair-faced one, for a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who, out of knowledge, approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman, the cutting off of the penis is declared to be the punishment. (38)
Having disfigured the Brahmin woman, the king shall banish her from the country;
such indeed is the prescribed punishment for those women who have intercourse with a hero. (39)
But for that evil-minded man who takes pleasure with the wife of another against her will,
his punishment shall be the confiscation of his wealth and subsisting on grain-particles for three months.
The same punishment is ordained for a woman who acts out of her own desire.
O Śivā, a wife who has been approached by force should be abandoned; she should not be protected.

Now, with the words beginning "O fair-faced one" (*rājanye*), he states the punishment for Kṣatriyas and others who intentionally have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman who is likewise desirous, as well as for her, when it occurs through knowledge [of her status].
O fair-faced one (*varānane*), for those who knowingly approach a Brāhmaṇī...
For Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and commoners of the lowest castes (antyajas), the cutting off of the male organ is declared to be the punishment. || 38 ||

Even a Brahmin woman who is willing, if she has been disfigured or deprived of a limb, the king should cause her to be banished and expelled from the country. Now, regarding those who approach the wives of heroes, he states their punishment: "of the heroes' wives," and so forth; [this refers to] those who have sexual intercourse with the wives of heroes when they are willing.
And in this very same way, as before, the rule of restraint (dama) is to be ordained; such is the meaning. Regarding the word "vidhi" (rule):
from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi*, the suffix *ki* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *upasarge dhoḥ kiḥ*. || 39 ||

Now, with the verse beginning "durātmā" (the evil-minded), the author states the punishment for men who have sexual intercourse with women of their own caste or of a higher caste, as well as for the woman herself if she is willing. For example: "The evil-minded man"—one whose mind is corrupt, whose intellect is wicked, or whose nature is depraved—who takes pleasure with the wife of another in the inverse order of castes. As follows:
It has been stated that [this applies] to a Śūdra by means of a Vaiśya woman. For such a man, the seizure of her wealth and a three-month diet of *kaṇa* grains shall be the punishment. || 40 ||

In the same way, a punishment is prescribed for a woman who acts out of her own desire, as previously stated. Now, with the words beginning with "by force" (*balāt*), [the author] states that in the case of a woman who has been approached by another man through coercion, it is the duty of the man to provide her with protection and maintenance: "O Śivā, by force... and so forth.
A wife who has gone over to another man should be abandoned; she should be maintained with food and other necessities. || 41 ||
Whether she be a Brāhmaṇī wife or a Śaiva wife, whether intentionally or unintentionally, she must be abandoned in every way if she has once gone to another man. (42)
O Goddess of the gods, for those who have gone among courtesans or into the wombs of animals such as cows, purification occurs after three nights of subsisting on *kaṇa* (grains).
If wicked men and women go about according to their lust, the king must, by the command of Śambhu, carry out their execution. 44.
If one should approach even a Cāṇḍāla woman by force, his execution must be carried out; he is never to be forgiven. (45)

Now, he states with the verse beginning "Brāhmī" that, whether out of desire or lack of desire, the abandonment of the two wives— the Brāhmī and the Śaivī— who have gone over to another [man], is indeed appropriate. *Brāhmī* refers to one married according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas, or alternatively, the *Śaivī*.
If a wife, though married according to the rites prescribed by Śiva, goes to another man even once, at a single instance, then she must be abandoned in every way and by all means. || 42 ||
Now, with the words beginning "of those who go," etc., he states the expiation for those who approach prostitutes and those who approach the wombs of animals such as cows: O Goddess of Gods,
for people who go among courtesans (vāranārī) and likewise among the wombs of animals such as cows, [the penance lasts] three nights.
Purification occurs through eating only grain. || 43 ||

Now, he states the expiation for a man and a woman who engage in the anus with the words beginning "gacchatām" (for those engaging). For the wicked-minded man and woman who intentionally engage in the anus— the rectum— the king, the upholder of the earth, [should prescribe the following].
By the command of Śambhu, his execution alone must be carried out. || 44 ||
He states, beginning with the word "by force," that even for those who approach the wives of others through compulsion, the punishment is indeed death.
He who approaches even a Cāṇḍāla woman by force must also be sentenced to death; he must never be pardoned. By the use of the word "even" (api), [it is implied that this applies to all such cases].
It is implied that for those who approach Brahmanical women and others, execution must certainly be carried out (p.
330): "But those women who have been married by Brahmans or followers of the Śaiva path—they alone are to be known as one's own wives; all others are the wives of others. (46)
If one looks at another's wife with lustful intent, converses with her in secret, touches her,
or embraces her, he shall be purified by fasting for double the duration of each successive act.
A noble woman who, while acting thus with desire, has intercourse with another man, shall purify herself by means of the prescribed method of fasting. 48.
A mortal who speaks blameworthy words to women, who looks upon the private parts of another's wife, or who laughs excessively, shall be purified by two fasts. (49)

Now, because they are required in the various verses that have been spoken and those yet to be spoken, he defines his own wives and the wives of others with the words beginning "those who are married," and so forth:
"Those women who [are wed] by the *brāhma* rites— the paths prescribed in the Vedas or the paths taught by Śiva— "
Those who have been married and wedded are to be understood as one's own wives;
all others, distinct from them, are to be understood as the wives of others. || 46 ||
Now, he states the expiation for one who intentionally looks at another's wife and so forth, beginning with the words "kāmāt" (intentionally): "Intentionally looking at another's wife,
likewise conversing with her in private— that is, engaging in speech with her— and likewise..."
By touching, embracing, and hugging her, a person may be purified through fasting in a double progression:
just as looking at another's wife intentionally is purified by one fast,
conversing with her by two fasts, touching her by four fasts, and embracing her [by eight].
Purification is achieved by means of those eight. || 47 ||
Now, he states with the verse beginning "kurvatī" that the same penance applies even to a lustful woman who engages in conversation and so forth with another man.
A woman of noble family (*kulāṅganā*), a protector of her lineage (*kulapālikā*), being lustful, [acts] thus with another man...
While engaging in conversation and other such activities, she should purify herself according to the previously mentioned rules for fasting. || 48 ||

Now, one might ask: how can there be purification for one who speaks ill of women, who looks upon the secrets of another's wife, or who laughs excessively? To this, he says "bruvan" and so forth. [The meaning is:
speaking indecent and censurable words regarding women, as well as looking upon the secret parts of another's wife...
A mortal who, while looking at her private parts, laughs excessively with her, shall be purified by two fasts. || 49 ||
By manifesting his own self as fire and likewise making another person fire, and by abstaining from food for three nights, a human being becomes pure. (50)
If the husband admits to having had sexual intercourse with another woman's wife, then the king shall punish her and her lover in accordance with the scriptures. (51)
If the husband of a woman who has an illicit lover is unable to provide for her,
he should abandon her and support himself with morsels of food, provided he remains under the authority of his husband.
At that time, seeing his wife taking pleasure with her paramour, the husband who was killing the lover with his woman was not at all deserving of death by the king. (53)
Now, one might ask: how can there be purification for one who exposes his own nakedness and causes another to do the same? To this, he says "darśayan" and so forth:
a man who exposes his own nakedness and likewise makes another naked—

By abstaining from eating for two nights, one becomes pure. Regarding the term *ātman*, the lexicon states: "The self [resides] in the body, mind, Brahman, inherent nature, fortitude, and intellect. (50)

Now, with the words beginning "of the wife," he states the punishment for a woman who has gone to another man as authorized by her own husband, and for her paramour. If the husband indeed authorizes the wife's going to another, then the king [should punish] her and her paramour.
In accordance with the treatises and according to the previously stated injunctions, one should be disciplined. || 51 ||
Now, regarding the abandonment or maintenance of a woman who is suspected of infidelity because her husband is incapable of providing proof against her misconduct, he says "pramāṇa" and so forth:
if the husband is incapable of providing proof (*pramāṇa*) against his beloved wife’s paramour (*upapati*), then...
If, having abandoned that beloved wife, he should abide by his husband's command and not transgress his master's order, then he should nourish her with morsels of food. || 52 ||

Indeed, he speaks to Girijā— who was doubting whether or not the husband of a woman who, while sporting with a paramour, was caught by her husband and killed, deserved death— using the verse beginning with "ramamāṇām" and so forth. When the husband, the master, [sees her] with the paramour...

Seeing his wife sporting with a paramour, the husband, while slaying that paramour, would not be subject to execution for the sake of the king, the lord of the earth. By the phrase "while slaying" (*tadā nighnan*), it is implied that at other times, one who slays [the paramour] would indeed be liable to execution.
This has been indicated. || 53 ||

In a case where there is a husband’s prohibition regarding a journey, or speech by which [a woman intends to go], a woman of good family becomes worthy of abandonment on account of that departure or that speech. (54)
When her husband has died, she who remains under the authority of her husband’s kinsmen in accordance with her own duty,
or in the absence of those, under the authority of her father’s kinsmen, is entitled to the inheritance.
A widow should avoid eating twice a day, food from others, sexual intercourse, meat, ornaments, using a couch, and wearing red garments. (56)
She should not rub her limbs with fragrant unguents, nor should she abandon even the avoidance of vulgar conversation;
observing the vow of devotion to the gods and relying on the dharma of widowhood, she should pass her time.

Now, by the verse beginning with "The husband [is entitled to] abandon," etc., it is established that a woman who goes to a place forbidden by her husband, and who converses with another man despite that prohibition,
is subject to abandonment by her husband; this applies to whichever place she goes.
If a conversation with a certain man occurs and the husband forbids it, then even a woman of noble family would deserve abandonment on account of that journey and conversation. || 54 ||

Now, as a corollary, [the author] states the right to inheritance for a woman whose husband has died, provided she remains under the authority of her husband’s kinsmen and abides by her own duty, with the words beginning "when the husband has died," etc. When the husband has died, she remains under the authority of her husband’s kinsmen according to her own duty; and in the absence of her husband’s kinsmen...
A virtuous woman who remains under the control of her paternal kinsmen is entitled to an inheritance. || 55 ||

Since the duties of a widow were intended [to be described] in the verse just mentioned, he defines them with the two verses beginning with "dvirbhojanam" (twice-eating). A widow woman [should observe] twice-eating...

One should completely avoid the food of another, sexual intercourse, sensual pleasure, meat and other delicacies, ornaments and decorations, a couch or bedstead, and red clothing— that is, dyed garments. || 56 ||

"Nor [should she adorn] her limbs": a widow, adhering to the dharma of widowhood, should not rub or anoint her limbs with *vāsas*—that is, fragrant substances ground or rubbed into powder (the suffix *ac* is used here in the sense of the instrument). She should also abandon vulgar conversation. Now, [one might ask]:...
To the question of how she should pass her time in the absence of vulgar conversation, he says "deva" and so forth.
Being devoted to the deity (*devavrata*), she should spend her time; the meaning is that she should pass the time by reciting the names and other attributes of her chosen deity. || 57 ||
For that infant who has no father, mother, or paternal grandfather, the maternal relative is invariably praised for his protection. (58)
The mother’s mother, father, and brother; likewise the sons of the mother’s brother;
and the uterine brothers of the mother’s father—these are to be known as the maternal relatives (mātṛbāndhava). || 59 ||

The father’s mother, the father, the brother, the sons of the father’s brother and of the paternal aunt, and the father’s father’s uterine brothers—these are to be known as the paternal kinsmen (pitṛbandhu). || 60 ||
The husband’s mother, father, and brother; the sons of the husband’s brother and of his sister;
and the husband’s paternal uncles—these are to be known as the husband’s kinsmen (patibandhava). || 61 ||
To the father, the mother, the father’s father, and likewise to the paternal grandmother;
to the unworthy son, and to the maternal grandfather who is without sons.

To the Goddess, who asks, "In the case of a child whose father, mother, and grandfather are deceased, between the father’s relatives and the mother’s relatives, which group is more commendable for the child's protection?
[the Lord] replies with the words beginning "na vidyate" (it does not exist), etc., regarding that child whose father and mother...
And since the grandfather is not present for his protection, it is certain and settled that the maternal kinsman is praised [as the guardian]. (58)
Now, he asks, "Who are those maternal relatives and so forth? and answers with the verse beginning with "mātuḥ":
the mother's mother is the *mātāmahī* (maternal grandmother); the mother's father is the *mātāmaha* (maternal grandfather); the mother's brother is the *mātula* (maternal uncle);
likewise, the sons of the mother's brother are the *mātulaputra*s (nephews); [and so on] of the mother.
The brothers of one's father and maternal grandfather are to be known as the maternal relatives (mātṛbāndhava). || 59 ||

Then, with the words beginning with "of the father," he speaks of the paternal relatives: the mother of the father is the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*); the father of the father is the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*); the brother of the father is the paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*);
the sons of the uterine brother of the father; the sons of the father’s sister (the paternal aunt); and the father of the father’s father (the great-grandfather).
And brothers and paternal kinsmen are to be understood [as such]. || 60 ||

Then, he speaks of the husband's kinsmen with the words beginning with "of the husband" (*patyuḥ*) and so forth: the husband’s mother is the mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*); the husband’s father is the father-in-law (*śvaśura*); the husband’s brother is the uterine brother (*sodara*);
the husband’s brother’s sons are the [husband’s] sons; and the husband’s sister’s [sons] are the daughters [of the sister].
The brothers of the husband, the father, and the father-in-law are to be known as the husband's kinsmen (patibandhava). || 61 ||

Now, [the author] states in the two verses beginning with "to the father" that a man should cause food and other necessities to be given by the king to his poor parents and others: "O Ambikā, O Mother of the World, to the father,
and likewise to the mother..."
O Ambikā, the king should cause clothing and food to be given to the maternal grandmother and to these poor men by the person, according to his means. (63)
Speaking harsh words to his wife, he shall abstain from food for one day;
for striking her, three days; and for causing blood to flow, seven days.
If one speaks abusively to his wife, mother, sister, or daughter out of anger or delusion,
he shall become pure by fasting for seven days, according to the teaching of Śiva.
If a king knows that a maiden has been married by a eunuch, he should marry her again even if the time limit has passed; this is the rule declared by Śiva. (66)
To the father’s father (the paternal grandfather), to the paternal grandmother, likewise to an unworthy son, to an unworthy daughter, to a motherless maternal grandfather,
and to such a maternal grandmother— to these poor ancestors and others, according to one's means.
Without exceeding his means, the king should cause clothing, as well as food and edibles, to be given to men. || 62 || 63 ||
Now, regarding one who speaks harsh words to his wife, strikes her, and causes her blood to flow— progressively, the expiation for these acts begins with "harsh words" (*durvācyam*) and so forth.
A person speaking harsh words, that is, speech unfit to be uttered, toward his wife...
One should abandon food for one day while striking her; one should abandon food for three days while beating her;
and by causing her blood to flow, one should abandon food for seven days.

Now, with the verse beginning "From anger," etc., he states the expiation for one who, out of anger, resentment, delusion, or lack of discrimination, speaks of his own wife as a mother, a sister, and so forth. From anger (*krodha*), which is indignation (*amarṣa*), or from delusion (*moha*), which is a lack of discernment (*aviveka*), [one might speak of] his wife as a mother or a sister.
A man who speaks of a daughter or a son [as his own] shall be purified by fasting for seven days, according to the teaching of Śiva. || 65 ||

The king should cause the remarriage of a woman wedded to a eunuch; thus he says, beginning with "by a *śaṇḍha*," and so forth: even when the [proper] time has passed, the king, the ruler, knowing [the situation], [should act regarding] a maiden wedded to a *śaṇḍha*, a eunuch.
One should marry her once again. Now, one might object that this [practice] is not to be respected because it is not sanctioned by the Vedas and other scriptures;

therefore, he says: "This is the rule. This is the rule (vidhi) spoken by Śiva, uttered by Śiva. Regarding the word *śaṇḍha*, the suffix *ḍha* is applied according to the rule "the root *śam* takes *ḍha*. || 66 ||
A maiden who has been betrothed but not enjoyed sexually shall become a widow;
she too must be married again by her father—this is the rule in the Śaiva dharma. (67)
If she gives birth to a worthy son in the twelfth fortnight after marriage, or in a year passed since her husband's death, she is not truly a wife, nor is he a true son.
If a woman intentionally causes an abortion within the first five months of pregnancy,
she shall be punished with severe beatings for that act committed by her own means.
If a woman causes an abortion after the fifth month [of pregnancy],
both she and the one who incited her shall incur the sin arising from murder.
Now, he states with the verse beginning "pariṇītā" that the father must perform the remarriage of a maiden whose husband has died and who has not been enjoyed by him. A maiden who, though married—
that is, wedded— by her husband, remains unenjoyed and becomes a widow, even though she was previously married...
The maiden should be married again by her father. He shows the authority for this here with the words "Śaiva": "This rule is established in the Śaiva doctrines. (67)

Now, by the words "from marriage" (*udvāhāt*) and so forth, [the author] negates both the status of being a wife for the woman who has given birth to a son and nourished him until the sixth month after marriage due to her husband's death, as well as the status of being a son for the boy, once a year has passed since she gave birth to him. From marriage...

In the twelfth fortnight of the sixth month, whatever son she brings forth who is fit and well-nourished— she who gives birth to such a son after a year has passed since her husband's death— that wife shall no longer be a wife, and that son shall no longer be a son. Her...
The meaning is that, having recognized her as an unchaste woman and the child as born of an adulterer, one should effect their abandonment.
Now, he states the punishment for a woman who causes an abortion within five months from conception, as well as for the one who performs the means to achieve it:

By the words "from the embryo" (*āgarbhāt*) and so forth: from the embryo (*garbha*), beginning from conception up until the end of the fifth month; within those five months, the king [should punish] her who causes the embryo to miscarry by means of her intellect (*dhiyā*), as well as the one who employs the means for that miscarriage—the perpetrator of the method for causing the miscarriage—with severe beatings.
He should cause to go [to hell] and cause to suffer. || 69 ||

Now, with the verse beginning "From the fifth month," etc., [the author] states the sin resulting from the murder of a human being for a woman who causes an abortion after the fifth month, as well as for the one who performs it.
A woman who, after the fifth month, [induces an abortion of] a *bhrūṇa*...

It would cause the fetus to fall; furthermore, both that person who administered it and the one who employed it would incur the sin arising from killing, namely the transgression born of taking human life. || 70 ||
If a man of cruel conduct kills a mortal intentionally, the ruler of the earth must by all means inflict the death penalty upon him. (71)
O subduer of enemies, one should purify that man who kills out of negligence, delusion,
or ignorance by means of seizing his wealth and severe beatings.
For that sinner who, whether by his own hand or through another, employs a means of killing, a punishment has been ordained for those who kill out of ignorance.
O Supreme Goddess, having slain an assailant who has come as an aggressor to fight in mutual combat, a man does not become liable for sin. (74)

Then, in response to Pārvatī, who asks, "How then can there be liberation?", he says, beginning with the words "He who," and so forth: "That man who, acting with cruelty, kills another mortal human being out of ignorance— of him, by every means and in every way, the Dharaṇībhṛt (the Mountain-Bearer), [speaks]."
Execution must be carried out; the meaning is that his purification occurs only through that, and not otherwise. || 71 ||
Now, [the text] shows the purification for one who kills a human being through negligence and so forth,

beginning with the words "through negligence" (*pramādāt*). The Tamer of Enemies (*arindama*) [says that] toward the person who kills a man— whether out of negligence (*pramādāt*), which is a lack of attention, or while wandering about in delusion (*bhramataḥ*), or through ignorance (*ajñānāt*)— [there is this rule].
The king, who acts as the subduer of adversaries, shall purify [the realm] by seizing wealth, confiscating property, and through severe punishments. || 72 ||

Now, he states the punishment for one who employs means to kill a person, whether by his own hand or through another, beginning with the words "svataḥ" (by himself) and so forth: "For that sinner who employs a means of killing—whether by himself or through another—whoever [the king] [punishes] those killers of men who act out of ignorance... [and so on].
That punishment has been ordained. || 73 ||

Now, in response to the doubt as to whether one who has slain a warrior in battle or one who has killed an approaching assassin would be subject to execution or not, [the author] says "mutually" (*mithaḥ*) and so forth:
"O Supreme Goddess, having slain a warrior mutually in battle..."
Having slain even a Tathāgata or an assassin, a man who would otherwise deserve the sin does not partake of that sin.
As for assassins, they are as follows:
one who sets fire [to a dwelling], one who administers poison, one who bears a weapon in hand, and one who robs another of wealth.
And one who seizes land or a wife—these six are assassins (ātatāyin). Thus [it is said]. || 74 ||
When those intent on committing evil against men desire to cut off his limbs, the king should cut off their own limbs; and when they desire to strike him, he should strike them with weapons. (75)
One who is difficult to subdue and should threaten or strike Brāhmaṇas or gurus shall be purified by the gradual removal of wealth or by the burning of his hand. 76.
If one whose body has been wounded by weapons or other means dies more than six months later,
the assailant shall be subject to punishment, but he is not liable for capital punishment from the sovereign.

Those who cause the kingdom to be disturbed, those who wish to seize the realm, those who are enemies of the king, secret servants seeking his welfare, and those who create dissension between the two royal armies—[these he should eliminate]. (78)
Now, he states the punishment for those who commit acts such as the amputation of limbs, beginning with the word "aṅga":

when there are persons desiring to commit, that is, wishing to perform, a sin, the king—that is, the ruler—should, upon the amputation of a limb, carry out the cutting off of the limb; and in the case of an assault...
The weapon must be fashioned. || 75 ||

Now, regarding those who raise sticks and other weapons for the purpose of striking or killing Brahmins and teachers, he states the penance in sequence, beginning with the words "viprān" (Brahmins) and so forth. The meaning is: "whosoever is an ill-behaved person, difficult to approach, who threatens to kill Brahmins and teachers"—the word "to kill" being understood as the remainder of the sense. "Avaguret" means he should threaten.
If one should raise a staff or the like against them, or strike them, the king shall purify that person by means of a fine, the taking of wealth, or the burning of the hand, respectively. || 76 ||

Now, regarding one whose body has been wounded by a weapon or the like, if death occurs more than six months later, the author states— by means of the verse beginning with "śastrādi"— that the assailant is subject to punishment but is not liable for capital punishment.
That is to say, when a man whose body was wounded by a weapon or the like dies after six months have passed.
If the king is alive, the striker should be punished; he should certainly not be subject to execution. || 77 ||

Then, while the king was slaying those who were afflicting the country, those desiring to seize the kingdom, enemies of the monarch, servants seeking to cause dissension within the royal army out of a desire for their own private benefit, those wishing to fight against the king, and armed men who oppressed travelers; ||| 10 ||
He says that there is no sharing of the sin [of killing] through the two verses beginning with "rāṣṭra," etc.
[The term refers to] those who cause the subversion of the kingdom, those who bring calamity upon the country, those who desire to seize the kingdom—
meaning those wishing to take away the realm— and the enemies of the king, [killing them] in secret.
When subjects desire to fight, the king, having slain those armed men who harass travelers, shall not incur any guilt for these acts. (79)
If one should kill a human being by the unavoidable command of his master, the killing belongs to the master alone; it does not belong to the striker, for it was by the command of Śiva.
If a man dies through an animal or by weapons without his own effort,
his purification is achieved through a monetary fine or the restraint of his body.
