The king should punish those who are averse to the royal commands, those who speak insolently in the presence of the king, and those who revile the family traditions, even if they are otherwise contemptible.
Those who appear to be well-wishers but secretly desire harm, those servants such as ministers who create dissension between the king and his army,
as well as subjects who wish to fight against the king, and those armed men who harass travelers— all these he should [punish].
Having killed [him], the king shall not become a partaker of sin. || 78 || 79 ||

Now, with the verse beginning with "ya," [the author] states that when a master causes a human being to be killed by a servant who is unable to disobey the master’s unavoidable command, the death must be attributed to the master alone, not to the servant. [The phrase] "by the master's unavoidable" means by a command that cannot be transgressed.
If one should kill a human being, there is no death for the assailant in that act of killing;

rather, by the command of Śiva, the death of the master alone is ordained. By the phrase "by way of what is unavoidable," it is meant that if a servant capable of disobeying his master's command should kill a human being, then—
It is indicated that his very [life] shall be the slaying. || 80 ||

Now, as for that man who through negligence causes a human being to die by means of weapons and the like, how can his purification be achieved? To this he replies with the verse beginning "ayatna," etc.: "of a man who is effortless," meaning of a person devoid of intent, [if death occurs] by means of an animal such as a cow or a horse, or by weapons...
Or if a man dies by means of a sword or similar weapons, his purification shall come through a monetary fine or a corporal punishment for that person. || 81 ||

Then, [the author] states with the verse beginning "outside" (*bahiḥ*) that the king should punish those who disobey his commands, those who speak insolently in his presence, and those who defile the family dharma.
Those who turn their faces away from the king's commands are those who transgress the royal edicts; [he should punish them] in the presence of the king.
The king shall punish those who speak with arrogance, those who speak haughtily, as well as those who revile and disparage the traditional duties of their families. || 82 ||
The king should banish from the country one who embezzles what has been deposited, one who is cruel, a deceiver, a sower of discord, and one who incites lawsuits among the people. (83)
The king should banish from the country those who give a daughter for a bride-price, those who bestow a son upon a eunuch, and those fallen ones of evil nature.
Those who, under the pretext of false accusation, desire to bring about the ruin of others, should be punished by the king who knows the Dharma in accordance with their accusation. (85)
The king shall cause the person who has inflicted a certain measure of harm to pay a corresponding amount of wealth to the person who suffered that harm. 86.

Now, the author states with the verse beginning "sthāpya" that the king should expel from his own country those who misappropriate deposits and so forth. One who misappropriates a deposit is a thief of what was entrusted; such a person may be cruel, harsh, or merciless, as well as a deceiver.
Likewise, the king should banish from the country—that is, expel—a person who causes dissension and incites people to quarrel. || 83 ||

Now, with the verse beginning "By means of a fee" (*śulkena*), the King issues a command that those people who give away a daughter or a son for the purpose of receiving a fee (*śulka*)— that is, money given as the cause for the gift— should be expelled from the country;
this applies especially to one who is impotent (*śaṇḍha*).

A king should expel from his realm those evil-minded and sinful-hearted people who give a daughter to a eunuch, or who, for a bride-price, bestow or give a son to one who is specifically a *śaṇḍha* (impotent). Regarding the term *śaṇḍhe*: [it refers to] one who is impotent.
Because the recipient (sampradāna) is intended to be expressed as the locus (adhikaraṇa), the locative case is employed by the rule "saptamy adhikaraṇe ca" [Pāṇini 2.3.36]. || 84 ||
Now, with the verse beginning "mithyā," he states the punishment for those who desire to cause harm to others under the pretext of false slander; that is,
those who wish to bring about an undesirable result for another by means of a false accusation or the guise of an untrue calumny.

Those men should be punished according to the accusation by the king, the lord of the earth, who knows the law and understands righteousness; the meaning is that for a grave accusation, a severe punishment must be imposed, and for a minor accusation, a light punishment. || 85 ||
To the question, "What punishment should be inflicted upon a man who causes harm to another even without any offense? he replies with the verse beginning with "yaḥ" (who):
"Whatever limited harm a man might inflict upon another, by that [act], he becomes a partaker of harm for that person."
The king should cause wealth equal to that amount to be given. || 86 ||
For those who commit theft of gems, pearls, gold, and other minerals, the king, after determining their value, shall order the cutting off of a hand or both arms. (87)
For men who have forcibly carried off buffaloes, horses, cattle, and the like, as well as gems and such, or even a child, the punishment prescribed is the same as that for a thief.
The king should clear a thief of an object of food that has little value by having him fast for one fortnight or for seven days while subsisting on grain-particles.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, there is no atonement through sacrifices, vows, austerities, gifts, or penances for a man who betrays trust or is ungrateful. (90)
Now, with the verse beginning with "maṇi," he states the punishment for those who steal minerals such as gems and pearls:

the king, having determined the value of the gems and other items, shall inflict the amputation of a hand or both arms upon the man who commits the theft of gems, pearls, gold, and other such minerals.

The meaning is that in the case of stealing gems and other items of small value, the cutting off of a hand should be performed; in the case of stealing gems and other items of great value, the cutting off of both arms should be performed. || 87 ||

Now, with the verse beginning with "mahiṣa," etc., he states the punishment for one who forcibly seizes buffaloes, horses, and so forth: for those who by force seize or carry away buffaloes, horses, cattle, and other such animals,
as well as jewels and the like, and even a child—
For men, punishment is ordained as being like that for a thief. || 88 ||

Now, he describes the purification for one who steals food or other objects of small value, such as gems and the like, beginning with the words "Of foods" and so forth: "That man who is a thief of foods or likewise of an object of small value, having subsisted on grain for one fortnight or seven days..."
While feeding [the guests], the king should purify [himself]. || 89 ||

Now, with the verse beginning with "viśvāsa" (trust), the author describes the lack of atonement even for one who performs various sacrifices, vows, and so forth, if they are a betrayer of trust or ungrateful.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, in the case of a man who is a betrayer of trust and likewise ungrateful— that is, one who destroys what has been done for him— [there is no purification].
Through sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha,
through vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa, through austerities, and through gifts that serve as expiations for the destruction of sin—
even by these, there would be no atonement for misdeeds nor liberation. || 90 ||
Those mortals who are false witnesses, whether acting as mediators or showing partiality, the king shall punish them with severe punishment and banish them from the country. (91)
Six witnesses may serve as authority, or four, or even three;
in their absence, even two may suffice, O Śivā, provided they are both well-known and righteous.
O beloved, if testimony is mutually inconsistent regarding place, time, or subject matter, the statement of the witnesses is inadmissible.
O beloved, the word of the blind may be authoritative, as may that of the deaf;
for the mute and the dumb, the written script accepted with the head serves as authority.

Now, with the verse beginning with "Those who," etc., he states the punishment for witnesses who speak falsely, as well as those who are partial and those who are neutral: "Those mortals who are false witnesses, speaking untruthfully in testimony, as well as those who are partial and those who are neutral."
The king, having punished them with severe punishment, should likewise banish them from the country. || 91 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to how many witnesses would constitute valid evidence, he says "six," and so forth: six, four, or three witnesses may be authoritative. O Śivā, in the absence [of such], that is, if there are no three, four, or more witnesses, if [the parties] are well-known and righteous—
Then both would be witnesses; they would be authoritative evidence. || 92 ||

He states with the words "deśataḥ" and so forth that the testimony of witnesses is not authoritative when it is mutually inconsistent due to differences in place and so on: "O dear one, if [the statements] differ by way of place (sthāna), by way of location (deśa), by way of time (kāla)— such as days or watches of the day— and likewise by way of subject matter (viṣaya) or by way of substance (vastu)."
At that time, the testimony of witnesses that is mutually inconsistent and lacks coherence shall be inadmissible. || 93 ||

Now, in response to the doubt as to whether those such as the blind—who are incapable of seeing and so forth—can be witnesses or not, he says "of the blind," and so on: "O beloved, [the witness] of the blind who lack eyes, and likewise of the deaf who lack ears... [and of those who lack speech].

Likewise, for the mute who lack speech, and for those who are both deaf and mute and thus devoid of hearing and speech, the acceptance by nodding the head, as well as writing and letters, would constitute valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). || 94 ||
Writing is the authority for all people and is praised everywhere; it is especially so in legal transactions, since it does not perish for a long time. (95)
If one creates a fabricated document for his own sake or for the sake of another, a punishment shall be imposed upon him; for a false witness, the fine shall be two hundred [paṇas].
When one who is free from pride and vigilant makes a single admission for his own sake, that shall be authoritative even against the testimony of many witnesses. (97)
O Pārvatī, just as merits endure by relying upon truth, so too do all sins endure by relying upon falsehood. 98.
Therefore, by the command of Śiva, the king incurs no sin by striking or subduing one who is devoid of truth and is a refuge for all manner of evil. 99.

Now, by means of the passage beginning with "lipi," [the author] states the excellence of the authority of writing (*lipipramāṇa*) over other authorities, because it endures for a long time. In all matters of action— specifically in all transactions such as buying and selling— writing is the authority for everyone.
It is praised. Showing the reason for its excellence, he says, "it shall not perish," and so forth.
This means that because the script shall not perish for a long time—that is, it shall endure for a long duration—[it is praised]. || 95 ||
Now, he states the punishment for one who fabricates written characters with the words "svīyārtham" and so forth:
for that person who fabricates a written script— whether for his own purpose or for the purpose of another— and for such a person who acts as a false witness, speaking untruth in testimony...
The king shall impose a double fine for stealing two pādas. || 96 ||

In order to demonstrate the extreme excellence of the means of proof consisting of a single-time acceptance made by oneself— by a person who is vigilant and free from delusion— as compared to the words of many witnesses, he says "of one who is not deluded," and so forth.
[This refers to] one who is not deluded (*abhramasya*), meaning free from error, and who is vigilant (*apramattasya*).
The acceptance— that is, the formal admission— even once or a single time by one who is attentive, shall be a proof superior to the testimony of many witnesses regarding one's own matter. || 97 ||

Now, with two verses beginning with "yathā" and ending with "śivājñayā," he declares that while falsehood is the locus of all sins, the king who punishes men based on such [falsehood] is not subject to sin.
O Pārvatī (p.
343), I speak the truth: having formed a resolve and touched the Kaula Guru, the twice-born, the water of the Gaṅgā, the divine form, the Kula scripture, and the Kula nectar—100.
Whether it be regarding the remains of an offering to a goddess or the telling of a secret,
if a mortal speaks a falsehood therein, he shall go to hell until the end of the kalpa.
Whether in abandoning or in undertaking actions that do not produce sin, mortals must by all means fulfill that task which has been accepted under oath. (102)
One may be purified from the transgression of an accepted [vow] by fasting for one fortnight;
even if it was transgressed through delusion, one is purified by eating grains for twelve days.

Just as meritorious deeds abide by relying upon truth, so too do all transgressions abide by relying upon falsehood and untruth. Therefore, for a person who is devoid of truth and is the refuge of all sins, [the king should act] through beating, subduing, and monetary fines.
By the command of Śiva, a king who is deserving of sin shall not partake in that sin. || 98 || 99 ||
Now, defining the nature of the oath, [the author] establishes that a mortal who speaks falsely therein goes to hell by means of two verses beginning with "Truth.
Having made the resolve, "I speak the truth," [one should address] the Kaula, the noble Guru...

Having touched a twice-born Brāhmaṇa who performs rites such as the *niṣeka*, the water of the Gaṅgā (*gaṅgātoya*), the image of a deity (*devamūrti*), a sacred text of the lineage (*kulaśāstra*) such as the Tantras,
the lineage-nectar (*kulāmṛta*) or *āsava*, or the remains of offerings to the Goddess (*devīnirmālya*), one makes a statement of oath.
In that case, a mortal speaking falsely in an oath shall go to hell for the duration of a kalpa, until the end of the kalpa; he shall pass from one hell to another hell. || 100 ||
Now,
with the verse beginning "apāpa," he states the necessity of performing those actions which, by means of an oath,
have been accepted as not producing sin: "of those actions from which there is no *januḥ*, i.e., no production (*utpattiḥ*), of sin."

The meaning is that whatever has been undertaken by mortals, whether through renunciation or even through acceptance under oath, must be carried out in every way and not transgressed. By the phrase "or even through acceptance," it is implied that regarding actions which produce sin, one should only undertake their renunciation.
It is thus intimated that this very [practice] is an obligatory duty. || 102 ||
Now, one might ask: how can a person who has committed an act that produces sin, having previously made a vow not to transgress it, be purified? To this, he says "svīkāra... and so forth:
by means of fasting for one fortnight [following] the transgression of his vow, a person may be purified.
Even if it was done through delusion, one who transgresses that acceptance shall be purified by eating only grains for twelve days. || 103 ||

Even the family tradition (kuladharma), if it is not practiced with truthfulness and according to the prescribed rule, will not lead to liberation or the highest good; in the Kaula system, it leads only to sin. (104)
Sura is liquid in nature, radiant, the sustainer of life, the mother of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and the destroyer of calamities and diseases. (105)
O Beloved, she is the destroyer of the multitudes of sins, the purifier of the worlds, the bestower of all perfections, and the increaser of knowledge, intellect, and learning. (106)

It is always resorted to by the liberated, those seeking liberation, the perfected ones, practitioners, and protectors of the earth, as well as by the gods, for the sake of attaining their primary desired goals. 107.
Those mortals who drink wine according to the correct ritual procedure with a well-composed mind are indeed immortals on this earth. 108.

Now, with the words beginning with "kula," he states that even a family tradition (*kuladharma*) produces sin if it is not practiced according to the prescribed rule: if it were not practiced by means of the true rule,
then even a family tradition would lead to liberation (*apavarga*), or rather, to the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) for one of noble lineage (*kulīna*) within the *Kaula* tradition.
It would not lead to welfare, but would result only in evil; therefore, the family tradition must be observed strictly according to the prescribed rule—this is the intended meaning. || 104 ||

Now, with these three verses beginning with "atha surā," he praises wine: Wine is liquid, having the nature of a fluid; it is *tārā*, that which effects the crossing over [of worldly existence]. It is the savior of living beings (*jīva*), the one who brings about their liberation; it is the mother, the progenitor of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is [the destroyer] of calamities...
It is the destroyer of misfortunes, pains, and diseases. || 105 ||
O beloved, she who burns—that is, consumes—the evil congregations, the masses of sin;
she who purifies—that is, effects the cleansing of—the worlds; she who bestows all perfections, the giver of all *siddhis*; and she who increases knowledge, intellect, and wisdom.

In liberation, *dhī* is wisdom, *jñāna* is the knowledge of the reality of the scriptures and so forth, *buddhi* is the intellect, and *vidyā* is self-knowledge; [the Goddess] is the increaser of these. O Primordial One! [She is worshipped] by the liberated who possess liberation, by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), by the perfected ones (*siddha*), by practitioners (*sādhaka*), and by the protectors of the earth.

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: that which is always served by kings and gods for the sake of attaining their own desired goals—that liquid *surā*, which is *tārā* (the Savior), is to be understood. The word "that" (*yā*) is to be supplied through ellipsis. 106–107.

Having praised *madirā* with the three verses beginning with "Suretyā," he now establishes that one who drinks it according to the prescribed rule attains the state of a god directly, starting with the verse beginning "samyak. Those mortals who, by means of the correct performance of the ritual procedure...

By means of a well-concentrated mind and an extremely attentive intellect, through the formal acceptance of each individual principle (*tattva*) according to the prescribed rite, a man may become Śiva.
I do not know what fruit might arise from the practice of the five principles. (109)
If this goddess Vāruṇī is consumed without following the prescribed rules, she destroys everything—intellect, lifespan, fame, and wealth—of men. (110)
Through excessive drinking of intoxicants, the intellect—which normally accomplishes the fourfold aims of life—is generally destroyed in people whose minds are intoxicated. 111.
From a person whose intellect is bewildered and who does not know what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, both his own misfortune and that of others arise at every step. (112)

Therefore, the king or the lord of the wheel should purify those people who are excessively attached to liquor and intoxicating substances by means of corporal punishment or fines on their wealth. || 113 ||
Those who drink liquor on this earth, on the ground, become indeed immortal gods. || 108 ||

Now, [the author] demonstrates that the five *tattvas*, beginning with wine (*madya*), when consumed according to the prescribed rule, yield an indescribable fruit, by means of the verse beginning with "pratyeka... and so forth. By the acceptance of each individual *tattva* according to the rule—that is, by the adoption of each single *tattva* such as wine and the rest—a person becomes Śiva through all five.
I do not know what fruit would arise from the consumption of the "principles" (tattvas), such as wine and the like.
Now, with the verse beginning "iyam" and so forth, he explains how the drinking of wine that is not performed according to the prescribed rules destroys all things such as intellect and longevity.
If (*ced*) this goddess Vāruṇī, the intoxicating liquor, were drunk in a manner devoid of ritual injunctions, then for men—
It would destroy everything, including intelligence, longevity, fame, and purity. || 110 ||

Since excessive drinking of liquor causes the destruction of the intellect, and because those who have drunk too much liquor are the cause of bringing about harm to themselves and others, [the author] states with the words beginning "excessive" (*atyanta*) that men whose minds are intensely addicted to it should be punished by both the lord of men and the lord of the circle.
By means of these three verses ending with the word "śodhayet" (one should purify),
[it is shown that] for people whose minds are intoxicated by the excessive drinking of liquor,
[this practice] is the accomplisher of the four aims of life— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
The intellect generally perishes. || 111 ||
From this man of deluded intellect, who does not distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done,

his own misfortune and that of others arise at every step; therefore, whether it be a king or a lord of a circle, [he should restrain] those people who are excessively addicted to liquor and intoxicating substances.
One should purify [the offense] by means of corporal punishment, fines, or flogging. || 112 || 113 ||
Due to differences in liquor, differences in individual constitution, or by the variation of place and time—whether by deficiency or excess—there occurs a derangement of the intellect in men. (114)
For this very reason, excessive drinking is not defined merely by the consumption of *surā* liquor;
one should recognize excessive drinking by those whose speech, hands, feet, and eyes falter. (115)
He whose senses are not under control, whose mind is overwhelmed by intoxication, who transgresses the boundaries of the gods and his gurus, is a personification of fear. (116)
The king should burn the tongue, seize the wealth, and beat that sinner who is fit for every misfortune and a slayer of Śiva. || 117 ||
The king shall punish that fierce man who moves his feet, speech, and hands erratically, who is confused, insane, or arrogant, and he shall confiscate his wealth from him.

Because intoxication from substances such as liquor varies in degree— whether slight or excessive— and because it causes a derangement of the intellect, it is impossible to know the extent of one's consumption by that measure alone; therefore, he says that it must be characterized by signs such as faltering speech and so forth.
By means of the two verses ending with "he should investigate by means of surety and so forth," [it is shown that] due to the difference between types of liquor,

the difference between individual persons, the specific nature of the people involved, and the distinction between place and time, the confusion of the intellect of men may occur even through a small or large amount of intoxicant. Therefore, regarding liquor...

Excessive drinking is not perceived through pride alone; rather, one should discern and recognize excessive drinking by the faltering of speech, hands, feet, and eyes, as they wander here and there with words, hands, feet, and eyes unsteady. || 114 ||

Now, with the two verses beginning with "Not the senses," he states the punishment for one who has transgressed the boundaries of gods and gurus and is intoxicated by the wine of the senses: for him whose senses are not under control,
whose mind is overwhelmed by intoxication, and whose heart is agitated by wine.
Of the sinner who transgresses the boundaries of the deities and the guru, who has violated the guru’s boundaries regarding the divine consecration and other rites,
who is the very embodiment of fear, whose nature is terror, who is fit for every misfortune, who deserves all manner of calamity, and who is a refuge for sin.

The king should burn the tongue of a man who harms Śiva, who violates the command of Śiva, who kills him, or who harms his own benefactor; he should confiscate his wealth and beat him. (116–117) Now, he states the punishment for one who is intoxicated by liquor and whose feet and other limbs are unsteady:

With the words beginning "vicalat" and so forth: the king should cause that fierce and cruel man—who has trembling feet, speech, and hands; who stumbles in his gait, words, and gestures; who is confused, possessed by delusion, insane, intoxicated with pride, and ill-mannered—to undergo punishment, and then he should confiscate his wealth. || 118 ||
A king who seeks the welfare of his subjects should punish with the confiscation of wealth that intoxicated person who speaks subversively and is devoid of shame and fear. (119)
O Kuleśvarī, if a Kaula who has received the hundredfold initiation drinks excessively,
he should be considered nothing but a bound soul (paśu), for he has been cast out from the Kula dharma.
One who drinks intoxicants in excess— whether they have been purified or unpurified—
is to be abandoned by the Kaulas and may even be punished by the king.
Twice-born men who, being intoxicated, cause their Brāhmaṇa wives to drink liquor shall be purified together with their wives by subsisting on grains for five days.
One becomes pure by drinking unfermented liquor after fasting for three days;
even having eaten meat that has not been purified, one should perform two fasts.
Now, he states the punishment for one who speaks what should not be spoken and is intoxicated, beginning with the words "apavāk" and so forth:

"The king, who brings joy to his subjects, shall punish that intoxicated man—who speaks words that ought not to be spoken and is devoid of shame and fear—by means of the confiscation of his wealth. (119)

By the words beginning with "śata," [the author] states that even a Kaula who has received the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣikta*) possesses the state of being a *paśu* (an uninitiated soul) because he has been excluded from the Kula-dharma due to excessive drinking of wine.
The word *cet* has the sense of *api*. O Kuleśvarī, even a Kaula who has received the hundredfold consecration, through over-indulgence in drinking...
He must be regarded as nothing more than a beast, since he has been cast out from the family dharma. || 120 ||

Now, with the verse beginning with "piban," [the author] describes how a man who drinks an excessive amount of liquor— whether refined or unrefined— is subject to punishment by the king and is to be censured by his family.
A mortal drinking an excessive or abundant quantity of liquor, whether purified or unpurified...
He must be abandoned by the Kaulas, and he may even be subject to punishment by the king. || 121 ||

Now, one might ask: "How can twice-born men who cause their Brāhmī wives to drink liquor be purified? To this, he says, beginning with the words "brāhmīm" and so forth: "Twice-born men who, being intoxicated, cause their Brāhmī wife—married according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas—to drink *surā* (liquor)..."
Together with his wife, they shall be purified by subsisting on grains for five days. || 122 ||

Now, one might ask: "How can one be purified from drinking unrefined liquor and eating such meat? To this, he says, beginning with the words "asaṃskṛta" and so forth: by fasting for three days—one period of three days—from drinking unrefined *surā* liquor, one is purified; likewise, even after eating unrefined meat.
One should observe two fasts; one should perform them. || 123 ||
On the day of the Mīna-mudrā in the unconditioned [state], one should fast for the day;
by performing the fifth [rite] according to the rule, one is purified from the king’s punishment. || 124 ||
O Śivā, one who knowingly eats the flesh of a human or the flesh of a cow shall become pure by fasting for a fortnight; this is recorded as the expiation.
O beloved, by eating the flesh of a human-shaped beast and the flesh of a meat-eater,
a man may be purified from that sin through three days of fasting.
By eating the food of Mlecchas, Śvapacas, or those who harbor hereditary enmity toward cattle,
one becomes purified by fasting for one fortnight.

O Mistress of the Family, if one should eat the leavings of these [initiates] out of ignorance, O Goddess, he is purified by a month-long fast; if out of ignorance, [he is purified] by a fortnight-long fast. (128)

Now, he states the penance for one who eats fish and meat without purification and for one who engages in non-sacred sexual intercourse, beginning with the words "asaṃskṛte" and so forth: "If a man eats [fish and meat] that are *asaṃskṛta*—that is, unpurified—he shall fast for one day and night. Non-sacred...
A man who engages in the fifth kind of sexual union while devoid of the prescribed ritual is purified by the king's punishment. || 124 ||

Now, one might ask: how can there be purification for a man who knowingly eats human flesh and beef? To this, he says "bhuñjāna" and so forth: O Śivā, [even] one who knowingly eats human flesh—that is, flesh belonging to a human—and beef...
By fasting for one fortnight, a man shall become pure; this is recorded in the Smṛtis as the expiation for eating those two.
Now, one might ask: how can a man who has eaten the flesh of a beast in human form, or who eats the flesh of a meat-eater, be purified?
To this, he says "nara... and so forth. O Dear One, regarding the eating of the flesh of a beast in human form, such as a monkey and the like—
Having eaten the flesh of a meat-eater, such as a tiger or the like, a man shall be purified from the sin by means of three fasts. || 126 ||
Now, he describes the expiation for a man who has consumed the food of Mlecchas and others,
beginning with the words "Of the Mlecchas": "A person eating the food of Mlecchas— Yavanas, Śvapacas— Cāṇḍālas, those who are hereditary enemies, or of animals..."
Having fasted for one fortnight, he shall become purified. || 127 ||

Now, one might ask: how can one who eats food and other things left over by Mlecchas and others be purified through either knowledge or ignorance? To this, he says "the leavings," and so forth: O Kuleśvarī, [regarding] the food and other things left over by these Mlecchas and others, [it is purified] through knowledge.
O Dear One, by eating the food of those of the same caste in the direct order (anuloma) even once, one shall become purified by fasting for three days through my command. (129)
If the food of cattle, dog-cookers, or barbarians has been offered to the Cakra,
or even placed in the hand of a Vīra, one who eats it incurs no sin whatsoever.
In the absence of food, during a famine, in times of calamity, or when life is in danger, one who preserves his life even by consuming forbidden food is not a sinner. (131)
Likewise, on the back of an elephant, or upon various stones and timber intended for transport,
there is no fault regarding the food of those who eat, even if it is not clearly visible.
If he should eat [forbidden food], then a man shall be purified by a month-long fast; if he should eat it through ignorance, then he shall be purified by a fortnight-long fast. || 128 ||

Now, he states the penance for Brāhmaṇas and others who eat the food of Kṣatriyas and so forth in successive order, beginning with the words "anulomena": "O dear one, having eaten the food of the castes once in the direct (anuloma) order, a Brāhmaṇa and others [should perform] a fast for three days."

By my command, he shall become purified. Just as a Brāhmaṇa [is not defiled by] the food of a Kṣatriya, so too, with the words beginning with "paśu," he declares that there is no sin for the one who eats the food of animals, dogs, cāṇḍālas, or mlecchas, provided it has been offered upon the discus or placed in the hand of a hero.

If the food of cattle, dog-eaters, or barbarians has been offered to the Discus (Viṣṇu), given by one who bears the Discus, or placed in the hand of a hero, then a man eating or consuming that food shall not become a partaker of sin. || 130 ||
Anticipating the doubt— namely, whether there might be sin for a person who preserves their life by eating prohibited substances during famine and the like—
he replies with the verse beginning "anna" and so forth. This refers to a time of famine where alms are difficult to obtain, as well as to times of calamity.

In cases such as fleeing from a regional calamity, when there is a lack of food and life is in danger, one who preserves his life— even by consuming what is forbidden or eating that which is unfit to be eaten— shall not become a sinner. || 131 ||
He states by means of the verse beginning with "karī" that there is no fault for those eating food and so forth on a boat or similar vessel:
"on the back of an elephant (karipṛṣṭhe)," meaning on the back of a tusker; likewise, on stones and wooden beams carried by many people;
and similarly, even when unobserved by the Dasyus, such as the Yavanas and others.

This applies to the Yavanas and others: "The Yavanas and so forth reside here"—even when the location is thus unknown, or [as it says on] page 350: "Or [one should avoid] animals whose meat is unfit for consumption, even if they are afflicted by disease, O Dear One."
One should not kill even for the sake of a deity; having killed, one becomes a sinner. || 133 ||
A man should perform the *kṛcchra* vow in the case of the intentional killing of a cow;
if it was done through ignorance, he should perform half the vow, according to the command of Śaṅkara.
One should not have one's hair shaved, nor likewise have one's nails clipped,
nor apply alkaline substances to one's garments, as long as one has not performed the vow.
One should spend one month on fasts, one month eating only grain-particles (kaṇa), and one month subsisting on alms-food; O Śivā, this is the Kṛcchra vow.
Regarding impure substances such as feces and urine, even if they are present and unobserved, no fault regarding the food exists provided they are not recognized. || 132 ||

Now, with the words beginning with "paśūn," [the author] declares the sinfulness of one who kills animals that are unfit for consumption or afflicted by disease for the sake of the deities: "O dear one,
one should not kill animals unfit for consumption or afflicted by disease for the sake of the deities."
The word "api" (even) indicates certainty. Now, [the author] asks: what fault is there in killing? To this he replies with the words "hatvā": having killed, a person becomes a sinner. || 133 ||

Now, he describes the penance for killing a cow committed through knowledge or ignorance, beginning with the words "kṛcchra" and ending with "priye": when a cow is killed intentionally, a man shall perform the *kṛcchra* vow; when a cow is killed unintentionally...
By the command of Śaṅkara, one should observe and perform half of the vow. || 134 ||
"Not with hair" means that as long as he does not perform his vow, he should not undergo the shaving of hair—
that is, the clipping of the hair— nor should he cut his nails, nor should he apply alkaline substances to his garments or clothes. || 135 ||

Now, one might ask: what indeed is the *kṛcchra* vow? Therefore, [the author] defines it with the words beginning "by fasts" (*upavāsaiḥ*) and so forth. O Śivā, one should spend one month by means of fasts;
one should spend one month eating only grains (*kaṇa*); and for one month, [one should subsist on] food obtained through alms (*bhaikṣānna*).
One should eat food obtained through alms; this is to be known as the *kṛcchra* vow.
(136) At the conclusion of the vow, having shaved one's head and fed the *kaula*s, kinsmen, and relatives, one shall be liberated from the sin of killing a knowledge-cow. (137)
O Dear One, one is purified from the sin of failing to protect or from killing a cow by means of eight fasts;
those born of the arms (kṣatriyas) and the others are purified by a quarter less in each successive order.
O Kaulinī, having intentionally killed an elephant, a camel, a buffalo, or a horse,
a man who has committed that sin shall be purified by three fasts.
One who kills a deer, a sheep, a goat, or a cat shall fast for one day; for killing a peacock, a parrot, or a swan, one shall abstain from food as long as the light lasts.

"At the end of the vow" means that at the conclusion of the vow, having had his head shaved (*vāpitaśirāḥ*, i.e., with a shorn scalp), and having fed his *kaula* relatives and those of the same lineage (*sagotra*), a person shall be liberated from the sin of killing a cow through [the power of] knowledge. || 137 ||
Regarding "non-protection": for the killing of a cow due to failing to protect it—that is, from not guarding against its slaughter—one is purified by an eight-day fast.
O beloved, those born of the arms and so forth—the Kṣatriyas and others—should be purified by a sequence [of fasts] decreasing by one quarter. By the Kṣatriyas and the rest, respectively...
The meaning is that the vow must be performed with one foot less [than the full duration]. || 138 ||
Now, he states the penance for killing elephants, camels, and so forth, beginning with the words "gajoṣṭra" and so on:
O Kaulinī, a man who, having committed the sin of intentionally killing elephants, camels, buffaloes, or horses of large body, shall be purified by three fasts. || 139 ||

Now, he describes the expiation for killing deer, sheep, and so forth, beginning with the words "mṛga" and so on: A man who kills a deer, a sheep, a cat, a gazelle, a ram, or a domestic cat (viḍāla) shall fast for one day. [He should likewise do so for] peacocks, parrots, and swans.

A person, while striking [the enemy] with light, should abandon the "sajyotis" meal—that is, eating during the day while the sun is present. The meaning is that one who abandons eating during the day should eat when the sun has set.
Rudra states: "The word *jyotis* is masculine when referring to the sun or fire; it is neuter when referring to a luminary or eyes. (140)
Having killed creatures possessing bones, one should eat at night without meat;
having killed those that live without bones, one is purified by mental remorse. (141)
O Goddess, a lord of the earth who kills beasts, fish, or birds while hunting does not incur sin; for this is the eternal duty of a king. (142)
O auspicious lady, one should avoid violence everywhere except when directed toward the gods;
when violence is performed for the sake of dharma, a man is not stained by sins. (143)
Upon the non-fulfillment of a vowed observance, upon stepping over the remains of an offering to a deity,
or upon touching a deity while impure, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.

Now, with the verse beginning "Having killed," etc., he states the expiation for a man who kills small creatures possessing bones, such as lizards, as well as boneless creatures. Because of their association with [the term] "boneless," one should understand that "possessing bones" refers to small-bodied beings like lizards. Having killed them—
At night, during the evening, one should eat without meat—that is, avoiding meat.

This is because, compared to the killing of peacocks and similar birds, there is a greater inclination toward killing lizards and the like; therefore, [the rule applies] on account of the punishment incurred for that specific killing.

The severity of the punishment for killing creatures such as lizards and the like should be understood [as grave]. One who kills boneless beings—creatures devoid of bones—is purified by mental remorse. || 141 ||
To her who asks, "Surely, for a king who slays deer, fish, and other creatures during the hunt, does sin arise caused by the killing of those animals or not?
he replies with the verse beginning with "paśv" and so forth: "O Queen, [regarding] beasts, fish, and birds..."
A king who kills deer, tigers, fish, birds, and other creatures during the hunt does not become subject to sin; for this constitutes the eternal and perpetual duty (*sanātana dharma*) of a king.
Now, he states that such killing is not to be performed because unrighteous violence (*avaidha-hiṃsā*) produces sin.

With the half-verse beginning "O Goddess": O auspicious one, O doer of good, one should avoid violence everywhere except for acts performed for the sake of the gods. He states that such [ritual] violence must be performed because it does not produce sin, with the half-verse beginning "When it has been committed," regarding ritual violence (*vaidhahiṃsā*).
When this has been performed, a person is not defiled by sins. || 143 ||

Now, one might ask: how can there be purification for a man who does not complete a vowed observance he has resolved upon, who steps over the remains of an offering to a deity (*devanirmālya*), or who touches a deity while impurity (*aśauca*) has not yet passed?
To this, he says "saṅkalpita... and so forth: [regarding] the non-completion of a resolved vow...
The mother, the father, and the giver of the Veda are remembered as great gurus.
By speaking harshly or reviling these, one is purified by five days of fasting. (145)
Likewise, O beloved, even by censuring other gurus, Kaulas, or Brahmins,
one becomes liberated from that sin through two and a half fasts.
A person seeking wealth ought to travel through all lands;
however, one should abandon even the sacred scriptures regarding a land where prohibited Kaulika practices prevail. (147)

If, however, one wanders at will in a region where the path of his family is forbidden, he falls again from the dharma of his lineage; he may be purified only by means of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).

If one fails to complete a vowed observance that was undertaken, or if one steps over the remains of an offering to a deity, or if one touches a deity while being impure or in a state of ritual impurity, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra. || 144 ||

Now, defining the great gurus, [the author] states the expiation for those men who revile or speak cruelly toward them, beginning with the word "mother" (*mātā*). The mother is the progenitress; the father is the progenitor;
and the giver of the Veda (*brahmadātā*), that is, the teacher of the Vedas—these are recorded as the great gurus. These...
A man who reviles his great gurus and speaks cruelly shall be purified by five days of fasting. || 145 ||
Now, with the words beginning with "evam," he states the expiation for those who revile their mother and others, as well as other gurus, Kaulas, and Brahmins: "O Dear One, in this way,
even one who censures or reviles others— meaning gurus, Kaulas, and Brahmins distinct from [one's own] mother and so forth."
A man who speaks cruelly is liberated from that sin by fasting for one and a half days.

Now, with the verse beginning "one who seeks wealth," etc., [the author] states that even a person who is otherwise fit to travel to all lands for the sake of wealth is unfit to wander through regions devoid of the Kaula practice. One who seeks wealth...
A human being may travel to all lands; however, a person should abandon such a land, as well as its scriptures, where the conduct of the Kaulas is prohibited. || 147 ||

Now, with the words beginning with "gacchan," he explains how a man who, out of greed for wealth, goes to a region where the Kaula conduct is prohibited, falls from his family dharma, and is subsequently purified by means of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*). [He speaks thus] regarding one on the prohibited path of the Kula.
(354) Fasting for eight watches (yāmas), beginning from sunrise, should be understood as *upavāsa*; it is prescribed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). || 149 ||
Even while drinking a single handful of water or consuming air, a person does not fall from the state of fasting, provided it is for the sake of preserving life. (150)
If one is unable to observe the fast due to illness or even old age,
then for each day of fasting, one should feed twelve twice-born men.
One who engages in censuring others, praising oneself, speaking what is improper, or performing unwholesome deeds, becomes purified through mental torments. 152.
If a man wanders at will to another region, he falls from his family dharma; he shall be purified again by means of a full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka). || 148 ||
Now, because it was required in the various verses previously mentioned, he defines fasting with the words beginning "tapanodayam" (at the rising of the sun).
Fasting is to be understood as that non-eating which lasts for eight *yāmas*— that is, eight watches— beginning from the rising of the sun (*tapanodaya*).
It is prescribed; it is performed as an expiation. || 149 ||
Now, explaining that fasting is not invalidated by drinking a single handful of water, he says "piban" (drinking): a person who drinks a single handful of water for the sake of preserving life,
and even consuming air (vāyu), shall not fall from his fast.
He shall fall [from his vow]. The truth is that by drinking even a single handful of water, the fast is not destroyed. || 150 ||
Now, he states with the words beginning "upavāse" that if a person is unable to perform a fast due to illness or the like, they should feed twelve Brāhmaṇas for every fast;
[he says this] with the verse beginning "rujā," meaning if, by "rujā" (illness) or by "jarasā" (old age/infirmity).
If a man is unable to observe a fast, then for each fast he should feed twelve twice-born Brāhmaṇas. || 151 ||

Now, he states the expiation for one who engages in such acts as disparaging others and exalting oneself, beginning with the words "paranindām" and so forth. "Paranindām" means the disparagement of another;
"nijotkarṣam" means self-exaltation, that is, speaking of one's own superiority; and "vyasanāyuktabhāṣaṇam" refers to speech associated with vice.
A person who engages in talk connected with slander and the like, as well as improper and unbecoming actions, is purified through mental anguish. || 152 ||
Whatever other sins there may be, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, they are destroyed by the recitation of the Goddess Sāvitrī and by partaking of the Kaula feast. (153)
One should apply the general rules for men to women and eunuchs;
however, there is this specific distinction for women: the husband alone is the great preceptor. 154.

Those men who are afflicted by great diseases and those who have been ill for a long time shall become purified by the gift of gold and thus qualified to participate in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
One should purify a house defiled by a death caused by lightning or fire with oblations performed one hundred times using the Vyāhṛtis.

Now, he states with the words beginning "anyāni" that the destruction of the remaining sins committed both knowingly and unknowingly occurs through the recitation of the Gāyatrī and the consumption of *kaula* food:
"those other sins which have been committed through knowledge and ignorance..."
They perish through the recitation of the Sāvitrī—the goddess Gāyatrī, whose deity is Savitṛ—and through the feeding of those belonging to the Kaula lineage. || 153 ||

Now, he states with the words beginning "sāmānya" that the general rules for men should also be applied to women and to those who are neuter (napuṃsaka). One should apply the general rules for men (*puṃsām puruṣāṇām*) to women, to eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍeṣu*), and to those who are neuter (*napuṃsakeṣu*).
For women, however, the husband alone is traditionally regarded as the supreme guru; this is the specific distinction. (154)

Now, with the verse beginning with "mahāroga," [the author] states that even those long-term sufferers afflicted by great diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) attain the qualification for rites pertaining to the gods and ancestors through the purification resulting from the gift of gold.
Those men who are afflicted by great diseases and those who have been ill for a long time, having become purified by the gift of gold—
They shall be entitled to participate in rites dedicated to the gods and to those dedicated to the ancestors. || 155 ||

Now, one might ask: how is the purification of a house defiled by lightning or by fire caused by a death other than [the aforementioned] "apaghāta"? To this, he says, beginning with "apaghāta... etc. "Apaghātamṛtena" means by one who has met death through an "apaghāta" (accidental or calamitous cause).

That is to say, [a house] destroyed by snakes, tigers, hanging, and so forth; or even one defiled by lightning-fire—one should purify it with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, beginning with *bhūḥ*, through one hundred oblations (*homa*). || 156 ||
(356) From seeing corpses containing bones in large oblong ponds, wells, and tanks, one should remove the carcasses from them and then purify those [sites]. || 157 ||
One should bathe them with pure water consecrated by mantras during the full ablution (pūrṇābhiṣeka), using twenty-one full jars; this is the purification. || 158 ||
If those [wells] should have very little water, being defiled by the foul odor of corpses, one should remove all the muddy water and flood them [with fresh water]. || 159 ||
There are many waters there, each as deep as an elephant;
one should purify [the site] by means of an ablution with water drawn from jars of gold. || 160 ||
If water reservoirs touched by the dead were not purified in this manner, their waters would be undrinkable; one should not even perform their consecration.

Now, with the verse beginning with "vāpī," he describes the general purification of ponds, wells, and other such bodies of water that have been defiled by bones, marrow, or corpses. From ponds, wells, and tanks—
specifically those containing bones (*sāsthnām*), meaning those possessing bones— from the sight of a corpse (*kuṇapa-darśanāt*), that is, from the observation of a dead body within them...
Having extracted a corpse or a dead body from ponds and other such bodies of water, he should then purify those ponds and other locations. || 157 ||

In response to the inquiry "How should one purify?", he explains the method of purification with the words beginning with "pūrṇā": by means of pure waters— sacred waters consecrated with the mantras of the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*.

One should flood those ponds and other water bodies with twenty-one jars—twenty-one being three times seven—full of [the liquid]; this is the purification, and this is the method of purification. || 158 ||

Now, because ponds and other water bodies differ according to whether they contain little water or are filled with much water, he describes the specific method of purification for them in two verses beginning with "yadi" (if).
If those ponds and so forth are defiled by the foul odor of a corpse and contain only a small amount of water, then...
Having drawn out all the water from them along with the mud, he should bathe them in the manner previously described. || 159 ||
"If there are" means: if in those ponds and so forth there exist abundant— that is, many— waters measuring a *gajadaghna*, which is the height of an elephant,
then by means of ablutions with waters from twenty-one jars, using water drawn from jars of gold (*śatakumbha*), [one should honor] them.
One should purify. || 160 ||

Now, with the words beginning "yadi," he explains that ponds and other water bodies that have not been purified become unfit for drinking and unworthy of consecration: "If water reservoirs touched by the dead"—
that is, ponds and so forth touched by corpses— were not thus purified, then their waters would be undrinkable.
(357) For those who bathe with these [impure] waters, their ritual action becomes fruitless. By fasting for one day and consuming the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one shall be purified. || 162 ||
One who sees a beggar as wealthy, a hero as turning his back in battle, a defiler of family traditions, or a woman of noble birth drinking liquor. (163)
Seeing a mortal who betrays his friends or one who is himself devoted to sin,
a wise man should remember Viṣṇu and perform a bath with his clothes on while looking at the sun.
Even if twice-born men sell donkeys, cocks, and pigs,
or follow the livelihood of the low-born, they may be purified by a three-day vow.
One should not perform, nor should one carry out, even the consecration ceremony for those ponds and other structures that have not been purified.
Now, he describes the penance for a man who performs bathing and other rites with water from uncleaned ponds and the like, and the fruitlessness of the rite thus performed,
beginning with the words "snānam" (bathing). Bathing in these [waters] such as uncleaned ponds, and of those...

Furthermore, a man performing other ritual acts with water while remaining without food for one day shall be purified by consuming the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); otherwise, the ritual act being performed would become fruitless.

Now, with two verses beginning with "yācakam," he describes the penance for a man such as one who has seen a wealthy person and a beggar, or a hero who has turned his back in battle, and so forth. [The verse begins: "Having seen a beggar... and "a wealthy person," as well as "one who has turned his back in battle."

Upon seeing a hero who has turned his back on battle, a brave man who defiles the traditions of his lineage, a woman of noble family who drinks liquor, a mortal who betrays his friends, or even a wise and learned scholar who is himself devoted to sin— one should look at the sun or Viṣṇu.
A man, remembering [this], should perform his bath while still wearing his clothes and garments. (163–164)
Now, one might ask: how can there be purification for twice-born men who sell donkeys and the like, or who engage in low occupations? To this, he says "kharādi" and so forth:
those who sell donkeys, cocks, and boars—that is, donkeys, birds with claws, and pigs—and even those who practice low occupations.
By performing this for three days, the twice-born Brāhmaṇas shall be purified. || 165 ||
O Ambikā, one should spend the first day without food, the second subsisting on grains, and the third day with only water; such is the vow for three days.
A man who enters a house with its door unopened without being invited,
or who speaks of matters that have been forbidden, shall abstain from food for five days.
He who, filled with pride, does not rise upon seeing his elders approaching,
as well as those who similarly disregard the family scriptures, shall be purified by a single fast.
In this Śāmbhava scripture, which is expanded by words of clear meaning, those who imagine a meaning through [arbitrary] code-words fall and go to a downward state. 169.

Now, one might ask: what is this three-day vow? To this, he says "dinam" and so forth. Being without food (*nirāhāra*), one should spend—that is, pass—one day; being subsisting on grains (*kaṇabhojana*), one should spend the second day;
and the other, the third day, one should spend with water alone (*adbhiḥ*). O Ambikā, this is the three-day vow.
Thus it is remembered. || 166 ||

Now, with the words beginning with "gṛhe," the author states the penance for one who enters a house whose door is closed without being invited, and speaks to prevent [the person inside] from being restrained. A man who enters a house whose door is not opened—
that is, whose door is barred— without being invited, even if he speaks to prevent [the occupant] from being restrained...
Even a man who speaks of a matter that has been forbidden should abstain from food for five days.
Now, regarding the penance for a man who approaches his father or other elders, or who rises [to greet them] after having examined the family scriptures, he says: "Upon approaching..."

By such statements as these: "If one who is filled with pride (*madānvita*) does not rise upon seeing elders such as his father or others approaching, or likewise upon seeing the family scriptures (*kulaśāstra*) approaching, he shall be purified by a single fast (*ekopavāsa*).
By the phrase "filled with pride," it is implied that there is no fault for one who does not rise due to incapacity caused by illness or similar reasons.
Thus it is intimated that [the speaker] shares in the fault. || 168 ||

Now, with the words beginning "In this," [the author] states the state of falling and downward descent for those who, under the guise of words, imagine other meanings within this scripture proclaimed by Śambhu.

O Goddess, this which is more essential than the essence, supreme among the supreme, bestowing the goals of this world and the next, righteous, purifying, and beneficial— has been told to you in words expanded by clear meaning and augmented by distinct expressions. (170)
Thus, in the glorious Mahānirvāṇa Tantra, the most supreme among all tantras,

the essence of the determination of all dharmas, within the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva, this is the chapter titled "The Description of Expiation for Sins that Cause One's Own or Others' Misfortune."
The Eleventh Chapter:

In this scripture proclaimed by Śambhu within the Śāmbhava tradition, those men who, under the pretext of "kūṭa"— that is, through verbal deception— fabricate meanings, fall and go to a downward state.
"Kūṭa" is used in the feminine gender to denote magical illusions, immovable machines, heaps of deceit and falsehood, an iron mace, a mountain peak, and the pole of a plough; thus says Amara.

Concluding the meaning of the section, he says "This," and so forth: "O Goddess, this is the essence of essences, more logical than the logical, higher than the highest, superior even to the most excellent,
bestowing the goals of this world and the next, yielding fruit in both this world and the hereafter, and righteous."

This which is not deviating from the Dharma, which is purifying, which brings about purity, and which is the cause of welfare has been told to you. Regarding the word *sāra*, Amara states: "It means strength, the solid part, and what is just; it is neuter when meaning excellent, and is used in three genders. Regarding the word *artha*, Amara states: "It means the expressed meaning, wealth, substance, purpose, and cessation."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. In the twelfth chapter,
the venerable Sadāśiva said:
O foremost one, I shall further declare to you the eternal legal procedures, by protecting which and understanding which, a king may govern his subjects according to his own will. || 1 ||
Without the rule of law, men greedy for wealth will dispute among themselves with their teachers, kinsmen, and relatives. (2)
Then, O Goddess, those seeking their own interests for the sake of wealth will strike one another down;
they will become the refuge of sin through violence and the desire to plunder.
Therefore, for their benefit, a discipline approved by Dharma is enjoined, relying upon which men shall not fall away from what is auspicious. (4)
Oṃ! Homage to Brahmā!
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, the supremely compassionate Mahādeva began once more to recount the eternal customs to Pārvatī.

With the words "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) and so forth: O first one, I shall tell you again— either to you or in your presence— those eternal and perpetual worldly transactions (*vyavahārān*), by protecting and maintaining which, and by knowing them thoroughly, a king may act according to his own will.
He should protect his subjects by governing them at his own will. || 1 ||
Due to the absence of restraint among the lords of the earth, men who crave wealth will engage in mutual disputes with their fathers and others; therefore,
Sadāśiva, desiring the welfare of the world, [will appear] to resolve them.
Just as a king should punish evildoers for the sake of removing their evil, so too should he distribute the inheritances of men according to the distinctions of their relationships. (5)
The relationship is to be known as twofold: through marriage and likewise through birth; therein, the relationship arising from birth is more powerful than that arising from marriage. (6)
In the *dāya* [of the lineage], O Śivā, the downward connection is considered superior to the upward one;
here, according to the sequence from below to above, the male is remembered as being more primary.

He establishes the rule by means of the three verses beginning with "by means of a rule" (*niyamena*) and ending with "men from auspicious [lineages]" (*śubhānnarāḥ*). O Goddess, because, in the absence of a rule, those men within the kingdom of a king—
those humans who are greedy for wealth, being intensely attached to the objects of riches— [act as they will].

They will dispute with one another along with their teachers, kinsmen, and relatives; likewise, in the absence of restraint at that time, those seeking their own interests and desiring wealth will strike one another down for the sake of riches, out of a desire to seize property through the wish to plunder wealth.

And through violence they will become reliant on evil. Therefore, for the benefit of those people, I ordain and set forth that law which is approved by righteousness— a law relying upon which men shall not fall away from or descend into what is auspicious and good.

Regarding the phrase "vyatighnantīti" (they strike down), the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the future according to the rule *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat* ("when there is proximity to the present, it is treated as the present"). Now, one might ask: by resorting to what rule would men not fall away from prosperity? To that, he says, beginning with "daṇḍayet" (he should punish): just as a king, a lord of men.

For the removal of evil and the destruction of sin, he should likewise punish sinful people; furthermore, he should divide—that is, apportion—the inheritances and wealth of men according to the distinctions of their relationships. *Dāya* (inheritance) refers to giving or wealth, and as a masculine noun it denotes the giver. (Verse 5)

Now, Mahādeva, while explaining the twofold nature of the relationship relevant to the partition of inheritance based on marriage and birth, establishes the superiority of the relationship by birth over the relationship by marriage with the words beginning "sambandha" (relationship).
From marriage as well as from birth— that is, from origin— the relationship is to be known as being of two kinds or two types. Among those two relationships,
the relationship by birth is stronger than the relationship by marriage.
It is to be known. || 6 ||

Regarding the taking of inheritance, [the author] states with the words "But in the case of inheritance" (*dāye tu*) and so forth that, in relation to those above, the connection belonging to those below alone possesses primacy;
and furthermore, according to the sequence from below to above, he declares that among women, the male alone is more preeminent. O Śivā, in the matter of inheritance...
Even in that case, one who is related by proximity is entitled to a share.
By this rule, the wise should divide the wealth in due order. (8)
When a man has died, while his son, grandson, daughters, and father are still living,
as well as his wife, the son alone is entitled to the inheritance and no one else.
Where there are many sons, all of them share equal portions;
however, the right to the kingdom belongs to the eldest, according to the tradition of the lineage.
However, regarding wealth,

the lower relationship (the relationship with those in a lower state of existence) is considered superior— that is, more excellent— than the higher relationship (the relationship with those in a higher state of existence). By the word "however" (tu), it is indicated that in matters such as salutation, the lower relationship is [superior].
It is implied that, regarding the relationship, the subsequent relationship alone is superior.

In this matter of inheriting the estate, according to the sequence from below upwards, the male person is recorded in the legal tradition as being more principal—that is, more preeminent—than the female. || 7 ||

Now, between one who is near and one who is not near, which one would be entitled to the inheritance? To this he says: "In that case also. Even among those who are more primary [in status], the relative who is connected by proximity—that is, by physical presence—is entitled to the inheritance; he becomes the rightful heir to the wealth. By this...
By the previously stated procedure, the wise and learned should divide and distribute the wealth in due order. || 8 ||

Now, among the wife, daughters, father, sons, and grandsons of a man who has met his death, whose right is it to take that wealth? To this he replies with the words beginning "of the deceased," etc.: "of the deceased human being."

When a son, grandson, and father are present, as well as daughters born of one's own body and a wife, the son alone is entitled to the inheritance because he is proximate, because he is preeminent by virtue of being male, and because he is superior due to his status as the offspring.

Nor would another person distinct from him, such as a grandson and so forth, be entitled to the inheritance; for the grandson is more remote than a son, while the wife and daughters are subordinate by virtue of being female, and the father, being a superior, is not [the primary claimant] because he exists after [the deceased]. This is the meaning. || 9 ||
Now, a question arises: when a king who has many sons passes away, do all his offspring have an equal share in the immovable and movable property, or do they receive unequal shares? To this, he says:

By the verse beginning with "bahavaḥ" [and so forth]: where there are many sons entitled to shares in any property of a king, whether immovable or movable, they shall all discharge that paternal debt from the paternal assets.
While he remains, the paternal wealth shall not be subject to partition.
If men should take paternal wealth after having divided it,
the king, having recovered that property from them, shall cause it to be given to the ancestors.
Just as men go to hell because of the evil they themselves have committed, so too are they bound by their own debt; it is not anyone else. 13.
The meaning is that they should be equal sharers, not those possessing unequal shares.

Now, an objection is raised: since it is both heard in scripture and observed in practice that, for the most part, the eldest son alone of a sovereign holds the right to the kingdom, how can it be said that "all there are equal sharers"? To this, he replies:

"Eldest," and so forth. That which constitutes the right to the kingdom for the eldest son of a king is to be understood according to the lineage (*vaṃśa*). If, within the lineage, only the eldest son receives the kingdom, then the right to the kingdom belongs to him alone; [it does not belong] to others.

[They become] recipients of food, clothing, and vessels; otherwise, however, the meaning is that everyone would take possession of all the wealth, such as the earth and so forth, after dividing it up. || 10 ||

Having paid the paternal debt, the remaining paternal property is to be divided by the brothers; this is stated by the verse beginning with "the debt" (*ṛṇam*). That which is the paternal debt—meaning the debt related to the father—is [to be paid] from the paternal assets, meaning the wealth related to the father.
One should clear [the debt]. While that debt remains outstanding, the paternal wealth—the property—would not be subject to division, meaning it would not be fit for partition. || 11 ||

The king should cause those mortals who have taken paternal property by dividing it, without having cleared the paternal debt, to pay that debt; this is stated by the words beginning with "vibhajya" (having divided).
If men, having divided the paternal wealth or property...
Then, having recovered and taken that paternal wealth from those men, the king, the ruler, shall cause them to pay the debt belonging to the ancestors. || 12 ||

Regarding the non-clearance of debt, he states with an illustration that the debtor alone shares in the fault, beginning with the words "Just as... Just as human beings go to hell (niraya) due to the sin committed by themselves, so too one becomes bound by debt oneself.
Nor could there be any other, distinct from that, who would be bound. || 13 ||
Whatever property is common, whether immovable or movable, the sharers are entitled to receive their respective shares according to the partition. (14)
Partition is established only when the sharers themselves agree; if they do not agree, the king shall distribute the shares with impartiality.
The king shall divide the value, or the proceeds from the sale, of immovable property, as well as movable property that is unfit for partition, among the sharers. || 16 ||
Even when the wealth has been divided, he who should claim his own share may have that property divided again and cause it to be given to one who did not receive a share. || 17 ||
He states, beginning with the words "sādhāraṇam" (common), that regarding all property— whether immovable or movable— all heirs have an equal right to take their shares.
That which is common or general, whether it be immovable or otherwise movable, is what is meant by "sādhāraṇa."
In that regard, all the sharers are entitled—that is, they are fit—to receive and obtain their respective shares from the division of the wealth. || 14 ||
He states with the half-verse beginning "of the sharers" (*aṃśinām*) that the division can only be accomplished when there is mutual consent among all the sharers.
Partition occurs only when there is agreement among the sharers, that is, those who are to receive the portions.

It is accomplished and brought to completion, but not otherwise. Now, one might ask: "In the case of the partition of paternal property, how can a division take place in the absence of the consent of all the heirs?
To this, he says, beginning with the words "teṣām" (of them): "In the event that there is no consent of those who are the sharers..."
The king should distribute the share—that is, the portion—with impartiality and an equal eye.
Now, one might ask: how can there be a division of an object such as immovable property, which is unfit for division?
To this, he says "of immovable property," etc.; that is, the value of an object—whether immovable or movable (jaṅgama)—which is unfit for division and incapable of being partitioned.

The king, the ruler, shall divide that property which belongs to them, as well as any other substance produced therein, among the sharers—the heirs—in order to cause it to be given to them; he shall effect its distribution. In the term "aṃśinām," the genitive case is used because the recipient (the dative) is intended to be expressed as a subordinate element (śeṣa).
"In the remainder" is the genitive case. || 16 ||
Now, even when the goods have been divided and taken by the co-sharers,
if they inform the king in the presence of witnesses that this is their own portion, the king should again divide those goods and cause them to be given back to those very persons; thus he says.
Once the division of the property has been completed with the consent of the owners, O Auspicious One, anyone who initiates a lawsuit regarding it again shall be punished by the king. (18)
When the grandson of the deceased, the wife, and the father are all present, the grandson alone shall be entitled to the wealth, due to the priority of his birth. (19)
While the father and the uterine paternal grandfather are alive,
the father alone shall take the wealth of the sonless man, on account of his proximity by birth.
"O beloved, even though daughters are present and nearby, the grandson of the deceased shall inherit the wealth, because he is the primary male heir. (21)

By the words "even when divided," etc.: even when the wealth has been divided— that is, partitioned— if a person should establish his own share, his own portion, before the king by means of witnesses, then for that person who has not received his share, [the king shall restore] that [wealth].
Having divided the property, the king shall cause it to be given by the heirs.

He states with the words beginning "kṛte" that once all the heirs have reached an agreement and the division of property has taken place, if a person should again engage in dispute over that matter, he shall be punished by the king. O Śivā, when there is agreement among the sharers...
When a division of property has been made, a person who subsequently initiates a dispute regarding that division of property becomes subject to punishment by the king, the ruler.
Now, among the father, the wife, and the son’s sons who exist after a man has died, whose is the entitlement to that wealth?
To this he replies with the words beginning "sthite": "When the son’s son and the father of the deceased man are both present."

And when the wife remains below, those whose birth [occurs] beneath her—due to their respectability and weight—the grandson alone shall be the heir to the wealth, being worthy of the inheritance. || 19 ||
Now, among the father, the paternal grandfather, and uterine brothers who are living, which one among them shall take the property of a deceased man who has no son?
To this, he says "of the sonless," and so forth: "of a person who has died without a son."

While the father, the uterine brother, and the paternal grandfather are still living, the father alone shall take— that is, receive— the wealth of this sonless man, on the grounds of his proximity to birth, that is, his close kinship.

He states with the words "vidyamānāsu" and so forth that, even when daughters who are closer [in kinship] exist, the grandson alone is the heir to the wealth because the male is more important for one who has departed for heaven and has no son. O beloved, for a deceased man...
When a son has died, the paternal grandfather’s wealth passes to his grandson;
therefore, it is said by people in this world that the father himself takes the form of the son. (22)
Even in the case of a marriage alliance, a wife wedded according to the Brāhma rite is most excellent;
she who takes half the body of her husband shall inherit his estate if he dies without a son.
But a woman who has lost her husband and sons, even if she has acquired wealth from her master, is not at all capable of giving it away or selling it without her own property. 24.

Since a man (pumān) is the most eminent (mukhyatara) and the most principal (pradhānatara) among all available girls— whether they be nearby or not— he alone, as the son of the grandson (pautra), shall be the heir to the wealth. || 21 ||
Now, explaining how the father himself takes on the form of a son through a specific cause,
[the author] restates that for a deceased man who has no son, the right to the wealth belongs to the grandson alone,
beginning with the words "The wealth," and so forth; because the wealth [was received] from the grandfather by the deceased son...

Because he goes to or enters the grandson (pautra), for this reason, in this worldly existence (saṃsāra), the father himself is sung of—that is, designated—by people as being "in the form of a son. || 22 ||
Now, it is said— in the passage beginning with "Even in the case of the wedding"— that between the two wives, Brāhmī and Śaivyā,

Brāhmī alone is the most excellent, as she is the one who takes possession of the wealth of her deceased husband who died without a son, even though that wealth was acquired on account of the wedding. "Even in the case of the wedding" (audvāhike) means even in the matter caused by the marriage.

In the matter of marriage, a Brāhmī wife—one wedded according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas—is superior to a Śaivī wife; she is the most excellent because she takes half the body of her husband, the master. Therefore, for one who is sonless or lacks progeny, only a Brāhmī wife [is truly his].

She shall take the inheritance—the wealth—of her deceased husband. The phrase "of one without a son" (*aputrasya*) is an elliptical expression meaning "devoid of sons, grandsons, and so forth. According to Amara, *varīyān* is a synonym for *uru* and *vara*. Furthermore, according to Amara, *riktha*, *ṛktha*, *dhana*, and *vasu* are synonyms for wealth. || 23 ||

Now, it is said that a woman who is deprived of her husband and sons, even if she has obtained her master’s wealth, is unable to give it away or sell it; this is expressed by the verse beginning with *patiputra* and so forth:
"A woman deprived of husband and sons, having obtained—that is, acquired—the wealth of her master..."
She would not be capable or able to take it or sell it, except for her own wealth; the meaning is that she is able to give or sell her own property. || 24 ||
That which is given by her father or her father-in-law, or that which is acquired through her own efforts, is proclaimed to be woman’s property (strīdhana) in accordance with the Dharma. (25)
When she has died, that inheritance shall again go to the position of the owner;
then the one most closely related [to her] shall take the inheritance, according to the sequence of those below and above.
When her husband has died, she remains under the authority of her husband's kinsmen by virtue of her own duty;
in their absence, remaining under the authority of her father's kinsmen, she is entitled to the inheritance.
Even if she is suspected of infidelity, she does not become an heir to her husband's property;
she receives only a means of subsistence from the husband who has seized his wealth.
Now, what indeed is called "women's property" (strīdhana)? To this he says, beginning with the words "by fathers," etc.

Since the plural number indicates many [sources], it refers to that wealth which has been given—whether by "fathers" such as the biological parents, or by "husbands' fathers" such as the father-in-law—in accordance with the Dharma, or that which she has acquired through her own efforts.
That which is acquired through one's own craft or similar activities is proclaimed—that is, declared—to be *strīdhana* (woman's property).
Now, one might ask: "When a woman who has acquired her husband's wealth dies, to whom does that property belong? To this, he says, beginning with the words "tasyām" (in her):
"When that woman who has acquired her husband's wealth has died, her inheritance..."

Furthermore, the wealth shall go to, or reach, the status of the owner. And that inheritance, having reached the status of the owner, shall be taken by the person most closely related to the owner—extremely near—according to the order of descent and ascent. This has been stated in general; however, the specific details will be explained further on. || 26 ||
