When the husband has died, a woman remains under the authority of her husband’s kinsmen and so forth, abiding by her own duty; she is entitled to her husband’s inheritance, as stated in the verse beginning with "mṛte" (when dead).
When the husband, the master, has died, she remains under the authority of her husband’s kinsmen, abiding by her own duty; and in their absence...
In the absence of her husband's kinsmen, a woman remaining under the authority of her father's kinsmen is entitled to the inheritance, the wealth of her husband. || 27 ||
A woman suspected of infidelity, however, is entitled only to food and clothing, and not to a share of her husband's wealth; this is stated by the verse beginning with "śaṅkitā" and so forth.
Even a woman suspected of infidelity is a sharer in her husband's inheritance.
(368) O lady of pure smiles, if that deceased man has many wives devoted to dharma, they shall share their husband’s wealth in equal portions. (29)
When the husband who took the wealth has died and the son of the husband remains,
the woman shall return to her own master's position, and the wealth shall go to the daughter.
When the daughter remains thus [unmarried], the inheritance passes to her son's wife;
upon her death, it reaches the husband, and from the father-in-law it goes to his daughter.

However, she obtains nothing more than mere subsistence from a man who robs her husband of his wealth. By using the word "api" (even), Sadāśiva has revealed that for a woman who commits adultery, there is absolutely no entitlement to her husband's inheritance.
This has been indicated by the word "not" (na). That by which one lives, such as food and so forth, is "living" (jīvana);

the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), according to the rule "in the sense of an instrument or a locus. According to Amara, "mātra" signifies entirety or restriction. || 28 ||

If the deceased has many wives devoted to dharma, they should all divide and take the husband’s property; this is what [the author] states with the words beginning "many" (*bahvyaḥ*). O lady of pure smiles—whether meaning one with a beautiful, gentle smile or one with a pure, gentle smile—for that man who has departed to heaven...

If there are many wives for a man who has gone to heaven— one who was devoted to dharma and dedicated to merit— then all of them shall share their husband’s wealth equally, that is, in equal portions. || 29 ||

He states by means of the verse beginning with "of the husband" (*patyuḥ*) that when a woman who has obtained her husband's wealth dies, that wealth returns to her original owner and from there passes to his daughter. [This refers to] one who takes the husband's wealth— that is, one who seizes the property of her master.
Upon the death of the wife and while the daughter remains alive, the wealth returns to its original owner; having reached that status of the owner, it goes to the daughter and then to her son.
By using the expression "husband's son," Mahādeva indicates that the wealth does not go to a daughter who is purchased or otherwise acquired.
"He should go"—thus he indicated. || 30 ||

When a woman who has received her husband's property dies, that property—having first gone to the husband and then to the father-in-law—shall go to the daughter-in-law; thus he says with the words beginning "In this way," etc., regarding the case of a maiden. In this manner, by this method, in the case of a maiden...
When she remains [alive], the inheritance— the wealth belonging to the son’s wife—
goes to her husband upon his death; then, upon the death of the son’s wife,
it goes again to the husband, and from the father-in-law, it goes to his daughter.
She should go as if she were her father-in-law’s daughter. Likewise, when the grandfather has passed away, the wealth belonging to the mother goes to Śiva;
once she has died, it shall belong to her son through her husband, as if it were his father-in-law's property. (32)
Just as the father of the deceased obtains the wealth that has gone upward after death,
so too does the mother obtain it, provided she be without a husband.
Therefore, while the biological mother is alive, the stepmother shall not take the wealth;
upon the death of the mother, having obtained it, he may go to the stepmother with his father.
Just as, due to the absence of those below, wealth does not go downward, so too that which has reached the lower [state] shall proceed upward by that very same means. || 35 ||
In the phrase "tan-mṛte" (in his death), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) according to the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*.
This [rule] should be understood as applying when there is an absence of [relations] starting from the husband’s daughter and ending with the brother’s son. || 31 ||

Now, one might ask: "When a mother who has already obtained sons and wealth dies, to whom does that wealth belong? To this, he says, beginning with the word *tathā*: "O Śivā, in that same manner (*tathā*), while the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*) is still living, [the property] belonging to the mother—that which was acquired by the mother—"

When that mother has died, her wealth (vittam) shall go to her son (putreṇa), her own offspring (ātmajena), and her husband (bhartrā); "it shall go to the father-in-law" (śvaśuragam) means it shall go to the father-in-law (śvaśuram).
[The form] *sanneva* is *sattvam*, where the suffix *tva* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). This [rule applies] to the son and his uterine brothers.
And it should be understood that this applies to the non-existence of his sons as well. || 32 ||

He states, by means of the two verses beginning with "of the deceased," that even when a man who has met his death— being devoid of [relatives] from son down to father— his wealth is seized by the mother and the father, and upon his death, it belongs even to his brother. Regarding the deceased person, "gone upwards" (*ūrdhvagata*) means having reached the state above.
Just as the father of a deceased person obtains that wealth, so too does her mother obtain it if she should become deprived of her husband, that is, bereft of her master. || 33 ||

"From this [it follows]" means: while the biological mother is alive, the stepmother shall not take his wealth, but the mother alone shall take it; however, upon the death of the mother, that wealth, having reached the son, shall go from the father to the stepmother. || 34 ||

Due to the absence of any heirs belonging to the lower realms to take the inheritance, the wealth that would otherwise descend downward instead ascends upward, thereby belonging to the childless woman who has received her brother's property.
When a sister has died, her property remains with her;

therefore, when a paternal uncle is present, both the wealth of the uncle and that which belonged to the sister should be considered his. If she dies childless while her husband is still living, she should then resort to her paternal uncle. (36)
Wealth descending from above reaches below and takes hold of the man;
therefore, when a uterine sister exists, the half-brother shall take the inheritance.
When the sister and the offspring of the stepmother have both passed away,
the wealth belonging to the half-brother shall be inherited by the lineage of that half-brother.
He states precisely that there would be dependence upon paternal uncles by means of the two [verses] beginning with "adhastanānām" (of those below).
When, due to the absence or non-existence of the people dwelling below— those who are lower—
the inheritance or wealth does not go down, then by whichever person...
Having obtained wealth from a person belonging to a lower level or a lower realm, one should go or proceed upward by means of that very same person. || 35 ||

Regarding the phrase "ataḥ" (therefore) and so forth: because the inheritance of those below [the deceased] is absent and because it moves upward, when a sister— who is childless, being devoid of both son and daughter— dies while her paternal uncle is present and her husband is [also] present...

Even when the husband of the sister is present, she should resort to her paternal uncle for the wealth belonging to her sister; he, along with her brother, father, and others, should maintain the paternal uncle [of that sister]. By the qualification "childless," it is indicated that in the case of the death of a sister who has children, [the rule regarding] the wealth belonging to her [does not apply].
Thus he indicated that it would surely go to his offspring. || 36 ||

Because wealth obtained from above or below depends upon the person [who received it], it would go to the half-brother even when a uterine sister exists; thus he says "from above," etc. For wealth—that is, property—is obtained from above or below.
Since he relies upon and takes refuge in a male person, therefore, even when a uterine sister exists, the half-brother born of a different mother shall take the inheritance. || 37 ||
Now, one might ask: "If a uterine sister and the offspring of a stepmother both exist, who should obtain the wealth belonging to that [stepmother's son] upon his death?
To this, he replies with the words beginning with "sthitāyām" (if she exists): "While a uterine sister exists, [the inheritance goes to her], not to the offspring of the stepmother."

And while she remains alive, the wealth belonging to the half-brother shall, upon his death, be enjoyed—that is, inherited—by the half-brother's lineage, meaning by the offspring of the stepmother. || 38 ||
O Śivā, when a man has died, his uterine brother and likewise his half-brother shall divide the paternal wealth equally as co-sharers. (39)
If the daughter is still living, her offspring does not inherit that property;
whatever wealth was set aside for her shall go to another upon her death. (40)
In the absence of sons, the daughters shall divide the father's wealth among themselves, provided they marry any unmarried sisters using the common property of the father. (41)
Upon the death of a woman who leaves no offspring, her property shall go to her husband;
however, whatever other wealth she acquired from another person, that shall revert to the status of its original source.

He states with the words "of the deceased," etc., that for a man who has died without offspring ranging from sons down to a mother, both his uterine brother and his half-brother have equal shares in that wealth.
O Śivā, for a deceased person, the uterine brother... [and so forth].

And the uterine brother and the half-brother, being equal sharers in that wealth by virtue of its having originated from the father, shall divide that wealth; the meaning is that they should take it after having divided it. || 39 ||

He states by means of the verse beginning with "kanyāyām" that while the daughter is living, her offspring does not have a share in the inheritance; the meaning is that as long as the daughter is alive, her offspring shall not be an heir to the property, but rather the daughter herself shall be the heiress. Where...

Whatever wealth or property a person possesses that may cause him distress, upon his death— that is, when that distressing person has died— that wealth shall go to, or pass into the hands of, another person.
By the words "they should divide," and so forth, [the author] states that daughters should marry their unmarried sisters using the paternal assets held in common,
and that upon the death of a father who leaves no son, all [the daughters] should divide and take the father's wealth. This applies when there is an absence of sons for the father.

Daughters who marry their father’s unmarried—meaning unmarriageable—daughter using common or shared wealth shall divide the father’s property, his assets; by the word "tu" (but), it is indicated that even the daughter being married herself shall share in the paternal estate. 41.

He states with the verse beginning "asantatyā" that the woman’s property belonging to a deceased woman who leaves no offspring reverts to her owner; however, as for other property acquired by her, it reverts to whoever was the source from which she obtained it.
A woman may provide for her own maintenance with wealth obtained by her deceased husband;
however, she is not empowered to give away or sell his property, as it remains under his control. (43)
And when the paternal grandmother’s daughter-in-law—
the father’s stepmother— is present, the paternal estate shall go to her son through that daughter-in-law.

When the grandfather, the paternal uncle, and likewise the brother are living, the brother alone shall be the sharer of the wealth, because he is the foremost among those belonging to the lower generation. || 45 ||

The woman's property (strīdhana) shall belong to her husband—that is, her spouse—if she has died without offspring, being devoid of a lineage; he shall serve and maintain it. However, as for other wealth—any property obtained or received from another person—he shall resort to and maintain that specific source [from whom it was acquired]. || 42 ||

A woman who is unable to give away or sell wealth obtained from the deceased shall enjoy it until her death; moreover, she may perform religious duties with the property belonging to that [deceased] relative.
This is stated by the verse beginning with "pretalabdhaiḥ" and so forth: "With wealth obtained from the deceased (pretalabdha)—that is, with riches acquired from one who has died—a woman..."

A woman should provide for her own nourishment and maintenance; however, she should perform meritorious religious duties (puṇya-dharma) with wealth other than that—namely, with assets acquired in addition to or separate from those [given by her husband]. She shall not be empowered or capable of giving them away or selling them. || 43 ||

Now, regarding the doubt as to whether the property of a deceased man who is destitute of everyone from sons down to paternal uncles should go to his paternal uncle’s wife or to his father’s sister-in-law (paternal aunt), he says "the grandfather's daughter-in-law," and so forth. [In the case] of the grandfather's daughter-in-law...

When the grandfather’s daughter-in-law— that is, his father’s wife— and his father’s stepmother are both present, the paternal grandfather’s inherited wealth and property shall go to his son, the grandson, who approaches the daughter-in-law, the wife of his [the grandfather's] son. (44)
Now, regarding a deceased man who is destitute of all [heirs] from sons down to the mother,

among his existing paternal grandfather, paternal uncle, and brothers, which one among them shall have a share in that wealth? To this, he replies with the two verses beginning with "the paternal grandfather."

While the grandfather, the paternal uncle, and the brother are alive, the brother alone shall be the sharer of the wealth because he is the foremost and principal among those belonging to the lower generation. From the deceased son, the wealth that had gone to the father belongs to the deceased's brother alone.
The meaning is that one should worship. || 45 ||
In this matter, due to proximity, the brother and the paternal grandfather are equal [in right] to the paternal uncle.
Having reached the status of a father regarding the wealth, the [wealth] should go to the brother of the deceased. (46)
Even when the daughter’s offspring exists, if the deceased father remains [as the primary heir],
the daughter’s offspring is the sharer of the wealth, because the wealth flows downward.
While his father has departed for heaven and his mother likewise remains in the state of Kālikā,
the father, by virtue of being the primary person, shall be the taker of the wealth.
Even while the maternal uncle is still living,
one who is sapinda with his father shall be the taker of the deceased's wealth, due to the weight of the paternal relationship.

Regarding the phrase "from the paternal uncle" (*pitṛvyāt*): in this world, although the brother and the grandfather are equal and identical in their proximity or closeness to one's father, nevertheless, because those situated below [in the hierarchy] are primary,
the wealth of a person who has departed for heaven goes to the brother after reaching the status of the father.
One should worship. || 46 ||

Now, one might ask: among the father and the daughter’s son—who are both present—of a deceased man who is otherwise destitute of offspring from sons down to daughters, which of the two shall take his wealth?
To this, he says "sthite" and so forth. [This refers to] the *preta*, the deceased person.

Since the wealth would be turned downward (lost) even when the father is present and the daughter's offspring is also present, therefore the daughter's offspring alone shall be the heir to the wealth. || 47 ||

Because among a deceased man and his living parents, the male is predominant, it is said— in the passage beginning with "svaḥprayātuḥ"— that the father alone is the inheritor of that wealth. O Kālikā, when the father (tāte) of the person who has departed for heaven (svaḥprayātuḥ), i.e., the deceased, is still present, likewise...
While the mother remains alive, the father shall be the taker of the wealth by reason of his being the primary [kinsman]. || 48 ||

Now, between the maternal uncle and the paternal *sapinda* who both exist for a deceased man, which one is entitled to that wealth? To this, he says "sthita" and so forth: even when the maternal uncle is present, because of the greater weight of the relationship with the father, the deceased's own paternal *sapinda* remains [the heir].
He would be a stealer of wealth. *Sapiṇḍa* itself is *sāpiṇḍa*; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the base word itself according to the rule *prajñādibhyaś-ca*. || 49 ||
p. 374) Since there is no downward movement [of the inheritance], wealth has gone upward;
even there, O Śivā, because men are primary, it has gone to the paternal lineage.
Therefore, in this case, even a maternal uncle who is closely related does not receive the wealth. (50)
O Pārvatī, a grandson whose father is deceased is entitled to his own father’s inheritance from the grandfather’s wealth, together with the paternal uncles.
Likewise, a daughter of one who died without brothers or sons— being gentle and having lost her mother— shall receive an equal share of the grandfather’s wealth from her paternal uncles.
O Goddess, when the daughter’s daughter, the paternal grandmother, and even the daughter’s father’s sister are present,
and the wealth has gone to the father, the daughter’s daughter is the one entitled to it.

Now, anticipating the objection that the right to take the estate of a deceased person should belong only to the maternal uncle— who is a *sapiṇḍa* of the father and thus more closely related— and not to the father’s *sapiṇḍa* who is more distantly related, he says the following to dispel this doubt:

The passage from "adhastāt" up to "dhanam" consists of one and a half verses. O Śivā, in the absence of downward movement, the wealth of the deceased (preta) would have gone to—that is, reached—the people existing above. Furthermore, even among those in the higher realms, for men—

Because wealth primarily belongs to the paternal lineage, it would go to them. For this reason, even if a maternal uncle is nearby or close at hand in this world, he shall not obtain nor receive the wealth of the deceased. || 50 ||

He states with the verse beginning "ajīvati" that when a man who has not divided his property among his brothers dies, his son shall receive his paternal share from the ancestral estate together with his paternal uncles. O Pārvatī, [this applies to one] whose father is living... [or] whose father is deceased.

The son of a deceased father—the grandson—is entitled to receive his own father’s inheritance from the estate of the grandfather, together with the paternal uncles, who are the father’s brothers. || 51 ||

He states by the verse beginning with "bhrātṛhīnā" that even a daughter’s daughter who has not lived (as a maiden), being without brothers, is entitled to receive her deceased father's share from the grandfather's property;
provided that she is "saumyā"— meaning she is one whose mother is deceased and who is without brothers, both uterine and half-brothers.

And if she is free from the defect known as *vyabhicāra* (incontinence), then in that manner, being an equal sharer with her paternal uncles, the daughter of the son (*pautrī*) shall take— that is, receive— the grandfather’s wealth. || 52 ||
Now, among the mother, sister, and daughter of a man who has met his death (attained the five elements), which of them would be the rightful heir to his wealth?
To this, he says, beginning with "satyām" and so forth: "O Goddess, [in the absence] of the paternal grandmother of the granddaughter..."
When wealth flows downward, the man who is lower is superior;
when wealth flows upward, the man who is born higher becomes the best. (54)
Therefore, when there exists a daughter-in-law, a granddaughter, and a beloved daughter,
the father of the deceased is not at all able to seize the estate.
When there is no heir to the wealth of one who has died in the paternal family,
the inheritance shall go to the maternal grandfather’s family according to the previously mentioned rule.
The wealth belonging to the maternal grandfather is to be approached by the maternal uncles, their sons, and so forth,
in this same downward and upward order, whether it pertains to a male or a female.

Likewise, even when a paternal aunt exists, the daughter of a paternal granddaughter (pautrī) shall be the one entitled to the wealth belonging to the father [of the deceased], because of the greater weight of her birth being lower [in the line]. || 53 ||

Now, one might raise this doubt: since the deceased’s son-in-law, daughter’s son, and granddaughter’s son are superior by virtue of being male, it follows that the inheritance of that wealth should belong to him while he is alive, and not to the daughter-in-law and the others; in order to dispel this doubt, the author says:

The two verses beginning with "among those moving downwards" and ending with "his father" are as follows: among riches that move downwards—that is, wealth—the man born from the lower [womb] would be superior (jyāyān), meaning more excellent, and not the one born from the upper [womb]. However, regarding wealth that moves upwards, it is the man born from the upper [womb] who is superior.
He would become the most excellent. || 54 ||

The meaning is that the father is not at all able to seize or take the wealth and property of the deceased; rather, it is those [female relatives] who, in due order, are able to take the wealth of the deceased. || 55 ||
Now, one might ask: if there is no heir to take the wealth in the lineage of the deceased father, would that property not remain with the family? To this, he says "yadā" and so forth:
when there is no recipient of the wealth—that is, no vessel for the wealth—within the paternal family of the deceased person, then...
According to the previously mentioned rule and the previously described procedure, the maternal grandfather’s family shall inherit—that is, receive—the estate, the wealth of the deceased. || 56 ||

He states, beginning with "mātāmaha," that property inherited from the maternal grandfather belongs to males according to the sequence of ascending and descending generations, and in their absence, it belongs to females. "Mātāmahagata" means wealth obtained from the maternal grandfather.
When there exists a descendant of the Brāhmaṇa lineage and the period of *sāpiṇḍya* with the parents has not expired,
the son of a deceased man born of a Śaiva woman shall not be an heir to his father’s property. (58)
O auspicious lady, his wife who is a Śaiva and his sons shall receive shares of the wealth,
as well as food and clothing, just like the estate of one who has departed for heaven.

A husband who follows the Śaiva path shall protect a woman who marries according to the Śaiva rite; however, O beloved, if she is gentle (Saumyā), her father and other relatives have no authority over her wealth.

In this same manner as in the paternal lineage, one should resort to and serve a man— starting from maternal uncles, their sons, and so forth, as well as the sons of maternal uncles and so forth, following the sequence from lower to higher— or, in his absence, a woman.

Now, [the author] states with the verse beginning "brāhmyanvaye" that, if a relative (sapiṇḍa) of the parents exists within the lineage of the deceased man's Brāhmaṇa wife, the son of a Śaiva wife has no right to share in that wealth.
[The term] "brāhmyanvaye" means in the lineage of the Brāhmaṇa wife.
While the lineage of both parents— that is, the maternal and paternal lines— still exists, or while a sapinda relative remains,
the son of a Śaiva wife shall not be an heir to the deceased father; rather, the inheritance belongs respectively to those two [parents] who are still living.

The meaning is that he is entitled to a share of that inheritance. By this, it is implied that in the absence of a son born of a Brāhmaṇa marriage, and in the absence of the mother, father, or a sapinda relative, the son of a Śaiva wife alone is entitled to the inheritance of the deceased father. || 58 ||

Now, one might ask: "If a member of the Brāhma lineage, or a paternal relative (*sapiṇḍa*), is still living, how can Śaiva sons—who lack the right to inherit from a deceased father—maintain themselves through such means as filling their bellies? To this, he replies with the verse beginning "śaivī," etc. "O blessed lady! [he says].

When a man has departed for heaven—that is, when he has gone to the celestial realm—his Śaiva wife, his sons by her, and his daughters by her shall be the sharers of his wealth; they shall receive and obtain food and clothing according to their respective wealth and means. || 59 ||
Now, one might raise the doubt: "Should not a woman who has undergone a Śaiva marriage be protected by her father and others, or rather by her Śaiva husband?
In response to this, he says, beginning with "The Śaiva marriage," etc.: "O beloved, because of this Śaiva woman..."

Since her father and others have no right to her wealth, if one should know that she—who is performing the Śaiva marriage—is gentle and chaste, then her Śaiva husband alone shall maintain and protect her. The word "should know" (*jānīyāt*) is to be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Regarding the phrase "performing [the marriage]" (*prakurvantīm*):
The addition of the augment *nu* is Vedic.
Therefore, if a father marries a girl born of a noble family to Śaiva practitioners, whether out of anger or greed, he shall be censured by the world. (61)

In the absence of a Śaiva or his lineage, the king—who is the giver of the water [of funeral rites] and the bestower of the sacred knowledge—shall take the wealth of the deceased in due order, according to the teaching of Śiva. (62)
O beloved, those up to the seventh person from the giver of the funeral ball (piṇḍa) are declared to be sapindas;
those up to the tenth are sodakas, and beyond that, they are merely born of the same lineage (gotra).

Now, in order to demonstrate that a father who marries a girl born of a noble family according to the Śaiva rite becomes censured by the world, he says "ataḥ" and so forth. Therefore, when a sapinda relative of the mother and father exists within the Brāhma lineage, or when the husband's property— that is, the property of his own father and so on— is present—

Furthermore, due to the absence of authority for this purpose, whether out of anger or even greed, he who marries a maiden born of a noble family and a virtuous lineage according to Śaiva rites shall become a father despised by the world and censured by the people. || 61 ||

He states that the eligibility belongs respectively to a man who has died without offspring down to the lineage of Śaivas, to a teacher of the Vedas who has offered water for the deceased, and to a king, over all things including immovable property.

By the words beginning with "śaivī" [it is meant]: in the absence of a Śaiva [initiate] or one belonging to his lineage, the *sodaka* (one who performs the water-libation), the *brahmadā* (the giver of the Veda), the teacher (*guru*), and the king (*rājā*) may, by the command of Śiva—that is, according to Śiva’s injunction—seize the wealth or property of the deceased in due order. As follows:
In the absence of a Śaiva or one of his lineage, the first among those entitled to the water-offering (sodaka) shall take the wealth of the deceased;
in his absence, a Vedic teacher; and in his absence, the king. || 62 ||

Now, for whom does sapinda-relationship exist, for whom does sodaka-relationship exist, and for whom does mere common lineage (gotra) exist? To this, he says, beginning with "piṇḍada": O beloved, starting from the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa), seven generations of persons [counting back] from the giver of the cake are sapindas.

Those mentioned above [the seventh] up to the tenth—meaning ending with the tenth person—should be accompanied by water (sodaka). Beyond that, they should be merely those born of the same lineage (gotraja). In the phrase "piṇḍadāt" (from the giver of the rice-ball), the ablative case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule "lyablope karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca. 63.
If property that was previously divided is later reunited by mutual consent, they shall divide that wealth again according to the rules for undivided inheritance. (64)
Whether the estate was undivided or divided, whatever the share of a person may have been, his heirs likewise partake of such wealth even after he has died. || 65 ||
Those who may be the takers of one’s wealth for as long as they live,
they alone shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for him, with the exception of a wife or son of Śiva.
Just as impurity is prescribed in this world due to the connection of birth, so too is a three-night period ordained due to the connection of sharing in the inheritance of wealth. (67)

Regarding property that was divided and subsequently reunited by mutual consent, he describes the method for its re-division again through the rule for those who are undivided, beginning with the words "vibhaktam" (if divided).
"Cet" means if; "vibhaktam" refers to the wealth (*draviṇa*) or property (*dravya*) that had been partitioned.
If it has been mixed together by their own will, then the heirs shall divide that wealth again according to the rules for undivided property. || 64 ||
He states with the words "among those undivided," etc., that for whatever man there exists a certain degree of shareholding in all his property—
whether divided or undivided— upon his death, those [heirs] shall indeed possess that same degree of shareholding therein. For whichever man [the property was] undivided or divided...
Or rather, whatever the nature of the division among those heirs may be regarding the property, even upon the death of that man, those heirs shall become partakers of such wealth. || 65 ||

Regarding the man who has died, those who should obtain his wealth must offer the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for him as long as they live; this is stated by the verse beginning with "ye" and so forth.
Those men who are the takers of a man's property, they alone [must perform the rites] until the end of their lives.
They should offer the *piṇḍa* for this man throughout his lifetime;

however, with the exception of the son of a Śaiva wife. The meaning is that he has no entitlement to offer that *piṇḍa*. By the phrase "the son of a Śaiva wife," [it is meant] the daughter and other descendants of that Śaiva woman.
This is an inclusive illustration. || 66 ||

Just as impurity (*āśauca*) arises for all kinsmen on account of birth due to their relationship by birth, so too does a three-night period of impurity arise for those who inherit wealth due to their relationship through the sharing of property.

He says "it may be so" with the words beginning "in the world," etc. Just as in this world, in relation to people, impurity (*aśauca*) caused by death or birth is prescribed—whether the period of impurity has been completed or not—if [the news] is heard within that time. (p. 379)
Upon hearing [this], the twice-born and others shall become purified within the remaining days. || 68 ||
But when the lapse of time is known, there is no impurity for a partial period;
if it is not beyond one year, three nights of impurity are prescribed once the full period has elapsed. (69)

Even if more than a year has passed, if a son hears of the death of his mother or father, he remains impure for three nights; likewise does a devoted wife remain impure upon hearing of her husband's death.

Likewise, because of the relationship of sharing in the inheritance, three nights of impurity are prescribed even for the one who takes the wealth. According to Amara, "loka" means the world, the earth, or people. || 67 ||

Now, for Brahmins and others residing in another region who hear of an impurity while it is still within the period of impurity— whether that period be full or partial— their impurity lasts for only the remaining days from the day they hear of the impurity.
In response to the doubt as to whether purification would occur starting from that very day or after other periods such as ten days once the impurity has ended, he says "when complete," and so forth:
"whether the impurity is complete or incomplete, or when the impurity is partial."
If [the news] is heard within that period— that is, during the interval of impurity— then from the day of hearing (śravaṇa),

meaning from the day the news of the impurity is heard, the twice-born and others, such as Brāhmaṇas and so forth, shall become pure by means of the remaining days, that is, the remaining ahorātras. It is called "śravaṇa" because it is heard in this [time].
Therefore, by the rule "karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca," the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). 68.

Now, one might ask: when the period of impurity has passed, if Brāhmaṇas and others hear of the death of a relative within the year itself, by how many days and nights would they be purified? To this, he says "when the time has elapsed," and so forth. When the time has elapsed...

However, if the period of impurity has elapsed and the partial impurity (*khaṇḍāśauca*) is subsequently recognized, then no impurity remains. This applies provided that more than a year (*saṃvatsara*)—that is, if more than a year has not passed since the event;
even though the time of impurity has elapsed, if the [period of] full impurity is recognized as having been completed, [then purification occurs].

Impurity (*aśauca*) for three nights has been prescribed. The term *kālātīta* is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* (Pāṇini 2.2.8), meaning "that which has passed beyond time. The word *atīta* is derived from the root *i-* preceded by the prefix *ati-*, with the suffix *kta* used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). This is supported by the statement of Devala: "There is no impurity regarding childbirth even when the days have elapsed."
This statement concerns death. || 69 ||

He states in the verse beginning with "Even when a year has passed," etc., that for a son who hears of the death of his parents, and for a devoted wife who hears of the death of her husband, there shall be impurity (aśauca) for three nights, even if a full year has elapsed.
If another period of impurity should occur during the midst of an existing period of impurity, for mortals, purification is prescribed there by means of the more significant (guru) impurity. (71)
The gravity of impurities is determined by the weight of their duration;
between that which is pervaded and that which pervades, the pervader is traditionally held to be more significant. (72)

If another birth-impurity (sūtaka) should fall on the day the previous impurity ends, purification shall occur through the first impurity; however, due to the increase of sin, there shall be [an extension of] two days.
Even after a year has passed— that is, even upon the lapse of a full year— if there should be news of the death of one's mother or father, then, such news of their death having occurred,
the son shall remain impure for three nights; likewise, a devoted wife [remains impure] upon hearing news of the death of her husband or master.
A woman shall be impure for three nights.
When one period of impurity exists and, before its remaining days have even concluded,
another period of impurity extending over a different duration falls upon it, the purification of mortals occurs through the period of impurity that covers the greater number of days.
He says "it may be so" with the words beginning "within the period of impurity," and so forth: when another period of impurity (*aśaucāntaram*)—
one that covers a different duration of time— should fall upon or arrive during a certain period of impurity (*aśauce*), that is, within the midst of that impurity (*aśaucābhyantare*).
When [the period of impurity] has arisen, once the impurity caused by the death of a guru—which extends over more days—has passed away, the purification of mortals is ordained. || 71 ||
Now, he defines the gravity of impurities (*aśauca*) with the words beginning "of impurities" (*aśaucānām*).

Due to the gravity of their temporal extension—that is, because of the gravity inherent in pervading a long duration—impurities become grave on account of extending over a greater length of time. This is because they occupy a larger span of time.
The meaning is that "heaviness" refers to its duration being longer, while "lightness" refers to its duration being shorter.
Between the two periods of impurity—the subsumed and the subsuming—that which is more pervasive (vyāpaka) is remembered as the weightier (garīyaḥ), that is, more significant. || 72 ||

Now, regarding the doubt as to whether purification occurs through the preceding impurity alone or through the subsequent impurity when another impurity falls on the day following the end of the first impurity, he says "yadi" (if), etc.

On the final day of the period of impurity— that is, during the last day and night of the birth-impurity— if another *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) should occur, meaning if a partial impurity caused by another birth should fall, then purification shall occur through the previous impurity itself once it has passed. However, if on the final day of the impurity...

If another period of impurity (āśauca) should occur while a full period of impurity is still in effect, there shall be an increase in that impurity; consequently, due to this increase, the impurity shall last for two additional days beyond the final day of the preceding period of impurity.
The term *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) is used here as an elliptical expression for *mṛtaka* (impurity due to death) as well.
In that case as well, it should be understood in exactly the same way. || 73 ||

(381) The period of impurity for the father’s family lasts as long as the woman has not been married; once the marriage has taken place, it is declared that upon the death of her parents, the impurity lasts for three days.
After marriage, a woman becomes a member of her husband's lineage;
likewise, the status of a son given in adoption is determined by the lineage of the adoptive father. (75)
Having taken up the sacred thread with the consent of his mother and father,
and having recorded the names of his own lineage and personal name, he should perform the consecration together with his kinsmen.

Now, one might raise the doubt: "In the case of women, does impurity (aśauca) belong only to the father's family, or only to the husband's family, or to both? In response to this, he says "tāvat" and so forth: as long as the wedding—the marriage—has not taken place, [so long does the impurity belong to the father's family].

Until the end of the [mourning] period, the impurity related to the father's family—that is, the impurity pertaining to the paternal kin—shall belong to the woman. By this, it is indicated that after marriage, the woman's impurity shall pertain only to the husband's family. Now, one might object: even after marriage, regarding the mother and father who gave her birth...
Since there might be the notion that there is no impurity (aśauca) upon the death of a woman, he says "jāte" and so forth.

Even when a marriage has taken place, if the death of both parents occurs—that is, upon the death of the mother and the father—the impurity for the woman is declared to be three days (tryaha), a period of three days. || 74 ||

Now, since it has been stated that the relationship by birth is stronger than the relationship by marriage, it might be argued that when impurity (aśauca) exists in the father's family alone, it is proper for the wife to remain impure there, but not when impurity exists in the husband's family; to this, he replies with the words beginning "vivāhāntaram" and so forth.
After marriage—that is, subsequent to the wedding—a woman becomes a member of her husband’s lineage (*gotra*).

The implication is that since she has exited her father’s lineage after the marriage, there would be no period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) for the woman when such impurity occurs within that [paternal] family. Now, one might object: what about a *dattaka* (adopted) son with respect to his biological father’s lineage?
Dispelling the doubt as to whether the adopted son possesses the lineage (*gotra*) of the adopter or that of his own [biological] lineage, he says "tathā" and so forth:
"In that manner," by that means, the adopted son's possession of a lineage—his state of belonging to a lineage—shall be through the lineage of the adopter. (75)

Now, he states with the words beginning "the son" (*sutam*) that the rite of consecration (*saṃskāra*) should be performed by the recipient, having taken the son with the consent of both parents and having uttered their own lineage names (*gotra*) and personal names.
With the consent of the mother— the progenitor— and the father— the begetter— he [should take] the son.

Taking that son and grasping him, having recorded the names of his own lineage and having uttered the names of one's own lineage, one should perform the sacramental rite together with the relatives and kinsmen who have gathered. || 76 ||

Just as the biological son has the right to the inheritance and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) of his parents, so too does the adopted son have that right with respect to his adoptive parents, for they are indeed his parents. (77)
One should adopt a child from a woman of the same caste and protect him until he reaches five years of age;
a boy older than five years is not recommended as an adopted son. (78)
O Kālikā, even if a brother’s son is given [in adoption], he becomes the adoptive father;
the biological progenitor becomes the paternal uncle in all ritual matters.
Whoever may be the taker of another's wealth should observe that person's religious duties;
he should protect their observances and satisfy their kinsmen. (80)

With the words beginning "even in the case of the legitimate son" (*aurase 'pi*), he states the entitlement of the adopted son (*dattaka-putra*) to the wealth and the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*) of his adoptive parents, along with an illustrative example. The word "even" (*api*) is to be construed with the term "oblation. Just as there is entitlement to the wealth and the oblation of the two parents in the case of the legitimate son, so it is for the adopted son.
In the same way, the right of adoption belongs to both the adopter and the biological father regarding the wealth and the *piṇḍa* (funerary cake) of the adopted son (*dattaka*).

Demonstrating the reason for the adopted son’s right to the *piṇḍa* and so forth for both the adopter and the biological father, he says "since," etc.; since those two—the adopter and the biological father—are indeed certainly his fathers.
Therefore, the meaning is that he shall have the right of inheritance over both that wealth and the funeral cake (piṇḍa). || 77 ||
Now, one might ask: "At what age is an adopted son (dattaka) considered recommended?

To this, he says, "Until the fifth year," and so forth. A Brāhmaṇa or other [caste], taking a child or infant from a person of the same caste (savarṇa)—that is, from one of equal caste—until the fifth year, that is, up to the end of the fifth year; [is thus recommended].
One should protect and guard [him]. "Up to five years" (*āpañcābdaṃ*) means from one who is five years old (*pañcābda*);
this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*. He who is more than five years of age...
That adopted son who is ignorant is not praised. || 78 ||

The father of Datta’s paternal uncle would indeed be his adoptive father, while Datta’s biological father would be that paternal uncle; this is stated in the passage beginning with "bhrātṛputro’pi" (even the brother’s son).
O Kālikā, if even the brother’s son were to be adopted as Datta, then in all ritual acts—
The one who takes her in hand shall indeed be her father; however, the biological progenitor would be his paternal uncle.

(Verse 79) By means of the words beginning with "ya" (he who), [the author] states that the man who takes away the wealth must protect the religious duties and observances of the owner of that wealth, and must satisfy his kinsmen.

For a man who seizes the wealth of another man— those born of an unmarried woman (kānīna), those born from a widow (golaka), those born from an adulterous union (kuṇḍa), and those who have committed heinous sins—
there is no impurity (aśauca) upon their death, nor do they possess any right to inheritance. (81)
For those men whose lingas are severed and for those women whose noses are cut off,
as well as for those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātaka), one should not observe impurity upon their death.
The king should maintain and protect the dependents and even the wealth of those men who are without a protector for as long as twelve years. 83.
He might protect his duties, preserve his observances, and even satisfy his kinsmen. || 80 ||

He states with the verse beginning "The *kānīna*s," etc., that those such as the *kānīna* and *golaka* do not have the right to inherit, nor is there impurity (*aśauca*) upon their death. Those who are *kānīna*s are sons begotten by a maiden in secret within her father's house; and those who are *golaka*s are [sons] [begotten] when the husband has died.

Those born of a paramour (*jāra*) while the husband is still living are *kuṇḍas*; those born of a paramour who possess the aforementioned characteristics are *atipātakin* (extreme sinners). Upon their death, there shall be no period of ritual impurity (*aśauca*), nor shall they have any right to inheritance. As Amara states: "A son born of a paramour while the husband is alive is a *kuṇḍa*; when the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*."
It is stated that for women who have committed the offense of cutting off a nose or a limb,
for men who have committed the offense of having their genitals cut off, and even for men who are great sinners (mahāpātakin), one should not observe impurity upon death; thus it says, "liṅgaccheda."

By these and other such statements, for those men for whom the cutting off of the *liṅga*— that is, the excision of the penis— is ordained as the punishment (*dama*), for those women who are great sinners (*mahāpātakinaḥ*) for whom the cutting of the nose— the excision of the nostril— is the punishment, [the same applies].
Furthermore, one should not observe, nor perform, the impurity (aśauca) upon the death or passing away of those such as the slayers of Brahmins. || 82 ||

He states with the verse beginning with "nṛṇām" that the dependents and wealth of men who have no designated heirs must be protected by the king for a period of twelve years. "Of men" refers to those who are without a designation, meaning those who have no designated heirs.
The king shall protect the dependents of men for twelve years, up to the end of the twelfth year; he alone shall also guard their wealth. || 83 ||
When twelve years have passed, one should cremate their bodies made of darbha grass;
at the end of three nights, their sons and others should liberate them from the state of a preta. (84)
Then the king, having divided the wealth among his attendants according to the order of their sons and so forth, should bestow it; otherwise, he would become a sinner. (85)
For one who is wretched and fallen into calamity, there is no protector whatsoever; the king alone is his protector, since the monarch is the lord of his subjects.

If one should arrive unannounced even at the conclusion of the partition during the period of temporary residence (kālika), his wife and sons belong to him alone, and his wealth likewise; it is not otherwise.
After twelve years, for those men whose bodies have not been designated [for cremation], the king or his sons and others must cause effigies made of *kuśa* grass to be cremated;
at the end of three nights, their state of being a *preta* must be released— so says the *Dvādaśābda*.

By such statements as these: when twelve years—twelve varṣas—have passed and gone by, the king, along with his sons and others, shall cause the bodies made of darbha grass (kuśa-maya-śarīrāṇi) of those men who were without designated heirs to be cremated; this is at the end of the three-night period for those who have no sons or other relatives to perform the rites.
And he should liberate them from that state of being a preta by means of those very same [deeds]. || 84 ||

Thereafter, he states with the words "tataḥ" and so forth that the king should distribute the property belonging to a person who has no heirs among the members of that person's retinue, starting from the sons and so on, after having divided it. Thus:
"tataḥ," meaning after that cremation, his wealth should be divided.

The king should bestow [the gifts] upon the retinues of his sons and others in due order. Now, what fault accrues to a king who does not act in this way? To this he says: "Otherwise. Otherwise, failing to do this, the king becomes a sinner. (85)
He states with the words beginning "na kaścit" that a mortal who has met with misfortune and has no other protector must be protected by the king alone. For that man who has fallen into calamity,
who is distressed and impoverished, and for whom no protector whatsoever exists, the king alone [is the protector].
The protector (*pātā*) should be the guardian; for the king alone is the lord and master of the subjects.
Regarding the terms *nisva*, *durvidha*, *dīna*, *daridra*, and *durgata*, Amara states: "He is *nisva*, *durvidha*, *dīna*, *daridra*, and also *durgata*. (86)

He says "yadi" and so forth, [anticipating the objection] that even after the division of the property, the wife and others might still be entitled to it if they arrive without having been previously designated. O Kālikā, if a person who was not designated should arrive even after the division of the property, then—
A man is not empowered to give away ancestral immovable property, whether to a kinsman or to another, without the consent of his heirs. (88)
Whatever property he has acquired himself, whether immovable or movable, as well as movable paternal property, he is entitled to give away according to his own will. (89)
Whether the son is present, or the wife, or the daughter, or even her son;
or the father, or the mother, or likewise the brother or even the sister—(in all these cases, one should not eat).
Whatever immovable property has been acquired by oneself, as well as movable property, and whatever movable property belongs to one's father—one would be capable of giving all of it away. (91)
His wife alone is his wife, his sons are his sons, and even his wealth belongs to him alone;
all this would not be otherwise. || 87 ||
He states with the words "is not capable," etc., that no one would be able to give immovable property owned by the father to anyone at all without the consent of the heirs (*aṃśikā*).
In the phrase "and immovable property" (*sthāvaraṃ ca*), the word *ca* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
It is connected with both "paternal" (paitṛka) and "immovable" (sthāvara). Then, this is the meaning:

without the consent of the heirs—that is, in the absence of the consent of the co-sharers—a man [is not entitled] to give that property which is both paternal and immovable to his own kinsmen or to another.
[The particle *ca*] is used in the senses of capability,
possibility, inclusion (*anvācaya*), collection (*samāhāra*), mutual conjunction (*itaretara-samuccaya*),
application (*viniyoga*), equal association (*tulyayogitā*), restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and cause (*hetu*).
It is stated that the indeclinable *api* is used for filling out a verse-foot as well as in nine other senses. (88)

By the phrase "that which is ancestral and immovable," it is indicated that one may freely give away all property acquired by oneself, such as immovables, as well as movable property obtained from one's father; that indeed is what is meant.

To clarify further, he says "yattu" and so forth: whatever immovable property (sthāvara) or movable property (jaṅgama)— that is, wealth (riktha)— is self-acquired, and whatever non-immovable, movable wealth is obtained as paternal inheritance (paitṛka), meaning related to the father, that indeed [may be disposed of] according to one's own will.
He ought to give it. || 89 ||

He states, beginning with the words "sthitaḥ" (established), that even in the absence of the consent of very closely related sons and others, a man is capable of giving away all property such as immovable assets acquired by himself, as well as non-immovable paternal wealth; [the opponent] says he is not capable.
Wealth given away or dedicated to religious duty (*dharma*) by a man according to such a procedure cannot be altered by his sons or others in any other way. (92)
The donor ought to protect property established for the sake of the Dharma;
he is not the master to take it back again, since the Dharma is its true master. || 93 ||

O Ambikā, either the root [owner] or one who holds subordinate rights over it may, according to their resolve, personally employ that property for the sake of dharma, or their representative may do so. || 94 ||
By means of these two verses ending with the word *bhavet*: even when a son (*putra*) or one's own offspring (*ātmaja*) is present,
or when a wife (*patnī*) or consort (*bhāryā*) is present, or when a daughter (*kanyā*) or child (*duhitṛ*) is present,
or when her son (*tatsuta*)— the son of a daughter— or a father (*janaka*) or progenitor (*pitṛ*) is present, or even when a mother (*jananī*) is present.

While the brother, the uterine brother, remains, and while the sister, the uterine sister, also remains, whatever immovable property— land or buildings— and whatever movable wealth— personal chattels— that has been acquired by oneself and earned by oneself [belongs to them].
A man is capable—that is, competent—to give away even all that non-immovable ancestral wealth. || 90 || 91 ||

He states with the verse beginning "The wealth," etc., that the property given by a man according to the procedure prescribed by Śaṅkara and established for the sake of dharma cannot be altered in any way by his sons or others; [this was done] by a man (puṃsā), that is, by a person, according to such a procedure.

Whatever wealth has been given according to such a procedure as declared by Śiva, or whatever wealth has been dedicated to Dharma— meaning made subject to Dharma or set aside for the purpose of Dharma—
that wealth cannot be altered in any other way by sons or others. || 92 ||

Because property set aside for the sake of Dharma belongs to the Dharma as its owner, the giver has no further right to it and must protect it; this is stated by the verse beginning with "dharmārtham.
Whatever inheritance or wealth has been set aside for the sake of Dharma, the giver ought to protect that.
The giver is not the master or lord capable of reclaiming or seizing that wealth; for, as is certain (*hi*), Dharma alone is the master and owner of this wealth. 93.

He states with the words beginning "the root," that one's principal wealth or its subordinate property should be employed for the sake of dharma, either by oneself or through a representative, according to one's resolve. O Ambikā, "according to one's resolve" means without transgressing one's intention.
One may employ for the sake of dharma either the root capital, or the interest derived from it, or one's own self, or a substitute for oneself;
for when the primary object is absent, that which is taken in its place is a substitute (pratinidhi). || 94 ||
If a wealthy man, out of affection, should give even half of his self-earned wealth to his heir, another person may not alter that [arrangement]. (95)
If one gives half of what he has earned to a moneylender, it cannot be prevented by other heirs. (96)

When wealth is acquired by means of paternal property belonging to one [co-heir], the heirs are entitled to equal shares in that paternal estate; they do not deserve a share of the profit except for the acquirer himself. (97)
If one recovers ancestral property that had been lost, he is entitled to two shares from that wealth among the heirs. (98)
Now, one might ask: "Is another person permitted to alter otherwise even that half of his self-acquired wealth which was given out of affection by the acquirer to the heir?
To this, he says, beginning with "of his self-acquired wealth," etc.: if the wealthy man, out of affection...

If one should give even half of one's own earned wealth out of affection to an heir or even to a taker of the property, then no other person is able— meaning, not fit— to alter that half of the self-earned wealth given out of such affection. Following this, that which is about to be stated...
Since this statement concerns multiple shares, it refers to a matter involving two shares. [Objection:
But surely, when property from one's own earnings is being given to one among many heirs, can the other heirs not oppose it?

To this he replies with the words beginning "yadi" (if): if the *arjaka* (the acquirer) gives half of his self-acquired property to one among the heirs who are claimants of the wealth, then he cannot be obstructed or prevented by the other heirs. || 96 ||

Now, regarding the doubt as to whether all heirs would be entitled to a share in wealth acquired solely from paternal property, he says "by one," and so forth. Among those heirs, by whichever single heir, and by whatever paternal wealth— that is, ancestral property— [it was acquired].

All those heirs shall have equal shares—that is, they shall be equal dividers—in that paternal wealth acquired through money; however, without that acquirer, they would not be entitled to the profit. The meaning is that the acquirer alone is entitled to the profit. || 97 ||

Regarding a person who recovers ancestral property that has been lost, it is stated by the verse beginning with "paitṛkāṇi" that he is entitled to two shares therein, while the others have equal shares; furthermore,
among the heirs, whichever heir [recovers it]...
Merit, wealth, and knowledge do not abide in one who is bodiless;
since the body belongs to the father, why should the paternal property not belong to him? (99)
Whatever has been acquired by men through separate foods and separate wealth—all that has passed over to the ancestors; how then can anything be one's own acquisition? (100)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, whatever wealth has been acquired by one through his own exertions, that alone shall be his own earnings; he is its owner, and no other.
Even when the father has perished or is lost, he who recovers the paternal assets is the rescuer;
he is entitled to two shares from those riches, while the others receive equal shares—this is the meaning. || 98 ||

Since the physical body is inherited from one's father, knowledge, wealth, and so forth— which depend upon that body— are likewise considered paternal; thus, even when acquired by humans through separate food and materials, all such riches belong to those very [ancestors].
Since the connection with the father does not cease [after his death], it would follow that ownership of what one has acquired oneself is not established; therefore,

it must be understood that for all goods acquired through one's own exertion, there is both the status of being self-acquired and ownership belonging solely to the acquirer— this is precisely what [the author] states.

By means of these three verses beginning with "merit" (*puṇya*) and ending with "nor anything else" (*na cāparaḥ*), [the author explains]: for what reason, merit (*puṇya*), righteousness (*dharma*), wealth (*vitta*) or riches (*dhana*), and knowledge (*vidyā*)—that is, the knowledge of the reality of the scriptures and so forth—would not resort to or support one who is bodiless (*aśarīrin*), that is, one without a physical body? Rather, [they do resort to him].

One should take refuge in the embodied soul alone; for the body belongs to the father and is related to the father. Therefore, why should wealth (vasu) not be paternal—that is, related to the father? Indeed, all wealth is paternal. || 99 ||

Regarding the phrase "with separate foods": therefore, whatever has been acquired by men—by human beings who possess separate food (meaning distinct portions of rice) and separate wealth (meaning divided property)—all that becomes transferred to the ancestors and connected with the ancestors; at that time, it becomes what they themselves have acquired.
"From where would wealth come? means that the fact of wealth being self-acquired would not be established.

Regarding "ataḥ" (therefore): O Maheśī, for this reason, whatever wealth has been acquired by a man through his own efforts and personal exertion—whether by means of separate food and so forth, or by means of non-separate food and so forth—[that is what is meant].
That very wealth would be self-earned; he alone who earned it is its owner, for one who has earned his own wealth is its master, and no one other than the earner is the owner. || 101 ||
O Goddess, one who strikes even with the hand his mother, father, teacher, paternal grandfathers, or maternal grandfathers, does not inherit the property. (102)
Even while killing others, one shall not acquire their wealth;
when they are slain, their other heirs shall become the sharers of that property.
O Mother, those who are eunuchs or cripples are entitled to food and clothing for as long as they live; they shall not be sharers in the inheritance.
If property with an owner is found on a road or anywhere else, the king, having investigated thoroughly, shall cause it to be returned to the owner by the finder. 105.

He states with the verse beginning "mātaram" that a man who strikes his mother and others even with his hand shall have no share in the inheritance: "O Goddess, [one who strikes] the mother, the progenitor;
the father, the begetter; and the guru, the instructor of mantras—the plural number [is used for the latter]."

Because it indicates many cases, a man who strikes even his paternal grandfathers and their ancestors, as well as his maternal grandfathers and their ancestors, with his hand— that is, with his very fist— shall not be an heir at all. By the use of the word "even" (*api*), it follows that one who strikes his mother and others with a staff or similar weapon is even more certainly excluded.
It is indicated that there shall be no entitlement to a share of the inheritance. || 102 ||

He states, beginning with the words "killing" (*nighnan*), that for a man who kills even his brothers and others for the sake of wealth, there shall be no share for him in the property of the deceased owner, while the other heirs shall receive equal shares; this applies to others as well.

Even by killing or depriving of life people who are distinct from his mother and others, a man shall not acquire—that is, he shall not obtain—the wealth of those slain; rather, other heirs distinct from the killer shall become the sharers of the wealth of the deceased. || 103 ||
Now, [the author] states with the words beginning "napuṃsakāḥ" that those who have no share— namely the impotent and the eunuchs— shall receive food and clothing for as long as they live:
"O Ambikā, O Mother of the World, the impotent and the lame [shall receive these] for as long as they live."
They are entitled only to food and clothing for as long as they live; they shall not be sharers in the inheritance. || 104 ||
Now, one might ask: regarding property with an owner that has been found on a journey or elsewhere, should it go to the person who finds it, or should it go to the owner?
To this, he says "sasvāmika" (with an owner), and so forth; [it refers to] on the road, or at some place along the way.
In the case of ownerless living beings and ownerless property, one who recovers them shall become their owner; he should present a tenth part of it to the king. (106)
While the owner of immovable property remains present and nearby, he is not empowered to sell that immovable wealth to another, even if a suitable buyer is available. (107)
Among those present, a kinsman or one of the same caste is preferred;
in their absence, a friend [is preferred], for the will of the seller carries the greatest weight. (108)

When wealth has been found in its proper place, the king, having investigated thoroughly, shall cause it to be given back to its owner—the master who is the rightful recipient of the recovered property—by the person who found it. (105)

Now, one might raise the objection: "Would not living beings such as cattle and horses, as well as such acquired riches, which have no owner, pass to the man who finds them or to the lord of the earth? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "of those without an owner" and so forth:

when living beings such as cattle and horses that lack an owner, or property that has no owner, are acquired by a person, he shall become the owner of them once they have been acquired. And in that case, [he shall give] a tenth share...

"Having obtained [it], one should offer it to the king; one should give it. In the phrases "of living beings" (jīvānām) and "of wealth" (dhanasya), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object, according to the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). || 106 ||
Now, one might ask: between two potential buyers, one who is distant and one who is nearby, to which of the two can the owner of immovable property rightfully sell that wealth?
To this, he says, beginning with "immovable property" (*sthāvaram*): [it may be sold] to the one who is capable and situated nearby (*sānnidhyavartini*).

The meaning is that while a buyer worthy of purchase—a purchaser—is present, the person who is the owner of the immovable property would not be able to sell that immovable wealth to another man situated at a distance; rather, he would only be able to sell it to one who is in close proximity. Proximity alone [is required].

[The suffix] -yaṅ [is applied] in the sense of proximity (*sānnidhya*). Regarding the statement "there is an addition for *caturvarṇa* and so forth in their own sense," the suffix -ṣyañ is applied in the sense of the base itself. 107.
Now, among many who are present, which one is distinguished in the purchase of immovable property? To this he says, beginning with "sānnidhya" (presence):
among those present, a kinsman born of the same lineage (*gotra*) who is of the same caste (*savarṇa*) is distinguished.

Either one of equal caste is preferred; in the absence of those two who are of the same lineage and caste, friends—that is, well-wishers—are preferred. Now, among many kinsmen of the same caste and friends, to whom should the owner of the property give the immovable asset?

To the objection "Sell it!", he says: "The will of the seller. (p. 391) Even when the price has been determined, if another person makes an effort to purchase immovable property, [the sale shall proceed] if the nearby bidder offers that same price, and no other does. || 109 ||
If one is unable to pay the price, or if he is otherwise approved for the sale, then the householder who has the goods in his possession may, being capable, sell them to another. (110)
O Goddess, if immovable property has been purchased in the absence of the neighbor, he is entitled to obtain it by paying its value upon merely hearing of the transaction. || 111 ||

It would be more weighty, that is, more significant. The sense is that, among them, one should sell it only to whichever person one desires to sell it to, strictly according to the sequence. || 108 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "Should immovable property whose value has been determined be purchased by someone standing nearby who pays that determined value, or by another person?
In response to this doubt, he says "nirṇīta" and so forth. This refers to the effort to purchase immovable property when its value has been fixed.
Even when the value has been determined by another person standing nearby—
meaning even though the price has been fixed—
if that price [is equal to] the value of the immovable property whose value was determined by the other person, provided that the person standing nearby...

When he gives it away, then another person standing nearby—one who is distinct [from the giver]—would not be a purchaser (*krayaka*), but rather the one standing nearby himself would purchase it by paying the price; such is the meaning. || 109 ||

Since the owner of immovable property is able to sell it even when he is unable to pay its price or does not give his consent for the sale, provided a person is nearby, whereas he would not be so able if that person were far away, the author says "the price," and so forth. [This refers to] one who is present.

If the person staying nearby is unable to pay the price for the immovable property, or if he is not in agreement with its sale— meaning he lacks consent— then the householder, the owner of the home, is able, that is, empowered, to sell it to another person distinct from the one staying nearby.

Now, one might raise this objection: "If a person standing nearby hears that immovable property or wealth has been purchased by another while it was out of his sight, should not the purchaser alone be entitled to obtain it, or should the one standing nearby be entitled to it upon merely hearing of it and paying its price? Anticipating this doubt, the author says, beginning with "If it has been purchased," etc. O Goddess!
If immovable property should have been purchased by another in the absence of the neighboring residents who were present at the time, then upon merely hearing of it,
the value of that immovable property purchased by another [must be paid].
Even after paying the price, a purchaser who remains nearby does not obtain the immovable property if the seller constructs or destroys houses and gardens thereon. (112)
Even if uncommanded, one who is free from debt, unimpeded, and accustomed to the wild forests and difficult terrains is capable of making that land prosperous. || 113 ||
Having bestowed upon the king a tenth part of that [revenue] which is to be accomplished with great effort, one should enjoy [the remainder], since the king is the lord of the earth. 114.

By the phrase "having paid the price, that neighbor deserves to obtain it," it is indicated that one does not deserve to obtain immovable property even by paying its price at a later time, merely because of having heard [of it]. || 111 ||

Regarding immovable property purchased—whether it be a temple and garden constructed by the buyer or a ruined temple and grove—even after the price has been paid, one who merely resides nearby is not entitled to obtain ownership;
this is stated by the verse beginning with "the buyer," etc. If the buyer, as a person, [acts] there regarding that purchased immovable property...

When one constructs or creates houses, gardens, and groves, yet subsequently destroys or crushes those very things he himself built, then even a person standing nearby does not obtain or acquire that immovable property, even after paying its price. || 112 ||
The king has declared that even by a man who has not been commanded, uncultivated land—whether produced from water or produced from the forest—should be made productive while exempt from taxes;
he says "exempt from taxes" and so forth. That which is produced from water is *vanyā*, and that produced from the forest is *kānanodbhavā*.

Furthermore, that land which is extremely difficult to traverse—and for that very reason unobstructed; which is barren—and for that very reason devoid of taxes, meaning free from the share to be taken by the king; such land, even if not assigned and even if not commanded by the king, a person may take when it is productive with crops and the like.

[The suffix] *yat* should be applied [to form the word *vanya*]. That which exists in the forest (*vana*) or in the water (*jala*) is *vanya*. [The suffix] *yat* is prescribed by the rule *digādibhyo yat*. According to Amara: "Water (*payaḥ*), nectar (*kīlāla*), ambrosia (*amṛta*), life-giving (*jīvana*), the world (*bhuvana*), and forest (*vana*).
Those that exist in the forest (*araṇya*) are *āraṇyāḥ*; the suffix *ṇa* is applied by the rule *araṇyāṇṇaḥ*. || 113 ||

He states with the words beginning "much" (*bahu*) and so forth that one should offer a tenth part of the produce grown on forest or wilderness land—which is obtained through manifold efforts—to the king by virtue of his ownership of the land, and enjoy all the remainder oneself; for since the king is the ruler, he is the owner of the land. Therefore...
The digging of ponds, wells, and tanks, and the planting of trees—tasks that are accomplished through great effort and produced by manifold exertion—[are performed] for that [purpose]. (p. 393)
One ought not to build a house in a place that causes harm to others. || 115 ||

In the case of wells and other such works given for the sake of the gods, as well as in the water of flowing rivers, all who have the right to drink [the water] are entitled to its sprinkling, provided they reside nearby. (116)
Because people would become fearful of water from the sprinkling of it, even those standing nearby would not sprinkle water. (117)
Without the consent of the sharers whose names for the wealth have not been divided, as well as for those whose property has not been formally determined, a deposit or a sale is not valid. (118)
Having given a tenth part— a tenth portion— of whatever object has grown on forest land to the sovereign king, one may enjoy the remainder oneself. || 114 ||

He states by means of the verse beginning with "vāpī" that one should not undertake the digging of ponds and the like, the planting of trees, or the construction of a house at a location where their production was not previously desired;
for [otherwise] there would be the existence of the digging of ponds and so forth, the planting of trees, and the making of houses [at inappropriate times].
In a place that causes harm to others or produces what is undesired by others, people ought not to dig ponds, wells, or tanks, nor plant trees, nor even build a house.

Regarding wells and the like dedicated for the sake of the gods, as well as river water, he states with the verse beginning "devārtham" that everyone has the right to drink from them, but the right to use them for irrigation belongs only to those residing in their vicinity.
Thus, in wells and such given for the sake of the gods, and likewise in the flowing water of rivers, all [have the right to drink].

Regarding the sprinkling [of water], however, those who reside nearby—those staying in close proximity—would be the ones authorized to perform it. According to Amara: "Srotasvatī, dvīpavatī, sravantī, nimnagā, and apagā" are synonyms for a river.
(116) Now, surely, by the sprinkling of that water, the people and folk situated near it would become agitated.
To address whether that water should be sprinkled or not, he says, "yattoya...

and so forth. From whatever well or source of water people might become distressed for water—that is, troubled by the lack of drink—on account of the sprinkling of that water, they would not sprinkle it even though it is nearby.
But what need is there to speak of those who are far away? || 117 ||

He states, beginning with the words "of wealth," that there can be no validity for the deposit or sale of undivided property by heirs or those not authorized, nor for a deposit or sale that lacks a formal decision. [He explains] the consent of the sharers, that is, the heirs...

(394) In the case of items that have been deposited and for which the value has been recorded, even if they are lost without negligence, the king shall cause their value to be paid to the owner by the [custodian]; thus all matters are settled. 119.

When a transaction is conducted based on the depositor’s conviction regarding the items deposited, such as cattle and so forth, the creditor shall nourish those cattle [until they are returned]. (120)
Wherever a person employs immobile property and the like for the sake of profit, it shall be done according to fixed rules; otherwise, there will be irregularity regarding both time and profit. 121.
Without [the consent] of those who have not divided their property, the depositing and selling of wealth cannot be accomplished; likewise, for wealth whose value is undetermined— that is,
for goods regarding which there is no determination as to whether "these are his" or "these are so many"— depositing and selling are not valid.
They may both be so. || 118 ||

The king should cause the man in whose house goods are deposited or tied up to be made to pay their value to the owner if they are lost through his negligence despite his prior knowledge; this is stated by the verse beginning with "sthāpyānām" (of those deposited).
If, through lack of effort— whether due to ignorance or due to a prior lack of diligence—

the wealth that was deposited, entrusted, or secured in someone's house should be lost or destroyed, then even though the wealth deposited or secured in that house has perished, that man [must pay] its value.

The king, the ruler, shall cause the value of the property deposited to be paid in every way and by all means to its owner, the master of that wealth; for Sadāśiva, by stating "even when lost without effort," implies that although an effort was made for its protection, if it should somehow be destroyed, [the king must compensate].
He indicated that the king should not be made to pay its price. || 119 ||

He states, beginning with "by consent," that the animals deposited by a person through the very practice of depositing objects such as livestock— by the agreement (*sammati*) of the depositor— are to be properly nourished. [This is] by the consent (*abhimati*) of the depositor, the one who makes the deposit of property.

When a transaction has been conducted with the consent [of the owner] regarding items deposited such as cattle and so forth, among those deposited items therein, the person who is the keeper (*dhāraka*) shall nourish the cattle;
