this is because the rule [prescribing the suffix *ṇini*] based on a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka-vidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), as in the case of the expression "items deposited such as cattle."

The term *nāmi* does not imply length [of the vowel], because even that which arises from an augment (*āgama*) is non-eternal; thus, in the word *dhārta*, there is no introduction of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ardhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*. || 120 ||
Without having fixed a restriction regarding time and gain,
he says "in gain," etc., meaning that there might be a change in that gain in which immovable property and other assets are employed. Where, without a restriction of time and gain—
One should never employ common property for the sake of personal gain while the father is alive, nor without the consent of all the co-sharers once the father has died. (122)
O Pārvatī, when goods are sold by reversing their proper sequence, the king is empowered to rectify that error.
Just as the birth and death of bodies occur but once,
so too the giving away of a daughter and the Brāhma marriage ceremony occur but once, each only once.
A person should employ immovable property and other assets for the purpose of profit;
otherwise, that profit would not be realized. According to Amara, "nīvī" refers to the capital or principal, while "lobha" refers to the excessive profit. || 121 ||

He states with the words "common" (*sādhāraṇāni*) and so forth that, after the death of the father, in the absence of the consent of all brothers, common property must not be employed for the sake of profit. When the father has died, [this applies] to all the sharers.
One should never employ common or general objects for the sake of profit or fruit without having reached a consensus. || 122 ||
He states with the words beginning "krama" that the King is unable to otherwise alter a sale of immovable property and other goods that has occurred at a price involving a reversed order.
O Pārvatī, "kramavyatyaya" means a reversal or inversion of the sequence; [the sale] is at such a price.
When there is the sale of goods— specifically when goods of high value are sold for a low price,
or goods of low value are sold for a high price— the king, as the lord of men, is empowered to rectify such sales. || 123 ||

Now, one might object: "A maiden married by one man according to the injunctions declared in the Vedas certainly remains alive; even when he has died, must she not be married again by another according to those very same injunctions?
To this, he says, beginning with the words "jananam" (birth), etc.: "Just as the birth—meaning the production—and the death of bodies..."

Death also occurs only once, just a single time; likewise, the giving away of a daughter and the Brāhma marriage ceremony occur only once, indeed just once. By using the term "Brāhma marriage," Mahādeva indicated that even for a daughter who has been married once, [the rite may be performed].
However, it was indicated that according to the Śaiva rites, remarriage indeed takes place. || 124 ||
A man who has only one son should not give away his son; likewise, one with only one wife should not give away his wife;
and one with only one daughter should not give away his daughter at a Śaiva marriage, if he is a man seeking the welfare of his ancestors. (125)
In matters concerning the gods, the ancestors, trade, and especially at the royal court,
whatever an agent may perform shall be considered the act of the principal.
O lady of virtuous vows, neither a substitute nor even a messenger deserves punishment for a fault committed by the one who employed them; this is the eternal rule. (127)
In matters of debt, agriculture, trade, and likewise in all undertakings,
whatever has been agreed upon by people should be carried out as it is sanctioned by dharma.

It is stated by the verse beginning with *naikaputra* that a man who has only one son, a woman who has only one husband, and a woman who has only one daughter— provided they are devoted to the welfare of their parents—
must never give away their son, their wife, or their daughter in a Śaiva marriage. A man with only one son [should not give] his son...
One should not give [anything] to anyone whatsoever. Likewise, a man with only one wife should not give away his wife;

and a man with only one daughter should not give away his daughter at a Śaiva marriage. Demonstrating the reason for not giving away sons and others, he qualifies the man: what kind of man? One who is devoted to the welfare of his father (*pitṛhita*).
The meaning is that since he is beneficial to his ancestors, one should not give [the offering] to him. || 125 ||
He states with the words "In matters divine," etc., that whatever ritual action dedicated to the gods or others is performed by a representative,
all of that shall be as if performed by oneself; this applies specifically to rites for the gods, rites for the ancestors, commercial dealings, and especially at the royal court.

Whatever a representative (*pratinidhi*) should perform, that becomes the action (*kṛti*) of the one who directs or impels [him]. In the phrase "in a rite for the gods, for the ancestors, or in trade," the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). It is called *kṛti* because it is performed (*kriyate*); the suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule "the suffix *ktin* occurs after roots to form feminine nouns. (126)
Now, one might ask: "Should the representative and the messenger be punished for an offense committed by the employer (niyantr)?
To this, he says "No," and so forth. O Suvrate, you who possess excellent vows;
[the representative] likewise [is not to be punished] for the fault committed by the employer, that is, the offense ordained by the employer.
Even a messenger or a spy shall not be subject to punishment; this is the eternal and constant rule. || 127 ||

With the verse beginning with "In debt," etc., he declares the necessity of performing all that has been undertaken in its entirety, including debt, agriculture, trade, mercantile work, and likewise all other activities. In debt, in agriculture, in trade, in mercantile work, and similarly in all others—

The universe is protected by the Supreme Lord; those who seek destruction meet their end, while the Lord of the Universe protects those who take refuge in Him. Therefore, one should act for the welfare of the world. (129)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Discourse on Eternal Conduct," in the *Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra*, the most excellent of all tantras, the essence of the determination of all dharmas, within the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva.

Whatever is accepted by people in their worldly activities as being in accordance with dharma (dharma-sammata), all that must be performed. By the phrase "in accordance with dharma," it is implied that whatever is accepted as being in accordance with sin (pāpa-sammata) is in every way unfit to be done by people. || 128 ||
He states, beginning with "by the Lord," that those humans who desire their own welfare must act solely for the benefit of the world;
for they are those desiring to cross over the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is protected by the Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe.
People who desire to destroy [others] go to their own destruction and reach it;
however, the Lord of the Universe protects those protectors of the world.
For that reason, one should be a person devoted to the welfare of the world. Here, the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is implied within the root *naś* (to perish).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. [The thirteenth chapter begins:
To Maheśa, the God of gods, who had thus spoken...

With a mind solely intent on purification for those afflicted by the impurities of the Kali age, Pārvatī— the mother of the people of the three worlds— devoutly spoke that which is the essence of all the Vedas and the sole seed of heaven and liberation. (1)

The Goddess said: How can there be a description of the form of Mahākālī, who is born from the Great Womb, the primordial Śakti, possessed of great luster, and who has become subtler than the subtlest?
"Form (rūpa) is the effect of primordial nature (prakṛti), yet it is directly higher than the highest;
O Lord, you ought to sever this doubt of mine specifically. (3)

"Oṃ! Salutations to Brahman!"—thus he spoke, having uttered these words. [He addressed] those whose minds are solely intent on purification, yet who are afflicted by the impurities of the Kali age; that is, for the sake of purifying people joined with the stains of the Kali age.
Firm-minded. || 1 ||

In response to the inquiry, "What did Pārvatī say to Maheśa?", he says, beginning with "mahadyoneḥ" (of the Great Womb). She is Mahākālī, who is the source from which the principle of Mahat (the Great Principle) arises. "Etat" means this. || 3 ||
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
O beloved, for the sake of the practitioners, I have previously described the form of the Goddess as it is fashioned according to their qualities and activities. (4)
Just as colors such as white and yellow dissolve into black,
so too do all beings enter into Kālī, O Daughter of the Mountain.
Therefore, the color black is prescribed for that power of Time (kāla-śakti), which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā), formless (nirākṛti), and beneficial for those who have attained yoga.
Because she is eternal, whose form is time, imperishable, and of the nature of Śiva,
the mark of the moon is depicted upon her forehead due to her immortality.
Since he perceives the entire world throughout all time by means of the eternal moon, sun, and fire, he is therefore conceived as possessing three eyes.
To this, the illustrious Sadāśiva replied with these ten verses beginning with "upāsakānām": "O Dear One, for the sake of those people who are practitioners (*upāsaka*),
the form of the Goddess Mahākālī [is manifested] according to their respective qualities and actions."
It has already been stated previously that this is conceptually constructed and not real.

"Śvetā," and so forth: O Śailajā Pārvatī, just as colors such as white and yellow dissolve—that is, become completely merged—into the color black, in that very same way, all beings enter and are absorbed into Kālī. For this reason, of her...

The connection [of the words] is as follows: "the color of Kālī is determined and described as black. For those who have attained yoga—that is, those who have acquired the means to liberation in the form of knowledge—[this is stated]. || 5 || 6 ||

By the words "of the eternal," etc.: because she is eternal (*nityā*), devoid of growth (*vṛddhiśūnyā*), immutable (*avyayā*), free from decay (*apakṣayarahitā*), of the nature of Śiva (*śivātman*), auspicious by essence (*kalyāṇasvarūpā*),
and of the form of Time (*kālarūpā*), this Kālī possesses a moon-mark on her forehead due to her immortality (*amṛtatva*).
It has been explained; it has been told. || 7 ||
That which pertains to time and arises from time. || 8 ||
(400) Because of devouring all sentient beings by chewing them with the teeth of Time, that assembly of their blood is described as being in the form of the garment of the Mistress of the Gods. 9.
At every moment, the protection of living beings from calamities is auspicious;
the impelling toward their respective duties and the granting of fearlessness are declared to be excellent.
Having pervaded and supported all things produced from *rajas*, she remains established there;
therefore, O auspicious lady, she is said to be seated upon a red lotus throne.
The Goddess, who consists of consciousness and is the nature of the witness of all, beheld Kālīkā playing with Kāla after he had drunk the wine made of delusion.
Thus, various forms have been fashioned according to [their] qualities for the benefit of devotees of limited intelligence. (13)
The Śrī Devī said:
"The meditation upon Kālī which has been described as the means for the liberation of living beings—corresponding to that [meditation], one should fashion an image made of clay or stone. (14)

Of all sentient beings, of every living creature; by the "Time-tooth," that is, by the tooth which has the form of Time; "that mass of blood" refers to the collection of the blood of all sentient beings. || 9 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "samaye" and so forth: O Śivā, at every moment, at every time, the protection of living beings from calamities and their impulsion toward their respective duties—this is declared to be the boon and the state of fearlessness granted by Kālikā. [This refers to] the protection of living beings from misfortune...
Protection is said to be the granting of fearlessness, and the meaning is that incitement toward one's respective duties is said to be the boon. || 10 ||
Having pervaded; having supported. || 11 ||
The world is temporal and arises in time; she is composed of consciousness and is the very nature of knowledge. 12.

Desiring to hear the ritual procedure for the consecration of the image of the primordial goddess Kālikā, as well as that of other deities, and the fruit of the consecration of houses and so forth, the Goddess spoke:
If a practitioner, having fashioned [an image] even from wood,
constructs a variegated temple and installs there the Goddess of Gods adorned with garments and ornaments, what fruit arises for him? (15)
O Lord, by what rite should the consecration of that image be performed?
Please reveal that to me in its entirety out of compassion. (16)
The installation of ponds, wells, houses, gardens, and images of deities was previously indicated, but it has not been explained in detail. (17)
I also wish to hear its ritual procedure from your lotus-like mouth;
O Supreme Lord, please tell it if it pleases you, out of your compassion. (18)
The illustrious Sadāśiva said: O Supreme Goddess, this which you have asked is a supreme secret and the ultimate reality;
out of affection for you, I shall tell it—listen with a concentrated mind. 19.
Human beings on earth are of two kinds: those with desire and those free from desire.
For those without desire, the goal is liberation; for those with desire, it is said to be the attainment of fruits.
O beloved, whoever installs an image of whichever deity attains that world as well as the enjoyments arising from it. (21)

"Regarding the passage beginning with 'dhyānam' (meditation): O Lord, for the sake of the liberation of living beings, that meditation which was taught by Kālī— corresponding to that meditation, one should fashion an image made of clay (a modification of earth), or stone, or wood, or metal."

The syntactical connection is as follows: if a practitioner, having fashioned a variegated mansion and having established therein the Goddess Kālī, the Queen of the Gods, adorned with garments and ornaments, then what fruit arises for that practitioner?
Of the image, that is, the representation. || 14–17 ||
Nor is there a fruit [arising] from the *api* (also/even). || 18 ||
Thus entreated by the Goddess, Śrī Sadāśiva said:
"This is a secret," and so forth. (19–21)
In a clay image, however, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas;
for images made of wood, stone, or metal, the reward increases tenfold respectively. (22)

Listen to the merit of that man who, for the sake of a deity or for the sake of his desire, constructs a temple made of grass, wood, and so forth, provided with banners and vehicles, and either consecrates it or abandons it. (23)
O Supreme Goddess, he who gives a house constructed from grass and other materials shall dwell in the abode of the gods for thousands of millions of years.
But for the gift of a house made of bricks, the fruit is a hundredfold greater than that; and from the gift of a stone house, the merit is ten thousandfold more than that. (25)
One who gives a bridge or a causeway in this world does not see the realm of Yama;
having attained the blissful abode of the gods, he rejoices with the inhabitants of heaven.
Having established groves of trees and gone to the abode of the Thirty-three gods,
dwelling among the clusters of wish-fulfilling trees in celestial mansions,
he enjoys delightful pleasures, whatever his heart desires.
Those who provide a reservoir of water for the pleasure of all sentient beings,
having shaken off their sins and attained the healthy world of Brahmā,
shall dwell there for a hundred years amidst the spray of waters. (28)
"In a reflection" means in an image; here, the word "when this has been installed" is to be supplied. "Observe" means listen. (23–27)
A reservoir of water, such as a pond or a well; free from disease, meaning devoid of affliction; at every spray, that is, at every drop of water. || 28 ||
O Goddess, he who gives a vehicle that brings pleasure to the deity shall be constantly protected by it and shall dwell long in that world. (29)
Whatever fruit arises on earth from giving a vehicle made of clay, that same fruit multiplied tenfold is obtained from one made of wood, and ten times more than that from one made of stone.
One obtains a hundredfold greater fruit, respectively, by giving a *rintikā*—a vehicle for the gods fashioned from bell-metal, copper, or other materials. || 31 ||
The best of practitioners should offer a great lion in the temple of the Goddess, a bull in the abode of Śaṅkara, and a Garuḍa in the house of Keśava.
With sharp fangs, a formidable mouth, and a neck adorned with a mane, having four legs and diamond-hard claws, he is celebrated as the Great Lion (Mahāsiṃha). || 33 ||
A bull is said to have horns as its weapon, a pure body, four feet with black hooves, a large hump, a black tail, and dark shoulders. || 34 ||
Garuḍa has the legs of a bird and the face of a man with a long nose; he stands with his feet tucked together, possesses wings, and has joined his palms in reverence. || 35 ||
In that world, in the world of that god. || 29 || 30 ||
Rintikā is brass. || 31 || 32 ||

He describes the form of the Great Lion with one verse beginning with "sharp-fanged": "with a formidable mouth" means having a face with protruding teeth; "with a neck adorned by a mane" means one whose neck is beautified by a mane (*śaṭā*), which is a mass of specific hairs joined together.
Being thus, he has four limbs; that is, he is four-footed. || 33 ||
He describes the true nature of the bull with the single verse beginning "śṛṅgāyudha" (armed with horns) and so forth. "Asitakṣuraḥ" means having black hooves. || 34 ||
He describes the form of Garuḍa with the single verse beginning with "Garuḍa": he has the face of a man (narāsya), meaning a human face. || 35 ||
By the gift of banners and flags, there is satisfaction of the gods for a hundred years. The flagstaff, moreover, should be made thirty-two cubits in length. (36)
It is very firm, devoid of knots, straight, and auspicious in appearance;
it is wrapped in a red cloth and provided with a disc at its tip. || 37 ||

A banner (patākā) should be attached there, marked with the emblem of the respective vehicle; it should have a sturdy base, a slender tip, and be fashioned from divine cloth. That which shines at the top of the flagpole is proclaimed as the banner. || 38 ||
Garments, ornaments, couches, vehicles, and lion-thrones;
as well as vessels for drinks, food, and betel, and a water-receptacle (patadgraha).
Whoever, endowed with faith and devotion, should offer gems such as jewels, pearls, and corals, as well as whatever is dear to oneself, for the sake of the God,
shall reach that world and obtain [the merit] multiplied ten millionfold.
It is said that for those possessed by desire, the fruit is perishable, like a kingdom seen in a dream;
but for those free from desire, it is Nirvana, which is devoid of rebirth. (41)
Upon the consecration of reservoirs, houses, gardens, bridges, pathways, trees,
and deities, one should worship the Vāstu-demon.

"Patākā," and so forth. By the gift of a banner and flag—that is, by the offering of a flag together with a banner—there is satisfaction of the gods for a hundred years (*śataṃ samāḥ*). Between those two, he first describes the nature of the flag:
By the half-verse beginning with "dhvajadaṇḍa" (the flagstaff), [it is explained]. "At the tip" means at the uppermost part. || 36 || 37 ||

Regarding that flagstaff (*dhvajadaṇḍa*), he describes the nature of the banner (*patākā*) with one and a quarter verses beginning with "marked by the emblems of their respective vehicles. At the tip of the flag (*dhvajāgre*),
meaning on the uppermost part of the flagstaff— 38.
A *patadgraha* is a specific type of vessel used to receive water, betel, and other such items falling from the mouth. || 39 ||
If a person performs building activities without having first worshipped the site (vāstu), that site, together with its retinue of deities, will create obstacles for him. (43)
He had a tawny face, reddish-brown hair, and terrifying red eyes;
he was cave-eyed, with long hanging ears, shanks, and a massive belly. || 44 ||
Aśvatuṇḍa, Kākakaṇṭha, Vajrabāhu, and Vratāntaka—these attendants of Vāstu should be worshipped with great effort. (45)
Listen to the mandala which I shall describe, wherein one should worship the site (vāstu).
On an altar or in a level place smeared with auspicious water, measuring one cubit in size between the directions of Vāyu and Īśa (the northwest and northeast). || 47 ||
One should fashion a single line according to the sequence of the sūtra-falling;
likewise, one should draw another from the northeast (īśāna) to the southeast (agni).
Having drawn lines from the southeast (āgneya) to the southwest (nairṛta), and from the southwest to the northwest (vāyava),
one should draw a single square mandala.
"Having approached," meaning having reached. || 40–43 ||
Now, with the half-verse beginning with "kapilāsya," he describes the retinue of the Daitya Vāstu;
"parikarāḥ" means attendants. (44–46)
For the purpose of worshiping the *vāstu*, he describes the mandala itself with the words beginning "on the altar" (*vedyām vā*) and so forth:
either on an altar, or on a level spot smeared with excellent water from a commendable source,
or between the corners of Vāyu and Īśa, by means of the sequence of dropping the measuring-line (*sūtra*), to the extent of one cubit (*hastamātra*).

One should fashion—that is, draw—one line. Likewise, in that very same manner, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) corner up to the southeast (Agni) corner, one should draw another line. Similarly, starting from the southeast (Agni) corner up to the southwest (Nairṛta) corner.

Having drawn two lines in sequence from the southwest corner (nairṛta) up to the northwest corner (vāyu), starting from the southwest and ending at the northwest, one should thus draw a single square mandala according to this procedure. (47–49)
Having cast the diagonal cords, one should divide that [space] into four parts, O Goddess, so that there may be four fish-tails therein. (50)
Then, having pierced the base of the tail, the wise man should draw two lines from the western direction to the eastern, and from the northern to the southern limit. 51.
Then, in the four corners— even those already provided with corner-lines—
one should lay down four lines by joining corner to corner.
Thus, by means of the conventional method, while drawing sixteen squares,
one should fashion this supreme yantra with powder of five colors.
In the four central squares, one should fashion a beautiful lotus with four petals,
a yellow and red pericarp, and red filaments.

"Regarding the diagonal lines," and so forth: O Goddess, one should divide that four-cornered mandala into four parts—that is, one should effect the division—by laying down the diagonal lines in such a way that a set of four "fish-tails" (matsyapuccha) is formed within that four-cornered mandala. || 50 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "tataḥ": thereafter, the wise person, having pierced the base of the tail, starting from the west (the direction of Varuṇa) up to the east (the limit of Vāsava), and starting from the north (the direction of Kubera) up to the south (the limit of Yama).
One should draw two lines. || 51 ||

With the words "tataḥ" and so forth: thereafter, one should lay down four lines by means of diagonal application (karṇākarṇi-prayoga) within all four squares that are already provided with corner-lines; by the word "api," [it is implied] that within those four squares provided with corner-lines, [the lines run] from west to east.
One should draw two lines from the north to the south, and likewise two lines [from east to west]. || 52 ||

"Thus," and so forth. "In this way," by means of the ritual of convention (*saṅketavidhi*), that is, by performing the ritual of convention in this manner, one should draw sixteen squares (*koṣṭha*). Now, in response to the expectation of what substance one should draw this mandala with, he says: "with five colors," and so forth. (53)
One should imagine the petals as being white in color or else yellow;
one may fill the junctions of the lotus with pigments as desired. (55)
Starting from the Śāmbhava square, one should fill the twelve squares in sequence with four colors: white, black, yellow, and red.
O Dear One, one should fill the squares by means of a clockwise rotation;
therein, one should perform the worship of the deities by means of a counter-clockwise rotation.
One should worship the Vāstu deity within the lotus for the pacification of obstacles;
and in the twelve compartments starting from the northeast (īśāna), one should worship the Dānavas beginning with Kapilāsya.
Performing the consecration of the fire according to the procedure taught in the Kuśaṇḍikā,
and having offered oblations according to his capacity, he should complete the Vāstuyajña.
Thus, O Goddess, this auspicious Vāstupūjā has been described to you;
by performing it, a man is never again afflicted by obstacles arising from the site (vāstu).
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have described the mandala of Vāstu and the procedure for its worship; however, the meditation (dhyāna) has not been told—reveal that now. (61)

"Regarding the four," and so forth. Then, in the four central squares, one should fashion a charming four-petalled lotus with four petals, having a pericarp (*karṇikā*) of yellow and red, a seed-vessel (*bījakośaka*) of yellow and red color, and red filaments (*kesara*). (54–56)

Having thus described the mandala of Vāstu, he now states the procedure for the worship of Vāstu together with his retinue in two and a half verses beginning with "vāmāvartena" (by turning to the left).
In those twelve squares, [one should place] the gods who sport by turning to the left.
One should accomplish the worship of the twelve Dānavas, beginning with Kapilāsya;
having thus heard the ritual procedure for the Vāstu-maṇḍala and the worship of Vāstu together with his retinue, she now desires to hear the meditation (dhyāna) upon Vāstu.
The Śrī Devī said, beginning with the words "the maṇḍala," etc. (verse 61).
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
O Maheśānī, I shall describe the meditation on the protector of the site (vāstu-rakṣasa); listen, for by its constant practice all calamities are instantly destroyed. (62)
Four-armed and of massive body, with his head adorned by matted locks, three-eyed and with a formidable face, he was beautified by necklaces and earrings. || 63 ||
He has a protruding belly, long ears, and is hairy; he wears yellow garments and holds a mace, a trident, an axe, and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his hands.
It was surrounded by heroes bearing swords and shields, such as Kapilāsya and others;
it was the manifest destroyer of enemies, resembling the rising sun. (65)
One should meditate upon the Lord Vāstupati, seated upon a tortoise-lotus throne,
in times of fear from Mārīs, fear of disease, and likewise fear of Ḍākinīs and other such beings.
In the event of the fault of having an ill-omened child, or even in the face of danger from wild beasts or demons,
one should meditate thus and worship Vāstu together with his retinue.
Having offered oblations of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and milk-rice, one shall attain all-pervading peace;
for in the prescribed rites, O lady of excellent vows, the Vāstu deity is to be worshipped in this manner.
The planets, together with the lords of the ten directions, should also be worshipped;
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Śaṅkarī.
Being thus entreated, Śrī Sadāśiva spoke [the verse] beginning with "Dhyānam" (Meditation), etc. || 62 ||
He describes the meditation on Vāstu itself with three and a half verses beginning with "four-armed" (caturbhujam).
"Lomaśa" means distinguished by abundant hair. || 64 ||
O Kālikā, the Mothers, along with Gaṇeśa and the Vasus, as well as the ancestors, must be worshipped if they are unsatisfied in these rites. (70)
All of that would become useless for him, and there would be obstacles at every step;
therefore, O Great Goddess, one must exert effort in the aforementioned rites of consecration.
One should perform the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha here for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
I shall now describe the planetary yantra, which brings about all forms of peace. (72)
Wherein the planets, together with Indra, grant one's desires when duly worshipped;
one should draw the diagram with three triple-triangles and write a circle around it.
One should fashion eight petals attached to the circumference, and outside of that,
one should construct a very beautiful outer square (bhūpura) provided with four gates.
Between the dwelling of Vāsava and the entrance, on the area outside the square enclosure (bhūpura),
one should fashion a single circle measuring one span (prādeśa).
Likewise, one should arrange another [altar] between the Rakṣas and Vāruṇa [directions].
Resembling the rising sun; like the rising sun. || 65–72 ||
"Accompanied by Indra," meaning together with the lords of the ten directions beginning with Indra; "they grant," meaning they bestow. || 73 ||
He describes the planetary diagram itself with the words beginning "with three triangles" and so forth.
First, one should draw a diagram distinguished by three triangles;
then, outside of those three triangles, one should draw a single circular mandala.

Then one should fashion eight petals or leaves attached to the circle; outside of that, one should construct a very beautiful *bhūpura* (enclosure) provided with four gates. Then, in the space situated outside the *bhūpura*, between the directions of Indra (East) and Īśāna (Northeast).

One should draw a single circular mandala measuring one span (prādeśa). Then, in the space outside the square enclosure (bhūpura), between the southwest (nairṛtya) and the west— the directions of Rakṣas and Varuṇa— one should likewise draw another circular mandala measuring one span.
One should fashion or create [it]. || 74–76 ||
One should fill the nine triangles with the colors of the nine planets;
the two sides of the central triangle are distinguished as left and right. (77)
The two [lotuses] should be made white and yellow, while the back portion is of a color other than white;
one should fill the eight petals with the colors of the lords of the eight directions.
One should construct a rampart in front with white, red, and black powders.
O Goddess, there are two circles outside the front, measuring a span in size.
Having arranged the red and white [colors] in the sequence of upper and lower,
the wise one should color the joints of the yantra according to his own desire.

Now hear the sequence of that which is to be worshipped in each chamber, which planet is to be honored in each leaf, which guardian of the direction resides there, and who are stationed at each gate. 81.
One should worship Sūrya in the central corner, Aruṇa and Śikhā on his two sides,
and thereafter one should worship the two Daṇḍas of Aṃśumālī behind the two Pracaṇḍas.
One should worship the Sun in the upper corner, the Moon in the east, Mars in the southeast, and Mercury in the southern corner. (83)

"Of the nine planets," and so forth: one should fill the nine triangles with powders distinguished by the colors of the nine planets, beginning with the Sun. Then, according to the distinction between left and right, the two sides of the central triangle [are filled] in sequence.

The [two] sides should be made white and yellow. The rear portion of the central triangle should be made other than white, namely black in color. Then, one should fill the eight petals with powders distinguished by the colors of the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra. || 77 ||
"White," and so forth.

Then, with white, red, and black powders—meaning powders of white, crimson, and dark colors—one should perform or construct a perimeter wall in front of the *bhūpura*. O Goddess, outside the *bhūpura* in front, there are two circles (*vṛtta*) measuring one span (*prādeśa*).

Having fashioned a circular mandala with red and white [sections] in the sequence from top to bottom, the wise practitioner should color the junction points of the mantra according to his own desire. || 79–83 ||

One should worship Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the Daityas, in the northwest; Śanaiścara in the northeast; and Rāhu and Ketu in the directions of Kubera and Īśāna respectively. One should worship the Moon and the hosts of stars surrounding it. (84)
The Sun is red, the Moon is white, and Mars has a crimson form;
Mercury and Jupiter are pale-yellow, Venus is white, and Saturn is black;
Rāhu and Ketu have variegated appearances—thus are the colors of the planets proclaimed. (85)

One should meditate on the Sun as four-armed, holding two lotuses and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; one should contemplate the Moon with hands like lotuses, making the gesture of charity and holding nectar.
One should meditate upon the son of Soma as a youth with a slightly hunched body, holding a staff in both hands, and with locks of hair dangling over his forehead.

One should meditate upon the Guru as being endowed with a sacred thread (yajñasūtra) and holding a book and a rosary in his hands; likewise, one should meditate upon the Preceptor of the Daityas and upon Śanaiścara, who is one-eyed and lame.
On all sides, everywhere. || 84 ||
Now, with the half-verse beginning with "sūra," he describes the colors of the nine planets starting with the Sun in their respective order. "Sūra" means the Sun. || 85 ||

Now, he describes the sequential meditation on the nine grahas, beginning with the Sun, using the verses starting with "four-armed" (caturbhujam). One should meditate upon the Sun, Ravi, as four-armed and distinguished by two lotuses, the boon-granting gesture (varada), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). The "lotus-hand with the nectar-gesture of giving" refers to the *dānamudrā*.
One should likewise meditate upon the moon, which has nectar in its two lotus-like hands—that is, in its two lotus-hands. || 86 ||

Budha, the son of Soma; "with locks of hair tossing on his forehead" means one whose *kuntalas*—that is, locks of hair—are *lolitās*, meaning moving or waving, upon the forehead (*bhāle*). || 87 || 88 ||
Rāhu and Ketu are the head and the body [respectively], deformed and of cruel disposition.
Having worshipped the planets with their respective meditations, one should sacrifice to the lords of the directions, beginning with Indra. (89)
On the eight petals, starting from the east in due order, the best of practitioners should first worship Sahasrākṣa (the Thousand-eyed One), who is clothed in yellow silk garments.
Vajrapāṇi, with a yellow luster, stands upon Airāvata;
Agni, with a red radiance, is mounted on a goat and holds a spear in his hand. 91.
One should meditate upon Nirṛti, who has a dark body, stands upon a buffalo, holds a staff, carries a sword in his hand, and is mounted on a horse. || 92 ||
One should meditate on Varuṇa, mounted upon a crocodile, holding a noose in his hand, and white in luster;
or one should meditate on Vāyu, who has a dark complexion, is seated on a deer, and has a goad as his weapon.
[He saw] Kubera, golden in form, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, praised by all the hosts of yakṣas, with his lotus-like hands holding a noose and a goad. (94)
Ishana, mounted upon a bull, bearing the trident and the boon-granting gesture, clad in a tiger-skin garment, with a radiance like that of the full moon. 95.
Having sacrificed and having worshipped. || 89 ||

Now, he describes in sequence the meditation and the color of the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, starting with the words "sahasrākṣam" and so forth. "Clad in yellow silk" (pītakauśeyavāsasam) means one whose garment (vāsas) is yellow silk (kauśeya), which is produced from the cocoon of a silkworm; thus he is described. || 90 || 91 ||
Kāla, Yama, seated upon a buffalo (lulāpa). || 92 ||
Nirṛti and the Rākṣasa. || 93–95 ||
Having meditated upon these and worshipped them in sequence, one should first worship Brahmā and Ananta outside in front;
then the deities of the upper and lower circles are to be worshipped, followed by the deities of the door.
Ugra, Bhīma, and Pracaṇḍeśa are proclaimed as the guardians stationed at the eastern gate; Jayanta, Kṣetrapāla, Nakuleśa, and Bṛhacchiras [are at the southern gate];
and Vṛka, Aśva, Ānanda, and Durjaya [are] at the western gate.
Triśiras, Puranjit, Bhīmanāda, and Mahodara—
these were the guardians of the northern gate, all of them with weapons and missiles in their hands.
Listen, O lady of virtuous vows, to the meditation upon Brahmā and also upon Ananta.
Brahmā resembles a red lotus; he has four faces and four arms, is mounted upon a swan, and holds in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a garland and a book. 100.
White as snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, with a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, and a thousand hands and faces—the infinite one is to be meditated upon by gods and demons alike. 101.
Meditation, the sequence of worship, and the yantra have been taught, O beloved;
now listen also to their mantras according to the sequence beginning with the Vāstu, O beloved. (102)
"Having meditated," and so forth: having thus meditated upon these eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, and having worshipped them in sequence,
one should [worship] Brahmā within the two circular maṇḍalas situated above and below the square enclosure (bhūpura) in front.
The two guardians of the quarters are to be honored and worshipped in succession; thereafter, the deities of the door are to be honored.

The deities of the door are indeed to be worshipped; [the author] describes the meditation on Brahmā with two and a half verses beginning with "Ugra," "Bhīma," and so forth, and describes the meditation on [the deity] beginning with "resembling a red lotus" and so forth. || 99 || 100 ||
Now, he describes the meditation on Ananta with the single verse beginning "white as snow, jasmine, and the moon."
Of these, beginning with *vāstu* and ending with *ananta*. || 102 ||
The syllable *kṣa*, situated upon the fire-carrier (*havyavāha*) and joined with the six long vowels, adorned with the *nāda* and the *bindu*, is the six-syllabled mantra of Vāstu. (103)
One should utter the Tāra (Oṃ), then Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by the word "tīgmaraśme" ending in the fourth case (tīgmaraśme), and then say "ārogyadam" (the giver of health);
after that, having added the Vahni-jāyā (Svāhā), one should extract the Sūrya-mantra.
*Kāma*, *māyā*, *vāṇī*, and then *amṛtakara*;
"O nectar, flood the pair, svāhā"—this is considered the mantra of Soma. (105)
Ai Hrā Hrī! Destroy, destroy all wicked beings from every quarter!
This mantra, ending with Svāhā, is proclaimed as that of Maṅgala. || 106 ||
He states the mantras for Vāstu and the others in their respective order with the words beginning with "the letter Kṣa" (kṣakāraḥ).
"Residing in Havyavāha" means that Havyavāha is the letter *ra*; the letter *kṣa* residing therein should be joined with the six long vowels and adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*.
And thus, the six-syllable mantra of Vāstu, *kṣrā kṣrī kṣrū kṣrai kṣrau kṣraḥ*, was extracted. || 103 ||

"Tāram" and so forth: First, one should utter the *tāra*, the *praṇava* (Om). Then, one should utter the *māyā* seed-syllable, *hrīḥ*. Then, one should utter "tīgmaraśme". Then, one should utter "ārogyadam" ending in the dative case (*ṅe*).
Then, having added the *vahnijāyā* (Svāhā), one should extract the Sūrya mantra through this conjunction.
"Oṃ hrīḥ tigmaraśme ārogyadāya svāhā"—thus was the mantra of the Sun extracted.

"Kāma," and so forth. First, "Kāma"—the seed-syllable *klīṃ*—is to be uttered. Then, "Māyā"—the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*—is to be uttered. Then, "Vāṇī"—the seed-syllable *aiṃ*—is to be uttered. Then, "Amṛtakarā" (the Nectar-maker) is to be uttered. Then, "Amṛta" (Nectar) is to be uttered. Then, "Plāvayat" (Flooding) and the pair [of hands] are to be uttered. Then, "Svāhā" is to be uttered.
By means of the application [of the mantra]: *klīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ amṛtakarā amṛtaṃ plāvaya plāvaya svāhā*, this is considered the Soma-mantra. || 105 ||

"AIM," and so forth. First, one should utter "AIḤ / HRĀḤ / HRĪḤ. Then, after all the words [of the name], one should say "destroy, destroy the wicked ones" (*sarvaduṣṭān nāśaya nāśaya*). By this combination, the mantra "AIḤ HRĀḤ HRĪḤ SARVADUṢṬĀN NĀŚAYA NĀŚAYA" is produced, ending with *svāhā*.
This mantra of Maṅgala is proclaimed to end with "svāhā. || 106 ||

Having uttered *hrīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, and the word "gentle one" (*saumya*), one should then say "all desires" (*sarvān kāmān*); at the end, say "fulfill" (*pūraya*) followed by the beloved of fire (*vahnikāntā*). This is the mantra for the son of the Moon (*somātmaje*). (107)

The mantra of Bṛhaspati is: the speech [TĀREṂ] encased by TĀRA (OṂ), followed by the word for the preceptor of the gods (GURU), then "grant what is desired, grant" (ABHĪṢṬAṂ YACCHA YACCHA), and ending with SVĀHĀ. 108.
Śā, śī, śū, śai, then śau, śa, and ḥ—this is declared to be the Śukra mantra.
Hrāḥ hrāḥ hrīḥ hrīḥ, "drive away all enemies"—these two words, followed by "to the son of Mārtaṇḍa, obeisance," constitute the mantra for Śanaiścara. 110.
*Rā hraum bhraum hrīḥ, O enemy of Soma, destroy the two enemies! Rāhave namaḥ*—this is declared to be the mantra of Rāhu. (111)
"Hrīṃ," and so forth. Having first uttered "Hrīṃ," "Śrīṃ," and the word "Saumya," one should then say "all desires. Then, at the end of "fulfill," one should utter the consort of Fire (Svāhā).
By this conjunction, it becomes: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Saumya, fulfill all desires, Svāhā. This is [the mantra].
When Budha is the son of Soma, Manu is considered [the lord]. || 107 ||
"By *tāra*, etc. means that speech should be uttered encapsulated by *tāra*, which is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), joined at both the beginning and the end.

Then one should say the word "suraguro" (O Teacher of the Gods). Then one should say "abhīṣṭaṃ yaccha yaccha" (grant what is desired, grant it). Then one should say "svāhā". By way of this construction: *oṃ aiṃ oṃ suraguro*.
"Grant what is desired, grant it, svāhā!"—this is considered the mantra of Bṛhaspati. || 108 ||
Śā, śī, śū, śai, śau, śa, ḥ—thus is the Śukra-mantra proclaimed and declared. || 109 ||

*Hrāḥ*, *hrām*, and so forth. First, one should utter *hrāḥ*, *hrāḥ*, *hrīḥ*, *hrīḥ*, and then say "all enemies" (*sarvaśatrūn*). Then, one should utter the two words "drive away" (*vidrāvaya*). Then, one should utter "to the son of Mārtaṇḍa" (*mārtaṇḍasūnave*).
After that, one should utter "homage" (*namaḥ*). By this combination: *hrāḥ*, *hrāḥ*, *hrīḥ*, *hrīḥ*, [drive away] all enemies.
"Drive away, drive away! Salutation to the son of Mārtaṇḍa!"—this is considered the mantra for Śanaiścara. || 110 ||
"Rā" and so forth: first one should say "rā/ hrau/ bhrau/ hrī/ somaśatro śatrūn"; then one should say the pair "vidhvaṃsaya"; then one should say "rāhave namaḥ". By way of application: rā/ hrau/...
KRŪ HRA KRAI KETAVE SVĀHĀ—this is proclaimed as the mantra of Ketu. || 112 ||
La, ra, mṛ, strū, va, yam, kṣa, hau, and brīṃ—these are declared to be, in order, the ten mantras of the world-protectors beginning with Indra and ending with Ananta. (113)
The name-mantras for other retinues have been proclaimed;
wherever no mantra is mentioned, this procedure taught by Śiva applies everywhere. (114)
O Queen of Devas, a wise man should not append "namaḥ" to a mantra that already ends with "namaḥ";
likewise, he should not offer "vahnivallabhā" (svāhā) to a mantra that already ends with "svāhā."
Flowers, garments, and ornaments should be offered to the planets and other deities according to their respective colors; otherwise, it will not lead to their satisfaction. (116)
The wise man, establishing the fire according to the procedure taught in the Kuśaṇḍikā,
should perform the oblation with various kinds of flowers or with sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh).
In rites of pacification and nourishment, he is Varada;
in consecrations, he is Lohitākṣa; and in cruel rites, he is Śatruhan.
"Bhrair / Hrīḥ / O Somaśatru, destroy, destroy the enemies! Salutation to Rāhu"—this is declared to be the mantra of Rāhu; thus it has been described. (111-112)

"Lam," "ram," "mṛm," "strūm," "vam," "yam," "kṣam," "haum," "brīm," and "am"— these ten mantras are proclaimed and taught as belonging, in order, to the ten guardians of the directions (dikpālas), beginning with Indra and ending with Ananta. || 113 || 114 ||
The word "svāhā" is the beloved of Fire (Agni). || 115 ||
Of those [planets] and so forth. || 116 ||
With *samidh* sticks, that is, pieces of wood. || 117 ||
O Maheśānī, by performing the sacrifice to the planets (grahayāga) during rites of pacification, nourishment, or even cruel acts, one shall attain one's desired object. (119)
Just as in the rites of consecration, the worship of the deities and the libation to the ancestors are prescribed,
so too are they ordained for the Vāstuyāga and the propitiation of the planets.

If the rites of installation and sacrifice are performed two or three times on a single day, then the worship of the deity, the ancestral śrāddha, and the consecration of the fire are to be carried out by way of a single ritual procedure (tantra).
Reservoirs of water, houses, groves, bridges, and pathways;
vehicles, seats, conveyances, garments, and ornaments. (122)
Those who desire the fruits [of their merit] should not offer to the God vessels for food and drink or any other objects that have not been consecrated. 123.

In every instance of optional ritual action, the wise person should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) according to the injunctions of the scriptures, for the sake of attaining the full merit of the deed. 124.
Having first uttered the name of the consecrated object that has been worshipped with Sanskrit mantras,
and having stated its designation as a gift, one obtains the full fruit by giving it correctly.
The mantras to be employed for the sprinkling of reservoirs, houses, groves, bridges, causeways, and trees are now declared; they are to be used with the Brahmavidyā.
Varada is named Varada; Lohitākṣa is known as Lohitākṣa; Śatruhā is designated as Śatruhā. (118–120)
By means of the tantra, [it is] indeed as one. || 121–124 ||
It is consecrated by ritual refinement (*saṃskṛta*), purified, and fully worshipped;
it is designated as "the gift" (*sampradāna*), meaning it bears the name of a gift. || 125 ||
Together with the Gāyatrī, the knowledge of Brahman. || 126 ||
O source of life for all living beings, O bestower of vitality, O Lord of the Waters! Through this sprinkling, may those who move upon the water, upon the earth, and in the sky be satisfied. (127)
O beloved of Brahmā, born from grass, wood, and other materials, I sprinkle you with water; may you be ever propitious. 128.
However, in the case of a temple made of bricks, it should be stated that it is produced from bricks and so forth.
May these trees, which bring delight with their fruits, leaves, branches, and shade, grant all my desires when they are sprinkled with the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites. 130.
You are the bridge over the oceans of worldly existence, the one who carries travelers across, and you are dear to those on the journey.
O Setu, having been consecrated by me, may you grant the fruits as described.
O Saṃkrama, I sprinkle you with water so that you may become a bridge for the worlds;
just as you provide a bridge here, let a bridge be granted to me in heaven.
O Dear One, the very same mantra that has been taught for the sprinkling of the grove should be employed by the wise for the consecration of the trees. (133)
Among these, he first states the mantra for sprinkling the reservoir of water:
"O support of life for living beings... [The term] *jīvanādhāra* means the support of life; *vāruṇa* means having Varuṇa as its deity. || 127 ||
Now he states the mantra for sprinkling the house, beginning with "arisen from grass, wood, and so forth. *Vāsya* means suitable for dwelling (*vāsāya hitam*). || 128 ||

Regarding the phrase "made of bricks, etc. (*iṣṭakādītyādi*): in the context of "in a house made of bricks, etc., which is to be sprinkled and produced from grass, wood, and so forth," one should rather say "produced from bricks, etc. (*iṣṭakādisamudbhūta*).
Now he states the mantra for sprinkling the grove: "With fruits, leaves, branches, and so forth. (130)
Now he states the mantra for the sprinkling of the bridge: "Thou art the bridge over the oceans of worldly existence."
Now he states the mantra for the sprinkling of the bridge:

"O bridge, I sprinkle you. That upon which people properly cross—that is, where the act of stepping forward is performed—is a "bridge" (*saṃkrama*), a specific kind of causeway; the address "O bridge" (*saṃkrama*) is used for its invocation. [The object of the action is] the bridge.
Right progress. || 132 || 133 ||
O Ambikā, one should employ the Praṇava, the Vāruṇa weapon-mantra, and the triad of seed-syllables for the sprinkling of all common ritual substances. (134)
If the vehicle is worthy of being bathed, one should bathe it with the Brahma-vidyā;
otherwise, one should purify it with arghya water using the tips of kuśa grass.
Having performed the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) by means of the respective names of the mounts, the mount—
being worshipped and adorned— should be given to the deity.
In a reservoir of water, Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, is to be worshipped;
in the home, Prajāpati Brahmā; and in a garden, a bridge, or a crossing, Viṣṇu—the protector of the world, the soul of all, the all-seeing, and the omnipresent—is to be worshipped.
The Goddess said:
"Various ritual procedures have been described for the prescribed rites,
but the sequence has not been shown by which a human being may accomplish the rite."
Even rites performed with great effort, if their sequence is inverted, do not yield the proper fruit for men who subsist upon ritual action. (139)

"Oṃ," and so forth: O Ambikā, one should employ this triad of seed-syllables—the *praṇava* (oṃ), the *vāruṇa* (vaṃ), and the weapon (*astra*, phaṭ)—for the sprinkling of all common ritual substances. || 134 ||
By means of the Gāyatrī, which is the knowledge of Brahman. || 135 ||

"Prāṇa," and so forth: having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) of the vehicle by means of the *devīprāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra— which possesses the previously mentioned indicative marks (*liṅga*) and words— the vehicle (*vāha*), which is the mount (*vāhana*), is worshipped and adorned under the name of that respective vehicle.
It becomes something to be given to the deity. || 136 ||
Sarvadṛk means the seer of all objects; vibhu means the pervasive one. || 137 ||

Then, desiring to know the sequence of those various rites and their specific procedures as they have been described, the Goddess spoke, beginning with the words "vividhāni" (various), and so forth. 138–139.

The venerable Sadāśiva said: O Supreme Goddess, you who act for our welfare like a mother, that which has been spoken by you concerns the supreme good for those people whose minds are occupied with the fruits [of their actions]. (140)
O Goddess, I shall now describe the performance of these aforementioned rites individually, according to the sequence of the Vāstuyāga; listen attentively.
Having restricted one's food on the previous day, one should perform the ritual bath tomorrow morning;
having performed the morning rites, one should worship the Guru, who is Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having formed a firm resolve with his own desired object in mind, the practitioner of mantras should worship Gaṇeśa and the other deities according to the path shown by the ritual rules.

Having the luster of the bandhūka flower, three-eyed, with the face of a noble elephant, wearing a sacred thread of serpents, holding in his lotus-hands a conch, a discus, a sword, and a stainless lotus;
with the rising young moon as his crest-jewel, and the beauty of his garments and limbs radiant with the rays of the sun.
Worship Gaṇapati, who is adorned with various ornaments and seated upon a red lotus.
Having meditated thus and having worshipped Gaṇeśvara according to one's ability,
one should then duly honor Brahmā, Vāṇī, Viṣṇu, and Lakṣmī.

Being thus entreated, Śrī Sadāśiva spoke with the words beginning "That which was said," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "those whose minds are occupied with results": it refers to those whose minds (*cetas*) are occupied with—that is, characterized by activity directed toward—results (*phala*). || 140 ||
Practice is the means of accomplishment. || 141 ||
He describes the sequence for performing the rites prescribed in the order of the *vāstuyāga* with the verses beginning "on the previous day," etc. (142–143).
Now, he describes the meditation on Gaṇapati with the single verse beginning with "bandhūkābham":

"Having the luster of a bandhūka flower" means possessing a radiance similar to the bandhūka blossom; "having the rising young moon as his crest-ornament" means that the young moon which is rising is upon his crest.

Having offered oblations of streams of clarified butter to Śiva, Durgā, the planetary deities (grahas), and likewise the sixteen Mothers (mātṛkāḥ), as well as to the Vasus, one should perform the rites for the ancestors (pitṛkriyā). || 146 ||
Then, having constructed the mandala of Vāstu-rakṣas according to the prescribed method,
one should worship the Daitya Vāstu there along with his attendants.
Then, having prepared the sacrificial ground and consecrated the fire as before,
and having performed the rites up to the *dhārā-homa*, one should commence the *vāstu-homa*.
Having offered oblations according to one's ability to him and to his retinue,
as well as to the deities who have been worshipped, one should bring the ritual to completion.
This sequence has been told to you for the Vāstuyāga when it is to be performed separately; by this very method, O beloved, the sacrifice to the planets is also ordained. (150)
Because the planets are the primary focus here, they are not worshipped as subordinate members;
rather, the sequence is that the worship of Vāstu should be performed immediately after the formal resolve (saṅkalpa). || 151 ||
The entire worship of Gaṇeśa and the others is to be performed according to the ritual procedure for the Vāstuyāga;
as for the yantras, mantras, and meditations of the planets, they have already been described previously. (152)
O auspicious lady, the procedures for planetary rites and house-consecration have been mentioned incidentally; now, the purification of wells regarding the matters at hand shall be described. (153)
One whose crown was thus; one whose bodily splendor was enhanced by a garment as radiant as the rays of the sun, possessing such beauty through a cloth shining like the rays of the sun.
Having sacrificed and having worshipped. || 146 || 147 ||
Having appointed an Ācārya. || 148 ||
To that Daitya Vāstu. || 149 ||
In this very sequence. || 150 ||
In this sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña): || 151–153 ||

Having performed the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the worship of Vāstu, either in a mandala, in a water-pot (kalaśa), or in a śālagrāma stone, according to one's capacity. (154)
Then Gaṇapati is to be worshipped, as well as Brahmā, Vāṇī, Hari, Ramā, Śiva, Durgā, the planets, and likewise the lords of the directions. || 155 ||
Then the two Mothers and the eight Vasus should be worshipped; after that, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkriyā) should be performed.
Varuṇa holds preeminence here, for he is especially worthy of worship. || 156 ||
Having worshipped Varuṇa with various offerings according to one's capacity,
one should perform the Vāruṇa oblation in a fire consecrated according to the rules.
Having offered an oblation to each of the deities who have been worshipped, one should complete the rite of fire-offering (homa) with the concluding act of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 158 ||
Then, one should sprinkle that excellent well, which has been adorned with banners, flags, garlands, perfumes, and vermilion, using the previously mentioned sprinkling mantra. 159.
Then, for the sake of his own desire or for the sake of the gods,
a man should dedicate a well or a reservoir of water for the gratification of all living beings.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the foremost of practitioners should pray:
"May all beings dwelling in the sky, on the earth, in water, and in fire be well-pleased. (161)
This excellent water has been released by me for the sake of all beings;
may all beings be satisfied by bathing, drinking, and immersion. 162.
This water has been offered by me as a common gift to all living beings, and to whoever may perish through the ripening of their own respective karma. (163)
He describes the sequence for the consecration of the well with the verses beginning with "saṃkalpam" (verse 154) and so on. (verse 155)
In this matter of the consecration of the well, he is Varuṇa. (156–160)
"May I not be defiled by those sins; may my actions bear fruit.
Then, having offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and performed the rites for pacification (śānti) and so forth, [he should proceed]. (164)
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas, the Kaulas, and even the poor who are hungry;
this is the procedure everywhere for the consecration of water reservoirs, O Śivā.
And in ponds and such places, one should construct pillars for the Nāgas and water-dwelling creatures. || 166 ||
Fish, frogs, crocodiles, and tortoises—these aquatic creatures should be fashioned from metal, according to the means and wealth of the maker. (167)
One should fashion two fish out of gold, and two frogs likewise made of gold;
the two crocodiles should be of silver, and the pair of tortoises should be made of copper.
Together with these aquatic creatures, having abandoned even the pond, the oblong pool,
and the ocean, one should worship the arriving guest while making this request.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the foremost of practitioners should pray for, he says [the following] with the words beginning "May they be well-pleased" (suprīyantām), etc. (verses 161–165).

He states the specific details regarding the consecration of tanks and similar works with the words beginning "In the case of a tank, etc. When a tank or the like is to be consecrated, a pillar for the Nāgas and water-dwelling creatures must be constructed. || 166 ||
Now, in response to the expectation of what aquatic creatures should be made and whether they should consist of substantial materials, he says "fish, frogs," and so forth. || 167 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to whether the aquatic creatures, such as fish and others, are to be made of metal and how many there are to be fashioned, he says: "The two fish are made of gold," and so forth.

"By these," and so forth: together with these aquatic creatures such as fish and others, having abandoned the pond, the long reservoir, and even the ocean, one who is praying for the Naga should worship.
Ananta, Vāsuki, Padma, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, Kulīra, Karkaṭa, and Śaṅkha—these are the guardians of the waters. (170)
Having written these eight names of the Nāgas upon an Aśvattha sprout,
and having recollected the Praṇava and the Gāyatrī, one should place them within the middle of the jar.
Having made the moon and the sun witnesses, one should stir [the water] and draw out a single [serpent];
whichever nāga rises up there, one should appoint him as the protector of the waters.
Having brought a single auspicious pillar, twenty cubits in length, made of straight wood, and smeared with oil and turmeric; 173.
One should bathe [the image] with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) while reciting the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava;
there, one should worship the Nāga accompanied by Hrī, Śrī, Kṣamā, and Śānti.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to in what place one should worship which nāga, or what one should pray for, he says "Ananta" and so forth. The grammatical connection is that these eight nāgas, beginning with Ananta, are the protectors of the waters (pāthasām). || 170 ||

"Thus eight," and so forth. Having written these eight names of the Nāgas, beginning with Ananta, upon the leaf of an Aśvattha tree, and having recollected the Praṇava and the Gāyatrī, one should cast them into the middle of the jar. || 171 ||

"Candrārka" and so forth. Then, having made the moon and the sun witnesses, one should stir together the *aśvattha* leaves upon which the names of the serpents (*nāga*) have been written, and draw out a single *aśvattha* leaf bearing the name of a serpent. Therein, whichever serpent...
One should cause that nāga who rises up to become the protector of the water. || 172 ||

"Stambham" and so forth: having brought a single auspicious pillar made of wood, measuring twenty cubits— meaning twenty *hasta*s in length— straight and without curvature, smeared and anointed with oils and turmeric, [one should perform the rite] with the *vyāhṛti* mantras.

And one should bathe [the pillar] with water from a sacred ford while reciting the *praṇava*. Once it has been bathed there, one should worship the Naga together with Hrī, Śrī, Kṣamā, and Śānti. (173–174)
O Naga, you are the bed of Viṣṇu and the ornament of Mahādeva; taking your station upon this pillar, provide protection for my waters. (175)
Having thus prayed, the builder should then erect a pillar of serpents (nāgastambha) in the middle of the reservoir and perform a circumambulation of the pond.
If the sacrificial post (yūpa) was previously erected, then one should worship the serpent in a water-pot, pour that water there [into the pit], and complete the remaining rites. || 177 ||
In this manner, the wise man who has formed the resolution regarding the establishment of a house should perform the ancestral rites (paitra-karma),
beginning with the worship of the site (vāstu) and ending with the worship of the Vasus, just as in the case of a well.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] here specifically, the best of practitioners should worship the god Prajāpati and perform the oblation dedicated to Prajāpati.
"O Nāga," and so forth: O Nāga, you are the bed of Viṣṇu and the ornament of Mahādeva; having taken your seat upon this pillar, provide protection for my water. || 175 ||

"Thus," and so forth. Having thus petitioned the Nāga, the performer should then install the Nāga-pillar in the middle of the reservoir—that is, in the center of the body of water—and perform a circumambulation of the tank. The phrase "in the middle of the reservoir" [is explained by the rule] *pāre madhye*.
The compound *ṣaṣṭyā vā* is an avyayībhāva. || 176 ||

"Yūpa," and so forth. If the *yūpa*—the pillar representing the serpent (*nāga*)—has already been established, then the performer, while worshipping the serpent in the jar, should pour that water—the water connected with the jar—into that pond and complete the remaining ritual acts. || 177 ||
Having thus described the procedure for the consecration of a reservoir of water,
he now states the procedure for the consecration of a house with the words beginning "In this way, regarding the consecration of a house."
In this regard, concerning the consecration of the house: || 179 ||

Having sprinkled the house with the previously mentioned mantra and worshipped it with fragrances and other offerings, one should stand facing the northeast and pray with palms joined in reverence. (180)
O Lord of Prajāpati, adorned with flowers, garlands, and other ornaments, grant us happiness in every way for our auspicious dwelling. 181.
Then, having performed the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), one should offer prayers for peace and blessings;
one should feed the Brahmins—both those of noble birth and the poor—according to one's own capacity.
If the installation is for another purpose, one should employ it here for the sake of that [other] residence;
O Daughter of the Mountain, hear now the procedure for constructing a house for a deity. (183)
Having thus consecrated the temple with the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments,
and having approached the presence of the deity, one should pray with palms joined in reverence.
Arise, O Lord of the gods of gods, you who grant the desires of your devotees!
O ocean of compassion, come and make my birth fruitful. 185.

"House," and so forth: Then, having sprinkled the house with the previously mentioned mantra and having consecrated it, the performer, while worshipping the house with perfumes and other offerings, should face the northeast (īśāna), join his palms in the prescribed manner (añjali), and pray to the house. || 180 ||
He expresses the very prayer directed toward the house with the single verse beginning "O Lord of Prajāpati" (prajāpatipate).
He whose lord is Prajāpati is the "Lord of Prajāpati" (prajāpatipati); the vocative address to him is "O Lord of Prajāpati" (prajāpatipate).

"Anyārtham tu," and so forth. If the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the house is prescribed for another purpose, then in the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to be performed here during the house-consecration, one should employ the phrase "for the sake of its [the house's] residence. O Śailajā Pārvatī, for a house constructed by the gods...
Listen now to the injunction for giving a gift of a house constructed under the authority of a deity. || 183 ||
He explains the procedure for constructing a house for the deities with the verses beginning with "ittham" (thus):

having thus consecrated the dwelling or house according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should go to the presence of the deity accompanied by the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he should pray to the deity. || 184 ||
He states what one should pray for with the words beginning "Arise," etc. (185).
Having thus entreated [the deity], the practitioner brings the god to the vicinity of his house;
having stationed him at the door of the house, he should place the vehicle in front. (186)
Having placed either a trident or a wheel upon the roof,
the wise man should erect a banner with a flag at the northeast of the temple.
Having properly adorned the house with moonlight-like decorations, small bells, flower garlands, and mango sprouts, one should cover it with a divine cloth.
One should bathe the deity facing north with the prescribed substances according to the procedure to be described; I shall tell you that sequence, so listen. (189)
At the end of the mantra *ai hrīḥ śrīḥ*, while reciting the root mantra:
"I bathe you with milk; protect me like a mother. (190)
Applying the root mantra in the same way at the end of the three previously mentioned seed-syllables:
"I bathe you with curd today; be the remover of my misfortunes. (191)

"Thus," and so forth. Having made this request, the practitioner should bring the deity near the house, station him at the threshold of the house, and place or set down the vehicle before him. || 186 ||

"Triśūlam," and so forth. A wise person, having placed or established a trident or a wheel upon the roof, should hoist a banner together with a flag in the northeast corner of the house—that is, in the northeastern direction of the temple. || 187 || 188 ||
The sequence for the bathing of the deity with substances prepared according to the procedure to be described hereafter. || 189 ||

He states that very sequence with "aiḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ" and so forth: at the end of the mantra "aiḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ," while reciting the root mantra, and at its conclusion, while reciting "I bathe you with milk; protect me like a mother," the practitioner first [bathes the deity] with milk.
One should bathe the deity. || 190 ||

"Prokta" and so forth: thereafter, having applied the root mantra in the same manner at the end of the three previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*), and reciting at its conclusion, "I bathe you with curd today; be the remover of [the devotee's] suffering," the practitioner should bathe the deity with curd.
Furthermore, the three seeds are the root, and [the mantra] "O you who bring about all bliss!
Having been bathed with honey, may he, being pleased, make me full of bliss. (192)
Having recited the root mantra as before, while remembering the Sāvitrī and the Praṇava, [he says]:
"O Lord, with the oblation dear to the gods, with long life, semen, and splendor, I prepare this bath for you; always keep me free from disease. (193)
Likewise, uttering the root *gāyatrī* along with the *vyāhṛtis*,
O Lord of Gods, grant my desire as I have bathed with water mixed with sugar.

Likewise, having recited the root mantra, the Gāyatrī, and the Vāruṇa mantra, I perform this bath with divine, pleasing, unctuous, and extraordinary coconut waters prepared by the Creator; salutations be unto You! (195)

"Again," and so forth. Again, while reciting the three seed-syllables *aiṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*; at the end of that, while reciting the root mantra; at the end of that, while reciting "O maker of all bliss" (*sarvānandakara*);
and at the end of that, [reciting] "bathed with honey, pleased, [make me] full of bliss" (*madhunā snāpitaḥ prīto māmānandamayam*).
Uttering "Do so," the performer should bathe the deity with honey. || 192 ||
"Prāgvat" (as before), and so forth. Just as before, having recited the root mantra,
then while remembering the Sāvitrī (Gāyatrī) and the Praṇava (Oṃkāra),
[one should offer] with the oblation dear to the gods, which is the luster of longevity and semen.
O Lord, at the conclusion of my bath, I offer this to you; always keep me free from disease.
Recalling this, the performer should bathe the deity with ghee, [with the mantra] "Obeisance to Āyuḥśukra," which increases longevity and semen, and "to Tejas," which increases splendor. || 193 ||

"In that same manner," and so forth. Reciting the root mantra, the *gāyatrī*, and the *vyāhṛtis* in that very way, and then reciting, "O Lord of Gods, having been bathed by me with sugar-water, grant my desire," the performer should bathe the deity with sugar-water. || 194 ||

"Thus," and so forth. Having likewise recited the root mantra, the Gāyatrī, the Vāruṇa mantra (*manu*), and the syllable *vaṃ*, one should then bathe [the deity] with juices derived from sugarcane using the Gāyatrī and the root mantra. (196)

Uttering the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), the Tāra (OM), the Sāvitrī, and the Mūlamantra, and having bathed well with waters of camphor, agallochum, saffron, musk, and sandalwood, [one should say]: "Be well-pleased; grant me both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (197)
Having thus caused the Lord of the World to be bathed with the eight pitchers,
one should bring him inside the house and place him upon a seat.
If the image is not fit for bathing, one should bathe it in its yantra, or in its mantra,
or upon a śālagrāma stone, and then worship it.
I perform this bath with divine, beloved, affectionate, and extraordinary coconut waters fashioned by the Creator; salutations be unto you.
Reciting this, the performer should bathe the deity with coconut water. || 195 ||
Then, one should bathe the deity with juices extracted from sugarcane, using both the Gāyatrī and the root mantra.

"Kāmabījam," etc. Reciting—that is, uttering—the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*), namely *klīm*, as well as the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), the *sāvitrī* (the *gāyatrī*), and the root-mantra; thereafter...
Well-bathed with waters of camphor, agallochum, saffron, musk, and sandalwood, be well-pleased and grant me both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Uttering this, the performer should bathe the deity with waters scented with camphor and other substances;
*kāśmīra* is saffron. || 197 ||

"Thus," and so forth. By this very procedure and sequence, having caused the bathing with eight jars—that is, with milk and other substances measured by eight jars—and having brought the Lord of the World, the God, inside the house, one should place him upon a seat. || 198 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "snāpanārha" (fit for bathing): if the arcā— the image of the deity— is not fit for bathing, that is, not suitable for the ritual bath, then one should bathe the Deity in its yantra (the deity-yantra), or in its mantra (the mantra of that deity), or upon a śālagrāma stone.
One should worship [them]. || 199 ||
If one is unable [to perform the full ritual], one should bathe [the image] with pure water using the root mantra, using eight jars, or else five or seven as appropriate. (200)
The measurement of the jar was already stated previously in the context of the worship of the wheel;
that same jar is prescribed for all ritual procedures according to the Āgamas.

Then one should worship Mahādeva according to the specific ritual procedures for one's own [deity]. O Goddess, Supreme among the supreme, I shall describe the articles of offering there; listen. (202)
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, again water for sipping, bathing materials, garments, and ornaments. (203)
Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise prostration—these sixteen services are prescribed for the worship of the deity. (204)

The water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture with a second sipping (madhuparkācamau), and the five beginning with fragrance (gandha)—these are recorded as the ten ritual services (upacāra). || 205 ||
O Kālikā, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings—these five modes of worship (pañcopacāra) are prescribed for the propitiation of the deity. (206)
Regarding the passage beginning with "aśaktau" (in case of inability): when it is impossible to bathe the deity with milk and other substances,
one should duly [bathe] the deity with pure water using eight, seven, or five jars, while reciting the root mantra.
One should bathe [the deity]. || 200 || 201 ||
Mahādeva means the great god; there, at that place of sacrifice for the gods. || 202 ||
He states the very *upacāras* (ritual services) with the words beginning "the seat" (*āsana*) and so forth; they are "indicated," meaning described. 203.
He explains the different varieties of *upacāra* with the two verses beginning "water for the feet" (*pādya*) and so forth; this is clear. 205.
Having sprinkled the substance with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, while displaying the *dhenu-mudrā*...
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should recite the exposition of the substances.
Having recollected the mantra to be recited hereafter and the root mantra, as well as the name of the deity with the dative case ending,
one should utter the formula for the purpose of relinquishment.
The procedure for the offering has been declared regarding the objects to be given to the deity;
by this rite, the wise man should present the substance to the celestial being. (209)
In the initial procedure of worship, the offering of water for the feet, the respectful oblation (arghya), and so forth,
as well as the entire ritual of the dedication of the causal deities and others, has been fully demonstrated.
O Dear One, listen now to those mantras for which no specific mantra has been mentioned;
one should employ them in the offering of the services beginning with the seat (āsana).
To you who abide within all beings, the inner self of all beings, I prepare this seat for your sitting; salutations, salutations to you!
Now, he describes the procedure for offering the seat and other requisites with the two verses beginning with "with the Astra-mantra":

having sprinkled and consecrated the substance— the seat and so forth— with the water of the *arghya* (offering water) using the *astra* mantra, namely the mantra *phaṭ*, the practitioner, while displaying the *dhenu-mudrā* over it, [proceeds].
Having fully worshipped the substance with perfumes and flowers, one should utter and recite the description and name of the substance; having recollected the mantra to be spoken hereafter,
one should pronounce the root mantra together with the name of the deity in the dative case.
One should recite the words for the purpose of renunciation. || 207–208 ||
To the god who dwells in heaven. || 209–211 ||

He states the mantras that were not mentioned in the initial procedure for worship, in their proper sequence, beginning with "To the one dwelling within all beings," and so forth. O God, He who dwells within all beings is the "Dweller within all beings" (*sarvabhūtāntarastha*); [the mantra is addressed] to Him, the Dweller within all beings.
"To you, the inner self of all beings, I prepare and offer this seat for the purpose of sitting; salutations, salutations unto you. With this mantra, one should offer the seat to the deity. || 212 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, having offered the supreme seat according to the stated sequence, one should then, with palms joined in reverence, pray for a welcome. (213)
To that Supreme Self, for the sake of whose vision the gods long in order to achieve their own desired goals—to you, my very welcome, welcome! (214)
Today my birth has become fruitful; my life and my actions have borne fruit. Since you have come here, the welcome result of my austerities has arrived.
Having addressed the deity and requested his welcome, O Ambikā, and having offered the water for washing the feet (pādya), one should utter this mantra while taking it. || 216 ||
O worthy recipient of water for the feet (pādya), I offer this water for the purpose of sprinkling those lotus-feet by the touch of whose foot-water the three worlds attained purity.

"Having spoken," and so forth: O Goddess of the Gods, having offered the supreme seat to the deity according to the stated sequence, and then, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), uttering these two statements beginning with "O God, for the sake of the attainment of your own desired goal," [he says] "O such-and-such God, by you..."
One should pray to the God with devotion, saying, "Welcome! A most hearty welcome! || 213 ||

"O gods," and so forth. O Supreme Self, since even the gods desire Your vision for the sake of accomplishing their own desired goals, by You—such as You are—I offer a welcome, a most hearty welcome; salutations to You, that Supreme Self. || 214 ||
"Today," and so forth. O Lord, since you have welcomed me, for that reason today my birth and my life have become fruitful; my ritual actions have also become fruitful;
