and the fruit of my austerities has arrived. || 215 ||

"O Goddess," and so forth: having addressed and invoked the God, O Mother, while reciting the two previously mentioned mantras, having requested a welcome and taken the offered water for the feet (pādya), one should recite—that is, speak—this mantra. || 216 ||
Regarding the mantra he recites, it says "that which is the water from his feet": O Supreme Lord,
for the purpose of sprinkling those lotus-feet by the touch of whose foot-water the three worlds attained purity, I offer this *pādya* (water for the feet) to you.
Having uttered this mantra, "I offer," one should present water for the feet to the deity. || 217 ||
I offer this water of bliss as an oblation to Him who has become the soul of all, by whose grace arises the mass of supreme bliss. (218)
Having taken water mixed with nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola, or even pure water alone, which has been sprinkled and honored, one should offer it while reciting this mantra: || 219 ||
To that lotus-face by whose mere touch even the entire world, though defiled by remnants of food, attains purity—to you I offer this ceremonial rinsing of the mouth (ācamana). 220.
Having taken the madhuparka, one should offer it with devotion by means of this [mantra]. || 221 ||
For the sake of destroying the threefold suffering and for the cause of indivisible bliss, I offer the honey-mixture today; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
Since even that which is impure becomes pure by the mere touch of his touch,
you have offered water for sipping once again to that lotus-face of yours.
"An abundance of supreme bliss," and so forth.
"An abundance of supreme bliss" means a collection of supreme bliss. With this mantra, one should offer arghya to the deity.

Regarding the passage beginning with *jāti* and so forth: having taken water that has been sprinkled (*prokṣita*) and honored (*arcita*), scented with nutmeg (*jātī*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and kakkola, or simply water alone, one should offer it to the Deity with this mantra which is about to be described. || 219 ||

He states that very mantra as "yad ucchiṣṭam" (that which is the remnant). It means "it attains. With this mantra, one should offer the water for sipping (ācamanīya) into the mouth of the deity. || 220 ||
Then, having taken the madhuparka with devotion, he should offer it to the God with this mantra which is about to be recited. || 221 ||
He states that very mantra for the purpose of destroying the threefold suffering: "tāpatrayavināśārtham" (for the sake of destroying the threefold suffering). || 222 ||
Then, with the mantra beginning "tato 'śuciḥ śucitām eti," he should again offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) into the mouth of the deity. || 223 ||
Having taken water for the purpose of bathing, as before sprinkled and worshipped, and having placed it before the deity, one should utter this mantra: || 224 ||
O support of the universe, I offer this water for your ablution to you, by whose splendor the world is pervaded and from whom this world was born.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) after the bath, the clothing, and the food offering;
at the conclusion of the presentation of each other substance, one should give water once for each.
Having brought the cloth and purified it before the deity according to the previous procedure, the wise one, holding it with both hands and lifting it up, should recite this mantra: || 227 ||
To you who are free from all obscurations, whose splendor is concealed by illusion, and who wear two garments—I offer these; homage be to you! || 228 ||
Having taken various ornaments made of gold, silver, and other materials,
and having sprinkled them with water and worshipped them, one should offer them to the God while reciting this mantra.
To You who are the ornament of all, the sole source of the beauty of the universe, I offer these ornaments for the purpose of adorning Your illusory form. (230)

"Regarding 'for the purpose of bathing' and so forth: then, as before, having taken water for the purpose of bathing that has been sprinkled and worshipped, and having placed it and established it before the deity, one should utter this mantra. || 224 ||
He spoke that mantra which one should utter, saying, "The world is pervaded by your splendor. With this mantra, one should offer water for the purpose of bathing to the deity. (225–227)
"Whichever mantra one recites, that one says [to the deity] as 'one who is free from all obscurations' (sarvāvaraṇahīna).
With this mantra, one should offer a garment to the deity. || 228 || 229 ||
He states that very mantra which one should recite while offering ornaments to the deity: "O you who are the ornament of the universe, to the one who has become all things. (230)
To you, the Supreme Self, by whom the earth that bears fragrance was created through the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra), I offer this supreme fragrance. || 231 ||
This flower, captivating, delightful, fragrant, and fashioned by the gods, has been offered by me with devotion; please accept this flower. (232)
This divine incense, the essence of the forest king, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, is offered for your sense of smell—the scent to be inhaled by all living beings. (233)
Well-illuminated, greatly radiant, and dispelling darkness on all sides—may this lamp, whose light shines both within and without, be accepted. (234)
O Supreme Lord, I offer with devotion this food offering (naivedya), endowed with delicious flavors and accompanied by various kinds of eatables; please accept it. 235.
O Lord, I offer you water for drinking, scented with camphor and other fragrances, pure and satisfying to all; salutations unto You. (236)
Then, having offered betel leaf prepared with camphor, khadira, cloves, cardamom, and other ingredients, as well as water for sipping (ācamana), one should perform the act of salutation.
"With the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra)": *dharā* means earth. With this mantra, one should offer fragrance to the deity. || 231 ||
One should offer a flower to the deity with the mantra beginning with "puṣpam" (the flower). || 232 ||
"The essence of the forest-king," and so forth. "The essence of the forest-king" refers to the juice of a specific tree.
With this mantra, one should offer incense to the deity. || 233 ||
One should offer a lamp to the deity with the mantra beginning with "suprakāśa. || 234 ||
With the words beginning "naivedyam" (the food offering), one should present the naivedya to the deity. || 235 ||
When offering a common support for a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), one should mention the shared substance;
or, pronouncing each respective name, one should offer a separate support for each. (238)
Having thus offered three handfuls of flowers to the deity who has been worshipped,
and having sprinkled the house along with its covering, one should recite this with palms joined in reverence.
O House, you are worthy of worship by all the worlds and the bestower of merit and fame;
in providing stability for the deities, may you be like Mount Sumeru. (240)
You are Kailāsa and Vaikuṇṭha; you are the abode and the home of Brahmā.
Since the Lord is supported by you, therefore you are praised by the gods.
Because he sustains that form whose belly contains the entire world of moving and non-moving beings,
even though his body is sustained by *māyā*.
For you are indeed equal to the divine mothers and likewise consist of all sacred fords;
having become the granter of all desires, grant me peace—homage to you! (243)

Having thus made this request and having worshipped [the deity] three times, the practitioner, aiming for his own desired goal, should offer a house equipped with wheels and other features to the God.
With the verse beginning "Water for drinking" (pānārthaṃ salilam), one should offer water scented with camphor and other fragrances for the purpose of drinking to the deity. (236–239)
In response to the expectation of what one should recite over this [image], he says: "O House, you... and so forth. || 240 ||
In the belly, in the abdomen. || 242 || 243 ||

"Thus," and so forth. Having thus requested the house and having worshipped it three times, three times over, the practitioner, with his own desire in mind, should offer the house—equipped with the [mandala] wheel and other features—to the deity. || 244 ||
To you, the abode of the universe and the universe itself, this dwelling is offered.
O Great Lord, accept it out of compassion; be present here. (245)
Having spoken thus and given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the deity who has been offered the house,
one should install him upon the altar amidst the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments.

Having touched the pair of the deity’s feet while reciting the root mantra, and having said, "Sthā / Sthī / Be firm! My dwelling has been prepared by me," one should thus stabilize the deity and then pray for the abode once more. (247)
Be in every way a source of joy for the residence of the household deities;
when you have been released, may my worlds remain stable and free from affliction. (248)
Reside in the abode of the gods with the fourteen generations of ancestors who have passed away, the fourteen future generations yet to come, as well as myself and my retinue.
By your grace, may that fruit which arises from performing all sacrifices and from visiting all sacred fords be mine this very day. (250)
"Viśva" and so forth: "To Viśvāvāsa"—he whose dwelling or home (*āvāsa*) is the universe (*viśva*), he is Viśvāvāsa; to him. || 245 ||

"Thus," and so forth. Having addressed this prayerful statement to the deity, the practitioner— being one who has given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to that deity to whom the house has been offered (*arpitageha*), meaning given (*arpita*)— [should lead] that deity with the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments.
One should place it upon the altar. || 246 ||

"Having touched," and so forth. Then, having touched the pair of the deity's feet while first reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should then say "sthā/ sthī/ sthiro bhava" (be established/steadfast), and subsequently recite "vāsaste kalpito mayā" (this dwelling has been prepared by me). By means of this [mantra] conjoined with the root mantra, [one says] "sthī."
Having stabilized the deity with the mantra, "Be firm; your dwelling has been prepared by me," one should then pray for a palace or a house. || 247 ||

Now, in response to the expectation of what one should request for the sake of the ritual cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he says: "A house for the residence of the gods," and so forth. "Utsṛṣṭe" means given. "Nirāmayāḥ" means free from calamities.
[This applies] as long as the earth (*vasundharā*) remains, and as long as these mountains (*dharādharāḥ*) endure.
As long as the two lords of day and night endure, so long may my lineage continue.
Having prayed thus, the wise man, worshipping the deity again at home,
should offer mirrors and other articles, as well as a banner.
Then one should offer a vehicle as prescribed for whichever deity it may be;
having offered a bull to Śiva, one should pray with palms joined in reverence. (253)
O Bull, you are massive in body, with sharp horns and a slayer of enemies;
you carry the Lord of Gods upon your back and are worthy of worship even by the thirty gods.
All sacred fords reside in his razor-like beard; the eternal Vedas dwell in his hair; and the Nigamas, Āgamas, and Tantras abide upon the tips of his teeth. (255)
O illustrious one, when this has been given to you, may the Lord of Pārvatī be well-pleased;
may he grant me residence on Kailāsa, and may you protect me at all times. (256)
Having given a lion to Mahādevī and likewise a Garuḍa to Viṣṇu, O Maheśānī, listen as I speak of how they should be praised. || 257 ||
Possessing great strength and prowess in the battles between the gods and the asuras, Bhīma was the bestower of victory upon the deities and the destroyer of the Danujas. 258.
The *dharādharas* are the mountains. || 251–253 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what one should pray for regarding the Bull (Vṛṣabha), he says:
"O Bull, you... and so forth. || 254 ||
"Daśanāgre" means on the tip of a tooth. || 255 ||
"May he be well-pleased"—this is the ellipsis. || 256 || 257 ||
p. 439) You are always beloved by the Goddess, and you are dear to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Having been offered to the Goddess with devotion, destroy the enemies; salutations be unto you! 259.
O Garuḍa, best of birds, who grants delight to the Lord of Śrī;
O you with the adamantine beak and sharp talons, whose wings are golden!
Homage be to you, the lord of birds; homage be to you, O king of winged creatures. || 260 ||
O destroyer of the pride of enemies, just as you stand here with palms joined in the presence of Viṣṇu, so place me before Viṣṇu.
When you are pleased, O Lord of the World, he who is pleased bestows perfection.
One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the deity for the materials offered to Him;
likewise, one should devotedly dedicate the fruit of the ritual action to Him.
Accompanied by ministers and kinsmen, one should do so with dances, songs, and musical instruments. (263)
Having circumambulated the house and bowed to the deity, he should feed the twice-born.
The same sequence that has been described for the consecration of a temple is also prescribed for groves, bridges, causeways, and trees. || 265 ||
In these specific rites, the eternal Viṣṇu is especially worthy of worship;
likewise, all acts such as worship and fire-offerings are to be performed according to the rules for the ritual donation of a house.
He offers praise to the Lion himself with these two verses beginning with "surāsura... and so forth.
Then, he offers praise to Garuḍa with three verses beginning with "O Garutmān.
O Garutmān, O Garuḍa! O best of birds, O supreme among winged creatures! (260–262)
To that god. || 263 ||

One should never give a house or similar property to a deity that has not been formally installed (*apratiṣṭhita*). When a deity is to be honored while uninstalled, the offering of worship and gifts is prescribed. (267)
Now, the procedure for the installation of the illustrious Primordial Goddess (Ādyā) is described therein;
by means of which, once installed, the Goddess swiftly grants one's desires. (268)
On that day, the practitioner, having bathed in the morning and being pure, facing north,
should perform the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the rules and then worship Vāstveśvara.
Having performed the worship of the planets, Āditya, Heramba, and others, as well as the ancestral rites (śrāddha),
the practitioners and Brahmins should approach the presence of the deity every month.
Having brought the image to a fixed residence or some other auspicious place, the best of practitioners should worship it and bathe it. (271)
First, one should bathe with ashes; then with clay from an anthill;
then with clay originating from the tusk of a boar or the tusk of an elephant;
and also with clay from the door of a courtesan, as well as that produced from the Pradyumna lake.
Then, having prepared [the image] with the five astringents (pañcakaṣāya), the five flowers, and the three-leaved plants,
the wise one should bathe the image with scented oils.
He should cause [them] to rest and feed [them]. 264–268.

He describes the very sequence for the installation of the venerable Ādyā with the words beginning "on that day, the practitioner," and so forth. "On that day" means on the day of the installation of the venerable Ādyā. || 269 ||
Heramba is Gaṇeśa. || 270 ||

"Pratiṣṭhitā" and so forth: Then the supreme practitioner, having brought the image—the object of worship—into a consecrated house or some other beautiful location, and having worshipped it, should bathe it. || 271 ||
Now, in response to the expectation of what substance one should bathe the image with, he says "with ashes," and so forth. || 272 || 273 ||
The *vāṭī*, *ālabadarī*, *jambu*, *vakula*, and likewise the *śālmali*—these five trees are declared to be the astringents (*kaṣāya*) for the ritual bath. (274)
Karavīra, as well as Jātī, Campaka, the lotus (sarasīruha), and the Pāṭalī flower—these are proclaimed as the five flowers. || 275 ||
Barbara, tulasī, and bilva are declared to be the three leaves. || 276 ||
In these aforementioned substances, the addition of water is prescribed;
however, in the case of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and scented oil, one should avoid adding water.
Reciting the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava, while uttering the root mantra, one should say, "I bathe [the deity] with the water of this substance; obeisance. (278)
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, the wise one should bathe the image with the eight substances beginning with milk, as well as with lukewarm water.
Having cleansed the Śivā with white wheat flour or sesame paste,
one should rub it dry with the powder of *śālī* rice.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to with which five *kaṣāyas*, which five flowers, and which three leaves one should bathe the image, he says "vāṭyālā" and so forth. (Verse 274) Now, should one bathe the image with ashes and the like alone, or with them combined with water?
In response to this inquiry, he says, beginning with "in these," etc. (verse 277).

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which mantra should be used to bathe the image with ashes and other substances, he says "savyāhṛtim" and so forth: first, while reciting the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, and then the Mūlamantra.
Then, while reciting the mantra, one should say: "I bathe this substance with water;
*namaḥ*. With this very mantra, one should bathe the image using ashes and other substances mixed with water.

Having bathed the image with eight jars of water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and having dressed it in fine garments, one should bring the image—its limbs now thoroughly cleansed—to the place of worship. (281)
In case of inability, the best of practitioners should devoutly bathe the image with twenty-five jars of pure water.

At each bath of the Great Goddess, one should perform worship with the Śakti-mantra. Then, having placed the image upon a well-adorned seat and having honored it with water for the feet, the arghya-offering, and other rites, one should pray with palms joined in reverence.
Salutations to you, O image fashioned by Viśvakarman;
salutations to you, the abode of the deities, who grants the desires of your devotees; salutations! (285)
In you I worship today the primordial Supreme Goddess, higher than the highest; may you make my body, which remains defective due to errors in craftsmanship, complete. Salutations to you! (286)
Then, placing his hand upon the head of that image, remaining silent, he should touch its limbs after reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Performing the six-limbed Mātṛkā-nyāsa by assigning [the letters] to the various limbs of the image,
one should carry out the six-limbed nyāsa with the root mantra accompanied by the six long vowels.
With lukewarm water, that is, with slightly warm water. || 279–281 ||
The image; that is, the idol. || 282–284 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what one should pray for regarding the image, he says: "Salutation to you, O Image," and so forth (verses 285–287).

"Six-limbed," and so forth. Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed *mātṛkā* upon the limbs of the image according to the previous rule, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should also perform the six-limbed placement upon the limbs of the image with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) accompanied by the six long vowels. He should do so.

One should perform the placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa) upon the limbs of the deity using the eight groups of consonants, preceded by *tāra* (om), *māyā* (hṛllekhā), and *ramā* (śrī), joined with the nasal bindu and ending with *namaḥ*. || 289 ||
The wise practitioner should place the vowels and the *ka*-group in the mouth, the *ca*-group in the region of the throat,
the *ca*-group in the belly, and the letters beginning with *ṭa* on the right arm.
One should place the *tavarga* on the left arm, the *pavarga* and *yavarga* on the pair of right and left thighs, and the *śavarga* on the head. (291)
Having thus performed the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
The earth element is in the two feet, and the water element is in the generative organ;
the fire element is in the region of the navel, and the air element is in the heart-lotus.
The element of space is in the mouth, the element of form in the eyes, the element of smell in the two nostrils, and the element of sound in the two ears. (294)
One should place the principle of taste (rasatattva) on the tongue and the principle of touch (sparśatattva) on the skin;
the principle of mind (manastattva) should be placed between the eyebrows in the thousand-petaled lotus.
The foremost of practitioners should place the Śiva-principle, the Knowledge-principle, and likewise the Supreme-principle upon the chest; then the Life-principle and the Nature-principle;
and subsequently, the Great-principle and the Ego-principle upon all the limbs in due order. (296)

"Tāra" and so forth: Then, one should perform the ritual placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*) upon the limbs of the deity using the eight groups of consonants, preceded by *tāra* (Oṃ), *māyā* (Hrīṃ), and *ramā* (Śrīṃ), ending with *namaḥ*, joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*), and accompanied by the *anusvāra*. || 289 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to which specific group of letters should be assigned to each specific limb of the deity, he says: "In the mouth, the vowels," and so forth. (290–291)

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which specific *tattva* should be assigned to each limb of the deity, he says: "The *pṛthivī-tattva* [is to be assigned] to the two feet," and so forth (verses 292–296).
One should perform the placement with the first [syllable] preceded by *tāra* (oṃ) and *māyā* (hrīḥ), ending with *namo* in the dative case (*ṅe*). || 297 ||

While reciting the root mantra encased within the letters of the Mātṛkā along with the bindu, one should perform the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) in the positions of the Mātṛkā, ending each with "namaḥ. || 298 ||
This splendor consists of all sacrifices; this body consists of all beings. This form has been fashioned for you; here I establish you. (299)
Then, having performed the visualization, invocation, and so forth according to the ritual procedure for worship,
and having accomplished the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), one should worship the Supreme Deity.
Whatever mantras have been prescribed for the offering of a temple to the gods,
those very same mantras should be employed here in the worship according to their indicative marks (liṅga).
Having offered oblations into the fire duly consecrated and worshipped,
and having invoked and fully honored the Goddess, one should perform the birth-rites.
Naming at birth, the rite of first exit, the first feeding of solid food, tonsure, and initiation—these six purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been proclaimed by Śiva. (303)
The Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, the Gāyatrī, the root mantra, the address with the mantra, the birth-rite and so forth, and the naming ceremony—[these you have taught]. (304)

Now, in response to the inquiry as to which mantra one should employ to assign the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) and the others to the feet and other parts of the body, he says "Tāra" and so forth: by means of the mantras beginning with the earth-principle, preceded by *tāra* (oṃ), *māyā* (hrīḥ), and *ramā* (śrīḥ), and ending with *ṅe namaḥ*.
One should place the earth-principle and the others upon the feet and other limbs.

"Along with the bindu," and so forth: Then, while reciting the root mantra ending in "namas," which is encased by the letters of the Mātṛkā with their bindus— meaning joined at the beginning and end by the letters of the Mātṛkā together with the anusvāras— one should perform the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) in the locations of the Mātṛkā.
One should perform [it]. || 298 ||

Then, one should pray to the Goddess with the words beginning "The splendor consisting of all sacrifices," and so forth; the word "vapuḥ" (body) is to be understood as the subject, with "tava" (of yours) as the implied complement. (299–303)
Having recited the *agnikāntā* mantra, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the rite of re-consecration by offering five sets of five oblations. (305)
Having offered a hundred oblations to the Goddess with the name "Datta" preceded by the recitation of the root mantra,
one should deposit a portion of the oblation upon the head of the image.
The wise man, completing the remaining rites through expiatory ceremonies and other means, should feed the practitioners and Brahmins and satisfy the poor and the helpless. (307)
If one is unable to perform the aforementioned rites, one should bathe the deity with seven jars of water, worship according to one's capacity, and cause the name of the deity to be heard.
Thus, O beloved, the installation of the venerable Ādyā has been described;
likewise [the installation] of the vidyās such as Durgā, and of the celestial beings such as Maheśa.
This is the procedure for the installation of a mobile Śivaliṅga;
it should be performed by those who know the ritual rules, preceded by the recitation of mantras and names. (310)
Thus, in the venerable Mahānirvāṇatantra— the supreme among all supreme tantras,
the essence of the determination of all dharmas— within the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva,
concerning the performance of the installation of Ādyākālī.

The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of All Installations of Deities, Including the Sacrifice for Taking Possession of a Site, the Consecration of Water Reservoirs and Temples, and the Giving of Gifts. Now, by which mantra is the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) and so forth performed for the Goddess?

In response to the expectation of how one should accomplish this, he says "the *praṇava*" and so forth: first the *praṇava*, which is the syllable *oṃ*; then the *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūr*; then the *gāyatrī*;
then the root mantra; and then the address of invocation.
Having uttered the name of the Goddess together with an invocation, then the word "tataḥ te" (then [for] you), then the name [derived from] the birth-rite and so forth,
then the word "sampādayāmi" (I accomplish), and then the word "svāhā" ending with "agnaye" (to Agni),
the practitioner who knows the ritual procedure should perform the birth-rites for the Goddess.
The logical connection with what precedes must be established. (304–3310)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra. Chapter Fourteen.
The Holy Goddess said:
O Lord of Compassion, through the performance of the primordial power (ādyā-śakti), you have out of grace described to me the manifold means; I am satisfied by your devotion.
The procedure for the installation of a movable Iśaliṅga has been declared;
now, what is the fruit of the installation of an immovable one, and what is its specific procedure? (2)
O Lord of the worlds, please explain this now in detail;
for I choose to ask about this supreme reality—tell me, whom shall I question?
Who else than you is omniscient, compassionate, all-knowing, and all-pervading?
You are easily pleased, the lord of the distressed, and the one who increases my bliss. || 4 ||
Oṃ! Salutations to Brahmā!
Having thus heard the ritual procedure and the fruit of the installation of all the deities as well as the mobile Śivaliṅga, [I shall now describe] the installation of the immobile Śivaliṅga.
Desiring to hear about the fruit and the ritual procedure, the Śrī Devī said: "Of the primordial power," and so forth. [She spoke] out of devotion—that is, out of love. (1) (2)
"Ask some other who is supremely compassionate, easily pleased, and omniscient;
why do you ask me again and again? To this, he replies with the words beginning, "For this is the supreme reality," and so forth. (3)
The all-knowing one, the investigator of all things. || 4 ||
The venerable Sadāśiva said:
What can I tell you of the greatness of installing a Śiva-liṅga?
By its installation, one is liberated from great sins and goes to the supreme state. (5)

From the gift of the earth filled with gold, from the performance of ten thousand horse-sacrifices, from creating water in a waterless place, and from the complete satisfaction of the poor and the distressed; || 6 ||
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains [from other acts], ten million times that fruit one obtains from the consecration of a Śiva-liṅga; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Kālikā, wherever Mahādeva resides in the form of a Liṅga,
there Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the deities including Indra remain present.
The three and a half crores of sacred fords, both those seen and those unseen,
and all holy fields of merit, abide in the presence of Śiva.
Śambhu, who bears the form of the Liṅga, is surrounded on all sides by the cardinal and intermediate directions;
the sacred precinct of Śiva (śivakṣetra) is proclaimed to extend for a measure of one hundred cubits.
The field of Īśa is of great merit, the most excellent of all sacred fords;
there the immortals and all holy sites shine eternally.
He who dwells for even a single moment in the sacred field of Śiva, being fully devoted to him,
is liberated from all sins and goes at the end to the abode of Śaṅkara.
First, regarding the fruit of the installation of the Śivaliṅga, Śrī Sadāśiva spoke [the verses] beginning with "of the establishment of the Śivaliṅga" (5–9).
On all sides, there is a whirlpool. 10–12.
p. 448) Whatever action is performed here, whether it be small or great, by the power of Dhūrjaṭi, each and every one becomes multiplied ten million-fold. || 13 ||
One is liberated from whatever sin has been committed by being in the presence of Śiva;
however, O beloved, a sin committed within a sacred field (kṣetra) of Śiva is like an adamantine cement.
Whatever preliminary rite, recitation, gift-giving, ancestral offering,
or libation one performs in a sacred field of Śiva, that becomes infinite in its merit.

Whatever fruit is obtained by performing a hundred preliminary rites (puraścaryā) during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one attains that same fruit by reciting [the mantra] once in the presence of Śiva. 16.
Whatever a man obtains by offering ten million funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Gayā, the Gaṅgā, and Prayāga,
he obtains that very same result here by offering a single funeral cake.
Even those who have committed minor transgressions and those who have committed great sins,
if they perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) at Śaiva-tīrtha, they too attain the supreme goal.
Where the Lord of the World exists in the form of a *liṅga* together with the venerable Durgā upon the sacrificial altar, there the fourteen worlds abide. (19)
This much of the majesty of the Lord established here has been revealed;
however, the greatness of the primordial Lord of all beings is beyond the reach of words. (20)
O Hari, who bears the form of the Liṅga, there exists no defilement from the touch of the untouchable in your worship at the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha). It does not exist. || 21 ||
Here, in this sacred field (kṣetra) of Śiva; [the field] of Dhūrjaṭi, that is, of Śiva. || 13–15 ||
In the seizing, in the grasping. || 16 || 17 ||
"Just as, O Goddess, no fault whatsoever is found in the worship of the discus, know it to be so, O Kālikā, regarding a great holy site in a field of Śiva. (22)
What is the use of saying much more here? I speak the truth before you: the power of the Śivaliṅga cannot be described by me.
Whether the *liṅga* is without a pedestal or even with a pedestal, the practitioner should worship it with devotion for the sake of attaining his desired fruit. (24)
The supreme practitioner who performs the preliminary consecration of the deity on the afternoon preceding the installation ceremony obtains the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices. || 25 ||
Earth, fragrance, stone, grain, dūrvā grass, flowers, fruit, curd, ghee, the svastika symbol, vermilion, conch shell, collyrium, and gorocana; || 26 ||
Siddhārtha, gold, silver, copper, a lamp, and a mirror—
these twenty substances one should employ in the rite of consecration (adhivāsa).
Taking each substance individually with the illusory power of the knowledge of Brahman, may there be an auspicious consecration (adhivāsana) for this [substance] from that [divine] state. || 28 ||
Those for whom the *śrāddha* has been performed are "those for whom the *śrāddha* has been performed" (*kṛtaśrāddhāḥ*). || 18–24 ||
Now, he describes the procedure for the installation of the immovable Śiva-liṅga with the verses beginning "pratiṣṭhāpūrvasāyāhne" (in the afternoon preceding the installation) and so forth. || 25 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what specific substances one should consecrate (*adhivāsayet*) the deity, he says "the earth," and so forth. *Siddhārtha* refers to white mustard seeds. || 26 || 27 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what ritual procedure one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of the deity,

he says "pratyekam" and so forth. Having taken— that is, having grasped— each individual substance such as the lotus and others, [one should do so] with the Brahma-vidyā distinguished by the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, which is *māyā*.
Thus, one should touch the forehead of the object to be consecrated with all the elements, beginning with earth;
thereafter, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) three times using the vessel of praise.

Having thus consecrated the deity according to this procedure, the one who knows the ritual rules should then bathe him with milk and other substances, following the prescribed method for the gift of a house.
Having wiped the linga with a cloth and placed it upon a seat,
one should worship Gaṇeśa and the other deities according to the prescribed rules for the performance of worship.
Having performed the placement of mantras on the hands (karanyāsa) and the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma) with the syllable Om (praṇava),
one should meditate upon Sadāśiva, the peaceful one, whose radiance is equal to ten million moons.
Clad in a tiger skin, wearing a serpent as his sacred thread,
with all his limbs smeared with holy ashes, and adorned with serpent ornaments.
The omnipresent Lord is endowed with five faces—smoky, yellow, crimson, white, and red—and possesses three eyes; he bears a mass of matted hair.
He holds the Gaṅgā, has ten arms, and his head is adorned by the moon;
he carries a skull, fire, a noose, a Pināka bow, and an axe in his hands.
Holding in his left hands a trident, a thunderbolt, a goad, and an arrow, and bearing a boon-granting gesture in all [his] right hands, he is praised by all the gods and the best of sages. (36)

With this mantra— "By means of this substance conjoined with the Gāyatrī, may there be the auspicious consecration (adhivāsana) of the deity [Name]"— one should touch the forehead of the deity to be accomplished with all the materials, such as the earth and so forth, using the Praśasti vessel. Thereafter, with the Praśasti vessel...
In this manner, one should consecrate the deity three times in three ways according to the prescribed rite.
"Bibhrat vibhratam" [is an example]; by the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39), there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *-ām*. 33–35.
Bearing, that is, bestowing. || 36 ||
His curved eyes flash with the effulgence of a mass of supreme bliss;
he resembles snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, and is resplendent upon his bull-throne. (37)
The beloved of Umā, who delights in exclusive refuge, was being sung of day and night on all sides by Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
Having thus meditated upon Maheśāna and worshipped him with mental offerings, one should invoke him into that liṅga and sacrifice according to the prescribed rule and with all one's power.
The mantras for the offering of the services beginning with the seat have been stated previously;
here, I shall state the root mantra of the high-souled Maheśvara. (40)

The syllable *māyā* (M), the syllable *tāra* (OM), and the seed-syllable of sound (H), joined with the final letter of the vowels (M) and enriched with the ornament of the half-moon and the bindu—this is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Śiva (HŪM). 41.
Having covered Śaṅkara with fragrant flowers, garlands, and cloth,
and having placed him upon a divine bed, one should purify the Goddess in this manner.
One should worship the Goddess on the sacrificial altar in this very manner according to the prescribed rule;
here, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa) with Māyā and practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).

"Whose curved eyes shine with a mass of supreme bliss"— that is, one whose curved eyes (*locanāni*) shine (*ullasanti*) by means of a mass (*sandohaḥ*), a collection (*samūhaḥ*), of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). [37–40]

He states the root mantra of Maheśa with the words beginning with "māyā" and so forth. First, "māyā," namely the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, is to be uttered; then the "tāra," that is, the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), should be spoken. Then, it is conjoined with the final syllable of the diphthongs—that is, it is joined with the last of the diphthong vowels.

The syllable that is the seed of sound, in the form of the letter *ha*, adorned with the crescent moon and the bindu, is to be expressed; through its conjunction with all the preceding words, *hrīṃ oṃ hrauṃ* is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Śiva.
By means of the *māyā* [vowel] *ī* and the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*. || 43 ||
Possessing the stainless splendor of a thousand rising suns, with eyes like fire, the sun, and the moon;
her lotus-face radiant with a smile framed by golden earrings set with pearls;
holding in her lotus-hands the gestures of fearlessness and boon-giving, as well as a discus and a lotus.
I meditate upon her who has full and lofty breasts, who removes fear, and who is clad in yellow garments. || 44 ||
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Great Goddess according to one's own capacity;
thereafter, one should duly honor the ten guardians of the directions and the Bull.
I shall declare the mantra of the Bhagavatī, by which the one who consists of the universe is to be propitiated. (46)

Having uttered "Māyā" (Hrīṃ) and "Lakṣmī" (Śrīṃ), one should join at the end the letter following "tha" (da) conjoined with the sixth vowel (ū) and the bindu, and thereafter append the beloved of Fire (Svāhā). 47.
Now, with the verse beginning "udyadbhānu... and so forth, he describes the meditation upon Mahādevī alone:
"I meditate upon Mahādevī. Of what nature is Mahādevī? She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns—that is, of rising *bhānus*, or suns.

One who possesses a luster and brilliance like that of a thousand [suns]; furthermore, of what nature? Immaculate, meaning stainless; furthermore, of what nature? Having fire, sun, and moon as her eyes—that is, one whose eyes (locanāni) are fire, sun, and moon; furthermore...
Of what sort? One whose lotus-face shines with a smile, fixed by pearls;
that is, whose lotus-face, which is radiant and characterized by a slight smile, is fixed—meaning bound—by two golden earrings set with pearls.

One whose face is like a lotus; furthermore, of what nature? One who, with her lotus-like hands—her palms—bears the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and boon (*vara*), as well as a discus, and likewise bears a fragrant lotus. Furthermore, of what nature?

One whose breasts are full, high, and elevated—that is, one whose two breasts (payodharau) are both large (pīnau), great (mahantau), and lofty (uttuṅgau)—elevated (unnatau). Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is the dispeller of fear (bhayaharām), the destroyer of fear (bhayahantrīm). Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is clad in yellow garments (pītāmbarām), meaning her clothing (ambaram) or garment is yellow (pītam).
Of her who was thus situated. || 44–46 ||

He states the mantra of the Bhagavatī with the words beginning with "māyām": having uttered "māyā" (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) and "lakṣmī" (the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*), one then utters the letter at the end of the sixth group (*th*), which is conjoined with the sixth vowel and the nasal drop (*bindu*).
As before, while establishing the Goddess, one should offer the bali-oblation for all the deities:
black gram rice mixed with curd and combined with sugar and other ingredients. (48)
Having taken the bali offering to the northeast, one should purify it with the Vāruṇa mantra;
having worshipped it with scents and flowers, one should offer it with this mantra: || 49 ||
All the gods, the hosts of Siddhas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
Piśācas, Mātṛs, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and likewise the Pitṛs. || 50 ||
"May the sages and the other gods, being self-restrained, accept their offerings;
let them stand surrounding Mahādeva as well as the Daughter of the Mountain."
Then one should recite this mantra of the Great Goddess as desired,
and one should perform auspicious rites with virtuous songs, instrumental music, and so forth.
Having thus granted his assent, on the following day, having performed the prescribed rites and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to rule, he should worship the five deities.

At the end of that, one should join the beloved of Fire (the syllable *svāhā*). By joining all these words together, the mantra *hrīḥ śrīḥ dūḥ svāhā* is produced. In some places, the word "ending with *tha*" (*thāntam*) is read as "ending with *sa*" (*sāntam*). 47.

"As before," and so forth. Then, as previously described, having covered [the deity] with fragrant flower garlands and cloth like those used for a Śiva-liṅga, while placing the Goddess upon a divine bed, [he offers] that which is joined with curd and provided with sugar and other ingredients.
One should take away and offer the bali-oblation for all the gods consisting of black gram cooked with rice. || 48 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what procedure one should offer the bali-oblation to all the gods, he says "in the northeast," and so forth. [He offers] with the Vāruṇa mantra, *vaṃ*. || 49 ||
He states the mantra for the offering of the bali-oblation to all the gods, beginning with "All the gods, the hosts of Siddhas," and so forth. (50–51)
Recite "enaṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ dūḥ svāhā" over this. || 52 ||
Performing the worship of the Mothers, the stream of Vasu (vasordhārā), and the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, one should,
with a concentrated mind and devotion, worship the gatekeepers of Maheśa.
Nandī, of great strength, with the face of a monkey, is the leader of the hosts;
these are all the gatekeepers of Śiva, holding weapons and missiles in their hands. (55)
Then, having brought the *liṅga* and the savior goddess (*Tāriṇī*) in the form of an altar,
one should place them upon an auspicious seat within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
Having bathed Śambhu with eight jars using the Tryambaka mantra, one should worship him with devotion through the sixteen types of service (upacāras).
Having likewise established the altar with the root mantra and worshipping it,
the virtuous one, with palms joined in reverence, should pray to Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara.
Come, O Blessed One, O Śambhu, who art saluted by all the gods!
O wielder of the Pināka bow, Lord of All, Mahādeva, homage be to you! (59)
Come to the temple, O Lord, you who bestow grace upon your devotees;
come together with the Goddess, show us mercy—salutations, salutations! (60)
O Mother Goddess, Mahāmāyā, you who bring about all auspiciousness!
Be gracious together with Śambhu; salutations to you, O beloved of Hara! 61.
The five gods, beginning with Brahmā. || 53 || 54 ||
Having worshipped the gatekeepers of Maheśa who are worthy of worship, he spoke with the single verse beginning with "Nandi," etc. (55).
With the mantra "manunā hrīḥ oḥ hauḥ," and with the Tryambaka mantra beginning with "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe," etc. || 57 ||
With the root mantra, namely the mantra *hrīḥ śrīḥ dūḥ svāhā*; in this context, "the altar" (*vedīm*) is sometimes [read as] "the goddess" (*devīm*). || 58 ||
Come, O boon-granting Goddess, to this abode, O bestower of boons!
Be pleased, O Great Sovereign; be the bringer of all prosperity. (62)
Arise, O Goddess of the lords of gods, together with your respective retinues;
may you dwell happily in this house, and may the two who are affectionate toward their devotees be pleased.
Having thus prayed to Śiva and the Goddess amidst auspicious sounds,
and having caused her to circumambulate the house three times, he should cause her to enter.
In a pit dug into stone or even one constructed of bricks,
one should plant the root [of the liṅga] beneath the lower third of the liṅga while reciting the Mūla-mantra.
As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth and the oceans remain, so long, O Mahādeva, be firm here; salutations be unto you!
Having firmly established Sadāśiva with this mantra,
one should cause him to enter the altar there, which has its edge pointing north, using the root mantra itself.
Be firm, O Sustainer of the World, you who cause the creation, preservation, and destruction [of all things];
remain steady here as long as the two lords of day and night endure.
Now, in response to the question of what one should pray for Śaṅkara and Śivā, he says: "Come, O Blessed Śambhu," and so forth.
Regarding the verse beginning with "pāṣāṇa" (stone), etc.: then, reciting the root mantra, the practitioner [should do so] upon a stone.
In a naturally occurring cavity or even one constructed with bricks, one should place [the pedestal] three parts below the base of the *liṅga* while reciting the mantra,
and so forth. Having made Sadāśiva very firm there by means of this mantra beginning with "As long as the moon and the sun," one should [place it] there using the root mantra itself.
One should cause [the disciple] to enter the altar at Sadāśiva. || 67 || 68 ||
Having firmly stabilized [the mind] by this means and touched the *liṅga*, one should recite this: || 69 ||
Tigers, spirits, and piśācas; gandharvas, siddhas, and cāraṇas; yakṣas, nāgas, and vetālas; the world-protectors and the great ṛṣis. || 70 ||
The Mothers, Gaṇanātha, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Bṛhaspati,
as well as those who move upon the earth and those who move through the sky, are all stationed upon his throne.
I invoke that three-eyed Lord, the imperishable Īśāna:
O Blessed One, come here to this machine fashioned by Brahmā. (72)
"Be firm for the welfare and happiness of all.
Then, according to the prescribed rite for the installation of a deity, he bathed Śiva.
O Dear One, having meditated as before, one should worship with mental offerings;
having prepared the special *arghya* water and worshipped the attendant deities (*gaṇadevatā*),
one should again meditate upon Maheśāna and place a flower upon the *liṅga*.

The Śakti, consisting of the letters from *yā* to *sā* with the noose (*pāśa*) and goad (*aṅkuśa*) as the two hands and accompanied by the nasal bindu—namely *hauṃ* and *haṃsa*—one should establish the vital breaths there with this mantra.
Then, having anointed the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain (Śiva) with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron... 75.
One should perform the sacrifice according to the previously mentioned procedure with the sixteen types of service (upacāras),
having performed the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) such as the naming ceremony (jātakarman) and others, in accordance with the earlier injunctions.
"Having made the altar very firm"—this is the ellipsis. || 69 ||
In response to the inquiry as to what one should recite here, he says: "Those who have become tigers," and so forth. (Verses 70–74)

"Enclosed by the noose and goad," etc.: "enclosed by the noose and goad" means that which has a conjunction at the beginning and end with the two seed-syllables *āḥ* and *kroḥ*. Such is the *śakti* [syllable] *hrīḥ*; this seed-syllable should be stated first. Then—
Having completed everything according to the rules, one should worship the Goddess Maheśvarī on the altar and there propitiate the eight forms of the God.
Śarva is declared to be the earth; Bhava is cited as water;
Rudra is fire; Ugra shall be wind; and Bhīma is designated as space.
The Lord of the Paśu, the Sacrificer, Mahādeva, Sudhākara, Īśāna, and Sūrya—these are proclaimed as the eight forms (mūrtis). || 79 ||
Preceded by the individual invocation with the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*,
one should worship the eight forms in sequence, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
Having worshipped Indra and the other guardians of the directions, as well as the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī,
the practitioner should offer a bull, a canopy, a house, and so forth, to Īśāna.
Then, with palms joined in devotion, one should pray to the Lord of Pārvatī.

The letters from *ya* to *sa*, together with their bindus and anusvāras, should be spoken. Then, *hauḥ* and *haṃsaḥ* should be uttered. Through this combination, the mantra is formed as follows: *āḥ hrīḥ kroḥ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hauḥ haṃsaḥ*. By means of this mantra...
One should cause the vital breaths to enter that liṅga by means of the procedure previously described. || 75 || 76 ||
In that regard, it is on the sacrificial altar itself. || 77 ||
Śarva [the Lord] declares the eight forms of Mahādeva worthy of worship with the two verses beginning with "The earth" (kṣitiḥ). || 78 || 79 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what procedure one should worship the eight forms of Mahādeva, he says "beginning with *praṇava*," and so forth.
This means by means of the name-mantra beginning with *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) and ending with *namaḥ*. Starting from the east (*pūrva*).

Having invoked him with the words, "O Śarva, you whose form is earth, come here, stay here, be present here, accept my worship," one should worship Śarva, whose form is earth, on the eastern part of the altar with scents, flowers, and other offerings, using the mantra: *oṃ śarvāya kṣitimūrtaye namaḥ*.
In this very manner, one should worship the other seven forms in sequence within the [directions] beginning with Agni.
Having sacrificed and having worshipped. || 81 || 82 ||
O Lord, ocean of compassion, you have been established by me in this house;
be gracious, O Blessed Śambhu, the cause of all causes. (83)
As long as the earth with its oceans endures, and as long as the moon and sun remain, so long may you abide in this house; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord! (84)
O Dhūrjaṭi, by your grace, may I not be defiled by the sins of any living being whatsoever who should meet their death in this house. (85)
Then, having circumambulated and paid homage, one should go home;
returning again at dawn, one should bathe the Moon-crested Lord.
First, one should perform the bathing with the five pure nectars (pañcāmṛta);
thereafter, with jars numbering one hundred filled with fragrant waters.
Having worshipped him according to one's ability, one should pray with a spirit of devotion. || 88 ||
Whatever has been worshipped by me deficient in ritual, deficient in action, or deficient in devotion—may all that become complete through your grace, O Lord of Umā. (89)
As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth and the oceans remain, may my incomparable fame abide forever in this world. (90)
Salutations to the three-eyed Rudra, the wielder of the excellent Pināka bow;
salutations again and again to him who is worshipped by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Sūrya, and the others.
Now, in response to the inquiry, "What indeed should one pray to the Lord of Pārvatī? he says:
"O Ocean of Compassion, in this house," and so forth (verses 83–86).
Now, in response to the inquiry as to with what substance one should bathe Śiva, he says "pure" and so forth. || 87 ||
To that Śiva. || 88 ||
Then, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should feed the Kaulika brahmins;
one should satisfy the poor with various kinds of foods, drinks, and garments. || 92 ||
One should worship the deity every day according to one's own means;
however, one must never move a stationary Śiva-liṅga.
O Supreme Goddess, the installation of the immovable *īśaliṅga* has thus been described to you in brief, as extracted from all the Āgamas. 94.
The Śrī Devī said:

"O All-pervading Lord, if by some accident there should be an obstruction to the worship of the deities, what should be done in that situation by the devotees? Tell me that in accordance with reality. (95)
By what defects would divine images become unworthy of worship, or by what defect should they be abandoned? Please explain the means for that as well. (96)
Śrī Sadāśiva said: If there is an obstacle to worship for one day, one should worship the Lord twice as much;
for two days, double that amount; and for three days, double that again.
Thereafter, if worship should not be possible for up to six months,
then the wise one, having bathed the deity with eight jars, should perform the sacrifice.
After six months, the foremost of practitioners, having again properly consecrated the deity according to the previously prescribed ritual procedure, should worship it.
Now, in response to the inquiry, "What indeed should one pray for from Śiva?", he says:
"Devoid of ritual injunctions," and so forth (verses 89–94).
The Śrī Devī said: "If," and so forth. In that context, it refers to when there is an obstruction to the worship. 95–96.
Being thus entreated, Śrī Sadāśiva said: "For one day, there shall be no hindrance to worship," and so forth (verses 97–99).
A wise person should not worship a deity that is broken, cracked, mutilated, touched by one suffering from leprosy, or fallen upon impure ground and the like. (100)
One should discard in water a deity that has missing limbs, is cracked, or is broken;
however, one that is defiled by defects such as contact with impurities should be consecrated again and then worshipped.
In the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of the beginningless Liṅga, which is free from all defects, one should always worship one's own respective chosen deity there for the attainment of happiness. 102.
O Great Illusionist, whatever was asked regarding the ultimate liberation of men who subsist by their actions—all that has been proclaimed in detail. (103)
Without karma, embodied beings do not remain still even for half a moment;
though unwilling, they are helplessly dragged along by the wind of karma. (104)
Through action they experience happiness; through action they experience suffering.
They are born, they perish, and they exist under the sway of action. 105.

Therefore, various kinds of ritual actions, accompanied by their means of accomplishment, have been taught for the sake of engaging those of limited understanding and for the cessation of their evil conduct. (106)
For action is indeed twofold: auspicious and inauspicious;
from inauspicious action, living beings undergo intense torment. (107)
O Goddess, even those whose minds are attached to the fruits of auspicious actions go and come between the next world and this one, bound by the chains of karma. (108)
"Vyaṅga" means one who is deprived of limbs. (100–107)
Having thus set forth various kinds of actions that bring about happiness and are accompanied by abundant means, [the author now states: "Now,
people shall attain liberation through the knowledge of Brahman alone, and not through ritual actions."
He begins to speak (p.
461): "As long as karma—whether auspicious or indeed inauspicious—is not exhausted, liberation does not arise for men even in hundreds of kalpas. (109)
Just as one might be bound by fetters made of iron or even by fetters made of gold,
so too is the living soul bound by both inauspicious and auspicious karmas.
Constantly performing ritual action, even after undergoing hundreds of hardships,
one does not attain liberation so long as one does not find knowledge.
Knowledge arises through the investigation of reality and through desireless action for those wise ones whose darkness has been destroyed and whose selves are stainless. (112)
The world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is fashioned by Māyā;
having realized that the one Supreme Brahman alone is real, one shall become happy. (113)
Having abandoned name-and-form within the eternal and immovable Brahman,
he who has attained firm certainty regarding reality is liberated from the bondage of karma.
"Even from auspicious action," and so forth. O Goddess, due to even auspicious action,
people whose minds are attached to its fruits— being bound by the shackles of karma, that is, fettered by the chain of action— depart from this world to the other world, the hereafter.
And from that world they return again to this one; the meaning is that they do not become partakers of liberation.
He does not find, he does not obtain. || 111 ||
Now, one might ask: how does that knowledge, which is the sole means to liberation, arise?

To this he says "jñānam" and so forth. For those whose darkness in the form of ignorance has been destroyed through the investigation of reality—that is, through the investigation of Brahman—and who possess stainless souls.
Of those whose internal faculties are stainless. || 112 || 113 ||
(462) There is no liberation through recitation, nor through burnt offerings, nor even through hundreds of fasts;
having realized "I am indeed Brahman," the embodied being becomes liberated. 115.
The Self is the witness, all-pervading, complete, true, non-dual, and higher than the highest;
though situated in the body, it is not situated in the body—knowing this, one becomes a partaker of liberation. (116)
Like the play of a child, one who abandons all conceptualization of forms, names, and so forth, and remains established in Brahman, is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (117)
If a form imagined by the mind were the means to liberation for men, then kings would have attained it through a kingdom obtained in a dream. (118)
Those who, regarding images made of clay, stone, metal, wood, and so forth as the Lord,
undergo the toil of asceticism, do not attain liberation without [true] knowledge.
If those who are afflicted by restraint regarding food, yet have their bellies distended by eating as they please, are devoid of the knowledge of Brahman, how can they attain liberation? (120)
If there are those who observe vows of eating only wind, leaves, grain-particles, or water who partake in liberation, then even snakes, beasts, birds, and aquatic creatures would be liberated. (121)

"Having abandoned," and so forth. "One who has ascertained the reality" (*pariniścitatattva*) refers to one by whom the *tattva*—the actual state of things (*yāthārthya*), which is thoroughly determined (*pariniścita*), correctly resolved (*samyak nirṇīta*), eternal (*nitya*), indestructible (*avināśin*), immovable (*niścala*), and not relinquishing its prior nature—is known. || 114 || 115 ||
"Self," and so forth. The Witness (*sākṣī*) is the observer of the auspicious and the inauspicious. The Pervasive (*vibhu*) is all-encompassing.
The Full (*pūrṇaḥ*) is of an undivided nature. The Non-dual (*advaitaḥ*) is devoid of internal, external, and other-internal distinctions. (116–118)
By austerity (tapas), such as the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances. || 119 ||
They go to, that is, they attain, *niṣkṛti*, which means deliverance. || 120 || 121 ||
The supreme state is the true nature of Brahman; the meditative state is the middling one; praise and recitation are the lower state; and external worship is the lowest of the low. (122)
Yoga is the unity of the individual soul and the Supreme Soul; worship is the relationship between the servant and the Lord.
For one who knows that "all is Brahman," there is neither yoga nor worship.
For one in whose mind the supreme knowledge of Brahman shines forth, what need is there for recitation, sacrifices, austerities, observances, or vows? (124)

For one who perceives that Brahman is truth, consciousness, and bliss—unique and one—and who has become Brahman by their very nature, what need is there for worship, meditation, or concentration? (125)
For one who knows that everything is Brahman, there is neither evil nor good deed, neither heaven nor rebirth, nor even an object of meditation, nor a meditator. 126.
This Self is eternally liberated and unstained by all things; what bondage could it have, and why do the dull-witted desire liberation for it? (127)
"Supreme," and so forth. Brahman alone is real; everything other than that is unreal—this is the supreme state (*bhāva*).
The construction is as follows: "The supreme devotion (*bhajana*) comes to be. Devotional state of meditation (*dhyānabhāva*) means devotion in the form of meditation. || 122 ||
"Yoga," and so forth: for a wise person who knows that "everything is indeed Brahman," the very identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Self (*ātman*) constitutes yoga.
Just as the very identity of the servant and the Lord constitutes worship, there is no yoga other than that.
For him, there is also no worship distinct from that. || 123 || 124 ||
"Truth," and so forth. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the very nature of consciousness. "One" means non-dual (*advaita*).
Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*). || 125 ||
There is no further existence, nor is there further rebirth. || 126 ||
Unstained means unattached. || 127 ||
The universe, fashioned by his own *māyā*, is inconceivable even to the gods;
he himself shines forth therein, though unentered, as if entered. (128)
Just as space exists both outside and inside all things,
so too does the Self, whose nature is Being, shine as the witness by its very essence.
There is no childhood, no old age, no youth, and no birth for the Self;
it is eternally of one form, consisting of pure consciousness, and entirely free from modification.
Birth, youth, and old age belong only to the body and not to the self;
yet those whose intellects are shrouded by illusion do not perceive this, even though they see it.
Just as one sees the sun reflected in the waters of a river in many ways, so too does one perceive the Self as manifold within the body through illusion (māyā). || 132 ||
Just as people perceive the flickering of water when the moon is reflected in it, so too do the unwise perceive the flickering of the intellect within the Self. (133)
Just as the space contained within a jar remains exactly the same even when the jar is broken,
so too the Self shines forth in its identical form when the body has perished.

[Objection: Surely the self does indeed have bondage in the form of the body; how then can it be said that "this self is eternally liberated," and so forth? To this he replies with the words "by its own māyā," etc. [It is] inconceivable (avitarkya), meaning it is not to be reasoned out or scrutinized. || 128 || 129 ||
*Januḥ* means birth. With the half-verse beginning with "sadaikarūpa" (always of one form), he states the reasons for the absence of childhood and other stages in the Self. || 130 ||
To the question, "In that case, for whom do birth and so forth occur?", he says "birth," etc. (verse 131).

Now, one might object: "The Self, residing within various bodies, is perceived in manifold forms; how then can it be said to be always of a single form? To this, he says "yathā" (just as), and so forth. 132.
(465) O Goddess, this knowledge of the Self is the supreme and sole means to liberation;
one who knows it shall be liberated even in this very life—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 135 ||
One is not liberated by ritual action, nor by lineage, nor by wealth;
having realized the Self through the Self, a human being becomes liberated. || 136 ||
For the self alone is dear to all; there is nothing else dearer than the self.
O Śivā, in this world, others become dear only through their connection with the self.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this triad appears through illusion (māyā).
When this triad is investigated, only the Self (ātman) alone remains. 138.

Knowledge is the Self alone, whose nature is consciousness; the object of knowledge is the Self alone, consisting of consciousness. The knower is the Self itself; he who knows thus is a knower of the Self.
This knowledge, the direct cause of liberation, has been told to you;
this alone is the supreme wealth of the four kinds of Avadhūtas.
Śrīdevī said:
"Two types of stages of life (āśrama) have been proclaimed: the householder's and the mendicant's.
What is this strange thing that is heard—that there are four kinds of Avadhūtas?"
Having heard this, O Lord, I desire to know it in its true essence; please describe in detail the characteristics of the four types of Avadhūtas.
When the moon has entered the water—that is, when the ritual procedure has been performed—those who are unskilled are the ignorant. 133.
Desiring to know the characteristics of the four kinds of *avadhūtas*, the venerable Goddess said, beginning with "the two types," etc. 141–142.

The venerable Sadāśiva said: O beloved, those Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others who worship the Brahma-mantra should be known as ascetics (yatayas), even while they dwell in the householder stage of life (gṛhāśrama). || 143 ||
Those men who have been consecrated by the rite of the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) are to be known as Śaiva-avadhūtas; they are worthy of worship in the Kulārcita.

Those who follow the Brahma-avadhūta and Śaiva traditions, remaining steadfast in the conduct of their respective stages of life (āśrama), should perform all rites according to the path proclaimed by me. 145.
Except for that which is offered to Brahman and likewise that which is offered to the Discus (Viṣṇu),
they should never accept prohibited food or water.
O fair-faced one, the dharma and conduct of the Brāhma, Avadhūta, and Kaula [practitioners], as well as those Kaulas who have received initiation, have already been described.
Bathing, twilight rituals, eating, drinking, giving gifts, and protecting one's wife—all these are performed by the Śaiva, the Brāhma, and the Avadhūta according to the path of the Āgamas. (148)
The Avadhūta has been described as being of two kinds, distinguished by the division of "complete" and "incomplete.
O Dear One, the complete one is called the Paramahaṃsa, while the other is the Parivrājaka. (149)
If one who has performed the purificatory rites of the Avadhūta should be weak in knowledge, then, while remaining in the abode of the world, he should purify himself. || 150 ||
Being thus entreated by the Goddess, Śrī Sadāśiva spoke [the verses] beginning with "Those who are worshippers of the Brahma-mantra," and so forth. (143–144)
"Vidadhyuḥ" means they would perform or do. || 145–148 ||
Another [type] is incomplete. || 149–153 ||
Protecting the signs of his own caste and performing his duties like a Kaula, always being devoted to Brahman, he should accomplish the supreme knowledge. (151)
Having uttered that very mantra while contemplating "I am He," one should always perform actions appropriate for oneself, relying upon dispassion. || 152 ||
Performing actions without attachment, like water on a lotus leaf,
one should strive to uplift oneself through the discernment of the knowledge of reality.
Whatever rite one may perform with the mantra "Oṃ Tat Sat"—whether he be a householder or even a neutral observer—that shall result in his desired goal. (154)
Recitation, fire-offerings, consecrations, and all other ritual acts, when performed with the mantra "Oṃ Tat Sat," shall be complete; of this there is no doubt. (155)
What is the use of many other mantras, or what is the use of numerous other ritual means?
One should accomplish all rites with this very mantra of Brahmā. || 156 ||
O Mother, there is no other means superior to this great mantra, which is easy to accomplish, requires little effort, and bestows the complete fruit. 157.
Having written this down, one should bear it either in the front part [of the house] or upon the body;
his home becomes a great sacred site (tīrtha), and his body shall become composed of merit.
O Goddess of gods, the Mantra is the essence of the essences of the Nigamas, Āgamas, and Tantras;
"Oṃ, Tat Sat"—this has been spoken truthfully before you. 159.
Now, [the author] describes the majesty of the mantra "Oṃ tat sat" with the words beginning "By means of the mantra 'Oṃ tat sat'": "one should perform," that is, one should carry out. (154–157)
This mantra, "oṃ tat sat," [is recited]. (158–160)
Having pierced through the palate, the head, and the crest-lock of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, this *oṃ tatsat* has manifested—the most excellent among all mantras. (160)
If food of the four kinds and other objects as well were purified by means other than mantras, it would be sufficient; yet, they are purified by this [mantra]. (161)

Seeing the form of the Real everywhere and muttering that great mantra which is the Reality itself, he who acts according to his own will with a pure mind is indeed the sovereign of the Kaulas on earth. 162.
Through the recitation of this, one becomes perfected; through contemplating its meaning, one becomes liberated.
A living being who recites this mantra along with its meaning becomes manifest equal to Brahman. (163)
This great mantra consists of three parts and is the cause of all causes;
by the practice of this mantra, one becomes a conqueror of death himself.
O Great Goddess, by reciting this either as a pair, or as two separate words, or even word by word, the practitioner shall become a possessor of siddhi. (165)
For one whose entire karma has been shaken off by the purificatory rites of a Śaiva Avadhūta,
there is no eligibility for rites performed for the gods, nor for those for the ancestors, nor for those pertaining to the Ṛṣis.
Among the four Avadhūtas, the fourth is called the Haṃsa;
the other three are rich in the enjoyment of yoga, and all are liberated and equal to Śiva. (167)
Like a swan, he should not engage in sexual union with women, nor should he take possession of the elements;
eating only what is presented by past karma, he should wander about, free from both prohibitions and injunctions.
"Of the four kinds," and so forth; that is, of the four kinds [of food]: those to be chewed, those to be crunched, those to be licked, and those to be sucked. (161–167)
Eating, that is, consuming. || 168 ||
One should abandon the marks of one's own caste and the duties of householders;
as a fourth [stage], one should wander the earth free from conceptual construction and devoid of effort. (169)
Always content with his own self-nature, free from sorrow and delusion, without a sense of "mine," he should be patient, fearless, and free from affliction. (170)
There is no offering of food or drink for him, nor does he possess meditations or mental fixations;
liberated, dispassionate, and free from the pairs of opposites, the ascetic is devoted to the conduct of the Haṃsa.
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you in detail the characteristics of these four virtuous Kulayogins, who possess my own nature.
From seeing, touching, conversing with, and pleasing these [deities], the attainment of the fruits of all sacred fords (tīrtha) arises for those born as human beings. || 173 ||
O beloved, whatever holy fords and sacred fields exist upon the earth, they all reside eternally within the body of one who has renounced his family life.
Blessed are they, successful are they, meritorious are they, and performers of sacrifice are they—
those men by whom virtuous members of their own lineage have been honored with ancestral offerings.
The impure becomes pure, the untouchable attains touchability, and even that which is unfit to be eaten becomes edible—simply by the touch of those [who have attained this state]. (176)
Of householders, that is, of those living as family men; "inactive," meaning devoid of activity for the sake of maintaining one's own body. || 169 ||
"Always the Self," and so forth. *Bhāva* means contemplation. *Nirniketa* means devoid of a fixed or constant dwelling. *Titikṣuḥ* means one whose nature is endurance. (170–172)
Now, he describes the greatness of the Avadhūtas with the words beginning "of these" (eteṣām) and so forth. || 173 ||
With family substances, such as wine and the like. || 175 || 176 ||
Kirātas, sinners, cruel Pulindas, Yavanas, and Khasas are purified by their touch; who else but them would one worship? (177)
Those who, even once, worship with devotion the Kaulikas—the yogis of the Kula—using the principles of the Kula and the substances of the Kula, they too are worthy of honor upon this earth. (178)
O lotus-faced one, there is truly no dharma higher than the Kaula dharma;
even an outcaste, by taking refuge in it, becomes purified and attains the state of a Kaula. (179)
Just as the feet of all living beings dissolve into the foot of an elephant,
so too, O beloved, do all phenomena submerge into the Kula-dharma.
"O Dear One, how most meritorious are the Kaulas, who are themselves the very embodiment of sacred fords; for through their connection, they purify even Mlecchas, Cāṇḍālas, and commoners. (181)
Just as the waters fallen into the Gaṅgā attain the state of being Gāṅgeya (belonging to the Gaṅgā),
so too all who enter into the conduct of a family attain the status of belonging to that family (kaulatā).
Just as water situated within the ocean does not attain a separate existence, so too people submerged in the ocean of the Kula do not become separate. 183.
From the Brahmins down to the lowest castes, all those who are bipeds upon this earth shall be eligible for this family tradition.
The Pulindas are a specific class of Cāṇḍālas; the Khasas are a specific mixed caste. As it has been said: "The Jhallas, the Mallas, the Rājanyas, the Vrātyas, and the Licchavis..."
The Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Drāviḍa as well. Thus [ends verse 177].
With the *kula*-principles such as meat and so forth; with the *kula*-substances, namely the intoxicants (*madya*). || 178–186 ||
Those who, when summoned to this family dharma, turn their faces away from it, fall away from all dharmas and go to the lowest state. (185)
Any men whatsoever who seek to follow the traditional conduct of their lineage—even if he is of noble birth, one who deceives them shall go to the Raurava hell. (186)
That Kaula who, regarding a Cāṇḍāla, a Yavana, or a low-born person as inferior, does not perform the Kaula rite with a woman out of contempt, is base and goes to a downward state. 187.

Whatever merit is gained from a hundred consecrations or even from a hundred preparatory rites (puraścaryā), ten million times that merit is obtained when a single Kaulika rite is performed. || 188 ||
Whosoever among the castes exist on earth, and whatever dharma they have resorted to, if they become Kaulas, they are liberated from the bonds and go to the supreme state. || 189 ||

The Kaulas, who take refuge in the Śaiva dharma, who are the very embodiment of sacred pilgrimage sites and whose nature is Śiva, should honor and respect one another with affection, faith, and love. (190)
What is the use of saying much more here? I speak the truth before you:
for the bridge for crossing the ocean of worldly existence is indeed one's own family dharma, and nothing else.
All doubts are severed, accumulations of evil are exhausted, and the webs of karma are burned away by the practice of the family dharma. 192.

Those who are devoted to the vow of truth, established in Brahman, and who, having compassionately summoned human beings, purify them through their family traditions, are to be known as the best of the Kaulikas. || 193 ||
Thus, O Goddess, I have explained to you the determination of all dharmas, the first half of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra, which purifies the world. (194)
By contempt, that is, by insult. || 187–194 ||
Whoever should constantly hear this, or should cause other men to hear it, being liberated from all sins, shall attain nirvāṇa at the end. || 195 ||
Having understood this King of Tantras—the essence of essences, higher than the highest among all Āgamas and Tantras—one becomes a knower of all scriptures. (196)
But what is the use of wandering to sacred fords, or sacrifices, or the practice of recitation for him who knows this great tantra? He is liberated from the bonds of karma. (197)
He is wise in all scriptures, the best among those who know all dharmas; he is the knower, the one who knows Brahman, the true practitioner—he who knows this, O Kālikā. (198)
Enough with the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the Smṛtis, the Saṃhitās, and so forth;
what is the use of many other Tantras? By knowing this, one becomes all-knowing. (199)
That which was my most secret means of accomplishment, the supreme knowledge—by your inquiry, all of that has been clearly revealed in this tantra. (200)
O lady of virtuous vows, know that this Mahānirvāṇatantra is to me as you are to Brahmā—my supreme power, even more dear than my own life-breaths. 201.
Just as Himavat is among mountains, as the moon is among stars, and as the sun is among luminous things, so is this King of Tantras among all tantras. (202)
Having studied or even taught this Tantra, which consists of all phenomena and is the sole means for the knowledge of Brahman, a person shall become a knower of Brahman. (203)
O Goddess of the Gods, in whose house exists this most excellent of all tantras, there shall never be a bound soul (paśu) born in that lineage. 204.
Now, he declares the greatness of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra with the verses beginning "Whoever should hear this constantly" (195–201).
Even one who is blinded by the cataracts of ignorance, or is a fool, or even one rendered inert by karma—by hearing this great tantra, such a person is liberated from the bondage of karma. (205)
O Supreme Goddess, the reading, hearing, worship, and likewise the salutation of this Tantra bestows liberation upon men. (206)
The Tantra has been described in many varieties, each joined with its own narrative;
this Tantra, which encompasses all dharmas, is unsurpassed anywhere else. (207)

He who knows the wheel of the netherworld (pātālacakra), together with the wheel of the earth (bhūcakra) and the wheel of light (jyotiścakra), up to the highest numerical limit (parārdha), is omniscient; of this there is no doubt.
A person who knows this treatise, consisting of one billion verses, shall be capable of recounting the events of the three times and the history of the three worlds. (209)
There are many tantras and various treatises as well,
yet they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
What shall I tell you of the greatness of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra? By knowing this great tantra, one attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman. || 211 ||
Thus, in the glorious Mahānirvāṇa Tantra, the most excellent among all tantras,
the essence of the determination of all dharmas, in the dialogue between the venerable Ādyā and Sadāśiva,
within the Pūrvakāṇḍa.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Fourfold Classification of the Installation of the Śiva-liṅga," is concluded.
This completes the first half [of the work].
Among those possessing splendor, [he is] the most splendid. || 202–211 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
